## FILE: work/ANSWER.md
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I. ROCKY v GRACE

Whether the February dealings formed a loan contract decides Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that he failed to lend. Grace’s 5 February call ‘proposed that Rocky offer’, promising nothing, so was likely an invitation to treat.[^1] Rocky could say his 12 February email only records discussions, like its ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’ points, which promise nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and the email seeks agreement: unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’, those words are promissory,[^2] so the first point is likely an offer.

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent.[^3] ‘Confirmed’ arguably vouched only for the email’s accuracy; but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ without new terms, so it was no counter-offer and likely accepted the first point, ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ included. Grace’s implied promise to repay would arguably be consideration, since a promise can be the price of another.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether this preliminary agreement showed intention to create legal relations. That is judged objectively, the alleging party bearing the onus;[^5] the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours intention. As nothing was made ‘subject to a formal contract’, the question is whether the terms were to ‘be put into form’ or left to ‘a new agreement’.[^6] Grace would say the fixed terms show the parties had ‘reached finality’, Masters’ first class.[^7] Rocky would invoke the third class, where parties ‘have dealt only with major matters’,[^8] as the email arguably did. Its ‘conditions’, unlike ‘subject to success of Hail Mary Project’, name no external event, so they are most naturally further loan terms; and ‘satisfactory’ leaves them to the protected party’s judgment,[^9] here Rocky’s as lender. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement: later conduct, admissible on formation, agrees, Grace taking AMPL’s loan on other terms.[^10] Were the conditions settled ‘this morning’, the email would bind.

The qualifier also arguably makes Rocky’s promise illusory, since a consideration is illusory if it ‘depends upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor’.[^11] Grace may reply that, as in Meehan, Rocky must judge honestly, perhaps reasonably,[^12] and the fixed terms are ‘specified parameters’.[^13] However, Meehan is distinguishable: its discretion related ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’, finance, within agreed terms;[^14] Rocky’s covers the loan’s own terms, which neither standard can supply and no range confines. Godecke bound because its added terms had to be ‘reasonable in an objective sense’.[^15] Gibbs J, obiter, doubted any ‘concluded bargain’ where ‘a vital matter’ is left to one party; his ‘[p]erhaps’ for subsidiary matters cited a case where parties had ‘imported the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness’,[^16] which these parties never did. The email therefore likely bound neither party, defeating Grace’s claim.

Rocky may instead claim AMPL’s advance, made because he ‘asked’, performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differed in amount and date. As Pierre ‘agreed to provide the money’ and the Loan Agreement named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, AMPL did not contract ‘as agent’ for him.[^17] Rocky’s 5 March demand under the Loan Agreement, arguably assuming a 27 February start, engages privity: outside insurance, ‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’, nor can ‘a stranger to the consideration’.[^18] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[^19] which ‘AMPL and Grace entered into’: Grace’s promises ran to AMPL alone, not even jointly to Rocky,[^20] who gave nothing for them, AMPL’s loan being their price. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is right in result but wrong in reason: signature is not necessary, Empirnall’s unsigned developer being bound,[^21] nor decisive, Mrs Coulls signing without becoming a party.[^22]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace: the Development Agreement repays him first ‘if the Project made a profit’, even a ‘minimal’ one, but none is yet shown; and Grace never promised to reimburse what he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

Rocky’s questions are whether he can claim $10,000 and must pay AMPL. At the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s expressed expectation promised nothing, so was likely an invitation to treat.[^23] Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ offered a bilateral contract,[^24] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^25] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing; but that ‘depends upon the intention disclosed by the language’ used,[^26] and Rocky reserved no right to withdraw pending a document he would not sign, so a contract likely formed orally.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if he had ‘authority … to act for’ it and contracted for it, not solely for himself.[^27] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, supplying that authority, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he promised personally, he alone owes the $10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: ‘also’ arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so, as in Sundell, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^28] However, the rule applies ‘at least when’ the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^29] and none is shown: on 27 February Rocky ‘asked’, and the clause, arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’, bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies, any duty running to AMPL.[^30] Rocky likely gave consideration, unless he also promised AMPL a guarantee when he ‘asked’.

On intention, Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^31] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised is ‘appropriately promissory in character’.[^32] Nor is Rocky’s undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ that a borrower could repay and a promise ‘to ensure’ it.[^33] Rocky’s words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must ‘ensure’, so his undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be void.[^34] His ‘I will do that’ contains no words of effort, and his ‘check in’ emails cannot construe it:[^35] it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. Nor is AMPL’s promise illusory: once Grace repays, it leaves ‘no discretion’.[^36]

On privity, the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky gave: he is its promisee, no stranger to the consideration.[^37] Read naturally, ‘the clause’ is the guarantee clause already described, not a $10,000 term; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky’s exposure turns on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, possibly only by his oral undertaking, and only ‘the parties to it’ are ‘bound by the obligations of a contract’.[^38] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^39] AMPL would say Rocky ‘attended’ as the clause was included, taking the $10,000 promise knowing the terms.[^40] However, the benefit he took priced his own words, so taking it is not conduct ‘of such a character as necessarily’ to infer assent to the clause.[^41] He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^42] which its $10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^43] which counts only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky ‘asked’, but, unlike the return in Pao On, understood ‘at the time of the main agreement’,[^44] no guarantee is shown then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause’s inclusion, arguably ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee;[^45] but Rocky priced his undertaking at $10,000, not at AMPL’s signature, so the clause then likely lacks consideration.

Whether the 9 March call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Construction is objective,[^46] and post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s interest payments or ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term;[^47] but, if it is ambiguous, pre-contractual conduct casting light on ‘the genesis of the contract’ is admissible.[^48] Naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, which the agreement ‘recorded’; but ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. If the March interest went unpaid, Rocky’s undertaking is arguably already broken.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once:[^49] nothing is yet payable. Read commercially, Rocky’s own payment arguably satisfies it;[^50] but the words name Grace, whose payment the $10,000 priced. AMPL’s call, not stopping Grace repaying, breaches no duty to ‘do everything necessary on [its] part’.[^51]

Accordingly, Rocky is likely liable on his oral undertaking, in damages to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. If the clause also binds him and AMPL promised the $10,000, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the $10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if he had 'authority ... to act for' it and contracted for it, not solely for himself.[^27] Rocky's 'you' points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, supplying that authority, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he promised personally, he alone owes the \$10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: 'also' arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so, as in *Sundell*, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^28] However, the rule applies 'at least when' the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^29] and none is shown: on 27 February Rocky 'asked', and the clause, arguably included after Pierre 'agreed', bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring 'all payments' 'promptly' exceeds guaranteeing 'repayment of the Loan'; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies, any duty running to AMPL.[^30] Rocky likely gave consideration, unless he also promised AMPL a guarantee when he 'asked'.

On intention, Pierre is Rocky's cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^31] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL's office as its loan was finalised is 'appropriately promissory in character'.[^32] Nor is Rocky's undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw 'no relevant difference' between a 'practice to ensure' that a borrower could repay and a promise 'to ensure' it.[^33] Rocky's words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must 'ensure', so his undertaking is not 'so obscure' as to be void.[^34] His 'I will do that' contains no words of effort, and his 'check in' emails cannot construe it:[^35] it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. Nor is AMPL's promise illusory: once Grace repays, it leaves 'no discretion'.[^36]

On privity, the \$10,000 was to be paid 'to me directly' for consideration Rocky gave: he is its promisee, no stranger to the consideration.[^37] Read naturally, 'the clause' is the guarantee clause already described, not a \$10,000 term; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky's exposure turns on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was 'provided by Rocky', possibly only by his oral undertaking, and only 'the parties to it' are 'bound by the obligations of a contract'.[^38] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^39] AMPL would say Rocky 'attended' as the clause was included, taking the \$10,000 promise knowing the terms.[^40] However, the benefit he took priced his own words, so taking it is not conduct 'of such a character as necessarily' to infer assent to the clause.[^41] He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^42] which its \$10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^43] which counts only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky 'asked', but, unlike the return in *Pao On*, understood 'at the time of the main agreement',[^44] no guarantee is shown then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause's inclusion, arguably 'really done in consideration of' the guarantee;[^45] but Rocky priced his undertaking at \$10,000, not at AMPL's signature, so the clause then likely lacks consideration.

Whether the 9 March call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Construction is objective,[^46] and post-contractual conduct, such as Grace's interest payments or 'I have until 8 April 2025', cannot construe the term;[^47] but, if it is ambiguous, pre-contractual conduct casting light on 'the genesis of the contract' is admissible.[^48] Naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, which the agreement 'recorded'; but 'recorded' equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. If the March interest went unpaid, Rocky's undertaking is arguably already broken.

The \$10,000 is payable 'once Grace repays the Loan', a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once:[^49] nothing is yet payable. Read commercially, Rocky's own payment arguably satisfies it;[^50] but the words name Grace, whose payment the \$10,000 priced. AMPL's call, not stopping Grace repaying, breaches no duty to 'do everything necessary on \[its\] part'.[^51]

Accordingly, Rocky is likely liable on his oral undertaking, in damages to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. If the clause also binds him and AMPL promised the \$10,000, he is liable for \$1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the \$10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he 'might not pay at all', repays.

## FILE: work/ANSWER_v1.md

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, on which both Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that Rocky failed to lend ‘by 15 February’ depend. Grace’s 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer, so it was not itself one,[^1] and Rocky declined. Rocky could argue that his 12 February email merely records their meeting, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its other points promise nothing; however, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ seeks assent, so, unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson,[^2] the first point is likely an offer, though made ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’.

Acceptance requires ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[^3] Rocky could say that ‘Confirmed’ vouched only for the email’s accuracy; however, it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ and added no terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Grace’s implied promise to repay with interest would stand in ‘the relation of a quid pro quo’ to Rocky’s promise to lend.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether the parties intended to be bound immediately, which is judged objectively, the onus lying on Grace, who alone would sue on the email, although their status as ‘project developers’ supports intention.[^5] Decisively, the third class in Masters covers parties who ‘have dealt only with major matters and contemplate that others will or may be regulated by provisions to be introduced’;[^6] that describes an email fixing the amount, date, term and rate while leaving unnamed ‘conditions’ to Rocky. Grace’s strongest counter is Godecke, where terms the vendor’s solicitors could add bound because they had to be reasonable ‘in an objective sense’;[^7] Rocky’s qualifier has no such standard, since ‘satisfactory’ leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects,[^8] here Rocky as lender. Gibbs J, in obiter, doubted that an agreement leaving ‘further terms to be settled by one of the parties’ binds, while allowing that it ‘may be different’ where only ‘subsidiary matters’ remain;[^9] were the conditions settled ‘this morning’ or mere documentation, the email would bind, so further information on them is needed. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement.

For the same reason Rocky’s promise is arguably illusory: in Placer a promise with no ‘identifiable criteria’, left ‘solely to the discretion’ of the promisor, was ‘wholly unenforceable’.[^10] Grace may reply that, as in Meehan, Rocky must judge ‘satisfactory’ honestly,[^11] a limit which ‘takes the case out of the principle’ that a promisor’s discretion over performance defeats the promise;[^12] however, the discretion in Meehan related ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’,[^13] obtaining finance, whereas Rocky’s concerns the content of his own loan, which honesty cannot supply. The email therefore likely bound neither party, so Grace has no claim that Rocky failed to lend.

Rocky may claim that AMPL’s 27 February advance, made because he ‘asked’, performed his promise, so that Grace owes him the money. This fails: the advance was $1,150,000, not $1 million, made after 15 February and in AMPL’s name, on terms first fixed on 8 April at 4%. Nor did AMPL lend as his agent: a principal is a party only where another ‘contracts as agent’ for him,[^14] and AMPL contracted in its own name. His 5 March demand under ‘the Loan Agreement with AMPL’ therefore meets privity, under which ‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’.[^15] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[^16] and Grace’s promises to repay were made to AMPL, not to Rocky, even as a joint promisee;[^17] Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ reaches the right result, but signature is not the test, as Mrs Coulls signed yet was not a party.[^18]

Thus Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace: the Development Agreement pays only ‘if the Project made a profit’ and is not shown breached, and Grace never promised to reimburse Rocky for anything he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

At the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s statement that he ‘expected’ Rocky to ensure Grace’s payments promised nothing, so it was a request rather than an offer;[^19] Rocky’s reply, ‘I will do that if you also promise’, offered a promise for a promise,[^20] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^21] AMPL may argue that nothing bound until the Loan Agreement was signed; however, parties are bound ‘when, and in the manner in which, they intend’, as Lord Greene MR said of exchanged contracts,[^22] and nothing suggests Rocky’s undertaking awaited a document he never signed, so a contract likely formed orally.

Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre, but Pierre controls AMPL and spoke at its office about its loan, so, objectively,[^23] he likely contracted ‘as agent’ for AMPL;[^24] further information on whose money was to pay the $10,000 would settle this; if Pierre promised personally, what follows runs against him.

AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, arguing that Rocky’s promise gave nothing beyond his guarantee.[^25] However, the rule bites on a promise ‘made to the promisee under that contract’,[^26] and none then existed: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’, and ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included’ suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even if it came first, ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’; and if Pierre promised, any duty was owed to AMPL, and ‘a pre-existing contractual obligation to a third party can be valid consideration’.[^27] Rocky likely gave consideration.

Although Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, family presumptions do ‘no more than invite attention to identifying the party who bears the onus of proof’,[^28] here Rocky; a promise of a fixed sum, made at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised, is ‘appropriately promissory in character’ and commercial.[^29] Rocky could argue that his own undertaking, like a letter of comfort, was only a moral assurance; however, Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ repayment and a promise ‘to ensure’ it,[^30] and Rocky’s ‘I will do that’ was given for a price, so intention likely exists on both sides.

Rocky’s undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[^31] Objectively,[^32] his ‘I will do that’, answering an expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, contains no words of effort, so he likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that he would try.

Privity is no bar: the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky himself gave, so he is the promisee and no ‘stranger to the consideration’.[^33] ‘The clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause; even if it means the $10,000 term, AMPL remains bound by its oral promise.

A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, but whether by assent to the clause or only by his oral undertaking is open; only the parties to a contract are bound by it,[^34] so AMPL must show assent. Silence while a clause is included is generally insufficient,[^35] but, having ‘attended’ with a reasonable opportunity to object, Rocky arguably took the benefit of the $10,000 promise with knowledge of the clause;[^36] he could answer that the $10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^37] which its $10,000 promise, if it made one, supplies. If Pierre promised, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration,[^38] counting only if done at Rocky’s request, understood to be ‘remunerated’, with payment ‘legally enforceable had it been promised in advance’;[^39] Rocky ‘asked’, but nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee,[^40] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

Whether AMPL’s 9 March 2025 call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s interest payments from 8 April 2024 and his ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term,[^41] but, the term being arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[^42] AMPL argues the term ran from its 27 February advance, since the agreement ‘recorded’ a loan already made; however, ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature unless the Loan Agreement dates it from the advance.

Interest is shown paid only until 8 February 2025; further information is needed on whether the March 2025 instalment was paid, for if not, Rocky’s undertaking that Grace make ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ is arguably already broken, whichever start date applies.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation rather than to the contract,[^43] so nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies the condition;[^44] however, the words name Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach its duty ‘to do everything necessary on [its] part’ to give Rocky the benefit of the contract,[^45] since its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, if the term ran from 27 February, or otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only by his oral undertaking, he faces damages for any payment Grace fails to make when due. His $10,000 claim against AMPL, or alternatively Pierre, likely stands, but it falls due only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

Although Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, family presumptions do ‘no more than invite attention to identifying the party who bears the onus of proof’,[^28] here Rocky; a promise of a fixed sum, made at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised, is ‘appropriately promissory in character’ and commercial.[^29] Rocky could argue that his own undertaking, like a letter of comfort, was only a moral assurance; however, Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ repayment and a promise ‘to ensure’ it,[^30] and Rocky’s ‘I will do that’ was given for a price, so intention likely exists on both sides.

Rocky’s undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[^31] Objectively,[^32] his ‘I will do that’, answering an expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, contains no words of effort, so he likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that he would try.

Privity is no bar: the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky himself gave, so he is the promisee and no ‘stranger to the consideration’.[^33] ‘[T]he clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause; even if it means the $10,000 term, AMPL remains bound by its oral promise.

A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, but whether by assent to the clause or only by his oral undertaking is open; only the parties to a contract are bound by it,[^34] so AMPL must show assent. Silence while a clause is included is generally insufficient,[^35] but, having ‘attended’ with a reasonable opportunity to object, Rocky arguably took the benefit of the $10,000 promise with knowledge of the clause;[^36] he could answer that the $10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^37] which its $10,000 promise, if it made one, supplies. If Pierre promised, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration,[^38] counting only if done at Rocky’s request, understood to be ‘remunerated’, with payment ‘legally enforceable had it been promised in advance’;[^39] Rocky ‘asked’, but nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee,[^40] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

Whether AMPL’s 9 March 2025 call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s interest payments from 8 April 2024 and his ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term,[^41] but, the term being arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[^42] AMPL argues the term ran from the 27 February advance, and may add that the agreement ‘recorded’ a loan already made; however, ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature unless the Loan Agreement dates it from the advance.

Interest is shown paid only until 8 February 2025; further information is needed on whether the March 2025 instalment was paid, for if not, Rocky’s undertaking that Grace make ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ is arguably already broken, whichever start date applies.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation rather than to the contract,[^43] so nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies the condition;[^44] however, the words name Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach its duty ‘to do everything necessary on [its] part’ to give Rocky the benefit of the contract,[^45] since its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, if the term ran from 27 February, or otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only by his oral undertaking, he faces damages for any payment Grace fails to make when due. His $10,000 claim against AMPL, or alternatively Pierre, likely stands, but it falls due only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

## FILE: work/ANSWER_v2.md
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, which decides both Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that he failed to lend ‘by 15 February’. Grace’s 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer and promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat,[^1] which Rocky declined. Rocky could argue his 12 February email merely records the meeting, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its other points promise nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ seeks assent; unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’,[^2] these words are promissory, so the first point is likely an offer, though ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’.

Acceptance requires ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[^3] ‘Confirmed’ arguably vouched only for the email’s accuracy; however, it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ and added no terms, so it was no counter-offer and likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Grace’s implied promise to repay would arguably be consideration, as the price of a promise ‘can be in the form of an act, forbearance or promise’.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether this preliminary agreement showed an intention to create legal relations, judged objectively, the onus lying on the party alleging the contract, though their status as ‘project developers’ favours it.[^5] Where nothing is ‘expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract’, the question is whether the terms were to ‘be put into form’ or were ‘subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not expressed in detail’.[^6] Grace would say they had ‘reached finality in arranging all the terms of their bargain’.[^7] However, unlike ‘subject to success of Hail Mary Project’, the ‘conditions’ name no external event, so they are most naturally further loan terms, and ‘satisfactory’ leaves their judgment to the party the condition protects,[^8] here Rocky as lender. Gibbs J, in obiter, doubted that leaving ‘further terms to be settled by one of the parties’ binds, while allowing that it ‘may be different’ for ‘subsidiary matters’;[^9] but he tied that to ‘the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness’,[^10] which ‘satisfactory’ lacks. Later conduct, admissible on formation,[^11] agrees: Rocky never lent, Grace never demanded it, and AMPL supplied the money. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement, unless the conditions were settled ‘this morning’.

The qualifier also arguably makes Rocky’s promise illusory, since a promisor with ‘a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out’ the promise makes ‘no contract on which an action can be brought at all’.[^12] Grace may reply that, as in Meehan, Rocky must decide honestly;[^13] however, that saved a discretion relating ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’ within ‘a concluded agreement as to the terms’,[^14] whereas Rocky’s covers the loan’s own terms, which honesty cannot supply. The email therefore likely bound neither party, defeating any claim that Rocky failed to lend.

Rocky may instead claim that AMPL’s advance, made because he ‘asked’, performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differs: $1,150,000, after 15 February, ‘advanced by AMPL’ and ‘recorded’ at 4%. Although a principal is a party where another ‘contracts as agent’ for him,[^15] Pierre ‘agreed to provide the money’ and AMPL named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, so AMPL was not his agent. Rocky’s 5 March demand under ‘the Loan Agreement with AMPL’ therefore meets privity, for ‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’.[^16] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[^17] and Grace’s promises to repay were made to AMPL, not to Rocky, even as joint promisee;[^18] Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is right in result, though Mrs Coulls signed yet was not a party.[^19]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace. The Development Agreement repays him first ‘if the Project made a profit’, even a ‘minimal’ one, but no breach is shown, and Grace never promised to reimburse anything Rocky pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

At the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s ‘expected’ promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[^20] Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ offered a bilateral contract,[^21] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^22] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing, but parties are bound ‘when, and in the manner in which, they intend’, as Lord Greene MR said of exchanged contracts,[^23] and Rocky’s undertaking did not await a document ‘signed by Grace and AMPL’, so a contract likely formed orally.

Who promised turns on what Pierre’s words objectively conveyed. Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre, but Pierre controls AMPL and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely contracted ‘as agent’ for it.[^24] If Pierre was to pay personally, he alone owes the $10,000, and AMPL, not Rocky’s promisee, cannot sue on his undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, arguing Rocky’s promise added nothing to his guarantee.[^25] However, the rule applies ‘at least when’ the promise is ‘made to the promisee under that contract’,[^26] and none then existed: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’, and ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included’ suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even otherwise, ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’. If Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies, as ‘a promise to perform … a pre-existing contractual obligation to a third party can be valid consideration’.[^27] Rocky likely gave consideration.

On intention to create legal relations, Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions do ‘no more than invite attention to identifying the party who bears the onus of proof’,[^28] here Rocky, and a fixed sum promised at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised is ‘appropriately promissory in character’.[^29] Rocky could call his own undertaking a mere letter of comfort; however, Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ repayment and a promise ‘to ensure’ it,[^30] and Rocky’s ‘I will do that’ was plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must ‘ensure’, so his undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be void;[^31] his ‘I will do that’ contains no words of effort, so it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that he would try. AMPL’s promise is not illusory either, because its condition, Grace’s repayment, relates ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’.[^32]

The $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky himself gave, so he is its promisee and no ‘stranger to the consideration’,[^33] and privity is no bar. ‘[T]he clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause, the only clause described, and Rocky’s claim rests on the oral promise either way.

Whether the guarantee clause binds Rocky is open: a guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, perhaps only by his oral undertaking, and only ‘the parties to it’ are ‘bound by the obligations of a contract’.[^34] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^35] AMPL would say the clause recorded Rocky’s own bargain, taken ‘with knowledge of its terms’,[^36] and that his 5 March demand invoked ‘the Loan Agreement’; but Rocky has received nothing, and nothing shows he saw it. He is therefore likely bound by his oral undertaking and arguably by the clause, which evidence that he read it would settle.

AMPL must show consideration moving from itself,[^37] which its $10,000 promise supplies, if AMPL made it. Otherwise its earlier advance is past consideration,[^38] counting only if requested, understood to be ‘remunerated’, and ‘legally enforceable had it been promised in advance’;[^39] Rocky ‘asked’, but nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL’s better answer is that it signed only after the clause was included, arguably ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee.[^40]

Whether the 9 March 2025 call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term in New South Wales,[^41] but, the term naming no start, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[^42] AMPL argues the term ran from the 27 February advance, perhaps adding that the agreement ‘recorded’ a loan already made; however, ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature. Interest is shown paid only to 8 February 2025; if the March 2025 instalment was unpaid, Rocky’s undertaking that Grace make ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ is arguably already broken.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation rather than to the contract, which bound immediately,[^43] so nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies it,[^44] but the words name Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach the duty to co-operate, to ‘do everything necessary on [its] part’,[^45] since nothing suggests its call stops Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, if the term ran from 27 February, otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only orally, he is liable in damages, to AMPL or else Pierre, for any payment Grace fails to make when due. No term requires him to pay early, and paying himself likely forfeits the $10,000, which falls due only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

Post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term in New South Wales,[^41] but, the term naming no start, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[^42] AMPL argues the term ran from the 27 February advance, perhaps adding that the agreement ‘recorded’ a loan already made; however, ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature. Interest is shown paid only to 8 February 2025; if the March 2025 instalment was unpaid, Rocky’s undertaking that Grace make ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ is arguably already broken.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation rather than to the contract, which bound immediately,[^43] so nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies it,[^44] but the words name Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach the duty to co-operate, to ‘do everything necessary on [its] part’,[^45] since nothing suggests its call stops Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, if the term ran from 27 February, otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only orally, he is liable in damages, to AMPL or else Pierre, for any payment Grace fails to make when due. No term requires him to pay early, and paying himself likely forfeits the $10,000, which falls due only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

## FILE: work/ANSWER_v3.md
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, which decides Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that he failed to lend. Grace’s 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer and promised nothing; it was likely an invitation to treat,[^1] which Rocky declined. Rocky could say his 12 February email merely records discussions, its other points, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promising nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and the email seeks agreement. Unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’, those words are promissory,[^2] so the first point is likely an offer.

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent.[^3] ‘Confirmed’ arguably vouched only for the email’s accuracy; but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ without new terms, so it was no counter-offer and likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Grace’s implied promise to repay would arguably be consideration, since a promise can be the price of a promise.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether this preliminary agreement showed an intention to create legal relations. That is judged objectively, the alleging party bearing the onus;[^5] the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours it. As nothing was made ‘subject to a formal contract’, the question is whether the terms were merely to ‘be put into form’ or left to ‘a new agreement’.[^6] Grace would say the fixed amount, date, term and rate show the parties had ‘reached finality’, as in Masters’ first class.[^7] Rocky would invoke the third class, where parties ‘have dealt only with major matters’;[^8] though no formal document was contemplated, the email likewise fixes only these. Its ‘conditions’, unlike ‘subject to success of Hail Mary Project’, name no external event, so they are most naturally further loan terms; and ‘satisfactory’ leaves them to the protected party’s judgment,[^9] here Rocky’s as lender. Later conduct, admissible on formation,[^10] agrees, AMPL later lending on other terms. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement. Were the conditions settled ‘this morning’, the email would bind, but Rocky’s duty would arise only once they were met.[^11]

The qualifier also arguably makes Rocky’s promise illusory, since a consideration is illusory if it ‘depends upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor’.[^12] Grace may reply that, as in Meehan, Rocky must judge honestly, perhaps reasonably.[^13] However, Meehan is distinguishable: its discretion related ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’, finance, within agreed terms;[^14] Rocky’s covers the loan’s own terms, which neither standard can supply. Gibbs J’s obiter ‘[p]erhaps’, allowing subsidiary matters to be left to one party once ‘all essential terms’ are agreed, assumed ‘the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness’,[^15] which ‘satisfactory’ lacks. The email therefore likely bound neither party, and Grace has no claim that Rocky failed to lend.

Rocky may instead claim that AMPL’s advance, made because he ‘asked’, performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differs: $1,150,000, after 15 February, by AMPL, recorded on 8 April at 4%. As Pierre ‘agreed to provide the money’ and AMPL named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, AMPL did not contract ‘as agent’ for him.[^16] Rocky’s 5 March demand under the Loan Agreement therefore faces privity: ‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’, nor can ‘a stranger to the consideration’.[^17] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[^18] and Grace’s promises were made to AMPL, not Rocky, even as joint promisee;[^19] nor did Rocky give Grace anything, AMPL having lent. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is right in result but wrong in reason: signature is not necessary, Empirnall being bound unsigned,[^20] nor decisive, Mrs Coulls signing without becoming a party.[^21]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace. The Development Agreement repays him first only ‘if the Project made a profit’, none yet shown; and Grace never promised to reimburse what he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

For Rocky, the questions are whether he can claim $10,000 and must pay AMPL. On offer and acceptance at the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s ‘expected’ promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[^22] Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ offered a bilateral contract,[^23] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^24] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing; but that ‘depends upon the intention disclosed by the language’ used,[^25] and Rocky reserved no right to withdraw pending a document signed only by Grace and AMPL. A contract likely formed orally, binding both promises.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if he contracted ‘as agent’ for it rather than for himself.[^26] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he said he would pay personally, he alone owes the $10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: ‘also’ arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so that, as in Sundell, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^27] However, the rule applies ‘at least when’ the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^28] and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’, and the clause, included after Pierre ‘agreed’, bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies.[^29] Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain.

On intention to create legal relations, Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^30] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised is ‘appropriately promissory in character’.[^31] Nor is Rocky’s undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ that a borrower could repay and a promise ‘to ensure’ it.[^32] Rocky’s words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind, even if Pierre promised.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must ‘ensure’, so his undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be void.[^33] His ‘I will do that’ contains no words of effort: it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. AMPL’s promise is not illusory either, because once Grace repays it leaves AMPL ‘no discretion’ whether to pay.[^34]

On privity, the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky himself gave; he is therefore its promisee and no stranger to the consideration.[^35] ‘[T]he clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause just described; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky’s exposure turns next on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, perhaps only by his oral undertaking, and only ‘the parties to it’ are ‘bound by the obligations of a contract’.[^36] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^37] AMPL would say Rocky ‘attended’ as the clause recording his bargain was included, taking the $10,000 promise knowing its terms,[^38] and later invoked the Loan Agreement. However, he has received nothing, and signature is no test for him either. He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^39] which its $10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^40] counting only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky ‘asked’, but unlike Pao On, where a return was understood ‘at the time of the main agreement’,[^41] nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause’s inclusion, arguably ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee;[^42] but Rocky priced his undertaking at $10,000, not at AMPL’s signature.

Whether the 9 March 2025 call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. In New South Wales, post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term;[^43] but, if it is ambiguous, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[^44] Naming no start, it is ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, the agreement having ‘recorded’ a loan already made; but ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. Interest is shown paid only to 8 February 2025; if the March instalment went unpaid, Rocky’s undertaking is arguably broken already.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once;[^45] nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies it;[^46] but the words name Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach the duty to co-operate, to ‘do everything necessary on [its] part’:[^47] its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only orally, he is liable in damages, to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the $10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

## FILE: work/ANSWER_v4.md
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, deciding Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that he failed to lend. Grace’s 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer and promised nothing; it was likely an invitation to treat.[^1] Rocky could say his 12 February email records discussions, its other points, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promising nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and the email seeks agreement. Unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’, those words are promissory,[^2] so the first point is likely an offer.

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent.[^3] ‘Confirmed’ arguably vouched only for the email’s accuracy; but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ without new terms, so it was no counter-offer and likely accepted the first point, ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ included. Grace’s implied promise to repay would arguably be consideration, since a promise can be the price of a promise.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether this preliminary agreement showed an intention to create legal relations. That is judged objectively, the alleging party bearing the onus;[^5] the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours intention. As nothing was made ‘subject to a formal contract’, the question is whether the terms were to ‘be put into form’ or left to ‘a new agreement’.[^6] Grace would say the fixed terms show the parties had ‘reached finality’, Masters’ first class.[^7] Rocky would invoke the third class, where parties ‘have dealt only with major matters’;[^8] though no formal document was contemplated, so did the email. Its ‘conditions’, unlike ‘subject to success of Hail Mary Project’, name no external event, so they are most naturally further loan terms; and ‘satisfactory’ leaves them to the protected party’s judgment,[^9] here Rocky’s as lender. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement. Were the conditions settled ‘this morning’, the email would bind, but Rocky’s duty would arise only once they were met.[^10]

The qualifier also arguably makes Rocky’s promise illusory, since a consideration is illusory if it ‘depends upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor’.[^11] Grace may reply that, as in Meehan, Rocky must judge honestly, perhaps reasonably, and that the fixed terms are ‘specified parameters’.[^12] However, Meehan is distinguishable: its discretion related ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’, finance, within agreed terms;[^13] Rocky’s covers the loan’s own terms, which neither standard can supply and no range confines. Godecke bound because its added terms had to be ‘reasonable in an objective sense’, and Gibbs J’s obiter ‘[p]erhaps’, for subsidiary matters once ‘all essential terms’ are agreed, likewise assumed ‘the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness’,[^14] which these parties never imported. The email therefore likely bound neither party, defeating Grace’s claim.

Rocky may instead claim that AMPL’s advance, made because he ‘asked’, performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differed in amount, date, lender and rate. As Pierre ‘agreed to provide the money’ and AMPL named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, AMPL did not contract ‘as agent’ for him.[^15] Rocky’s 5 March demand under the Loan Agreement, arguably assuming a 27 February start, faces privity: ‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’, nor can ‘a stranger to the consideration’.[^16] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[^17] and Grace’s promises were made to AMPL, not Rocky, even as joint promisee;[^18] nor did Rocky give Grace anything, AMPL having lent. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is right in result but wrong in reason: signature is not necessary, Empirnall being bound unsigned,[^19] nor decisive, Mrs Coulls signing without becoming a party.[^20]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace. The Development Agreement repays him first only ‘if the Project made a profit’, none yet shown; and Grace never promised to reimburse what he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

Rocky’s questions are whether he can claim $10,000 and must pay AMPL. On offer and acceptance at the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s expressed expectation promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[^21] Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ offered a bilateral contract,[^22] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^23] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing; but that ‘depends upon the intention disclosed by the language’ used,[^24] and Rocky reserved no right to withdraw pending a document signed only by Grace and AMPL, so a contract likely formed orally.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if, with its consent, he contracted ‘as agent’ for it rather than solely for himself.[^25] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he said he would pay personally, he alone owes the $10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: ‘also’ arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so, as in Sundell, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^26] However, the rule applies ‘at least when’ the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^27] and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’, and the clause, arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’, bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies, any duty running to AMPL.[^28] Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain.

On intention to create legal relations, Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^29] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised is ‘appropriately promissory in character’.[^30] Nor is Rocky’s undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ that a borrower could repay and a promise ‘to ensure’ it.[^31] Rocky’s words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must ‘ensure’, so his undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be void.[^32] His ‘I will do that’ contains no words of effort: it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. AMPL’s promise is not illusory either: once Grace repays, it leaves ‘no discretion’.[^33]

On privity, the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky himself gave: he is its promisee, no stranger to the consideration.[^34] ‘[T]he clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky’s exposure turns next on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, possibly only by his oral undertaking, and only ‘the parties to it’ are ‘bound by the obligations of a contract’.[^35] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^36] AMPL would say Rocky ‘attended’ as the clause was included, taking the $10,000 promise knowing its terms,[^37] and later invoked the Loan Agreement. However, the benefit he took, AMPL’s promise, priced his own words, and nothing shows ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’ the clause. He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^38] which its $10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^39] counting only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky ‘asked’, but unlike Pao On, where a return was understood ‘at the time of the main agreement’,[^40] nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause’s inclusion, arguably ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee;[^41] but Rocky priced his undertaking at $10,000, not at AMPL’s signature, so the clause may lack consideration.

Whether the 9 March call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Construction is objective, and in New South Wales post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s interest payments or ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term;[^42] but, if it is ambiguous, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[^43] Naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, which the agreement ‘recorded’; but ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. Interest is shown paid only to 8 February 2025; if the March instalment went unpaid, Rocky’s undertaking is arguably broken.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once:[^44] nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies it;[^45] but the words name Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach the duty to co-operate, to ‘do everything necessary on [its] part’:[^46] its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only orally, he is liable in damages, to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the $10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

## FILE: work/ANSWER_v5_src.md
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, deciding Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that he failed to lend. Grace’s 5 February call, which ‘proposed that Rocky offer’ a loan and promised nothing, was likely an invitation to treat.[^1] Rocky could say his 12 February email only records discussions, as its other points, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and the email seeks agreement. Unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’, those words are promissory,[^2] so the first point is likely an offer.

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent.[^3] ‘Confirmed’ arguably vouched only for the email’s accuracy; but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ without new terms, so it was no counter-offer and likely accepted the first point, ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ included. Grace’s implied promise to repay would arguably be consideration, since a promise can be the price of a promise.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether this preliminary agreement showed an intention to create legal relations. That is judged objectively, the alleging party bearing the onus;[^5] the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours intention. As nothing was made ‘subject to a formal contract’, the question is whether the terms were to ‘be put into form’ or left to ‘a new agreement’.[^6] Grace would say the fixed terms show the parties had ‘reached finality’, Masters’ first class.[^7] Rocky would invoke the third class, where parties ‘have dealt only with major matters’,[^8] as the email arguably did, though it mentions no formal document. Its ‘conditions’, unlike ‘subject to success of Hail Mary Project’, name no external event, so they are most naturally further loan terms; and ‘satisfactory’ leaves them to the protected party’s judgment,[^9] here Rocky’s as lender. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement; later conduct, admissible on formation, agrees, as Grace took AMPL’s loan on other terms.[^101] Were the conditions settled ‘this morning’, the email would bind.

The qualifier also arguably makes Rocky’s promise illusory, since a consideration is illusory if it ‘depends upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor’.[^11] Grace may reply that, as in Meehan, Rocky must judge honestly, perhaps reasonably,[^12] and that the fixed terms are ‘specified parameters’.[^102] However, Meehan is distinguishable: its discretion related ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’, finance, within agreed terms;[^13] Rocky’s covers the loan’s own terms, which neither standard can supply and no range confines. Godecke bound because its added terms had to be ‘reasonable in an objective sense’; and Gibbs J, obiter, doubted any ‘concluded bargain’ where ‘a vital matter’ is left to one party, his ‘[p]erhaps’ for subsidiary matters invoking a case where parties had ‘imported the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness’,[^14] as these parties never did. The email therefore likely bound neither party, defeating Grace’s claim.

Rocky may instead claim that AMPL’s advance, made because he ‘asked’, performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differed in amount and date. As Pierre ‘agreed to provide the money’ and the Loan Agreement named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, AMPL did not contract ‘as agent’ for him.[^15] Rocky’s 5 March demand under the Loan Agreement, arguably assuming a 27 February start, engages privity: outside insurance, ‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’, nor can ‘a stranger to the consideration’.[^16] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[^17] and ‘AMPL and Grace entered into’ this one, so Grace’s promises ran to AMPL alone, Rocky being not even a joint promisee;[^18] nor did Rocky give Grace anything, AMPL’s loan being their price. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is right in result but wrong in reason: signature is not necessary, the unsigned developer in Empirnall being bound,[^19] nor decisive, Mrs Coulls signing without becoming a party.[^20]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace. The Development Agreement repays him first ‘if the Project made a profit’, even the ‘minimal’ one expected, though none is yet shown; and Grace never promised to reimburse what he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

Rocky’s questions are whether he can claim $10,000 and must pay AMPL. On offer and acceptance at the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s expressed expectation promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[^21] Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ offered a bilateral contract,[^22] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^23] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing; but that ‘depends upon the intention disclosed by the language’ used,[^24] and Rocky reserved no right to withdraw pending a document signed only by Grace and AMPL, so a contract likely formed orally.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if he had ‘authority … to act for’ it and contracted for it, not solely for himself.[^25] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, supplying that authority, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he promised personally, he alone owes the $10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: ‘also’ arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so, as in Sundell, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^26] However, the rule applies ‘at least when’ the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^27] and none is shown: on 27 February Rocky ‘asked’, and the clause, arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’, bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies, any duty running to AMPL.[^28] Rocky likely gave consideration, unless he also promised AMPL a guarantee when he ‘asked’.

On intention to create legal relations, Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^29] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised is ‘appropriately promissory in character’.[^30] Nor is Rocky’s undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ that a borrower could repay and a promise ‘to ensure’ it.[^31] Rocky’s words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must ‘ensure’, so his undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be void.[^32] His ‘I will do that’ contains no words of effort, and his ‘check in’ emails cannot construe it:[^103] it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. Nor is AMPL’s promise illusory: once Grace repays, it leaves ‘no discretion’.[^33]

On privity, the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky gave: he is its promisee, no stranger to the consideration.[^34] The clause later ‘included’ is most naturally the guarantee clause already described, not a $10,000 term; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky’s exposure turns on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, possibly only by his oral undertaking, and only ‘the parties to it’ are ‘bound by the obligations of a contract’.[^35] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^36] AMPL would say Rocky ‘attended’ as the clause was included, taking the $10,000 promise knowing the clause’s terms.[^37] However, the benefit he took, AMPL’s promise, priced his own words, so taking it is not conduct ‘of such a character as necessarily’ to infer assent to the clause.[^104] He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^38] which its $10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^39] counting only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky ‘asked’, but unlike Pao On, where a return was understood ‘at the time of the main agreement’,[^40] nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause’s inclusion, arguably ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee;[^41] but Rocky priced his undertaking at $10,000, not at AMPL’s signature, so the clause then likely lacks consideration.

Whether the 9 March call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Construction is objective,[^105] and in New South Wales post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s interest payments or ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term;[^42] but, if it is ambiguous, pre-contractual conduct casting light on ‘the genesis of the contract’ is admissible.[^43] Naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, which the agreement ‘recorded’; but ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. Interest is shown paid only to 8 February 2025; if the March instalment went unpaid, Rocky’s undertaking is arguably broken.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once:[^44] nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies it;[^45] but the words name Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Rocky might also say AMPL’s call breached its duty to ‘do everything necessary on [its] part’;[^46] but the call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, Rocky is likely liable on his oral undertaking, in damages to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. If the clause also binds him and AMPL promised the $10,000, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the $10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.
