## 2. Margin comments, paragraph by paragraph (his marker's style)

Part I
1. Offer (123 words). Good framing from the client's risk (Grace's claim that Rocky failed to lend). 'Grace invited an offer rather than making one' and 'unlike 'may be prepared to sell' in Gibson, these words are promissory' are correct on Gibson 298. However: 'its other points promise nothing' is conclusive; classify the bullets on their own words ('Potential', 'wait and see'). The paragraph of the Council's letter in the indicative mood, which Lord Diplock said 'might have been understood ... as indicating a firm offer' only without its disclaimer (Gibson 298), is the closest analogy to 'subject to satisfactory conditions' and is not named.
2. Acceptance and consideration (60 words). 'an external manifestation of assent to an offer' (Empirnall 534, McHugh JA) correctly stated and Rocky's counter put. Name the doctrine: no counter-offer. '15 minutes later' unused. 'likely accepted' understates a strong point. 'Consideration would also exist' is unqualified while the next paragraph but one finds the promise 'arguably illusory': 'Ensure your conclusions stand on one footing.' Brambles 177 states that a typical contract is an exchange of promises (McHugh JA quoted by Heydon JA); it is not the course statement of the price requirement: 'Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied.' 'Grace's implied promise' is an inference: mark it arguably.
3. Intention (152 words). Strong: objective test, onus correctly placed on Grace as the party alleging the contract (Ermogenous [26]), status weighed, Winn v Bull at 363 in the Court's adopted words, Godecke (Walsh J) put for Grace and distinguished on 'reasonable in an objective sense'. Missing: Masters asked whether the document was 'only a record of terms' (360) and Jessel MR's question arises 'When it is not expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract' (363); say that no formal contract is stipulated here and that the authorities apply by analogy.
4. Certainty (102 words). Excellent use of Meehan: the honesty fetter put for Grace (Gibbs CJ 581; Mason J 589 to 590 quoting Thorby) and met on Gibbs CJ's own limit ('only to the fulfilment of a condition'), with 'honesty cannot supply terms never agreed'. Verdict properly 'arguably' with further information and its direction. But Gibbs J's dictum (used in the paragraph above) is given without its 'Perhaps it may be different where agreement has been reached on all essential terms but the determination of subsidiary matters has been left to one of the parties' (Godecke 647): state the exception and say why the loan's own conditions are not subsidiary.
5. Privity (129 words). Correct and well sourced: Windeyer J at 494 (dissent disclosed in the footnote), 'the written instrument itself' (487), the joint promisee met (486), Grace's planted line right in result and wrong in reason, Mrs Coulls compared. Only the party limb of the general rule is stated here; the consideration limb (Windeyer J 495) appears only in Part II. 'Nor was AMPL his agent:' states the verdict before its proof. The agency criterion is applied ('so it contracted for itself') but never stated as a test in this Part; the contrast of '$1,150,000' with '$1 million' is half made. Routes around privity other than agency (the contracting party enforcing; trust; estoppel) are not tried: 'Try every route for the non-party, briefly, on the facts.'
6. Conclusion for Part I (54 words). Good: the Development Agreement disposed of as conditional, and reimbursement for paying AMPL named and disposed of. One 54-word sentence.

Part II
7. Offer and acceptance (96 words). 'expected' classified on its word, 'likely an invitation to treat'; Rocky's reply offers a promise for a promise (name it: a bilateral contract). AMPL's execution argument put and answered with Lord Greene MR's words, but they were said of exchanges of contracts for land (Brambles 176): disclose the analogy. Masters 361 (reservation of a right to withdraw) not used. Say that the $10,000 and the undertaking stand or fall together.
8. Who promised (62 words). Both agency questions framed in one clause; 'you' met with control, office and loan. 'Identify the further information and how it would change your conclusion': what Pierre said about whom he spoke for. Footnote 22 pins Port Jackson 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ); the extract of their joint judgment begins at [271], and Lord Reid's requisites appear in the extract only at 240 (Barwick CJ).
9. Existing legal duty rule (96 words). Rule named and premise tested; 'none existed' tied to 27 February 'asked'; 'Pierre agreed and the clause was included' hedged ('suggests'); the 'more than' limb is excellent. Missing: Mason J's hedge 'at least when'; the word 'also', AMPL's best fact; the alternative that Pierre promised (promise made to Pierre while any duty was owed to AMPL; a duty to a third party is good consideration, Pao On 632); further information with direction (the order of clause and $10,000). 'Answer with specificity to individual Ps.' The price of the $10,000 and that it moved from Rocky (and, if Pierre promised, Rocky's detriment) is never stated as the consideration criterion.
10. Intention (53 words). Ermogenous [26] correctly used; Banque Brussels 523 quoted accurately. 'Further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive': the undertaking resembles a letter of comfort; name the difference from Banque Brussels (there the facility was 'subject to BBL obtaining a suitable letter of comfort'; here AMPL had already advanced) and say which way it cuts. Say the same finding binds Rocky to his undertaking. 'Intention to create legal relations' is never named in full anywhere in the answer.
11. Certainty (46 words). Opens with its verdict, reason in the same sentence (acceptable). Result versus effort on 'I will do that' is a good addition. AMPL's own promise ('once Grace repays') is not shown to be other than illusory (Meehan 581 to 582).
12. Burden and assent (119 words). Burden aspect correct (Trident, Deane J, per R-Y); Empirnall 534 and 535 to 536 applied with the benefit named ('retaining the $10,000 promise') and the knowledge fact ('attended', marked arguably). Rocky's counter put but not met; no further information with direction (whether he saw the clause's words). 'A guarantee was 'provided by Rocky'' used and tested: good. Signature is not the test for Rocky either (Empirnall 536; Coulls 487): say so here.
13. Consideration for the guarantee (83 words). Conditional on who promised; past consideration named; Pao On's request met on 'asked'; fallback put and accepted with 'really done in consideration of' (AWM 456). 'and that is doubtful' is conclusive: in Pao On the parties understood 'at the time of the main agreement'; nothing shows that understanding on 27 February. 65-word sentence.
14. The 12 months (121 words). Very good: later conduct excluded (Brambles 164), ambiguity decided with a reason, genesis admitted only conditionally (191), the 'recorded' point turned against AMPL with the 4% rate, lean 'arguably' to 8 April with further information and direction. Missing the objective-meaning limb (Brambles 168 or Ermogenous [25]).
15. The condition (74 words). Condition precedent to the obligation, not to the contract, with its reason (Meehan 582); commercial reading put (Upper Hunter 437) and met with the pricing point. 'his own repayment' is the wrong word (Rocky does not repay the Loan; he pays under the guarantee). Rocky's best answer, the duty to co-operate (Beaton 185, McHugh JA citing Mason J), is neither put nor met.
16. Bottom line (112 words). Exposure stated precisely on both readings of the 12 months and both sources of liability (R-AD(1) met); T13 drawn. Missing: on the 8 April reading, interest is shown paid only to '8 February 2025', so a March 2025 instalment is arguably unpaid and engages the oral undertaking ('all payments ... promptly').

## FILE: work/LAWS1150 Mid-Term T3 2026 - Rocky (v3).docx
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[.docx converted to text]

**I. ROCKY v GRACE**

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, which decides Rocky's claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that he failed to lend. Grace's 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer and promised nothing; it was likely an invitation to treat,[^1] which Rocky declined. Rocky could say his 12 February email merely records discussions, its other points, 'Potential' and 'wait and see', promising nothing. However, 'I will lend' fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and the email seeks agreement. Unlike 'may be prepared to sell', those words are promissory,[^2] so the first point is likely an offer.

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent.[^3] 'Confirmed' arguably vouched only for the email's accuracy; but it answered a request to 'confirm agreement' without new terms, so it was no counter-offer and likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Grace's implied promise to repay would arguably be consideration, since a promise can be the price of a promise.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether this preliminary agreement showed an intention to create legal relations. That is judged objectively, the alleging party bearing the onus;[^5] the parties' status as 'project developers' favours it. As nothing was made 'subject to a formal contract', the question is whether the terms were merely to 'be put into form' or left to 'a new agreement'.[^6] Grace would say the fixed amount, date, term and rate show the parties had 'reached finality', as in *Masters*' first class.[^7] Rocky would invoke the third class, where parties 'have dealt only with major matters';[^8] though no formal document was contemplated, the email likewise fixes only these. Its 'conditions', unlike 'subject to success of Hail Mary Project', name no external event, so they are most naturally further loan terms; and 'satisfactory' leaves them to the protected party's judgment,[^9] here Rocky's as lender. Later conduct, admissible on formation,[^10] agrees, AMPL later lending on other terms. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement. Were the conditions settled 'this morning', the email would bind, but Rocky's duty would arise only once they were met.[^11]

The qualifier also arguably makes Rocky's promise illusory, since a consideration is illusory if it 'depends upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor'.[^12] Grace may reply that, as in *Meehan*, Rocky must judge honestly, perhaps reasonably.[^13] However, *Meehan* is distinguishable: its discretion related 'only to the fulfilment of a condition', finance, within agreed terms;[^14] Rocky's covers the loan's own terms, which neither standard can supply. Gibbs J's obiter '\[p\]erhaps', allowing subsidiary matters to be left to one party once 'all essential terms' are agreed, assumed 'the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness',[^15] which 'satisfactory' lacks. The email therefore likely bound neither party, and Grace has no claim that Rocky failed to lend.

Rocky may instead claim that AMPL's advance, made because he 'asked', performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differs: \$1,150,000, after 15 February, by AMPL, recorded on 8 April at 4%. As Pierre 'agreed to provide the money' and AMPL named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, AMPL did not contract 'as agent' for him.[^16] Rocky's 5 March demand under the Loan Agreement therefore faces privity: 'a third party cannot sue upon a contract', nor can 'a stranger to the consideration'.[^17] Party status turns on 'the written instrument itself',[^18] and Grace's promises were made to AMPL, not Rocky, even as joint promisee;[^19] nor did Rocky give Grace anything, AMPL having lent. Grace's 'I never signed anything with you' is right in result but wrong in reason: signature is not necessary, *Empirnall* being bound unsigned,[^20] nor decisive, Mrs Coulls signing without becoming a party.[^21]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace. The Development Agreement repays him first only 'if the Project made a profit', none yet shown; and Grace never promised to reimburse what he pays AMPL.

**II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)**

For Rocky, the questions are whether he can claim \$10,000 and must pay AMPL. On offer and acceptance at the 8 April meeting, Pierre's 'expected' promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[^22] Rocky's 'I will do that if you also promise' offered a bilateral contract,[^23] which Pierre accepted when he 'agreed'.[^24] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing; but that 'depends upon the intention disclosed by the language' used,[^25] and Rocky reserved no right to withdraw pending a document signed only by Grace and AMPL. A contract likely formed orally, binding both promises.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if he contracted 'as agent' for it rather than for himself.[^26] Rocky's 'you' points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he said he would pay personally, he alone owes the \$10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: 'also' arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so that, as in *Sundell*, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^27] However, the rule applies 'at least when' the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^28] and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only 'asked', and the clause, included after Pierre 'agreed', bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring 'all payments' 'promptly' exceeds guaranteeing 'repayment of the Loan'; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies.[^29] Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain.

On intention to create legal relations, Pierre is Rocky's cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^30] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL's office as its loan was finalised is 'appropriately promissory in character'.[^31] Nor is Rocky's undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw 'no relevant difference' between a 'practice to ensure' that a borrower could repay and a promise 'to ensure' it.[^32] Rocky's words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind, even if Pierre promised.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must 'ensure', so his undertaking is not 'so obscure' as to be void.[^33] His 'I will do that' contains no words of effort: it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. AMPL's promise is not illusory either, because once Grace repays it leaves AMPL 'no discretion' whether to pay.[^34]

On privity, the \$10,000 was to be paid 'to me directly' for consideration Rocky himself gave; he is therefore its promisee and no stranger to the consideration.[^35] '\[T\]he clause' most naturally means the guarantee clause just described; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky's exposure turns next on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was 'provided by Rocky', perhaps only by his oral undertaking, and only 'the parties to it' are 'bound by the obligations of a contract'.[^36] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^37] AMPL would say Rocky 'attended' as the clause recording his bargain was included, taking the \$10,000 promise knowing its terms,[^38] and later invoked the Loan Agreement. However, he has received nothing, and signature is no test for him either. He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^39] which its \$10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^40] counting only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky 'asked', but unlike *Pao On*, where a return was understood 'at the time of the main agreement',[^41] nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause's inclusion, arguably 'really done in consideration of' the guarantee;[^42] but Rocky priced his undertaking at \$10,000, not at AMPL's signature.

Whether the 9 March 2025 call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. In New South Wales, post-contractual conduct, such as Grace's 'I have until 8 April 2025', cannot construe the term;[^43] but, if it is ambiguous, mutually known facts showing 'the genesis of the transaction' are admissible.[^44] Naming no start, it is ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, the agreement having 'recorded' a loan already made; but 'recorded' equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. Interest is shown paid only to 8 February 2025; if the March instalment went unpaid, Rocky's undertaking is arguably broken already.

The \$10,000 is payable 'once Grace repays the Loan', a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once;[^45] nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies it;[^46] but the words name Grace, and the \$10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach the duty to co-operate, to 'do everything necessary on \[its\] part':[^47] its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for \$1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only orally, he is liable in damages, to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the \$10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he 'might not pay at all', repays.

The email therefore likely bound neither party, defeating Grace's claim.

Rocky may instead claim that AMPL's advance, made because he 'asked', performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differed in amount, date, lender and rate. As Pierre 'agreed to provide the money' and AMPL named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, AMPL did not contract 'as agent' for him.[^15] Rocky's 5 March demand under the Loan Agreement, arguably assuming a 27 February start, faces privity: 'a third party cannot sue upon a contract', nor can 'a stranger to the consideration'.[^16] Party status turns on 'the written instrument itself',[^17] and Grace's promises were made to AMPL, not Rocky, even as joint promisee;[^18] nor did Rocky give Grace anything, AMPL having lent. Grace's 'I never signed anything with you' is right in result but wrong in reason: signature is not necessary, *Empirnall* being bound unsigned,[^19] nor decisive, Mrs Coulls signing without becoming a party.[^20]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace. The Development Agreement repays him first only 'if the Project made a profit', none yet shown; and Grace never promised to reimburse what he pays AMPL.

**II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)**

Rocky's questions are whether he can claim \$10,000 and must pay AMPL. On offer and acceptance at the 8 April meeting, Pierre's expressed expectation promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[^21] Rocky's 'I will do that if you also promise' offered a bilateral contract,[^22] which Pierre accepted when he 'agreed'.[^23] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing; but that 'depends upon the intention disclosed by the language' used,[^24] and Rocky reserved no right to withdraw pending a document signed only by Grace and AMPL, so a contract likely formed orally.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if, with its consent, he contracted 'as agent' for it rather than solely for himself.[^25] Rocky's 'you' points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he said he would pay personally, he alone owes the \$10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: 'also' arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so, as in *Sundell*, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^26] However, the rule applies 'at least when' the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^27] and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only 'asked', and the clause, arguably included after Pierre 'agreed', bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring 'all payments' 'promptly' exceeds guaranteeing 'repayment of the Loan'; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies, any duty running to AMPL.[^28] Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain.

On intention to create legal relations, Pierre is Rocky's cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^29] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL's office as its loan was finalised is 'appropriately promissory in character'.[^30] Nor is Rocky's undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw 'no relevant difference' between a 'practice to ensure' that a borrower could repay and a promise 'to ensure' it.[^31] Rocky's words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must 'ensure', so his undertaking is not 'so obscure' as to be void.[^32] His 'I will do that' contains no words of effort: it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. AMPL's promise is not illusory either: once Grace repays, it leaves 'no discretion'.[^33]

On privity, the \$10,000 was to be paid 'to me directly' for consideration Rocky himself gave: he is its promisee, no stranger to the consideration.[^34] '\[T\]he clause' most naturally means the guarantee clause; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky's exposure turns next on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was 'provided by Rocky', possibly only by his oral undertaking, and only 'the parties to it' are 'bound by the obligations of a contract'.[^35] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^36] AMPL would say Rocky 'attended' as the clause was included, taking the \$10,000 promise knowing its terms,[^37] and later invoked the Loan Agreement. However, the benefit he took, AMPL's promise, priced his own words, and nothing shows 'a reasonable opportunity to reject' the clause. He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^38] which its \$10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^39] counting only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky 'asked', but unlike *Pao On*, where a return was understood 'at the time of the main agreement',[^40] nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause's inclusion, arguably 'really done in consideration of' the guarantee;[^41] but Rocky priced his undertaking at \$10,000, not at AMPL's signature, so the clause may lack consideration.

Whether the 9 March call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Construction is objective, and in New South Wales post-contractual conduct, such as Grace's interest payments or 'I have until 8 April 2025', cannot construe the term;[^42] but, if it is ambiguous, mutually known facts showing 'the genesis of the transaction' are admissible.[^43] Naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, which the agreement 'recorded'; but 'recorded' equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. Interest is shown paid only to 8 February 2025; if the March instalment went unpaid, Rocky's undertaking is arguably broken.

The \$10,000 is payable 'once Grace repays the Loan', a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once:[^44] nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies it;[^45] but the words name Grace, and the \$10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach the duty to co-operate, to 'do everything necessary on \[its\] part':[^46] its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for \$1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only orally, he is liable in damages, to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the \$10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he 'might not pay at all', repays.

## 1. CERTAIN DEFECTS

Each is provable from the verbatim text of the answer, the problem or the casebook. Word costs are body words.

### CD1. The agency reason is refuted by the very passage cited for it (Part I, para 5; fn 14)

Sentence: 'Nor did AMPL lend as his agent: a principal is a party only where another ‘contracts as agent’ for him,[^14] and AMPL contracted in its own name.'

Proof: Deane J at Trident 145 (CB14 ch11, [11.70], after the [145] marker): 'If the promisee contracts as agent for a disclosed or undisclosed principal, the principal will ordinarily himself be, for the purposes of the requirement of privity, a party to the contract.' Two faults. (a) The passage expressly includes an *undisclosed* principal, that is, an agent contracting in its own name. 'AMPL contracted in its own name' is therefore no reason at all on Deane J's own words; it is the fact pattern his sentence says still binds the principal. (b) Deane J says 'If', and his very next sentence gives a second route to direct rights (a third party accepting an offer incorporated in the contract, 'compare Coulls at 478–9, 486, 493'). 'only where' turns a sufficient condition into a necessary one; the authority is used for more than it says. The result (Rocky lent nothing) is right; the reason given for it is wrong. The previous version's reason ('took his guarantee') was the right one; it was removed to cure Marker B's consistency point and replaced with a reason the source defeats. 'Rocky asked', Rocky's best fact, is also never met on the purporting question.

Fix (+12): 'Nor did AMPL lend as his agent: a principal is a party where another ‘contracts as agent’ for him,[^14] but AMPL lent its own money, for interest payable to itself, and named Rocky its guarantor, so it acted for itself and not for him.' (If the colon order is also cured under CD8: 'AMPL lent its own money, for interest payable to itself, and named Rocky its guarantor, so, although Rocky ‘asked’, it did not contract ‘as agent’ for him.') 'named Rocky its guarantor' is the narrator's description of the clause and answers Marker B's C3 without asserting assent.

### CD2. A derived fact stated as fact, contradicting the answer's own II.G reasoning (Part I, para 5)

Sentence: '…made after 15 February and in AMPL’s name, on terms first fixed on 8 April at 4%.'

Proof: the problem says only 'The loan was recorded as $1,150,000 (‘Loan’) with an interest rate of 4% per annum.' When the terms were first agreed is nowhere stated; on 27 February the problem says only that 'Pierre agreed to provide the money'. The answer itself, in II.G, writes that the 4% rate is a rate 'which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April', and puts AMPL's argument that the agreement 'recorded' a loan already made. Part I asserts as fact what Part II treats as contested. Sheet D4 (derived fact not marked; the sheet's own II.G note rejects 'were fixed on 8 April' for exactly this reason): −2, unit capped at Fair.

Fix (0): 'on terms recorded on 8 April at 4%'.

### CD3. The onus framing contradicts the paragraph that follows it (Part I, paras 3 and 5)

Sentence (para 3): '…which is judged objectively, the onus lying on Grace, who alone would sue on the email…'

Proof: para 1 says 'both Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that Rocky failed to lend … depend' on the email, and para 5 runs that very claim: 'Rocky may claim that AMPL’s 27 February advance … performed his promise, so that Grace owes him the money.' That is Rocky suing on the email. 'who alone would sue' is false on the answer's own structure. The fault was introduced when Marker B's point 1 (frame Rocky's claim) was added without revisiting Marker A's K12 wording. R10 tension.

### CD4. Masters' third class quoted without its limiting words and applied 'Decisively' beyond its premise (Part I, para 3; fn 6)

Sentence: 'Decisively, the third class in Masters covers parties who ‘have dealt only with major matters and contemplate that others will or may be regulated by provisions to be introduced’; that describes an email fixing the amount, date, term and rate while leaving unnamed ‘conditions’ to Rocky.'

Proof: Masters 361 (CB14 ch05, [5.95]): '…because they have dealt only with major matters and contemplate that others will or may be regulated by provisions to be introduced **into the formal document**, as in Summergreene v Parker'. The quotation stops one phrase short of the words that confine the class. The classes are framed at 360 for parties who 'reach agreement upon terms of a contractual nature and also agree that the matter of their negotiation shall be dealt with by a formal contract', and the third class itself is a case where the parties do not intend a concluded bargain 'unless and until they execute a formal contract'. The email contemplates no formal document. Applying the class without disclosing that it is an analogy, and cutting the quotation so the premise disappears, uses the authority for more than it decided. The course passage that does fit a qualifier which mentions no formal contract is the Court's adoption of Jessel MR at 363: 'When it is not expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract it becomes a question of construction, whether the parties intended that the terms agreed on should be put into form, or whether they should be subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not expressed in detail'. The previous version used exactly that passage (its fn 6); this version dropped it. Worse, Godecke, which the answer cites in the next sentence, reversed a first-instance holding that further terms left to one side's solicitors put the case 'within the third class of the cases discussed in Masters v Cameron' (Walsh J, 643, CB14 ch06 [6.175]), so the class is not 'decisive' of anything on this kind of qualifier. 'Decisively' then sits two sentences before 'On balance', which is a contradiction in the answer's own strength signals.

Severity: the words quoted are verbatim, so I do not apply D2 automatically; a strict reading of D2 ('an ellipsis that changes meaning') would, and I show that figure in Part 4.

Fix (+12 net): 'Masters’ third class, for parties who leave other terms ‘to be introduced into the formal document’, assumes a contemplated formal contract, absent here, so the question is whether the terms were to be ‘put into form’ or left ‘subject to a new agreement’;[^Masters 361, 363 quoting Winn v Bull] an email fixing the amount, date, term and rate while leaving unnamed ‘conditions’ to Rocky arguably leaves a new agreement.' Delete 'Decisively,'.

### CD5. Gibbs J's dictum loses its 'Perhaps' and is then converted into a holding (Part I, para 3; fn 9)

The answer drops 'Perhaps' and then says that if the conditions were 'mere documentation, the email would bind'. Gibbs J said only that it 'Perhaps … may be different'. Fix (+1): 'while allowing that ‘Perhaps it may be different’ where only ‘subsidiary matters’ remain; were the conditions settled ‘this morning’ the email would bind, and were they mere documentation it might'.

The missing or thin arguments in detail:

**M1. Mason J's hedge in Wigan (II.C2).** 'the rule bites on a promise ‘made to the promisee under that contract’, and none then existed'. Wigan 594 (CB14 ch04): 'The general rule is that a promise to perform an existing duty is no consideration, **at least when** the promise is made by a party to a pre-existing contract, when it is made to the promisee under that contract, and it is to do no more than the promisor is bound to do under the contract.' 'at least when' marks the core case, not the limit of the rule. The answer's point (no existing duty because no prior contract) is sound, but the sentence states Mason J's sufficient case as the rule's only field. Fix (+3): 'the rule applies ‘at least when’ the promise is ‘made to the promisee under that contract’, and no such contract then existed'. Also missing: the order of clause and $10,000 as further information with its direction (sheet II.C2 core (5)); +8: 'though a guarantee agreed before the $10,000 would favour AMPL'.

**M2. Grace's answer to Placer (I.E).** Placer is distinguishable on its own reasoning. Kitto J (CB14 ch06 [6.185]): 'A promise of a governmental subsidy is meaningless in the absence of a specification of some amount or some basis of calculation. It carries no implication that at least a reasonable subsidy shall be paid, for there is no general standard of reasonableness with respect to the quantum of a subsidy.' Grace's best reply is that loan 'conditions' between project developers do have an objective standard (market lending terms), as Gibbs CJ himself contemplated for finance at Meehan 579 to 580 (a purchaser 'should not find it unduly difficult to decide what finance a reasonable man … would regard as satisfactory'), so the honesty or reasonableness fetter can operate. Rocky's answer is Mason J at 587 (CB14 ch06, before [588]): the point 'would have force if the contract left the court at large to assess what is ‘finance on satisfactory terms and conditions’, yielding no indication as to what the parties meant by that expression', and the email names no object for the conditions. About +25 words; marks at risk about 0.75 (I.E VG to Excellent).

**M3. No conclusion on assent to the written clause (II.I2).** The paragraph ends on Rocky's counter ('he could answer that the $10,000 priced his own words, not the clause') and never says which way it goes or what would decide it. Empirnall 536: 'taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms'. The decisive facts are whether Rocky saw the clause's words; the answer should lean ('likely assented, unless he never saw its words') or say the opposite with its reason. The closing paragraph's conditional ('if Rocky assented') cannot substitute for the lean at the unit. +14 words; II.I2 0.875, R6.

**M4. Rocky's pricing counter to AMPL's fallback consideration (II.I3).** 'AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee'. Australian Woollen Mills 456 states two limbs: the promise must be 'really offered as consideration for the doing of the act, and that the act was really done in consideration of' it. The answer applies the second limb only. Rocky's words price his undertaking at $10,000, not at AMPL's signing, which goes to the first limb. +10: '…though Rocky offered his undertaking for the $10,000, not for AMPL’s signing'.

**M5. The Banque Brussels difference (II.D).** Rogers CJ (CB14 ch05, between [521] and [523]): 'it was made quite clear to both Spedley and ANI that the facility was subject to BBL obtaining a suitable letter of comfort'. In Banque Brussels the comfort conditioned the lending; here AMPL had already advanced on 27 February, which makes the commercial-seriousness inference weaker; the answer's price point is what supplies it. Also the 'far more thorny' hedge Rogers CJ attached to the 525 passage is omitted. +12; II.D 1.25.

**M6. The Development Agreement is a live contingent claim, not a dead one (Part I conclusion).** The problem says the profit 'would be minimal and, due to the terms of their Development Agreement, Grace was unlikely to make a profit'. A minimal profit is still a profit, and Rocky is to be 'repaid his investment and a portion of the profit in priority to Grace'. 'is not shown breached' answers a question nobody asked; the advice should be that the condition is likely to be met on completion and Rocky's priority claim then arises. This is the one contractual claim Rocky has against Grace on the facts. +18.

**M7. Pierre alternative in consideration and intention (II.C1, II.D).** If Pierre promised personally, Rocky's consideration is his own detriment (Musumeci 745 is in CB14 ch04) and the cousinhood bears directly on the promisor; the answer never re-weighs intention on that alternative ('a promise of a fixed sum, made at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised' is the AMPL weighing). +12.

**M8. Routes around privity (Part I).** Only agency is run. Trident (CB14 ch11, Mason CJ and Wilson J, set reading) names the trust route, 'a party to a contract can constitute himself a trustee for a third party of a right under a contract' (115), and the class slides list estoppel; AMPL, the contracting party, is itself enforcing ('AMPL contacted Grace directly'). One line disposes of all three. +18; I.F3 0.4.

**M9. The consideration limb in Part I's privity rule.** Only 'a third party cannot sue upon a contract' is quoted; the same sentence at Trident 115 continues 'and that a stranger to the consideration cannot maintain an action at law upon it', and Rocky gave Grace nothing for his promise to AMPL. +8; I.F2 1.9.

**M10. The 8 April 2024 interest payment (II.G, credit).** Payments ran 'Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025'. A monthly payment on 8 April 2024, the day the agreement was made, is appropriate only if interest had already accrued, which points to the 27 February advance; equally, the record stops at 8 February 2025, consistent with a term expiring 27 February 2025. This is post-contractual conduct, inadmissible on meaning (Brambles 164), so it cannot decide the start date, but a strong answer would say why it is excluded rather than leave AMPL's best factual point unmentioned. Credit only.

**M11. 'once Grace repays' not illusory (II.E).** Meehan 581 to 582: 'The fact that the condition is one whose performance lies wholly or partly within the power of one of the parties to the contract does not mean that there is no binding contract once the condition is fulfilled.' The condition here lies with a third party, so a fortiori. +10; II.E 0.6.

**M12. Gibson's second paragraph (I.A).** Gibson 298: 'If the final sentence had been omitted the wording of the second paragraph, unlike that of the first, with its use of the indicative mood … might have been understood … as indicating a firm offer'. 'I will lend' is indicative but carries 'subject to satisfactory conditions', which is the disclaimer's analogue; naming that similarity is why the qualifier goes to intention. The bullets are also disposed of without their deciding words ('Potential', 'wait and see'). +20; I.A 0.75.

**M13. Pao On pin (contestable, not deducted).** fn 39 pins 629; the quoted words sit before the [630] marker, so 629 is precise. Sheet D11 literally lists only '629–30 or 632'. I do not deduct; a literal marker might.

## 3. MARGIN COMMENTS (paragraph by paragraph)

**I ¶1 (offer).** Good close reading of 'I will lend' against 'may be prepared to sell'. Name the category: the 5 February call is an invitation to treat. 'its other points promise nothing': further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive; quote the words that make them non-promissory ('Potential'; 'wait and see'). Gibson's second paragraph is the closer comparison for a qualified indicative promise.

**I ¶2 (acceptance, consideration).** Clean. Name the doctrine you exclude: no counter-offer. The quid pro quo citation is from a unilateral-contract passage ('In cases of this class'); acceptable, but say it is the bargain requirement.

**I ¶3 (intention).** The strongest paragraph in Part I, but its decisive step is wrong in method. Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied: Masters' third class concerns terms 'to be introduced into the formal document'; your quotation stops before those words, and the email contemplates no formal document. Use the Court's adopted words at 363. 'Decisively' cannot sit beside 'On balance'. 'who alone would sue on the email' is contradicted by your own paragraph 5. Keep Gibbs J's 'Perhaps'.

**I ¶4 (certainty).** Very good: Meehan named, its similarity stated, and distinguished on Gibbs CJ's own limit; the honesty fetter is put and met with a reason. Consider Grace's answer that, unlike Placer's subsidy, loan terms have an objective standard.

**I ¶5 (Rocky's claim; privity).** Begin with the hypothesis: even if the email bound. 'This fails:' and 'Nor did AMPL lend as his agent:' state the conclusion before the analysis. 'first fixed on 8 April' is not a fact in the problem. Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied: Deane J's sentence covers an undisclosed principal, so 'in its own name' is no answer; the answer is that AMPL lent its own money for itself and named Rocky its guarantor. State both limbs of the rule.

**I ¶6 (conclusion).** One-sentence paragraph. 'not shown breached': a 'minimal' profit is still a profit; advise on the contingent claim.

**II ¶1 (offer, acceptance).** Correct. Name the bilateral contract. Lord Greene MR's analogy is properly disclosed. Hedge 'a request' ('likely').

**II ¶2 (who promised).** One-sentence paragraph. State the agency criterion (authority, and whether Pierre purported to act for AMPL or himself) before applying it. 'would settle this': identify the further information and how it would change your conclusion. 'what follows runs against him' is not advice.

**II ¶3 (existing legal duty rule).** Good: the rule named, Mason J's premise applied, the order inference marked, 'exceeds' well found, Pao On 632 added. Keep Mason J's 'at least when'. State what the order of clause and $10,000 would do to the result.

**II ¶4 (intention).** Good use of Ermogenous [26] and Rogers CJ at 525. Name the difference from Banque Brussels (the comfort there conditioned the facility). Re-weigh if Pierre promised personally.

## 1. CERTAIN DEFECTS

### CD1. A derived fact stated as fact, contradicted by Part II (D4; I.F1 capped at Fair)
Sentence (Part I, para 5): ‘This fails: the advance was $1,150,000, not $1 million, made after 15 February and in AMPL’s name, on terms first fixed on 8 April at 4%.’
Proof: the problem says only ‘The loan was recorded as $1,150,000 (‘Loan’) with an interest rate of 4% per annum’. When the terms were first fixed is nowhere stated. The answer itself says so in Part II: ‘‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April’. SHEET_v12 II.G core (4) names this exact slip (‘v5’s ’were fixed on 8 April’ stated a derived fact as fact’) and D4 lists it. It is also the fact on which AMPL’s whole 27 February argument turns, so stating it as settled in Part I pre-decides II.G.
Fix (0 words): ‘… and in AMPL’s name, and ‘recorded’ on 8 April at 4%.’

### CD2. The cited judge’s own sentence defeats the reason given (I.F1; R2; R8)
Sentence (Part I, para 5): ‘Nor did AMPL lend as his agent: a principal is a party only where another ‘contracts as agent’ for him,[^14] and AMPL contracted in its own name.’
Proof: Trident 145 (Deane J, CB14 355): ‘If the promisee contracts as agent for a disclosed or undisclosed principal, the principal will ordinarily himself be, for the purposes of the requirement of privity, a party to the contract.’ Two faults. (a) Deane J states a sufficient condition (‘will ordinarily … be’); ‘only where’ turns it into a necessary one, which he did not say. (b) An agent for an undisclosed principal always contracts in its own name; Deane J expressly includes that case. So ‘AMPL contracted in its own name’ is no reason at all against agency on the very authority cited. The facts that do answer agency (purporting) are left unused: AMPL lent a different sum on its own recorded terms, took the interest to itself, and the Loan Agreement includes ‘a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, which no lender takes from its own principal. ‘Rocky asked’ is put in the claim sentence but never met on the purporting criterion (SHEET I.F1 core). Separately, Deane J’s passage is about a promisee who contracts as agent; it is a privity statement, not a statement of the agency criterion.
Fix (+6 words): ‘Nor, although Rocky ‘asked’, did AMPL lend as his agent: an undisclosed principal is a party only if the agent acted for him,[^14] whereas AMPL lent a different sum on its own terms and named Rocky as guarantor, which no lender does of its own principal.’ (Prefer the set reading, Mason CJ and Wilson J at 115, for ‘an agency relationship’ if a case is wanted for the route; see C11.)

### CD3. Three unit verdicts stated before their proof (D5 x3; R3; R-AC(2))
Sentences: (i) Part I para 5: ‘This fails: the advance was $1,150,000 …’; (ii) Part I para 5: ‘Nor did AMPL lend as his agent: …’; (iii) Part II para 6: ‘Privity is no bar: the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ …’.
Proof: SHEET §1 and D5: ‘a unit’s VERDICT before a colon (‘Rocky lent nothing: …’) is conclusion-first whatever follows it’; R-AC(2): each paragraph ‘opens by naming the issue … states the rule … works through the facts … and ends with a hedged conclusion’. Paragraph 6 of Part II opens with its verdict. Each is −1; two or more cap R3 at Fair.
Fix (0 to +2 words each): put the facts first, eg ‘Because the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky himself gave, he is the promisee and no ‘stranger to the consideration’, so privity is no bar.’

### CD4. Inconsistent onus: ‘Grace alone would sue’, then Rocky sues on the same email (R10)
Sentence (Part I para 3): ‘… the onus lying on Grace, who alone would sue on the email …’
Proof: two paragraphs later the answer puts Rocky’s own claim on the email: ‘Rocky may claim that AMPL’s 27 February advance … performed his promise, so that Grace owes him the money.’ Rocky would then be the party alleging the contract and, on Ermogenous [26] (CB14 135 to 136, report 106: ‘it was for the appellant to demonstrate that there was such a contract’), would bear the onus. The answer’s own framing sentence (‘on which both Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace … depend’) makes the inconsistency visible.
Fix (−3 words): ‘the onus lying on whichever party alleges the contract’.

### CD5. The decisive authority is cut off just before its own premise (I.D; R2)
Sentence (Part I para 3): ‘Decisively, the third class in Masters covers parties who ‘have dealt only with major matters and contemplate that others will or may be regulated by provisions to be introduced’;[^6] that describes an email fixing the amount, date, term and rate while leaving unnamed ‘conditions’ to Rocky.’
Proof: Masters 361 (CB14 153) continues ‘… provisions to be introduced into the formal document’, and the three classes are framed at 360 for parties who ‘also agree that the matter of their negotiation shall be dealt with by a formal contract’. The email contemplates no formal document. The quotation stops one phrase before the words that show the class does not fit, and the sentence calls it ‘Decisively’ without disclosing that it applies only by analogy. The passage of Masters that does fit a qualifier which mentions no formal contract is the Court’s adoption of Jessel MR at 363: ‘When it is not expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract it becomes a question of construction, whether the parties intended that the terms agreed on should be put into form, or whether they should be subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not expressed in detail’. The previous version used exactly that passage; this version dropped it, and the paragraph’s own verdict (‘left to a new agreement’) still borrows Jessel MR’s words without his authority. This is a regression.
Fix (about +4 words): ‘Decisively, where nothing is ‘expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract’, the question is whether the terms were to ‘be put into form’ or left ‘subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not expressed in detail’;[fn: Masters 363, quoting Winn v Bull (1877) 7 Ch D 29, 32 (Jessel MR)] the email fixes …’. If class 3 is kept, add ‘by analogy, Masters assuming a formal document’ (+6).

## 2. CONTESTABLE POINTS AND MISSING ARGUMENTS
Ranked by marks at risk per word (highest first). ‘Marks’ are SHEET_v12 units and rows; ‘holistic’ means it would move a senior academic’s mark although the sheet treats it as credit.

**M1. Explicit legal consequence of paying, and of waiting (R-AD(1), R-AE; II.H, II.I4; holistic). About +20.** The answer never says the two things Rocky most needs: no term obliges him to pay before the Loan is due, and if he pays it himself the $10,000 likely never falls due. The condition paragraph says only that the words ‘name Grace’; the bottom line says the $10,000 ‘falls due only if Grace … repays’. R-AD(1): ‘paying early likely forfeits it’; R-AE: ‘paying before the Loan is due is not required by any term and, the $10,000 being conditional on Grace’s repayment, likely forfeits it’. Source: Meehan 582 (‘Once the condition is fulfilled … the contract becomes completely binding’). Form: ‘No term requires Rocky to pay before the Loan is due, and his own payment would likely leave the $10,000 never payable.’

**M2. The Development Agreement is a live, contingent claim, so ‘Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace’ overstates (P; holistic). About +15.** The problem: ‘if the Project made a profit, Rocky … would be repaid his investment and a portion of the profit in priority to Grace’, and the parties ‘realised that the profit from the Project would be minimal’. A minimal profit is a profit. The Project was ‘near completion’. Rocky’s priority repayment may therefore yet fall due; it is the only money claim he has against Grace. The answer says only that the Development Agreement ‘is not shown breached’. Form: ‘…, though the ‘minimal’ profit expected, once made, would entitle him to priority repayment of his investment.’

**M3. Post-contractual conduct is admissible on formation, and here it all points one way (I.D; credit; holistic). About +25.** Brambles 164 (Heydon JA, CB14 73): ‘post-contractual conduct is admissible on the question of whether a contract was formed’. The answer cites 164 only for the exclusion on meaning. After 12 February nobody acted on the email: Rocky lent nothing ‘by 15 February’, nothing suggests Grace complained, and the money came from AMPL on its own recorded terms. That is the strongest objective evidence that the email was ‘left to a new agreement’, and it costs one sentence with an authority already in the footnotes. Grace’s counter, McHugh JA’s ‘cure by later conduct’ (Brambles 177: terms ‘too uncertain or too illusory to enforce at a particular time … may by reason of the parties’ subsequent conduct become sufficiently specific’), is met because no later conduct ever specified the ‘conditions’.

**M4. Grace’s best certainty answer from the majority in Placer itself (I.E; credit; both-sides). About +20.** Kitto J (majority), CB14 188: in service cases the question is whether ‘a promise to pay a reasonable amount is to be implied’, Placer failing because ‘there is no general standard of reasonableness with respect to the quantum of a subsidy’. Grace will say loan terms, unlike a governmental subsidy, have a market standard. The answer to it is in the course: Mason J at Meehan 587 (CB14 182), the point ‘would have force if the contract left the court at large … yielding no indication as to what the parties meant’, which is what unnamed ‘conditions’ do. The answer’s ‘which honesty cannot supply’ asserts this without the authority.

**M5. Gibbs J’s own reason why discretion left to the promisor is fatal (I.D/I.E; R2). About +12.** Godecke 646 to 647 (CB14 187): the price ‘left to be settled by the buyer himself’ falls within Thorby’s principle; ‘if the determination of the price were left to the seller, then it would be the promisee, not the promisor, who was left with the discretion’. Rocky is promisor and judge. Also 647: Gibbs J disagreed with Bray CJ that the omission of ‘reasonably’ made no difference, which directly answers Godecke as Grace’s ‘strongest counter’. And keep his ‘Perhaps’: the answer’s ‘allowing that it ‘may be different’’ converts a hesitation into a concession.

**M6. II.D does not re-weigh the Pierre alternative (II.D; VG drop). About +10.** Every objective factor used (‘made at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised’) points to AMPL. If Pierre promised personally, the cousinhood bears directly on the promisor and ‘at AMPL’s office’ bears less; the price (‘$10,000 … to me directly’) is what must carry the finding. One clause: ‘the price carrying it even if Pierre, a cousin, promised personally’.

**M7. The Pierre alternative in the bottom line (II.I4 core (4); R10). About +15.** The final paragraph states Rocky’s exposure without distinguishing AMPL and Pierre. On the answer’s own reasoning, if Pierre promised personally, Rocky’s undertaking ran to Pierre, and AMPL can enforce only the clause, and only with assent and its own consideration (which the answer finds ‘likely’ through signing). Say so: ‘If Pierre promised, the claim lies against him and the undertaking runs to him, AMPL keeping only the clause.’

**M8. II.H: give the classification its reason and state the verdict (II.H; VG drops). About +10.** ‘a condition precedent to that obligation rather than to the contract’ needs Gibbs CJ’s reason, which is the answer’s own II.B finding: the oral bargain bound at once, as ‘Certain obligations under the contract attached immediately’ (Meehan 582). The paragraph then never says ‘so his payment likely does not meet it’; the reader must infer the verdict from ‘however, the words name Grace’.

**M9. II.E: AMPL’s $10,000 promise is not illusory (II.E; VG drop). About +12.** A promise ‘once Grace repays’ leaves AMPL no discretion once the condition is met (Meehan 581 to 582: ‘There is a concluded agreement as to the terms of the contract which, if the condition is satisfied, leaves no discretion in either party’). AMPL will run Placer against the $10,000 if Grace never repays; one clause closes it.

**M10. What AMPL actually gave by signing (II.I3; credit; holistic). About +15.** The answer says signing was ‘an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee’ but never says what the act cost AMPL. On 27 February AMPL advanced with no stated term; on 8 April it bound itself to leave $1,150,000 with Grace for ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’. That is a forbearance, the very example Australian Woollen Mills gives (CB14 99 to 100: ‘cases in which there is forbearance by a creditor in return …’). Without it, ‘likely’ rests on sequence alone.

**M11. Trident: use the set judges (R8 risk; residual).** The reading guide sets Trident ‘(Mason CJ and Wilson J only)’. The answer cites Deane J three times (fn 14, 24, 34). R-Y(1) makes the full judgment a course reading, so this is not deducted on the sheet, but a cold UNSW marker reading the guide may write ‘not part of the set readings’. Mason CJ and Wilson J at 115 state both limbs and name ‘an agency relationship’ as a route (CB14 345, ‘in the absence of a trust, an agency relationship or an enforceable agreement’). Zero body words.

**M12. Routes around privity in one line (I.F3; Good to Excellent, 0.4). About +15.** Only agency is tried. AMPL, the contracting party, is already enforcing its own loan; nothing suggests a trust for Rocky or a representation by Grace on which he relied (Mason CJ and Wilson J at 115 on the trust route).

**M13. I.F2: the second limb and the 12 months cross-reference (I.F2; VG drops). About +14.** Part I states only the party limb (‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’); the consideration limb (Trident 115: ‘a stranger to the consideration cannot maintain an action at law upon it’) is used only in Part II. Rocky also gave Grace nothing for her promises to AMPL. And the 5 March demand arguably assumed the 27 February start (SHEET I.F2 core (5)).

**M14. I.C: the Loan Agreement’s consideration (I.C core (2)). About +15.** Grace’s promises to AMPL were likely given for AMPL’s promise of the ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’; this is also what makes Grace’s promises AMPL’s, not Rocky’s.

**M15. Empirnall’s fit (II.I2; credibility).** McHugh JA’s criterion is an offeree who ‘takes the benefit of [goods or services]’ (535). Rocky took no performance; he received a conditional promise that was the price of his own offer. A clause conceding the analogy is strained would make the ‘arguably’ honest (SHEET Part 9 item 33). About +10.

**M16. Gibson’s second paragraph (I.A core (4)).** The closest feature of Gibson is not ‘may be prepared to sell’ but the mortgage paragraph, whose indicative mood ‘might have been understood … as indicating a firm offer’ only if the disclaimer ‘had been omitted’ (298). ‘I will lend’ is indicative; ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ is the disclaimer’s analogue. About +18; lowest priority.

**M17. Wigan’s hedge.** ‘the rule bites on a promise ‘made to the promisee under that contract’’ turns Mason J’s ‘at least when’ into ‘only when’. The answer’s real point is that no prior duty existed at all, which needs no narrowing of the rule. Write ‘the rule applies at least to a promise ‘made to the promisee under that contract’, and none then existed’ (+1).

Not met or newly broken: K2 (Crossley, official-only, rightly left); K12 adopted as ‘who alone would sue’, which now contradicts B1’s new paragraph (CD4); K6’s replacement (Deane J) brings its own error (CD2); the Winn v Bull passage was replaced by a truncated class 3 (CD5); fn 20 and fn 31 short titles moved after the tail (CD7); the B1 paragraph added a D4 fact and two verdict-first colons (CD1, CD3); B11’s ‘a request’ removed the answer’s only ‘invitation to treat’ (CD6).

## 3. MARGIN COMMENTS (UNSW marker’s style)

**I, para 1 (offer).** Good close reading of ‘I will lend’ against ‘may be prepared to sell’, and the qualifier is carried forward. Name the category: the 5 February call was an invitation to treat. ‘its other points promise nothing’: further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive; quote the deciding words (‘Potential’; ‘wait and see’). The second sentence runs to 62 words; break it. Consider the second paragraph of the Council’s letter, the closer analogy.

**I, para 2 (acceptance, consideration).** Well done: ‘Confirmed’ answered ‘confirm agreement’ and added nothing; say ‘so no counter-offer’. Australian Woollen Mills was speaking of a promise for an act; acceptable, but Beaton 168 states the price for a promise.

**I, para 3 (intention).** Name the doctrine in full: intention to create legal relations. You place the onus on Grace ‘who alone would sue’, but two paragraphs later Rocky sues on the same email; be consistent. Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied: the third class in Masters concerns terms ‘to be introduced into the formal document’ and the email contemplates none; the Court’s words at 363 (Winn v Bull) fit this qualifier. Godecke is put fairly and met. Gibbs J said ‘Perhaps’; keep the hedge. Further information with its direction: good.

**I, para 4 (certainty).** The strongest paragraph: Placer’s criterion, Meehan named as the similar case, distinguished on Gibbs CJ’s own limit, and the honesty fetter put and met. ‘which honesty cannot supply’ needs Mason J’s ‘left the court at large’ (587). Consider Kitto J’s reasonable-standard point for Grace.

**I, para 5 (Rocky’s claim; privity).** Good to test Rocky’s own best claim. ‘This fails:’ and ‘Nor did AMPL lend as his agent:’: do not state the conclusion before the analysis. ‘on terms first fixed on 8 April’: your statement of the facts is incorrect; the problem says only that the terms were ‘recorded’. Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition: Deane J includes an ‘undisclosed principal’, for whom an agent always contracts in its own name. Answer ‘Rocky asked’ on whether AMPL purported to act for him. The Coulls reasoning and the treatment of Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ are excellent.

**I, para 6 (conclusion).** Clear, and reimbursement is named. ‘no contractual claim against Grace’ overstates: a ‘minimal’ profit would still trigger his priority repayment under the Development Agreement.

**II, para 1 (offer, acceptance).** Correct; Lord Greene MR’s analogy is properly disclosed. Name the bilateral contract. ‘a document he never signed’: the problem says it was ‘signed by Grace and AMPL’; say that rather than asserting a fact about Rocky.

**II, para 2 (who promised).** Sensible weighing of ‘you’ against control, office and loan. State the test: authority, and whether Pierre purported to act for AMPL or for himself. ‘would settle this’: identify the further information and how it would change your conclusion. ‘what follows runs against him’ is unclear: what follows?

**II, para 3 (existing legal duty rule).** Very good: the rule is named, its premise applied to the 27 February facts, the ‘more than’ limb found and the Pao On third-party point put. Keep Mason J’s ‘at least when’.

**II, para 4 (intention).** Good: Ermogenous on presumptions and onus, and the letter of comfort point put for Rocky and met by the price and Rogers CJ’s ‘no relevant difference’. Answer with specificity to individual Ps: does the finding hold if Pierre promised personally?

**II, para 5 (certainty).** Sound. ‘contains no words of effort’ is the right reading of ‘ensure’. Address whether AMPL’s conditional $10,000 promise is illusory.

**II, para 6 (privity of the $10,000).** Correct, but do not open with the conclusion. Give the reason why ‘the clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause.

**II, para 7 (the guarantee clause).** Careful: the proven ‘provided by Rocky’ is now used properly, the burden aspect is stated and Empirnall is applied with ‘attended’ marked ‘arguably’. Further analysis is required: you put both sides and stop. Which is the better view, and what fact would change it?

**II, para 8 (AMPL’s consideration).** Accurate on Roscorla and all three Pao On conditions, with the timing contest. Say what AMPL gave by signing (a 12-month term on money already advanced).

**II, para 9 (the 12 months).** Very good: the excluded conduct is named, the ‘recorded’ argument is turned with the 4% rate, and the lean carries its reason and its further information with direction.

**II, para 10 (March instalment).** Good: the bad news is drawn and hedged correctly.

**II, para 11 (condition).** Correct classification, and the commercial reading and the duty to co-operate are both put and met. Name the duty to co-operate; give the classification its reason; state the verdict on his own payment.

**II, para 12 (bottom line).** Exposure precisely stated on both readings of the 12 months, as required. Advise the client on the consequence, including the bad news: paying early is not required and would likely forfeit the $10,000. Distinguish AMPL and Pierre.

**Global.** Accurate, well sourced, both sides argued: this reads as a lawyer working the problem, not a checklist. But the sentences are too long for clarity (mean 32 words; eleven over 45). Quotations are stitched into nearly every clause (83 spans), which at points reads as a mosaic (‘ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’’). Use the course’s names for the doctrines you apply.

## 4. MARKS

### Holistic mark: 83 / 100 (Distinction, high)
Reasons. This is, on substance, a better script than the previous version. Almost every argument the two earlier markers asked for is now present: Rocky’s own claim on the email, privity of the $10,000, the letter of comfort, Pao On 632, the duty to co-operate, the March instalment and the excluded conduct. The certainty paragraph (Placer, Meehan on Gibbs CJ’s limit, honesty put and met) and the existing legal duty paragraph are High Distinction work. Every quotation is verbatim and every judge is right.

It stops short of 85 for five reasons. (1) The two authorities doing decisive work in Part I are used for more than they decide: Masters class 3 is cut before its formal-document premise (CD5), and Deane J’s sentence includes the undisclosed principal that defeats the stated reason (CD2). (2) Part I states as fact what Part II rightly calls unknown (CD1), and puts the onus on Grace while letting Rocky sue (CD4). (3) The guarantee-assent paragraph, the one on which the $1,150,000 turns, ends without a view (CD8). (4) The course’s names for six doctrines are absent (CD6). (5) The prose is dense: a mean sentence of 32 words is far outside both his own range and what a marker reads comfortably.

Against the task as actually set (1,500 words), the script is 100 words over; a real UNSW marker would apply the penalty, and I would not award above 78 on submission in this form.

Sensitivity: if a marker counts only the two clearest D5 instances and treats ‘bilateral’ and ‘preliminary agreement’ as not required, the mark is 73 to 74. Fixing CD1 to CD9 alone, at about +38 words, would take the rubric mark to about 84; adding M1, M6, M7 and M8 to about 88.

### Is this the objectively best answer within 1,600 words?
No. What would make it so, in order:
1. The zero-cost fixes: CD1 (‘recorded’), CD3 (facts before verdicts), CD4 (onus on the party alleging), CD7 (footnote forms).
2. Restore Winn v Bull at Masters 363 as the decisive passage for a qualifier that mentions no formal contract (CD5).
3. Replace ‘AMPL contracted in its own name’ with the purporting facts, meeting ‘Rocky asked’ (CD2), and use the set judges in Trident (M11).
4. Name the six doctrines in the course’s words (CD6; +17).
5. Give II.I2 a lean with its further information (CD8), and II.F2 its test and the direction of its further information (CD9).
6. State the client’s legal position on paying (M1), the Development Agreement’s contingent priority right (M2), and the Pierre alternative in the bottom line (M7).
7. Fund it by breaking the 45-plus-word sentences into his 20 to 25-word sentences and cutting quotation fragments that the paraphrase already carries. That also brings the voice measures back into range.
8. To submit, cut to 1,500. The surest cuts are the 62-word opening of the email analysis, the Banque Brussels sentence, and the duplicated condition reasoning in the bottom line.

## 1. Certain defects (proved at source)

**D1. Footnote 34 is mis-pinned (certain); the words it supports are not in the readings.**
Answer: "only the parties to a contract are bound by it,[^34] so AMPL must show assent." fn 34: "Ibid (Deane J)." The immediately preceding fn 33 is "Trident (n 14) 115 (Mason CJ and Wilson J)", so 'Ibid' imports page 115.
Source: page 115 lies inside the joint judgment of Mason CJ and Wilson J, which runs from "[113]" (CB14_ch11, cb p 343, "MASON CJ AND WILSON J: [113] Although the principle…") to "[124]" (cb p 348). Deane J's extract begins "[11.70] DEANE J: [143] Circumstances can undoubtedly arise…" (cb p 354). Deane J does not speak at 115. Further, the paraphrased words ('only the parties to a contract are bound by it') appear nowhere in the casebook's Deane J extract (pp 354-357; grep of CB14.txt for "bound by, and entitled to enforce" returns nothing); the RUBRIC R-Y(2) quotation comes from the full official judgment, which is not among the readings supplied here, so the pin cannot be proved from the readings. The only casebook statement of the burden limb is Brennan J (dissenting) at 129, quoting Kitto J in Wilson: "the only persons entitled to the benefits or bound by the obligations of a contract are the parties to it" (cb p 350), a dissent and outside the 'Mason CJ and Wilson J only' set range.
Fix (0 words): fn 34 → "Trident (n 14) (Deane J)." (R-Y(1): judge named, no pin), and the tracer should confirm the words against the official text before release.

**D2. Footnote 4 uses Australian Woollen Mills for what it did not decide (a bilateral promise-for-promise).**
Answer: "Grace's implied promise to repay with interest would stand in 'the relation of a quid pro quo' to Rocky's promise to lend.[^4]"
Source: the Court (Dixon CJ, Williams, Webb, Fullagar and Kitto JJ) speaks of "that type which is commonly said to be constituted by an offer of a promise for an act, the offer being accepted by the doing of the act", and the quid pro quo sentence opens "In cases of this class it is necessary…" and links "the statement or announcement" to "the act which is put forward as the executed consideration" (CB14_ch04, cb pp 98-99, AWM 456-7). The Court found no contract. Both earlier hostile markers flagged this exact use (Marker A K3; Marker B C2). The readings contain the exact bilateral statement: Kirby P, Beaton 168: "consideration must be satisfied in the form of a price in return for the promisor's promise or a quid pro quo. The price can be in the form of an act, forbearance or promise." (cb p 102; Kirby P in the majority on the result, appeal dismissed; the definition is uncontested by McHugh JA, who uses Pollock's same words at 182.)
Fix (−4 words): "Grace's implied promise to repay with interest would be 'a price in return for' Rocky's promise to lend.[^4]" fn 4 → "Beaton v McDivitt (1987) 13 NSWLR 162, 168 (Kirby P) ('Beaton')." AWM's first full citation moves to fn 40 (where its promise-for-an-act use is apt); fn 45 becomes "Beaton (n 4) 185 (McHugh JA dissenting), citing …".

**D3. The 12-months paragraph rests on two skip-range passages and does not meet a set reading that points the other way.**
Answer: "Post-contractual conduct, such as Grace's interest payments from 8 April 2024 and his 'I have until 8 April 2025', cannot construe the term,[^41] but, the term being arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing 'the genesis of the transaction' are admissible.[^42]"
Status (certain): Brambles 164 (Heydon JA, the third principle, cb p 73) lies in the 1B skip range [3.290]-[3.300] (pp 73-76); Brambles 191 (Ipp AJA, cb p 82) lies in the 1B skip range [3.330]-[3.360] "(the first part of Ipp JA's judgment; pp82-84)" (ReadingGuide.txt). Both are casebook text and correct, but neither is set reading.
Set reading against: Mayo J, Todd v Nicol (CB14_ch05, cb p 145, between report markers [74] and [77]): "It is an accepted principle that regard may be had to the subsequent conduct of, and communications between, parties for the purpose of discovering whether the intention to be attributed to them was to make a binding arrangement or otherwise, and if the former what the parties understood the terms to be … The acts of parties, where meaning is in doubt, may be used to remove uncertainty, or to explain, but not to contradict, the language used." (single judge, SA Supreme Court, 1957; holding on intention.) This helps Rocky (Grace's payments from 8 April and his 'I have until 8 April 2025' point to an 8 April start, which makes AMPL's call premature), and the answer never puts it. The decisive answer is in the readings: Heydon JA's own hedge at 164 that the High Court position "is unclear: hence unless it is demonstrated that the later decisions … against admissibility … are clearly wrong or they are overruled, they should be followed in New South Wales" (cb pp 73-74); the problem is set in New South Wales.
Fix (+6 words): "Grace's interest payments from 8 April 2024 and his 'I have until 8 April 2025' might 'explain' the term,[^T] but in New South Wales post-contractual conduct cannot construe it;[^41] however, the term being arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing 'the genesis of the transaction' are admissible.[^42]" New fn: "Todd v Nicol [1957] SASR 72, 7x (Mayo J) ('Todd')." Pin caution: the passage sits between the printed markers [74] and [77] with no [75]/[76] shown; the tracer must fix the page from the student's extract before use. No set-reading substitute exists for 'genesis' (191) — keep it, knowing its status.

**D4. A planted fact is never used: "Throughout this period Rocky would check in consistently with Grace via email" (narrator).** It is the best fact AMPL has, with Rocky's 5 March demand "requiring repayment of the principal amount under the Loan Agreement with AMPL", on whether Rocky assented to the guarantee clause, and subsequent conduct is admissible on whether a binding arrangement was intended (Todd, above; also Brambles 164, second principle, skip range: "post-contractual conduct is admissible on the question of whether a contract was formed"). Fix: see A2 in §5.

## 2. Issue-by-issue (the order in MARKERS_PROMPT ROLE 2)

For each: the answer's use; the best passage for each side (verbatim, cb page, report pin, speaker, status); facts set beside ours; verdict; replacement and word cost.

### 2.1 The 5 February call
Answer: "Grace's 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer, so it was not itself one,[^1] and Rocky declined." fn 1 Gibson 298 (Lord Diplock).
Best for 'not an offer': Bowen LJ, Carlill 268 (cb p 46; CA, unanimous in result): "Such advertisements are offers to negotiate – offers to receive offers – offers to chaffer". Grace "proposed that Rocky offer Grace a … loan": exactly an 'offer to receive an offer'. Gibson 298 decides that "may be prepared to sell" and an invitation "to make formal application to buy" are not an offer (cb p 42) — the Council invited Gibson to make the offer; analogous, not exact. Facts: Gibson, a seller inviting a buyer's application; ours, a would-be borrower inviting a lender's offer; same structure (the speaker asks the other to make the offer).
Verdict: adequate; Carlill is the tighter fit. Optional replacement (+4): "Grace's 5 February call, proposing that Rocky 'offer' a loan, was an offer 'to receive offers',[^1] not an offer, and Rocky declined." fn 1 → Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co [1893] 1 QB 256, 268 (Bowen LJ). Gibson's full cite then moves to fn 2. ADD IF FUNDED (low).

### 2.2 The 12 February email as offer
Answer: "'I will lend' fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and 'Please confirm agreement' seeks assent, so, unlike 'may be prepared to sell' in Gibson,[^2] the first point is likely an offer".
Best for Rocky (not an offer): Gibson 298 ("may be prepared to sell" fatal; cb p 42) — distinguishable on our words 'I will lend'. Felthouse 876 (Willes J, cb p 70): a later letter "may be treated either as an acceptance then for the first time made by him, or as a memorandum of a bargain complete before" — the 'Confirming discussions' opening raises the same choice; if the morning meeting concluded a bargain, the email is a memorandum and the problem moves to the meeting (helps Grace, not Rocky). ### 2.6 Certainty and illusory promises (12 February)
Answer: "in Placer a promise with no 'identifiable criteria', left 'solely to the discretion' of the promisor, was 'wholly unenforceable'.[^10]" (Taylor and Owen JJ 361); then Meehan 581 (Gibbs CJ), 589 (Mason J, "takes the case out of the principle"), 581 ("only to the fulfilment of a condition"); "whereas Rocky's concerns the content of his own loan, which honesty cannot supply."
Weakness 1 (wrong-fit passage): Taylor and Owen JJ speak of "the amounts or rates to be determined" (cb p 189) — a discretion over quantum. Rocky's amount is fixed; his reserved discretion is whether, on 'conditions', he lends at all. The majority statement that fits is Kitto J, Placer 356 (cb p 188; majority 3-2; the pin is the one Gibbs CJ gives at Meehan 581): "wherever words which by themselves constitute a promise are accompanied by words showing that the promisor is to have a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out that which purports to be the promise, the result is that there is no contract on which an action can be brought at all." 'I will lend' = words which by themselves constitute a promise; 'subject to satisfactory conditions' = words reserving the option. It is also the very principle Mason J's "takes the case out of the principle" refers to (he quotes it at 589-90 via Thorby), so the paragraph becomes one chain.
Weakness 2 (unsupported step): "which honesty cannot supply" has no authority. Gibbs CJ supplies it at 582 (cb p 181): "There is a concluded agreement as to the terms of the contract which, if the condition is satisfied, leaves no discretion in either party as to whether he shall carry them out." Meehan rested on agreed terms; Rocky's unnamed 'conditions' are themselves unagreed terms.
Grace's best counter not met: Kitto J in Thorby, quoted by McHugh JA, Biotech 151 (cb p 164): "an agreement is not void for uncertainty because it leaves one party or group of parties a latitude of choice as to the manner in which agreed stipulations shall be carried into effect" — amount, date, term and rate were agreed. (McHugh JA, Beaton 185). SHEET R7: 'describing the doctrine in the answer’s own words (... ‘the duty ’to do everything necessary’’) is ... one proxy instance'.
- Fix (+2): 'Nor does AMPL breach its duty' to 'Nor does AMPL breach the duty to co-operate,'.

- Course term: CB14_ch05 p 152 heading 'PRELIMINARY AGREEMENTS'; p 133 '[5.05] ... 4. Where parties reach a preliminary agreement, the question may arise whether the parties intend to be bound immediately'; Class 3A slide 22 'What are preliminary agreements? What are the 3 categories and which are binding on the parties?'; Reading Guide 3A 'preliminary agreements'. SHEET R7: the term is required 'where the answer relies on the category'.

**C7. 'Bilateral contract' is not named; the answer writes 'a promise for a promise'.**
- Answer S25: 'Rocky’s reply, ‘I will do that if you also promise’, offered a promise for a promise,[^20] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^21]'

Source cited (fn 20) uses the term: McHugh JA in Integrated Computer Services, quoted by Heydon JA in Brambles 177 (CB14_ch03 p 78): 'In classical theory, the typical contract is a bilateral one and consists of an exchange of promises by means of an offer and its acceptance'. **C8. The exception to the existing legal duty rule for promises to third parties is applied but not named.**

SHEET R7 lists 'promises to third parties' among the required names.

**C9. The Pao On quotation is cut so that its subject changes.**

The Board's subject is the promise to perform or the performance; the quoted words, read as a sentence, make the obligation itself the consideration. Status: the Board's holding on its second question (the extrinsic evidence showed 'the real consideration for [632] the indemnity was the promise to perform, or the performance of, the plaintiffs pre-existing contractual obligations to Fu Chip', p 125 to 126). The answer's use (Rocky's duty owed to AMPL, his new promise made to Pierre) puts our parties in the Board's positions correctly.
