## 7. Residual risks (recorded, not changed)

- 'likely an offer' beside 'likely left to a new agreement'. A purist says an offer requires willingness to be bound. The answer sequences offer and acceptance first and intention second, carries the qualifier forward ('‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ included'), and the course itself treats offer and acceptance as 'an aid to analysis'. Acceptable.
- The commencement conclusion (8 April) rests on rebuttal. No reading gives a default rule, so the hedge is the right form.
- Duty to co-operate (C21): Rocky's sharper counter is unstated. It is answered by 'No term requires him to pay early'.
- Trident: the reading guide sets 'Mason CJ and Wilson J only'. The answer also uses Deane J and Brennan J (dissenting), which R-Y permits.

---

## 8. Holistic mark (Step 4)

**86/100 as submitted; about 88 with the section 5 package.**

Reasons: every issue that changes Rocky's position is identified and decided in course terms with correct, well-placed authority. Both sides are put almost everywhere, the exposure is exact, and nothing is misattributed. Points are lost for one argument from the cited page left unanswered (B), one-sided use of later conduct (A), a small internal tension (C), two unused planted facts (E, F), and density: several steps are shown in a phrase rather than reasoned. At 1,600 words the last of these is largely the price of completeness, which is why 90 is out of reach for me without a lower issue count, and a lower issue count is ruled out by his instruction never to drop an argument.

**Possible defects (most significant first)**

- P1. The text that ‘Construction is objective’ and the ‘in New South Wales’ limb rest on is at *Brambles* 164 (Heydon JA). The pin is right, but the text sits on casebook p 74. That page is inside the reading guide's skip range ([3.290] to [3.300], pp 73 to 76) and is missing from the student's supplied W1L2 extract, which runs pp 72, 73, then 76. In-range alternatives are given in 5.4.
- P2. ‘[T]he genesis of the transaction’ (*Brambles* 191, Ipp AJA) is on p 82, inside the guide's ‘Skip … the first part of Ipp JA's judgment; pp82-84’. Heydon JA at 163 (p 73, in range and in the extract) says the same thing: ‘casts light on the genesis of the contract’. Ipp AJA adopted his reasons on the July 1990 contract, and Mason P agreed with Ipp AJA. The swap saves 1 word (5.4).
- P3. The *Pao On* holding at 632 (the third-party duty) comes from the casebook's full extract, whose pages appear to fall in the 2B skip range. That inference is from the 2-page offset: Wigan is at [4.350] p 131 in the student's edition and at p 129 in CB14. The holding is otherwise carried only by slide 2B (‘promises to third parties (Pao On v Lau Yiu Long)’). R-Z(2) makes 632 the citation, so this is a status note, not a fault.
- P4. Fn 38 (‘AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself’) pins *Trident* 115. The on-point passage is 115 to 116 (Mason CJ and Wilson J): ‘C cannot compel A to carry out his promise, because, though a party to the contract, C is a stranger to the consideration’. That passage is slide 4A's ‘multi-party agreement where privity is satisfied but one party has not given consideration’. Change the pin to 115–16 (0 words).
- P5. Hedges dropped. In *Banque Brussels* 525, Rogers CJ called the third-paragraph point ‘far more thorny’ before holding it promissory, and he sat at first instance. In *Trident* 115 the plurality says ‘This court has hitherto accepted’ before reforming the rule for insurance. Neither omission misstates the law. A harsh marker could still note it.
- P6. *Roscorla* (fn 39) gives the pinpoint for the nominate report only (3 QB 234, 237). AGLC practice for English Reports parallels is to pin both. The ER page cannot be verified from the readings because the casebook carries only QB markers. This is settled only by the official report.
- P7. Fact nuance. ‘The Development Agreement repays him first only ‘if the Project made a profit’, none yet shown’ is accurate as far as it goes. But the narrator says the parties ‘realised that the profit from the Project would be minimal’, which implies a profit that would trigger Rocky's priority. ‘[N]one yet shown’ is not wrong, but it reads as though there will be no profit.
- P8. ‘AMPL named Rocky guarantor’ is a derived actor. The problem says only that ‘[t]he Loan Agreement also included a clause’ and that ‘the clause was included … before it was signed by Grace and AMPL’. Write ‘the Loan Agreement named Rocky guarantor’ (plus 1 word).
- P9. ‘[S]o it was no counter-offer’ applies the counter-offer rule with no authority attached. R-Z requires a case for every proposition. Brambles 176 (Heydon JA: ‘the rejection of the offer by a counter-offer’) is available.
- P10. The .docx sectPr has no pgSz or pgMar, so Word applies its own defaults (normally US Letter and 1-inch margins). Set A4 and explicit margins in reference.docx. The instructions ask for margins for comments.
- P11. The .docx and ANSWER.md match exactly: 20 paragraphs, 46 footnotes, identical text. The stated count is correct: the body is 1,596 words and the line says 1,599.

**Net word effect of the recommended fixes:** C1 Option A (minus 2), C4 (minus 1) and P2 (minus 1) take the body to 1,592 and the count line to ‘Word count: 1,595’. That frees 5 words for P8 (plus 1) and, if wanted, the clarity fix in 6.2.

- **Option B (keeps both elements, from a case; minus 1 word).** ‘Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if, with its authority, he contracted ‘as agent’ for it, not solely for himself.[^25]’ Footnote: `Trident (n 15) 145 (Deane J); Port Jackson Stevedoring Pty Ltd v Salmond & Spraggon (Aust) Pty Ltd (1978) 139 CLR 231, 240 (Barwick CJ dissenting).` Barwick CJ at 240 (cb 334) states Lord Reid's requisites: ‘(2) the carrier by the bill contracted for the stevedore's protection as well as for his own, (3) the authority of the carrier to act for the stevedore … whether antecedently or by ratification’. ### 6.2 Voice and mechanics

- **No dashes, double quotation marks or contractions** (all apostrophes are possessives). No meta language and no invented abbreviations. Longest sentence: 45 words (‘Otherwise its advance is past consideration …’), at the limit. Next longest: 42, 42, 41.
- **One-clause sentences** (Yusuf ‘despises’ them): ‘Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent.’ (it opens a paragraph); ‘Naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous.’; ‘Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace.’; ‘Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.’ Each can be joined to its neighbour with a semicolon at no word cost. Examples: ‘Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent;[^3] ‘Confirmed’ arguably …’; ‘… are admissible;[^43] naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous.’
- **Elliptical clause (clarity, possible zeugma):** in ‘…‘have dealt only with major matters’; though no formal document was contemplated, so did the email’, ‘so did the email’ borrows ‘have dealt’ from ‘parties’. Clearer: ‘…; though no formal document was contemplated, the email likewise dealt only with major matters.’ (plus 4 words, affordable after 5.1A, 5.4 and 5.5).
- **Ambiguous list:** ‘Rocky could say his 12 February email records discussions, its other points, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promising nothing.’ This can be read as three items. Clearer: ‘… merely records discussions, and that its other points, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing.’ (plus 3 words).
- **No fragments after semicolons** (every post-semicolon segment has a finite main verb).

## 1. Margin comments, paragraph by paragraph (in his marker's style)

P1 (offer). 'Good issue framing from the client's position. Grace's call is classified correctly, but quote the deciding words ("proposed that Rocky offer") rather than paraphrase them. Gibson is distinguished on "may be prepared to sell"; however, Lord Diplock's second-paragraph point (the indicative paragraph that "might have been understood ... as indicating a firm offer" only absent its disclaimer: Gibson 298) is the passage that resembles this email and is not met. "Rocky could say his 12 February email records discussions, its other points, ... promising nothing": the subject of "promising nothing" is unclear.'

P2 (acceptance, consideration). 'Acceptance is well done: criterion, both readings of "Confirmed", counter-offer excluded, qualifier carried. Consideration is one sentence tacked onto acceptance; give it its own step. Identify the price on both sides: what did AMPL give for Grace's Loan Agreement promises?'

P3 (intention). 'Excellent use of Winn v Bull in Jessel MR's own condition, the onus, and the status of "project developers". The textual point (no external event, unlike bullet 2) is exactly the analysis required. "though no formal document was contemplated, so did the email" is elliptical, and "contemplated" states more than the email shows: write "mentions no formal document".'

P4 (certainty). 'Meehan is distinguished on Gibbs CJ's own limit, and the honesty fetter is put and met: well done. But you answer Gibbs J's "Perhaps" without stating the dictum it qualifies (that terms left "to be settled by one of the parties" would give "no binding contract": Godecke 646 to 647). Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied: Gibbs J attributes "the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness" to the Court of Appeal in Sweet & Maxwell; he does not say that his "Perhaps" assumes it. Certainty alone is arguable at most; your "likely" rides on D.'

P5 (agency and privity v Grace). 'Strong: both limbs of the rule, the instrument test, the joint promisee, and Grace's line right in result but wrong in reason. Two problems. (1) Agency is decided without stating its criterion; Deane J at 145 gives the route ("contracts as agent"), not what must be shown. (2) "differed in ... rate" sits badly with your later point that nothing shows the 4% "predated 8 April"; and "lender" assumes the answer to the agency question. Quote the deciding fact for party status: "AMPL and Grace entered into a written loan agreement". "faces privity" is loose.'

P6 (Part I close). 'Good: the Development Agreement and the reimbursement claim are disposed of in substantive terms.'

P7 and P8 (Part II, offer and acceptance). 'Clear. Pierre's expectation, the bilateral offer, acceptance on "agreed", and AMPL's execution argument met from Masters 362. Good.'

P9 (who promised). 'Answer with specificity to individual Ps: you do, and the further information has its direction. State consent as its own question ("owned and controlled") rather than folding it into a list. The footnote does not state the two elements your sentence attributes to it.'

P10 (existing legal duty rule). 'Very good: the rule is named with Mason J's hedge, Sundell is met, the request is tied to 27 February, the "more than" limb is drawn, and the third-party exception is applied if Pierre promised. However, your closing "unless the clause preceded the bargain" contradicts the reason you have just given ("bound no one before signing"). Further analysis is required: which fact would actually give Rocky a prior duty?'

P11 (intention, 8 April). 'Good use of Rogers CJ's "practice to ensure" passage. But meet the difference that cuts against Rocky: in Banque Brussels the comfort conditioned the facility, whereas AMPL had already advanced. Answer with specificity to individual Ps: if Pierre promised personally, the cousin relationship bears on the promisor itself; say what still carries the finding.'

P12 (certainty, 8 April). 'Good, including the promise of result against a promise of effort.'

P13 (privity, $10,000). 'Correct. But give the reason why "the clause" most naturally means the guarantee clause. Do not begin a sentence with a quotation.'

P14 (does the clause bind Rocky). 'The burden aspect, silence, and McHugh JA's criterion with the benefit named: good. You put AMPL's "later invoked the Loan Agreement" but never answer it; and "nothing shows a reasonable opportunity to reject" is asserted against your own "attended" fact. Further information with its direction is well placed.'

P15 (AMPL's consideration). 'Very good: past consideration is named, Pao On is run on its timing, and the fallback is put and met. "may lack consideration" is not a conclusion: lean.'

P16 (the 12 months). 'Method, ambiguity decided with reasons, both readings, a lean and further information: excellent analysis. "Construction is objective" needs authority.'

P17 (condition). 'Excellent: condition precedent with its reason, the commercial reading put and met, and the duty to co-operate named and met on its own terms.'

P18 (advice). 'Precise exposure, both readings, the bad news and the forfeiture point. But "if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable" overlooks your own P15: on the Pierre alternative the clause may lack consideration.'

## 4. Certain defects and contestable points

Certain:
1. P10: 'Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain' contradicts 'the clause ... bound no one before signing'. Rocky's promise necessarily preceded signing ('Pierre agreed and the clause was included ... before it was signed').
2. P5 against P16: 'the advance differed in amount, date, lender and rate' against '‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April'. Also, 'lender' assumes the answer to the agency question.
3. fn 25 (and the I.F1 criterion): Trident 145 (Deane J) states only 'If the promisee contracts as agent for a disclosed or undisclosed principal, the principal will ordinarily himself be, for the purposes of the requirement of privity, a party to the contract'. It does not state consent or purporting, which the sentence attributes to it. The elements are the editors' agency note (14th ed [11.32]; the student's edition [11.70] per the sheet) or Lord Reid's requisites (2) and (3) at Port Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ, whom the casebook heading marks 'dissenting').
4. P16: 'Construction is objective' has no authority.
5. P13: a sentence begins with a quotation, and 'most naturally' is given no reason.
6. fn 12: one marker carries two sources for two propositions.
7. P14: AMPL's 'later invoked the Loan Agreement' is put and never met.
8. P18: the clause liability is stated without P15's consideration caveat.
9. P15: 'may lack consideration' has no lean.

Contestable (with what would settle each):
- 'Gibbs J’s obiter ‘[p]erhaps’ ... likewise assumed ‘the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness’'. At Godecke 647 the words describe what the Court of Appeal in Sweet & Maxwell relied on, given in rejecting Bray CJ's extension. Inferring that Gibbs J's exception depends on reasonableness is defensible but is not his statement. Saying 'resting on Sweet & Maxwell, where the parties had imported ...' would settle it.
- 'AMPL named Rocky guarantor'. The problem says only that the Loan Agreement 'included a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment'. Who drafted it is not stated, and the sheet lists 'AMPL drafted the Loan Agreement' as a D4 example. 'AMPL’s agreement named Rocky guarantor' would settle it.
- Trident beyond Mason CJ and Wilson J (fn 15, 25 and 35). The Reading Guide limits Trident to 'Mason CJ and Wilson J only'. R-Y(1) makes the full judgment a course reading, so I do not deduct, but a real cold marker reading the guide might query Deane J and Brennan J (dissenting).
- Brambles 191 (Ipp AJA) and Heydon JA 163 to 164 sit in Reading Guide skip ranges. R-F: never deducted.

## 5. Holistic mark

**84 / 100.** As a senior contracts lecturer would read it, this is a genuinely high-level answer. It identifies every live issue. It reads the problem's words closely ('recorded' governing the rate; 'conditions' against the Eastwood 'subject to success'; 'no words of effort'). It uses every authority for what it decided, with statuses kept, and ends with precise exposure advice. It does not reach 90 for three reasons:
- a handful of logic slips a careful marker will catch (the II.C2 'unless', the 'rate' inconsistency, the uncaveated clause liability);
- density that sometimes tips into note-like compression;
- two opponent points left at half strength (the Banque Brussels timing difference; AMPL's 'later invoked' argument), with Gibbs J's core dictum missing.

**Does it reach 90? No.** It scores 83 on SHEET_v12 and 84 holistically.

## 1. Holistic mark first: senior contracts academic, rubric set aside

**Mark: 85/100. A high Distinction, not in the 90s.**

This is a serious, legally literate advice. It reads the facts closely and is well organised by client claim. The doctrinal choices are almost all right:
- Gibson is distinguished on its words.
- Masters is used through Jessel MR's Winn v Bull passage for a qualifier that mentions no formal contract, and the analogy is disclosed.
- Meehan is distinguished on Gibbs CJ's own limit, not on its result, and the honesty fetter is put and met.
- The existing legal duty rule is run on Mason J's premises, with Sundell for AMPL and the Pao On third-party point if Pierre promised.
- Coulls is used correctly on signature, and Grace's planted line is answered with the correct "right result, wrong reason".
- Pao On's three conditions are run on the facts, and the timing is identified as the contest.
- The Brambles construction method is stated in NSW terms.
- Rocky's exposure is stated in dollars and dates.

Few undergraduate answers reach this level of authority control.

**Why it is not 90 or above on a hard reading:**
1. **Density over explanation.** Several steps are asserted in compressed or elliptical prose, and a reader has to reconstruct the logic:
   - "though no formal document was contemplated, so did the email"
   - "Grace's promises were made to AMPL, not Rocky, even as joint promisee"
   - "taking the $10,000 promise knowing its terms"

   The many two-to-four-word quotations (244 quoted words in 69 sentences) sometimes read as quote-stitching rather than analysis.
2. **One internal contradiction in the consideration paragraph** (section 3, defect C1). The clause "bound no one before signing", yet the verdict turns on whether "the clause preceded the bargain".
3. **Some leans are reasoned only negatively.** The 12 months is the main example: AMPL's reasons are neutralised, but no positive reason is given for 8 April.
4. **Some authorities are stretched slightly:**
   - Gibbs J's "Perhaps" is said to have "likewise assumed" the reasonableness standard.
   - Mason J's "at least when" is turned into a limit on the rule.
   - Deane J's bare agency sentence is cited for a two-element test.
5. **Missed or thin points a contracts academic expects:**
   - the Banque Brussels timing difference (the facility there was conditioned on the letter; here AMPL had already advanced);
   - the price of Grace's promises in the Loan Agreement;
   - a reason for reading "the clause" as the guarantee clause;
   - Lord Greene MR's "when and how they contemplate becoming bound" for AMPL's "nothing until signing" point.
6. **Length.** Against the Instructions it is 99 words over. A UNSW marker applying the Instructions would penalise that whatever the quality (section 5).

## 2. Margin comments, paragraph by paragraph (in his UNSW marker's style)

**P1 (offer; 100 words).** The 5 February call is classified on its deciding effect and Gibson is distinguished on "may be prepared to sell": good. *Grace's best analogy is missing.* Gibson's second paragraph was indicative in mood but read as no "firm offer" only because of its disclaimer (Gibson 298: "If the final sentence had been omitted … might have been understood … as indicating a firm offer"). "Subject to satisfactory conditions" is the email's analogue of that disclaimer. "Rocky could say … promising nothing" bundles the bullets into Rocky's argument; the result for the bullets is only implied by "the first point is likely an offer". **Marker comment:** "Distinguish Gibson fully: meet the paragraph that resembles the email."

**P2 (acceptance and consideration; 61 words).** The acceptance sentence is excellent: the criterion, the counter put ("vouched only for the email's accuracy"), and "no counter-offer". The consideration sentence is folded into the acceptance paragraph (R-AC(2): each element in its own paragraph). The Loan Agreement's price, AMPL's 12 months at 4% for Grace's promises, is never identified, here or in P5. **Marker comment:** "Identify the price on both sides."

**P3 (intention; 164 words).** The strongest paragraph in Part I:
- the objective test and the onus;
- the status of the parties as "project developers";
- Winn v Bull in Jessel MR's own condition;
- both classes with the analogy disclosed;
- "conditions" read against "subject to success of Hail Mary Project", which is close textual analysis;
- an "On balance … likely" verdict, with further information that carries its direction.

One clarity lapse: "though no formal document was contemplated, so did the email". The subject shifts from "parties" to "the email", and the clause reads as note form.

**P4 (certainty; 130 words).** The criterion is right (Pace 151) and Meehan is distinguished on Gibbs CJ's limit (581–2), the correct method. The honesty fetter is met ("which neither standard can supply") and "no range confines" answers Pace's "specified parameters". *Two contestable steps:*
- "Gibbs J's obiter '[p]erhaps' … likewise assumed 'the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness'". At 647 Gibbs J says that Sweet & Maxwell "placed considerable reliance" on that standard, and he disagrees with Bray CJ's extension. He does not say his own "Perhaps" assumed it. Write "as his reliance on Sweet & Maxwell suggests" or "arguably".
- The verdict "likely bound neither party" is one tier stronger than certainty supports on its own; intention decided it.

**Marker comment:** "Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied."

**P5 (Rocky through AMPL's advance; privity; 153 words).** "Rocky asked" is met with the guarantee clause, which is good reasoning. *The criterion is not stated:* "did not contract 'as agent' for him" names the category, not its test, which is purporting to act for the principal and not solely for itself. The footnote, Trident 145 (Deane J), states only the bare route. The privity limbs (Trident 115), "the written instrument itself" (Coulls 487) and the Grace's-line answer (Empirnall 536; Coulls 487) are all correct and pinned. "Even as joint promisee" is note form: say that nothing makes Grace's promise one to Rocky.

**P6 (Part I conclusion; 34 words).** Claim C3 and the Development Agreement are disposed of in substantive terms. "None yet shown" is defensible, but "minimal" is still a profit, and one clause on that would show the point was seen (credit only).

**P8 (offer and acceptance on 8 April; 94 words).** The client-goal opening ("Rocky's questions are …") is exactly right. The bilateral contract (Brambles 177) and acceptance on "agreed" (Empirnall 534) are correct. AMPL's "nothing bound before signing" is met through Masters 361–2. This works, but it omits the passage built for this point: Lord Greene MR, through Heydon JA at Brambles 176, "Parties become bound by contract when, and in the manner in which, they intend and contemplate becoming bound."

**P9 (who promised; 72 words).** Both questions are put, consent is answered on control, purporting is contested and "you" is met, with a "likely" verdict and further information that carries its direction. **Citation fault:** consent and "rather than solely for himself" are footnoted to Deane J at 145, who states neither. Port Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ; set out in the casebook at [11.35]) states Lord Reid's requisites (2) and (3). The editors' note at [11.32] states consent and purporting. **Marker comment:** "Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied."

**P10 (existing legal duty rule; 108 words).** This is the right structure: AMPL's best argument through Sundell, Mason J's premises, the "more than" limb, and the Pao On 632 exception if Pierre promised. *Two problems:*
- Mason J's "at least when" marks a floor of the rule's application, not a ceiling. The real answer is that no duty yet existed: "Rocky only 'asked'".
- **Internal contradiction:** "the clause … bound no one before signing", yet "Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain". If the clause bound no one before signing, its order cannot matter unless Rocky had assented to it earlier. Say that.

**Marker comment:** "Further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive."

**P11 (intention; 81 words).** Ermogenous [26] on presumptions is correct, and the Banque Brussels "practice to ensure" comparison is used in the right direction. *Missing:* the difference that cuts against Rocky. In Banque Brussels "the facility was subject to BBL obtaining a suitable letter of comfort" (CB 142, between [521] and [523]), whereas AMPL had already advanced on 27 February. Rogers CJ's own hedge, "far more thorny", is also dropped. Pierre is weighed as a cousin, but the paragraph never says what carries the finding if Pierre promised personally. **Marker comment:** "Answer with specificity to individual Ps."

**P12 (certainty; 57 words).** Correct and economical: Upper Hunter 437 is applied to "ensure"; the promise of result is distinguished from a promise of effort; and AMPL's promise is shown not illusory (Meehan 582).

**P13 (privity of the $10,000; 41 words).** The promisee and the consideration are correct. "[T]he clause most naturally means the guarantee clause" gives no reason; one is needed, such as the definite article pointing back to the only clause named.

**P14 (assent to the guarantee clause; 109 words).** The burden aspect is cited correctly: Brennan J, dissenting, quoting Kitto J at 129, in the right AGLC form. The benefit is named, "attended" serves as the knowledge fact, and further information carries its direction. *Contestable:* "nothing shows 'a reasonable opportunity to reject' the clause". He attended the meeting, so he arguably had the opportunity; the gap is knowledge of the clause's words, which the last clause rightly makes decisive. "Later invoked the Loan Agreement" is AMPL's point and goes unanswered. The demand is described in the problem in the narrator's words, not Rocky's, and in any case it is not assent to the guarantee. "Knowing its terms" has an unclear antecedent.

**P15 (consideration from AMPL; 97 words).** This is the strongest paragraph in Part II:
- the point is conditional on who promised;
- past consideration is named (Roscorla 237);
- all three of Pao On's conditions are stated;
- the first condition is met on "asked";
- the second is the contest, with the timing comparison ("at the time of the main agreement", 629);
- AMPL's fallback is put and met with the pricing point.

**P16 (the 12 months; 136 words).**
- The method is right: objective construction; post-contractual conduct excluded in NSW (Heydon JA 164); the genesis admissible only if the terms are ambiguous (Ipp AJA 191).
- Ambiguity is decided with a reason, and the March instalment is put in the approved form.
- *The lean is negative only:* AMPL's two reasons are neutralised, but no positive reason for 8 April is stated.

**Marker comment:** "Further analysis is required: why 8 April?"

**P17 (the condition; 75 words).**
- The condition precedent is named, with Meehan 582's reason (bound at once).
- The commercial reading is put through Upper Hunter 437 and met with the pricing point.
- *The duty to co-operate* is stated as a verdict before its reason ("Nor does AMPL breach …: its call does not stop …"). The stronger form of the argument is not put: by calling on Rocky and taking his payment, AMPL ends the chance that Grace repays.
- "Its call does not stop Grace repaying" is an inference and should read "nothing suggests …".

**P18 (exposure; 74 words).** Exactly what R-AD requires: $1,150,000; "now" on a 27 February start, otherwise from 8 April 2025; damages if Rocky is bound only orally; and payment likely forfeits the $10,000. **Note:** under the Instructions' 1,500 cap this paragraph would not be read.

## 3. Source verification: every finding, with its status

**Proved against the source (certain under the rubric or against the text):**

**C1. II.C2 internal tension (logic, proved from the answer's own words).**
- Sentence: "and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only 'asked', and the clause, arguably included after Pierre 'agreed', bound no one before signing … Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain."
- Wigan 594 (Mason J, majority reasoning; CB 129) requires "a party to a pre-existing contract". A clause that bound no one creates no pre-existing duty, whatever its order.
- The further-information clause only works if Rocky had assented to the clause before the bargain.
- Fix: "Rocky likely gave consideration unless he had assented to the clause before the bargain, which would favour AMPL" (+4 words).

**C2. Agency criterion cited to a source that does not state it (fn 15, fn 25).**
- Deane J at 145 (CB 355): "If the promisee contracts as agent for a disclosed or undisclosed principal, the principal will ordinarily himself be, for the purposes of the requirement of privity, a party to the contract." This states no consent element and no "not solely for himself".
- The criterion is stated by:
  - the editors' note [11.32] (CB 332–3): "expressly or impliedly consented" and "purporting to act on behalf of the principal and not solely on his or her own behalf";
  - Barwick CJ at Port Jackson 240 (CB 334; dissenting on the result but stating the requisites the Privy Council adopted): "(2) the carrier by the bill contracted for the stevedore's protection as well as for his own, (3) the authority of the carrier to act for the stevedore in this respect whether antecedently or by ratification was made out".
- Grid: Port Jackson 240 or [11.70] is the required authority for I.F1 and II.F2, so both units drop to Very Good, and R8 takes a citation imprecision.

**C3. fn 12 carries two sources (Meehan; Pace) for two propositions under one marker.** Honesty comes from Meehan 581 and 589; "specified parameters" comes from Pace 151. That is one minor R8 non-compliance; split the footnote at "perhaps reasonably,".

**C4. Word limit.** 1,599 stated against the Instructions' "no more than 1,500 words". Certain; consequences in section 5.

**Rubric core items missing (certain under SHEET_v12):**
- I.A: the Gibson second-paragraph similarity, with its direction, is not named.
- I.C: the Loan Agreement's price (AMPL's 12 months at 4% for Grace's promises) is not identified.
- II.B: Brambles 176 (Lord Greene MR) is absent.
- II.D: the Banque Brussels "weaker here" point is not given its reason (AMPL had already advanced), and the Pierre alternative is not re-weighed in a clause.
- II.F1: "most naturally" carries no reason.

**Contestable, with what would settle each:**

**K1. Gibbs J's "Perhaps" said to have "likewise assumed" reasonableness (fn 14, Godecke 646–7).**
- The 647 text: "Perhaps it may be different where agreement has been reached on all essential terms but the determination of subsidiary matters has been left to one of the parties." Gibbs J then says Sweet & Maxwell "placed considerable reliance on the fact that the parties had imported the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness" and disagrees with Bray CJ, and adds "it is unnecessary to express any concluded opinion".
- Reading the "Perhaps" as confined to reasonableness is an inference from the same passage, not his statement.
- Settled by writing "arguably" or "as his reliance on Sweet & Maxwell suggests", and by adding the rubric's reason: the loan's own conditions are arguably not "subsidiary".

**K2. "the rule applies 'at least when' … and none existed" (fn 27).**
- Mason J (594): "The general rule is that a promise to perform an existing duty is no consideration, at least when the promise is made by a party to a pre-existing contract …". "At least when" sets the core case; it does not exclude others.
- The conclusion is right because no duty existed, not because of the hedge.
- Settled by resting the point on the absence of any existing duty.

**K3. "nothing shows 'a reasonable opportunity to reject' the clause" (Empirnall 535, McHugh JA).**
- The problem says Rocky "attended a meeting at AMPL's office" at which the Loan Agreement was entered into, and the clause "was included … before it was signed".
- Attendance arguably shows an opportunity; it does not show knowledge of the words. The knowledge limb (536: "taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms") is the better ground.

**K4. I.E's verdict "likely".** The rubric wants "arguably", with intention deciding the outcome. The sentence's subject is the email overall, not certainty alone, so this is borderline; I grade it Very Good.

**K5. Duty to co-operate stated verdict-first.** "Nor does AMPL breach the duty …: its call does not stop Grace repaying" is a D5 conclusion before analysis on the sheet's literal rule (a unit's verdict before a colon). It is −1 on that reading; a real UNSW marker would probably not deduct.

**K6. Trident judges outside the set reading.**
- The reading guide sets Trident [11.130] "(Mason CJ and Wilson J only)". The answer cites Deane J (fn 15, fn 25) and Brennan J, dissenting (fn 35).
- R-Y(1) makes the full Trident a course reading for this run, so there is no deduction. It is a residual risk with a real lecturer. Mason CJ and Wilson J at 115, already cited, state the party and consideration limbs.

**K7. SHEET D13 (a Trident CLR pin as a fault) does not apply.** Its premise is "none can be verified". CB14 prints the Trident markers [113] to [148]; I verified all three pins against them:
- 115: "a third party cannot sue upon a contract and that a stranger to the consideration cannot maintain an action at law upon it";
- 129: Kitto J, quoted by Brennan J;
- 145: Deane J.

No deduction.

**Minor and credit-level points:**
- fn 19 pin 535–6: the unsigned point is at 536 only.
- Banque Brussels: the "far more thorny" hedge is not kept.
- "Its call does not stop Grace repaying" should read "nothing suggests".
- Masters and Australian Woollen Mills name the judges of a whole-Court judgment. The sheet prefers no names; AGLC allows them. Not deducted.

**Verified correct: every other proposition and pin.** Gibson 298; Empirnall 534 and 535–6; Beaton 168 (Kirby P), and 185 (McHugh JA dissenting, citing Mason J); Ermogenous [25]–[26]; Masters 360, 361, 361–2 and 363, quoting Winn v Bull; Meehan 580–1, 581–2 and 582 (Gibbs CJ) and 589 (Mason J); Pace 151 (McHugh JA, citing Placer); Godecke 642–3 (Walsh J); Trident 115 (Mason CJ and Wilson J); Coulls 486–7 (Taylor and Owen JJ); Brambles 164 and 177 (Heydon JA) and 191 (Ipp AJA); Sundell 327 paraphrased and cited by report (an accepted form); Wigan 594; Pao On 629 and 632 (Lord Scarman for the Board); Banque Brussels 523 and 525 (Rogers CJ); Upper Hunter 437 (Barwick CJ, quoting Lord Wright); Roscorla 237; Australian Woollen Mills 456.

Every "Ibid" follows a single-source footnote, and short titles are introduced at the first full citation. All facts are the problem's words or are marked "arguably"; there are no D4 faults.

## 1. Certain defects (proved from the text)

**D1. Internal contradiction in the consideration paragraph (para "On consideration…").**
- The answer says: "However, the rule applies 'at least when' the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract, and none existed: … the clause, arguably included after Pierre 'agreed', bound no one before signing … Rocky likely gave consideration unless the clause preceded the bargain."
- Source: Wigan v Edwards 47 ALJR 586, 594 (Mason J; Walsh and Gibbs JJ agreeing on this point), CB p 129: "The general rule is that a promise to perform an existing duty is no consideration, at least when the promise is made by a party to a pre-existing contract, when it is made to the promisee under that contract…".
- Fact (narrator): "the clause was included in the Loan Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL."
- On the answer's own reasoning, the rule needs an existing duty. A clause that "bound no one before signing" creates none, whenever it was drafted. Signing followed Pierre's agreement. The "unless" therefore contradicts the sentence before it.
- Fix: cut "unless the clause preceded the bargain" (−6).

**D2. Garbled clause in the intention paragraph.**
- The answer says: "Rocky would invoke the third class, where parties 'have dealt only with major matters'; though no formal document was contemplated, so did the email."
- "so did the email" has no verb it can take back, so the reader cannot work out that it means the email also dealt only with major matters.
- Fix: replace with "the email, though contemplating no formal document, did likewise." (−1).

**D3. The exposure paragraph does not match the answer's own findings, which R-AD(1) forbids.**
- The consideration-for-the-guarantee paragraph finds that the clause has consideration only "if AMPL made" the $10,000 promise, and otherwise "may lack consideration". The exposure paragraph then says: "if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for $1,150,000". That drops the consideration condition.
- The guarantee-clause paragraph concludes: "He is likely bound by his oral undertaking". The exposure paragraph then treats oral liability as an alternative: "If bound only orally, he is liable in damages…". On the answer's own findings, the oral undertaking binds in any event. It covers "all payments", including any unpaid March instalment, which the clause ("repayment of the Loan") does not.
- Fix: "if Rocky assented to the clause and AMPL promised the $10,000, he is liable…" (+5), and "By his oral undertaking he is also liable in damages, to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses." (+1).

**D4. Footnote 25 (Deane J) does not contain the words paraphrased into it.** Words certain; whether the paraphrase may rest on this footnote is contestable.
- The answer says: "Pierre bound AMPL if, with its consent, he contracted 'as agent' for it rather than solely for himself.[^25]" Footnote 25 is Trident 145 (Deane J).
- What Deane J says at 145 (CB p 355): "If the promisee contracts as agent for a disclosed or undisclosed principal, the principal will ordinarily himself be, for the purposes of the requirement of privity, a party to the contract."
- The consent element and "not solely on his or her own behalf" come from the editors at [11.32] (CB pp 332–3): "the principal expressly or impliedly consented to the agent acting on his or her behalf … the agent was purporting to act on behalf of the principal and not solely on his or her own behalf."
- Deane J also speaks of the *promisee* as agent. That fits Part I (AMPL as promisee-agent for Rocky) and AMPL's claim to the benefit of Rocky's undertaking. It does not, in terms, fit the *burden* of the $10,000, where Pierre is the promisor.
- R-Y(2) prefers Deane J for the burden aspect, so I do not demand a change of source. The reviser should know that the consent words are the editors', not Deane J's. One answer is to keep the paraphrase and accept the risk. The other is to drop "with its consent" and "rather than solely for himself", which costs the test its elements.

## 1. The new v5 material, tested at source

### 1.1 Later conduct on formation: 'later conduct, admissible on formation, agrees, Grace taking AMPL's loan on other terms.[^10]'

Source. Brambles 164, Heydon JA: 'The second relevant principle is that post-contractual conduct is admissible on the question of whether a contract was formed … The third relevant principle is that post-contractual conduct is not admissible on the question of what a contract means as distinct from the question of whether it was formed.' (CB14 ch03 p 73.) Speaker: Heydon JA, stating 'conventional and accepted principles' before construing the 12 July 1990 contract. Status: Ipp AJA at 184 ('For the reasons set out by Heydon JA, I agree that the July 1990 contract governed …') and Mason P at 155 (agreeing with Ipp AJA) adopt that construction, so the principles are majority-backed. The passage sits in the reading guide's skip range (pp 73 to 76), but R-F (SHEET line 322) records skip status 'for the register and never required or deducted'. Not a defect.

Use. Correct proposition, correct use (formation, not meaning), consistent with the answer's later use of the third principle for the 'check in' emails. The slide 1B question 'Can post-formation conduct be relevant to the question of whether a contract was formed?' is answered in the lecturer's terms.

Grace's counsel's strongest reply (contestable, not a defect). Later conduct does not point one way. The Loan Agreement's term ('repayable at the expiry of 12 months') matches the email's 'for 1 year', and AMPL advanced at Rocky's request twelve days after the promised date. Grace would say this is Rocky arranging his own performance through AMPL, not evidence that nothing bound. The answer meets this, though not in that sentence: Part I's next paragraph puts Rocky's own version of the argument ('AMPL's advance, made because he "asked", performed his promise') and answers it ('the advance differed in amount and date'; AMPL lent for itself). Read together, the two paragraphs answer the point. 'Agrees' is a fair conclusion, given the different lender, the 4% rate, the $1,150,000 amount and the later date.

Better pin at zero body cost. In the part of Brambles that is read (p 81), Heydon JA applies the same principle to find no contract: the absence of protest at a later variation 'is admissible on the issue of whether there was a contract at all, and points strongly against it' (Brambles 182, Heydon JA). That is an application, against formation, on facts of the same kind (a party's later conduct inconsistent with contractual rights). Proposed: footnote 10 becomes '… 53 NSWLR 153, 164, 182 (Heydon JA)'. Body cost 0. Note that 182 is Heydon JA alone (Ipp AJA took a different route on consideration), so 164 stays as the main pin and 182 only adds the application.

### 1.2 Gibbs J in Godecke: 'concluded bargain', 'a vital matter', '[p]erhaps'

Source. Godecke 646 to 647, Gibbs J: 'it seems to me that there would be no binding contract in such a case … the same conclusion might have been reached by holding that there can be no concluded bargain if a vital matter (such as price or rental) has been left to the determination of one of the parties … Perhaps it may be different where agreement has been reached on all essential terms but the determination of subsidiary matters has been left to one of the parties. In Sweet & Maxwell … "such other covenants and conditions as shall be reasonably required" … I am, with respect unable to agree with that observation [Bray CJ in Powell v Jones, upholding a lease without "reasonably"], for it seems to me that the members of the Court of Appeal in Sweet & Maxwell … placed considerable reliance on the fact that the parties had imported the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness … However, it is unnecessary to express any concluded opinion on these matters' (CB14 ch06 p 187).

(verify.py lists 'a vital matter' and 'concluded bargain' first at Meehan 577, where they appear in the vendor's submission. The words also appear verbatim at Godecke 647 in Gibbs J's own judgment, so footnote 16's attribution is correct.)

Fidelity. 'Obiter' is correct. 'Doubted' is a fair gloss on 'might have been reached'. The answer says the '[p]erhaps' 'cited a case where parties had "imported …"'. Gibbs J also cited Powell v Jones, which had no reasonableness qualifier, but only to reject Bray CJ's extension. So the answer's reading, that the 'perhaps' is confined to clauses importing reasonableness, is the better reading and arguably understates the point. Not a defect.

Grace's counsel's strongest reply (partly met). The email 'fixes the amount, date, term and rate', which are the essentials of a loan, as the answer itself says in its first paragraph. Grace would say the 'conditions' are subsidiary matters, so Gibbs J's 'perhaps' applies, and Mason J in Meehan 589 implies 'honestly, or honestly and reasonably' into 'satisfactory'. That would supply the reasonableness standard Gibbs J required. The answer's reply ('which these parties never did') relies on the parties not having imported reasonableness expressly. Implication is Grace's point, and the answer meets it only through the Meehan distinction (see 1.3). The answer never says why the 'conditions' are 'a vital matter' rather than subsidiary ones. A harsh marker could write 'label asserted'. This is contestable. Proposed edit E3 below sharpens the decisive reason so that the label carries less weight.

### 1.3 The Meehan distinction: 'Rocky's covers the loan's own terms, which neither standard can supply and no range confines.'

Grace's counsel's strongest reply (contestable, and the weakest clause in the paragraph). Gibbs CJ in Meehan 579 said that on an objective test a court 'should not find it unduly difficult to decide what finance a reasonable man, in the position of the purchaser, would regard as satisfactory', even though the clause was 'silent as to amount, term of the loan, rate of interest, conditions of repayment …'. So a reasonableness standard can supply loan terms. Pace 151 (McHugh JA) adds that 'even when no objective criterion of measurement is available, it may still be possible to infer a promise to act honestly and/or reasonably'. 'Which neither standard can supply' is therefore open to direct contradiction from Meehan 579. That is the same case the answer distinguishes, and the second passage is on the same Pace page the answer cites at footnote 13.

The decisive reason is a different passage, which the answer half-quotes. Gibbs CJ, Meehan 581: the Placer principle 'does not apply where the discretion or option of the contracting party relates, not to the performance of the contractual obligations themselves, but only to the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends.' Rocky's 'satisfactory conditions' are the terms of his own lending, so they go to the performance of his own obligation. That is the Placer side of Gibbs CJ's line, and it matches Pace 151's Placer example ('a subsidy "of an amount or at a rate determined by the Commonwealth"'). Quoting the other half of Gibbs CJ's sentence makes the distinction from the source's own words and drops the contestable 'neither standard' clause. See edit E3.

### 1.4 Agency: Port Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ dissenting) and 'Pierre controls AMPL, supplying that authority'

Source. Port Jackson 240, Barwick CJ (dissenting in the result): the Eurymedon adoption of Lord Reid's requisites, '(2) the carrier by the bill contracted for the stevedore's protection as well as for his own, (3) the authority of the carrier to act for the stevedore in this respect whether antecedently or by ratification was made out' (CB14 ch11 p 334). The editors' note [11.32] (p 333) supplies the answer's 'not solely for himself': 'the agent was purporting to act on behalf of the principal and not solely on his or her own behalf'.

Fidelity. Correct quotation and pin. 'Dissenting' is correct under AGLC, because he dissented on the construction point that decided the appeal. On agency, though, he was in the majority (editors at p 333: the 'agency' point was 'rejected by the majority of the court: Barwick CJ, Mason and Jacobs JJ'), so relying on him for the agency criterion is sound. The requisites are Lord Reid's as the Privy Council adopted them, paraphrased by Barwick CJ, and 'authority … to act for' are his words. The answer does not misattribute. R-Z(3) names Port Jackson for agency, and the SHEET (lines 2490 to 2492) accepts this form. Port Jackson is outside the reading guide's set pages, but R-Z(3) governs.

'Supplying that authority': AMPL's or Pierre's counsel would say this is an unhedged legal inference. Under [11.32], authority is the principal's express or implied consent. In Port Jackson (241), authority was found as a fact from a course of dealing. The answer's chain is: 'owned and controlled' (narrator), then authority, then 'likely acted for AMPL'. The conclusion is hedged ('likely') but the middle step is not, and the SHEET's credit line accepts inferring authority from ownership and control. Contestable at most, low risk. An optional fix ('Pierre's control arguably supplies that authority') costs about +2 words. It is not funded here, because the edits below rank higher per word.

Pierre's own counsel. If Pierre spoke for AMPL, Pierre personally owes nothing. The answer's alternative branch ('If he promised personally, he alone owes the $10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking') states the other result. Met.

### 1.5 'Rocky likely gave consideration, unless he also promised AMPL a guarantee when he "asked".' CERTAIN DEFECT (internal inconsistency)

The paragraph runs: (a) the rule applies 'at least when' there is an existing contract, and none is shown; (b) 'Even otherwise, ensuring "all payments" "promptly" exceeds guaranteeing "repayment of the Loan"'; (c) the closing caveat above. Sentence (b) holds that a prior duty to guarantee 'repayment' leaves fresh consideration, because the 8 April undertaking promised more. A 27 February promise of 'a guarantee' therefore defeats consideration only if it already covered every payment, promptly. As written, the caveat contradicts (b): it says any guarantee promised on 27 February would defeat consideration. Source for the test: Wigan 594 (Mason J): the rule applies where the new promise 'is to do no more than the promisor is bound to do'; Sundell 327: 'every promise allegedly given … was identical with a promise given under the original agreement'.

Fix (E1, saves 1 word): 'unless, when he "asked", he already undertook the same.' 'The same' refers back to 'ensuring "all payments" "promptly"', which is exactly the Sundell or Wigan identity test.

### 1.6 'Check in' emails and post-contractual conduct

'His "I will do that" contains no words of effort, and his "check in" emails cannot construe it:[^35]' is correct (Brambles 164, third principle) and is consistent with the formation use at footnote 10. AMPL could use the same emails on formation (second principle) to show Rocky treated himself as bound, which favours intention. The answer already finds intention ('both promises likely bind'), so nothing turns on it. Met.

### 1.7 Brambles 195 (Brogden) for acceptance by conduct

Source. Ipp AJA, 195 (Mason P agreeing, so the majority): conduct must be '"of such a character as necessarily to lead to the inference … that the agreement had been accepted … and was to be acted upon"'; 'The question is one of fact' (CB14 ch03 p 85). Correct speaker, pin and status.

AMPL's strongest reply (met, though not at full strength). Ipp AJA's own application: where the benefit and the conditions 'were dependent on each other and inextricably linked … the fact that the appellant charged the higher fees is conclusive evidence that it agreed to all the conditions … by accepting those benefits the appellant accepted the Council's offer in accordance with its terms' (p 86). AMPL would say the $10,000 and the clause were linked in the same way ('Pierre agreed and the clause was included'). The answer's reply, 'the benefit he took priced his own words', is exactly the right answer to that argument: the $10,000 was bought by the oral undertaking, not by the clause, so there is no indivisible offer. 'AMPL would say Rocky "attended" … taking the $10,000 promise knowing the terms' states AMPL's case at Empirnall strength rather than at Ipp AJA's 'inextricably linked' strength. Optional upgrade only, not funded.

Two things pull it below 90: the one internal inconsistency, and a clause in the illusory-promise paragraph that the distinguished case itself contradicts. With E1 to E4 applied: 90/100.

6.1 Rulings that override SHEET_v12 (binding on the markers)
R-P. Word count line and judge forms. The ‘Word count: N’ line states the total of all text excluding footnotes as Word
would count it, which is the body count plus the three words of the line itself (so a body of 1,495 is stated as ‘Word count:
1,498’); the body must therefore be at most 1,497 for the stated total to be at most 1,500, and the sheet’s floors use 1,495
as the body ceiling. Pao On may be cited either as the Board (no judge) or as ‘(Lord Scarman for the Board)’, since the
course extract is headed ‘Judgement delivered by Lord Scarman’; neither is deducted. Roscorla may name Lord Denman
CJ, who delivered the judgment of the Court, on the same basis. Slides are cited as ‘Class 4A Slides, slide 16’ only where
no course case states the point; a slide citation where a course case states the point is over-citation.

and round-2 rulings. (1) Trident General Insurance Co Ltd v McNiece Bros Pty Ltd (1988) 165 CLR 107 is a Class 4A
reading; it is saved at ‘W4 C4A Privity/Trident (course reading, supplied by Yusuf 2026-10-11).txt’ and added to the
corpus by judge. R-J and R-N are superseded: Trident may be quoted and cited as a course case, one source per marker;
because the reading carries no CLR page markers, it is cited by report with the judge named and no pin, and the no-pin
lint is an accepted, disclosed consequence. (2) For the burden aspect of privity, Deane J’s words (‘the general rule that
only the parties to a contract are bound by, and entitled to enforce, its terms’) are the preferred source over Class 4A
slide 2 (R-P: a slide only where no course case states the point). For the routes around privity, a Trident judge who states
them is preferred over slide 3 if one does so in terms; otherwise slide 3 stays. (3) The textbook is never a source, including
as a page locator: Ermogenous stays pinned by paragraph (as his LAWS1061 answer pinned Wicks) and Pao On stays at
the brief’s verified 632 and 629 to 630. (4) Round-2 marker and panel findings are triaged by the reviser at source; II.I3
takes ‘likely’ (both markers); Brambles 182 is replaced by Heydon JA at 179 or 181 where he applies Empirnall, if the
page states it, marked as his reasoning; guarantee-law statements (‘only postpones liability’) are removed (the answer’s
own scope line excludes guarantee law).

R-Z. No meta language and no slide citations (Yusuf, 11 October 2026, 16:08 and 16:10: ‘you cant cite a slide like this is
an actual advise right? so you cant use meta language of weeks 1 to 4 explicitly in the … answer’; ‘having the words

answer simply does not say so. (5) Markers grade a meta reference or a slide citation as an R1 and R8 fault (VG for one
instance, Good for two or more), and P’s core no longer requires naming excluded matters.

going through it critically reasoning … be explicit i feel like you skip over a lot … be clean’; 19:21 approving
REBUILD/CALIBRATION_SAMPLE.md and ‘run till completion’). Binding on every later agent and overriding SHEET_v12

Headings are by parties only (eg ‘I. ROCKY v GRACE’; ‘II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)’; a further party-
pair heading only if needed); no element headings (no ‘A. Offer’ etc.). (2) Under each party heading, the elements are
taken in chronological and course order, each in its own full paragraph that opens by naming the issue in course terms
(eg ‘The first issue is whether Rocky’s 12 February email was an offer.’), states the rule with authority, then works
through the facts explicitly (‘Employing textual analysis’, the words weighed one by one, both readings, why one wins),
and ends with a hedged conclusion; each Part ends with a short concluding paragraph for that party pair. (3) No one-
sentence paragraphs; no choppy runs of short sentences; transitions between paragraphs make the reasoning flow. (4)
Times New Roman 12 pt, double spaced (the builder already does this). (5) The sample is a style reference only: it is

REBUILD/STYLE_REFERENCE_sample_distinction.pdf/.txt. (6) The heading words freed (about 50) go to explicit

R-AC(7). Authenticity review (Yusuf, 22:48: ‘even outside of the rubric … in case issues with rubric, genuinely just try and
find any other downsides which would stray from an authentic problem solving legal reasoning flow … showing the full
and proper thinking of the mind critically with all sources always in context to truly be right’). From now on every round
includes an AUTHENTICITY CRITIC who ignores the rubric and judges the answer as a senior contracts academic and
practitioner would: does it read as a real lawyer thinking a problem through (question framed from the client’s goal, facts
read closely, the governing test identified and applied step by step, authorities used for what they actually decided in
their full context and distinguished on their facts, both sides’ best arguments, a decisive reason, a conclusion and its
practical consequence), or does it read as box-ticking, name-dropping, quote-mosaic, label-assertion, or reasoning shaped
by a checklist? Its findings bind the reviser on the same footing as markers’.

R-AD. Exposure and completeness (Yusuf, 12 October 2026, 00:21: ‘wdym waiting till april 8th costs little? and what about
the personal guarantee so does he have to come up with all of it … making sure you really actually did everything in full,
and not just a botched effort getting half things and skipping half including key shi or strong arguments’). (1) The advice
states Rocky’s exposure precisely: if bound by the written clause (‘personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’), he is
liable for the Loan, $1,150,000, once it is due and unpaid (now, on the 27 February reading; from 8 April 2025 if Grace
has not repaid, on the 8 April reading); if bound only by his oral undertaking and it promised a result, Grace’s default
breaches it (damages not assessed, per the Instructions); Grace’s ‘I might not pay at all!’ makes default a real risk; if
Grace never repays, the $10,000 never falls due; paying early likely forfeits it and nothing gives him a contractual claim
against Grace. Resisting the premature call buys time only; the advice must not say waiting ‘costs little’. (2) A
completeness audit precedes the final version: every sentence of the problem is either used or deliberately set aside with
a reason, and every strong argument for either side is put and met.

R-AE. Every point through legal principle (Yusuf, 12 October 2026, 00:33: ‘everything is through law principles not just …
commentary and truly getting to the gist of it, although arguments … should be lawful not feelings or glibs like costs
little’). Every sentence of reasoning and advice, including the closing advice, rests on a legal rule applied to the facts: the
source of each consequence is named (the condition precedent: Meehan 582; the terms of the guarantee clause; the oral
undertaking as a promise of result; privity; consideration), never on impressions, risk talk or practical colour (‘a real risk’,
‘buys time’, ‘costs little’, ‘weak’ without the legal reason). A practical recommendation is stated only as the legal
consequence of each course (eg paying before the Loan is due is not required by any term and, the $10,000 being
conditional on Grace’s repayment, likely forfeits it), with the facts that decide it.
