being certain on either reading (II.E, II.I2).
Strength and tilt. Moderate to strong if AMPL promised, a disclosed departure from ISSUES_SETTLED’s ‘strong’
(S-33; header C6) with its reason stated here from the source page as R-R(9) requires (CRIT_round4 m12):
Ermogenous [25] makes the inquiry ‘an objective assessment of the state of affairs between the parties’ that ‘may
take account of the subject-matter of the agreement, the status of the parties to it, their relationship to one another,
and other surrounding circumstances’, and [26] puts the onus on the party alleging the contract; the casebook’s own
note at [5.90] says ‘the nature of the relationship between the parties and the context in which the agreement was
made remain important considerations’; Banque Brussels 523 is a first-instance NSW judgment about a commercial
letter between companies, not a cousin’s oral undertaking. No High Court authority in the materials decides a
family-and-company weighing on these facts, so a well-reasoned contrary conclusion that applies [25] and [26] to the
onus, the relationship, the unpriced request of 27 February and ‘expected’ is a reasoned application of the governing
authority, not law wrong, and R-E’s ‘strong’ consequence (Poor) would misgrade it; it is capped at Very Good
(CRIT_complete_bias_2 B-4; Part 9 item 6). A contrary conclusion resting on a family presumption is Poor and D6.
Moderate to strong if Pierre promised, likewise.
Consistency (T3). Rocky cannot argue family honour to escape the undertaking while claiming the $10,000.
Citation. Ermogenous [25]–[26] (Gaudron, McHugh, Hayne and Callinan JJ); Banque Brussels Lambert SA v
Australian National Industries Ltd (1989) 21 NSWLR 502, 521–3 or 523 (Rogers CJ), 525–6 for the ‘practice to
ensure’ passage.

II.E Certainty: ‘all payments … promptly’ measurable; ‘once Grace repays’ not illusory (2.5; L; floor 35) [Upper
Hunter 437 (Barwick CJ, quoting Lord Wright); Meehan 581 to 582]

    Rules at source. ‘So long as the language employed by the parties … is not “so obscure and so incapable of any
    definite or precise meaning that the court is unable to attribute to the parties any particular contractual intention”,
    the contract cannot be held to be void or uncertain or meaningless.’ [CB3B 161 | 437 | Barwick CJ, ‘to use Lord
    Wright’s words in G Scammell & Nephew Ltd v Ouston’, Upper Hunter | the inner quotation never nested; the
    quoted words are Lord Wright’s, so the footnote reads ‘(Barwick CJ, quoting Lord Wright in G Scammell & Nephew
    Ltd v Ouston)’ and R8’s second-hand list includes him; Mason J RECITES the same words at 587 as the respondents’
    first proposition (‘The respondents’ case rests on three propositions: (1) a contract which is expressed in language
    “so obscure …” is void for uncertainty’), which he does not dispute, so 587 is a recited submission and not a second
    adoption; Upper Hunter 437 is the adoption and the citation (CRIT_fidelity_4 Finding 4, adopted; CRIT_fidelity_3
    m8)]; contrast Mobil: ‘find a way’ ‘is simply too vague and uncertain to be capable of giving rise to contractual
    obligation’ [CB1A 58 | 499 | the Court] (credit); ‘The fact that the condition is one whose performance [582] lies
    wholly or partly within the power of one of the parties to the contract does not mean that there is no binding
    contract once the condition is fulfilled.’ [CB3B 184 | 581 to 582 | Gibbs CJ, Meehan].
    Facts (deciding). ‘all payments … promptly’; ‘once Grace repays the Loan’. Supporting: ‘$10,000’; ‘to me directly’.
    Core. One or two sentences: the criterion (a term fails only if ‘so obscure’ that no contractual intention can be
    attributed to it) applied to ‘all payments … promptly’, which takes its content from the Loan Agreement’s own
    timetable (monthly interest; principal at the expiry of 12 months); and AMPL’s promise not illusory, its condition
    depending on a third party’s act, Grace’s repayment (credit: ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ quoted here; AMPL has no
    discretion once it is met). The counted form is two sentences, each carrying its own footnote (Upper Hunter 437 on
    the first; Meehan 581 to 582 on the second), the second a ten-word element sub-verdict with its reason in an
    absolute clause (‘AMPL’s promise is not illusory, its condition depending on Grace’), which is his form under R1; v5’s
    single sentence carried one marker for two sources (CRIT_fidelity_5 Finding 5).
    Credit. Mobil compared (similar: ‘find a way’ and ‘ensure’ both leave the means to the promisor; different: Mobil’s
    result was itself undefined, whereas Rocky’s result is defined by the timetable); the contrast with I.E (the same
    doctrine, opposite result, the discretion there lying with the promisor); any dispute about the 12 months is
    construction, not certainty (II.G); the sum, payee and trigger stated.
    Strength. Strong; a contrary conclusion is Poor.
    Drops. VG: the criterion absent (a bare ‘capable of meaning’); AMPL’s promise not addressed for illusoriness (the
    second sentence, the first-demotion item in Part 8, mirrored here: CRIT_round6 m8). Good: bare. Fair: the condition
    called uncertain. Poor: ‘ensure’ held void for vagueness; AMPL’s promise held illusory because Grace might never
    repay. Omitted.

II.F1 Privity: Rocky the promisee; ‘the clause’ both ways with the reason (1.0; L; floor 38) [Coulls 494 to 495
(Windeyer J dissenting) alone; never a slide (R-Z(2)) or [11.10] (R-Z(3); R-U(1)); Coulls 487 is not the citation]

    Rules at source. The two limbs (I.F2): Windeyer J at 494 (‘only those who are parties to a contract can sue upon it’)
    and 495 (‘a plaintiff who sues on a promise must show a consideration for it provided by him’), dissenting on
    construction, alone: S4A slide 2 states only the party limb, and [11.10] is an editors’ note for a rule a course case
    states, so neither is the citation (R-Z(2), (3); R-U(1); CRIT_fidelity_9 Finding 1, v9’s ‘or S4A slide 2, or [11.10]’
    withdrawn); Coulls 487 decides that signature does not make one a party and that there was no express or implied
    promise to the wife, and does not state the two-limb rule, so it is not the citation for ‘promisee for consideration, not
    barred’ (CRIT_fidelity_3 m6 and CRIT_round3 m6, adopted); example 1: ‘If A and B enter into a contract under which
    A promises B (for consideration) to pay $1,000 to C, and A fails to honour this promise, C has no right to sue A to
    recover the money.’ [CB4 327 | [11.10] | editors]; Coulls 487; Trident [14] (Mason CJ and Wilson J: ‘a stranger to the
    consideration cannot maintain an action at law upon it’; by report, no pin; [15] asks whether the two rules are one)
    (credit; CRIT_complete_bias_2 A-7 adopted).
    Facts (deciding). ‘to me directly’; ‘the clause’. Supporting: ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included in the Loan
    Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL.’
    Core. One sentence: Rocky is the promisee and named payee (‘to me directly’) of an oral promise made to him for
    his own consideration, so he is a party who gave consideration and privity does not bar the oral claim; and, in a
    clause, both readings of ‘the clause’ (CRIT_harsh_2 F7, adopted): it most naturally means the guarantee clause
    named before it (the reason stated in a few words: the definite article refers back to the only clause previously
    named; v10’s ‘just named’ pointed at a place in the answer rather than in the problem, an answer-external deictic a
    cold reader could not resolve, and is from v11 an R1 lapse; the v11 form is ‘the guarantee clause named before it’,
    +1: UPGRADES_r1 U29; ‘the guarantee clause the problem names first’ is equally Excellent; v3’s floor gave no
    reason, which the harsh critic graded VG: CRIT_round3 table 1.1), and even a written $10,000 term leaves him the
    oral promise made to him (accepted bare in the counted form; its reason, that Rocky is party to neither document
    and the materials state no rule displacing an oral promise by a later written record (gap G8), is credit, ‘he being
    party to neither document’ (+6) where words allow: CRIT_round4 m8, disclosed; credit also: example 1 named,
    Rocky being then a non-party to the Loan Agreement; the order of clause and $10,000 weighed in terms).
    Credit. The gap disclosed if relied on (no rule in the materials on an oral promise and a later written record); Grace
    is not a party to the $10,000 bargain; the order of the clause and the $10,000 weighed in terms, marked ‘arguably’
    (R-M). From v11 (UPGRADES_r1 U17, credit only; its proposed weight change REJECTED, the weights being R-C
    calibrated): the written-term reading’s reason, ‘he being party to neither document’ (+6), stays credit, example 1 at
    [11.10] (‘C has no right to sue A to recover the money’, CB4 327) supporting it.
    Strength and tilt. Either reading of ‘the clause’ is Excellent if both are run, the preferred reading carries its reason
    (the definite article for the guarantee reading; the order of clause and $10,000, marked ‘arguably’, for the written-
    term reading), and the result is shown unchanged; weighing the other reading’s reason in terms is credit
    (CRIT_round10 M1) (CRIT_complete_bias_2 B-5, adopted: the ambiguity is textual, not legal); one reading only is
    Good.
    Drops. VG: the criterion (party plus consideration) absent; ‘most naturally’ with no reason; Coulls 487 cited for the
    two-limb rule (a citation fault); [11.10] cited for the rule where Coulls 494 to 495 states it (a citation fault: R-Z(3); R-
    U(1)); a slide cited for either limb or for the rule is graded at R1 and R8 under R-Z(5), not here (v11’s slide-2
    citation-fault line is withdrawn). Good: bare; one reading only. Fair: the written-term reading adopted and the claim
    said to fail on privity with the oral contract ignored. Poor: Rocky treated as a third-party beneficiary of the Loan

II.F2 Privity: who promised, AMPL through Pierre or Pierre personally (4.0; K; floor 95) [the doctrine of
agency, one source per marker (R-R(3)): a case first under R-Z(3), Port Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ) for the
criterion stated in Lord Reid’s form; the casebook [11.70] only as a last resort, per R-A(4) as amended by R-
X(1); either suffices for the criterion; Ermogenous [24] credit]

    Issue. Whether the $10,000 promise (and so Rocky’s counterparty, and the promisee of his undertaking) is AMPL or
    Pierre.
    Rules at source. The doctrine of agency: S4A slide 16 (as at I.F1; a locator only, never cited: R-Z(2)); the course’s
    statement of what must be shown: the principal ‘expressly or impliedly consented to the agent acting on the
    principal’s behalf so as to effect the principal’s relations with third parties’ and, ‘with respect to the particular
    transaction under consideration, the agent was purporting to act on behalf of the principal and not solely on the
    agent’s own behalf. Ratification refers to the principal’s adoption or confirmation of a contract made without prior
    authorisation.’ [CB4 336 | [11.70] | editors’ note; cited from v12 as at I.F1: a case first, Port Jackson 240 (Barwick
    CJ) for the elements stated in Lord Reid’s form (‘contracted for the stevedore’s protection as well as for his own’;
    authority ‘antecedently or by ratification’), Trident (Brennan J or Deane J) by report only for the bare route, The New
    York Star only for authority; the casebook [11.70] a last resort (R-Z(3)), at most twice in the answer, never stacked
    with a case for the same proposition (R-R(3)); no slide (R-Z(2))]; ‘To be a legally enforceable duty there must, of
    course, be identifiable parties to the arrangement’ [CB3A 137 | [24] | Ermogenous] (credit); Windeyer J’s ‘the
    company (by its agent O’Neil) promised’ [CB4 332 | 492 | dissenting on construction] (illustration only). No court in
    the set states a rule of ratification in terms (O-7): ratification is not used to supply the purporting element.

    personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ (AMPL’s later call, quoted in the narrator’s words, the inference that it was a
    call on the undertaking marked ‘arguably’: R-M; CRIT_round3 M8, adopted). Supporting (credit): ‘Pierre agreed to

    loan; ‘a cousin’ at ‘you’; on the guarantee reading of ‘the clause’ the $10,000 is nowhere in AMPL’s document.

    put in the answer’s own words as ‘whether’ clauses, never as a direct question with a question mark (his Part A has
    none; the counted form: ‘turns on agency: whether AMPL consented to Pierre acting on its behalf, and whether

the Loan Agreement’ and AMPL’s later call under ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’, ‘arguably’ his

in part). (4) A conclusion in the open-point tier (‘On balance … likely …, because …, though …’) whose ‘because’ is
Pierre’s dealing throughout about AMPL’s loan (v3’s ‘AMPL asserted its other side’ deleted as cryptic and as
restating the R-M inference: CRIT_round3 M8); the other party pleaded in the alternative, which the trailing clause
‘though ’you’ keeps Pierre arguable’ does (the counted form from v8; v7’s ‘keeps Pierre arguable in the alternative’

the alternative’ are not required and a drafter who writes them loses nothing) (credit: the consequence stated here

(5) The further information that decides it, with its direction, in the trailing clause (from v11 CORE, a K unit carrying
none being the contradiction five of six Stage-5 round-1 markers graded at R6: UPGRADES_r1 U3): what Pierre said
about whom he spoke for, and which way it cuts; the v11 form adds ‘, decisively so if he spoke for himself’ after
‘though ’you’ keeps Pierre arguable’ (+7); a form naming AMPL’s later adoption of the $10,000 promise, with its
direction, is equally Excellent.
Credit. Ratification named and set aside (it concerns a contract ‘made without prior authorisation’, and prior
authorisation is not the difficulty); in Port Jackson the carrier’s antecedent authority to contract for the stevedore
was found as a fact on the evidence of their course of dealing (OFF Port Jackson, Barwick CJ [2] ‘(at p236)’: the
stevedore ‘had for years acted as stevedore in the discharge of the carrier’s ships’ and ‘was aware of the use by the
carrier of a form of bill of lading’ including the Himalaya clause; [21] ‘(at p241)’: the appellate Court ‘having
reviewed the evidence’ found the carrier ‘was acting with the appellant’s authority’, ‘i.e. with its antecedent

Finding 2); the stevedore’s knowledge of the offer and its reliance on it go to acceptance and consideration (OFF

shipper’s promise or offer when he discharges the goods so long as he has knowledge of the existence of that
promise or offer’), and, in the authority finding Mason and Jacobs JJ adopted from Glass JA (OFF Port Jackson [5] ‘(at
p271)’: the stevedore ‘proved that it was familiar with the terms of the bill of lading in general and with the clauses
purporting to exempt independent contractors in particular’, and claims had been ‘rejected in reliance upon the
exemption clauses’, from which there was ‘a clear implication’ that the carrier acted ‘as agent with the authority of
its principal the stevedore’; ‘On this point we need do no more than state our agreement with what Glass J.A. has
said’), the stevedore’s familiarity with the clauses and its reliance on them in rejecting earlier claims were part of
the course of dealing from which authority was implied (CRIT_fidelity_9 Finding 3; R-U(6): v9’s ‘not to authority’ was
too wide and is withdrawn); so the cases support inferring Pierre’s authority from AMPL’s ownership and control, as
a course of dealing supported it there, but neither addresses ‘purporting’ (v7’s gloss, ‘infer authority from the
principal’s knowledge of and reliance on the clauses’, was imprecise rather than wrong, naming the familiarity and
reliance without the course of dealing they formed part of, and is replaced by the statement above: CRIT_fidelity_7
Finding 2 and CRIT_fidelity_9 Finding 3, adopted as corrections under R-T(3) and R-U(6); every span above checked
verbatim against the saved official texts, which are credit, never cited for a course-stated proposition, and never
quoted in the answer); Ermogenous [24]; intention re-weighed if Pierre promised (II.D); a second further-information
item beyond core (5) (AMPL’s later adoption of the $10,000 promise, or what Pierre said, whichever core (5) does
not use), with its direction.

pleaded, and the consequences for II.C2, II.D, II.I1, II.I3 and II.I4 are drawn conditionally on the conclusion (T11).

Spraggon (Aust) Pty Ltd (1978) 139 CLR 231, 240 (Barwick CJ), where the sentence states the criterion in Lord

II.G The 12 months (5.0; C; floor 76) [Brambles 163 to 164 and 191; for the objective reading eg Brambles 168
or Ermogenous [25]]

Why it is here (R-Q). ‘repayable at the expiry of 12 months’ states no start; it decides (i) whether AMPL’s 9 March 2025
call was premature, (ii) whether Rocky’s undertaking was broken on 27 February 2025 (breach exposure, which the
answer does not argue and never frames as outside any scope: R-Z(1), (4)), (iii) when the $10,000 condition can be met. It
does not decide Rocky’s claim against Grace (privity defeats it on either reading), which is why it sits in Part II after F,
with Part I carrying only the one-clause cross-reference at I.F2 (the 5 March demand assumed the earlier date). The
reader of II.I4’s ‘turns on the 12 months (G)’ is then in the same Part (CRIT_round3 M9, adopted).

     Issue. Whether ‘the expiry of 12 months’ ran from the advance of 27 February 2024 or the agreement of 8 April
     2024: a question of construction on which no reading or slide states when such a period begins (gap disclosed: Z9),
     and of construction, not uncertainty (Meehan 578: ‘It is only if the court is unable to put any definite meaning on the
     contract that it can be said to be uncertain’; the former I.E2 point, now carried here).
     Rules at source.
           Objective meaning: Ermogenous [25] (I.D; ‘in the same sense as it is used in other contractual contexts’) (eg).
           Ambiguity and genesis: ‘if the language of a contract is ambiguous, evidence of surrounding circumstances is
           admissible for the purposes of construing the contract … Where ambiguities exist, mutually known facts
           establishing the commercial purpose of the contract, the genesis of the transaction, the background and the
           context in which the parties are operating will be admissible … the shared beliefs of the parties as to their
           respective rights as they existed immediately before the contract was entered into are admissible’ [CB1B 82 |
           191 | Ipp AJA (Mason P agreeing on the contractual claim), Brambles | majority; conditional on ambiguity
           throughout; RG skip (register only); ‘Ipp AJA’ per R-K, the casebook heading ‘IPP JA’ accepted and not
           deducted]; ‘pre-contractual conduct is only admissible on questions of construction if the contract is ambiguous
           and if the pre-contractual conduct casts light on the genesis of the contract, its objective aim, or the meaning of
           any descriptive term’ [CB1B 73 | 163 | Heydon JA | unanimous by adoption (O-9) | RG skip]; ‘whatever might
           flow from the factual matrix, it cannot be resorted to unless the 12 July 1990 contract is ambiguous’ [CB1B 76 |
           167 | Heydon JA].
           Exclusion: post-contractual conduct ‘not admissible on the question of what a contract means’ [CB1B 73 | 164 |
           Heydon JA, unanimous by adoption]; ‘the actual opinions of the parties are irrelevant’ absent rectification or
           estoppel by convention [CB1B 76 | 168 | Heydon JA]. Contra, older (credit): Mayo J admits subsequent conduct
           ‘where meaning is in doubt … to explain, but not to contradict, the language used’ [CB3A 147 | 74 | Mayo J,
           Todd v Nicol | first instance, SA, 1957; the passage sits after the [74] marker and before any [75] marker:

II.I AMPL’s call of 9 March 2025 (16.5; a further heading inside Part II; the Part III option was
withdrawn in v6, §5)

Why it is in the advice: it is the setter’s final fact and the reason advice is sought now; it is the other side of the bargain
Rocky sues on, so every argument on it is an argument on the $10,000; the 12 months (II.G) decides its timing. The
elements of the bargain are not re-run here; I is confined to the burden aspect, the content of what Rocky promised and
his assent to the written words, AMPL’s consideration, timing and consequences; intention and certainty of the
undertaking are carried by the II.D clause. The four paragraphs sit under the one heading ‘I. AMPL’s call’ (the Part III
option is withdrawn: §5; CRIT_round5 m2); they may open ‘Whether …’ or with a classification; II.I2’s counted opening
(‘Rocky promised what Pierre ’expected’, whereas …’) is a classification of the two contents and is not a conclusion first
(CRIT_round3 Part 3.5 noted the visible inconsistency; it is not a fault).

II.I1 The burden aspect; the clause alone; Rocky likely bound by his own undertaking, to AMPL only if Pierre
acted for it (4.0; C; floor 56) [Trident (Deane J) by report, judge named, no pin (R-Y(1), (2)), never a slide (R-
Z(2)); Empirnall 534 and 536; Coulls 487]

     Issue. Whether a clause in a contract between AMPL and Grace, described by the narrator as one ‘that Rocky
     personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, can by itself bind Rocky; and, if not, whether he is bound by his own
     undertaking, and to whom.
     Rules at source. ‘Nor can it impose an enforceable burden on a non-party.’ [S4A slide 2 | slide; a locator only, never
     cited: R-Z(2)]; ‘nor can it impose an enforceable burden on a non-party’ [CB4 327 | [11.10] | editors; ‘This chapter
     will focus on the benefit aspect of the rule’; a last resort only, never needed here: R-Z(3)]; the case statement of both
     aspects, the preferred source from v12 (R-Y(2)): ‘the general rule that only the parties to a contract are bound by,
     and entitled to enforce, its terms’ [Trident, course reading (R-Y(1)) | Deane J, his opening sentence | verified in the
     corpus’s Deane J segment | by report, judge named, no pin, the reading carrying no CLR page markers], and Deane
     J’s further statement, ‘a contract between two or more parties does not, of itself, directly confer rights or impose
     liabilities upon persons who are not parties to it’ [same | Deane J | verified likewise]; either may be quoted or
     paraphrased; Trident being a course reading, the footnote never counts toward the R-H cap of three and there is no
     cap of one Trident footnote (R-J and R-N superseded: R-Y(1)); ‘The objective theory of contract requires an external
     manifestation of assent to an offer.’ [CB1B 71 | 534 | McHugh JA, Empirnall]; signature NOT NECESSARY: ‘Eric does
     not sign contracts’ and ‘Since Empirnall has taken the benefit of the work with knowledge of the terms on which it
     was offered, an objective bystander would conclude that Empirnall had accepted the offer’ [CB1B 72 | 536 | McHugh
     JA, Empirnall | a party bound without signing]; signature NOT DECISIVE: ‘the mere fact that her signature appears
     does not make her a party; this is a question to be resolved upon a consideration of the written instrument itself’
     [CB4 331 | 487 | Taylor and Owen JJ, Coulls | signature not sufficient; whether it is necessary was not in issue, so
     487 is never cited for ‘not necessary’: CRIT_fidelity_3 m7, adopted].
     Facts (deciding). ‘that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ (the narrator’s description); ‘I will do
    that’. Supporting: ‘signed by Grace and AMPL’; ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ (R-M).
    Core. (1) The burden aspect stated: a contract cannot impose an enforceable burden on a non-party, so ‘the clause
    as described’ (the narrator’s description is quoted or paraphrased at II.I2, whose unit it is: Appendix B; never ‘the
    clause states’ or ‘records’: D4) binds Rocky only if he manifested assent to it (Empirnall 534), the question for II.I2;
    the reason is not that Rocky did not sign, signature being ‘neither necessary nor decisive’ (not necessary: Empirnall
    536; not decisive: Coulls 487; T10), each footnoted to its own authority. (2) Rocky is LIKELY bound by his own ‘I will
    do that’, a promise in a bargain to which he was party (the hedge matching ‘bound to someone (moderate to strong)’:
    CRIT_round4 M4, adopted; the counted form is ‘His own ’I will do that’ likely binds him’); AMPL may enforce it only
    if Pierre accepted for AMPL (II.F2); if Pierre accepted for himself, AMPL is a non-party to the undertaking and can
    enforce only the clause, on II.I2’s assent and II.I3’s consideration, its entry into the Loan Agreement remaining
    arguable consideration on that alternative (S-13, moderate), so Rocky’s exposure to AMPL is then likely absent but
    arguable and is never stated as settled (CRIT_round9 M1; R-U(2): v9’s ‘has nothing to enforce’ stated as settled a
    consequence II.I3 leaves arguable).
    Credit. The T2 reconciliation in four words, ‘as to that clause only’, after ‘binds him only if he assented’ (Rocky’s
    assent, if found, makes him party to the guarantee promise alone, not promisee of Grace’s promise to repay, so I.F2’s
    ‘not a party’ and II.I2’s ‘likely assented’ do not contradict: CRIT_round5 m12, credit, +4, written where words
    allow); Rocky differs in kind from Mrs Coulls (named as promisor, not payee); (v12: v11’s credit ‘the gap disclosed
    (no extracted judgment develops the burden aspect …)’ is withdrawn, Trident being a course reading that states it
    (R-Y(1)) and a statement about what the readings extract being meta language (R-Z(1))); joint promisees on the
    undertaking (if given to Pierre and AMPL jointly, ‘an action to recover must have been brought by both promisees’:
    Coulls 486; weak for Rocky); the Loan Agreement’s text not narrated (the answer never asserts it ‘purports
    expressly’ to be between AMPL and Grace: D4). From v11 (UPGRADES_r1 U11, credit only): ‘as to that clause only’
    remains the first credit to write here; R10 accepts the T2 reconciliation without it only where I.F2’s joint-promisee
    clause states that no promise by Grace runs to Rocky, Taylor and Owen JJ framing two questions, ‘whether the
    testator’s wife was a party to the contract and whether, upon its true construction, the contract contains a promise
    by the company to pay to her’ (CB4 330, Coulls 486).
    Strength and tilt. The clause alone cannot bind Rocky (strong, S-8): ‘Rocky is bound because the clause is in the
    Loan Agreement’ is Poor with the D6 deduction; so is ‘Rocky is not bound to anyone because he never signed’. Bound
    to someone (moderate to strong); bound to AMPL (moderate, capped by the II.F2 conclusion and stated conditionally
    on it).
    Citation. Trident General Insurance Co Ltd v McNiece Bros Pty Ltd (1988) 165 CLR 107 (Deane J), by report with
    the judge named and no pin (R-Y(1), (2)): Trident is a Class 4A reading, so it is cited as any course case is, one
    source per marker, with no cap on the number of Trident footnotes; the reading carries no CLR page markers, so no
    pin can be verified, and the verifier’s lint ‘report citation with no pinpoint’ is an accepted, disclosed consequence,
    not a fault (R-Y(1); Part 9 item 7). v11’s alternative ‘Class 4A Slides, slide 2’ is withdrawn (R-Z(2)); a slide citation
    here is graded at R1 and R8 under R-Z(5). Residual risk, disclosed (CRIT_round7 m6, carried): the real marker reads
    the footnote, not this sheet, and may record a report citation with no pinpoint as a minor non-compliance at R8; the
    slide form that once removed that risk is barred, so the risk stands, and this sheet grades the no-pin form as no fault
    (Part 9 item 7); Empirnall 534 for assent; Empirnall 536 for ‘not necessary’; Coulls 487 only for ‘not decisive’ and
    ‘the written instrument itself’. One footnote marker per proposition inside the sentence (CRIT_round3 m2, adopted):
    the counted form reads ‘neither necessary[fn Empirnall 536] nor decisive[fn Coulls 487]’, two markers; v5’s single
    marker listing both sources is withdrawn (CRIT_fidelity_5 Finding 5, adopted).
    Drops. VG: the AMPL/Pierre dependency not drawn; signature-not-the-test absent (T10); Coulls 487 cited for ‘not
    necessary’ (a citation fault); ‘binds him’ unhedged (the tier). Good: ‘the clause cannot bind a non-party’ bare; ‘Rocky
    is bound by his oral promise’ bare; ‘a fortiori because he did not sign’ as the reason for the right result (right result,
    wrong reason, conclusive: the same grade as I.F2’s ‘Grace is right because Rocky did not sign’, because the same
    signature reasoning with the same right result carries the same grade whichever party it helps: CRIT_round4 M11;
    R-R(4); v4’s Poor was asymmetric). Fair: the benefit aspect only; the oral route missed and liability rested on the
    clause; the clause said to ‘state’ or ‘record’ a guarantee as a stated fact (D4). Poor: either D6 conclusion. Omitted.
    Marker comments. ‘Privity has two aspects: the burden aspect decides whether the clause alone binds Rocky;
    signature is not the test either way.’ ‘Answer with specificity to individual Ps: to whom was Rocky’s undertaking
    given?’

II.I2 Content: what Pierre ‘expected’ against the clause as described; assent to the written words on Empirnall
535 to 536; the benefit named; ‘attended’ as the knowledge fact, the inference marked; ‘provided by Rocky’
(3.5; C; floor 80) [Empirnall 535 to 536]

    Rules at source. ‘A more accurate statement is that where an offeree with a reasonable opportunity to reject the
    offer of goods or services takes the benefit of them under circumstances which indicate that they were to be paid for
    in accordance with the offer, it is open to the tribunal of fact to hold that the offer was accepted according to its
    terms. A useful analogy is to be found in the “ticket cases” where an offeree, who has or ought to have knowledge of
    the terms of a contract of carriage or bailment, is generally bound unless he raises objection’ [CB1B 72 | 535 |
    McHugh JA (Samuels JA agreeing; Kirby P to substantially the same effect), Empirnall | ratio. McHugh JA’s OWN
    criterion has three elements: an offeree with a reasonable opportunity to reject the offer of goods or services; who
    takes the benefit of them; under circumstances which indicate that they were to be paid for in accordance with the
    offer; and his holding at 536 rests on actual knowledge (‘taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms
    and knowledge of the offeror’s reliance’). The ‘has or ought to have knowledge of the terms’ words are the
ANALOGY (‘A useful analogy’), confined by its own words to ‘a contract of carriage or bailment’ (MacRobertson
Miller is the course’s ticket case, CB1A 48); v3 spliced the analogy’s words into the rule as its second limb and
deducted for omitting an ‘ought to have’ limb the rule does not contain: CRIT_fidelity_3 M2 and CRIT_round3 M3,
adopted]; ‘Since Empirnall has taken the benefit of the work with knowledge of the terms on which it was offered, an
objective bystander would conclude that Empirnall had accepted the offer on those terms and conditions’ [CB1B 72 |
536]; ‘The ultimate issue is whether a reasonable bystander would regard the conduct of the offeree, including his
silence, as signalling to the offeror that his offer has been accepted’ [535]; contra: ‘an offeror cannot erect a contract
between himself and the offeree by the device of stating that unless he hears from the offeree he will consider the
offeree bound’ [CB1B 71 | 534 | McHugh JA]; Felthouse 876 (uncommunicated assent); ‘In all the circumstances it
was for the defendant to make plain that its conduct amounted only to taking advantage of the proposal but not to
submitting to the disadvantages’ [CB1B 81 | 181 | Heydon JA, Brambles | his route] (credit). Lord Denning MR’s ‘last
shot’ (Butler 404 to 405) is his alone and concerns standard forms: a remote analogy at most.
Facts (deciding). ‘expected’ (and the narrator’s ‘ensure that Grace made all payments … promptly’); ‘that Rocky
personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ (the narrator’s description); ‘the personal guarantee provided by
Rocky’ (R-M); ‘attended’ (Rocky, Grace and Pierre ‘attended a meeting at AMPL’s office’, at which the Loan
Agreement was entered into and the clause ‘was included … before it was signed’: the attendance is the one fact in
the problem that goes to McHugh JA’s knowledge element, so it is DECIDING and is quoted in the counted
paragraph, ‘included at the meeting he ’attended’‘: CRIT_round4 M5, adopted; Appendix B). That the inclusion
happened at the meeting rather than in a draft before it is itself an inference from ’At the meeting … entered into’
and ‘included … before it was signed’; the counted form is now ‘included, arguably at the meeting he ’attended’’
(CRIT_fidelity_6 Finding 2 and CRIT_round6 m6, adopted, +1 from the slack), so that the inference that helps AMPL
is marked exactly as the inference that helps Rocky at II.C2 (‘The facts arguably place the clause after the
exchange’) is, §3’s one rule applied identically whichever party it helps. v6 carried the unmarked form ‘included at
the meeting he ’attended’’ and its changes file attributed that acceptance to words in R-S(6) that the ruling does not
contain; the acceptance was a reviser’s judgment call (CRIT_round5 m4, recorded rather than funded), disclosed as
such in SHEET_v7_changes.md and now moot. A drafter who writes the unmarked form is graded as the identity
table graded v6: Excellent, the inference being carried by the quoted word and by ‘likely’ in the verdict, though the
marked form is the counted one. Supporting: ‘included … before it was signed’; his presence at the inclusion is an
inference from attendance, so ‘in his presence’ is written ‘arguably’ or as ‘at the meeting he attended’
(CRIT_fidelity_3 m2, adopted); no objection shown; nothing narrated says Rocky read or was shown the clause’s
words; ten months of check-ins (admissible on formation of the oral bargain and on Rocky’s assent, inadmissible on
the meaning of ‘ensure’ or of the clause).
Core. (1) The two contents distinguished with the right speakers: what Rocky promised is what Pierre ‘expected’,
reported by the narrator as ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ (interest included; procuring performance), whereas
the clause is described as one ‘that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ (the defined principal; ‘on
default’ is guarantee law and is not said). (2) Assent to the written content decided on McHugh JA’s own criterion as
the source states it: whether, with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’, Rocky took the benefit of AMPL’s written
offer ‘with knowledge of its terms’, THE OFFER NAMED so that ‘its’ keeps its antecedent (McHugh JA at 536:
‘taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms’, CB1B 72; v10’s prescribed ‘took the benefit ’with
knowledge of its terms’’ detached ‘its’ from ‘an offer’; the v11 form ‘took the benefit of AMPL’s written offer ’with
knowledge of its terms’‘, +4: UPGRADES_r1 U13; knowledge of the offeror’s reliance, which describes Empirnall’s
facts and appears in no statement of the rule, and the disclosure of the analogy (Part 9 item 33) remain credit) (535
to 536; the ’under circumstances which indicate’ element may be stated in terms, credit); the BENEFIT NAMED,
because the criterion has a benefit element and a paragraph that names none is conclusive under §1(b): the $10,000
promise, taken as the other side of the clause recording the bargain he had just proposed (CRIT_round3 M3,
adopted: moved from credit to core); the KNOWLEDGE ELEMENT APPLIED TO A FACT, because the holding at 536
rests on ‘taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms’ and a paragraph that states the knowledge
element and names no fact going to it before concluding ‘assented’ is the conclusive shape his marker graded Good
(§1(b); CRIT_round4 M5, adopted: moved from credit to core): the fact is Rocky’s attendance at the meeting where
the clause was included, carried by the quoted word (‘included, arguably at the meeting he ’attended’‘, the counted
form from v7), the inference from attendance to knowledge being marked by ’arguably’, by the quotation and by
‘likely’ in the verdict, and a drafter who wants the knowledge inference itself explicit writes ‘arguably knew’; the
ticket-case analogy (‘has or ought to have knowledge’) is CREDIT, usable only with its confinement to ‘a contract of
carriage or bailment’ disclosed; for AMPL, the clause was included without objection shown (never ‘without narrated
objection’: R-R(1)), to record the bargain he had just proposed (credit), and the narrator’s ‘the personal guarantee
provided by Rocky’ proves that he provided one; for Rocky, that stipulation establishes neither the clause’s words
nor that he saw them (R-M) (credit: ‘provided’ arguably describes the oral undertaking; he was the offeror of ‘that’).
(3) A conclusion in the tier for the strength, with the further information named in the trailing clause (the clause’s
words; whether Rocky saw them; whether he objected) AND ITS DIRECTION (eg on a ‘likely assented’ verdict,
‘unless he never saw its words’; on a ‘likely did not assent’ verdict, ‘unless he saw and accepted its words’; a same-
count rewording of the counted trailing clause, which named the information without its effect: UPGRADES_r1 U3;
R6), which is also the answer to Rocky’s strongest counter, that the $10,000 was the price of his own completed oral
offer and not of the written clause (Kirby P at 170 by analogy: an additional term arising after acceptance ‘cannot
represent consideration’; credit in terms, met by the trailing clause because whether he assented to the written
content turns on the words he saw: CRIT_round4 M5).
Credit. Heydon JA’s ‘make plain’ (his route); the oral bargain complete before the clause was written (Kirby P at
170, by analogy: an additional term arising after acceptance ‘cannot represent consideration’); Proscour only to
    frame the difference; on either content Rocky is exposed if Grace defaults on a due date, the measure (a debt on call
    or damages) being remedies law, which the answer does not argue and never frames as outside any scope (R-Z(1),
    (4)); whether the clause was in the draft before the conversation; on the Pierre alternative the benefit taken was
    Pierre’s promise, not AMPL’s, which weakens assent to AMPL’s written content (S-18, weak to moderate;
    CRIT_round9 M1, credit: the counted ‘the $10,000 promise being his benefit’ names the promise whoever made it,
    and a drafter who states the weakening in a clause loses nothing).
    Strength and tilt. Assent to the written ‘personally guaranteed’ content moderate on the guarantee reading of ‘the
    clause’, weak to moderate on the other (S-9). Either conclusion can be Excellent if it applies McHugh JA’s criterion
    with the benefit named, meets the other side’s best fact (including ‘provided by Rocky’ on the R-M line), and names
    the further information; no method and no lean is Good (§2). An answer that treats ‘provided by Rocky’ as stipulated
    evidence of assent is eligible for Excellent provided it says what the stipulation does and does not establish (not the
    clause’s exact words).
    Drops. VG: further information missing, or given without its direction (U3); the offer whose benefit was taken not
    named, so that ‘its terms’ has no antecedent (U13); ‘provided by Rocky’ neither used nor tested; the ‘reasonable
    opportunity to reject’ or the knowledge element omitted so that AMPL’s best words are understated. Good: ‘Rocky is
    bound as guarantor’ bare; the benefit taken not named (§1(b)); the knowledge element stated and applied to no fact
    before ‘assented’ (§1(b); ‘attended’ or an equivalent fact absent). Credit wrong: the ticket-case ‘ought to have’ words
    stated as McHugh JA’s rule without the confinement (VG; a wrong rule). Fair: ‘ensure’ and ‘guarantee’ treated as the
    same with no reasons; ‘ensure … promptly’ attributed to Rocky as his words (D4); the clause said to ‘state’ or
    ‘record’ a guarantee (D4). Poor: Proscour’s damages statement applied as the Australian rule; Rocky’s silence held
    acceptance on Felthouse’s facts; Butler’s ‘last shot’ used as more than a remote analogy. Omitted.
    Marker comment. ‘Empirnall asks whether an offeree with a reasonable opportunity to reject took the benefit with
    knowledge of the terms: what benefit did Rocky take, and what does the problem tell us he knew of the clause?’

II.I3 Consideration moving from AMPL, conditional on II.F2; Pao On’s second condition on timing; AMPL’s
fallback put (4.0; C; floor 73) [Pao On 629 to 630; Roscorla 237]

    Issue. Whether AMPL, as promisee calling on Rocky’s undertaking, gave consideration for it.
    Rules at source. ‘Must flow between the parties in both directions’ [S2A slide 2 | slide only]; past consideration: ‘a
    consideration past and executed will support no other promise than such as would be implied by law’ [CB2A 113 |
    237 | Lord Denman CJ delivering the judgment of the Court, Roscorla]; Pao On: ‘An act done before the giving of a
    promise to make a payment or to confer some other benefit can sometimes be consideration for the promise. The act
    must have been done at the promisors’ request: the parties must have understood that the act was to be
    remunerated either by a payment or the conferment of some other benefit: and payment, or the conferment of a
    benefit, must have been legally enforceable had it been promised in advance.’ and its application, ‘The parties
    understood at the time of the main agreement that the restriction on selling must be compensated for by the benefit
    of a guarantee against a drop in price’ [PO | [1980] AC 614, 629–30 | the Board (Lord Scarman delivering) | ratio on
    the First Question]; the Board’s gloss, read in the official text; course-stated in substance only (Roscorla 237;
    Australian Woollen Mills (PC) 550, ‘The presence of a request does not, however, in itself establish a contract’), the
    words themselves sitting in the casebook’s omitted pp 126 to 130; never quoted, unpinnable (CRIT_fidelity_8 Finding
    4; ISSUES_SETTLED’s register line, ‘course-stated in substance’): the recital of a prior request ‘is not sufficient in
    itself’ and the second precondition ‘is simply one of the construction of the words of the contract in the
    circumstances of its making’ (O-3); a duty owed to a third party: Pao On 632 (II.C2); Glidewell LJ: ‘Pao On is a case of
    a tripartite relationship’ [CB2B 119 | 15]; AWM ‘really offered as consideration … really done in consideration’ (456
    to 457); Asquith LJ’s whole sentence [CB2A 102 | 460 | quoted by the Court | never cut to ‘an agreement to forbear
    … is a good consideration’ (D2)]; detriment to the promisee suffices (Musumeci 745).
    Facts (deciding). ‘27 February’ as the date of the advance; ‘Rocky asked’ (from v11 the first condition, the request,
    met on that word: UPGRADES_r1 U32, reversing CRIT_round3 M5 option (a)‘s move to credit); ’I will do that if you
    also promise to pay $10,000’ (the pricing that meets AMPL’s fallback: U2). Supporting (credit): Pierre’s expectation
    narrated only on 8 April and AMPL’s return being Grace’s interest (the two reasons why nothing shows a 27
    February understanding; credit for the same reason); nothing narrated on 27 February about a guarantee; AMPL
    entered the Loan Agreement with Grace at the same meeting.
    Core. (1) The point stated conditionally on II.F2: if AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise is fresh consideration
    moving from AMPL (strong on that view); if the $10,000 was Pierre’s, AMPL needs its own consideration and the 27
    February advance is past (Roscorla 237 footnoted on the words ‘the past advance’, its own marker, with Pao On 629
    to 630 on the exception carrying a second marker: one source for one proposition, R-R(3); the counted form is
    ‘AMPL’s own promise suffices; if Pierre promised, the past advance,[fn] under Pao On, suffices only where the
    parties ’understood that the act was to be remunerated’[fn]‘; from v11 the doctrine is NAMED once in the course’s
    term, past consideration (RG2A: ’What is the rule with respect to past consideration? Are there any exceptions to the
    general rule?’; S2A PDF page 20, ‘Past consideration’; S2A PDF page 23, ‘Exception to past consideration rule’; the
    v11 form ‘the past advance, past consideration,’ +2: UPGRADES_r1 U7; R-X(4)); v5’s ‘if AMPL, that promise suffices;
    if Pierre, the past advance’ elided the verb of each ‘if’ clause and read as note form, an R1 lapse under the type
    added in v6: CRIT_round5 M7, adopted under R-S(2)). (2) Pao On’s FIRST condition met on its fact, as the Board
    itself runs each condition on its fact (‘The act must have been done at the promisors’ request … All three features
    are present in this case. The promise given to Fu Chip under the main agreement not to sell the shares for a year
    was at Lau’s request’, Pao On extract, [1980] AC 614, 629 to 630): the advance was made at Rocky’s request, ‘Rocky
    asked’ (the v11 form ‘the past advance, made at Rocky’s request,’, +4: UPGRADES_r1 U32, folded into this item
because the ‘similar shape’ below is a guarantee given after an act done at the guarantor’s request); the third
condition is credit to state; and the SECOND condition as the contest: nothing narrated shows that the parties
understood on 27 February that the advance was to be remunerated by a benefit from Rocky, whereas in Pao On the
understanding existed ‘at the time of the main agreement’ (the comparison named: similar shape, different timing;
credit: the two reasons, Pierre’s ‘expected’ narrated only on 8 April and AMPL’s return being Grace’s interest). (3) A
conclusion in the tier for the strength on the alternative that Pierre promised (‘likely’), written ‘if Pierre promised’,
never ‘on that branch’ (R7), WITH AMPL’S FALLBACK PUT in a clause (CRIT_round5 M6, adopted in the ‘put’ form
under R-S(3)): AMPL’s entry into the Loan Agreement at the same meeting, tied by Pierre’s expectation to ‘payments
under the Loan Agreement’, is the course’s second candidate for consideration moving from AMPL
(ISSUES_SETTLED S-13, moderate), and a verdict that AMPL ‘gave none’ without naming it overstates the tier and
leaves a C unit’s counter unput; the counted form is the absolute clause ‘its entry into the Loan Agreement
remaining arguable consideration’ after ‘AMPL likely gave none’ (the noun ‘consideration’ added in v8, +1, so that
the clause says what the entry is arguable as: CRIT_round7 m7, adopted; v7’s ‘remaining arguable’ is not deducted,
the sentence being about consideration throughout); and, from v11, the fallback MET, not only put, or ACCEPTED
with the bargain requirement applied (UPGRADES_r1 U2, adopted as core and as a grading fix, §2 already listing
‘the fallback limb of II.I3’ among the units where a paragraph with no lean and no method is Good while v10’s
‘remaining arguable consideration’ gave that limb neither): the bargain test asks whether AMPL’s entry was ‘really
done in consideration of’ the undertaking (‘it should be made to appear that the statement or announcement which is
relied on as a promise was really offered as consideration for the doing of the act, and that the act was really done in
consideration of a potential promise inherent in the statement’, CB2A 101, Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457, the
Court), and Rocky’s own words name another price, ‘I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly’;
the v11 form adds ‘, though Rocky priced his undertaking at’$10,000’’ after ‘remaining arguable consideration’ (+7),
on its own marker to Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457. Accepting the fallback with the bargain requirement
applied (AMPL may read ‘also’ as ‘in addition to entering the Loan Agreement’) is equally Excellent (S-13,
moderate). Meeting it in the fuller form (the critic’s +12, the entry not ‘really done in consideration of’ the
undertaking stated in terms) is credit.
Credit. AMPL’s fallback met or accepted in a fuller form than core (3) requires: its entry into the Loan Agreement is
arguably ‘really done in consideration of’ the undertaking (or, if AMPL was already bound to Grace from 27
February, a promise to perform a duty owed to a third party: Pao On 632), a detriment sufficing though the benefit
went to Grace; against which the express words price the undertaking at $10,000 and AMPL had already advanced
(S-13; either conclusion Excellent if the bargain requirement is applied and the pricing point met or accepted);
Lampleigh’s ‘request’ and Bowen LJ’s ‘implication that at the time it was rendered it was to be paid for’ (the extract;
cited as quoted by Lord Scarman without an AC page pin); the recital of consideration in the guarantee clause as
further information (O-3); the AWM creditor-forbearance example labelled an analogy; the consistency points (T7:
Rocky cannot say his undertaking was given only for past consideration while claiming the $10,000 was given for it;
T17), each stated once; the further information that would reverse it (evidence of an understanding on 27 February).
Strength and tilt. Two limbs, each with its own rating (corrected to ISSUES_SETTLED S-12 and S-13: CRIT_round5
M6; R-S(3)): the past advance as consideration, unproven under Pao On’s second condition (moderate to strong
against AMPL; S-12), a contrary conclusion on that limb capped at Very Good; AMPL’s consideration on the Pierre
alternative taken as a whole, once the fallback is live, MODERATE (S-13), so that a conclusion that AMPL gave
consideration which rests on the fallback with the bargain requirement applied and the pricing point met or
accepted is Excellent, and ‘AMPL gave none’ is Excellent only with the fallback put and met (from v11: U2). v5’s
single ‘moderate to strong against AMPL’ line rated the whole question by its first limb and tilted the unit against
AMPL beyond the settled ratings, which on the Pierre alternative was bad advice to Rocky (told that AMPL has
nothing to enforce). An answer that uses Pierre’s ‘expected’ as evidence, marked ‘arguably’, that an understanding
existed on 27 February (the narrator’s past tense permits the inference) is that capped contrary conclusion; an
answer that places the understanding on 8 April misapplies the second condition’s timing (the condition’s own words
do not state the time; the timing is read from the Board’s application, ‘at the time of the main agreement’) and is

Part 7. Global rows (20%), scoring rule and automatic deductions

Global-row cap (R-C). A global row cannot be graded above the lowest grade, among the units, of the core item it
summarises: R2 at most the lowest application grade (the authority applied by its own criterion; the comparison named at
K and C units); R4 at most Very Good if any unit is Omitted and at most Good if a claim is missed; R6 at most the lowest
further-information or strength grade; R8 at most the lowest citation grade; R10 at most the lowest consistency grade; R1,
R3, R5, R7 and R9 are graded independently. Reason: his real marker left the global rows ungraded in Part A, so the
global block must compound unit failures, never offset them.

R1. Style, clarity of expression, conciseness, grammar & spelling, persuasiveness of argument: his voice (4.0)

Measured against his LAWS1061 Part A (the authority) and VOICE.md (the measurement), with python3 -I voice_stats_v2.py
on the body (headings, footnotes and the count line are stripped by the script). - Excellent requires all of: flowing multi-
clause sentences joined by semicolons (the next step) and colons (claim, then proof); whole-answer measures within the
range of his Parts I to VI (mean sentence length 17.8 to 24.7 words; sentences under 12 words 9.1% to 36.4%, all verdicts
or one-line frames and never two in a row inside a paragraph; semicolons 0.85 to 2.02 per 100 words; colons 0.81 to 2.57
per 100 words; sentences containing a semicolon or colon 36.4% to 72.7%); the ranges apply to the whole body, not per
unit, so K and C units are written in his 20 to 25-word sentences and the one-sentence L forms are balanced by short
verdicts (the appendix shows the balance: mean 24.0; 10.0% under 12 words; 1.04; 0.90; 41.7%; the mean sits near the
top of his range, so a drafter who lengthens sentences further falls out of it: every fix that adds a clause to an existing
sentence pushes the mean up, so additions go in as new sentences or by splitting a long one, never as a further clause:
CRIT_round4 m14); a short counter-frame (‘AMPL would say nothing bound until execution’) and an element sub-verdict
(‘AMPL being ’owned and controlled’ by Pierre supplies consent’; ‘His payment therefore likely does not meet it’) count as
his frames and verdicts under VOICE.md F9 (his Part A: ‘On the other hand, only SPC knew its finances and that GR
would rely’), so a drafter does not merge them to be safe and fall below the 9.1% floor (CRIT_round4 m14, adopted); the
rule-then-proof join written as a colon, because the L form (‘fact, rule, so result’) produces semicolons and ‘so’ but few
colons; every semicolon joins a step to the step it follows from (a sentence of three or more semicolon-joined clauses each
a conclusion without its reason is conclusive and an R1 lapse); his signposts (‘Firstly’, ‘Secondly, however,’, ‘Decisively,’,
‘Nor does … assist:’, ‘… is distinguishable:’, ‘… is analogous because …’, ‘The strongest counter is …’, ‘On balance,’, ‘the
better view is that … likely …’) used where they fit and never at a required rate: the requirement is ‘no signpost he never
uses’, ‘Whether … turns on’ as an opener in at most about 1 in 6 sentences, ordinals where three or more factors are
weighed as separate sentences (his stacked-facts sentence, VOICE.md 2.3 examples 14 and 15, weighs three or four
quoted facts inside one sentence without ordinals and is equally his form), valence tags only on factor sentences

Scoring rule

For each unit and each global row: points × multiplier (Excellent 1.00; Very Good 0.75; Good 0.60; Fair 0.45; Poor 0.20;
Omitted 0). Mark out of 100 = sum of all items − automatic deductions, never below 0, rounded down to a whole mark.
100 is awarded only if every unit and every global row is Excellent (each with the quoted sentence that earns it
and the source check) and no automatic deduction applies.

Calibration (R-C). His real LAWS1061 Part A grades, re-read cell by cell from the .pdf pages (v5; the recount stands,
was re-run for v6 and v8, and was confirmed by the round-7 critic and, from the rendered pages, by the round-8 critic; the
arithmetic is recomputed for v10): Preliminary Exc; 1(a) 3 Exc, 2 VG, 1 Good; 1(b) 1 Exc, 5 VG; 1(c) 2 Exc, 1 Good; 1(d) 2
Exc, 1 VG; 2 (statutory authorities) 2 Exc, 3 VG, 1 Good: 11 Excellent, 11 Very Good, 3 Good, no Fair, no Poor (25 cells);
the three global rows ungraded; Part A mark 82%. On these multipliers, with the printed Part weights (15/25/15/15/30,
the preliminary row unweighted) and equal weight within each Part, his dot grades give 0.850 × 15 + 0.792 × 25 + 0.867
× 15 + 0.917 × 15 + 0.808 × 30 = 83.5% of the dot points (v3 printed 83.7; the recount is 83.5); with the global block (20
of 100) capped at the grade of the units it summarises (Very Good on his sheet), the whole-sheet mark is 0.835 × 80 + 20
× 0.75 = 81.8, and 81.4 if R2 is capped at Good (his two ‘conclusive’ units); both within one mark of 82. The disclosure
the result depends on (CRIT_round4 m15, adopted): the dot points alone give 83.5, which is 1.5 off, and the within-one-
mark result holds only on the assumption that every ungraded global row is graded Very Good, the grade of the units it
summarises; if the five independent rows (R1, R3, R5, R7 and R9, 9.5 points) were Excellent, as his marker’s Part B style
comment might suggest, with R2 Good and the rest Very Good, the figure is 83.76 (v9 printed ‘83.7’, a truncation beside
the rounded 81.4: CRIT_round9 m6; R-U(6)). The assumption is a judgment call and is stated as the one on which the
calibration rests. The multipliers and the cap are unchanged from v2 and the grid change (23 units) does not touch the
calibration, which is run on his sheet’s own weights. The multipliers are a disclosed judgment call; the global-row cap is
what makes them reproduce his result.

Automatic deductions (applied after the grades; each instance counts)

One error, one deduction (R-U(6); CRIT_round9 m3 to m5). Each error is graded once: where the same fault
appears under two Drops lines or two automatic deductions, only the heaviest applicable applies (eg ‘ensure … promptly’
attributed to Rocky is D4 and not also D2; Knox CJ’s severance words as the joint judgment’s own are D2 at I.A and not
also a VG credit-wrong line; ‘[1980] AC 615’ is VG with D11 at II.I3 and not also Poor). The global-row cap (R-C) is not a
deduction and still applies, because it is what makes the global rows compound unit failures rather than offset them; D6’s
‘−2 each, in addition to the Poor grade’ is that deduction’s own rule and is unchanged. One error carried into a later
unit is deducted once, at the unit where it is made (R-V(1); CRIT_round10 m9): a later unit that applies the earlier
finding is graded on its own question and drops only for a new error of its own (eg ‘AMPL clearly gave none’ at II.I3 is
graded there, and ‘AMPL has nothing to enforce’ at II.I4, its consequence, is not deducted again; but a later unit that
turns the carried finding into new advice that the strength does not support, such as II.I4’s ‘so do nothing’ or ‘so pay now’
on an overstated date from II.G, makes a new error in the advice and is graded at that unit, R-U(4)).

     three words are counted by Word): −2 (R-R(6); CRIT_round4 M13, adopted: the verifier’s own lint, ‘Stated word
     count N does not match the count N−3’, is the expected R-P consequence and is disclosed in the appendix, not a
     fault).
     D8. Format. Bullet or numbered points in the body; an extended quotation (any single quotation over 20 words, his
     longest in Part A being 19); quoted words over 20% of the body (R-G); a coversheet, an unnecessary title page,
     unnecessary headers or footers (page numbers excepted: R-R(8)), a bibliography: −1 each.
     D9. Voice mechanics. Em dash or en dash as punctuation, double quotation marks, contraction, first person: −0.5
     each, to a maximum of −3. A dash or contraction reproduced inside a quotation counts (this is Yusuf’s own rule, not
     his marker’s, who would not deduct for quoting the problem verbatim: CRIT_round3 m16, disclosed) (the problem
     itself contains both: ‘Bowral Project – wait and see’; ‘the Loan – the $1.15m’; ‘you can’t enforce anything’; ‘you won’t
     see a cent’; ‘if you don’t leave off’): quote around it, or quote only the words on one side of it. An en dash in a
     footnote pin range (eg 629–30) is correct AGLC and is not a fault. A quotation that itself contains a quotation is never
     reproduced with the inner quotation: quote only the outer words that carry the point, or paraphrase; an inner
     quotation reproduced is −0.5 under this item.
     D10. Italics. A case name or statute title not italicised (text or footnote): −0.5 each, to a maximum of −2.
     D11. Pao On cited other than [1980] AC 614 with pins 629–30 or 632, or with a wrong judge named (any name
     other than Lord Scarman for the Board); or a Pao On pin other than 629–30 or 632 given for the Lampleigh or Re
       Casey’s Patents passages: −1 each. ‘(Lord Scarman for the Board)’ is not a fault (R-P). A pin to Hobart 106 or 1 Ch
       115–16 inside an AGLC ‘quoted in’ form is the course extract’s own and is not a fault (CRIT_fidelity_2 m10, adopted).
       D12. Proxy terminology beyond R7’s cap: −0.5 each, to a maximum of −2.
       D13. Official texts and Trident. A fourth footnote resting on a proposition the course never states; a Trident CLR
       pin (none can be verified, the reading carrying no page markers: R-Y(1)); an official quotation not checked verbatim
       against the saved file: −1 each, and R8 capped at Good. (v12: v11’s ‘a second Trident footnote (R-N)’ is withdrawn,
       R-N being superseded; a Trident quotation is checked against the course reading as any course case is.)



Part 8. The v11 core costs (R-X(3)); the v10 floors kept as a record

What changed in v11. Until v10 this Part printed a floor table: each floor was the count of a real paragraph in his voice
carrying exactly the unit’s core (the paragraphs in SHEET_v10_appendix_NOT_FOR_DRAFTERS.md, 1,442 words with 52 heading words,
1,494 of 1,495, slack 1, verified with verify.py and voice_stats_v2.py), and that table was the proof that the Excellent standard
was attainable in 1,495 words (R-L(2) and (4)). The v11 cores, adopted from UPGRADES_r1 and R-X, cost more than that
table holds, so the floors no longer fit and are no longer the proof. Under R-X(3) the cores are the requirement and the
floors are a feasibility record, not a quota: the answer, not the appendix, is now the feasibility proof. The answer
reviser funds the v11 cores in R-X(3)‘s order ((a) zero-cost rewrites; (b) cutting duplication, cross-references,
restatements and credit text; (c) compressing units whose result is not in doubt: I.F1, P, I.F3, II.E, II.F1), never dropping a
unit’s core, and records anything still unfunded in the map as a residual risk graded by the unit’s Drops. No appendix
paragraph has been written or counted for v11; the costs below are the UPGRADES_r1 deltas (verify.py’s rule: whitespace
tokens containing a letter or digit) against the v10 counted forms, and the rulings’ own deltas, and they measure what the

draft also needs U24’s reason clause at II.G, and about 1,576 if condition precedent is named in II.H’s text rather than its
heading). The 76 words are found by the answer reviser under R-X(3), never by relaxing a core. UPGRADES_r1 section 2
ranks the paid items by marks at risk per word (rank 1, U16, 2.38 per word; rank 16, U7’s remainder, 0.04 to 0.06) for

inside sentences and splitting long ones, and the R1 voice test is run on the answer itself (R-L(4) as R-X(3) now applies it).

What this means for the standard. The Excellent standard is the v11 cores, unchanged by length: (i) every unit’s core
is graded whatever the unit’s length (§1); (ii) every credit item is optional; (iii) the decide-once rules are applied; (iv) the L
units remain one or two sentences carrying the rule’s operative words; (v) the verdict sentences carry the strength, the
reason and the trailing further-information clause with its direction. If the answer reviser shows that a core cannot be met
within 1,495 words in his voice, the remedy is a disclosed demotion under the first-demotion list below, graded as printed,
or a ruling; never a silent relaxation. v4’s merge order is deleted (R-R(5); CRIT_round4 M12, adopted): each of its four
merges shrank an item its unit lists as core without saying whether the merged form still earned Excellent, which is the
silent relaxation R-B forbids. The ledgers below record how the v10 floors were reached; they are history, kept because
the first-demotion list and Part 9 refer to them.

  1. Weights carry v2’s (ISSUES_SETTLED S-28 re-balanced per CRIT_harsh F16), each merged unit taking the sum of

     for v9 and v10: 83.5% of the dot points; 81.8 and 81.4 whole-sheet).
  3. Strength caps follow R-E: strong, contrary Poor; moderate to strong, contrary Very Good; moderate or weaker or
     open, either conclusion Excellent if best-reasoned; misstated strength Very Good, or Good where it changes the
     advice, symmetric both ways; no lean and no method at any open unit, Good (§2).
  4. The condition (II.H) is moderate to strong against Rocky under R-O (restoring S-16), v2’s ‘moderate’ being
     withdrawn: the fact of the events as described, that AMPL’s call does not itself prevent Grace from repaying, is a
     fact, not guarantee law, and answers Rocky’s co-operation and prevention arguments; since v5 it is the unit’s
     decisive reason in the counted paragraph and in core (4), now written in his ‘nothing suggests’ form and meeting the
     duty in its own words (‘omitted nothing necessary’), Mobil’s prevention analogy being credit from v6 (R-S(4)); the
     pricing point (‘no reward for the failure he undertook to prevent’) being, from v8, core (2)‘s answer to the
     commercial reading of Rocky’s words (CRIT_round7 M1; R-T(1)), while remaining no answer to the co-operation
     argument in its call form (that AMPL’s call stops Grace repaying), which core (4) meets on its own terms
     (CRIT_round4 M9; R-O); the stronger form of that argument (that AMPL, by accepting Rocky’s payment, would end
     any possibility that ’Grace repays the Loan’) is met in substance by the same pricing point, because a duty ‘to do
     everything necessary on their part to enable the plaintiff to have the benefit of the contract’ (CB2A 109, 185) enables
     the benefit S2’s construction defines, a reward priced on Grace’s repayment, and does not require AMPL to forgo
     payment under the undertaking to preserve it; the discharge question (what Rocky’s payment does to Grace’s debt)
     is guarantee law, not argued, never relied on and, from v12, never flagged as outside any scope (R-Z(1), (4);
     CRIT_round8 m6, recorded at II.H Core (4) at no cost); Lindley LJ’s ‘It is for the defendants to shew what it does
     mean’ remains no rule of onus (CB1A 44 to 45, read in full context). The duty to co-operate is cited as Mason J’s
     principle applied by McHugh JA (CB2A 109, 185), with no status word in the text (R-F), because McHugh JA’s
     minority on the result does not change the weight a court gives Mason J’s principle.
  5. The 12 February intention (I.D) is moderate on the course materials; the sheet allows either conclusion to reach

    no core carries; (c) a grading rule that contradicts the brief, the Instructions, ISSUES_SETTLED or R-A to R-Z (the

    discretion. Later markers and critics apply this definition before labelling a finding.

Appendix A. Consistency traps (ISSUES_SETTLED 3.X, reduced to those a position
engages)

Required, one clause each where it bites (R10): T4 asserting the 12 February email invites Grace’s counterclaim (I.D
credit; engaged only if the answer holds the email binding); T8 class 3 or a writing requirement for the 8 April bargain
loses both sides (II.B or II.C2); T10 signature cuts both ways (I.F2 and II.I1); T11 one counterparty, or Pierre on both
sides (II.F2 and II.I4); T13 Rocky could pay $1,150,000 and lose the $10,000 (II.H or II.I4; the counted structure states it
at II.I4); T17 AMPL cannot have both 27 February arguments (II.C2 or II.I3; engaged only if the answer accepts AMPL’s
sequence and runs past consideration).

Avoided without words (no clause required; a breach is graded at R10): T1 the 12 months (demand v defence;
decided once at II.G); T2 party to the Loan Agreement v burden defence (reconciled, where words allow, by the four-word
credit clause ‘as to that clause only’ at II.I1: CRIT_round5 m12); T3 ‘I will do that’ binds both ways (carried by II.D’s
clause); T5 ‘the Loan Agreement with AMPL’ (the narrator’s description of the demand, usable as its proven content
under R-D, never as Rocky’s words) undercuts any claim that the money was Rocky’s; T6 class 3 or illusory defeats the
email claim but protects against the counterclaim; T7 past consideration for the undertaking v consideration for the
$10,000; T9 ‘once Grace repays’ read to include Rocky’s payment fights his own words; T12 attacking Grace’s
consideration destroys the $10,000 trigger; T14 check-ins go to formation, not meaning; T15 keep the 12 February email
and the Loan Agreement separate; T16 the two readings of ‘the clause’ (both run at II.F1); T18 the a fortiori reasoning
confined to the guarantee reading.

Avoided by the core’s own wording (from v11; a breach is graded once, at R10): T19 I.D’s ‘Confirmed’ settling ‘the
essentials’ (or ‘all essential terms’) concedes the premise of Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps it may be different where agreement has
been reached on all essential terms but the determination of subsidiary matters has been left to one of the parties’ (CB3B
190, Godecke 647), which I.E core (3) then resists; avoided by naming what ‘Confirmed’ settled, ‘amount, term and rate’
(UPGRADES_r1 U26). T20 I.C finding consideration without qualification while I.E finds Rocky’s promise illusory stands
on two footings, ‘A contract made for a consideration which is illusory is unenforceable’ (CB3B 166, Pace 150); avoided by
I.C’s ‘in form’, whether the promise is illusory, and so the consideration good, being decided at E (UPGRADES_r1 U10).

from this sheet alone)

Claims (ISSUES_SETTLED 1.4, condensed). C1 repayment of the principal ‘under the Loan Agreement with AMPL’
against Grace (fails: privity); C2 repayment under the 12 February email (fails: no binding contract and Rocky lent
nothing); C3 any implied promise by Grace to repay, reimburse or indemnify (no promise by Grace to Rocky appears;
disposed of in a substantive clause in P or wherever the answer first meets it, never with guarantee law named as
excluded: R-Z(1)); C4 the Development Agreement (stipulated ‘legally binding’; Rocky’s entitlement contingent on a profit
‘not yet shown’; a non-issue to be named as one, not a claim, in a clause in P: CRIT_round7 m11; R4 grades its omission as
a non-issue unnamed, VG); C5 the Eastwood and Bowral items (not promissory; I.A); C6 the $10,000 against AMPL,
alternatively Pierre (formed; not yet payable; conditional); C7 the $10,000 as a clause of the Loan Agreement on the other
reading of ‘the clause’ (adds nothing; II.F1); C8 Rocky’s answer to AMPL’s 9 March 2025 call (II.H).

Deciding planted facts (mandatory, quoted) by unit (R-L(7)); each is quoted in the counted paragraph of its
unit. P: ‘legally binding’; ‘if the Project made a profit’; claim C3 identified and named in a substantive clause, ‘Grace
promised Rocky no reimbursement for paying AMPL’ (from v11: U31; from v12 never attached to a clause naming
excluded matters: R-Z(1); frustration’s planted fact, ‘unavoidable delays’, no longer deciding: R-X(7)) (no quoted fact: the
problem contains no promise by Grace to Rocky, ‘Confirmed’ being her only promissory word, and that at I.C:

‘at a rate of 5% interest’; ‘4% per annum’ (the counted form quotes ‘12 months’ as well, with ‘likely’ marking the
inference that the recorded term carries AMPL’s promise; ‘not the past advance’ is credit). I.D: ‘satisfactory conditions’

# TRACE_v1: source trace of ANSWER.md

Scope: every footnote (1 to 45) and every fact in ANSWER.md, checked at source in CB14_ch03/04/05/06/11.txt, W1L2_casebook.txt, the Pao On extract PDF and ACTUAL TASKKK.txt. verify.py first pass: 83 quoted spans, 0 not found. The body is 1,597 words, so the count line ('1,600') is correct.

Key: CORRECT / CERTAIN ERROR / POSSIBLE ERROR. 'Pin' means the report page marker in force where the words sit.

## Summary of errors

| # | Status | Where | Defect | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | CERTAIN ERROR | Body I para 5 + fn 14 | 'a principal is a party only where another "contracts as agent" for him, and AMPL contracted in its own name'. Deane J at 145 says 'If the promisee contracts as agent for a disclosed or undisclosed principal, the principal will ordinarily himself be ... a party'. An undisclosed principal's agent contracts in its own name, so 'in its own name' does not exclude agency. 'only' also turns Deane J's sufficient condition into a necessary one. | Reason from the facts instead: 'Nor did AMPL lend as his agent: Pierre "agreed to provide the money" and AMPL advanced and later lent it as principal, so nothing suggests it "contracts as agent" for Rocky.' Drop 'only' and 'contracted in its own name'. About the same word count. |
| E2 | CERTAIN ERROR | fn 34 | 'Trident (n 14) (Deane J).' comes straight after fn 33 (Trident, Mason CJ and Wilson J), so AGLC r 1.4.3 needs 'Ibid'. The answer uses Ibid with a change of judge elsewhere (fns 12, 15). | 'Ibid (Deane J).' Also see P8 on the missing pin. |
| E3 | CERTAIN ERROR | Body I para 3 + fn 5 | 'the onus lying on Grace, who alone would sue on the email'. Ermogenous [26] puts the onus on the party asserting the contract ('it was for the appellant to demonstrate that there was such a contract'). Part I para 5 has Rocky claim that AMPL's advance performed 'his promise, so that Grace owes him the money', which is a claim on the email contract. Grace is not the only party who would rely on it. | 'the onus lying on whichever party relies on the email' (+1 word), or 'on Grace, as the party suing on it for failure to lend'. |
| E4 | CERTAIN ERROR (minor form) | Body II, privity para | ‘The clause’ is capitalised, but the problem has 'the clause' in lower case. A changed initial capital needs square brackets. | ‘[T]he clause’. |
| P1 | POSSIBLE ERROR | Body I para 3 + fn 6 | The Masters quotation stops before 'into the formal document'. All three Masters classes assume parties who 'agree that the matter of their negotiation shall be dealt with by a formal contract' (360). The email contemplates no formal document, only 'satisfactory conditions'. 'Decisively' also overstates a point the answer itself then weighs against Godecke and Gibbs J, ending 'On balance ... likely'. | Drop 'Decisively'. Say the email is 'analogous to' the third class, or meet the formal-document point in a clause. |
| P2 | POSSIBLE ERROR | fn 20 | Integrated Computer Services, quoted by Heydon JA at 177, is cited for 'offered a promise for a promise'. The passage does say 'the typical contract is a bilateral one and consists of an exchange of promises', but its point is that commercial dealings often do NOT fit that analysis. The words are right; the passage's purpose runs the other way. | Keep (accurate), or cite Australian Woollen Mills 456 ('an offer of a promise for an act', which contrasts with a promise for a promise). |
| P3 | POSSIBLE ERROR | fns 20 and 31 | The short title comes after the 'quoting' case, so ('Brambles') and ('Upper Hunter') read as titles of Integrated and Scammell. | Put the short title straight after the cited case's pin and judge, before ', quoting': '... 177 (Heydon JA) ('Brambles'), quoting ...'. |
| P4 | POSSIBLE ERROR | Body II assent para + fn 36 | 'having "attended" with a reasonable opportunity to object, Rocky arguably took the benefit of the $10,000 promise with knowledge of the clause'. In Empirnall the offeree takes the benefit of the very offer whose terms are in issue (535–6). Here the benefit (the $10,000 promise) was bargained for Rocky's oral undertaking, not offered on the terms of the clause. The answer concedes this in the next clause, but the analogy is weak. Source says 'reasonable opportunity to reject' (unquoted, so no quotation error). | Keep 'arguably'. Optionally name the benefit as the loan to Grace that Rocky asked for (27 February), which is closer to Empirnall's 'takes the benefit of [the offer]'. |
| P5 | POSSIBLE ERROR | fn 22 | Case name. Brambles' text has 'Eccles v Bryant', but the report name (as Masters at 363 gives it) is 'Eccles v Bryant and Pollock [1948] Ch 93'. | 'Eccles v Bryant and Pollock [1948] Ch 93, 104'. |
| P6 | POSSIBLE ERROR | fn 25 | Sundell: no judge in brackets, against the student's rule 'judge named in brackets'. The casebook gives it only as 'The court ... said (at 327)', with no judges named. | Leave as is (AGLC does not require a judge), or add '(the Court)'. Not deductible under AGLC. |
| P7 | POSSIBLE ERROR | fn 38 | Parallel citation 'Roscorla v Thomas (1842) 3 QB 234, 237; 114 ER 496'. AGLC pins each parallel report when one is pinned, but the ER pin cannot be checked from the casebook. | Drop the ER parallel ('(1842) 3 QB 234, 237') or add the ER pin if it can be verified. |

Deane J's burden words ('only the parties to a contract are bound by...') are not in the CB14 extract (143–8), so the pin cannot be checked here. R-Y(1) allows no pin for the full reading. Note also that the Reading Guide sets Trident as 'Mason CJ and Wilson J only'; R-Y accepts Deane J. | Add the CLR pin from the full reading if it is available. Otherwise keep it unpinned under R-Y and accept the lint. |
| P9 | POSSIBLE ERROR | Body I para 5 (fact) | 'on terms first fixed on 8 April at 4%'. The problem says only 'The loan was recorded as $1,150,000 ... with an interest rate of 4%'. 'first fixed' is an inference stated as fact. Later the answer hedges correctly ('nothing shows was agreed before 8 April'). | 'on terms recorded only on 8 April at 4%'. |
