### The rules those messages require (verbatim from the brief)

R1. To the book, verbatim, in full context. Every rule is stated as the readings and slides state it, in their terms, read with the sentence before and after, the question the judge was answering, the result, the speaker and the status. Never condensed, never metaphorised, never relabelled into your own shorthand.
R2. Truth is the readings and the slides. The readings are the casebook extracts and the Pao On extract. Nothing else is truth: not the textbook, not any earlier answer, not any earlier mark, not your memory of contract law.
R3. No textbook. Paterson and Robertson, Principles of Contract Law (and any file named Textbook or Optional) is never cited and is never the sole basis of any proposition. If a rule exists only there, it is dropped or found in a reading or slide.
R4. Lecturer's terminology, never proxy terminology. Write as the course's own lecturer would: every rule, test, element and exception named in the exact words of the reading guides, slides and casebook. No invented labels, no synonyms that sound right, no "gap-filling test" where the course says "implying objective standards", no "Agreement" heading standing in for offer and acceptance.
R5. Structure is the course's elements of formation, in the course's order, under claimant v defendant Parts (later overridden by R-AC: party headings only, each element in its own paragraph in chronological and course order).
R6. Strict IRAC in every sub-heading. Issue, rule with authority, application of the quoted facts with the opposing argument, the decisive reason, then the conclusion. Never a conclusion first, at any level, including the first line of the answer.
R7. Reasoned conclusions, never "finely balanced" where authority decides. If any course authority tips a point, find it and use it. "On balance ... likely ... because ..." is the form.
R8. His voice. Taken only from his submitted LAWS1061 mid-term (Part A). He "despises" one-clause sentences: flowing multi-clause sentences joined by semicolons and colons, his signposts, no em dashes, no double quotation marks in the body, no contractions, no metaphor, no rhetoric, no fluff.
R9. The rubric ... must be able to fail our answer and must reward correct advice even when the advice is bad news for Rocky.
R10. Issues are never pre-set by the orchestrator. Independent agents find them from the facts and the book; disagreements are resolved by the source, not by vote.
R11. Past papers are used to learn the setters' patterns, read in full, never parsed.
R12. Zero hallucination. The process must drive invented law, invented facts, wrong pins and misattributed words to zero.
R13. Autonomous, adversarial, dynamic loop. Fresh agents every round, adversaries added where new risk appears.
R14. Source check and mark check on the exact final text. Nothing ships that was polished after its last trace and last mark.

His standing preferences: no em dashes ever; disclose assumptions and judgment calls rather than hiding them; read sources verbatim page by page and never substitute a parsed or summarised document; one consolidated deliverable; adversarial review before he sees anything; finish end to end; aim at perfection, never a safe floor presented alone.

### Zero-hallucination protocol (verbatim, Part 5, abridged only where it names Cowork file paths)

Z1. No proposition without a register line: the passage copied verbatim from the source text; file; page; report pin; speaker; status (ratio, obiter, dissent, minority on the result, first instance, editors' note, slide only, skip-range passage); the question the court was answering; the result; any hedge in the sentence before or after ("Perhaps", "But", "However", "though", "I would doubt"). A sentence of the answer with no register line is deleted.
Z2. Facts are quoted exactly or marked. Every fact used comes from the problem in its exact words; a derived fact is written as "arguably" or as further information. Speaker matters: the narrator's words are not a party's words.
Z4. The verifier checks quotations, not paraphrase. So an independent tracer traces every sentence (paraphrase included) to the source page in full context.
Z5. Bench and speaker are counted, never assumed. Find the judge heading that precedes the passage; count the bench; name the judge unless the whole Court or Board speaks; write "dissenting" where it applies. Words a judge quotes from someone else are attributed to the original speaker.
Z6. Read what a passage excludes and what it was answering. A dictum applies only to the question the court was asking; compare the court's facts with ours, name what is similar and what is different, and keep confining words.
Z7. Disagreement is resolved by the source, never by vote or seniority. Every reviewer finding is itself verified at source before it is applied (earlier adversarial reviewers were right about four fifths of the time).
Z8. No earlier work is truth.
Z9. Gaps are disclosed, not filled.

### What Excellent requires at every point (verbatim, Part 8)

The issue framed in one sentence in the course's terms, never as a conclusion. The rule stated as the source states it, in the course's vocabulary, with the right authority, pin and speaker, its status disclosed where it matters (obiter, dissent, minority on the result, first instance, editors' note), and its hedge kept. Every planted fact that bears on the point, quoted briefly and exactly, with the right speaker. Application in his voice: the rule's own test applied to those facts, with each authority shown to be analogous or distinguishable by naming what is similar and what is different. The strongest opposing argument, put at full strength with its authority, and met. The decisive reason, from authority where any exists, never "finely balanced" where a course authority tips it. A conclusion that follows ("On balance, ... likely ..., because ..."), with its consequence for Rocky. Further information, only where it would change the advice, and how it would change it. Consistency with every other Part. Citation that precisely supports the proposition, no over-citation, AGLC 4 correct, case names italicised. Very Good: one of these missing or thin. Good: a correct but conclusive statement, or two missing. Fair: law stated generally rather than for this issue, or the counter absent. Poor: law wrong, misattributed or misstated against the source. Omitted: not addressed.

Part 10. "Nothing ships until a harsh UNSW lecturer, reading every sentence against the readings, the slides and this rubric, would have no ground to deduct a single mark; and nothing in the answer exists that cannot be found, word for word and in context, in the course materials."

### Pre-submission checklist (verbatim lines most relevant to this answer)

- Before writing any claim the advisee brings, or a threshold that goes against the advisee, write the advisee's case first as a full paragraph from every planted fact, its own words included, with its closest authority, then answer each point.
- Before answering a contested issue, list every argument for the losing side, lead with the one a good opponent would lead with at full strength, then answer it; if words are short, cut the weak counter, not the strong one.
- Before relying on a fallback rule, state the presumption the opponent invokes in the source's words with its pin (Masters 363, 'of similar import' prima facie an overriding condition), then answer it.
- Before resting a conclusion on one contested threshold, give the other branch and its result in two sentences.
- Before submitting, find every fact used in two Parts or two issues and write the reconciling sentence on one doctrinal footing.
- Before quoting any test, write one line on whether the court found it met, on what facts, and which side of ours that result lies.
- Before labelling a bench, count it in the casebook; recall Lord Denning MR's Butler patterns were his alone, Birkett LJ adopts Lord Goddard CJ in Boots, Lord Diplock quotes Lord Denning MR in Gibson to reject him.
- Three-question footnote pass: (a) does the passage or its next sentence say 'Perhaps', 'But', 'However' or 'though'? quote or state the hedge (Gibbs J's 'Perhaps it may be different', Godecke 647, obiter and only where essential terms are agreed); (b) is it the whole Court or Board? (c) is the judge dissenting, or one judge's words credited to several? write 'dissenting'.
- Before applying a dictum, check whose position it describes (promisor or promisee, offeror or offeree) and whether our party holds it.
- Before distinguishing or transposing a case, read the editors' facts bracket and the passage the court made decisive, and set the clause construed beside ours.
- Before applying a qualification, use its own test, not its rationale (Wigan 595: an honest claim, not vexatious or frivolous).
- Before quoting, read the next sentence and keep confining words; never put a judge's words about his case into his mouth about our parties.
- Before describing a case's facts, read them in the judgment, not memory.
- Before citing Brambles, write 'Ipp AJA' (Mason P agreeing) for the majority; Heydon JA's 'much to be said' and revival are minority obiter.
- Before citing Beaton, state the split (Kirby P no consideration; Mahoney JA and McHugh JA a promise for an act; appeal dismissed with McHugh JA dissenting).
- Before citing Meehan, say it has no majority on honest versus reasonable (Gibbs CJ honesty 581; Mason J undecided 590–1; Wilson J 597–8).
- Before citing Pao On, keep its two points apart: (1) Lord Scarman's conditions ('was to be remunerated'); (2) the third-party-duty holding at 632.
- Before drafting, list every verb of who did, said, instructed or proposed what, and match each to a quoted line; any adjective doing legal work needs a quoted fact.
- Before quoting a fact, check the speaker (party or narrator) and read the whole utterance.
- Before using a derived fact, drop it; facts are quoted exactly or marked 'arguably' or further information.
- AGLC: first citation in full with a short title; 'quoting Case (year) report pin (Judge)'; pins after a comma, no 'at', paragraphs in [ ], en dash ranges in footnotes only; full stop at the end; 'and' not '&' in case names (except as reported).
- Style: rule first, facts quoted into the sentence; 'Firstly, ... Secondly, however, ...'; 'Decisively,' once per claim; 'X is distinguishable: ...'; 'The strongest counter is ...'; 'On balance, the better view is that ..., though ...'; 'Further information is needed on whether ...; if ..., then ...' only where it changes the advice. Remove 'cuts both ways', 'it is trite law', 'it is submitted', 'in the present case', 'turning to', 'it is clear that'; no invented abbreviations; no bullets; no dashes, double quotation marks or contractions in the body. One quotation per source per sentence; none over 45 words; no fragments after semicolons; varied openers.

body,_,rest=s.partition('\n[^1]:')

def ital(text, names):
    pat=re.compile('|'.join(r'(?<![\w])'+re.escape(n)+r'(?![\w])' for n in sorted(names,key=len,reverse=True)))
    return pat.sub(lambda m:'*'+m.group(0)+'*', text)
# footnotes: full names and short titles (also inside the ('Short') parentheses)
foot=ital(foot, CASES+SHORT)
# body: short titles only where used as case names (not 'Mrs Coulls')
body=ital(body, [x for x in SHORT if x!='Coulls'])
body=re.sub(r'^(I{1,3}\. [A-Z][A-Z v()]+)$', r'**\1**', body, flags=re.M)
md=body+'\n[^1]:'+foot[5:]
open('build_tmp.md','w',encoding='utf-8').write(md)
subprocess.run(['pandoc','build_tmp.md','-f','markdown-smart','-o',out,'--reference-doc','reference.docx'],check=True)
# A4 page, 2.54 cm margins
import zipfile, shutil, os
tmp=out+'.tmp'
with zipfile.ZipFile(out) as zi, zipfile.ZipFile(tmp,'w',zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as zo:

            d=x.encode('utf-8')

shutil.move(tmp,out)

**I. ROCKY v GRACE**

Whether the February dealings formed a loan contract decides Rocky’s claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that he failed to lend. Grace’s 5 February call ‘proposed that Rocky offer’, promising nothing, so was likely an invitation to treat.[^1] Rocky could say his 12 February email only records discussions, like its ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’ points, which promise nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and the email seeks agreement: unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’, those words are promissory,[^2] so the first point is likely an offer.

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent.[^3] ‘Confirmed’ arguably vouched only for the email’s accuracy; but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ without new terms, so it was no counter-offer and likely accepted the first point, ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ included. Grace’s implied promise to repay would arguably be consideration, since a promise can be the price of another.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether this preliminary agreement showed intention to create legal relations. That is judged objectively, the alleging party bearing the onus;[^5] the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours intention. As nothing was made ‘subject to a formal contract’, the question is whether the terms were to ‘be put into form’ or left to ‘a new agreement’.[^6] Grace would say the fixed terms show the parties had ‘reached finality’, *Masters*’ first class.[^7] Rocky would invoke the third class, where parties ‘have dealt only with major matters’,[^8] as the email arguably did. Its ‘conditions’, unlike ‘subject to success of Hail Mary Project’, name no external event, so they are most naturally further loan terms; and ‘satisfactory’ leaves them to the protected party’s judgment,[^9] here Rocky’s as lender. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement: later conduct, admissible on formation, agrees, Grace taking AMPL’s loan on other terms.[^10] Were the conditions settled ‘this morning’, the email would bind.

The qualifier also arguably makes Rocky’s promise illusory, since a consideration is illusory if it ‘depends upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor’.[^11] Grace may reply that, as in *Meehan*, Rocky must judge honestly, perhaps reasonably,[^12] and the fixed terms are ‘specified parameters’.[^13] However, *Meehan* is distinguishable: its discretion related ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’, finance, within agreed terms;[^14] Rocky’s covers the loan’s own terms, which neither standard can supply and no range confines. *Godecke* bound because its added terms had to be ‘reasonable in an objective sense’.[^15] Gibbs J, obiter, doubted any ‘concluded bargain’ where ‘a vital matter’ is left to one party; his ‘[p]erhaps’ for subsidiary matters cited a case where parties had ‘imported the familiar and objective standard of reasonableness’,[^16] which these parties never did. The email therefore likely bound neither party, defeating Grace’s claim.

Rocky may instead claim AMPL’s advance, made because he ‘asked’, performed his promise, so Grace owes him. Even had the email bound, the advance differed in amount and date. As Pierre ‘agreed to provide the money’ and the Loan Agreement named Rocky guarantor, which no lender acting for him would need, AMPL did not contract ‘as agent’ for him.[^17] Rocky’s 5 March demand under the Loan Agreement, arguably assuming a 27 February start, engages privity: outside insurance, ‘a third party cannot sue upon a contract’, nor can ‘a stranger to the consideration’.[^18] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[^19] which ‘AMPL and Grace entered into’: Grace’s promises ran to AMPL alone, not even jointly to Rocky,[^20] who gave nothing for them, AMPL’s loan being their price. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is right in result but wrong in reason: signature is not necessary, *Empirnall*’s unsigned developer being bound,[^21] nor decisive, Mrs Coulls signing without becoming a party.[^22]

Thus Rocky has no present claim against Grace: the Development Agreement repays him first ‘if the Project made a profit’, even a ‘minimal’ one, but none is yet shown; and Grace never promised to reimburse what he pays AMPL.

**II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)**

Rocky’s questions are whether he can claim $10,000 and must pay AMPL. At the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s expressed expectation promised nothing, so was likely an invitation to treat.[^23] Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ offered a bilateral contract,[^24] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[^25] AMPL may argue that nothing bound before signing; but that ‘depends upon the intention disclosed by the language’ used,[^26] and Rocky reserved no right to withdraw pending a document he would not sign, so a contract likely formed orally.

Who promised turns on agency: Pierre bound AMPL if he had ‘authority … to act for’ it and contracted for it, not solely for himself.[^27] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre; but Pierre controls AMPL, supplying that authority, had agreed to its 27 February advance, and spoke at its office about its loan, so he likely acted for AMPL. If he promised personally, he alone owes the $10,000, and AMPL cannot sue on the undertaking.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule: ‘also’ arguably presupposes a guarantee already given, so, as in *Sundell*, promising to ensure performance already owed adds nothing.[^28] However, the rule applies ‘at least when’ the promise is made to the promisee under an existing contract,[^29] and none is shown: on 27 February Rocky ‘asked’, and the clause, arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’, bound no one before signing. Even otherwise, ensuring ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’; and if Pierre promised, the exception for promises to third parties applies, any duty running to AMPL.[^30] Rocky likely gave consideration, unless he also promised AMPL a guarantee when he ‘asked’.

On intention, Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions at most identify who bears the onus,[^31] here Rocky; and a fixed sum promised at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised is ‘appropriately promissory in character’.[^32] Nor is Rocky’s undertaking a mere letter of comfort: Rogers CJ saw ‘no relevant difference’ between a ‘practice to ensure’ that a borrower could repay and a promise ‘to ensure’ it.[^33] Rocky’s words were plainer and priced, so both promises likely bind.

On certainty, the Loan Agreement fixes the payments Rocky must ‘ensure’, so his undertaking is not ‘so obscure’ as to be void.[^34] His ‘I will do that’ contains no words of effort, and his ‘check in’ emails cannot construe it:[^35] it likely promised that Grace would pay, not that Rocky would try. Nor is AMPL’s promise illusory: once Grace repays, it leaves ‘no discretion’.[^36]

On privity, the $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’ for consideration Rocky gave: he is its promisee, no stranger to the consideration.[^37] Read naturally, ‘the clause’ is the guarantee clause already described, not a $10,000 term; either way, Rocky relies on the oral promise.

Rocky’s exposure turns on whether the guarantee clause binds him. A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, possibly only by his oral undertaking, and only ‘the parties to it’ are ‘bound by the obligations of a contract’.[^38] Silence while a clause is included is generally not acceptance.[^39] AMPL would say Rocky ‘attended’ as the clause was included, taking the $10,000 promise knowing the terms.[^40] However, the benefit he took priced his own words, so taking it is not conduct ‘of such a character as necessarily’ to infer assent to the clause.[^41] He is likely bound by his oral undertaking, and by the clause only if he saw its words.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^42] which its $10,000 promise supplies if AMPL made it. Otherwise its advance is past consideration,[^43] which counts only if requested, understood to be remunerated, and enforceable if promised in advance; Rocky ‘asked’, but, unlike the return in *Pao On*, understood ‘at the time of the main agreement’,[^44] no guarantee is shown then contemplated. AMPL might add that it signed after the clause’s inclusion, arguably ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee;[^45] but Rocky priced his undertaking at $10,000, not at AMPL’s signature, so the clause then likely lacks consideration.

Whether the 9 March call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Construction is objective,[^46] and post-contractual conduct, such as Grace’s interest payments or ‘I have until 8 April 2025’, cannot construe the term;[^47] but, if it is ambiguous, pre-contractual conduct casting light on ‘the genesis of the contract’ is admissible.[^48] Naming no start, it is arguably ambiguous. AMPL argues it ran from the 27 February advance, which the agreement ‘recorded’; but ‘recorded’ equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows predated 8 April, and the genesis shows only when money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature, unless the Loan Agreement says otherwise. If the March interest went unpaid, Rocky’s undertaking is arguably already broken.

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to that obligation, not to the contract, which bound at once:[^49] nothing is yet payable. Read commercially, Rocky’s own payment arguably satisfies it;[^50] but the words name Grace, whose payment the $10,000 priced. AMPL’s call, not stopping Grace repaying, breaches no duty to ‘do everything necessary on [its] part’.[^51]

Accordingly, Rocky is likely liable on his oral undertaking, in damages to AMPL or Pierre, for any payment Grace misses. If the clause also binds him and AMPL promised the $10,000, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, on a 27 February start; otherwise from 8 April 2025. No term requires him to pay early, and paying likely forfeits the $10,000, payable only if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, repays.

## FILE: work/renumber.py
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

import re,sys
p=sys.argv[1]; s=open(p).read()
body,_,rest=s.partition('\nWord count:')
countline,_,foots=('Word count:'+rest).partition('\n\n')
defs=dict(re.findall(r'^\[\^(\d+)\]: (.*)$',foots,flags=re.M))
order=[]
for m in re.finditer(r'\[\^(\d+)\]',body):
    if m.group(1) not in order: order.append(m.group(1))
mp={old:str(i+1) for i,old in enumerate(order)}
body=re.sub(r'\[\^(\d+)\]',lambda m:'[^'+mp[m.group(1)]+']',body)
newdefs=[]
for old in order:
    t=defs[old]
    t=re.sub(r'\(n (\d+)\)',lambda m:'(n '+mp.get(m.group(1),'??'+m.group(1))+')',t)
    newdefs.append(f'[^{mp[old]}]: {t}')
open(p,'w').write(body+'\n'+countline+'\n\n'+'\n'.join(newdefs)+'\n')
print('footnotes',len(order), 'unmapped refs' if '??' in ''.join(newdefs) else 'ok')

import re,sys
s=open(sys.argv[1]).read()
body=re.sub(r'\[\^\d+\]','',s.split('Word count:')[0])
words=body.split(); n=len(words)
q=re.findall(r"‘(.+?)’(?![a-z])",body,flags=re.S)
qw=sum(len(x.split()) for x in q)
flat=' '.join(body.split())
ss=[x for x in re.split(r'(?<=[.])\s+(?=[A-Z‘])',flat) if len(x.split())>2 and not re.match(r'^I+\.',x)]
L=[len(x.split()) for x in ss]
semi=flat.count(';'); colon=flat.count(':')
withmark=sum(1 for x in ss if ';' in x or ':' in x)
print(f'body {n} stated {n+3} | quoted {qw} ({100*qw/n:.1f}%) | sentences {len(L)} mean {sum(L)/len(L):.1f} | under12 {100*sum(1 for l in L if l<12)/len(L):.1f}% | >45 {[l for l in L if l>45]} | semi/100 {100*semi/n:.2f} colon/100 {100*colon/n:.2f} | sent w/ ;: {100*withmark/len(L):.1f}%')

**I. ROCKY v GRACE**

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, on which both Rocky's claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that Rocky failed to lend 'by 15 February' depend. Grace's 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer, so it was not itself one,[^1] and Rocky declined. Rocky could argue that his 12 February email merely records their meeting, as it opens 'Confirming discussions' and its other points promise nothing; however, 'I will lend' fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and 'Please confirm agreement' seeks assent, so, unlike 'may be prepared to sell' in *Gibson*,[^2] the first point is likely an offer, though made 'subject to satisfactory conditions'.

Acceptance requires 'an external manifestation of assent to an offer'.[^3] Rocky could say that 'Confirmed' vouched only for the email's accuracy; however, it answered a request to 'confirm agreement' and added no terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Grace's implied promise to repay with interest would stand in 'the relation of a quid pro quo' to Rocky's promise to lend.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether the parties intended to be bound immediately, which is judged objectively, the onus lying on Grace, who alone would sue on the email, although their status as 'project developers' supports intention.[^5] Decisively, the third class in *Masters* covers parties who 'have dealt only with major matters and contemplate that others will or may be regulated by provisions to be introduced';[^6] that describes an email fixing the amount, date, term and rate while leaving unnamed 'conditions' to Rocky. Grace's strongest counter is *Godecke*, where terms the vendor's solicitors could add bound because they had to be reasonable 'in an objective sense';[^7] Rocky's qualifier has no such standard, since 'satisfactory' leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects,[^8] here Rocky as lender. Gibbs J, in obiter, doubted that an agreement leaving 'further terms to be settled by one of the parties' binds, while allowing that it 'may be different' where only 'subsidiary matters' remain;[^9] were the conditions settled 'this morning' or mere documentation, the email would bind, so further information on them is needed. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement.

For the same reason Rocky's promise is arguably illusory: in *Placer* a promise with no 'identifiable criteria', left 'solely to the discretion' of the promisor, was 'wholly unenforceable'.[^10] Grace may reply that, as in *Meehan*, Rocky must judge 'satisfactory' honestly,[^11] a limit which 'takes the case out of the principle' that a promisor's discretion over performance defeats the promise;[^12] however, the discretion in *Meehan* related 'only to the fulfilment of a condition',[^13] obtaining finance, whereas Rocky's concerns the content of his own loan, which honesty cannot supply. The email therefore likely bound neither party, so Grace has no claim that Rocky failed to lend.

Rocky may claim that AMPL's 27 February advance, made because he 'asked', performed his promise, so that Grace owes him the money. This fails: the advance was \$1,150,000, not \$1 million, made after 15 February and in AMPL's name, on terms first fixed on 8 April at 4%. Nor did AMPL lend as his agent: a principal is a party only where another 'contracts as agent' for him,[^14] and AMPL contracted in its own name. His 5 March demand under 'the Loan Agreement with AMPL' therefore meets privity, under which 'a third party cannot sue upon a contract'.[^15] Party status turns on 'the written instrument itself',[^16] and Grace's promises to repay were made to AMPL, not to Rocky, even as a joint promisee;[^17] Grace's 'I never signed anything with you' reaches the right result, but signature is not the test, as Mrs Coulls signed yet was not a party.[^18]

Thus Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace: the Development Agreement pays only 'if the Project made a profit' and is not shown breached, and Grace never promised to reimburse Rocky for anything he pays AMPL.

**II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)**

At the 8 April meeting, Pierre's statement that he 'expected' Rocky to ensure Grace's payments promised nothing, so it was a request rather than an offer;[^19] Rocky's reply, 'I will do that if you also promise', offered a promise for a promise,[^20] which Pierre accepted when he 'agreed'.[^21] AMPL may argue that nothing bound until the Loan Agreement was signed; however, parties are bound 'when, and in the manner in which, they intend', as Lord Greene MR said of exchanged contracts,[^22] and nothing suggests Rocky's undertaking awaited a document he never signed, so a contract likely formed orally.

Rocky's 'you' points to Pierre, but Pierre controls AMPL and spoke at its office about its loan, so, objectively,[^23] he likely contracted 'as agent' for AMPL;[^24] further information on whose money was to pay the \$10,000 would settle this; if Pierre promised personally, what follows runs against him.

AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, arguing that Rocky's promise gave nothing beyond his guarantee.[^25] However, the rule bites on a promise 'made to the promisee under that contract',[^26] and none then existed: on 27 February Rocky only 'asked', and 'Pierre agreed and the clause was included' suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even if it came first, ensuring 'all payments' 'promptly' exceeds guaranteeing 'repayment of the Loan'; and if Pierre promised, any duty was owed to AMPL, and 'a pre-existing contractual obligation to a third party can be valid consideration'.[^27] Rocky likely gave consideration.

Although Pierre is Rocky's cousin, family presumptions do 'no more than invite attention to identifying the party who bears the onus of proof',[^28] here Rocky; a promise of a fixed sum, made at AMPL's office as its loan was finalised, is 'appropriately promissory in character' and commercial.[^29] Rocky could argue that his own undertaking, like a letter of comfort, was only a moral assurance; however, Rogers CJ saw 'no relevant difference' between a 'practice to ensure' repayment and a promise 'to ensure' it,[^30] and Rocky's 'I will do that' was given for a price, so intention likely exists on both sides.

Rocky's undertaking is not 'so obscure' as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[^31] Objectively,[^32] his 'I will do that', answering an expectation that he 'ensure' payment, contains no words of effort, so he likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that he would try.

Privity is no bar: the \$10,000 was to be paid 'to me directly' for consideration Rocky himself gave, so he is the promisee and no 'stranger to the consideration'.[^33] 'The clause' most naturally means the guarantee clause; even if it means the \$10,000 term, AMPL remains bound by its oral promise.

A guarantee was 'provided by Rocky', but whether by assent to the clause or only by his oral undertaking is open; only the parties to a contract are bound by it,[^34] so AMPL must show assent. Silence while a clause is included is generally insufficient,[^35] but, having 'attended' with a reasonable opportunity to object, Rocky arguably took the benefit of the \$10,000 promise with knowledge of the clause;[^36] he could answer that the \$10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^37] which its \$10,000 promise, if it made one, supplies. If Pierre promised, AMPL's earlier advance is past consideration,[^38] counting only if done at Rocky's request, understood to be 'remunerated', with payment 'legally enforceable had it been promised in advance';[^39] Rocky 'asked', but nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL's stronger answer is that it signed only after the clause was included, an act likely 'really done in consideration of' the guarantee,[^40] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

Whether AMPL's 9 March 2025 call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct, such as Grace's interest payments from 8 April 2024 and his 'I have until 8 April 2025', cannot construe the term,[^41] but, the term being arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing 'the genesis of the transaction' are admissible.[^42] AMPL argues the term ran from its 27 February advance, since the agreement 'recorded' a loan already made; however, 'recorded' equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature unless the Loan Agreement dates it from the advance.

Interest is shown paid only until 8 February 2025; further information is needed on whether the March 2025 instalment was paid, for if not, Rocky's undertaking that Grace make 'all payments' 'promptly' is arguably already broken, whichever start date applies.

The \$10,000 is payable 'once Grace repays the Loan', a condition precedent to that obligation rather than to the contract,[^43] so nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies the condition;[^44] however, the words name Grace, and the \$10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach its duty 'to do everything necessary on \[its\] part' to give Rocky the benefit of the contract,[^45] since its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for \$1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, if the term ran from 27 February, or otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only by his oral undertaking, he faces damages for any payment Grace fails to make when due. His \$10,000 claim against AMPL, or alternatively Pierre, likely stands, but it falls due only if Grace, who said he 'might not pay at all', repays.

**I. ROCKY v GRACE**

The first issue is whether the February dealings formed a loan contract, on which both Rocky's claim to repayment and any claim by Grace that Rocky failed to lend 'by 15 February' depend. Grace's 5 February call asked Rocky to make an offer, so it was not itself one,[^1] and Rocky declined. Rocky could argue that his 12 February email merely records their meeting, as it opens 'Confirming discussions' and its other points promise nothing; however, 'I will lend' fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and 'Please confirm agreement' seeks assent, so, unlike 'may be prepared to sell' in *Gibson*,[^2] the first point is likely an offer, though made 'subject to satisfactory conditions'.

Acceptance requires 'an external manifestation of assent to an offer'.[^3] Rocky could say that 'Confirmed' vouched only for the email's accuracy; however, it answered a request to 'confirm agreement' and added no terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Grace's implied promise to repay with interest would stand in 'the relation of a quid pro quo' to Rocky's promise to lend.[^4]

The qualifier raises whether the parties intended to be bound immediately, which is judged objectively, the onus lying on whichever party relies on it, although their status as 'project developers' supports intention.[^5] Where nothing is 'expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract', the question is whether the terms were to 'be put into form' or to be 'subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not expressed in detail';[^6] the email fixes the amount, date, term and rate but leaves unnamed 'conditions' to Rocky. Grace's strongest counter is *Godecke*, where terms the vendor's solicitors could add bound because they had to be reasonable 'in an objective sense';[^7] Rocky's qualifier has no such standard, since 'satisfactory' leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects,[^8] here Rocky as lender. Gibbs J, in obiter, doubted that an agreement leaving 'further terms to be settled by one of the parties' binds, while allowing that it 'may be different' where only 'subsidiary matters' remain;[^9] were the conditions settled 'this morning' or mere documentation, the email would bind, so further information on them is needed. On balance, the loan was likely left to a new agreement.

For the same reason Rocky's promise is arguably illusory: in *Placer* a promise with no 'identifiable criteria', left 'solely to the discretion' of the promisor, was 'wholly unenforceable'.[^10] Grace may reply that, as in *Meehan*, Rocky must judge 'satisfactory' honestly,[^11] a limit which 'takes the case out of the principle' that a promisor's discretion over performance defeats the promise;[^12] however, the discretion in *Meehan* related 'only to the fulfilment of a condition',[^13] obtaining finance, whereas Rocky's concerns the content of his own loan, which honesty cannot supply. The email therefore likely bound neither party, so Grace has no claim that Rocky failed to lend.

Rocky may claim that AMPL's 27 February advance, made because he 'asked', performed his promise, so that Grace owes him the money. This fails: the advance was \$1,150,000, not \$1 million, made after 15 February and in AMPL's name, and 'recorded' on 8 April at 4%. Nor did AMPL lend as his agent, for, although a principal is a party where another 'contracts as agent' for him,[^14] AMPL took Rocky's own guarantee of the Loan, which no agent lending for him would need. His 5 March demand under 'the Loan Agreement with AMPL' therefore meets privity, under which 'a third party cannot sue upon a contract'.[^15] Party status turns on 'the written instrument itself',[^16] and Grace's promises to repay were made to AMPL, not to Rocky, even as a joint promisee;[^17] Grace's 'I never signed anything with you' reaches the right result, but signature is not the test, as Mrs Coulls signed yet was not a party.[^18]

Thus Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace: the Development Agreement pays only 'if the Project made a profit' and is not shown breached, and Grace never promised to reimburse Rocky for anything he pays AMPL.

**II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)**

At the 8 April meeting, Pierre's statement that he 'expected' Rocky to ensure Grace's payments promised nothing, so it was a request rather than an offer;[^19] Rocky's reply, 'I will do that if you also promise', offered a promise for a promise,[^20] which Pierre accepted when he 'agreed'.[^21] AMPL may argue that nothing bound until the Loan Agreement was signed; however, parties are bound 'when, and in the manner in which, they intend', as Lord Greene MR said of exchanged contracts,[^22] and nothing suggests Rocky's undertaking awaited a document 'signed by Grace and AMPL', so a contract likely formed orally.

Rocky's 'you' points to Pierre, but Pierre controls AMPL and spoke at its office about its loan, so, objectively,[^23] he likely contracted 'as agent' for AMPL;[^24] further information on whose money was to pay the \$10,000 would settle this; if Pierre promised personally, what follows runs against him.

AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, arguing that Rocky's promise gave nothing beyond his guarantee.[^25] However, the rule bites on a promise 'made to the promisee under that contract',[^26] and none then existed: on 27 February Rocky only 'asked', and 'Pierre agreed and the clause was included' suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even if it came first, ensuring 'all payments' 'promptly' exceeds guaranteeing 'repayment of the Loan'; and if Pierre promised, any duty was owed to AMPL, and 'a pre-existing contractual obligation to a third party can be valid consideration'.[^27] Rocky likely gave consideration.

Although Pierre is Rocky's cousin, family presumptions do 'no more than invite attention to identifying the party who bears the onus of proof',[^28] here Rocky; a promise of a fixed sum, made at AMPL's office as its loan was finalised, is 'appropriately promissory in character' and commercial.[^29] Rocky could argue that his own undertaking, like a letter of comfort, was only a moral assurance; however, Rogers CJ saw 'no relevant difference' between a 'practice to ensure' repayment and a promise 'to ensure' it,[^30] and Rocky's 'I will do that' was given for a price, so intention likely exists on both sides.

Rocky's undertaking is not 'so obscure' as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[^31] Objectively,[^32] his 'I will do that', answering an expectation that he 'ensure' payment, contains no words of effort, so he likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that he would try.

Privity is no bar: the \$10,000 was to be paid 'to me directly' for consideration Rocky himself gave, so he is the promisee and no 'stranger to the consideration'.[^33] '\[T\]he clause' most naturally means the guarantee clause; even if it means the \$10,000 term, AMPL remains bound by its oral promise.

A guarantee was 'provided by Rocky', but whether by assent to the clause or only by his oral undertaking is open; only the parties to a contract are bound by it,[^34] so AMPL must show assent. Silence while a clause is included is generally insufficient,[^35] but, having 'attended' with a reasonable opportunity to object, Rocky arguably took the benefit of the \$10,000 promise with knowledge of the clause;[^36] he could answer that the \$10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

AMPL must also show consideration moving from itself,[^37] which its \$10,000 promise, if it made one, supplies. If Pierre promised, AMPL's earlier advance is past consideration,[^38] counting only if done at Rocky's request, understood to be 'remunerated', with payment 'legally enforceable had it been promised in advance';[^39] Rocky 'asked', but nothing shows a guarantee was then contemplated. AMPL's stronger answer is that it signed only after the clause was included, an act likely 'really done in consideration of' the guarantee,[^40] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

Whether AMPL's 9 March 2025 call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct, such as Grace's interest payments from 8 April 2024 and his 'I have until 8 April 2025', cannot construe the term,[^41] but, the term being arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing 'the genesis of the transaction' are admissible.[^42] AMPL argues the term ran from the 27 February advance, and may add that the agreement 'recorded' a loan already made; however, 'recorded' equally governs the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the call premature unless the Loan Agreement dates it from the advance.

Interest is shown paid only until 8 February 2025; further information is needed on whether the March 2025 instalment was paid, for if not, Rocky's undertaking that Grace make 'all payments' 'promptly' is arguably already broken, whichever start date applies.

The \$10,000 is payable 'once Grace repays the Loan', a condition precedent to that obligation rather than to the contract,[^43] so nothing is yet payable. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own payment satisfies the condition;[^44] however, the words name Grace, and the \$10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay. Nor does AMPL breach its duty 'to do everything necessary on \[its\] part' to give Rocky the benefit of the contract,[^45] since its call does not stop Grace repaying.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, he is liable for \$1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: now, if the term ran from 27 February, or otherwise from 8 April 2025. If bound only by his oral undertaking, he faces damages for any payment Grace fails to make when due. His \$10,000 claim against AMPL, or alternatively Pierre, likely stands, but it falls due only if Grace, who said he 'might not pay at all', repays.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Verify quotations in a draft against the casebook text (14th ed chapters, W1 casebook, Pao On extract, problem).
Usage: python3 -I verify.py draft.md
Reports, for each quoted span: FOUND/NOT FOUND, source, printed casebook page, and the nearest preceding report-page marker [nnn]."""
import re, sys, unicodedata, glob
BASE='/home/user/new/drive'
SRC={}
for f in sorted(glob.glob(BASE+'/casebook/CB14_ch*.txt')):
    SRC[f.split('/')[-1]]=open(f,encoding='utf-8').read()
for f,n in [('/txt/W1L1_casebook.txt','W1L1'),('/txt/W1L2_casebook.txt','W1L2'),('/txt/ACTUAL TASKKK.txt','PROBLEM')]:
    SRC[n]=open(BASE+f,encoding='utf-8').read()
import subprocess
SRC['PAOON_EXTRACT']=subprocess.run(['pdftotext','-layout',BASE+'/readings/W2 L1 - Consideration_ Part 1/Extract from Pao On v Lau Yiu Long 1980 Privy Council.pdf','-'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout
def norm(s):
    s=unicodedata.normalize('NFKC',s).replace('​','').replace('­','')
    s=s.replace('‘',"'").replace('’',"'").replace('“','"').replace('”','"').replace('–','-').replace('—','-')
    s=s.replace('ﬁ','fi').replace('ﬀ','ff').replace('ﬂ','fl')
    return s
# build normalised stream with position map to page and report markers
INDEX={}
for name,t in SRC.items():
    t=norm(t)
    out=[];meta=[];page='?';rep='?'
    lines=t.split('\n')
    for ln in lines:
        m=re.match(r'===== PDF \d+ \| expected printed p (\d+)',ln)
        if m: page=m.group(1); continue
        if re.match(r'^\s*(Part [IVX]+:|.*Chapter \d+\s*$)',ln): continue
        if re.search(r'\[\d+\.\d+\]\s+\d+\s*$|^\s*\d+\s+\[\d+\.\d+\]\s*$',ln): continue
        if re.search(r'\bcont\.\s*$',ln): continue
        # strip report markers from text but record them
        pieces=re.split(r'(\[\d{2,4}\])',ln)
        for p in pieces:
            mm=re.fullmatch(r'\[(\d{2,4})\]',p)
            if mm and not (len(mm.group(1))==4 and 1500<=int(mm.group(1))<=2100):
                rep=mm.group(1); continue
            for ch in p+' ':
                out.append(ch); meta.append((page,rep))
    s=''.join(out)
    # de-hyphenate line-break hyphens and collapse spaces, keep map
    s2=[];m2=[];i=0
    while i<len(s):
        ch=s[i]
        if ch=='-' and i+1<len(s) and s[i+1]==' ' and i>0 and s[i-1].isalpha():
            j=i+1
            while j<len(s) and s[j]==' ': j+=1
            if j<len(s) and s[j].islower():
                i=j; continue
        if ch.isspace():
            if s2 and s2[-1]==' ': i+=1; continue
            ch=' '
        s2.append(ch); m2.append(meta[i]); i+=1
    INDEX[name]=(''.join(s2),m2)
def find(q):
    qn=re.sub(r'\s+',' ',norm(q)).strip()
    parts=[p.strip() for p in re.split(r'\s*(?:…|\.\.\.)\s*',qn) if p.strip()]
    res=[]
    for name,(s,m) in INDEX.items():
        ok=True;pos=0;hits=[]
        for p in parts:
            p2=re.sub(r'\[[^\]]*\]','',p).strip() if '[' in p else p
            k=s.find(p,pos) if p in s else -1
            if k<0:
                # allow bracketed alterations: match segments around brackets
                segs=[x.strip() for x in re.split(r'\[[^\]]*\]',p) if x.strip()]
                kk=pos;seg_ok=True;first=None
                for sg in segs:
                    k2=s.find(sg,kk)
                    if k2<0: seg_ok=False;break
                    if first is None: first=k2
                    kk=k2+len(sg)
                if not seg_ok: ok=False;break
                hits.append((first,kk));pos=kk
            else:
                hits.append((k,k+len(p)));pos=k+len(p)
        if ok and hits:
            a=hits[0][0];b=hits[-1][1]-1
            res.append((name,m[a][0],m[b][0],m[a][1],m[b][1]))
    return res
if __name__=='__main__':
    txt=open(sys.argv[1],encoding='utf-8').read()
    body=txt
    qs=re.findall(r"(?<![A-Za-z])‘(.+?)’(?![A-Za-z])",body,flags=re.S)
    bad=0
    for q in qs:
        if len(q.split())<2: continue
        r=find(q)
        if not r:
            bad+=1;print('NOT FOUND :',q)
        else:
            srcs='; '.join(f"{n} p{a}{'-'+b if b!=a else ''} rep[{ra}{'-'+rb if rb!=ra else ''}]" for n,a,b,ra,rb in r[:3])
            print('FOUND     :',q[:70],'=>',srcs)
    print('TOTAL',len(qs),'NOT FOUND',bad)

LAWS1061 Torts

Mid-Term Assignment

Term 2 2026

Name: Yusuf Ahmed

zID: z5686965

Part A (Problem): 1,652 words

Part B (Essay): 848 words

Total: 2,500 words

PART A

No claim assessed is excluded by s 3B of the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW) ('CLA'), which thus applies alongside the common law.[1]

I. SPC'S DUTY OF CARE TO JIA

A. Physical injury

Jia's 'serious spinal injury, causing partial paralysis' is a 'personal injury' ('PI').[2] SPC's careless securing of the carabiner is not an omission but part of its act of running the activity.[3] Within this established category, whether SPC owes a duty of care ('DoC') turns on reasonable foreseeability ('RF') of injury to a class of persons; salient features arise only for a novel duty.[4] Under Lord Atkin's neighbour principle, SPC must take reasonable care to avoid acts it can 'reasonably foresee would be likely to injure' its neighbour; carelessly securing a carabiner on a 20-metre jump risked injuring participants.[5] That the carabiner loosened as others turned to Marcus doesn’t negate such duty: 'injury to a class of persons of which [Jia] was one' was foreseeable, not the 'precise manner' or 'sequence of events'.[6] SPC therefore owes Jia a DoC for her PI.

B. Consequential mental harm

Jia's 'Major Depressive Disorder' ('MDD') is consequential mental harm ('CMH'), 'a consequence of' her PI.[7] Whether the duty extends turns on s 32(1): no duty arises unless SPC ought to have foreseen that a person of normal fortitude ('NF') might suffer a 'recognised psychiatric illness' ('RPI'), the circumstances including her PI.[8] Jia is partially paralysed, in 'ongoing pain', and 'can no longer work in the tech industry': lasting impairment and lost livelihood apt to produce MDD, an RPI, in a person of NF.[9] Thus, SPC likely owes Jia a DoC for her CMH.[10]

II. SPC'S DUTY OF CARE TO MARGRET

Margret suffered no physical injury, thus her 'Cotard's Delusion' is pure mental harm ('PMH').[11] Whether SPC owes her a DoC depends on s 32(1): no duty arises unless SPC ought to have foreseen that a person of NF might suffer some RPI, not Cotard's; and four circumstances in the CLA guide this, although none are decisive.[12]

Firstly, sudden shock: Margret 'heard the loud thump and screaming' and 'immediately froze', a 'sudden and disturbing impression'; this supports foreseeability.[13] Secondly, however, she likely did not witness Jia 'being ... injured or put in peril': she 'did not see the impact', finding Jia already with paramedics; this weakens the claim.[14] Thirdly, the cousins 'grew up together': although not immediate family, the “nature of the relationship” is strong.[15] Fourthly, SPC's marketing of a 'fun and safe environment' to 'families and friends' arguably thickens their relationship; yet a pre-existing relationship between Margret and SPC is still weak; attendee to operator.[16]

Decisively, the ‘yardstick’ is the person of NF: 'a duty does not arise if mental harm would only be suffered by a person with an eggshell psyche', which her psychiatrist calls hers.[17] Nor does the knowledge provision assist: nothing suggests SPC knew or ought to have known of her fragility, and her 'racked by the guilt of ... not looking' reaction is idiosyncratic.[18] At common law, Jaensch is distinguishable: Margret was not immediate family and did not see the accident or Jia’s immediate injury.[19] Lederer is analogous because Margret’s harm turned on an eggshell psyche and guilt, not a foreseeable psychiatric response in a person of normal fortitude.[20]

Therefore, the better view is that SPC likely owes no DoC.

III. SPC'S DUTY OF CARE TO PATSY

A. Physical injury

Patsy's 'minor friction burns' are likewise a PI caused by an act; whether SPC owes a DoC again turns on RF alone.[21] SPC left Patsy supervising 'by herself' for 'the very first time', on 'five days of training' against its protocol of 'two staff members and seven days'; injury to her was foreseeable. Her attempt to catch the rope, at some risk to herself, is the intervention Chapman holds foreseeable.[22]

SPC therefore owes Patsy a DoC for her PI.

B. Pure mental harm

Patsy's 'Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder' ('PTSD') is PMH, stemming from witnessing Jia's fall, rather than her burns.[23] Whether SPC owes a DoC turns on the same s 32(1) threshold, and PTSD is an RPI.[24]

Firstly, the failure was a sudden shock seen first-hand, though shock is neither necessary nor sufficient.[25] Secondly, and most strongly, Patsy witnessed, at the scene, a person being injured: 'eyes glued to Jia', she 'saw the accident unfold', unlike Margret, who only heard.[26] Thirdly, although no pre-existing relationship is required; her relationship with SPC as 'general consultant' supports foreseeability.[27] Her “commando” and “active combat duty” background does not defeat duty: s 32 asks whether a person of normal fortitude might suffer an RPI in Patsy’s position, not whether Patsy personally was more or less likely to suffer one.[28]

On balance, a person of NF so placed might suffer an RPI; Patsy saw the accident itself, distinguishable from a Jaensch ‘aftermath’; the common law supports that conclusion.[29] SPC therefore likely owes Patsy a DoC for her PMH.

IV. SPC'S DUTY OF CARE TO GR

GR's loss of 'many customers' is pure economic loss ('PEL').[30] The claim is negligent misstatement; whether SPC owes a DoC turns on a special relationship, beyond RF, shown by reliance and assumption of responsibility.[31]

A. Reasonable reliance and assumption of responsibility

A duty arises where, on a serious matter, the representor realises it is 'trusted ... as a basis for action' and loss is foreseeable; reasonable reliance is 'a cornerstone of liability'.[32] SPC 'encourage[d]' GR to open 'directly across the road', supplying projections, with 'an interest in the recipient so acting'; this supports reliance, though only one indicator.[33] However, the main defence is that SPC told GR to 'make any final financial decisions themselves', a disclaimer negating assumption of responsibility, as in Hedley Byrne and Mallonland.[34] Yet the disclaimer was general, whereas the specific 'healthy bank balance' claim was a fact only SPC could verify; SPC's debts 'far outweighed' its 'cash liquidity', so the claim conveyed an incomplete impression of strength.[35]

B. Vulnerability

Vulnerability is a powerful PEL control factor favouring SPC: GR, a 'long-established Australia-wide business' like Esanda's 'sophisticated investors', could have sought warranties.[36] On the other hand, only SPC knew its finances and that GR would rely.[37] Indeterminacy is contained because GR was identified, but commercial autonomy still weighs against recognising a duty.[38]

On balance, the better view is that SPC owes GR no DoC: the disclaimer, GR's capacity to protect itself and the absent assumption of responsibility outweigh the induced reliance, though the bank-balance claim keeps this arguable.[39]

V. RECOVERY

Whether Part 3 precludes recovery arises for the mental-harm claims of Jia, Margret and Patsy, not GR's PEL.[40]

A. Jia

Jia's MDD is consequential, not pure, so the PMH limits do not apply; only the s 33 economic-loss bar remains, and MDD is an RPI.[41] Jia's recovery is not precluded.

B. Margret

Even if a duty arose, Margret's PMH faces two independent preclusions.

Firstly, recovery requires witnessing 'at the scene, the victim being killed, injured or put in peril', or being 'a close member of the family'.[42] Jia arguably remained “in peril” during treatment, but Wicks is distinguishable: Margret did not encounter the accident scene as a rescuer or see Jia’s injury directly, instead finding her already with paramedics; a cousin is outside the exhaustive family list.[43]

Secondly, liability requires an RPI; Cotard's, 'not included in the DSM-5' and backed only by 'homeopaths and some psychologists', is likely not one, though recognition is for the court.[44]

Margret's recovery is accordingly likely precluded.

C. Patsy

By contrast, Patsy clears both statutes: her PTSD is an RPI, and she 'witnessed, at the scene', Jia being injured. Jia's recovery not being precluded, the s 30(4) derivative bar does not operate.[45]

Patsy's recovery is not precluded.

VI. SAFE TECH'S DUTY OF CARE

Safe Tech, 'constituted' by 'regional development regulations' ('the Regulations'), is a 'public or other authority' 'constituted by or under an Act'.[46] The Regulations impose a duty to 'maintain structural oversight' and a power to 'inspect ... and give directions'; the former strengthens the plaintiffs' case but creates no common-law duty.[47] The claims concern the manner of exercise: Safe Tech 'conducted an inspection' and its inspector, Ming, 'simply approved it'.[48]

A. Jia

Whether Safe Tech owes Jia a DoC turns on Crimmins' six questions. Firstly, approving an unsafe activity foreseeably 'would result in injury' to participants.[49] Secondly and thirdly, the power protects a 'specific class'; Jia could not 'adequately safeguard' herself from failures the inspection existed to catch.[50]

Fourthly, having inspected, Safe Tech ought to have known the risk: WorkCover found the accident 'would likely have been avoided if proper safety systems were in place'. The strongest counter is Amaca: on similar inspection powers the State owed no duty, neither 'the sole entity with knowledge' nor, per Stuart, the party that created the risk.[51] Fifthly, 'stretched' hiring of 'brand new graduates' is 'core policy-making', 'not open to challenge' (s 42); the claim targets the operational approval.[52] Sixthly, no 'supervening reasons in policy' deny a duty: the inspection power is a 'special statutory power', but s 43A limits liability, not duty, requiring an exercise 'so unreasonable that no authority ... could properly consider [it] to be a reasonable exercise'; Ming's approving the jump on Patsy's 'military background' arguably qualifies.[53]

The better view is that Safe Tech likely owes Jia a duty, its mandatory oversight and positive approval distinguishing Amaca, though finely balanced.

B. Patsy

On the six questions, Patsy, on-site supervisor, is within the 'specific class'; her PI runs as Jia's; for PMH, a person of NF witnessing the accident might suffer an RPI.[54] Safe Tech likely owes her a duty for both.

C. Margret

Margret fails the first and second questions: her 'eggshell psyche' and guilt defeat NF foreseeability, and an attended is arguably outside the 'specific class'.[55] Safe Tech owes her no duty.

D. GR

GR fails the second and sixth questions: the power protects ventures utilising Fire Up, not neighbours; its loss is PEL.[56] Safe Tech owes GR no duty.

PART B

Statement:

“If you can reasonably foresee that a particular class of people might suffer any type of harm as a possible consequence of your acts or omissions, then accordingly, you should owe them a duty of care. If it were otherwise, we are saying that it is acceptable to harm certain people in certain ways.”

Reasonable Foreseeability and the Boundaries of the Duty of Care

Introduction

Reasonable foreseeability is necessary to a duty of care, but it cannot be sufficient, thus the statement would be wrong to treat it as such. Its first proposition, that foreseeability of 'any type of harm' to a class of persons, as a 'possible consequence' of one's 'acts or omissions', should found a duty, must be rejected, because a duty must rest on an interest the law can protect fairly and coherently. Its second proposition, that to refuse a duty is to call the harm 'acceptable', is mostly wrong, because a refusal usually draws a justified limit rather than licensing harm. Yet the second proposition is right in one case: where the law refuses a duty not to keep liability within proper limits but because of the plaintiff's own constitution, as the normal-fortitude rule does to Margret, it does decide that her injury need not count, and there it is unjust.

Foreseeability alone cannot found a duty

A duty of care cannot rest on foreseeability alone; it must rest on an interest the law can protect fairly and coherently. Consider the first proposition applied to GR: its loss of 'many customers' was foreseeable once SPC's venture failed, so on the statement's logic SPC would owe GR a duty. The same reasoning would make SPC liable to every business whose trade foreseeably fell with it, for an indeterminate loss owed to an indeterminate class, and worse, it would turn competition itself into a wrong: if a business had to answer for every foreseeable loss its failure caused its neighbours, few businesses would open at all, and the enterprise the economy depends on would be deterred.[57] That is why the law leaves pure economic loss where it falls unless more than foreseeability is shown: a special relationship, reliance and an assumption of responsibility.[58]

GR, a 'long-established' business told to 'make any final financial decisions themselves', could have protected itself, and the law is right not to make SPC its insurer. Jia's case shows the contrast: her 'serious spinal injury' founds a duty on foreseeability alone,[59] because bodily integrity is an interest the law protects and can protect without absurd consequences. The difference is not that Jia's harm was more foreseeable, but that a duty must rest on an interest whose protection is fair, which foreseeability of 'any type of harm' can never guarantee.

The one limitation to the second proposition

To refuse a duty is usually not to license the harm but to draw a justified limit; the second proposition fails except where that limit cannot itself be justified. To deny GR a duty is not to declare its loss acceptable, but to decide, for good reason, that the loss lies where it falls. Abel presses further, arguing that the malleable concepts of duty and proximate cause are invoked to curtail liability and to distribute protection unequally, so that no such limit is truly principled; but his remedy, replacing fault-based tort with a no-fault scheme overreaches: the manipulability of a concept does not make every use of it unprincipled.[60] The sounder view is that a limit stands or falls on whether it can be justified, and by that test the normal-fortitude rule cannot.

Applied to Margret, s 32(1) of the Civil Liability Act denies a duty for her 'Cotard's Delusion' unless the defendant ought to have foreseen that a person of normal fortitude might suffer a recognised psychiatric illness in her position, so her 'eggshell psyche' is held against her;[61] the objection here is to that s 32 duty threshold, not the recovery limits in ss 30 and 31.[62] Physical injury faces no such test: the eggshell skull rule already makes defendants answer for the unforeseeably frail, so that exposure cannot justify barring the mind. As Forster and Engel show, the rationale for that difference is 'nebulous', the reforms serving to 'reinforce and magnify historic distinctions between physical and mental harm',[63] even though Tame v New South Wales had already loosened such controls, treating sudden shock and direct perception as relevant, rather than decisive.[64] Their criticism is sound, but it does not condemn every control: they accept that some rest on 'credible rationales'.[65] The objection is narrow yet true in that one can no more choose one's fortitude than the thickness of one's skull, so to bar Margret for a frailty she never chose, when the law would not bar the physically injured, is exactly to treat her harm as an injury that need not count.

On this, the statement is right, and the law should raise the duty owed for psychiatric injury to the standard it already applies to the body.

Conclusion

Thus, in short; both propositions within the statement fault respectively, foreseeability cannot found a duty, because a duty must rest on an interest the law can protect fairly and coherently; and refusing to protect an interest is usually a just limit, not a licence to harm. However, the exception vindicates the concern behind the second proposition: the normal-fortitude bar limits liability not by any principled measure but by the plaintiff's own vulnerability, and there, and only there, the law does decide whose injury will count. It should not, and the mind should be taken as found, as the body already is.

                    LAWS1150/JURD7150 Principles of Private Law

                            Mid-Term Assignment for T3, 2026

                          Maximum Word Length: 1,500 words

                    Due Date: Monday, 19 October 2026 at 9:00am

                        (see Moodle for additional instructions)



PROBLEM QUESTION

Mr Grace and Mr Rocky are both project developers who pursued various projects
together since 2017 to stellar success.

In January 2020, Grace and Rocky agreed to develop a project which they named the
‘Hail Mary Project’. Grace and Rocky entered into a legally binding agreement that
determined the scope of their development relationship and included a valid and
binding clause that if the Project made a proﬁt, Rocky, as the investor for the Project,
would be repaid his investment and a portion of the proﬁt in priority to Grace (the
‘Development Agreement’).

Over the course of the Hail Mary Project, there were a number of unavoidable delays
due to COVID-19 related public health orders that aQected the ability for construction to
proceed. In January 2024, the Hail Mary Project was near completion, and Rocky and
Grace realised that the proﬁt from the Project would be minimal and, due to the terms
of their Development Agreement, Grace was unlikely to make a proﬁt.

At this time, Grace was experiencing signiﬁcant ﬁnancial diQiculties and had been
relying on expected proﬁts from the Hail Mary Project. He was quite angry at Rocky, who
he blamed for the delays to the Project, and demanded Rocky’s assistance. On 5
February 2024, Grace called Rocky and proposed that Rocky oQer Grace a ‘$1 million
dollar working capital loan for 2 years at 5% interest’. Rocky told Grace he was not
interested in oQering Grace a long-term loan but proposed that they meet in person to
discuss.

On 12 February 2024, Rocky and Grace met in person. Later that same day, Rocky sent
an email to Grace conﬁrming the details of their discussion. The email read as follows:

       ‘Mr Grace,

       Conﬁrming discussions from our meeting this morning:

       -   I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest
           subject to satisfactory conditions.
       -   Potential project over in Eastwood subject to success of Hail Mary Project.
       -   Threatened litigation from subcontractor from Bowral Project – wait and see
           at present.

       Please conﬁrm agreement.

       Rocky’

Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying, ‘Mr Rocky, Conﬁrmed. Best,
Grace.’

On 27 February 2024, Rocky asked A-Maize Pty Ltd, (‘AMPL’) a company owned and
controlled by Rocky’s cousin, Pierre, to advance $1,150,000 to Grace. Pierre agreed to
provide the money to Grace and the $1,150,000 was advanced by AMPL on the same
day.

On 8 April 2024, Rocky, Grace, and Pierre attended a meeting at AMPL’s oQice. At the
meeting, AMPL and Grace entered into a written loan agreement (the ‘Loan
Agreement’). The loan was recorded as $1,150,000 (‘Loan’) with an interest rate of 4%
per annum. Interest was to be paid by Grace monthly, and the Loan was repayable at
the expiry of 12 months.

The Loan Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed
repayment of the Loan. Pierre expressed during the meeting that he expected Rocky to
ensure that Grace made all payments under the Loan Agreement promptly. Rocky said,
‘I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the
Loan.’ Pierre agreed and the clause was included in the Loan Agreement before it was
signed by Grace and AMPL.

Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025, Grace made appropriate monthly
repayments of the interest on the Loan to AMPL. Throughout this period Rocky would
check in consistently with Grace via email.

On 13 February 2025, Rocky sent an email to Grace asking, ‘when and how [Grace]
intend[ed] to repay the principal of the Loan – the $1.15m?’. Grace did not respond to
Rocky’s email by 27 February 2025 and did not respond to Rocky’s subsequent emails
of 28 February 2025 and 2 March 2025.

On 5 March 2025, Rocky instructed his solicitor to send a letter of demand to Grace
requiring repayment of the principal amount under the Loan Agreement with AMPL. In
response to the letter of demand, on 7 March 2025, Grace called Rocky and said, ‘I
never signed anything with you, so you can’t enforce anything. Leave me alone!’

On that same date, AMPL contacted Grace directly, however, Grace refused to pay,
saying, ‘I have until 8 April 2025 to repay and you won’t see a cent before then’. AMPL
argued that the Loan was advanced on 27 February, and thus the 12 months had begun
then. Grace disagreed, saying, ‘if you don’t leave oQ, I might not pay at all!’
Unfortunately, AMPL required the $1,150,000 as soon as possible and so on 9 March
2025, when Grace had not yet repaid the Loan, AMPL called for payment of the Loan
under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky.

Assuming that all of the above takes place in New South Wales, advise Rocky on
the success of any contractual claims he could make.

In your answer, only consider the course materials from weeks 1 to 4 of Principles
of Private Law.

Revision of basic concepts


Concept               Definition
Offer                 An expression of willingness to enter into a contract on specific
                      terms.
Invitation to treat   An invitation for others to make an offer or enter into a
                      negotiation.
Unilateral contract   A contract in which the offeree accepts the offer by performing
                      their side of the bargain. It is unilateral because one party has
                      performed his or her obligations by the time of formation, only
                      the other party is ever under a contractual obligation.
Bilateral contract    A contract in which both parties are under a contractual
                      obligation to perform their side of the bargain at the time of
                      formation.

Broad view – per Bowen CJ in Eq in Bressan v Squires [1974]
  2 NSWLR 460, 461-2. [Pages 86-87 of Casebook]

• Postal Acceptance Rule: Where the circumstances are such
  that it must have been within the contemplation of the
  parties that, according to the ordinary usages of mankind, the
  post might be used as a means of communicating the
  acceptance of an offer, the acceptance is complete as soon as
  it is posted.

  ie: all that needs to be in contemplation of the parties is
  the post as a possible or permitted mode [of acceptance].

                                     Bargains or Conditional Gifts


Australian Woollen Mills Pty Ltd v Commonwealth
Example 1 – No request

➢ A said to B: “I will pay you £1000 on your arrival in Sydney”: no contract as there may be no relation
  whatever between A’s statements and B’s act. It is consistent with the facts proved that B intended to go to
  Sydney anyhow, and that A is merely announcing that, if and when B arrives in Sydney, he will make a GIFT
  to him.

➢ The necessary relation is not shown to exist between the announcement and the act

Example 2 – Additional facts

➢ A had told B, before the mentioning of the money, that it was a matter of vital important to A that B should
  come to Sydney; B objected that to go to Sydney at the moment might involve him in financial loss. B goes
  to Sydney because of the money offered.

➢ This suggests:

➢ (1) the statement to pay the money was intended as an offer of a promise;

➢ (2) the promise was offered as the consideration for the doing of the act by B;

➢ (3) the doing of the act was at once the acceptance of the offer and the providing of an executed
  consideration for a promise

Three questions call for decision by their Lordships' Board.

(1) Does the guarantee upon its proper construction state a valid con
    sideration for the defendants' promise of indemnity?

(2) Does the extrinsic evidence as to the circumstances in which the
guarantee was given establish the existence of a valid consideration
additional to the consideration, if any, stated in the agreement?

(3) If there be consideration for the promise of indemnity, is the
guarantee nevertheless unenforceable, the consent of the defendants
having been induced by duress? Upon the third question there are
concurrent findings of fact. It would have to be shown, therefore, that

                 Existing Legal Duty Rule

TA Sundell & Sons Pty Ltd v Emm Yannoulatos
  (Overseas) Pty Ltd (1955) 56 SR (NSW) 323
The general rule is that a promise to perform an existing duty is
  not consideration, at least:
• when the promise is made by a party to a pre-existing
  contract,
• when it is made to the promisee under that contract, and
• it is to do no more than the promisor is bound to do under
  that contract. (Wigan v Edwards (1973) 1 ALR 497, 512 (Mason
  J))

Often arises in cases of a variation to the terms of an agreement
General rule

• A promise to perform an existing contractual duty is not
   regarded as sufficient consideration


3 exceptions to the rule:

• practical benefit (Williams v Roffey; Musumeci v Winadell)
• promises to third parties (Pao On v Lau Yiu Long – class 2A)
• Genuine/ bona fide compromise (Wigan v Edwards)

•   Selectmove owed tax.

        Masters v Cameron (1954) 91 CLR 353;
Subject to a formal contract on terms acceptable to the vendor’s
solicitors
• Category 1 – parties have reached finality in all parts of their
   bargain and intend to be bound with no changes
   – Immediately binding
• Category 2 – parties have agreed all terms but made one or
  more terms conditional on execution of contract
   – Import a binding obligation to have a binding contract
   – Once the formal contract exists they will be bound
• Category 3 – no bargain intended until a formal contract is
  signed, satisfactory to my solicitors “subject to contract” (M v
  C)
   – Not binding at all

        followed in Baulkham Hills Private Hospital case

• 4th category
• The parties intend to be bound “immediately and exclusively”
  by the terms they have agreed on, “while expecting to make a
  further contract in substitution for the first contract

                                                                        Intention to Create Legal Relations

•   Sean and Patrick, owned a group of companies and trusts
•   Their relationship deteriorated
•   Sean fired Patrick
•   Sean and Patrick executed a heads of agreement. In broad terms, the agreement
    provided for Sean to buy Patrick out of the group for $10 million. It also provided
    for further negotiations (including as to tax issues) and allowed a short period of
    time in which a more formal agreement might be concluded.
•   No further agreement was concluded. Within weeks, Patrick purported to
    terminate the agreement.
•   Incomplete Heads of Agreement
•   Tax details of deal not resolved
• [60] The first inquiry is whether agreement has been reached on the essential terms
    constitutive of a contract; the second inquiry is whether the parties have (by agreeing on
    enough other important terms) expressed an intention to be bound by those terms.. These
    are distinct inquiries and may yield different answers. The parties may intend to make a
    contract but fail to do so by not agreeing on the essential terms. Conversely, the parties may
    have reached agreement on the essential terms but not yet intend to be bound.
•   [78] In all the circumstances, the trial judge was correct in our opinion to find that it was
    established that the parties to the heads of agreement intended to enter into a binding
    agreement to complete the sale and purchase transaction.

What might make a contact uncertain, and thus not a n
enforceable contract?

• Incompleteness
    – Failure to agree on an essential term, or an agreement to agree
• Unresolvable ambiguity
    – Contract hopelessly vague or imprecise
• Illusory promise
    – Usually because promisor expresses the nominally contractual promise in
       such a way that reserves to him/ herself a discretion whether he/she will
       actually carry it out.

• The categories often overlap
• NOTE: courts will strive to give effect to a contract if possible

                           Upper Hunter County District Council v
                           Australian Chilling and Freezing Co Ltd
                                                                                Certainty




A contract of which there can be more than one possible meaning or which when
construed can produce in its application more than one result is not void for
uncertainty. As long as it is capable of meaning, it will ultimately bear that meaning
which the courts, …, decide is its proper construction …
The question becomes one of construction, of ascertaining the intention of the
parties, and of applying it.
So long as the language employed by the parties is not so obscure and so incapable
of any definite or precise meaning that the court is unable to attribute to the parties
any particular contractual intention, the contract cannot be held to be void or
uncertain or meaningless. In the search for that intention, no narrow or pedantic
approach is warranted, particularly in the case of commercial arrangements.
… the concept of a cost of doing something is certain in the sense that it provides a
criterion by reference to which the rights of the parties may ultimately and logically
be worked out, if not by the parties then by the courts… In this case, the contract
itself provided the means of resolution… by the decision of an arbitrator whose
judgment … was agreed to be final and binding … (Barwick CJ)

Recognition that there are questions of construction

improvident, does not mean that the clause is
meaningless, nor, does recognition that, in particular
circumstances, there may be more than one view about
the true effect of the clause.
Ambiguities of the sort that I have been discussing, do
not however involve that kind of uncertainty which
defeats the intention of the parties to make a binding
contract; viz., the use of language which, as a matter of
construction and not mere speculation, cannot be given
any one meaning rather than another.

How might gap be filled?
1. Every case depends on its own facts – objective determination or may need
   extrinsic evidence.
2. Court will try not to frustrate the wishes of the contracting parties.
3. Court will not make a call when the parties themselves have failed to agree.
4. JJ views will differ about classification of the challenged provision.
5. Court will pay regard to the features of the agreement, the relationship
   between the parties and relevant external reference points to decide whether
   the term which is challenged can or cannot be sustained.
6. Relevant matters in determining these cases:
   1.   Provision may be settled by an identified 3 rd party who has been given power to resolve
        ambiguities / uncertainties.
   2.   If term is so vital that leaving it to one of the parties unacceptably removes certainty, court
        may or may not refuse to enforce it as illusory.
   3.   Existence of a readily ascertainable external standard
   4.   If a contract contains a range of possibilities, ct will opt for the minimum within the range.
