“The percentage is fixed by comparison, and ‘[P’s loss, stated as those cases state theirs]’ is set against four decided cases. Khan gives 20% for a testicle removed after a delayed diagnosis, work capacity unchanged and no ongoing physical disability. Jopling gives 28% for a fractured patella from a defective balcony, with chronic leg pain, restricted movement, snowboarding lost, surfing impaired, knee scarring and a risk of early arthritis. Wighton gives 45% for negligent surgery producing intense neck pain, shoulder damage, an inability to walk more than twenty minutes and difficulty with nappy-changing, bathing, breast-feeding and driving. George v Survery gives 65% for a heart transplant after a negligent failure to diagnose, with fatigue, muscle wasting, cognitive impairment, depression and lifelong immunosuppressants. Earlier decisions may be cited (CLA s 17A(1)), thus ‘[the severity percentage]’ follows from that comparison.”

A · above the mid decided cases

  “‘[The two nearest decided cases, and the respect in which P sits between them]’ place [P] above the middle of the ladder: worse off than Jopling’s 28%, chronic leg pain, restricted movement, snowboarding lost and knee scarring, and approaching Wighton’s 45%, intense neck pain, shoulder damage and an inability to walk more than twenty minutes, while George v Survery’s 65%, a heart transplant with lifelong immunosuppressants, stays above. ‘[The severity percentage]’ accordingly follows, earlier decisions citable (CLA s 17A(1)).”

B · below the mid decided cases

  “‘[The function P retains that the higher decided case had lost]’ holds [P] below the middle of the ladder: Khan is analogous at 20%, its work capacity unchanged and no ongoing physical disability, while Jopling’s 28%, chronic leg pain, restricted movement and snowboarding lost, is not reached, function largely intact, and Wighton at 45% and George v Survery at 65% stand far above. ‘[The severity percentage]’ arguably follows, earlier decisions citable (CLA s 17A(1)).”

C · two decided cases pulling opposite ways

  “The ladder cuts both ways on ‘[P’s loss, stated as those cases state theirs]’: Jopling’s 28% is analogous because [P] shares its chronic pain, restricted movement and lost sport, yet Wighton’s 45% is analogous too, [P] sharing that plaintiff’s difficulty with nappy-changing, bathing and driving. Therefore, the better view is that ‘[the severity percentage]’ sits between the two, nearer the decided case whose functional loss [P] more closely matches (CLA s 17A(1)), the Table converting only what the comparison fixes.”

State the percentage and the decided cases it rests on, never the percentage alone · To convert it under the Table → B11

B25 The three types of recoverable loss (CSR v Eddy) · when the facts give a loss that answers no obvious head

“Losses divide into three types. Firstly, non-pecuniary losses ‘such as pain and suffering, disfigurement, loss of limbs or organs, loss of the senses: sight, taste, hearing, smell and touch; and loss of the capacity to engage in hobbies, sport, work, marriage and child-bearing’, recoverable ‘even if no actual financial loss is caused’. Secondly, ‘loss of earning capacity both before the trial and after it’, ‘awardable only to the extent that the loss has been or may be productive of financial loss’. Thirdly, ‘actual financial loss, for example, ambulance charges; charges for medical, hospital and professional nursing services; travel and accommodation expenses incurred in obtaining those services; the costs of rehabilitation needs, special clothing and special equipment; the costs of modifying houses; the costs of fund management; and the costs of professionally supplied home maintenance services’ (CSR v Eddy [28]–[31] per Gleeson CJ, Gummow and Heydon JJ). ‘[The expense or loss claimed]’ is put to one of the three.”

A · recoverable as actual financial loss

  “‘[The expense claimed]’ answers ‘[the Eddy item it answers, quoted]’ within the third type, actual financial loss (CSR v Eddy [28]–[31]), and ‘[the evidence the need arose from the injury and not otherwise]’ shows the need is one the injury created. Where fund management is claimed, ‘[the evidence P cannot manage her own affairs]’ supports it, the court notifying the NSW Trustee and Guardian where it ‘considers that the person may be a person in need of protection’ (CLA s 23(3)). It is recoverable at ‘[the cost claimed]’.”

B · not a recoverable loss

  “‘[The expense claimed]’ answers none of the Eddy items: not ‘travel and accommodation expenses incurred in obtaining those services’, nor ‘the costs of rehabilitation needs, special clothing and special equipment’, nor ‘the costs of modifying houses’, nor ‘the costs of fund management’ (CSR v Eddy [28]–[31]), and ‘[why the expense fails to answer a named Eddy item]’ is the reason. Nor is it lost earning capacity, ‘awardable only to the extent that the loss has been or may be productive of financial loss’. It is not recoverable here, although the first type may yet take it as non-economic loss.”

C · Eddy both ways on the item

  “Eddy cuts both ways on ‘[the expense claimed]’. It sits within the third type because it answers ‘[the Eddy item it answers, quoted]’, the list running from ambulance charges to ‘the costs of professionally supplied home maintenance services’; yet ‘[why the expense arguably fails to answer a named Eddy item]’ points the other way, and the second type is ‘awardable only to the extent that the loss has been or may be productive of financial loss’. Therefore, the better view is that it is recoverable as actual financial loss, though the characterisation is arguable.”

Route the type, do not merge them: for the first type, non-pecuniary loss → B23A; for the second, loss of earning capacity before and after trial → 3; for the third, actual financial loss, value it here and then → 6

B26 The claim is [P]’s, not the carer’s · when the facts dwell on what the carer gave up, a job left, income forgone, a life rearranged, or a defendant says the carer should…

“What [the carer, named] gave up founds nothing of [the carer, named]’s own: it is the need for the services which gives [P] the right to an award, so the damages ‘are not determined by reference to the actual cost to the plaintiff of having them provided or by reference to the income forgone by the provider of the services’ (Van Gervan 333), and ‘the case will be rare indeed where the income forgone by the care provider is ever an appropriate guide to the fair value of the services required by the injured person’. [P] is ‘beneficially entitled to the judgment he obtains without question of the imposition of any trust in respect of some part of his damages in favour of one who has rendered … gratuitous services to him’ (Griffiths per Stephen J).”

A · the carer’s forgone income is not the measure

  “[The carer, named] gave up ‘[the job, income or life the carer gave up]’, and that is not the measure: damages answer the need, not the provider, so they ‘are not determined … by reference to the income forgone by the provider of the services’, ‘the case … rare indeed’ where that income is any guide (Van Gervan 333); market cost governs instead. The award is [P]’s, ‘beneficially entitled to the judgment’ without any trust in the carer’s favour (Griffiths per Stephen J), ‘no legal obligation’ existing to pay it over (Grincelis [51] per Callinan J).”

B · the carer has no claim of her own

  “[The carer, named] has no action of her own for ‘[the job, income or life the carer gave up]’: the head belongs to [P], the definition reaching services ‘provided by another person to a claimant’ for which ‘the claimant has not paid or is not liable to pay’ (CLA s 15(1)), and [P] is ‘beneficially entitled to the judgment’ without any trust in the carer’s favour (Griffiths per Stephen J). That the carer is unlikely to be able to distribute the loss is why the claim runs through [P], the wrongdoer ‘a much better loss distributor’ (Griffiths per Stephen J).”

→ 5 → 6

## FILE: drive/txt/LAWS1150 Mid-Term - Final Marker Feedback.txt
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Final adversarial marker feedback (verbatim)
Two independent hostile markers marked the final text and tried to break it against the readings. Their sheets follow word for word.
After they marked, the one certain defect both found (treating ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ as unproven) was fixed, as
were two further points from Marker A that the source text confirms (‘unqualified’ removed, since Rocky’s words were conditional;
‘supports it’ changed to ‘supports intention’). Points raised by only one marker that the other marker disputes, and arguments that
would need words the 1,500 limit does not leave, have not been applied; they are set out in the sheets.

Marker A

Marker A: hostile examination of the final answer
Marked against SHEET_v12 read with RULINGS R-P, R-Y, R-Z, R-AB, R-AC, R-AD and R-AE. Every authority in the footnotes was re-
read at its page in the casebook transcription or, where the point is official-only, in the saved official judgment. Verifier run: 40
quotations, 0 FAIL, 2 CHECK PIN (Brambles 176 and Pao On 629 to 630, both known artefacts and both correct on re-reading). Body
1,488 words; the stated 1,491 is body plus three under R-P, so no fault.


1. Certain defects

C1. A proven fact treated as unproven, and the narrator’s words put in AMPL’s mouth (Part II, guarantee paragraph).

Sentence: “AMPL’s call ‘under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ assumes, but does not prove, his assent, and because
privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[^29] AMPL must show that assent.”

Proof: the problem (question.txt, final page) reads “AMPL called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided by
Rocky”. The words ‘provided by Rocky’ are the problem’s own description, not AMPL’s assertion, and the Instructions (p 1) say “You
may assume the facts provided in the scenario to be proven”. What is proven is that Rocky provided a guarantee; what is open is only
what ‘provided’ consisted of (assent to the written clause, his oral undertaking, or both). The sentence attributes the words to
“AMPL’s call” and then says they do “not prove” his assent, which denies a proven fact and misidentifies the speaker (sheet D4,
which lists this exact phrase; sheet §3, second bullet).

Fix (+4 words): “A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, but whether by assent to the clause or only by his oral undertaking is open,
and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[^29] AMPL must show that assent.”

C2. ‘Unqualified’ misdescribes words the problem qualifies (Part II, certainty paragraph).

Sentence: “Read objectively, his unqualified ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, likely promised
that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.”

Proof: Rocky’s words are “I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the Loan” (question.txt).
They carry an express ‘if’ qualifier, and the answer’s own offer paragraph relies on it (“offered a promise for a promise”). The point
intended is that the words contain no language of effort, which ‘unqualified’ does not say.

Fix (−1 word): “Read objectively, his ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, contains no words of
effort and likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.” Net cost +3 if the clause is added; the cheapest
certain fix is simply to delete ‘unqualified’ (−1).

C3. A pronoun with two possible antecedents (Part I, intention paragraph).

Sentence: “The qualifier, however, raises whether the parties intended immediate obligations, which is assessed objectively, with the
onus on Grace as the party alleging the contract, although their commercial status as ‘project developers’ supports it.”

Proof: ‘it’ can be read as ‘the onus’ or as the intention; only the second makes sense (Ermogenous [25], which the answer cites, lists
‘the status of the parties’ as a factor going to intention). Sheet R1 and R-V(1): a pronoun is a lapse where its antecedent is unclear.

Fix (0 words): replace “supports it” with “supports intention”.

Word cost of all three: +4 −1 +0 = +3, taking the body to 1,491 and the stated count to 1,494; within 1,497.


2. Contestable points, with fixes

K1. Whose satisfaction (Part I, intention paragraph), an inference stated without its reason. “‘satisfactory’ leaves the
judgment to the party the condition protects,[^8] here Rocky”. Gibbs CJ at 581 grounds the rule in the clause being “generally
entirely for the protection of the purchaser” and leaves room for “a clear indication to the contrary”. Nothing in the email says whose
satisfaction; Grace could say the conditions were to be satisfactory to both, or objectively. Fix (+2): “here Rocky as lender”.

K2. Rocky’s best authority on the qualifier is missed. Masters v Cameron (1954) 91 CLR 353, 362 quotes Jessel MR in Crossley
v Maycock (1874) LR 18 Eq 180, 181 to 182: “if the agreement is made subject to certain conditions then specified or to be specified
by the party making it, or by his solicitor, then, until those conditions are accepted, there is no final agreement”. That is Rocky’s
‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ almost word for word, stated in a High Court joint judgment’s survey, and far stronger than a
single judge’s dictum in Godecke (Gibbs J at 646 to 647, where he says only that it “does not necessarily follow” that such an
agreement binds). The casebook elides this sentence, so it is credit and official-only; but the objectively best answer would use it,
with Jessel MR named, at fn 9.

K3. Brambles 177 cited for consideration (fn 4). The passage (Heydon JA quoting McHugh JA in Integrated Computer Services)
describes ‘classical theory’ (“an exchange of promises by means of an offer and its acceptance”) as a prelude to saying commercial
dealings often do not fit it. It is not a statement of the consideration rule. Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457 (“the relation of a quid
pro quo”) is the course authority for consideration as the price of the promise. Fix (footnotes only, 0 body words): fn 4 becomes the
full Australian Woollen Mills citation at 456 to 457 with the short title; fn 31 and fn 36 become “(n 4)”; fn 19 takes the full Brambles
citation and short title; fn 21 and fn 37 become “(n 19)”.

K4. Gibson for the 5 February call (fn 1). Gibson at 298 decides that “may be prepared to sell” lacks commitment. It does not
decide that a request that the other party make an offer is an invitation. The use is analogical and passes, but a stricter marker
would want the point stated as the absence of any promise by Grace, which is what Gibson actually turns on.

K5. Port Jackson (fn 16, fn 22). The words quoted are Lord Reid’s requisites as Mason and Jacobs JJ set them out at 269, and the
pin is right. But Mason and Jacobs JJ were in the majority that the Privy Council reversed; Barwick CJ (dissenting in the High Court,
whose view the Board preferred) states the same requisites at 240, and the sheet names 240. The answer’s ‘rev’d’ is honest, but
citing the reversed majority when the vindicated judge states the same rule is the weaker choice. Fix (footnotes only): cite Port
Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ). Separately, fn 16 puts ‘quoting’ inside the judge’s brackets, unlike every other ‘quoting’ footnote in the
answer (fn 4, 6, 11, 21, 27); AGLC form is “269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), quoting Scruttons Ltd v Midland Silicones Ltd [1962] AC 446,
474 (Lord Reid)”.

K6. Lord Reid’s requisites for the director question (Part II, agency paragraph). The requisites concern a carrier contracting
as agent for a stevedore to secure an exemption. Using them to decide whether a controlling director spoke for his company is a
stretch; the answer’s own facts (‘controls AMPL’, ‘at its office’, ‘about its loan’) do the work. Fix: state the question as authority to
act for AMPL and keep fn 22 as the general agency source, or cite Ermogenous [24] for objective attribution (credit).

K7. Privity of the $10,000 promise is never addressed (sheet II.F1). If ‘the clause’ that was ‘included in the Loan Agreement’
is the $10,000 term, AMPL will say the term lives in a document between AMPL and Grace to which Rocky is no party. The answer
needs one sentence: Rocky is the promisee and named payee (‘to me directly’) of an oral promise for which he gave consideration, so
privity is no bar; and, in a clause, ‘the clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause the problem names first. About 30 words.

K8. The letter of comfort point (sheet II.D). Rocky’s ‘ensure’ undertaking is the obvious candidate for comparison with the letter
in Banque Brussels; the answer applies ‘appropriately promissory’ only to the $10,000 promise and never weighs whether Rocky’s
own undertaking binds him likewise. About 15 words.

K9. The existing legal duty rule if Pierre promised personally (sheet II.C2). If Pierre is the promisee, any duty Rocky owed
under the guarantee was owed to AMPL, a third party; Pao On 632 holds that a promise to perform a duty owed to a third party is
good consideration. The answer’s “with the promisee” gestures at this but never states the branch. About 15 words.

K10. The duty to co-operate (sheet II.H). AMPL called the guarantee before the Loan was due on the 8 April reading; Rocky can
argue AMPL cannot rely on its own premature call to put the condition ‘once Grace repays’ out of reach. The answer never names or
meets the duty to co-operate. About 20 words.

K11. The interest payments (sheet II.G; R-AA(3)). “Grace made appropriate monthly repayments of the interest on the Loan to
AMPL” between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025 is the fact AMPL’s opponents will reach for on the start date. The answer’s rule
excludes post-contractual conduct (Brambles 164, correct), but never applies it to this fact, so a cold reader cannot tell whether it
was seen. About 12 words.

K12. The onus in Part I. The answer places the onus on Grace as the party alleging the 12 February contract. That is coherent
with its defensive framing (Rocky never lent, so only Grace would sue on the email), and I accept it; but the sheet’s I.D core frames
Rocky as the party alleging, so a marker reading the sheet literally will query it. The framing should be stated once (“Grace, who
alone would sue on it”).

Funding for K7 to K11 (about 92 words against 6 words of headroom after C1 to C3): cut “and likely never if Rocky pays it himself”
in the final paragraph, which repeats the II.H paragraph’s last sentence (−8); cut “Rocky could argue his 12 February email was
merely a negotiating step, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its other points promise nothing” to “Its other points promise
nothing” (−17); compress the Pao On and Roscorla paragraph, whose fallback the answer itself calls “doubtful” (about −20);
compress the Part I conclusion (about −10). Even so, not all five fit; on marks at risk per word the order is K7, K10, K9, K8, K11.

4. Is this the objectively best answer?

No. It is a very strong answer, and on the authorities it uses it is almost faultless: every quotation checks verbatim, every pin is right,
every judge is correctly named, the one dissent is labelled, the one reversed case is flagged, and the single-judge dictum is hedged.
It is not the best answer for four reasons.

First, C1 is a substantive error, not a slip. The problem proves that Rocky provided a guarantee; the live question is what he
provided. By saying AMPL’s call “does not prove” his assent, the answer frames Rocky’s exposure on a premise the facts deny, and a
marker who reads the problem’s last paragraph closely will see it.

Second, it misses the authority that most squarely fits the 12 February qualifier (K2). Rocky’s email made the loan ‘subject to
satisfactory conditions’; Jessel MR’s words quoted at Masters 362 deal with an agreement “subject to certain conditions then
specified or to be specified by the party making it”. The better answer leads with that and uses Godecke only to distinguish Grace’s
best case.

Third, it leaves four arguments unmet that a contracts academic would expect for one side or the other: privity of the $10,000
promise (K7), the duty to co-operate against AMPL’s premature call (K10), the third-party branch of the existing legal duty rule (K9),
and whether Rocky’s own ‘ensure’ undertaking is promissory or mere comfort (K8).

Fourth, two citations are used for less than they say (K3, K6).

The better answer would: fix C1 to C3; put Crossley (through Masters 362) against Grace on the qualifier; add the one-sentence
privity answer for the $10,000 claim; name and meet the duty to co-operate in the condition paragraph; state the Pao On 632 branch
in a clause; and fund it by cutting the repeated ‘pays it himself’ point, compressing the Part I opening and the doubtful past
consideration fallback.


5. Margin comments, paragraph by paragraph

I, para 1 (offer). Good close reading of ‘I will lend’ against ‘may be prepared to sell’. Gibson is stretched for the 5 February call; the
point is that Grace promised nothing. “Rocky could argue … negotiating step” is fair but costs words the answer needs later.

I, para 2 (acceptance and consideration). Clean. ‘Confirmed’ answered against ‘Please confirm agreement’ is exactly right.
Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied: fn 4 (Brambles 177) describes classical theory; it is not
the consideration rule.

I, para 3 (intention). The strongest paragraph in Part I. The pronoun ‘it’ at the end of the first sentence is unclear (C3). “here
Rocky” needs its reason (K1). Rocky’s best authority, Jessel MR at Masters 362, is missing (K2).

I, para 4 (certainty). Excellent distinction of Meehan: honesty governing an external condition against discretion over the loan’s
content. ‘Perhaps’ and the honest-and-reasonable variant could be met in a clause, but this is well done.

I, para 5 (privity). Correct and well sourced; the signature point using Mrs Coulls is effective. “took his guarantee” is consistent
with the problem’s ‘provided by Rocky’, which makes the Part II sentence in C1 all the harder to reconcile.

I, para 6 (conclusion). Clear bottom line; reimbursement disposed of in substantive terms.

II, para 1 (offer and acceptance). Correct; Lord Greene MR’s words are properly attributed. Disclose that Eccles concerned a
formal contract, so the words apply by analogy.

II, para 2 (who promised). Sensible weighing of ‘you’ against control, office and loan. Lord Reid’s requisites are an odd vehicle for
a director question (K6). Further information (whom Pierre spoke for) is implicit; state it.

II, para 3 (consideration). The existing legal duty rule is named and well met on timing. The Pao On 632 branch is missing (K9).

II, para 4 (intention). Correct use of Ermogenous [26]. Further analysis is required: Rocky’s ‘ensure’ undertaking against the
letter of comfort in Banque Brussels is never weighed (K8).

II, para 5 (certainty). “unqualified” misdescribes Rocky’s conditional words (C2). Otherwise sound.

II, para 6 (the guarantee). Your statement of the facts is incorrect: the problem proves a guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, and
those are not AMPL’s words (C1). The Empirnall 535 to 536 analysis that follows is good and fairly hedged.

II, para 7 (consideration for the guarantee). Accurate on Pao On and Roscorla; the fallback through signing the Loan Agreement
is a good point. The third Pao On condition is not stated; not fatal.

II, para 8 (the 12 months). Good textual analysis of ‘recorded’ against the 4% rate. The interest payments fact is not applied
(K11).

II, para 9 (condition). Correct classification with Meehan 582; the commercial reading is put and met. The duty to co-operate is
missing (K10).

II, para 10 (conclusion). Exposure stated precisely, as R-AD requires. The last clause repeats para 9.


6. Marks

Holistic mark: 84 (Distinction, at the top of the band). The law is accurate and the citations are exact, which is rare; the
reasoning is explicit and hedged. It stops short of High Distinction because it misreads a proven fact on the most valuable issue
(Rocky’s exposure on the guarantee), misses the best authority on the 12 February qualifier, and leaves four arguments for one side
or the other unmet.

Rubric mark (SHEET_v12 with R-AB to R-AE): 77.

Answer marked: MARKS/final/in/ANSWER.md, taken at face value. Body 1,488 words on verify.py’s count; the stated ‘Word count:

person in the body.

1. Certain defects (provable from the verbatim text)

C1. The narrated guarantee is treated as AMPL’s assumption rather than as a proven fact. - Sentence: “AMPL’s call ‘under
the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ assumes, but does not prove, his assent, and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s
contract imposing obligations on Rocky, AMPL must show that assent.” - Proof: the words are the problem’s, not AMPL’s: ‘AMPL
called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ (question, final paragraph). The Instructions say
‘You may assume the facts provided in the scenario to be proven’ (Instructions p 1). On R-M, that phrase proves that Rocky provided
a personal guarantee; only what ‘provided’ consisted of (his oral undertaking, assent to the written clause, or both) is open. Saying
the fact ‘does not prove’ anything denies a narrated fact its force, and the sheet’s D4 list names ‘personal guarantee provided by
Rocky’ treated as a party’s assertion. - Fix (+5 words; body 1,493): “Rocky ‘provided’ the guarantee, but whether by assenting to the
clause or only by his oral undertaking is unclear, and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on
Rocky, AMPL must show assent to the clause.”

C2. Footnote 31 cites a passage about a different kind of contract. - Sentence: “but Rocky’s ‘I will do that’, given for the
$10,000 promise, likely binds him at least to his oral undertaking.[^31]” (fn 31: Australian Woollen Mills 456–7). - Proof: the passage
at 456 is about ‘cases of this class’, in which ‘the consideration on the part of the offeree is completely executed by the doing of the
very thing which constitutes acceptance of the offer’, that is, a promise given in exchange for an act; the ‘quid pro quo’ at [457] is
the link between an announcement and an act (CB2A 103, [4.20]). On the answer’s own analysis Rocky’s undertaking was ‘a promise
for a promise’ (fn 19), so it is a bilateral contract, and the passage does not deal with it. The Court in Australian Woollen Mills also
found no contract. Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied on. - Fix (0 words): replace fn 31 with
‘Brambles (n 4) 177 (Heydon JA).’, the authority the answer already uses at fn 19 for the exchange of promises, or delete the footnote
and write ‘as formed above’ (+2 words).

C3. The two Parts take inconsistent positions on the guarantee. - Sentence (Part I): “it lent in its own name and took his
guarantee, so it contracted for itself”. - Proof: Part II then says AMPL ‘must show that assent’ and concludes he is bound by the
clause only ‘if Rocky assented to the clause’. Part I says, without qualification, that AMPL took his guarantee, which is the point Part
II leaves open. R10 (one doctrinal footing). - Fix (0 words): “it lent in its own name and named him guarantor, so it contracted for
itself”.

No authority is misquoted, mis-pinned, attributed to the wrong judge or given the wrong majority or dissent label. Every pin was
checked against the casebook or official text: Gibson 298; Empirnall 534 and 535–6; Brambles 164, 176, 177 and 191 (Ipp AJA, with
whom Mason P agreed, so the majority); Ermogenous [25]–[26]; Masters 363; Godecke 642–3 (Walsh J) and 646–7 (Gibbs J); Meehan
580–2 (Gibbs CJ) and 589–90 (Mason J); Coulls 486, 487 (Taylor and Owen JJ) and 494, 495 (Windeyer J, correctly marked as
dissenting); Port Jackson 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ quoting Lord Reid); Sundell 327; Wigan 594; Banque Brussels 523; Upper Hunter
437; Roscorla 237; Pao On 629–30; Trident (Deane J), with no pin because the reading has no page markers (R-Y).

2. Contestable points, with fixes

  1. Part I is framed around Grace’s claim, not Rocky’s. The question asks for the ‘contractual claims he could make’. The
     opening says the primary issue is whether ‘Grace could claim that Rocky failed to lend’. The claim Rocky would actually make
     against Grace under the February dealings is that AMPL’s advance, made at his request, performed his 12 February promise,
     so that Grace owes him repayment. The answer dismisses this in a clause (‘neither performed his email’). Further analysis is
     required as your statement is conclusive. The fix is to frame the opening on Rocky’s claim (word-neutral). Then give one
     sentence of reasons: the advance was $1,150,000 rather than $1 million, made on 27 February rather than ‘by 15 February’,
     and in AMPL’s name, with terms first fixed at 4% on 8 April (about +25 words).
  2. The Lord Reid conditions are used to decide whether Pierre contracted for AMPL (fn 22: ‘The same agency conditions
     guide whether Pierre … contracted on its behalf’). Lord Reid’s four requisites govern whether a carrier contracted as agent for
     a stevedore so that the stevedore could take the benefit of exemption clauses. Requisites (1) and (4), that the bill makes the
     protection clear and that consideration moves from the stevedore, have no counterpart in whether a director’s oral promise
     binds his company. The better course is to frame the question as which party Rocky’s ‘you’ objectively addressed (Ermogenous
     [25]), with the authority and purporting facts as the answer already weighs them. The ‘further information’ about whom Pierre
     spoke for should also be named (R6).
  3. Port Jackson is cited at 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), the majority that the Privy Council reversed. The ‘rev’d’ history is
     disclosed, which is correct AGLC practice. However, the sheet prefers 240 (Barwick CJ, who would have upheld the stevedore’s
     protection), and the reversal invites a marker to query the source. Since the requisites themselves were never doubted, either
     pin is defensible.
  4. Footnote 4 (consideration) rests on McHugh JA’s description of ‘classical theory’, where ‘the typical contract is a
     bilateral one and consists of an exchange of promises’ (Brambles 177). That passage is about the limits of offer-and-acceptance
     analysis, not a statement of consideration doctrine. Australian Woollen Mills 456–7 states the bargain (quid pro quo) principle
     directly and is the better footnote here, unlike at fn 31.
  5. II.C2 misses Pao On’s third-party point. If Pierre promised personally, any existing guarantee duty was owed to AMPL, not
     to Pierre. A promise to perform a duty owed to a third party is good consideration (Pao On 632), and Mason J’s own limit,
     ‘made to the promisee under that contract’ (Wigan 594), already points there. This is the strongest answer to AMPL’s or
     Pierre’s existing legal duty argument, and it costs one clause (+15).
  6. II.D omits the argument that most helps Rocky on his own exposure. The answer finds intention ‘whoever promised’
     because a fixed sum is ‘appropriately promissory’. It does not put the opposite point for Rocky’s own undertaking: that ‘ensure’
     is closer to the comfort given in Banque Brussels, where the letter of comfort conditioned the facility. Only after that is met
     should it be found ‘weaker here’ because Rocky’s words were given for a price. As it stands, Banque Brussels is cited without
     saying what the case was about (+20).
  7. II.H omits the duty to co-operate. Rocky’s best answer to ‘once Grace repays’ is not only a commercial reading (Upper
     Hunter 437). He can also argue that AMPL may not rely on a condition whose fulfilment its own call frustrates. That argument
     should be put and met: the call does not stop Grace repaying (R-O), so it fails (+20).
  8. II.I4 omits the March instalment. Interest is shown paid only ‘Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025’. On the 8 April
     reading, whether a March 2025 instalment was missed decides whether Rocky’s oral undertaking (to ‘ensure … all payments’)
     is already breached. The closing paragraph speaks only of ‘any amount when due’ (+15, hedged under R-M).
  9. II.F1 is never stated. The $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’, so Rocky is the promisee, and privity is no bar to his claim
     against whoever promised (Coulls 494). It needs one line (+12).
 10. Gibbs J in Godecke (646–7) is dictum. ‘Doubted’ is a fair verb, but the answer then relies on it as the decisive reason (‘so on
     balance’). A strict marker would want ‘in obiter’ (+2), as the sheet’s D3 entry for Godecke 646 to 647 shows.
 11. Pierre’s ‘expected’ is labelled an ‘invitation to treat’. That is defensible, because it drew Rocky’s offer, but ‘a request, not
     an offer’ is the safer course term and costs the same.
 12. Pao On conditions are stated incompletely. The answer gives the request and ‘was to be remunerated’, but omits that the
     payment ‘must have been legally enforceable had it been promised in advance’. That is harmless on these facts but incomplete
     (+8).
 13. The lender’s opening act is not named on the facts in II.G. ‘Post-contractual conduct cannot interpret the term’ is stated
     without the fact it excludes: Grace’s ‘appropriate monthly repayments’ from 8 April 2024 (and his own ‘I have until 8 April
     2025’). Name them (+10). A reader should not have to infer which conduct is meant.
 14. Footnote style is inconsistent. Judges are named in every footnote except Masters (fn 6: Dixon CJ, McTiernan and Kitto JJ)
     and Australian Woollen Mills (fn 31 and 36: the Court). Either name them or adopt one convention.

4. Is this the objectively best answer?

No. It is a very good answer, accurate at source to a degree few scripts reach, and its reasoning on the 12 February email, Meehan
and illusoriness, and privity is close to the best that 1,500 words allow. It is not the best answer for five reasons:

  1. Part I answers the wrong claimant’s question first. It defends against Grace instead of testing Rocky’s own best claim,
     that AMPL’s advance at his request was his lending.
  2. Three points that matter to Rocky’s exposure are missing. The letter-of-comfort argument against his being bound by
     ‘ensure’ is not made. The Pao On third-party answer on consideration is absent. The duty to co-operate is not put on ‘once
     Grace repays’.
  3. Two authorities are stretched beyond what they decide. Australian Woollen Mills is used for a bilateral promise. Lord
     Reid’s carrier and stevedore requisites are used for whether a director binds his company.
  4. One narrated fact is downgraded to a party’s assumption (C1), and Part I and Part II disagree on the guarantee (C3).
  5. The March instalment and the further information about whom Pierre spoke for are not used. Both decide parts of
     the bottom line.

A better answer would, within the same words, do the following: - Funding. Cut the restatements to pay for about +100 words of
missing argument: the final paragraph’s re-quotation of the clause, ‘Grace’s … is therefore right, but signature is not the test’
compressed, and the duplicated condition reasoning in the last paragraph. - Part I. Open on Rocky’s claim against Grace and
dispose of it on the four mismatches. - II.C2 and II.D. Put Pao On 632 for the Pierre branch, and the comfort-letter point both ways
for Rocky’s undertaking. - II.H and II.I4. Name and meet the duty to co-operate, and give the March instalment as the ‘arguable’
breach on the 8 April reading. - Citations and the guarantee. Fix C1 to C3.

5. Margin comments per paragraph

     I ¶1 (offer). Good use of Gibson’s contrast with ‘may be prepared to sell’. However, the opening frames Grace’s claim; Rocky
     is the client and the question is his claims. Further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive on ‘Rocky declined, so
     no contract formed’: say why a ‘not interested’ reply to a proposal for Rocky to offer leaves nothing to accept.
     I ¶2 (acceptance, consideration). Acceptance is well done: ‘Confirmed’ answered ‘confirm agreement’. On consideration,
     ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied (fn 4 is a passage on offer-and-acceptance theory).
     I ¶3 (intention). Strong. Godecke is put for Grace and distinguished on ‘in an objective sense’, and whose satisfaction counts
     is decided once. Name the third Masters class you are applying. Gibbs J at 646–7 is obiter; say so.
     I ¶4 (certainty). Excellent: honesty is put and met on Gibbs CJ’s own limit, ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’. Raising ‘this
     morning’ as further information is apt.
     I ¶5 (privity). Accurate on Coulls 486–7 and the signature point. However, ‘took his guarantee’ contradicts Part II (C3).
     ‘Neither performed his email’ needs its reasons.
     I ¶6 (conclusion). Clean. ‘Whenever the 12 months began’ is a good cross-reference.
     II ¶1 (offer, acceptance). Correct. Disclose that Lord Greene MR spoke of exchanges of contracts before borrowing his
     words.
     II ¶2 (who promised). The reasoning on ‘you’ against AMPL’s office is good, but the agency requisites are the wrong test
     (contestable 2). Name the further information.
     II ¶3 (existing legal duty). Good: the rule is named, Mason J’s limit is applied, and ‘goes beyond’ is well found. Add Pao On
     for the Pierre branch.
     II ¶4 (intention). The onus is correctly placed. The opposing point for Rocky’s own undertaking (letter of comfort) is not put.
     II ¶5 (certainty). Sound. Reading ‘ensure’ as a promise of a result is the right lean.
     II ¶6 (guarantee clause). The handling of Empirnall 534 and 535–6 is careful and the inference is marked. However, the
       ‘provided by Rocky’ sentence misreads a proven fact (C1), and fn 31 is the wrong authority (C2).

Final adversarial marker feedback (verbatim)
Two independent hostile markers marked the final text and tried to break it against the readings. Their sheets follow word for word.
After they marked, the one certain defect both found (treating ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ as unproven) was fixed, as
were two further points from Marker A that the source text confirms (‘unqualified’ removed, since Rocky’s words were conditional;
‘supports it’ changed to ‘supports intention’). Points raised by only one marker that the other marker disputes, and arguments that
would need words the 1,500 limit does not leave, have not been applied; they are set out in the sheets.

Marker A

Marker A: hostile examination of the final answer
Marked against SHEET_v12 read with RULINGS R-P, R-Y, R-Z, R-AB, R-AC, R-AD and R-AE. Every authority in the footnotes was re-
read at its page in the casebook transcription or, where the point is official-only, in the saved official judgment. Verifier run: 40
quotations, 0 FAIL, 2 CHECK PIN (Brambles 176 and Pao On 629 to 630, both known artefacts and both correct on re-reading). Body
1,488 words; the stated 1,491 is body plus three under R-P, so no fault.


1. Certain defects

C1. A proven fact treated as unproven, and the narrator’s words put in AMPL’s mouth (Part II, guarantee paragraph).

Sentence: “AMPL’s call ‘under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ assumes, but does not prove, his assent, and because
privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[^29] AMPL must show that assent.”

Proof: the problem (question.txt, final page) reads “AMPL called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided by
Rocky”. The words ‘provided by Rocky’ are the problem’s own description, not AMPL’s assertion, and the Instructions (p 1) say “You
may assume the facts provided in the scenario to be proven”. What is proven is that Rocky provided a guarantee; what is open is only
what ‘provided’ consisted of (assent to the written clause, his oral undertaking, or both). The sentence attributes the words to
“AMPL’s call” and then says they do “not prove” his assent, which denies a proven fact and misidentifies the speaker (sheet D4,
which lists this exact phrase; sheet §3, second bullet).

Fix (+4 words): “A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, but whether by assent to the clause or only by his oral undertaking is open,
and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[^29] AMPL must show that assent.”

C2. ‘Unqualified’ misdescribes words the problem qualifies (Part II, certainty paragraph).

Sentence: “Read objectively, his unqualified ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, likely promised
that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.”

Proof: Rocky’s words are “I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the Loan” (question.txt).
They carry an express ‘if’ qualifier, and the answer’s own offer paragraph relies on it (“offered a promise for a promise”). The point
intended is that the words contain no language of effort, which ‘unqualified’ does not say.

Fix (−1 word): “Read objectively, his ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, contains no words of
effort and likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.” Net cost +3 if the clause is added; the cheapest
certain fix is simply to delete ‘unqualified’ (−1).

C3. A pronoun with two possible antecedents (Part I, intention paragraph).

Sentence: “The qualifier, however, raises whether the parties intended immediate obligations, which is assessed objectively, with the
onus on Grace as the party alleging the contract, although their commercial status as ‘project developers’ supports it.”

Proof: ‘it’ can be read as ‘the onus’ or as the intention; only the second makes sense (Ermogenous [25], which the answer cites, lists
‘the status of the parties’ as a factor going to intention). Sheet R1 and R-V(1): a pronoun is a lapse where its antecedent is unclear.

Fix (0 words): replace “supports it” with “supports intention”.

Word cost of all three: +4 −1 +0 = +3, taking the body to 1,491 and the stated count to 1,494; within 1,497.


2. Contestable points, with fixes

K1. Whose satisfaction (Part I, intention paragraph), an inference stated without its reason. “‘satisfactory’ leaves the
judgment to the party the condition protects,[^8] here Rocky”. Gibbs CJ at 581 grounds the rule in the clause being “generally
entirely for the protection of the purchaser” and leaves room for “a clear indication to the contrary”. Nothing in the email says whose
satisfaction; Grace could say the conditions were to be satisfactory to both, or objectively. Fix (+2): “here Rocky as lender”.

K2. Rocky’s best authority on the qualifier is missed. Masters v Cameron (1954) 91 CLR 353, 362 quotes Jessel MR in Crossley
v Maycock (1874) LR 18 Eq 180, 181 to 182: “if the agreement is made subject to certain conditions then specified or to be specified
by the party making it, or by his solicitor, then, until those conditions are accepted, there is no final agreement”. That is Rocky’s
‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ almost word for word, stated in a High Court joint judgment’s survey, and far stronger than a
single judge’s dictum in Godecke (Gibbs J at 646 to 647, where he says only that it “does not necessarily follow” that such an
agreement binds). The casebook elides this sentence, so it is credit and official-only; but the objectively best answer would use it,
with Jessel MR named, at fn 9.

K3. Brambles 177 cited for consideration (fn 4). The passage (Heydon JA quoting McHugh JA in Integrated Computer Services)
describes ‘classical theory’ (“an exchange of promises by means of an offer and its acceptance”) as a prelude to saying commercial
dealings often do not fit it. It is not a statement of the consideration rule. Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457 (“the relation of a quid
pro quo”) is the course authority for consideration as the price of the promise. Fix (footnotes only, 0 body words): fn 4 becomes the
full Australian Woollen Mills citation at 456 to 457 with the short title; fn 31 and fn 36 become “(n 4)”; fn 19 takes the full Brambles
citation and short title; fn 21 and fn 37 become “(n 19)”.

K4. Gibson for the 5 February call (fn 1). Gibson at 298 decides that “may be prepared to sell” lacks commitment. It does not
decide that a request that the other party make an offer is an invitation. The use is analogical and passes, but a stricter marker
would want the point stated as the absence of any promise by Grace, which is what Gibson actually turns on.

K5. Port Jackson (fn 16, fn 22). The words quoted are Lord Reid’s requisites as Mason and Jacobs JJ set them out at 269, and the
pin is right. But Mason and Jacobs JJ were in the majority that the Privy Council reversed; Barwick CJ (dissenting in the High Court,
whose view the Board preferred) states the same requisites at 240, and the sheet names 240. The answer’s ‘rev’d’ is honest, but
citing the reversed majority when the vindicated judge states the same rule is the weaker choice. Fix (footnotes only): cite Port
Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ). Separately, fn 16 puts ‘quoting’ inside the judge’s brackets, unlike every other ‘quoting’ footnote in the
answer (fn 4, 6, 11, 21, 27); AGLC form is “269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), quoting Scruttons Ltd v Midland Silicones Ltd [1962] AC 446,
474 (Lord Reid)”.

K6. Lord Reid’s requisites for the director question (Part II, agency paragraph). The requisites concern a carrier contracting
as agent for a stevedore to secure an exemption. Using them to decide whether a controlling director spoke for his company is a
stretch; the answer’s own facts (‘controls AMPL’, ‘at its office’, ‘about its loan’) do the work. Fix: state the question as authority to
act for AMPL and keep fn 22 as the general agency source, or cite Ermogenous [24] for objective attribution (credit).

K7. Privity of the $10,000 promise is never addressed (sheet II.F1). If ‘the clause’ that was ‘included in the Loan Agreement’
is the $10,000 term, AMPL will say the term lives in a document between AMPL and Grace to which Rocky is no party. The answer
needs one sentence: Rocky is the promisee and named payee (‘to me directly’) of an oral promise for which he gave consideration, so
privity is no bar; and, in a clause, ‘the clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause the problem names first. About 30 words.

K8. The letter of comfort point (sheet II.D). Rocky’s ‘ensure’ undertaking is the obvious candidate for comparison with the letter
in Banque Brussels; the answer applies ‘appropriately promissory’ only to the $10,000 promise and never weighs whether Rocky’s
own undertaking binds him likewise. About 15 words.

K9. The existing legal duty rule if Pierre promised personally (sheet II.C2). If Pierre is the promisee, any duty Rocky owed
under the guarantee was owed to AMPL, a third party; Pao On 632 holds that a promise to perform a duty owed to a third party is
good consideration. The answer’s “with the promisee” gestures at this but never states the branch. About 15 words.

K10. The duty to co-operate (sheet II.H). AMPL called the guarantee before the Loan was due on the 8 April reading; Rocky can
argue AMPL cannot rely on its own premature call to put the condition ‘once Grace repays’ out of reach. The answer never names or
meets the duty to co-operate. About 20 words.

K11. The interest payments (sheet II.G; R-AA(3)). “Grace made appropriate monthly repayments of the interest on the Loan to
AMPL” between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025 is the fact AMPL’s opponents will reach for on the start date. The answer’s rule
excludes post-contractual conduct (Brambles 164, correct), but never applies it to this fact, so a cold reader cannot tell whether it
was seen. About 12 words.

K12. The onus in Part I. The answer places the onus on Grace as the party alleging the 12 February contract. That is coherent
with its defensive framing (Rocky never lent, so only Grace would sue on the email), and I accept it; but the sheet’s I.D core frames
Rocky as the party alleging, so a marker reading the sheet literally will query it. The framing should be stated once (“Grace, who
alone would sue on it”).

Funding for K7 to K11 (about 92 words against 6 words of headroom after C1 to C3): cut “and likely never if Rocky pays it himself”
in the final paragraph, which repeats the II.H paragraph’s last sentence (−8); cut “Rocky could argue his 12 February email was
merely a negotiating step, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its other points promise nothing” to “Its other points promise
nothing” (−17); compress the Pao On and Roscorla paragraph, whose fallback the answer itself calls “doubtful” (about −20);
compress the Part I conclusion (about −10). Even so, not all five fit; on marks at risk per word the order is K7, K10, K9, K8, K11.

4. Is this the objectively best answer?

No. It is a very strong answer, and on the authorities it uses it is almost faultless: every quotation checks verbatim, every pin is right,
every judge is correctly named, the one dissent is labelled, the one reversed case is flagged, and the single-judge dictum is hedged.
It is not the best answer for four reasons.

First, C1 is a substantive error, not a slip. The problem proves that Rocky provided a guarantee; the live question is what he
provided. By saying AMPL’s call “does not prove” his assent, the answer frames Rocky’s exposure on a premise the facts deny, and a
marker who reads the problem’s last paragraph closely will see it.

Second, it misses the authority that most squarely fits the 12 February qualifier (K2). Rocky’s email made the loan ‘subject to
satisfactory conditions’; Jessel MR’s words quoted at Masters 362 deal with an agreement “subject to certain conditions then
specified or to be specified by the party making it”. The better answer leads with that and uses Godecke only to distinguish Grace’s
best case.

Third, it leaves four arguments unmet that a contracts academic would expect for one side or the other: privity of the $10,000
promise (K7), the duty to co-operate against AMPL’s premature call (K10), the third-party branch of the existing legal duty rule (K9),
and whether Rocky’s own ‘ensure’ undertaking is promissory or mere comfort (K8).

Fourth, two citations are used for less than they say (K3, K6).

The better answer would: fix C1 to C3; put Crossley (through Masters 362) against Grace on the qualifier; add the one-sentence
privity answer for the $10,000 claim; name and meet the duty to co-operate in the condition paragraph; state the Pao On 632 branch
in a clause; and fund it by cutting the repeated ‘pays it himself’ point, compressing the Part I opening and the doubtful past
consideration fallback.


5. Margin comments, paragraph by paragraph

I, para 1 (offer). Good close reading of ‘I will lend’ against ‘may be prepared to sell’. Gibson is stretched for the 5 February call; the
point is that Grace promised nothing. “Rocky could argue … negotiating step” is fair but costs words the answer needs later.

I, para 2 (acceptance and consideration). Clean. ‘Confirmed’ answered against ‘Please confirm agreement’ is exactly right.
Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied: fn 4 (Brambles 177) describes classical theory; it is not
the consideration rule.

I, para 3 (intention). The strongest paragraph in Part I. The pronoun ‘it’ at the end of the first sentence is unclear (C3). “here
Rocky” needs its reason (K1). Rocky’s best authority, Jessel MR at Masters 362, is missing (K2).

I, para 4 (certainty). Excellent distinction of Meehan: honesty governing an external condition against discretion over the loan’s
content. ‘Perhaps’ and the honest-and-reasonable variant could be met in a clause, but this is well done.

I, para 5 (privity). Correct and well sourced; the signature point using Mrs Coulls is effective. “took his guarantee” is consistent
with the problem’s ‘provided by Rocky’, which makes the Part II sentence in C1 all the harder to reconcile.

I, para 6 (conclusion). Clear bottom line; reimbursement disposed of in substantive terms.

II, para 1 (offer and acceptance). Correct; Lord Greene MR’s words are properly attributed. Disclose that Eccles concerned a
formal contract, so the words apply by analogy.

II, para 2 (who promised). Sensible weighing of ‘you’ against control, office and loan. Lord Reid’s requisites are an odd vehicle for
a director question (K6). Further information (whom Pierre spoke for) is implicit; state it.

II, para 3 (consideration). The existing legal duty rule is named and well met on timing. The Pao On 632 branch is missing (K9).

II, para 4 (intention). Correct use of Ermogenous [26]. Further analysis is required: Rocky’s ‘ensure’ undertaking against the
letter of comfort in Banque Brussels is never weighed (K8).

II, para 5 (certainty). “unqualified” misdescribes Rocky’s conditional words (C2). Otherwise sound.

II, para 6 (the guarantee). Your statement of the facts is incorrect: the problem proves a guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, and

II, para 10 (conclusion). Exposure stated precisely, as R-AD requires. The last clause repeats para 9.


6. Marks

Holistic mark: 84 (Distinction, at the top of the band). The law is accurate and the citations are exact, which is rare; the
reasoning is explicit and hedged. It stops short of High Distinction because it misreads a proven fact on the most valuable issue
(Rocky’s exposure on the guarantee), misses the best authority on the 12 February qualifier, and leaves four arguments for one side
or the other unmet.

2. Contestable points, with fixes

  1. Part I is framed around Grace’s claim, not Rocky’s. The question asks for the ‘contractual claims he could make’. The
     opening says the primary issue is whether ‘Grace could claim that Rocky failed to lend’. The claim Rocky would actually make
     against Grace under the February dealings is that AMPL’s advance, made at his request, performed his 12 February promise,
     so that Grace owes him repayment. The answer dismisses this in a clause (‘neither performed his email’). Further analysis is
     required as your statement is conclusive. The fix is to frame the opening on Rocky’s claim (word-neutral). Then give one
     sentence of reasons: the advance was $1,150,000 rather than $1 million, made on 27 February rather than ‘by 15 February’,
     and in AMPL’s name, with terms first fixed at 4% on 8 April (about +25 words).
  2. The Lord Reid conditions are used to decide whether Pierre contracted for AMPL (fn 22: ‘The same agency conditions
     guide whether Pierre … contracted on its behalf’). Lord Reid’s four requisites govern whether a carrier contracted as agent for
     a stevedore so that the stevedore could take the benefit of exemption clauses. Requisites (1) and (4), that the bill makes the
     protection clear and that consideration moves from the stevedore, have no counterpart in whether a director’s oral promise
     binds his company. The better course is to frame the question as which party Rocky’s ‘you’ objectively addressed (Ermogenous
     [25]), with the authority and purporting facts as the answer already weighs them. The ‘further information’ about whom Pierre
     spoke for should also be named (R6).
  3. Port Jackson is cited at 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), the majority that the Privy Council reversed. The ‘rev’d’ history is
     disclosed, which is correct AGLC practice. However, the sheet prefers 240 (Barwick CJ, who would have upheld the stevedore’s
     protection), and the reversal invites a marker to query the source. Since the requisites themselves were never doubted, either
     pin is defensible.
  4. Footnote 4 (consideration) rests on McHugh JA’s description of ‘classical theory’, where ‘the typical contract is a
     bilateral one and consists of an exchange of promises’ (Brambles 177). That passage is about the limits of offer-and-acceptance
     analysis, not a statement of consideration doctrine. Australian Woollen Mills 456–7 states the bargain (quid pro quo) principle
     directly and is the better footnote here, unlike at fn 31.
  5. II.C2 misses Pao On’s third-party point. If Pierre promised personally, any existing guarantee duty was owed to AMPL, not
     to Pierre. A promise to perform a duty owed to a third party is good consideration (Pao On 632), and Mason J’s own limit,
     ‘made to the promisee under that contract’ (Wigan 594), already points there. This is the strongest answer to AMPL’s or
     Pierre’s existing legal duty argument, and it costs one clause (+15).
  6. II.D omits the argument that most helps Rocky on his own exposure. The answer finds intention ‘whoever promised’
     because a fixed sum is ‘appropriately promissory’. It does not put the opposite point for Rocky’s own undertaking: that ‘ensure’
     is closer to the comfort given in Banque Brussels, where the letter of comfort conditioned the facility. Only after that is met
     should it be found ‘weaker here’ because Rocky’s words were given for a price. As it stands, Banque Brussels is cited without
     saying what the case was about (+20).
  7. II.H omits the duty to co-operate. Rocky’s best answer to ‘once Grace repays’ is not only a commercial reading (Upper
     Hunter 437). He can also argue that AMPL may not rely on a condition whose fulfilment its own call frustrates. That argument
     should be put and met: the call does not stop Grace repaying (R-O), so it fails (+20).
  8. II.I4 omits the March instalment. Interest is shown paid only ‘Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025’. On the 8 April
     reading, whether a March 2025 instalment was missed decides whether Rocky’s oral undertaking (to ‘ensure … all payments’)
     is already breached. The closing paragraph speaks only of ‘any amount when due’ (+15, hedged under R-M).
  9. II.F1 is never stated. The $10,000 was to be paid ‘to me directly’, so Rocky is the promisee, and privity is no bar to his claim
     against whoever promised (Coulls 494). It needs one line (+12).
 10. Gibbs J in Godecke (646–7) is dictum. ‘Doubted’ is a fair verb, but the answer then relies on it as the decisive reason (‘so on
     balance’). A strict marker would want ‘in obiter’ (+2), as the sheet’s D3 entry for Godecke 646 to 647 shows.
 11. Pierre’s ‘expected’ is labelled an ‘invitation to treat’. That is defensible, because it drew Rocky’s offer, but ‘a request, not
     an offer’ is the safer course term and costs the same.
 12. Pao On conditions are stated incompletely. The answer gives the request and ‘was to be remunerated’, but omits that the
     payment ‘must have been legally enforceable had it been promised in advance’. That is harmless on these facts but incomplete
     (+8).
 13. The lender’s opening act is not named on the facts in II.G. ‘Post-contractual conduct cannot interpret the term’ is stated
     without the fact it excludes: Grace’s ‘appropriate monthly repayments’ from 8 April 2024 (and his own ‘I have until 8 April
     2025’). Name them (+10). A reader should not have to infer which conduct is meant.
 14. Footnote style is inconsistent. Judges are named in every footnote except Masters (fn 6: Dixon CJ, McTiernan and Kitto JJ)
     and Australian Woollen Mills (fn 31 and 36: the Court). Either name them or adopt one convention.

4. Is this the objectively best answer?

No. It is a very good answer, accurate at source to a degree few scripts reach, and its reasoning on the 12 February email, Meehan
and illusoriness, and privity is close to the best that 1,500 words allow. It is not the best answer for five reasons:

  1. Part I answers the wrong claimant’s question first. It defends against Grace instead of testing Rocky’s own best claim,
     that AMPL’s advance at his request was his lending.
  2. Three points that matter to Rocky’s exposure are missing. The letter-of-comfort argument against his being bound by
     ‘ensure’ is not made. The Pao On third-party answer on consideration is absent. The duty to co-operate is not put on ‘once
     Grace repays’.
  3. Two authorities are stretched beyond what they decide. Australian Woollen Mills is used for a bilateral promise. Lord
     Reid’s carrier and stevedore requisites are used for whether a director binds his company.
  4. One narrated fact is downgraded to a party’s assumption (C1), and Part I and Part II disagree on the guarantee (C3).
  5. The March instalment and the further information about whom Pierre spoke for are not used. Both decide parts of
     the bottom line.

A better answer would, within the same words, do the following: - Funding. Cut the restatements to pay for about +100 words of
missing argument: the final paragraph’s re-quotation of the clause, ‘Grace’s … is therefore right, but signature is not the test’
compressed, and the duplicated condition reasoning in the last paragraph. - Part I. Open on Rocky’s claim against Grace and
dispose of it on the four mismatches. - II.C2 and II.D. Put Pao On 632 for the Pierre branch, and the comfort-letter point both ways
for Rocky’s undertaking. - II.H and II.I4. Name and meet the duty to co-operate, and give the March instalment as the ‘arguable’
breach on the 8 April reading. - Citations and the guarantee. Fix C1 to C3.

5. Margin comments per paragraph

     I ¶1 (offer). Good use of Gibson’s contrast with ‘may be prepared to sell’. However, the opening frames Grace’s claim; Rocky
     is the client and the question is his claims. Further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive on ‘Rocky declined, so
     no contract formed’: say why a ‘not interested’ reply to a proposal for Rocky to offer leaves nothing to accept.
     I ¶2 (acceptance, consideration). Acceptance is well done: ‘Confirmed’ answered ‘confirm agreement’. On consideration,
     ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied (fn 4 is a passage on offer-and-acceptance theory).
     I ¶3 (intention). Strong. Godecke is put for Grace and distinguished on ‘in an objective sense’, and whose satisfaction counts
     is decided once. Name the third Masters class you are applying. Gibbs J at 646–7 is obiter; say so.
     I ¶4 (certainty). Excellent: honesty is put and met on Gibbs CJ’s own limit, ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’. Raising ‘this
     morning’ as further information is apt.
     I ¶5 (privity). Accurate on Coulls 486–7 and the signature point. However, ‘took his guarantee’ contradicts Part II (C3).
     ‘Neither performed his email’ needs its reasons.
     I ¶6 (conclusion). Clean. ‘Whenever the 12 months began’ is a good cross-reference.
     II ¶1 (offer, acceptance). Correct. Disclose that Lord Greene MR spoke of exchanges of contracts before borrowing his
     words.
     II ¶2 (who promised). The reasoning on ‘you’ against AMPL’s office is good, but the agency requisites are the wrong test
     (contestable 2). Name the further information.
     II ¶3 (existing legal duty). Good: the rule is named, Mason J’s limit is applied, and ‘goes beyond’ is well found. Add Pao On
     for the Pierre branch.
     II ¶4 (intention). The onus is correctly placed. The opposing point for Rocky’s own undertaking (letter of comfort) is not put.
     II ¶5 (certainty). Sound. Reading ‘ensure’ as a promise of a result is the right lean.
     II ¶6 (guarantee clause). The handling of Empirnall 534 and 535–6 is careful and the inference is marked. However, the
       ‘provided by Rocky’ sentence misreads a proven fact (C1), and fn 31 is the wrong authority (C2).
       II ¶7 (consideration for the guarantee). Very good: Roscorla, Pao On and AMPL’s fallback (signing after the clause) are all
       well put. Pao On’s third condition is omitted.
       II ¶8 (12 months). Very good: the ‘recorded’ answer on the 4% rate is a sharp point. Name the conduct that is excluded.
       II ¶9 (condition). Correctly classed as a condition precedent to the obligation, not to the contract. The duty to co-operate is
       absent.
       II ¶10 (conclusion). Exposure is stated precisely on both readings, as R-AD requires. The point that he forfeits the $10,000 if
       he pays himself is correctly drawn from the condition. Add the March instalment.

6. Marks

Holistic: 84/100 (Distinction, high; one step below HD). It is accurate, well hedged and well cited. It falls short of HD because
of the misframed Part I and the three missing arguments that bear on Rocky’s own exposure.

Rubric (SHEET_v12 read with R-AB to R-AE): 80/100.

  b. Issue. Whether anything Grace or Rocky said or wrote in February was an offer; it matters because a binding loan would let Grace sue Rocky for failing to lend by 15 February.

  c. Arguments. Rocky (‘could argue’): the email was ‘merely a negotiating step’, a minute of talks (‘Confirming discussions’); two of its three points promise nothing (Eastwood ‘subject to
     success’, Bowral ‘wait and see’), so the first is a record too. Grace: the first point is in promissory form (‘I will lend’), complete on amount, date, term and rate, and asks for assent (‘Please
     confirm agreement’).

  d. Rule and authority. fn 1 and fn 2: Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294, 298, Lord Diplock (unanimous House of Lords). CB1A p 42: “The words “may be prepared to sell”
     are fatal to this; so is the invitation, not, be it noted, to accept the offer, but “to make formal application to buy” upon the enclosed application form.”

Pinpoint (PINPOINT_MAP.md): fn 1: W1 C1A Offer/Casebook (casebook/reading p 42, pdf p 4); source words: “…quite impossible to construe this letter as a contractual offer capable of being

noted, to accept the offer, but “to make formal application to buy” upon the enclosed application form. It is, to quote Geoffrey Lane LJ, a letter setting out the financial terms on which it may …”
/ fn 2: W1 C1A Offer/Casebook (casebook/reading p 42, pdf p 4); source words: “…quite impossible to construe this letter as a contractual offer capable of being converted into a legally

offer, but “to make formal application to buy” upon the enclosed application form. It is, to quote Geoffrey Lane LJ, a letter setting out the financial terms on which it may …”

  e. Why this source. Gibson is the course’s leading case on the line between promissory words and an invitation, and its contrast phrase (‘may be prepared to sell’) lets the answer show the
     difference in one clause. Alternatives rejected: Carlill (CB1A p 43; a unilateral offer to the world, wrong shape) and the Boots invitation-to-treat line (display of goods, not correspondence).

   f. Appropriateness. Used for what it decided: tentative words are not an offer; the answer applies the converse (promissory words can be). Lord Diplock’s speech is the leading speech. Fn 1
      is also used for Grace’s 5 February proposal; Gibson does not itself use the term ‘invitation’ for a request that the other side make an offer, so that use is by analogy.

  g. Calculus. ‘I will lend’ plus fixed terms plus a request for agreement outweighs the minute-style opening; the other points are severable because each has its own qualifier. Flip: evidence
     that the meeting left the loan open, which is the same evidence that drives P3. Strength: moderate. Hedge ‘likely an offer, though made ’subject to satisfactory conditions’’ is right, and
     carrying the qualifier forward is what sets up P3. Drafting note: FIXED in the final text. The f9 wording ‘since Grace could otherwise claim’ had the wrong connective; P1.1 now reads
     ‘since, if they did, Grace could claim’, and P1.2 now states the 5 February reasoning before its conclusion (‘so no contract formed’).

       McHugh JA in Integrated Computer Services) states that the typical contract is an exchange of promises, exactly the promise-for-promise shape here; it replaces Australian Woollen Mills,

      but the words are McHugh JA’s general description of a bilateral contract, uncontroversial and used for exactly what they say. This replaces the earlier use of Australian Woollen Mills,
      whose passage concerns unilateral offers; the fit is now better.

  b. Issue. Whether the parties intended to be bound now or left the loan to a further agreement.

  c. Arguments. Grace (strongest): the parties are commercial developers; Godecke shows a bargain can bind even though one side may add terms, so ‘satisfactory conditions’ is a mechanism
     inside a concluded contract. Rocky: ‘satisfactory’ is his own judgment, the ‘conditions’ are unstated terms of his own loan, so the case is Masters’ third class, a new agreement still to be
     made.

  d. Rule and authority. fn 5: Ermogenous (2002) 209 CLR 95, [25] to [26] (Gaudron, McHugh, Hayne and Callinan JJ; majority). CB3A p 137 at [25]: “the status of the parties to it, their
     relationship to one another, and other surrounding circumstances”; at [26]: “it was for the appellant to demonstrate that there was such a contract.” fn 6: Masters v Cameron (1954) 91
     CLR 353, 363 (Dixon CJ, McTiernan and Kitto JJ), quoting Winn v Bull 32 (Jessel MR). CB3A p 156: “When it is not expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract it becomes a question
     of construc- tion, whether the parties intended that the terms agreed on should be put into form, or whether they should be subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not
     expressed in detail” (line-break hyphen as printed). fn 7: Godecke v Kirwan (1973) 129 CLR 629, 642 to 643, Walsh J (Mason J agreeing; majority). CB3B p 189: “It means that what is
     required must be reasonable in an objective sense, and in case of [643] dispute this is a matter which the court can decide.” fn 8: Meehan v Jones (1982) 149 CLR 571, 580 to 581, Gibbs CJ
     (majority). CB3B p 183: “its natural effect is to leave it to the purchaser to determine whether or not the available finance is suitable to his needs” and “Such a condition is generally
     entirely for the protection of the purchaser”. fn 9: Godecke 646 to 647, Gibbs J (concurring). CB3B p 190: “it does not necessarily follow from what I have said that an agreement which left
     further terms to be settled by one of the parties, rather than by his solicitors, would be treated as a concluded contract.”

  e. Why this source. Ermogenous is the course’s statement of the objective test and the onus. Masters supplies the exact construction question for an agreement not expressly ‘subject to
     contract’ (Winn v Bull passage), which fits an email that says ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ rather than ‘subject to contract’. Godecke is Grace’s best authority and is met head on.
     Meehan supplies who judges ‘satisfactory’. Alternatives rejected: Placer Development (cited by Gibbs J at CB3B p 190; a discretion over payment, closer to P4’s illusory-promise point and
     already covered there by the Thorby words); the ‘subject to finance’ line beyond Meehan (no extra value).

   f. Appropriateness. Ermogenous, Masters, Walsh J in Godecke and Gibbs CJ in Meehan are majority reasoning, used for what they decided. Meehan concerned a condition protecting a
      purchaser of land; transferring ‘satisfactory’ to a lender’s conditions is an analogy, fairly drawn. Gibbs J’s Godecke passage is obiter in a concurring judgment; the answer signals this only
      by ‘doubted’. Two limits not disclosed: (1) Gibbs J at 647 immediately adds “Perhaps it may be different where agreement has been reached on all essential terms but the determination of
      subsidiary matters has been left to one of the parties” (CB3B p 190), the final text drops the earlier ‘at all’ (‘binds’), which removes the overstatement, though the reservation itself is still
      not mentioned (section 3, item 7); (2) Walsh J, the majority, at 642 (OFF only; not in the casebook) said “there is no reason in principle for holding that there cannot be any binding
      contract if some matter is left to be determined by one of the contracting parties”. The answer survives both because what was left to Rocky is the content of his own loan, an essential
      matter, not a subsidiary one.

  g. Calculus. The deciding contrast is between an objective standard (Godecke: terms ‘reasonable in an objective sense’, so a court can police them) and a bare ‘satisfactory’ to the promisor
     with no standard (Meehan: his own satisfaction). With no standard and no stated content, the terms were not ‘agreed on’ to be ‘put into form’. Gibbs J at 647 adds a further point the
     answer could have used: discretion left to the promisor (here Rocky, the lender) is the case for the Thorby principle. Flip: evidence that ‘conditions’ meant routine security or
     documentation already settled at the meeting (Gibbs J’s subsidiary-matters reservation, Walsh J’s majority view). Strength: moderate. ‘on balance the loan was likely left to a new
     agreement, negating intention to be bound immediately’ is right.

P4. Certainty: was Rocky’s promise illusory?

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                         Submission (verbatim)
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   On certainty, Grace may argue that, as in Meehan, Rocky must decide honestly,[fn 10] which takes a promise
conditions.                                                                                                       outside the principle that a promisor with ‘a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out’ the promise
                                                                                                                  makes no contract.[fn 11]
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   However, honesty in Meehan governed a judgment on an external condition, the availability of finance,
conditions.                                                                                                       whereas Rocky’s discretion arguably concerns the content of his loan rather than relating ‘only to the
                                                                                                                  fulfilment of a condition’,[fn 12] and honesty cannot supply terms never agreed.
F10: On 12 February 2024, Rocky and Grace met in person. F13: ’Mr Grace, Confirming discussions from our          Rocky’s promise is therefore arguably illusory, and unless the conditions were settled ‘this morning’, the email
meeting this morning:                                                                                             likely bound neither party.

  b. Issue. Whether a promise to lend ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ leaves Rocky a discretion whether to perform, making it illusory.

  c. Arguments. Grace: Meehan implies honesty into a ‘satisfactory’ clause, and Mason J held that limit takes the case out of the illusory-promise principle. Rocky: Meehan’s discretion went to
     an external condition (finance); his goes to the content of the very obligation, which the honesty limit cannot fill.

  d. Rule and authority. fn 10: Meehan 581, Gibbs CJ. CB3B p 183: “No doubt it may be implied that the purchaser will act honestly in deciding whether or not he is satisfied.” fn 11: Meehan
     589 to 590, Mason J (Wilson J agreeing; majority), quoting Thorby v Goldberg 605. CB3B p 185: “The limitation that the purchaser must act honestly, or honestly and reasonably, takes the
     case out of the principle that: where words which by themselves constitute a promise are accompanied by words which show that the promisor is [590] to have a discretion or option as to
     whether he will carry out that which purports to be the promise, the result is that there is no contract on which an action can be brought.” fn 12: Meehan 581, Gibbs CJ. CB3B p 183: “that
     principle does not apply where the discretion or option of the contracting party relates, not to the performance of the contractual obligations themselves, but only to the fulfilment of a
     condition upon which the contract depends.”

satisfaction of the purchaser, not that of some hypothetical reasonable man, that will satisfy the condition. No doubt it may be implied that the purchaser will act honestly in deciding whether or
not he is satisfied. However, it does not seem to me necessary, in order to give business efficacy to a contract, that a condition should be implied that the purchaser will make reasonable efforts
to obtain finance. Th…” / fn 11: W3 C3B Certainty/Casebook (casebook/reading p 185, pdf p 21); source words: “…The limitation that the purchaser must act honestly, or honestly and
reasonably, takes the case out of the principle that: where words which by themselves constitute a promise are accompanied by words which show that the promisor is [590] to have a discretion
or option as to whether he will carry out that which purports to be the promise, the result is that there is no contract on which an action can be brought. [6.260] 185 …” / fn 12: W3 C3B
Certainty/Casebook (casebook/reading p 183, pdf p 19); source words: “…ntract on which an action can be brought at all. . In my opinion that principle does not apply where the discretion or
option of the contracting party relates, not to the performance of the contractual obligations themselves, but only to the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends. That this is so
is illustrated by the case of an option to purchase which is, in many cases at least, a contract to sell the land upon condition that the grantee gives the notice and does the othe…”

  e. Why this source. Meehan is the course’s case on ‘satisfactory’ clauses and contains both sides: Grace’s (honesty, Mason J) and Rocky’s distinction (Gibbs CJ’s condition versus obligation).
     Alternatives rejected: Placer Development (cited by Gibbs J at CB3B p 190; discretion as to amount payable, a strong analogy for Rocky but it would add a case for a point Meehan already
     makes); Upper Hunter (saves uncertain words, not discretionary ones).

   f. Appropriateness. Both judges were in the majority; the Thorby words are correctly attributed through ‘, quoting’. Gibbs CJ’s distinction is applied as he drew it. Limit: Meehan’s ratio is
      that the finance clause was valid; the answer uses the distinction drawn within that reasoning to reach the opposite result on different facts, which is legitimate distinguishing, openly
      done.

  g. Calculus. Honesty can police a yes-or-no judgment on an outside event; it cannot write the missing terms of a loan. So the discretion is over performance itself and the Thorby principle
     bites. Flip: proof that the conditions were settled at the meeting (‘this morning’), in which case ‘satisfactory’ would refer to known conditions and honesty could operate. Strength:
     moderate. ‘arguably illusory’ and ‘likely bound neither party’ are correctly pitched, and the conditional (‘unless the conditions were settled’) names the flip.
