     22). Alternatives rejected: Trident for the rule (used at P12 for the ‘bound by’ limb, where it fits better); Dunlop v Selfridge (not extracted in the course).

      majority. Port Jackson 269 is official-only and was reversed (see P8 (f) for both limits); here it is applied by analogy to a lender acting in its own name. Taylor and Owen JJ’s passages are
      majority. The joint promisee route at 486 is put correctly: it is available only to a promisee, and none of Grace’s promises was made to Rocky.

(F30), formerly used at the end of P11.2 (‘, as his check-ins did’); they show effort only, so they matter only on the effort reading the answer rejects, and the cut has no effect on the advice. Also
not addressed, correctly: anticipatory breach or repudiation by Grace (‘I might not pay at all’) and termination, which fall outside weeks 1 to 4; a guarantor’s right of indemnity or subrogation
against Grace, which is equitable or restitutionary and not a contractual claim on these facts; any claim by Grace for the delays (F4 ‘unavoidable’).

4. BOTTOM LINE
    1. Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace (beyond the Development Agreement, which is not shown breached): the email was probably not binding because the loan was left ‘subject to
       satisfactory conditions’ that Rocky alone would settle (P3, P4), and his 5 March demand fails on privity because Grace’s promises in the Loan Agreement were made to AMPL, not to him,
       and AMPL lent for itself, not as his agent (P5, P6).
    2. For the same reason Grace probably cannot sue Rocky for failing to lend by 15 February (P1 to P4, P6).
    3. Rocky probably made a binding oral contract with AMPL (or, if Pierre spoke for himself, with Pierre): he promised that Grace would make all payments promptly, in return for $10,000 (P7
       to P11).
    4. Rocky is probably liable to AMPL at least on that oral undertaking if Grace does not pay when due, and for $1,150,000 under the written clause only if he assented to it, which is arguable
       but not certain because he signed nothing (P12, P13, P16).
    5. Whether AMPL’s 9 March 2025 call was premature turns on whether the 12 months ran from 27 February 2024 (call timely) or 8 April 2024 (call premature until 8 April 2025); this is open
       and depends on the Loan Agreement’s own words (P14, P16).
    6. Rocky’s $10,000 is owed only once Grace repays, so it is likely never payable if Grace defaults and Rocky pays instead (P15, P16).

‘any amount when due’.

Marker feedback on the submission (verbatim)
Two independent hostile markers read the submission cold and tried to break it. Their sheets follow verbatim. They marked the text
immediately before the final file. Since then, the certain defect both found (the past consideration sentence) has been fixed with Pao
On 629 to 630, and the zero-cost points they agreed on have been applied (conclusion-first opening, ‘clearly’, ‘as his check-ins did’,
‘though not necessarily by signing’, ‘Silence while a clause is included’). Marker A’s second certain defect (the agency branch) was
raised by one marker only, so it has not been applied.

Marker A

MARK A (hostile examiner): f9
Answer marked: MARKS/f9/in/ANSWER.md, taken at face value. Every pin and quotation below was read at the casebook page or
the saved official judgment. The verifier run (scratchpad f9mA.json) returns 38 quotations, 0 FAIL, and one CHECK PIN (Brambles
176), which is the known parser artefact: the Lord Greene MR passage sits between the [176] and [177] markers on casebook page
77, so 176 is right. The body counts 1,495 words, so the stated ‘Word count: 1,498’ is correct under R-P, and the slack to the 1,497
ceiling is 2 words.

1. Certain defects

C1. The past consideration sentence states the law categorically and ignores the exception that the facts trigger (II.I3)

Exact sentence (paragraph II.7): “If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration and cannot support it,
[^33] but AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed the Loan Agreement only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done
in consideration of’ the guarantee,[^34] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.”

Source evidence: the Pao On extract (W2 C2A, Lord Scarman for the Board) states that ‘An act done before the giving of a promise to
make a payment or to confer some other benefit can sometimes be consideration for the promise. The act must have been done at
the promisors’ request: the parties must have understood that the act was to be remunerated either by a payment or the conferment
of some other benefit: and payment, or the conferment of a benefit, must have been legally enforceable had it been promised in
advance.’ In Pao On the later benefit was itself a guarantee, so the case is directly in point. The facts say that on 27 February ‘Rocky
asked’ AMPL to advance the money, which is the first Pao On condition, and the answer itself relies on ‘asked’ in paragraph II.3 to
show that no guarantee then existed. Roscorla at 237 states only the general rule, and the sheet (II.I3 core) requires Pao On’s first
condition to be met on ‘Rocky asked’ and its second on timing. ‘Cannot support it’ is therefore wrong as a statement of the law the
answer is confined to, and the same fact is used one way in II.3 and ignored in II.7 (R10).

Exact fix: replace “is past consideration and cannot support it,[^33] but” with “is past consideration[^33] unless, Rocky having
‘asked’ for it, both understood it ‘was to be remunerated’,[^new] but”, and add the footnote “Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614,
629–30 (Lord Scarman for the Board).” The words ‘but AMPL’s stronger answer’ that follow already signal that the second condition
is the weak link, because on 27 February the parties understood the advance to be repaid by Grace, not rewarded by Rocky.

Word cost: +9. Funding, all zero-loss: delete ‘clearly’ in II.3 (-1, it is also rhetoric); ‘so on balance the loan’ to ‘so the loan’ in I.3 (-2, a
double hedge with ‘likely’); ‘Finally, the $10,000’ to ‘The $10,000’ (-1); ‘Further, having’ to ‘Having’ (-1); ‘Rocky would say that his’
to ‘Rocky would say his’ (-1); ‘AMPL would argue that the term’ to ‘AMPL would argue the term’ (-1). Net +2, body 1,497, at the
ceiling.

C2. The Part I conclusion rests on a branch the answer never analyses: whether AMPL’s advance was Rocky’s loan (I.F1,
omitted)

Exact sentence (paragraph I.6): “Thus Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace, whenever the 12 months began, and Grace
likely has none against him for failing to lend.”

Source evidence: paragraph I.4 leaves the email binding as a live possibility (‘unless the conditions were settled ’this morning’‘). On
that branch Grace’s implied promise to repay (paragraph I.2) ran to Rocky, and Rocky’s best claim against Grace is that the advance
he ’asked’ AMPL to make performed his promise to lend, AMPL acting as his agent. The answer never puts or meets this, although it
is the only route by which Rocky could be owed anything by Grace, and the facts that decide it are in the problem: Rocky offered ‘$1
million’, AMPL advanced ‘$1,150,000’ on 27 February (not ‘by 15 February’), at 4% not 5%, and took Rocky’s personal guarantee,
which a principal lending through an agent would not need. The criterion is already in the answer at fn 21 (Lord Reid’s conditions,
quoted by Mason and Jacobs JJ in Port Jackson at 268 to 269: the contracting party must be ‘contracting as agent’ with ‘authority’).
The unqualified conclusion is therefore unsupported on one of the answer’s own branches, and the sheet grades I.F1 as Omitted (2.5
points) and marks it ‘Strong’.

Exact fix: replace “Thus Rocky has no contractual claim” with “Even if the email bound, AMPL, though Rocky ‘asked’ it, advanced
‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and took his guarantee, so it likely lent for itself rather than as his agent,[^new] and thus Rocky has no
contractual claim”. The new footnote takes the full Port Jackson citation now at fn 21 (the first citation moves earlier): “Port Jackson
Stevedoring Pty Ltd v Salmond & Spraggon (Aust) Pty Ltd (1978) 139 CLR 231, 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), rev’d (1980) 144 CLR 300
(‘Port Jackson’).” Old fn 21 then reads “Port Jackson (n X) 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), quoting Scruttons Ltd v Midland Silicones Ltd
[1962] AC 446, 474 (Lord Reid).”

Word cost: +31, which C1’s funding cannot also carry. This is a real trade-off, so the dial is shown rather than picked: - (a) Delete
“Their only binding contract, the Development Agreement, operates only ‘if the Project made a profit’, and no breach of it is shown;
nor did” and start “Nor did Grace promise…” (-22). Cost: the P unit loses the Development Agreement as stipulated (Excellent to
Very Good, about -0.5), against +2.5 gained at I.F1. - (b) Delete “as his check-ins did” in II.5 (-4). Cost: the check-ins fact goes
unused; its present use is cryptic anyway. - (c) Delete “, though not necessarily by signing,” in II.6 (-5). Cost: the link to Mrs Coulls’
signature in I.5 is lost, but I.5 already makes the point. (a) + (b) + (c) = -31 exactly; with C1 funded as above the body ends at 1,497.

No other certain defect survived checking. Every quotation passes, every pin below was confirmed, the word count line is right,
there are no em dashes, contractions, double quotation marks or first person, and no meta language or slide citation (R-Z).
2. Contestable points

  1. Gibbs CJ’s view stated as the law (I.3, fn 8). “‘satisfactory’ leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects” is Gibbs CJ’s
     subjective reading at 580 to 581 (‘it is the satisfaction of the purchaser, not that of some hypothetical reasonable man’); Mason
     J at 589 to 590 requires the judgment to be reached ‘honestly, or honestly and reasonably’, so the proposition is not the Court’s
     (the sheet’s D3 example). The footnote names Gibbs CJ, which softens it. Fix: ‘satisfactory’ to ‘satisfactory’ arguably (+1). Also,
     ‘here Rocky’ is asserted; a reason (‘as the lender who set the conditions’) costs +6.
  2. ‘Silence while others draft a clause’ (II.6) implies that others drafted it and that Rocky was silent, neither of which is narrated
     (D4 risk; R-M). Zero-cost fix: ‘Silence while a clause is included’.
  3. ‘since Pierre spoke as AMPL’s controller rather than as a cousin’ (II.4) states a derived fact without a hedge (D4 risk). Fix:
     ‘since Pierre arguably spoke’ (+1).
  4. Pierre’s ‘expected’ is labelled an ‘invitation to treat’ (II.1). Gibson’s distinction is between an offer and an invitation to treat; a
     statement of what one party expects the other to do is better called a request, which is also what the consideration analysis
     needs (the sheet’s II.A core). Zero-cost fix: ‘so it was likely a request, not an offer’.
  5. Lord Greene MR’s words in Eccles were said of exchanges of contracts for land, which Heydon JA lists as one example among
     several (Brambles 176). The answer uses them for an oral bargain at a meeting without noting that context (II.B core: ‘the
     analogy disclosed’). Fix: add ‘said of exchanges of contracts,’ (+5).
  6. Integrated Computer Services at 11,117 to 11,118 (fn 18) is a passage whose point is that commercial dealings often do not fit
     offer and acceptance; it is cited for the classical ‘exchange of promises’. The words are there (‘the typical contract is a bilateral
     one and consists of an exchange of promises’), so this is accurate, but a lecturer may write ‘check this passage supports your
     point’. No change needed.
  7. Rocky’s bullets (I.1) are dismissed as points that ‘promise nothing’ without quoting their deciding words (‘Potential’, ‘wait and
     see’). Fix: “its other points, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing” (+5).
  8. The 12 months (II.8) does not use the interest pattern (monthly interest ‘Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025’, which fits
     a term running from 8 April) or say which post-contractual conduct is excluded (Grace’s ‘I have until 8 April 2025’ and AMPL’s
     reply on 7 March). Fix: after ‘cannot interpret the term,’ add ‘so the 7 March exchanges are irrelevant,’ (+6). The interest point
     costs about +15 and is a credit, not a core.
  9. II.C2 does not name Pao On at 632 for the Pierre branch (a promise to perform a duty owed to a third party is good
     consideration). The answer’s ‘with the promisee’ reasoning reaches the same result, so this is a citation gap rather than an
     error. Fix only if words allow (+12).
 10. fn 21 places ‘rev’d (1980) 144 CLR 300’ after the ‘quoting Scruttons’ clause, so a reader may think Scruttons was reversed.
     AGLC4 puts subsequent history immediately after the citation it relates to. Zero-cost fix: move it before ‘quoting’ (done in C2’s
     footnote form above).
 11. Roscorla fn 33 pins 237; the general rule runs across 236 to 237 (‘subject to excep-[237]tions’). Fix: ‘236–7’ (0 words, footnote).
 12. II.9’s ‘which bound immediately’ gives Meehan’s reason in two words; the sheet wants it visible (‘Certain obligations under the
     contract attached immediately’, Meehan 582: here Rocky’s undertaking). Fix: ‘which bound immediately, Rocky’s undertaking
     attaching at once’ (+4).
 13. The Part II conclusion’s ‘once the Loan is due and unpaid’ does not address the arguable March interest instalment (II.I4
     credit): if the term ran from 8 April, interest for March fell due before the call, and non-payment of it, if any, is not narrated. A
     credit, not a core.

earlier advance, though made at Rocky’s request, is past consideration, good only if both understood it would be compensated,[^33]

Two independent hostile markers read the submission cold and tried to break it. Their sheets follow verbatim. They marked the text
immediately before the final file. Since then, the certain defect both found (the past consideration sentence) has been fixed with Pao
On 629 to 630, and the zero-cost points they agreed on have been applied (conclusion-first opening, ‘clearly’, ‘as his check-ins did’,
‘though not necessarily by signing’, ‘Silence while a clause is included’). Marker A’s second certain defect (the agency branch) was
raised by one marker only, so it has not been applied.

Marker A

MARK A (hostile examiner): f9
Answer marked: MARKS/f9/in/ANSWER.md, taken at face value. Every pin and quotation below was read at the casebook page or
the saved official judgment. The verifier run (scratchpad f9mA.json) returns 38 quotations, 0 FAIL, and one CHECK PIN (Brambles
176), which is the known parser artefact: the Lord Greene MR passage sits between the [176] and [177] markers on casebook page
77, so 176 is right. The body counts 1,495 words, so the stated ‘Word count: 1,498’ is correct under R-P, and the slack to the 1,497
ceiling is 2 words.

1. Certain defects

C1. The past consideration sentence states the law categorically and ignores the exception that the facts trigger (II.I3)

Exact sentence (paragraph II.7): “If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration and cannot support it,
[^33] but AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed the Loan Agreement only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done
in consideration of’ the guarantee,[^34] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.”

Source evidence: the Pao On extract (W2 C2A, Lord Scarman for the Board) states that ‘An act done before the giving of a promise to
make a payment or to confer some other benefit can sometimes be consideration for the promise. The act must have been done at
the promisors’ request: the parties must have understood that the act was to be remunerated either by a payment or the conferment
of some other benefit: and payment, or the conferment of a benefit, must have been legally enforceable had it been promised in
advance.’ In Pao On the later benefit was itself a guarantee, so the case is directly in point. The facts say that on 27 February ‘Rocky
asked’ AMPL to advance the money, which is the first Pao On condition, and the answer itself relies on ‘asked’ in paragraph II.3 to
show that no guarantee then existed. Roscorla at 237 states only the general rule, and the sheet (II.I3 core) requires Pao On’s first
condition to be met on ‘Rocky asked’ and its second on timing. ‘Cannot support it’ is therefore wrong as a statement of the law the
answer is confined to, and the same fact is used one way in II.3 and ignored in II.7 (R10).

Exact fix: replace “is past consideration and cannot support it,[^33] but” with “is past consideration[^33] unless, Rocky having
‘asked’ for it, both understood it ‘was to be remunerated’,[^new] but”, and add the footnote “Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614,
629–30 (Lord Scarman for the Board).” The words ‘but AMPL’s stronger answer’ that follow already signal that the second condition
is the weak link, because on 27 February the parties understood the advance to be repaid by Grace, not rewarded by Rocky.

Word cost: +9. Funding, all zero-loss: delete ‘clearly’ in II.3 (-1, it is also rhetoric); ‘so on balance the loan’ to ‘so the loan’ in I.3 (-2, a
double hedge with ‘likely’); ‘Finally, the $10,000’ to ‘The $10,000’ (-1); ‘Further, having’ to ‘Having’ (-1); ‘Rocky would say that his’
to ‘Rocky would say his’ (-1); ‘AMPL would argue that the term’ to ‘AMPL would argue the term’ (-1). Net +2, body 1,497, at the
ceiling.

C2. The Part I conclusion rests on a branch the answer never analyses: whether AMPL’s advance was Rocky’s loan (I.F1,
omitted)

Exact sentence (paragraph I.6): “Thus Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace, whenever the 12 months began, and Grace
likely has none against him for failing to lend.”

Source evidence: paragraph I.4 leaves the email binding as a live possibility (‘unless the conditions were settled ’this morning’‘). On
that branch Grace’s implied promise to repay (paragraph I.2) ran to Rocky, and Rocky’s best claim against Grace is that the advance
he ’asked’ AMPL to make performed his promise to lend, AMPL acting as his agent. The answer never puts or meets this, although it
is the only route by which Rocky could be owed anything by Grace, and the facts that decide it are in the problem: Rocky offered ‘$1
million’, AMPL advanced ‘$1,150,000’ on 27 February (not ‘by 15 February’), at 4% not 5%, and took Rocky’s personal guarantee,
which a principal lending through an agent would not need. The criterion is already in the answer at fn 21 (Lord Reid’s conditions,
quoted by Mason and Jacobs JJ in Port Jackson at 268 to 269: the contracting party must be ‘contracting as agent’ with ‘authority’).
The unqualified conclusion is therefore unsupported on one of the answer’s own branches, and the sheet grades I.F1 as Omitted (2.5
points) and marks it ‘Strong’.

Exact fix: replace “Thus Rocky has no contractual claim” with “Even if the email bound, AMPL, though Rocky ‘asked’ it, advanced
‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and took his guarantee, so it likely lent for itself rather than as his agent,[^new] and thus Rocky has no
contractual claim”. The new footnote takes the full Port Jackson citation now at fn 21 (the first citation moves earlier): “Port Jackson
Stevedoring Pty Ltd v Salmond & Spraggon (Aust) Pty Ltd (1978) 139 CLR 231, 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), rev’d (1980) 144 CLR 300
(‘Port Jackson’).” Old fn 21 then reads “Port Jackson (n X) 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ), quoting Scruttons Ltd v Midland Silicones Ltd
[1962] AC 446, 474 (Lord Reid).”

Word cost: +31, which C1’s funding cannot also carry. This is a real trade-off, so the dial is shown rather than picked: - (a) Delete
“Their only binding contract, the Development Agreement, operates only ‘if the Project made a profit’, and no breach of it is shown;
nor did” and start “Nor did Grace promise…” (-22). Cost: the P unit loses the Development Agreement as stipulated (Excellent to
Very Good, about -0.5), against +2.5 gained at I.F1. - (b) Delete “as his check-ins did” in II.5 (-4). Cost: the check-ins fact goes
unused; its present use is cryptic anyway. - (c) Delete “, though not necessarily by signing,” in II.6 (-5). Cost: the link to Mrs Coulls’
signature in I.5 is lost, but I.5 already makes the point. (a) + (b) + (c) = -31 exactly; with C1 funded as above the body ends at 1,497.

2. Contestable points

  1. Gibbs CJ’s view stated as the law (I.3, fn 8). “‘satisfactory’ leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects” is Gibbs CJ’s
     subjective reading at 580 to 581 (‘it is the satisfaction of the purchaser, not that of some hypothetical reasonable man’); Mason
     J at 589 to 590 requires the judgment to be reached ‘honestly, or honestly and reasonably’, so the proposition is not the Court’s
     (the sheet’s D3 example). The footnote names Gibbs CJ, which softens it. Fix: ‘satisfactory’ to ‘satisfactory’ arguably (+1). Also,
     ‘here Rocky’ is asserted; a reason (‘as the lender who set the conditions’) costs +6.
  2. ‘Silence while others draft a clause’ (II.6) implies that others drafted it and that Rocky was silent, neither of which is narrated
     (D4 risk; R-M). Zero-cost fix: ‘Silence while a clause is included’.
  3. ‘since Pierre spoke as AMPL’s controller rather than as a cousin’ (II.4) states a derived fact without a hedge (D4 risk). Fix:
     ‘since Pierre arguably spoke’ (+1).
  4. Pierre’s ‘expected’ is labelled an ‘invitation to treat’ (II.1). Gibson’s distinction is between an offer and an invitation to treat; a
     statement of what one party expects the other to do is better called a request, which is also what the consideration analysis
     needs (the sheet’s II.A core). Zero-cost fix: ‘so it was likely a request, not an offer’.
  5. Lord Greene MR’s words in Eccles were said of exchanges of contracts for land, which Heydon JA lists as one example among
     several (Brambles 176). The answer uses them for an oral bargain at a meeting without noting that context (II.B core: ‘the
     analogy disclosed’). Fix: add ‘said of exchanges of contracts,’ (+5).
  6. Integrated Computer Services at 11,117 to 11,118 (fn 18) is a passage whose point is that commercial dealings often do not fit
     offer and acceptance; it is cited for the classical ‘exchange of promises’. The words are there (‘the typical contract is a bilateral
     one and consists of an exchange of promises’), so this is accurate, but a lecturer may write ‘check this passage supports your
     point’. No change needed.
  7. Rocky’s bullets (I.1) are dismissed as points that ‘promise nothing’ without quoting their deciding words (‘Potential’, ‘wait and
     see’). Fix: “its other points, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing” (+5).
  8. The 12 months (II.8) does not use the interest pattern (monthly interest ‘Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025’, which fits

  9. II.C2 does not name Pao On at 632 for the Pierre branch (a promise to perform a duty owed to a third party is good

     error. Fix only if words allow (+12).

     AGLC4 puts subsequent history immediately after the citation it relates to. Zero-cost fix: move it before ‘quoting’ (done in C2’s
     footnote form above).

 12. II.9’s ‘which bound immediately’ gives Meehan’s reason in two words; the sheet wants it visible (‘Certain obligations under the
     contract attached immediately’, Meehan 582: here Rocky’s undertaking). Fix: ‘which bound immediately, Rocky’s undertaking

Answer marked: MARKS/f9/in/ANSWER.md, at face value, against question.txt, the Instructions, SHEET_v12 read with RULINGS (R-
P, R-Y, R-Z, R-AB, R-AC, R-AD and R-AE prevailing), the casebook transcriptions, the Pao On extract, the Trident reading and the
saved official judgments.

Verifier: 38 quotations, 0 FAIL; the one CHECK PIN (Brambles 176) is the known parser artefact, and the page image confirms that
Lord Greene MR’s words sit on 176, before the [177] marker. Body count 1,495; the stated ‘Word count: 1,498’ is body plus three, as
R-P requires, so D7 does not apply. Quoted words are about 13% of the body, with no quotation over 11 words; there are no dashes
in the body, no double quotation marks and no contractions; every case name is italicised. The only lint is the expected Trident no-
pin line (R-Y(1)).


1. CERTAIN DEFECTS (100% sure)

C1. Conclusion before analysis (D5, minus 1; R-R(2)). Sentence: ‘Grace’s 5 February call formed nothing: by asking Rocky to
offer a two-year loan, Grace invited an offer rather than making one, and Rocky declined.[^1]’ Evidence: R-R(2) and D5 treat a
verdict placed before a colon as conclusion-first ‘whatever follows it’, and the sheet gives ‘Rocky lent nothing: …’ as the example;
this sentence has the same shape. Fix: ‘By asking Rocky to offer a two-year loan on 5 February, Grace invited an offer rather than
making one,[^1] and Rocky declined, so that call formed nothing.’ Word cost: 0 (25 for 25).

C2. Past consideration is stated as an absolute rule, although the course authority creates an exception and the facts set
it up (II.I3). Sentence: ‘If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration and cannot support it,[^33] but
AMPL’s stronger answer is …’ Evidence: in the Pao On extract (Lord Scarman for the Board, [1980] AC 614, 629 to 630), ‘An act
done before the giving of a promise … can sometimes be consideration for the promise’, where the act was ‘done at the promisors’
request’, both parties understood it ‘was to be remunerated’, and the payment would have been enforceable if promised in advance.
In Pao On itself, a guarantee was upheld on that basis because the earlier act was done at the guarantor’s request. The problem says
that on 27 February ‘Rocky asked’ AMPL to advance the money. ‘Cannot support it’ is therefore wrong as a statement of law on
these facts. The question that decides the point is whether the parties understood on 27 February that the advance would be
compensated, and the answer never asks it. Roscorla (fn 33) gives only the general rule. Fix: ‘If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s
earlier advance, though made at Rocky’s request, is past consideration, good only if both understood it would be compensated,[^33]
which nothing shows; AMPL’s stronger answer is …’, with fn 33 reading ‘Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614, 629–30 (Lord
Scarman for the Board).’ Word cost: plus 11. Funding, with no core lost: (a) in II.I2, delete ‘, though not necessarily by signing’
(minus 5), because Part I has already made the signature point through Mrs Coulls; (b) in II.C2, change ‘the rule clearly applies’ to
‘the rule applies’ (minus 1), which also removes an overstatement, since Mason J’s words are ‘at least when’; (c) in II.E, delete ‘, as
his check-ins did’ (minus 4); see contestable point K9. The net change is plus 1, giving a body of 1,496 and a stated count of 1,499.

Nothing else is certain. Every other quotation, pin and speaker was checked at the source page and is right; the points below are
matters of judgement or omission.


2. CONTESTABLE POINTS (with fixes and costs)

K1. The 12 February offer is not reconciled with the finding of no intention (I.A against I.D; R10). The first paragraph
concludes that bullet 1 is ‘likely an offer’, and the third concludes that ‘intention to be bound immediately is likely absent’. An offer is
a promise made with the intention to be bound on acceptance, so a strict reader sees a contradiction. Fix: end the first paragraph
with ‘… so the first point is likely an offer in form, its qualifier deciding whether it was meant to bind’ (plus 7; fund it by deleting
‘Consideration would also exist,’ and starting the sentence ‘Rocky’s promise to lend was exchanged for …’, minus 4, plus a 3-word
cut elsewhere).

K2. Rocky’s claim against Grace through AMPL is never addressed (I.F1, 2.5 points). The answer never asks whether, if the
email bound, Rocky performed it by procuring AMPL’s advance (‘Rocky asked’), and so whether he is owed repayment or AMPL lent
as his agent. The conclusion ‘Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace’ rests only on the email failing and on Grace’s promises
running to AMPL; it does not deal with the bound branch, in which Rocky still lent nothing himself. Fix: one clause in the privity
paragraph, such as ‘and even if the email bound, Rocky lent nothing, AMPL advancing on its own account rather than as one
contracting for Rocky,[^21]’, citing the agency criterion (about plus 22). R-AB(2) allows this to be compressed but not dropped,
because it changes whether Rocky has any claim against Grace.

K3. Pao On 632 is missing on the Pierre branch of the existing legal duty rule (II.C2, a required authority). If Pierre
promised and the guarantee came first, Rocky’s prior duty was owed to AMPL, a third party. The answer’s ‘with the promisee’ gloss
on Wigan points that way but does not say so, and does not cite Pao On 632. Fix: ‘… and if Pierre promised, a promise to perform a
duty owed to AMPL is good consideration,[^x]’ (plus 15).

K4. The duty to co-operate is not put (II.H, a required authority: Beaton 185, McHugh JA in the minority on the result).
Rocky’s best answer to the condition ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ is that AMPL may not rely on non-fulfilment of a condition that its
own call helped bring about. The rebuttal is short: AMPL’s call does not prevent Grace from repaying. Fix: one clause (about plus
20).

K5. Lord Greene MR’s analogy is not disclosed (II.B). Lord Greene MR spoke of the exchange of contracts for the sale of land
(Brambles 176). The answer applies his words to an oral undertaking without saying it is reasoning by analogy, and Masters 361
(required) is absent. Fix: add ‘said of exchanges of land contracts’ after the quotation (plus 6).

K6. Niesmann (Masters 360 to 361) is missing (I.D, a required authority). This is Rocky’s best case that ‘subject to’ words
leave the parties unbound until a further agreement is made. Masters 363 (Winn v Bull) carries the test, but the grid requires 360
and 361 as well. This was recorded as a residual risk at R-R(7).

K7. The letter of comfort point is not made, and its direction is not given (II.D). Banque Brussels concerns a letter of
comfort. The answer borrows ‘appropriately promissory in character’ without saying that Rocky’s undertaking resembles such a
letter, or that the analogy is weaker here because a price was paid. Fix: one clause (about plus 14).

K8. Port Jackson is cited through a judgment that was reversed, when the report contains one that was upheld (fn 21;
II.F2). Mason and Jacobs JJ at 269 were in the High Court majority that the Privy Council reversed in The New York Star (1980) 144
CLR 300, where ‘their Lordships are in agreement with the judgment of the Chief Justice’ (official PC text [28]). Lord Reid’s
requisites survive, so the proposition is sound, and the answer correctly flags ‘rev’d’. Still, Barwick CJ at 240 states the same
requisites and is the judgment the Privy Council adopted. Fix: ‘Port Jackson Stevedoring Pty Ltd v Salmond & Spraggon (Aust) Pty
Ltd (1978) 139 CLR 231, 240 (Barwick CJ)’, with the subsequent history kept or dropped (0 words). AGLC: the placement of ‘rev’d’
after the ‘, quoting’ clause is also open to argument, because the subsequent history belongs to Port Jackson, not to Scruttons.

K9. ‘as his check-ins did’ (II.E) is unclear. It reads as though post-contractual conduct is being used to fix what Rocky promised,
which the answer itself rules out at II.G (Brambles 164). This is an R1 clarity lapse. Fix: delete it (minus 4); it is used to fund C2.

K10. Two planted facts on the 12 months are not used (II.G). These are the ‘appropriate monthly repayments of the interest’
from 8 April 2024 to 8 February 2025, and Rocky’s own 13 February 2025 email and 5 March 2025 demand. ‘Post-contractual
conduct cannot interpret the term’ disposes of them correctly in law, but a strict marker wants the facts named and set aside (R-
AA(3); R-AD(2)). Fix: ‘… cannot interpret the term, so the monthly interest payments and the parties’ later assertions are irrelevant
to its meaning,’ (plus 14).

K11. ‘The clause’ is read only one way (II.F1; R-M). The answer assumes throughout that the clause included before signing
was the guarantee. If it was the $10,000 promise, the written clause is in AMPL and Grace’s contract, and Rocky could not enforce it
by privity, so his claim would rest on the oral bargain alone. Fix: one clause (about plus 18).

K12. Rocky’s answer at II.I2 is put but never met. The paragraph ends on ‘Rocky would answer that the $10,000 priced his own
words, not the clause’, with no lean. The final paragraph’s ‘if Rocky assented’ then carries an open question with no indication of
which way it falls. Fix: ‘…, which is the stronger view, since nothing shows the clause was read out’ (plus 12), or the contrary lean
with its reason.

K13. Gibbs J’s dictum is obiter, and the answer relies on it to decide intention (I.D; R-F). ‘Gibbs J doubted’ signals that it is
tentative, but the dictum carries part of the decision. Fix: ‘Gibbs J doubted, obiter, that …’ (plus 1).

K14. Privity is stated as a single rule (fn 13). ‘Only a party who provided consideration may enforce a contract’ merges the two
requirements, whereas the casebook at [11.10] says the privity rule ‘is separate from the rule that consideration must move from the
promisee’. Windeyer J at 495 (‘Doubtless the two requisites merge in the strict view of a contract as a bargain’) supports the merged
form, so this is defensible. Fix if wanted: ‘… only a party may enforce a contract, consideration also having to move from that party’
(plus 3).

K15. Pace 150 to 151 is not cited, and Beaton 181 and Musumeci 745 are absent (I.E, II.C1; required authorities). Each
costs a footnote and a few words.

4. Margin comments (paragraph by paragraph, in the marker’s style)

  1. I, the offer. A good, close textual reading of ‘I will lend’ against ‘may be prepared to sell’. The opening verdict comes before
     its reasons (C1). ‘Likely an offer’ is in tension with your later finding of no intention, so reconcile the two (K1).
  2. The acceptance and consideration. Correct, and Empirnall’s criterion is applied to ‘confirm agreement’. Your note that
     Grace’s promise to repay is ‘implied’ is well marked.
  3. Intention. This is the strongest paragraph: you put the objective test and the onus, put Grace’s case on Godecke and
     distinguish it on ‘reasonably’ against ‘satisfactory’. Rocky’s best authority, Niesmann, is not used (K6), and you should flag
     Gibbs J’s dictum as obiter if it is to carry the decision (K13).
  4. Certainty. You put and meet the duty of honesty, and Gibbs CJ’s ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’ is used precisely. Pace is
     absent (K15).

  6. Conclusion for Part I. Clean. The Development Agreement and reimbursement are disposed of correctly.
  7. II, the offer and acceptance. You identify the bilateral offer correctly. Lord Greene MR’s words were said of exchanges of

  8. Agency. The facts are well weighed (‘you’ against office and control). Cite Barwick CJ at 240, not the reversed joint judgment
     (K8), and say what further information would decide whom Pierre spoke for.
  9. Consideration and the existing legal duty rule. You put the rule and meet it on ‘asked’ and on ‘more than’ the guarantee.

 12. Is Rocky bound by the clause? You state the burden aspect correctly and apply Empirnall at 535 to 536 well. You put
     Rocky’s answer but never meet it, so give a lean (K12). ‘The clause’ is read only one way (K11).
 13. AMPL’s consideration. ‘Cannot support it’ is wrong on these facts: Rocky asked for the advance, which engages Pao On (C2).
     The fallback based on AMPL’s signing is good.
 14. The 12 months. The method is careful (ambiguity, genesis, post-contractual conduct excluded), and the ‘recorded’ argument
     is a strong one. Name the monthly payments and the 13 February email and set them aside (K10).
 15. The condition. The condition precedent is correctly placed, and you put and meet the commercial reading. The duty to co-
     operate is missing (K4).
 16. Conclusion for Part II. This states Rocky’s exposure precisely on each reading of the 12 months, as R-AD requires; the advice
     is clear.


5. Marks

Holistic mark (senior contracts lecturer, at face value): 83 / 100 (Distinction, high)

This is a disciplined, well-sourced piece of advice with no misquotation. It reads close to the problem’s words, puts each opponent’s
best point and meets most of them, and its consequence paragraph is exact. Four things keep it out of the High Distinction band. It
states past consideration wrongly on a fact the problem plants (C2). It omits Pao On entirely, even though the problem has a request
followed by a guarantee. It leaves gaps in the second half: the duty to co-operate, the letter of comfort, the reading of ‘the clause’,
and Rocky’s unmet answer on assent. And it omits the agency question for Rocky’s claim against Grace.

2. PARAGRAPH MAP

P1. Was the 12 February email an offer?

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                           Submission (verbatim)
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory     The primary issue between Rocky and Grace is whether their February dealings formed a binding loan, since,
conditions.                                                                                                         if they did, Grace could claim that Rocky failed to lend ‘by 15 February’.
F8: On 5 February 2024, Grace called Rocky and proposed that Rocky offer Grace a ‘$1 million dollar working         By asking Rocky on 5 February to offer a two-year loan, Grace invited an offer rather than making one,[fn 1]
capital loan for 2 years at 5% interest’. F9: Rocky told Grace he was not interested in offering Grace a long-      and Rocky declined, so no contract formed.
term loan but proposed that they meet in person to discuss.
F11: Later that same day, Rocky sent an email to Grace confirming the details of their discussion. F13: ’Mr         Rocky would say his 12 February email only records their meeting, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its
Grace, Confirming discussions from our meeting this morning: F15: - Potential project over in Eastwood              other points promise nothing.
subject to success of Hail Mary Project. F16: - Threatened litigation from subcontractor from Bowral Project –
wait and see at present.
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory     However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ invites
conditions. F17: Please confirm agreement. Rocky’                                                                   acceptance; unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson, these words are promissory,[fn 2] so the first point is
                                                                                                                    likely an offer, though made ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’.

  b. Issue. Whether anything Grace or Rocky said or wrote in February was an offer; it matters because a binding loan would let Grace sue Rocky for failing to lend by 15 February.

  c. Arguments. Rocky: the email is a minute (‘Confirming discussions’); two of its three points promise nothing (Eastwood ‘subject to success’, Bowral ‘wait and see’), so the first is a record
     too. Grace: the first point is in promissory form (‘I will lend’), complete on amount, date, term and rate, and asks for assent (‘Please confirm agreement’).
  d. Rule and authority. fn 1 and fn 2: Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294, 298, Lord Diplock (unanimous House of Lords). CB1A p 42: “The words “may be prepared to sell”
     are fatal to this; so is the invitation, not, be it noted, to accept the offer, but “to make formal application to buy” upon the enclosed application form.”

  e. Why this source. Gibson is the course’s leading case on the line between promissory words and an invitation, and its contrast phrase (‘may be prepared to sell’) lets the answer show the
     difference in one clause. Alternatives rejected: Carlill (CB1A p 43; a unilateral offer to the world, wrong shape) and the Boots invitation-to-treat line (display of goods, not correspondence).

  f. Appropriateness. Used for what it decided: tentative words are not an offer; the answer applies the converse (promissory words can be). Lord Diplock’s speech is the leading speech. Fn 1
     is also used for Grace’s 5 February proposal; Gibson does not itself use the term ‘invitation’ for a request that the other side make an offer, so that use is by analogy.

  g. Calculus. ‘I will lend’ plus fixed terms plus a request for agreement outweighs the minute-style opening; the other points are severable because each has its own qualifier. Flip: evidence
     that the meeting left the loan open, which is the same evidence that drives P3. Strength: moderate. Hedge ‘likely an offer, though made ’subject to satisfactory conditions’’ is right, and
     carrying the qualifier forward is what sets up P3. Drafting note: FIXED in the final text. The f9 wording ‘since Grace could otherwise claim’ had the wrong connective; P1.1 now reads
     ‘since, if they did, Grace could claim’, and P1.2 now states the 5 February reasoning before its conclusion (‘so no contract formed’).

P2. Acceptance and consideration on the email

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                         Submission (verbatim)
F18: Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying, ‘Mr Rocky, Confirmed. Best, Grace.’                    Acceptance requires ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[fn 3]
F17: Please confirm agreement. Rocky’ F18: Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying, ‘Mr Rocky,       Rocky may argue that ‘Confirmed’ only confirmed the email’s accuracy, but it answered a request to ‘confirm
Confirmed. Best, Grace.’                                                                                          agreement’ and added no new terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included.
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   Consideration would also exist, Rocky’s promise to lend being exchanged for Grace’s implied promise to repay
conditions. F18: Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying, ‘Mr Rocky, Confirmed. Best, Grace.’        with interest.[fn 4]

  b. Issue. Whether ‘Confirmed’ accepted the first point, and whether there was consideration.

  c. Arguments. Rocky: ‘Confirmed’ verifies the minute’s accuracy, it does not assent. Grace: it answers ‘Please confirm agreement’ in its own terms, within 15 minutes, adding nothing, so it is
     assent to the offer as made.

  d. Rule and authority. fn 3: Empirnall Holdings v Machon Paull Partners (1988) 14 NSWLR 523, 534, McHugh JA (Samuels JA agreeing; majority). CB1B p 71: “The objective theory of
     contract requires an external manifestation of assent to an offer.” fn 4: Australian Woollen Mills v Commonwealth (1954) 92 CLR 424, 456 to 457, the Court (unanimous). CB2A p 101:
     “there must subsist, so to speak, [457] the relation of a quid pro quo.”

  e. Why this source. Empirnall states the objective test of acceptance in one line and is reused in P7 and P12, so one authority carries three acceptance points. AWM states the bargain
     requirement (quid pro quo). Alternatives rejected: the mirror-image and counter-offer cases in 1B (no new term was added, so they would only confirm); Felthouse (silence; not in issue
     here).

  f. Appropriateness. Empirnall 534 is a general statement of principle, correctly used. AWM’s passage is framed for unilateral offers (an act done for a promise); using it for a promise
     exchanged for a promise is a fair use of its general ‘quid pro quo’ language but not its exact context.

  g. Calculus. The reply mirrors the request (‘confirm agreement’ and ‘Confirmed’), so the objective reading is assent; Rocky’s ‘accuracy’ reading is possible but would make his request for
     ‘agreement’ pointless. Flip: a later course of dealing showing both treated the email as a minute. Strength: moderate. ‘likely accepted the first point, qualifier included’ is right; ‘qualifier
     included’ is essential, as acceptance cannot remove the qualifier. Consideration (‘would also exist’) is strong if a promise was made, and correctly conditional.

P3. Intention: did ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ postpone obligations?

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                         Submission (verbatim)
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   The qualifier, however, raises whether the parties intended immediate obligations.
conditions.
F1: Mr Grace and Mr Rocky are both project developers who pursued various projects together since 2017 to         Intention is assessed objectively, with the onus on Grace as the party alleging the contract, although their
stellar success.                                                                                                  commercial status as ‘project developers’ supports it.[fn 5]
F13: ’Mr Grace, Confirming discussions from our meeting this morning: F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by     The question is whether the terms were settled and merely to be ‘put into form’, or were ‘subject to a new
15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory conditions.                               agreement’.[fn 6]
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   Grace would rely on Godecke, where an agreement letting the vendor’s solicitors add terms still bound
conditions.                                                                                                       because those terms had to be reasonable ‘in an objective sense’.[fn 7]
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   Rocky’s qualifier contains no such standard: ‘satisfactory’ leaves the judgment to the party the condition
conditions.                                                                                                       protects,[fn 8] here Rocky, and the ‘conditions’, naming no external event, are most naturally further terms of
                                                                                                                  the loan itself.
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   Gibbs J doubted that an agreement leaving ‘further terms to be settled by one of the parties’ binds at all,[fn 9]
conditions.                                                                                                       so on balance the loan was likely left to a new agreement, and intention to be bound immediately is likely
                                                                                                                  absent.

  b. Issue. Whether the parties intended to be bound now or left the loan to a further agreement.

  c. Arguments. Grace (strongest): the parties are commercial developers; Godecke shows a bargain can bind even though one side may add terms, so ‘satisfactory conditions’ is a mechanism
     inside a concluded contract. Rocky: ‘satisfactory’ is his own judgment, the ‘conditions’ are unstated terms of his own loan, so the case is Masters’ third class, a new agreement still to be
     made.

  d. Rule and authority. fn 5: Ermogenous (2002) 209 CLR 95, [25] to [26] (Gaudron, McHugh, Hayne and Callinan JJ; majority). CB3A p 137 at [25]: “the status of the parties to it, their
     relationship to one another, and other surrounding circumstances”; at [26]: “it was for the appellant to demonstrate that there was such a contract.” fn 6: Masters v Cameron (1954) 91
     CLR 353, 363 (Dixon CJ, McTiernan and Kitto JJ), quoting Winn v Bull 32 (Jessel MR). CB3A p 156: “When it is not expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract it becomes a question
     of construc- tion, whether the parties intended that the terms agreed on should be put into form, or whether they should be subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not
     expressed in detail” (line-break hyphen as printed). fn 7: Godecke v Kirwan (1973) 129 CLR 629, 642 to 643, Walsh J (Mason J agreeing; majority). CB3B p 189: “It means that what is
     required must be reasonable in an objective sense, and in case of [643] dispute this is a matter which the court can decide.” fn 8: Meehan v Jones (1982) 149 CLR 571, 580 to 581, Gibbs CJ
     (majority). CB3B p 183: “its natural effect is to leave it to the purchaser to determine whether or not the available finance is suitable to his needs” and “Such a condition is generally
     entirely for the protection of the purchaser”. fn 9: Godecke 646 to 647, Gibbs J (concurring). CB3B p 190: “it does not necessarily follow from what I have said that an agreement which left
     further terms to be settled by one of the parties, rather than by his solicitors, would be treated as a concluded contract.”

  e. Why this source. Ermogenous is the course’s statement of the objective test and the onus. Masters supplies the exact construction question for an agreement not expressly ‘subject to
     contract’ (Winn v Bull passage), which fits an email that says ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ rather than ‘subject to contract’. Godecke is Grace’s best authority and is met head on.
     Meehan supplies who judges ‘satisfactory’. Alternatives rejected: Placer Development (cited by Gibbs J at CB3B p 190; a discretion over payment, closer to P4’s illusory-promise point and
     already covered there by the Thorby words); the ‘subject to finance’ line beyond Meehan (no extra value).

  f. Appropriateness. Ermogenous, Masters, Walsh J in Godecke and Gibbs CJ in Meehan are majority reasoning, used for what they decided. Meehan concerned a condition protecting a
     purchaser of land; transferring ‘satisfactory’ to a lender’s conditions is an analogy, fairly drawn. Gibbs J’s Godecke passage is obiter in a concurring judgment; the answer signals this only
     by ‘doubted’. Two limits not disclosed: (1) Gibbs J at 647 immediately adds “Perhaps it may be different where agreement has been reached on all essential terms but the determination of
     subsidiary matters has been left to one of the parties” (CB3B p 190), so ‘binds at all’ slightly overstates his doubt (the reservation was cut for words; section 3, item 7); (2) Walsh J, the
     majority, at 642 (OFF only; not in the casebook) said “there is no reason in principle for holding that there cannot be any binding contract if some matter is left to be determined by one of
     the contracting parties”. The answer survives both because what was left to Rocky is the content of his own loan, an essential matter, not a subsidiary one.

  g. Calculus. The deciding contrast is between an objective standard (Godecke: terms ‘reasonable in an objective sense’, so a court can police them) and a bare ‘satisfactory’ to the promisor
     with no standard (Meehan: his own satisfaction). With no standard and no stated content, the terms were not ‘agreed on’ to be ‘put into form’. Gibbs J at 647 adds a further point the
     answer could have used: discretion left to the promisor (here Rocky, the lender) is the case for the Thorby principle. Flip: evidence that ‘conditions’ meant routine security or
     documentation already settled at the meeting (Gibbs J’s subsidiary-matters reservation, Walsh J’s majority view). Strength: moderate. ‘on balance … likely absent’ is right.

P4. Certainty: was Rocky’s promise illusory?

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                         Submission (verbatim)
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   On certainty, Grace would argue that, as in Meehan, Rocky must decide honestly,[fn 10] which takes a promise
conditions.                                                                                                       outside the principle that a promisor with ‘a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out’ the promise
                                                                                                                  makes no contract.[fn 11]
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   However, honesty in Meehan governed a judgment on an external condition, the availability of finance,
conditions.                                                                                                       whereas Rocky’s discretion concerns the content of his own loan rather than relating ‘only to the fulfilment of
                                                                                                                  a condition’,[fn 12] and honesty cannot supply terms never agreed.
F10: On 12 February 2024, Rocky and Grace met in person. F13: ’Mr Grace, Confirming discussions from our          Rocky’s promise is therefore arguably illusory, and unless the conditions were settled ‘this morning’, the email
meeting this morning:                                                                                             likely bound neither party.

  b. Issue. Whether a promise to lend ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ leaves Rocky a discretion whether to perform, making it illusory.
  c. Arguments. Grace: Meehan implies honesty into a ‘satisfactory’ clause, and Mason J held that limit takes the case out of the illusory-promise principle. Rocky: Meehan’s discretion went to
     an external condition (finance); his goes to the content of the very obligation, which the honesty limit cannot fill.

  d. Rule and authority. fn 10: Meehan 581, Gibbs CJ. CB3B p 183: “No doubt it may be implied that the purchaser will act honestly in deciding whether or not he is satisfied.” fn 11: Meehan
     589 to 590, Mason J (Wilson J agreeing; majority), quoting Thorby v Goldberg 605. CB3B p 185: “The limitation that the purchaser must act honestly, or honestly and reasonably, takes the
     case out of the principle that: where words which by themselves constitute a promise are accompanied by words which show that the promisor is [590] to have a discretion or option as to
     whether he will carry out that which purports to be the promise, the result is that there is no contract on which an action can be brought.” fn 12: Meehan 581, Gibbs CJ. CB3B p 183: “that
     principle does not apply where the discretion or option of the contracting party relates, not to the performance of the contractual obligations themselves, but only to the fulfilment of a
     condition upon which the contract depends.”

  e. Why this source. Meehan is the course’s case on ‘satisfactory’ clauses and contains both sides: Grace’s (honesty, Mason J) and Rocky’s distinction (Gibbs CJ’s condition versus obligation).
     Alternatives rejected: Placer Development (cited by Gibbs J at CB3B p 190; discretion as to amount payable, a strong analogy for Rocky but it would add a case for a point Meehan already
     makes); Upper Hunter (saves uncertain words, not discretionary ones).

  f. Appropriateness. Both judges were in the majority; the Thorby words are correctly attributed through ‘, quoting’. Gibbs CJ’s distinction is applied as he drew it. Limit: Meehan’s ratio is
     that the finance clause was valid; the answer uses the distinction drawn within that reasoning to reach the opposite result on different facts, which is legitimate distinguishing, openly
     done.

  g. Calculus. Honesty can police a yes-or-no judgment on an outside event; it cannot write the missing terms of a loan. So the discretion is over performance itself and the Thorby principle
     bites. Flip: proof that the conditions were settled at the meeting (‘this morning’), in which case ‘satisfactory’ would refer to known conditions and honesty could operate. Strength:
     moderate. ‘arguably illusory’ and ‘likely bound neither party’ are correctly pitched, and the conditional (‘unless the conditions were settled’) names the flip.

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                      Submission (verbatim)

of the principal amount under the Loan Agreement with AMPL.                                                    only a party who provided consideration may enforce a contract.[fn 13]

by Grace monthly, and the Loan was repayable at the expiry of 12 months.                                       Rocky, even as a joint promisee.[fn 15]
F34: In response to the letter of demand, on 7 March 2025, Grace called Rocky and said, ‘I never signed        Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ therefore reaches the right result for the wrong reason, as Mrs
anything with you, so you can’t enforce anything. Leave me alone!’                                             Coulls signed and was still not a party.[fn 16]

  b. Issue. Whether Rocky can enforce Grace’s repayment promise in a contract between AMPL and Grace.

  c. Arguments. Rocky: the Loan Agreement contains his guarantee and he arranged the loan, so he is within it. Grace: ‘I never signed anything with you’. Best answer: Rocky provided no
     consideration for Grace’s promise and is not its promisee, so the result is Grace’s but the reason is privity, not signature.

  d. Rule and authority. fn 13: Coulls v Bagot’s Executor & Trustee Co (1967) 119 CLR 460, 494 to 495, Windeyer J (dissenting). CB4A p 333: “By the common law of England only those who
     are parties to a contract can sue upon it.” and “For us the rule prevails that a plaintiff who sues on a promise must show a consideration for it provided by him” (OFF prints ‘shew’). fn 14
     and fn 16: Coulls 487, Taylor and Owen JJ (majority). CB4A p 331: “But the mere fact that her signature appears does not make her a party; this is a question to be resolved upon a
     consideration of the written instrument itself.” fn 15: Coulls 486, Taylor and Owen JJ. CB4A p 330: “We do not accept the contention advanced on behalf of the appellant that if one, only, of
     two joint promisees provides the consideration for a promisor’s promise the other prom- isee cannot, in any circumstances, sue” (line-break hyphen as printed).

  e. Why this source. Coulls is the course’s privity case and supplies all three steps: the rule, the test for party status (the instrument), and the answer to ‘I never signed’ (Mrs Coulls signed
     and was not a party). Its joint promisee passage closes Rocky’s only route in. Alternatives rejected: Trident for the rule (used at P12 for the ‘bound by’ limb, where it fits better); Dunlop v
     Selfridge (not extracted in the course).

  f. Appropriateness. The rule at 494 to 495 is Windeyer J’s, in dissent, and is disclosed as such; the dissent was on the construction of the document, and the privity and consideration rule is
     common ground with the majority. Taylor and Owen JJ’s passages are majority. The joint promisee route at 486 is put correctly: it is available only to a promisee, and none of Grace’s
     promises was made to Rocky.

  g. Calculus. Rocky is a guarantor, not a promisee of Grace’s repayment promise; nothing he gave was the price of Grace’s promise. Flip: wording in the Loan Agreement making Grace’s
     promises run to Rocky jointly with AMPL (unknown, and unlikely given F22). Strength: strong. ‘therefore reaches the right result for the wrong reason’ is a firm statement and justified.

     ‘cannot support it’, ignoring the Pao On exception; P13.2 now says the advance ‘counts only if both understood it ’was to be remunerated’‘, concedes the request limb (’though Rocky
     ’asked’ for it’), and finds the remuneration limb unmet (‘nothing suggests that’). That is Lord Scarman’s test applied as stated by the Board, for what the case decided; the third limb
     (enforceable if promised in advance) is not reached because the second fails. The only limit is that the pin 629 to 630 rests on the brief, as the course extract carries no page markers.
     AWM’s passage concerns an act done for a promise; AMPL’s signing for Rocky’s guarantee fits it directly.

  g. Calculus. On the Pierre branch the past advance fails Pao On’s second limb: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’ and nothing shows a guarantee or other return was then contemplated
     (moderate to strong). On the AMPL branch, the $10,000 promise is plainly consideration (strong). On the Pierre branch, AMPL’s signing after the clause’s inclusion is a present act likely
     done in return for the guarantee (moderate). Flip: proof that AMPL had already committed to sign regardless. Overall ‘likely supported if Rocky assented’ is right, and correctly conditional
     on P12.

     the other way, to 27 February.

    g. Calculus. The text names Grace, and the bargain priced Rocky’s promise that Grace would pay; Rocky paying instead is the failure of what he promised, so it cannot earn the reward for it.

‘unavoidable’).

4. BOTTOM LINE
    1. Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace: the email was probably not binding because the loan was left ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ that Rocky alone would settle (P3, P4), and
       his 5 March demand fails on privity because Grace’s promises in the Loan Agreement were made to AMPL, not to him (P5, P6).
    2. For the same reason Grace probably cannot sue Rocky for failing to lend by 15 February (P1 to P4, P6).
    3. Rocky probably made a binding oral contract with AMPL (or, if Pierre spoke for himself, with Pierre): he promised that Grace would make all payments promptly, in return for $10,000 (P7
       to P11).
    4. Rocky is probably liable to AMPL at least on that oral undertaking if Grace does not pay when due, and for $1,150,000 under the written clause only if he assented to it, which is arguable
       but not certain because he signed nothing (P12, P13, P16).
    5. Whether AMPL’s 9 March 2025 call was premature turns on whether the 12 months ran from 27 February 2024 (call timely) or 8 April 2024 (call premature until 8 April 2025); this is open
       and depends on the Loan Agreement’s own words (P14, P16).
    6. Rocky’s $10,000 is owed only once Grace repays, so it is likely never payable if Grace defaults and Rocky pays instead (P15, P16).

Where the submission is not the best possible:

       view at 642 (official only) is broader in Grace’s favour than the answer shows.
       P3 could have used Gibbs J’s own point at 647 that a discretion left to the promisor attracts the Thorby principle; it fits Rocky (the lender) exactly and costs few words.
       P8 relies on an official-only and later-reversed authority (Port Jackson 269) for the agency test when the casebook’s own note at CB4A p 336 or Trident (Mason CJ and Wilson J) would

       suggests that’).
       P12.4 states ‘with a reasonable opportunity to object’ as fact; the facts show only attendance and the clause’s inclusion before signing.
       The March 2025 interest instalment (section 3, item 5) is the one excluded point that could change Rocky’s exposure on the oral undertaking, and it is covered only by the general words
       ‘any amount when due’.
       Brambles 176 and 177 are cited to Heydon JA, whose offer-and-acceptance discussion was not the majority’s route; harmless for general statements but a strict marker may note it.

P1. Was the 12 February email an offer?

  a.

conditions.                                                                                                         if they did, Grace could claim that Rocky failed to lend ‘by 15 February’.

capital loan for 2 years at 5% interest’. F9: Rocky told Grace he was not interested in offering Grace a long-      and Rocky declined, so no contract formed.
term loan but proposed that they meet in person to discuss.

Grace, Confirming discussions from our meeting this morning: F15: - Potential project over in Eastwood              other points promise nothing.
subject to success of Hail Mary Project. F16: - Threatened litigation from subcontractor from Bowral Project –

F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory     However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ invites
conditions. F17: Please confirm agreement. Rocky’                                                                   acceptance; unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson, these words are promissory,[fn 2] so the first point is
                                                                                                                    likely an offer, though made ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’.

  b. Issue. Whether anything Grace or Rocky said or wrote in February was an offer; it matters because a binding loan would let Grace sue Rocky for failing to lend by 15 February.

  c. Arguments. Rocky: the email is a minute (‘Confirming discussions’); two of its three points promise nothing (Eastwood ‘subject to success’, Bowral ‘wait and see’), so the first is a record
     too. Grace: the first point is in promissory form (‘I will lend’), complete on amount, date, term and rate, and asks for assent (‘Please confirm agreement’).
  d. Rule and authority. fn 1 and fn 2: Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294, 298, Lord Diplock (unanimous House of Lords). CB1A p 42: “The words “may be prepared to sell”
     are fatal to this; so is the invitation, not, be it noted, to accept the offer, but “to make formal application to buy” upon the enclosed application form.”

  e. Why this source. Gibson is the course’s leading case on the line between promissory words and an invitation, and its contrast phrase (‘may be prepared to sell’) lets the answer show the
     difference in one clause. Alternatives rejected: Carlill (CB1A p 43; a unilateral offer to the world, wrong shape) and the Boots invitation-to-treat line (display of goods, not correspondence).

  f. Appropriateness. Used for what it decided: tentative words are not an offer; the answer applies the converse (promissory words can be). Lord Diplock’s speech is the leading speech. Fn 1
     is also used for Grace’s 5 February proposal; Gibson does not itself use the term ‘invitation’ for a request that the other side make an offer, so that use is by analogy.

  g. Calculus. ‘I will lend’ plus fixed terms plus a request for agreement outweighs the minute-style opening; the other points are severable because each has its own qualifier. Flip: evidence
     that the meeting left the loan open, which is the same evidence that drives P3. Strength: moderate. Hedge ‘likely an offer, though made ’subject to satisfactory conditions’’ is right, and
     carrying the qualifier forward is what sets up P3. Drafting note: FIXED in the final text. The f9 wording ‘since Grace could otherwise claim’ had the wrong connective; P1.1 now reads
     ‘since, if they did, Grace could claim’, and P1.2 now states the 5 February reasoning before its conclusion (‘so no contract formed’).

P2. Acceptance and consideration on the email

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                         Submission (verbatim)
F18: Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying, ‘Mr Rocky, Confirmed. Best, Grace.’                    Acceptance requires ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[fn 3]
F17: Please confirm agreement. Rocky’ F18: Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying, ‘Mr Rocky,       Rocky may argue that ‘Confirmed’ only confirmed the email’s accuracy, but it answered a request to ‘confirm
Confirmed. Best, Grace.’                                                                                          agreement’ and added no new terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included.
F14: - I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory   Consideration would also exist, Rocky’s promise to lend being exchanged for Grace’s implied promise to repay
conditions. F18: Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying, ‘Mr Rocky, Confirmed. Best, Grace.’        with interest.[fn 4]

  b. Issue. Whether ‘Confirmed’ accepted the first point, and whether there was consideration.

  c. Arguments. Rocky: ‘Confirmed’ verifies the minute’s accuracy, it does not assent. Grace: it answers ‘Please confirm agreement’ in its own terms, within 15 minutes, adding nothing, so it is
     assent to the offer as made.

  d. Rule and authority. fn 3: Empirnall Holdings v Machon Paull Partners (1988) 14 NSWLR 523, 534, McHugh JA (Samuels JA agreeing; majority). CB1B p 71: “The objective theory of
     contract requires an external manifestation of assent to an offer.” fn 4: Australian Woollen Mills v Commonwealth (1954) 92 CLR 424, 456 to 457, the Court (unanimous). CB2A p 101:
     “there must subsist, so to speak, [457] the relation of a quid pro quo.”

  e. Why this source. Empirnall states the objective test of acceptance in one line and is reused in P7 and P12, so one authority carries three acceptance points. AWM states the bargain
     requirement (quid pro quo). Alternatives rejected: the mirror-image and counter-offer cases in 1B (no new term was added, so they would only confirm); Felthouse (silence; not in issue
     here).

  f. Appropriateness. Empirnall 534 is a general statement of principle, correctly used. AWM’s passage is framed for unilateral offers (an act done for a promise); using it for a promise
     exchanged for a promise is a fair use of its general ‘quid pro quo’ language but not its exact context.

  g. Calculus. The reply mirrors the request (‘confirm agreement’ and ‘Confirmed’), so the objective reading is assent; Rocky’s ‘accuracy’ reading is possible but would make his request for
     ‘agreement’ pointless. Flip: a later course of dealing showing both treated the email as a minute. Strength: moderate. ‘likely accepted the first point, qualifier included’ is right; ‘qualifier
     included’ is essential, as acceptance cannot remove the qualifier. Consideration (‘would also exist’) is strong if a promise was made, and correctly conditional.

P3. Intention: did ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ postpone obligations?

  a.

Mid-term facts (verbatim)                                                                                         Submission (verbatim)
