## FILE: drive/txt/LAWS1150 Mid-Term T3 2026 - Rocky.txt
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The primary issue between Rocky and Grace is whether their February dealings formed a binding loan, since, if they did, Grace could claim that Rocky failed to lend ‘by 15 February’. By asking Rocky on 5 February to offer a two-year loan, Grace invited an offer rather than making one,[1] and Rocky declined, so no contract formed. Rocky could argue his 12 February email was merely a negotiating step, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its other points promise nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ invites acceptance; unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson, these words are promissory,[2] so the first point is likely an offer, though made ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’.

Acceptance requires ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[3] Rocky could argue that ‘Confirmed’ only confirmed the email’s accuracy, but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ and added no new terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Consideration would also exist, Rocky’s promise to lend being exchanged for Grace’s implied promise to repay with interest.[4]

The qualifier, however, raises whether the parties intended immediate obligations, which is assessed objectively, with the onus on Grace as the party alleging the contract, although their commercial status as ‘project developers’ supports intention.[5] The question is whether the terms were settled and merely to be ‘put into form’, or were ‘subject to a new agreement’.[6] Grace may rely on Godecke, where an agreement letting the vendor’s solicitors add terms bound because those terms had to be reasonable ‘in an objective sense’.[7] Rocky’s qualifier contains no such standard: ‘satisfactory’ leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects,[8] here Rocky, and the ‘conditions’, naming no external event, are most naturally further terms of the loan itself. Gibbs J doubted that an agreement leaving ‘further terms to be settled by one of the parties’ binds,[9] so on balance the loan was likely left to a new agreement, negating intention to be bound immediately.

On certainty, Grace may argue that, as in Meehan, Rocky must decide honestly,[10] which takes a promise outside the principle that a promisor with ‘a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out’ the promise makes no contract.[11] However, honesty in Meehan governed a judgment on an external condition, the availability of finance, whereas Rocky’s discretion arguably concerns the content of his loan rather than relating ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’,[12] and honesty cannot supply terms never agreed. Rocky’s promise is therefore arguably illusory, and unless the conditions were settled ‘this morning’, the email likely bound neither party.

Rocky’s 5 March demand for repayment under ‘the Loan Agreement with AMPL’ faces privity, under which ‘only those who are parties to a contract can sue upon it’.[13] Party status is determined from ‘the written instrument itself’,[14] and the Loan Agreement was made between AMPL and Grace, whose promises to repay were made to AMPL; none was made to Rocky, even as a joint promisee.[15] Nor was AMPL his agent: though Rocky ‘asked’ it to lend, it lent in its own name and took his guarantee, so it contracted for itself,[16] and its $1,150,000 advance neither performed his email nor made him a party. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is therefore right, but signature is not the test, as Mrs Coulls signed yet was not a party.[17]

Thus, beyond the Development Agreement, which pays only ‘if the Project made a profit’ and is not shown breached, Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace, whenever the 12 months began, and Grace likely has none against him for failing to lend; nor did Grace promise to reimburse Rocky for anything he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

On whether a contract for the $10,000 formed at the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s statement that he ‘expected’ Rocky to ensure Grace’s payments promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[18] Rocky’s reply, ‘I will do that if you also promise’, offered a promise for a promise,[19] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[20] AMPL may argue that nothing bound until the Loan Agreement was signed, but parties are bound ‘when, and in the manner in which, they intend’,[21] and little suggests Rocky’s undertaking was to await any signature, so a contract likely formed orally.

The same agency conditions guide whether Pierre, with AMPL’s authority, contracted on its behalf rather than solely for himself.[22] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre, but Pierre controls AMPL and spoke at its office about its loan, so AMPL likely made the promise; if Pierre instead contracted for himself, Rocky’s undertaking ran to Pierre, and AMPL can rely only on the guarantee clause.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, arguing that Rocky had already guaranteed the Loan, so his promise to ensure Grace’s payments gave it nothing new.[23] However, the rule presupposes a duty, as under ‘a pre-existing contract’ with the promisee,[24] and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’ AMPL to advance the money, and ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included’ suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even if the guarantee came first, ensuring that Grace made ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ goes beyond guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’, so Rocky likely provided consideration.

Intention is in issue because Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions about family arrangements at most identify who bears the onus,[25] here Rocky. A promise to pay a fixed sum, made at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised, is ‘appropriately promissory in character’ and commercial,[26] so intention is likely present whoever promised.

Rocky’s undertaking to ‘ensure’ payment is not ‘so obscure’ as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[27] Read objectively, his ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.[28]

A separate issue is whether the guarantee clause binds Rocky. A guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’, but whether by assent to the clause or only by his oral undertaking is open, and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[29] AMPL must show that assent. Silence while a clause is included is generally not ‘an external manifestation’ of assent,[30] but Rocky’s ‘I will do that’, given for the $10,000 promise, likely binds him at least to his oral undertaking.[31] Having ‘attended’ with a reasonable opportunity to object, he arguably knew the clause’s terms and assented to them by retaining the $10,000 promise,[32] although Rocky could answer that the $10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

Consideration for the guarantee must move from AMPL,[33] and if AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise supplies it. If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration,[34] which, though Rocky ‘asked’ for it, counts only if both understood it ‘was to be remunerated’,[35] and that is doubtful; AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed the Loan Agreement only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee,[36] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

Whether AMPL’s call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct cannot interpret the term,[37] but because the term apparently specifies no start and is arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[38] AMPL may argue the term ran from its 27 February advance, since the agreement ‘recorded’ a loan already made. However, ‘recorded’ applies equally to the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved, not that a term first agreed on 8 April began earlier. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the 9 March 2025 call premature unless the Loan Agreement dates it from the advance.

The $10,000 is payable only ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to the obligation rather than to the contract, which bound immediately,[39] so nothing was payable on 9 March 2025, when Grace ‘had not yet repaid’. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own repayment satisfies the condition;[40] however, the words refer to Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay, so his payment likely leaves the condition unfulfilled.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, by which he ‘personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: immediately if the term ran from 27 February, or from 8 April 2025 if Grace has still not repaid. If bound only by his oral undertaking, he likely breaches it, and faces damages, if Grace fails to pay any amount when due. His $10,000 claim, against AMPL or alternatively Pierre, likely stands but is conditional:[41] it falls due only when Grace repays, so never if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, never repays, and likely never if Rocky pays it himself.

Rocky’s undertaking to ‘ensure’ payment is not ‘so obscure’ as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[26] Read objectively, his unqualified ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.[27]

A separate issue is whether the guarantee clause binds Rocky. AMPL’s call ‘under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ shows that a guarantee was given but not its terms, and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[28] AMPL must show that he assented to the clause. Silence while a clause is included is generally not ‘an external manifestation’ of assent,[29] but Rocky’s ‘I will do that’, given for the $10,000 promise, likely binds him at least to his oral undertaking.[30] Having ‘attended’ with a reasonable opportunity to object, he arguably knew the clause’s terms and assented to them by taking the $10,000 promise,[31] although Rocky would answer that the $10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

Consideration for the guarantee must move from AMPL,[32] and if AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise supplies it. If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration,[33] which, though Rocky ‘asked’ for it, counts only if both understood it ‘was to be remunerated’,[34] and nothing suggests that; AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed the Loan Agreement only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee,[35] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

Whether AMPL’s call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct cannot interpret the term,[36] but because the term specifies no start and is arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[37] AMPL would argue the term ran from its 27 February advance, since the agreement ‘recorded’ a loan already made. However, ‘recorded’ applies equally to the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved, not that a term first agreed on 8 April began earlier. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the 9 March 2025 call premature unless the Loan Agreement dates it from the advance.

Finally, the $10,000 is payable only ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to AMPL’s obligation rather than to the contract, which bound immediately,[38] so nothing was payable on 9 March 2025, when Grace ‘had not yet repaid’. Rocky may argue that, read commercially, his own repayment satisfies the condition;[39] however, the words refer to Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay, not his paying instead, so his payment likely leaves the condition unfulfilled.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, by which he ‘personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: immediately if the term ran from 27 February, or from 8 April 2025 if Grace has still not repaid. If he is bound only by his oral undertaking, Grace’s failure to pay any amount when due likely breaches it and exposes him to damages. His $10,000 claim, against AMPL or alternatively Pierre, likely stands but is conditional:[40] it falls due only when Grace repays, so never if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, never repays, and likely never if Rocky pays the Loan himself.

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The primary issue between Rocky and Grace is whether their February dealings formed a binding loan, since, if they did, Grace could claim that Rocky failed to lend ‘by 15 February’. By asking Rocky on 5 February to offer a two-year loan, Grace invited an offer rather than making one,[1] and Rocky declined, so no contract formed. Rocky could argue his 12 February email was merely a negotiating step, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its other points promise nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ invites acceptance; unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson, these words are promissory,[2] so the first point is likely an offer, though made ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’.

Acceptance requires ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[3] Rocky could argue that ‘Confirmed’ only confirmed the email’s accuracy, but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ and added no new terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Consideration would also exist, Rocky’s promise to lend being exchanged for Grace’s implied promise to repay with interest.[4]

The qualifier, however, raises whether the parties intended immediate obligations, which is assessed objectively, with the onus on Grace as the party alleging the contract, although their commercial status as ‘project developers’ supports it.[5] The question is whether the terms were settled and merely to be ‘put into form’, or were ‘subject to a new agreement’.[6] Grace may rely on Godecke, where an agreement letting the vendor’s solicitors add terms bound because those terms had to be reasonable ‘in an objective sense’.[7] Rocky’s qualifier contains no such standard: ‘satisfactory’ leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects,[8] here Rocky, and the ‘conditions’, naming no external event, are most naturally further terms of the loan itself. Gibbs J doubted that an agreement leaving ‘further terms to be settled by one of the parties’ binds,[9] so on balance the loan was likely left to a new agreement, negating intention to be bound immediately.

On certainty, Grace may argue that, as in Meehan, Rocky must decide honestly,[10] which takes a promise outside the principle that a promisor with ‘a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out’ the promise makes no contract.[11] However, honesty in Meehan governed a judgment on an external condition, the availability of finance, whereas Rocky’s discretion concerns the content of his own loan rather than relating ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’,[12] and honesty cannot supply terms never agreed. Rocky’s promise is therefore arguably illusory, and unless the conditions were settled ‘this morning’, the email likely bound neither party.

Rocky’s 5 March demand for repayment under ‘the Loan Agreement with AMPL’ faces privity, under which only a party who provided consideration may enforce a contract.[13] Party status is determined from ‘the written instrument itself’,[14] and the Loan Agreement was made between AMPL and Grace, whose promises to repay were exchanged for AMPL’s promises; none was made to Rocky, even as a joint promisee.[15] Nor was AMPL his agent: though Rocky ‘asked’ it to lend, it advanced $1,150,000, not $1 million, and took his guarantee, so it contracted for itself,[16] and its advance neither performed his email nor made him a party. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ therefore reaches the right result for the wrong reason, as Mrs Coulls signed yet was not a party.[17]

Thus, beyond the Development Agreement, which pays only ‘if the Project made a profit’ and is not shown breached, Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace, whenever the 12 months began, and Grace likely has none against him for failing to lend; nor did Grace promise to reimburse Rocky for anything he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

Whether a contract for the $10,000 formed at the 8 April meeting begins with Pierre’s statement that he ‘expected’ Rocky to ensure Grace’s payments promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[18] Rocky’s reply, ‘I will do that if you also promise’, offered a promise for a promise,[19] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[20] AMPL may argue that nothing bound until the Loan Agreement was signed, but parties are bound ‘when, and in the manner in which, they intend’,[21] and nothing suggests Rocky’s undertaking was to await any signature, so a contract likely formed orally.

The same agency test decides whether Pierre, with AMPL’s authority, contracted on its behalf rather than solely for himself.[22] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre, but Pierre controls AMPL and spoke at its office about its loan, so AMPL likely made the promise; if Pierre instead contracted for himself, Rocky’s undertaking ran to Pierre, and AMPL can rely only on the guarantee clause.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, arguing that ‘also’ implies Rocky had already guaranteed the Loan, so his promise to ensure Grace’s payments gave nothing new.[23] However, the rule applies to a duty under ‘a pre-existing contract’ with the promisee,[24] and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’ AMPL to advance the money, and ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included’ suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even if the guarantee came first, ensuring that Grace made ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ goes beyond guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’, so Rocky likely provided consideration.

Intention is contested because Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions about family arrangements at most identify who bears the onus,[25] here Rocky. A promise to pay a fixed sum, made at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised, is ‘appropriately promissory in character’ and commercial,[26] so intention is likely present whoever promised.

Rocky’s undertaking to ‘ensure’ payment is not ‘so obscure’ as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[27] Read objectively, his unqualified ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.[28]

A separate issue is whether the guarantee clause binds Rocky. AMPL’s call ‘under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ shows that a guarantee was given but not its terms, and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[29] AMPL must show his assent to the clause. Silence while a clause is included is generally not ‘an external manifestation’ of assent,[30] but Rocky’s ‘I will do that’, given for the $10,000 promise, likely binds him at least to his oral undertaking.[31] Having ‘attended’ with a reasonable opportunity to object, he arguably knew the clause’s terms and assented to them by taking the $10,000 promise,[32] although Rocky could answer that the $10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

Consideration for the guarantee must move from AMPL,[33] and if AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise supplies it. If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration,[34] which, though Rocky ‘asked’ for it, counts only if both understood it ‘was to be remunerated’,[35] and nothing suggests that; AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed the Loan Agreement only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee,[36] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

The $10,000 is payable only ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to AMPL’s obligation rather than to the contract, which bound immediately,[39] so nothing was payable on 9 March 2025, when Grace ‘had not yet repaid’. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own repayment satisfies the condition;[40] however, the words refer to Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay, not his paying instead, so his payment likely leaves the condition unfulfilled.

## FILE: drive/txt/LAWS1150 Mid-Term T3 2026 - Rocky_5.txt
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I. ROCKY v GRACE

The primary issue between Rocky and Grace is whether their February dealings formed a binding loan, since, if they did, Grace could claim that Rocky failed to lend ‘by 15 February’. By asking Rocky on 5 February to offer a two-year loan, Grace invited an offer rather than making one,[1] and Rocky declined, so no contract formed. Rocky could argue his 12 February email was merely a negotiating step, as it opens ‘Confirming discussions’ and its other points promise nothing. However, ‘I will lend’ fixes the amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ invites acceptance; unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson, these words are promissory,[2] so the first point is likely an offer, though made ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’.

Acceptance requires ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[3] Rocky could argue that ‘Confirmed’ only confirmed the email’s accuracy, but it answered a request to ‘confirm agreement’ and added no new terms, so it likely accepted the first point, qualifier included. Consideration would also exist, Rocky’s promise to lend being exchanged for Grace’s implied promise to repay with interest.[4]

The qualifier, however, raises whether the parties intended immediate obligations, which is assessed objectively, with the onus on Grace as the party alleging the contract, although their commercial status as ‘project developers’ supports it.[5] The question is whether the terms were settled and merely to be ‘put into form’, or were ‘subject to a new agreement’.[6] Grace may rely on Godecke, where an agreement letting the vendor’s solicitors add terms bound because those terms had to be reasonable ‘in an objective sense’.[7] Rocky’s qualifier contains no such standard: ‘satisfactory’ leaves the judgment to the party the condition protects,[8] here Rocky, and the ‘conditions’, naming no external event, are most naturally further terms of the loan itself. Gibbs J doubted that an agreement leaving ‘further terms to be settled by one of the parties’ binds,[9] so on balance the loan was likely left to a new agreement, negating intention to be bound immediately.

On certainty, Grace may argue that, as in Meehan, Rocky must decide honestly,[10] which takes a promise outside the principle that a promisor with ‘a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out’ the promise makes no contract.[11] However, honesty in Meehan governed a judgment on an external condition, the availability of finance, whereas Rocky’s discretion arguably concerns the content of his loan rather than relating ‘only to the fulfilment of a condition’,[12] and honesty cannot supply terms never agreed. Rocky’s promise is therefore arguably illusory, and unless the conditions were settled ‘this morning’, the email likely bound neither party.

Rocky’s 5 March demand for repayment under ‘the Loan Agreement with AMPL’ faces privity, under which ‘only those who are parties to a contract can sue upon it’.[13] Party status is determined from ‘the written instrument itself’,[14] and the Loan Agreement was made between AMPL and Grace, whose promises to repay were made to AMPL; none was made to Rocky, even as a joint promisee.[15] Nor was AMPL his agent: though Rocky ‘asked’ it to lend, it lent in its own name and took his guarantee, so it contracted for itself,[16] and its $1,150,000 advance neither performed his email nor made him a party. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ is therefore right, but signature is not the test, as Mrs Coulls signed yet was not a party.[17]

Thus, beyond the Development Agreement, which pays only ‘if the Project made a profit’ and is not shown breached, Rocky has no contractual claim against Grace, whenever the 12 months began, and Grace likely has none against him for failing to lend; nor did Grace promise to reimburse Rocky for anything he pays AMPL.

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

On whether a contract for the $10,000 formed at the 8 April meeting, Pierre’s statement that he ‘expected’ Rocky to ensure Grace’s payments promised nothing, so it was likely an invitation to treat.[18] Rocky’s reply, ‘I will do that if you also promise’, offered a promise for a promise,[19] which Pierre accepted when he ‘agreed’.[20] AMPL may argue that nothing bound until the Loan Agreement was signed, but parties are bound ‘when, and in the manner in which, they intend’,[21] and little suggests Rocky’s undertaking was to await any signature, so a contract likely formed orally.

The same agency conditions guide whether Pierre, with AMPL’s authority, contracted on its behalf rather than solely for himself.[22] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre, but Pierre controls AMPL and spoke at its office about its loan, so AMPL likely made the promise; if Pierre instead contracted for himself, Rocky’s undertaking ran to Pierre, and AMPL can rely only on the guarantee clause.

On consideration, AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, arguing that Rocky had already guaranteed the Loan, so his promise to ensure Grace’s payments gave it nothing new.[23] However, the rule presupposes a duty, as under ‘a pre-existing contract’ with the promisee,[24] and none existed: on 27 February Rocky only ‘asked’ AMPL to advance the money, and ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included’ suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even if the guarantee came first, ensuring that Grace made ‘all payments’ ‘promptly’ goes beyond guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’, so Rocky likely provided consideration.

Intention is in issue because Pierre is Rocky’s cousin, but presumptions about family arrangements at most identify who bears the onus,[25] here Rocky. A promise to pay a fixed sum, made at AMPL’s office as its loan was finalised, is ‘appropriately promissory in character’ and commercial,[26] so intention is likely present whoever promised.

Rocky’s undertaking to ‘ensure’ payment is not ‘so obscure’ as to be uncertain, because the Loan Agreement fixes the payments.[27] Read objectively, his unqualified ‘I will do that’, answering Pierre’s expectation that he ‘ensure’ payment, likely promised that Grace would pay, not merely that Rocky would try.[28]

A separate issue is whether the guarantee clause binds Rocky. AMPL’s call ‘under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ assumes, but does not prove, his assent, and because privity prevents AMPL and Grace’s contract imposing obligations on Rocky,[29] AMPL must show that assent. Silence while a clause is included is generally not ‘an external manifestation’ of assent,[30] but Rocky’s ‘I will do that’, given for the $10,000 promise, likely binds him at least to his oral undertaking.[31] Having ‘attended’ with a reasonable opportunity to object, he arguably knew the clause’s terms and assented to them by retaining the $10,000 promise,[32] although Rocky could answer that the $10,000 priced his own words, not the clause.

Consideration for the guarantee must move from AMPL,[33] and if AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise supplies it. If Pierre promised personally, AMPL’s earlier advance is past consideration,[34] which, though Rocky ‘asked’ for it, counts only if both understood it ‘was to be remunerated’,[35] and that is doubtful; AMPL’s stronger answer is that it signed the Loan Agreement only after the clause was included, an act likely ‘really done in consideration of’ the guarantee,[36] so the guarantee is likely supported if Rocky assented.

Whether AMPL’s call was premature depends on when the 12 months began. Post-contractual conduct cannot interpret the term,[37] but because the term apparently specifies no start and is arguably ambiguous, mutually known facts showing ‘the genesis of the transaction’ are admissible.[38] AMPL may argue the term ran from its 27 February advance, since the agreement ‘recorded’ a loan already made. However, ‘recorded’ applies equally to the 4% rate, which nothing shows was agreed before 8 April, and the genesis shows only when the money moved, not that a term first agreed on 8 April began earlier. The term therefore arguably ran from 8 April 2024, making the 9 March 2025 call premature unless the Loan Agreement dates it from the advance.

The $10,000 is payable only ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition precedent to the obligation rather than to the contract, which bound immediately,[39] so nothing was payable on 9 March 2025, when Grace ‘had not yet repaid’. Rocky could argue that, read commercially, his own repayment satisfies the condition;[40] however, the words refer to Grace, and the $10,000 priced his promise that Grace would pay, so his payment likely leaves the condition unfulfilled.

Accordingly, if Rocky assented to the clause, by which he ‘personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, he is liable for $1,150,000 once the Loan is due and unpaid: immediately if the term ran from 27 February, or from 8 April 2025 if Grace has still not repaid. If bound only by his oral undertaking, he likely breaches it, and faces damages, if Grace fails to pay any amount when due. His $10,000 claim, against AMPL or alternatively Pierre, likely stands but is conditional:[41] it falls due only when Grace repays, so never if Grace, who said he ‘might not pay at all’, never repays, and likely never if Rocky pays it himself.

How to read this

Each past paper was answered by the same pipeline that will run on the 2026 T3 paper: three independent issue spotters, a lead drafter writing in your voice from your torts paper, the verifier (every quotation checked against the scanned page and its pinpoint), a blind panel of four markers (examiner, issue auditor, accuracy tracer, AGLC and style), and a reviser who checked every marker finding against the source before accepting it. Only Weeks 1 to 4 materials were used, even where that year’s course differed. The marks are the panel examiner’s, who was told to be strict; they measure progress between drafts, not the mark a real marker would give.

In this book the footnotes run on continuously, so an answer’s ‘(n X)’ cross-references point to its own numbering, not the book’s; each paper’s standalone final.docx, formatted for submission, keeps the right numbers. Every final answer passes the verifier with no failed quotation; the few CHECK lines left are explained in each paper’s triage file (mostly Pao On, whose extract prints no page).

Pre-submission checklist

Pre-submission checklist (from eight practice runs)

Drafter runs it before handing draft_v1 to the markers; reviser runs it again before final.docx. Every line rests on LESSONS.md (run in brackets) or STYLE.md. RECURRED = came back despite an earlier lesson: do these twice. [repeat] = recurred once and was sharpened.

1. Issue finding and structure

-   Before spotting issues, open question_pages and treat italics, pencil, handwriting, strike-through and attachments as planted facts; question.txt drops them (2019_T3).
-   Before budgeting, map every planted phrase to every doctrine it could serve (‘needs to be further negotiated’ to the fourth Masters class; ‘two fees for no extra work’ to reliance and to third-party-duty consideration) and read ambiguous words (‘Claim it if you can’) in each meaning (2022_T1, 2023_T3).
-   Before cutting a doctrine as ‘casebook note only’, check whether a planted phrase matches its definition; if so argue it and cut weaker analysis instead (2022_T1).
-   Before any formality or Masters analysis, classify each message once (offer, acceptance, counter-offer, inquiry) on the majority’s analysis (Butler 404 Lord Denning MR, 405–6 Lawton LJ), never on a both-ways formula only the minority supports (2022_T3, 2024_T1).
-   Before a Part with three or more people, name the parties to each contract and promise (Ermogenous [33], identifying parties only), then run privity both ways and the third-party-duty point before any existing-duty defence (2021_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before a third-party advisee’s section, list her routes (joint promisee; acceptance by her own act on an implied request, Woollen Mills 458, Clarke 244; duty owed to a third party via Pao On; the dissent’s reading of the instrument), write them first, then answer each on whether the promise was bargained for (2024_T1).
-   Before an existing-duty answer, exhaust the promisee’s routes in the parties’ own words (‘estimated’, ‘will be prepared’, completion, a separately priced category, a variation in the acceptance call), ask the first question (Stilk ‘at liberty’) before any exception, then ask who proposed the extra (2021_T3, 2022_T1, 2026_T1) [repeat].
-   Before using a promisee’s outlay, give her own route first (request; Pao On ‘was to be remunerated’; Roscorla ‘implied by law’) and then the condition that defeats it; a planted ‘on your behalf’ gets a one-line agency flag (2026_T1).
-   Before writing headings, use ‘I. X’S CLAIM AGAINST Y’ per claimant and defendant, lettered sub-issues, a concluding line per claim; anything beyond Weeks 1 to 4 (estoppel, duress as vitiating factor, frustration, termination, damages quantum, ACL) gets one line only (standing, STYLE).
-   Before answering any ‘is X entitled’ question, give the per-unit figure, the total on each scenario and the clause that limits the base, and tie Part totals together (2019_T3, 2024_T1).

2. Argument

-   RECURRED 1. Before writing any claim the advisee brings, or a threshold that goes against the advisee, write the advisee’s case first as a full paragraph from every planted fact, its own words included (Mary’s ‘If you finish … I will pay’ as a unilateral offer), with its closest authority, then answer each point; compare the word counts of the two sides (2024_T1 gave 46 words against 200) (2020_T3, 2021_T3, 2023_T3, 2024_T1).
-   Before answering a contested issue, list every argument for the losing side, lead with the one a good opponent would lead with at full strength, then answer it; if words are short, cut the weak counter, not the strong one (2019_T3).
-   Before relying on a fallback rule, state the presumption the opponent invokes in the source’s words with its pin (Masters 363, ‘of similar import’ prima facie an overriding condition), then answer it (2022_T3).
-   Before concluding a point worth real money or a whole claim, write ‘likely …, though …’ with the figure each way; argue even easy elements both ways in a sentence (intention: onus Ermogenous [26], counter, decisive answer) (2019_T3).
-   Before settling a point the register maps as contested (revoking a unilateral offer after commencement), walk the authority each way with its status and who rejected it, then the factor test on the facts, then the remedy (2020_T3).
-   Before resting a conclusion on one contested threshold, give the other branch and its result in two sentences, and for each branch of a multi-class doctrine write one sentence on what it does to every later Part, down to the money (2021_T3, 2022_T3, 2023_T3) [repeat].
-   Before submitting, find every fact used in two Parts or two issues and write the reconciling sentence on one doctrinal footing (eg Ermogenous [25] plus privity), pointing to the quoted fact that differs; never supply the differing fact (2019_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before applying one doctrine in two claims, apply it the same way and say why it helps one claimant and not the other (‘up to’ has a ceiling but no floor) (2020_T3).
-   Before construing a disputed clause, state its effect as a promise, as a condition and as no term, and say which reading each Part relies on (2022_T1).
-   Before characterising a deal as unilateral, reconcile each element of the test that speaks of a promise (2022_T1).
-   Before quoting any test, write one line on whether the court found it met, on what facts, and which side of ours that result lies (Ipp AJA’s ‘necessarily’ was met in Brambles, 197) (2026_T1).

3. Law and attribution

-   Before stating any rule, point to its register entry or add the passage to register_supp.md verbatim with a pin; otherwise cut it; never cite slides or editors’ notes as law (standing).
-   Before using any passage, including a register_supp entry, write the question the court was answering there and compare any hypothetical with our facts (Bowen LJ’s lost dog answers notice, not who performed) (2023_T3).
-   Before labelling a bench, count it in the casebook (four joint plus one concurring is a majority, Ermogenous); recall Lord Denning MR’s Butler patterns were his alone, Birkett LJ adopts Lord Goddard CJ in Boots, Lord Diplock quotes Lord Denning MR in Gibson to reject him (standing, 2021_T3).
-   RECURRED 2. Before the verifier, run the three-question footnote pass on every citation: (a) does the passage or its next sentence say ‘Perhaps’, ‘But’, ‘However’ or ‘though’? quote or state the hedge (Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps it may be different’, Godecke 647, obiter and only where essential terms are agreed; Santow J’s ‘though by no means conclusively’, 744; proportionality after ‘unfair pressure’); (b) is it the whole Court or Board (Woollen Mills HC, Mobil, Masters, Roscorla, Pao On)? name no judge; (c) is the judge dissenting, or one judge’s words credited to several? write ‘dissenting’ in body and footnote and name the one judge (2020_T3, 2022_T3, 2023_T3, 2024_T1, 2026_T1).
-   Before applying a dictum, check whose position it describes (promisor or promisee, offeror or offeree, payer or payee) and whether our party holds it (‘within specified parameters’ is a promisor’s discretion) (2020_T3).
-   Before distinguishing or transposing a case, read the editors’ facts bracket and the passage the court made decisive, and set the clause construed beside ours (Mason J’s ‘each party’ rests on ‘null and void’); if its facts suit the other side, present it as the opponent’s best case (Empirnall) (2020_T3, 2021_T3, 2022_T1) [repeat].
-   Before applying a test, read what the passage says may not be used to satisfy it (Whitlock 461 excludes extrinsic evidence of importance), and test every marker-proposed application against that limit (2022_T1, 2022_T3).
-   Before applying a qualification, use its own test, not its rationale (Wigan 595: an honest claim, not vexatious or frivolous; not ‘threatening unscrupulously’) (2021_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before stating when or from whose view a test applies, find words in the passage that say so; else reason from the element’s own words (Santow J’s ‘obtains in practice’, ‘capable of being viewed by B’) (2024_T1).
-   Before writing a threshold sentence, confirm the pinned passage states the proposition (Ermogenous [33] only identifies parties); pin ‘left open’ points where they are left open (Meehan 591, 597–8) (2019_T3, 2020_T3).
-   Before quoting, read the next sentence and keep confining words (‘of a contract of carriage or bailment’); put the footnote straight after the quoted words when the rest of the sentence is your inference; never put a judge’s words about his case into his mouth about our parties (2019_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before describing a case’s facts, read them in the judgment, not memory (Meehan’s condition went to completion, 582; Empirnall had an admitted oral contract; Roffey’s own surveyor persuaded it to pay, 10) (2019_T3, 2021_T3, 2023_T3).
-   Before citing a case for a rule, find the rule’s words in that judgment; if only the textbook states it (revocation communicated, Byrne; bare promise to hold open, Goldsbrough Mort; postal rule and email; privity’s burden side, Taddy; agency, Port Jackson, Scruttons), cite the footnoted case by report only, no pin, no quoted words, and never borrow a neighbouring case (Felthouse for revocation) (standing, 2021_T3, 2022_T3, 2023_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before stating ETA s 13A, give its conditions in full (designated address, or awareness if none designated) and say it fixes the time of receipt, not knowledge of terms (2026_T1).
-   RECURRED 3. Before any sentence on a promisee’s remedies in Coulls, copy Windeyer J’s four holdings verbatim into plan.md from W4 C4A Casebook pp 334 to 336: he rejects the nominal view (‘I do not see why’, 501; ‘(I do not think it is)’, 503); three substantial-loss examples (creditor; someone A feels a duty to reward or recompense; an activity A wishes to promote), damages ‘less, or more’; the damages are A’s own (‘why should A hold for C the proceeds’, 502); ‘not persuaded’ C could force A to sue, on the assumptions of no trust and a wholly gratuitous transaction (502), specific performance only ‘as at present advised’ (503). Check every sentence against that block and write ‘dissenting’ (2019_T3, 2024_T1).
-   Before relying on Coulls joint promisees, say four judges support it but it is not ratio (Taylor and Owen JJ conditional, 486); read ‘brought by both’ as joinder, not a bar (Barwick CJ 479, C sues joining B as defendant, judgment for both; Windeyer J 493, after an offer of indemnity against costs; both dissenting); party status is construction of the instrument (487) (standing, 2022_T3, 2023_T3).
-   Before citing Brambles, write ‘Ipp AJA’ (Mason P agreeing) for the majority, pin his words from ‘the increase in fees’ on at 197 (misprinted ‘[172]’), state that a protesting offeree that took benefits that ‘could not be severed’ accepted; Heydon JA’s ‘much to be said’ and revival are minority obiter (standing, 2022_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before using revocation of a unilateral offer, cite Mobil as the whole Court: it refused any universal rule and its revocation reasoning is arguably obiter; its factors are at 501 (knowledge of commencement is factor (i)), 506 and 507. Abbott v Lance and McPherson J are known only as Mobil reports them at 505 and are the first roll call to cut (standing, 2020_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before citing Beaton, state the split (Kirby P no consideration; Mahoney JA and McHugh JA a promise for an act; appeal dismissed with McHugh JA dissenting) and that Kirby P rejected McHugh JA’s analysis at 171 (standing, 2020_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before citing Meehan, say it has no majority on honest versus reasonable (Gibbs CJ honesty 581; Mason J undecided 590–1; Wilson J 597–8); Mason J’s ‘acting honestly, or honestly and reasonably’ is 590, ‘mere declaration’ 589 (standing, 2019_T3, 2024_T1).
-   Before citing Pao On, keep its two points apart: (1) Lord Scarman’s conditions (‘was to be remunerated’) from the extract, [1980] AC 614 with no pin, Board so no judge; (2) the third-party-duty holding only as textbook [4.200] and Glidewell LJ (Williams v Roffey 15, ‘a tripartite relationship’) report it, ‘citing Pao On’, never in Lord Scarman’s words (standing, 2021_T3, 2023_T3, 2024_T1).
-   Before using Trident, go only through the textbook: Deane J alone, a sufficient two-limb test (‘should be inferred if … and if …’) on the promisee’s intention, cited ‘quoted in’ Paterson and Robertson 295 [11.110]; describe the gate illustration by its facts (A, B, C, the act) and put no textbook sentence in the judges’ mouths (2019_T3, 2024_T1).

4. Facts

-   RECURRED 4. Before drafting, list every verb of who did, said, instructed or proposed what, in the problem and in each distinguished case, and match each to a quoted line; any adjective doing legal work (‘uncommunicated’, ‘unprompted’, ‘all day’, ‘absent’) needs a quoted fact; a performance the narrator only implies becomes ‘if, as planned, …’ (2020_T3, 2022_T3, 2023_T3, 2024_T1, 2026_T1).
-   Before quoting a fact, check the speaker (party or narrator: ‘merely a handful of minor edits’ was the narrator’s) and read the whole utterance; if the omitted half bears on the issue, quote it or do not quote (2022_T1, 2026_T1).
-   Before saying who wrote or added any word on a document, check the page image for exactly which words (only ‘Kays’ was pencilled) (2019_T3).
-   Before using a derived fact (a weekday from a date, ‘immediately’ moved onto another verb), drop it; facts are quoted exactly or marked ‘arguably’ or further information (STYLE; 2021_T3, 2024_T1 triage).

5. AGLC

-   Before finalising, check each first citation is in full with a short title, every short form used in the body is defined, and unused short titles are removed (2020_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before writing an embedded source, use ‘quoting Case (year) report pin (Judge)’ or ‘citing’, never ‘adopting’, ‘discussing’ or ‘describing’, never a citation inside the judge’s brackets, and name the original speaker (Lord O’Hagan, Jessel MR, Megaw J) (2020_T3, 2022_T3, 2024_T1).
-   Before submitting, check pins: after a comma, no ‘at’, paragraphs in [ ], en dash ranges in footnotes only (261–2), ‘Ibid 535 (McHugh JA)’ when the judge changes, full stop at the end; split or range-pin a quotation crossing a printed page marker; keep pins where markers are missing (Roffey 11, Todd 74–6) (standing, 2020_T3, 2022_T1, 2026_T1).
-   Before submitting, check settled forms: ‘Ipp AJA’; ‘and’ not ‘&’ in case names; The Crown v Clarke; Rogers CJ Comm D; Ermogenous [2002] HCA 8; (2002) 209 CLR 95; Stilk ER 1168–9; UNCITRAL Guide named in full (standing, 2019_T3, 2022_T3, 2026_T1).
-   Before citing any source, cite the report from the casebook heading, never the casebook or slides; the textbook only for ‘quoted in’ or a contested academic point (STYLE).

6. Style (Yusuf’s voice, STYLE.md)

-   Before drafting, read Part A of his LAWS1061 torts mid-term and use his moves: rule first, facts quoted into the sentence; ‘Firstly, … Secondly, however, …’; ‘Decisively,’ once per claim; ‘X is distinguishable: …’; ‘The strongest counter is …’; ‘On balance, the better view is that …, though …’; ‘Further information is needed on whether …; if …, then …’ only where it changes the advice.
-   Before submitting, search for and remove: ‘cuts both ways’, ‘it is trite law’, ‘it is submitted’, ‘in the present case’, ‘turning to’, ‘it is clear that’; any introduction restating facts; invented abbreviations (define only parties and documents); bullets, lists, block quotes; dashes, double quotation marks and contractions in the body.
-   Before submitting, check every sentence: one quotation per source per sentence; none over 45 words; no absolute constructions (‘X being obiter’), fragments after semicolons, or semicolon before a dependent clause; no quoting of bare function words; quotations rarely over 20 words; varied openers (not ‘strongest’ four times) (2019_T3, 2020_T3, 2022_T1, 2023_T3).
-   Before submitting, check mechanics: Australian spelling; numerals for 10 and above; bracketed capitals for mid-sentence quotations; footnotes citation only; ‘intention to create legal relations’ in full; each claim ends with its own concluding line (STYLE, 2022_T1, 2024_T1).

7. Word budget method

-   RECURRED 5. Before writing, put a budget per claim summing to 1,450 (about 36% to the most valuable claim); before revising, list every accepted addition with its word cost beside a named cut; draft each section at 90% of its budget and run the verifier’s count after each section (first revisions ran 1,633; 2,036; 1,882; 1,838; 1,813; 1,815; 1,783; 1,823) (every run).
-   Before cutting, take in this order: a second authority or judge roll call for one point; unplanted further-information lines; facts quoted twice; the threshold sentence; the weakest third factor of a walk; a second illustration of one point; a quotation where paraphrase plus the footnote carries it; a sentence restating a footnoted characterisation. Never cut a planted doctrine (2020_T3 to 2026_T1).
-   Before submitting, set ‘Word count: N’ to the verifier’s body count (headings in, footnotes and that line out), at or under 1,500 (PIPELINE).

8. Verifier

-   Before running, use your own scratch folder (never a shared r.json): python3 -I /home/claude/LAWS1150/_tools/verify.py check draft.md -c /home/claude/LAWS1150/_tools/corpus.json --facts question.txt --crops crops -o verify.json (standing).
-   Before accepting the result, require 0 FAIL, lint clean, every CHECK fixed or listed in plan.md with its reason, and the crop opened for every OCR quotation; since 9 Oct a CHECK usually means a real pin or attribution fault (standing, 9 Oct).
-   Before ‘fixing’ a CHECK by changing a pin, compare it with the expected list: Pao On no AC pin (also a lint line); Meehan 589; Milne 473; Henthorn, Bressan, Tallerman via [3.210]; Heydon JA quoting Lord Wilberforce 176–7; Pao On duress passage; Trident via the textbook short form; report-only textbook cases (lint); record each as expected (standing, 2021_T3, 2024_T1).
-   Before trusting a PASS, remember the parser merges two quotations separated only by a footnote marker (put words between), skips one-word quotations (check by hand), passes problem words as facts even where a source has them, and needs ‘found N times’ rows checked for the cited hit (standing, 2022_T1, 2023_T3).
-   Before building the .docx, remove paired dollar signs and any possessive after a closing bracket (“(k)’s”); after make_docx.py, scan word/document.xml for oMath and reversed marks and rerun the verifier on the .docx (2023_T3).

2019 T3: QueenBea and Kim Kay: battle of forms, variation, reasonable fee, Rob’s 10%

First draft 79/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 79/100; main losses were one-sided argument on the two most valuable contested points, and three source misreadings.

-   Typography is fact. question.txt drops italics; here they marked pencil on a printed form, which decides the battle of forms and the third party’s status. Read the page images and treat italics, handwriting, strike-through and attachments as planted facts. Then quote only what the image shows: v1 said Bea pencilled the whole heading when only one word was pencilled. Rule: never describe who wrote or added a word without checking the image for exactly which words.
-   Strongest counter, not the easiest one. v1 rebutted a weak counter (a narrow, price-limited dictum) and omitted the opponent’s best (the planted remark plus a broader alternative test). Rule: for each contested issue list every argument for the losing side, pick the one a good opponent would lead with, state it at full strength, then answer it; if a word budget forces a cut, cut the weak counter.
-   No contested issue settled in one flat sentence. Rule: any point worth real money or a whole claim gets ‘likely … though …’ and, where it changes the advice, the figure each way.
-   Meet the other side’s best facts on formation, and keep Parts consistent. v1 used the third party’s signature line to make him a party in Part II while calling it irrelevant to formation in Part I. Rule: when the same facts serve two issues, write the reconciling sentence (eg the offer to one offeree was accepted, the offer to the other was not).
-   Argue even the easy elements both ways in a sentence. Intention on social facts needs the onus, the counter, and the decisive answer (later conduct, Todd v Nicol).
-   Quantify every ‘is X entitled’ question: give the per-unit figure and the totals on each scenario, and say which clause limits the base.
-   Read remedy passages of dissents to the end. v1 turned Windeyer J’s doubt about nominal damages into a rule that damages are nominal unless the promisee owed a debt; he gave several substantial-loss examples and rejected the nominal view. Rule: before stating what a judge ‘would’ award, read the whole passage and the next pages for the judge’s own conclusion and the ‘as at present advised’ or dissent label.
-   Describe a distinguished case’s facts from the judgment, not memory: Meehan’s condition went to the obligation to complete, not to whether the contract bound at all. A test quoted from a case (Trident, Deane J) must keep its form: ‘should be inferred if … and if …’ is sufficient, not necessary, and has two limbs.
-   Pin each footnote to the passage that supports the proposition stated, not only the quoted words (a ‘left open’ proposition needs the page where it is left open).
-   Quote-stitching and length: one quotation from a source per sentence, split at the footnote; no sentence over about 45 words. Absolute constructions (‘X being obiter’) and trailing ‘besides’ read as broken.
-   Do not quote three function words (‘at least where’); paraphrase. Do not put a judge’s words about the case before him into his mouth about your parties (‘on his view a promisor in X’s position …’).
-   Verifier: the false CHECK PIN from a statute year in the .docx is fixed in the tool (8 Oct). The first full rewrite ran to 1,633 words: write it, count with the verifier, then cut low-yield roll calls of judges and repeated facts first.

Final answer

Word count: 1,498

I. KIM’S CLAIM AGAINST QUEENBEA

A. Formation

The advertisement gives Kim no right to ‘$500 per post’. A website proposal invites offers unless it ‘clearly indicates’ an intention to be bound,[1] and ‘Apply through the link below’ seeks applications, like the invitation ‘to make formal application’ in Gibson.[2] Decisively, Kim saw it only after the Festival, so could not have accepted it.[3]

Intention to create legal relations is likely present, though Kim bears the onus.[4] QueenBea may point to the ‘third round of drinks’ between friends who laughed at the sudden formality. Yet the test is what ‘would objectively be conveyed by what was said or done’,[5] and paid promotion of a commercial festival by a ‘prominent’ influencer, on standard forms, conveys legal commitment. Decisively, Kim signed and emailed the form three days later and both performed, conduct admissible to discover that intention.[6]

Kim’s signed form was an offer to which Bea, who ‘read it quickly and put it in her bag’, manifested no assent.[7] Kim having proposed that ‘we can write it down on yours’, Bea’s signed form was a counter-offer operating, in words Lawton LJ adopted, ‘to kill the original offer’.[8] Kim accepted it by signing and emailing ‘this all looks great to me’.

Acceptance likely took effect on 31 August, when the email became ‘capable of being retrieved’ at an address Bea designated.[9] Bea will say a business card is a ‘mere indication’ of an address, so receipt awaited her awareness.[10] Yet an offer that ‘expressly specifies’ an address designates it,[11] as Bea did in asking for the agreement at the card’s address. Otherwise, Kim’s performance was arguably acceptance by conduct,[12] though placing her hashtag first makes it equivocal.

QueenBea’s best answer is Rob’s missing signature: Bea pencilled ‘Kays’ and ‘Rob Kay’ onto the form, nodded when told Rob would sign, and asked for the ‘finalised agreement’. Whether a contract awaits every signature ‘depends upon the intention disclosed by the language’,[13] and the form imposed every obligation on Kim and none on Rob, so his signature could only make him a party. Bea’s payment for ‘images which complied with the agreement’ confirms formation, being admissible post-contractual conduct.[14] A contract between QueenBea and Kim was therefore likely formed, the offer to Rob remaining unaccepted.

B. The hashtag order

Butler is analogous: the sellers’ conditions ‘had disappeared from the story’ once they signed the buyers’ acknowledgment,[15] and Kim’s email never mentioned her own form, so printed clause 4, with the QueenBea hashtag ‘listed first’, governs. Kim’s strongest counter is that Bea, having read Kim’s ‘condition’ that #valYOUable ‘must appear first’, said ‘you can include it in all posts’, objectively assenting to it. Alternatively, Lord Denning MR might scrap irreconcilable terms,[16] leaving no order requirement. Yet Bea read Kim’s form only ‘quickly’, and her words address inclusion, not order, beside a printed clause settling order expressly. Lord Denning MR’s view was his alone; Lawton LJ applied ‘set rules’,[17] under which Kim’s unqualified signature accepted clause 4.

The six posts of 1 to 3 September, carrying ‘#valYOUable and #empowHERment hashtags, in that order’, therefore likely breached clause 4 and, by clause 7, earned nothing, though Bea’s remark keeps this arguable. Waiver, and restitution for unpaid posts, are outside scope.

C. The 4 September posts

Clause 5’s proviso does not make Kim’s promise illusory, since it leaves her only ‘a latitude of choice as to the manner’ of performance.[18] On whether she validly invoked it, Meehan has no majority: Gibbs CJ required only honest satisfaction, ‘not that of some hypothetical reasonable man’;[19] Mason J and Wilson J left reasonableness open, though both read the authorities as favouring honesty.[20]

Firstly, Kim was plainly honest: she ‘looked in the mirror’ and was ‘looking incredibly tired’. Secondly, however, if reasonableness applies, Bea will say tiredness is not unfitness, since Kim was fit to attend, and that her face was what QueenBea bought. Yet Bea pencilled the proviso subjectively, turning on whether ‘Kim is not satisfied’, and Kim still posted two Festival images with QueenBea’s hashtag first. Meehan is distinguishable in Kim’s favour: there the condition decided whether the purchaser had to complete a land purchase at all,[21] which is why Mason J feared escape ‘on a mere declaration’,[22] whereas clause 5 alters only the manner of one day’s images. The 4 September posts therefore likely complied, though finely balanced if reasonableness applies.

D. The 5 September posts

Clause 2 required each image to ‘remain visible for the duration of the Festival’, so deleting the 5 September posts after a full day’s visibility breached it unless the 3 September concession binds. QueenBea will say Kim gave nothing, since a promise ‘to do no more than the promisor is bound to do’ is no consideration,[23] and this was no bona fide compromise, as Kim never asserted she was not bound.[24]

Kim’s answer is practical benefit, as recast in Musumeci.[25] Firstly, Kim had contracted to supply services for payment. Secondly, her ‘thinking about discontinuing’ gave Bea reason to doubt completion. Thirdly, Bea promised an ‘other concession (such as reducing A’s original obligation)’,[26] cutting visibility to a day. Fourthly, Bea ‘knew it was unlikely that she could find a replacement at such short notice’, so, as in Roffey, she avoided ‘engaging other people’.[27] Four more days of posts were therefore ‘capable of being viewed by B as worth more to B than any likely remedy against A’.[28] Kim, too, risked her other sponsorships by staying, as the Musumeci tenants stayed ‘rather than walking away at the cost of damages’.[29]

The strongest counter is unfair pressure: Glidewell LJ’s paradigm is a subcontractor who ‘declines to continue with it unless’ paid more.[30] Yet Kim demanded nothing, her reason was genuine, and Bea proposed the concession; one ‘extended by B, without extortion’ supports an inference of consideration.[31] Nor was it ‘expressly limited to a period of difficult circumstances’,[32] its only condition being a day’s visibility. The better view is that the variation binds, so clause 7 does not bite, though Musumeci is a first-instance decision; promissory estoppel, the fallback, is outside scope.

E. The fee

Clause 3’s ‘reasonable fee’ is certain: Hall v Busst concerned land, and Fullagar J’s contrary view was obiter.[33] For services, ‘The usual standard is that of reasonable remuneration based on market or industry criteria’,[34] which must be ‘readily ascertainable’ and proved;[35] Bea’s reliance on ‘the prevailing market rate’ concedes one exists. Kim may answer that the relevant market is for a ‘prominent’ influencer, of which QueenBea’s own ‘$500 per post’ is evidence. Her other sponsors’ rates would decide whether the fee exceeds $400.

Kim is therefore likely entitled to a reasonable fee for the eight images of 4 to 7 September, leaving $1,600 unpaid at $400 or $2,400 at $500, rising to $4,000 at $400 if she also wins on the hashtag order.

II. ROB’S ENTITLEMENT TO PAYMENT

A. Rob’s own claim

Only a party may sue,[36] and Bea’s reason that Rob ‘didn’t sign the agreement’ misstates the test, since ‘the mere fact that her signature appears does not make her a party’.[37] Coulls is distinguishable in Rob’s favour: there the heading and operative words named only the husband and the company, which McTiernan J held to ‘countervail against the inference’ from Mrs Coulls’s signature,[38] whereas Bea pencilled ‘Kays’, Rob’s name and clause 6. Decisively, however, Rob gave no ‘external manifestation of assent’,[39] having ‘already left for a vacation’, and Kim signed only her own line, not as his agent. Even as a party, Rob gave no consideration, so could enforce only as a joint promisee, Kim’s services being ‘a consideration given on behalf of them all’.[40] Four Coulls judges accepted that principle, though not as ratio, and it requires Kim to be a party to the action.[41] Deane J would infer a trust if Kim intended that Rob ‘should himself be entitled to insist on performance’ and a trust were appropriate;[42] Rob could then sue QueenBea, joining Kim, so further information is needed. Rob therefore likely cannot sue in his own right.

B. Kim’s enforcement of clause 6

Kim, however, gave consideration, and on Windeyer J’s dissenting view a promisor in QueenBea’s position ‘would break its contract if it did not’ pay.[43] Clause 7 likely confines clause 6’s fee ‘for each image posted by Kim’ to compliant images, so at $400 Rob is owed $40 an image: $160 on the four Bea accepts, or $320 on eight. Windeyer J would specifically enforce promises ‘to pay money … to a third person’;[44] Barwick CJ, also dissenting, would do so at least where the promisee’s own consideration was specifically enforceable,[45] which Kim’s services were not. Otherwise, some authorities allow Kim only nominal damages, but Windeyer J would award substantial ones where Rob was her creditor or someone she felt a duty to recompense,[46] as a brother and manager may be; further information is needed. Kim can therefore arguably obtain an order that QueenBea pay Rob, though only dissenting judges support it; otherwise she recovers her own loss.

2020 T3: Felted Hats: ATGS grant, Gerard’s past services, Ethereal Sounds’ fee range, Bloom

First draft 82/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 82/100; main losses were a one-sided treatment of the client’s own claim, dicta applied to the wrong party, and AGLC form.

-   RECURRED, sharpened: one opening sentence for the advisee followed by five factors for the other side is still one-sided. Rule: on a claim the advisee brings, give its case a full paragraph built from every planted fact (costing, promotion, a minister’s ‘committing’, the closest case on its side), then answer each point, even when you expect the claim to fail.
-   Where the register maps a point as contested (eg revoking a unilateral offer once performance has begun), work through each layer: the authority each way with its status and who rejected it, then the factor test applied to the facts, then the remedy. Settling it on the decisive fact alone loses most of the marks.
-   Before applying a dictum, check whose position it describes (promisor or promisee, offeror or offeree, payer or payee) and whether your party is in that position. v1 applied ‘a discretion within specified parameters’ (a promisor’s discretion) to a payee’s choice of its own fee.
-   When distinguishing a case or a court’s illustration, rely on the ground the court made decisive; reread the passage. The Woollen Mills Sydney example turns on request, not on benefit to A.
-   When one doctrine appears in two claims (eg the range rule), apply it the same way in both and say why it helps one claimant and not the other (‘up to’ has a ceiling but no floor; ‘$2,000 to $4,000’ has a floor).
-   RECURRED: never let a phrase like ‘like X in Case’ carry a single judge’s view, least of all a dissent’s. Write the judge, his status and his words. No adjective doing legal work (‘uncommunicated’, ‘expressly’, ‘all members’) may go beyond the problem’s own words.
-   RECURRED: a threshold sentence still needs a pinpoint that states the proposition. If the cited paragraph only implies the point, cut the sentence or restate it as the paragraph says it.
-   AGLC: name no judges for a judgment of the whole court or the whole Board (Woollen Mills HC, Mobil, Roscorla, Pao On). Use ‘quoting Case (year) report pin (Judge)’ and ‘citing’; never ‘adopting’ or ‘discussing’, and never a citation inside the judge’s brackets. Put en dashes in footnote pin ranges. Define a short title for every case later named in short form, in the body or by (n x). (The verifier quirk with two (‘Short’) titles in one footnote is fixed in the tool, 8 Oct.)
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2019_T3 ran to 1,633): the first full revision, with every marker addition, ran to 2,036 words. Rule: before revising, set a word budget for each claim (about 36% for the claim worth the most marks) and pay for each addition with a named cut; cut repeated authorities for one point and unplanted further-information lines first.

Final answer

Word count: 1,500

I. FELTED HATS’ CLAIM AGAINST THE COMMONWEALTH

A. Offer and intention

Felted Hats’ strongest argument is that the ATGS offered grants to any group performing an Australian play, so, as in Carlill, ‘the performance of the conditions is the acceptance of the offer’.[47] Its heavy promotion, ‘$7M’ costing and the Minister’s speech ‘committing her government’ arguably show a real promise, like the deposit there.[48]

However, the better view is that the ATGS was a policy statement: the Privy Council held that subsidy letters ‘cannot be read as an offer or offers to contract’.[49] Firstly, grants for ‘bold, confident productions’ that ‘may be up to $25 000’ raise the ‘uncertain factors’ that made an administrative basis natural there,[50] and a cost estimate, unlike a deposit, backs no individual claim. Secondly, the Opposition promised only ‘if they are elected’, without power to commit Crown funds, a factor against contract in Woollen Mills.[51] Thirdly, in Mobil a seriously meant commitment was still too vague to be an offer.[52] Decisively, Kitto J in Leahy asked only whether parties dealt contractually or were ‘arranging the manner and extent of gratuitous assistance’ under a policy;[53] these grants are the latter, and Felted Hats bears the onus.[54]

B. Certainty

Placer,[55] where a Commonwealth subsidy whose amount was to ‘rest in the discretion of the promisor’ was illusory, is the closest case.[56] Felted Hats would answer that size and duration made it ‘eligible for a $25 000 grant’, and a discretion exercised ‘within specified parameters’ is not illusory.[57] Yet ‘up to’ sets a ceiling with no floor, so holding the Commonwealth to ‘the minimum provision in the range’ yields nothing certain.[58]

C. Acceptance and consideration

If there were an offer, Felted Hats would invoke Starke J’s rule that one who knows of an offer and performs its conditions ‘establishes prima facie an acceptance’.[59] Though ‘her turn to decide’ suggests Danger would have been chosen anyway, a member ‘referred to the ATGS when making her case’, and a mixed motive ‘not inconsistent with’ acting on the offer need not displace that inference.[60] The votes of several members, however, are not consideration ‘moving from the plaintiff’.[61] The overspend is mere reliance, which ‘is not itself sufficient to create a contract’.[62]

D. Revocation

Acceptance by performance had not begun when the ATGS was suspended in June. Felted Hats would argue that its ‘well advanced’ preparations began the requested act, making the offer irrevocable. McPherson J read Abbott v Lance that way,[63] and in Beaton McHugh JA, dissenting in the result, said the McDivitts could not withdraw once Beaton began working the block.[64] However, Kirby P rejected that analysis,[65] and the Full Federal Court in Mobil, in alternative reasoning, rejected any universal rule, asking instead whether an ancillary contract not to revoke should be implied.[66] That Felted Hats ‘spent considerably more than normal’ supports one, unlike the ‘little or no actual detriment’ in Mobil.[67] Yet preparation is ‘such an ill-defined act’ as Mobil would not lightly protect,[68] and Starke J suggested no right to the reward arises until the conditions are ‘completely performed’.[69] Decisively, the Government protected only performances commenced ‘by 30 June’, and Danger was set to open on 10 July.

Felted Hats therefore likely recovers none of the $25,000 or its overspend in contract; estoppel lies outside this advice. Further information is needed on whether it applied once the scheme was ‘set up and running’; if an approved application stated terms, those would govern.

II. GERARD’S CLAIM AGAINST FELTED HATS

Despite Gerard’s volunteer history, a fixed rate answered by his invoice objectively shows intention.[70] The real problem is consideration, since the sets ‘took him four days to complete’ and the promise came ‘[o]n the fourth day’. A past consideration ‘will support no other promise than such as would be implied by law’.[71] As a completed sale could not support a later warranty in Roscorla, finished painting cannot support a later promise.

Gerard’s best answer is Lord Scarman’s exception: the act must be requested, ‘the parties must have understood that the act was to be remunerated’, and an advance promise must have been enforceable.[72] Enforceability is met, and request is likely if Felted Hats asked him to paint as in past years. Gerard would add Bowen LJ’s statement that a past service ‘raises an implication that at the time it was rendered it was to be paid for’.[73] Decisively, however, three years ‘without charging a fee’ rebut it, and the treasurer’s ‘this year he would be paid’ marks a new reward, unlike the restriction in Pao On that ‘must be compensated for’.[74]

The strongest counter is that if painting remained after the promise, finishing was fresh consideration, whose adequacy is not weighed.[75] Yet praise of ‘excellent’ sets and a rate covering all four days reads as a reward for past work. Nor would Felted Hats’ hope of the grant make payment conditional, unless made a term; McHugh JA, dissenting in the result, called a comparable motive in Beaton ‘a motivating factor’ but ‘not a condition’.[76]

Gerard therefore likely recovers none of his $1,400. Further information is needed on whether work remained after the promise or payment was discussed beforehand; if so, he likely recovers $1,400.

III. ETHEREAL SOUNDS’ CLAIM AGAINST FELTED HATS

A. Agreement

Ethereal Sounds’ reply, adding a fee ‘between $2 000 and $4 000’, was the operative offer: either Felted Hats’ email merely invited offers, or the new term operated ‘to kill the original offer’.[77] Silence on the fee is not acceptance of it.[78] Yet Felted Hats replied in words, and a reasonable bystander would read ‘look forward to receiving the score’, sent after the fee was stated, ‘as signalling to the offeror that his offer has been accepted’.[79] A paid commission shows intention, and the mutual promises supply consideration.

B. The brief

Gillian’s verdict that the score is ‘unusable’ does not defeat the claim. Unlike the finance clause in Meehan, nothing made the commission subject to Felted Hats’ satisfaction,[80] and ‘as you see fit’ gave Ethereal Sounds ‘a latitude of choice as to the manner’ of performance.[81] Felted Hats would reply that the latitude runs only within the brief, and one note and a backwards kookaburra convey ‘hidden menace’ but arguably no ‘surface beauty’. Even an implied satisfaction term would demand honesty,[82] which Gillian’s single listen tests. Conformity is a breach question, outside this advice.

C. The fee

Felted Hats could argue that a fee left to Ethereal Sounds means ‘no concluded bargain’, as Gibbs J suggested without deciding.[83] However, Kirby P would hold a party to ‘at least the minimum provision in the range’,[84] as Lewandowski enforced a $7,000 to $9,000 salary range at its minimum.[85] It is analogous as pay for services, though here the payee named the range. Ethereal Sounds would claim ‘reasonable remuneration based on market or industry criteria’,[86] but with ‘no further information about how the fee would be calculated’, no proved standard supports more.[87]

On balance, Felted Hats likely owes $2,000, not $4,000. Further information is needed on market rates; if a reasonable fee is proved, Ethereal Sounds could recover up to $4,000.

IV. FELTED HATS’ CLAIM AGAINST BLOOM

A. Agreement and intention

Bloom’s letters promise $5,000 for ‘just doing your thing’, and Felted Hats accepted its July selection, so a contract formed then or, at latest, on performance. Bloom may call its ‘unusual promotional campaign’ binding in honour only, but Rogers CJ held at first instance that promises ‘uttered in the course of business’ should be enforced absent a clear contrary indication.[88] Bloom’s post, ‘This week we paid the members’, is later conduct confirming that intention.[89]

B. Consideration

Bloom’s strongest argument is that Felted Hats gave nothing: it need only do ‘[w]hatever you like’, and the post says ‘Nothing else’. Like B in the Woollen Mills illustration, who may have ‘intended to go to Sydney anyhow’, Felted Hats would receive a conditional gift.[90] The better view favours consideration. Firstly, unlike A, who was not shown to have requested B’s journey, Bloom expressly paid ‘$5 000 in return for’ the role.[91] Secondly, and decisively, Bloom bargained for the right to ‘promote our relationship with you’, which it exercised by posting ‘Brought to you by Bloom’. That is a ‘benefit accruing to one party’.[92] Thirdly, ‘Whatever you like’ gives latitude as to manner, not as to whether Felted Hats lends its name.[93] Further information is needed on Bloom’s existing sponsorship; if it already permitted such publicity, Felted Hats did ‘no more than the promisor is bound to do under the contract’, and consideration fails.[94]

C. The withdrawal and the multivitamins

Once the appointed week had passed, a ‘change of policy’ is no answer, since an offer binds whoever performs ‘before it is retracted’.[95] Felted Hats should decline the ‘large box of multivitamins’ or accept it expressly not in satisfaction, since an accepted substitute may discharge the debt where it ‘operates by way of accord and satisfaction’.[96]

Felted Hats therefore likely recovers $5,000, though finely balanced on whether ‘Nothing else’ shows Bloom sought nothing.

2021 T3: Mary Stefas: Klaus’s variation, Luna’s deposit, Faulkner’s cleaning clause

First draft 78.5/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 78.5/100; main losses were a case distinguished on facts it did not have, a rule cited to a case that does not state it, and a multi-party Part analysed without its parties.

-   Check a case’s own facts before distinguishing it. v1 said Mary, unlike the Empirnall offeree, took no benefit she was not already owed; the casebook facts say Empirnall had admitted an oral contract, so the case was Faulkner’s best authority. Rule: before writing ‘unlike X in Case’, read the editors’ facts bracket and the passage the court decided on; if the case’s facts match the other side, present it as the opponent’s best case and distinguish on the ground the court made decisive (here knowledge of the terms, 536).
-   Some basic rules are stated only in the textbook or slides, never in an extracted judgment: revocation must be actually communicated (textbook [3.110], fn to Byrne v Van Tienhoven); a bare promise to hold an offer open is not binding (textbook, Goldsbrough Mort); the postal rule’s probable non-application to email (textbook, Olivaylle); privity’s burden side (textbook [11.60]); the Pao On third-party holding (casebook note, Glidewell LJ, textbook). Rule: before citing a case for a rule, find the rule’s words in that judgment; if only the textbook states it, cite the case the textbook footnotes (report only, no pin, no quoted words) or reason from what the extracted cases do say. Never borrow a case that decides a neighbouring point (v1 used Felthouse, an acceptance case, for revocation).
-   When a Part has three or more organisations or people, first name the parties to each contract and promise (Ermogenous [33]), then run privity both ways and the third-party-duty exception before any existing-duty consideration defence; v1’s ‘which it already owed’ ignored that the duty might be owed to a third party.
-   Where a Part’s conclusion rests on one contested threshold (here a binding oral contract before the documents), give the other branch and its result in two sentences; otherwise the conclusion is unreasoned if the threshold fails.
-   Apply a qualification by its own test, not by the words that explain its rationale. v1 used Mason J’s ‘threatening unscrupulously’ as a bar; the Wigan test is an honest claim, not vexatious or frivolous. Likewise ask the first question of a doctrine before its exceptions (did the event change the existing duty: Stilk ‘at liberty’).
-   RECURRED, sharpened: the advisee’s best argument can lie in its own words (Mary’s ‘If you finish … I will pay’ reads as a unilateral offer). Read the advisee’s own communications for the reading that defeats formation.
-   Bench labels in the register can be wrong: four judges in a joint judgment with a fifth concurring is a majority, not a plurality. Check the bench in the casebook before labelling.
-   RECURRED: the revision with every marker addition ran to 1,882 words. Rule: draft the revision against a 1,450 budget and cut whole low-yield sentences (second authorities, unplanted further-information lines, duplicate quotations of the same fact) before polishing. Verifier: a (‘Short title’) after a pin page where the case name does not appear gives a false CHECK, and a report citation the materials cannot pin (Pao On) gives a lint line; both are expected and explained, not ‘fixed’ with an invented pin.

Final answer

Word count: 1,498

Frustration, termination, duress, estoppel and restitution are outside this advice.

I. KLAUS’S CLAIM AGAINST MARY

A. The variation

Mary accepted Klaus’s Quotation; on 26 August she answered his $3,000 demand with an offer of $2,500 extra.

Mary’s strongest argument is that this offer was unilateral: ‘[i]f you finish the whole job by 7 September, I will pay’ asks for an act, which is then ‘also an executed consideration for the promise offered’.[97] If so, her 31 August notice revoked it before Klaus began. Yet ‘Let me know by 31 August’ asks for a reply, so the offer was likely bilateral, and the dated sentence fixes only when $8,000 falls due.
