Hiring another painter on 28 August revoked nothing, since a withdrawal takes effect only when actually communicated.[98] Nor was Klaus’s email complete on sending: on the High Court’s view the postal rule needs an offeror who ‘contemplated and intended’ acceptance by that act,[99] and Mary asked to be told.

If Mary designated her address, the email was received on 29 August, read or not.[100] Arguably she did by sending her offer from it, though merely showing an address is not designation.[101] Otherwise receipt also required that she ‘has become aware’ it had been sent,[102] which arguably occurred when Klaus told her so on 31 August, before she mentioned the other painter; his words were arguably themselves an oral acceptance.[103] Either way acceptance arrived by her deadline, so a variation was likely formed.

B. Consideration for the extra $2,500

A promise ‘to do no more than the promisor is bound to do under the contract’ is generally no consideration.[104] Klaus’s first answer is that the health orders freed him from the 7 September date, so promising to meet it exceeded his duty, as Lord Ellenborough CJ accepted crew ‘at liberty to quit the vessel’ could have done.[105] Yet Klaus promised to ‘recommence work as soon as he is permitted’, treating himself as bound, and whether the date survived is a frustration question.

Klaus’s main answer is practical benefit, as Santow J, at first instance, recast Williams v Roffey.[106] With the exterior unstarted, Mary had reason to doubt completion; she promised more for his promise to finish on time; and, as ‘no one is currently available’, his performance was capable of being viewed as worth more than any likely remedy.[107] The $6,000 painter appeared only later.

Mary’s strongest point is Santow J’s fifth element, which excludes a promise ‘induced as a result of unfair pressure’.[108] Klaus demanded more and drove away, near Glidewell LJ’s subcontractor who ‘declines to continue with it unless’ paid more,[109] though Klaus threatened only lateness. Williams v Roffey is distinguishable, as there the payer proposed the increase. Yet Mary fixed her own capped figure after canvassing other painters, and a concession extended ‘without extortion’ supports, though not conclusively, an inference of consideration.[110]

Alternatively, ‘I agreed to that before the movement restrictions came in’ arguably asserted Klaus was no longer bound. A Wigan compromise needs no threat to sue or winning claim, only one honestly made and, on the stricter test, not ‘vexatious or frivolous’.[111] A claim resting on health orders meets both, though Mary may say ‘the COVID lockdown put me behind’ asserts only delay.

On balance, the better view is that practical benefit likely supports the promise, though finely balanced, as duress may decide the fifth element. If so, the price is $13,500 rather than $11,000.

C. The demand for $8,000

Mary promised $8,000 only ‘[i]f you finish the whole job by 7 September’, and the original balance fell due only ‘on satisfactory completion’. Klaus never finished, so he has at most a damages claim against a contract sum of $8,000 or $5,500. Klaus therefore likely has a binding variation, but no debt of $8,000.

II. LUNA’S CLAIM AGAINST MARY

A. Agreement and intention

Mary’s tentative ‘I’m wondering if you could do me a favour’ became an offer once she stated firm terms, and Luna, after protesting, ‘eventually agrees’ and took the $1,000.

Luna bears the onus, and Ermogenous doubted the utility of presumptions.[112] The test is what would ‘objectively be conveyed by what was said or done’.[113]

Luna’s strongest case is that Mary used the language of a paid booking: a ‘jazz singer and pianist’ asked to play four Saturday nights at ‘your usual fee’, with a deposit and a balance. When Luna protested that she was a ‘charity case’, Mary insisted she had ‘been trying to work out entertainment for those Saturdays’. Mary’s later remark that she was ‘just offering you that work to help you out’ cannot contradict those words,[114] and earlier in that call she spoke of Luna coming to ‘start your performances’.

Mary’s answer is the setting: the parties were romantically involved, she asked ‘a favour’, she paid the deposit ‘so you have something in the meantime’, and Luna herself saw charity. Unlike the plaintiffs in Todd, who sold their belongings and left Scotland, Luna has changed nothing.[115] Yet affection no more excludes a contract than spirituality did in Ermogenous,[116] and Mary’s aim of sparing ‘Luna’s pride’ was never conveyed. On balance, the better view is that intention is likely present, because commercial form does the work that emigration did in Todd, though the romance keeps it arguable.

B. Consideration and certainty

Luna’s promise was the price of Mary’s, since Mary requested the performances,[117] and ‘[m]otive is not the same thing with consideration’.[118] Nor is ‘your usual fee’ uncertain, being an external standard that can be proved,[119] here $1,800. ‘[W]hen the restaurant opens’ leaves Mary discretion only over ‘the fulfilment of a condition’,[120] now set for 29 October.

C. The $1,000

Mary’s demand for ‘the $1,000 I let you borrow’ fails either way: under a contract it was a ‘deposit’ on the fee, and without one Luna never promised to repay. Mary is therefore likely bound to Luna, exposed on the $800 balance, and cannot recover the $1,000 in contract.

III. FAULKNER LOCATIONS’ CLAIM AGAINST MARY

A. The 28 August contract

Identifying the parties demands ‘close attention’.[121] On 28 August Trent negotiated the hire for Shock Value, which paid the $8,000, but said that ‘Faulkner Locations takes care of a COVID clean’, a promise by his company to Mary. Read with ‘so you don’t need to worry about that’, it was promissory and made in the course of business,[122] so Faulkner was to bear the cost.

Faulkner’s strongest case is that nothing bound Mary before its ‘usual Location Agreement which is a bit more detailed’, since where a contract ‘involving the possibility of new terms’ remains to be adopted, the parties are still negotiating.[123] Mary blocked the dates only ‘in my calendar in the meantime’.

The better view is that the parties proposed only a restatement ‘fuller or more precise but not different in effect’.[124] Mary had only to ‘dot the i’s and cross the t’s’, and Trent offered ‘all of that’ in ‘black and white’. Conduct after formation is admissible on formation,[125] and Shock Value paid before any document was handed over. Masters is distinguishable: there the solicitors could add whatever they ‘may fairly consider appropriate’.[126]

B. Clause 13

Faulkner’s best case is Empirnall, where an admitted oral contract did not stop the offeree accepting later written terms by taking the benefit of continued work ‘with knowledge of its terms’.[127] Mary likewise read that the parties would carry out ‘their respective obligations set out in this Agreement’, then let three more days of filming and cleaning proceed. Stephen J treated failing to reject ‘after he has had an opportunity of learning of the conditions’ as acceptance.[128]

Decisively, Mary lacked the knowledge Empirnall required. There a letter ‘made clear what was the basis’ of the work,[129] whereas Trent presented the document as ‘all of that’, Mary read only two paragraphs saying nothing of cleaning, and that morning she had handed over contrary terms. Stephen J addressed a ticket offered before any contract, not a document after one. Mary’s conduct, equally explained by the existing bargain, was not such ‘as necessarily to lead to the inference’ of acceptance.[130]

Even if she assented, clause 13 offered only that Faulkner ‘will arrange’ cleaning it already owed her, so her promise to pay half lacked consideration.[131] Faulkner may say that duty was owed to Shock Value, and a promise to perform a third party’s duty can be consideration, as in Pao On,[132] but Trent promised Mary directly. Clause 24 cannot help Mary either: who is a party turns on construing the instrument,[133] and it binds ‘the person hiring the venue’, Shock Value. Faulkner, a party with obligations under the Location Agreement, faces no privity bar.

If instead nothing bound Mary before the documents, Trent’s ‘That’s right’ acknowledged an exchange of terms rather than accepting hers, and the later Location Agreement, a counter-offer, killed her Hire Terms.[134] Three days of filming, unexplained by any prior contract, would likely accept it. Mary therefore likely owes Faulkner nothing rather than $420, provided the 28 August contract stands.

2022 T1: Best Power, New Auto and Baker & Associates: Masters, supply term, extra fee

First draft 80.5/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 80.5/100; main losses were a planted doctrine cut as ‘note only’, a test applied with the very evidence it excludes, and misquoted facts.

-   A doctrine whose definition matches a planted phrase must be argued even if the materials hold it only in a casebook note (the fourth Masters class and Sunny’s ‘needs to be further negotiated’). Rule: map every planted phrase to its doctrine before budgeting, and cut weak analysis, never the doctrine the examiner planted.
-   Apply a test by its own evidential limits. v1 proved essentiality under Whitlock from James’s later outburst, though Whitlock (461) excludes extrinsic evidence of importance. Rule: before applying a test, read what the passage says may not be used to satisfy it, and apply it only to what it admits (there, the contract’s terms).
-   Read a party’s words in every legal character they could bear and keep the readings consistent. v1 read ‘we do need to ensure there will be sufficient supply’ only as a promise; as a condition for the buyer it is certain (Meehan’s crude oil condition). Rule: for each disputed clause, state its effect as a promise, as a condition and as no term, and say which reading each Part relies on.
-   Quote the speaker, the whole utterance and the right speaker. v1 gave the narrator’s ‘merely a handful of minor edits’ to Sunny, halved James’s 18 July sentence and cut Nathan’s ‘but we will need to charge an extra A$5,000’. Rule: before quoting, check who says it in the problem and read the full sentence; if the omitted half bears on the issue, quote it or do not quote at all.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2020_T3 decisive ground): a judge’s conclusion about a clause rests on its words (Mason J’s ‘each party’ on ‘null and void’). Rule: before transposing a judge’s result, set the clause he construed beside ours and say whether the operative words match.
-   When a fact names a non-party entity (‘will be the buyer’), run privity with the majority’s holding, not a dissent’s general statement, and reconcile it with the formation finding (who is party on each branch).
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2021_T3 first question): on an existing-duty point, exhaust the promisee’s routes around the duty from the problem’s own words (‘estimated’, ‘will be prepared’, a variation agreed in the same call as acceptance) before any exception; and when you characterise a deal as unilateral, reconcile each element of the test that speaks of a promise.
-   RECURRED: the revision with every accepted finding ran to 1,838 words; per-section estimates ran about 10% under the verifier’s count. Rule: draft each section at 90% of its budget and run the verifier after each section, not at the end.

Final answer

Word count: 1,496

I. BEST POWER’S CLAIM AGAINST NEW AUTO

A. Offer and acceptance

Sunny’s 15 June email was likely only an invitation to treat: ‘We expect to sell’ is no firmer than ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson,[135] and Best Power asked only ‘whether your company may be interested’, as the council invited only an application.[136] James’s 25 June email was therefore New Auto’s offer, which Sunny’s ‘sounds good’ accepted; were Sunny’s email an offer, the added finance term would make the reply a counter-offer.[137]

B. Whether New Auto was bound before execution

Parties contemplating a formal contract are bound if they meant to be bound at once (the first class) or made only performance conditional on execution (the second), not if they intended no ‘concluded bargain at all, unless and until they execute a formal contract’ (the third).[138]

Best Power’s strongest case is that nothing remained to agree: no words made the deal subject to contract, James called the proposal ‘acceptable to us’, and the agreement was to be ‘based on what we have discussed’. Lord Blackburn treated a contract as complete once the drafters cannot vary the settled terms,[139] and Best Power made ‘merely a handful of minor edits’. Its best authority is the fourth class, where parties are ‘content to be bound immediately and exclusively by the terms which they had agreed upon’ while expecting further terms by consent,[140] just as Sunny said supply ‘needs to be further negotiated’.

However, the better view is the third class. Decisively, Sunny’s assent asked for an agreement ‘for our review’, reserving Best Power’s approval of the formal terms. In Masters, a contract acceptable to the vendor’s solicitors could include ‘whatever else the solicitors may fairly consider appropriate’, so no contract arose;[141] review by Best Power itself is wider. Nothing limited Best Power’s review, it revised the draft, and nothing records signing; while a contract ‘involving the possibility of new terms’ remains to be adopted, the parties are still negotiating.[142] The fourth class fails too, since New Auto, having said it did ‘need to ensure’ supply, was never content to be bound ‘exclusively’ without it. Nor does the absence of subject to contract words matter, since ‘no special form of words is essential’.[143]

New Auto, like Best Power, was therefore likely free to withdraw on 18 July, though this is finely balanced given the minor edits. On the first, second or fourth class, New Auto was bound to buy 49% for A$10 million, subject to the conditions below.

C. The buyer

Only a party may enforce a contract, and party status turns on the instrument itself.[144] Any contract formed on 27 June is New Auto’s, as offeror; but if one arises only on execution of an agreement naming New Auto Australia Pty Ltd as buyer, as James proposed, Best Power must sue the subsidiary, and New Auto, a stranger, could not enforce any supply promise ‘for New Auto’.

D. The conditions

If New Auto was bound, its finance condition was neither uncertain nor illusory: New Auto judges satisfaction honestly, for Gibbs CJ, and perhaps also reasonably, for Mason J,[145] so it could not invoke finance to escape a supply grievance. Mason J let each party avoid because the Meehan clause made the contract ‘null and void’;[146] New Auto’s clause lacks those words, so the right to avoid may be New Auto’s alone.

Were the supply words a condition rather than a promise, they would be certain, like the Meehan condition meant to ensure ‘a sufficient supply of crude oil’,[147] and Sunny’s refusal would let New Auto honestly treat them as unmet; but, unlike the finance term, they carry no ‘subject to’.

Sunny should therefore be advised that Best Power likely cannot enforce the sale.

II. NEW AUTO’S CLAIM AGAINST BEST POWER

New Auto’s strongest argument is that its supply requirement sat in the very email Sunny answered with ‘sounds good’. Yet the test is what ‘would objectively be conveyed by what was said’:[148] ‘we do need to ensure’ states New Auto’s need, not a promise by Best Power, which had ‘decided not to renew’ supply. Even if promissory, it fixes no quantity, price or delivery. New Auto would answer that commercial arrangements attract ‘no narrow or pedantic approach’[149] and that the expired contract supplies the standard; yet Best Power refused to renew it, and nothing adopted its terms. Unlike the Whitlock lease clause, which at least invoked terms in common use, these words fix no standard.[150]

Were the term void, severance would turn on ‘the intention of the parties as disclosed by the contract’, not James’s later ‘the battery supply was all we wanted’.[151] New Auto’s offer put supply beside price, but the draft it forwarded ‘without reviewing it’ presumably omitted supply, so the contract’s own terms leave essentiality doubtful.

New Auto therefore has no supply claim.

III. BAKER & ASSOCIATES’ CLAIM AGAINST NEW AUTO

A. The Engagement Letter

James’s strongest argument is that he never returned the signed copy requested and stayed silent for 12 days, and silence is generally not acceptance.[152] Yet an offeree with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’ services who takes their benefit, in circumstances indicating payment according to the offer, may be held to accept.[153] Empirnall is closely analogous: the developer never signed the contract sent for signature, kept taking the work and was bound, because its objection went only ‘to the manner of acknowledging’ the terms.[154] Here James, on 28 June, said ‘well done. Please proceed with the other work’, a request stronger than Empirnall’s continued receipt of work. His private view that the fee was ‘a bit high’ is irrelevant.[155] A contract on the letter’s terms was likely formed on 28 June.

Stage 1 preceded acceptance, a point Empirnall left undecided,[156] but the Pao On conditions are met: New Auto requested it, ‘Can you please let us know your fee?’ shows both parties expected payment, and a promise to pay for requested legal work would have been enforceable in advance.[157] Nathan is entitled to A$30,000, now paid.

B. The extra A$5,000

Because Nathan promised only to ‘try’, James’s promise was accepted by delivery of the draft, which was ‘also an executed consideration’.[158] A promise to perform an existing duty is no consideration, at least where one contracting party promises the other ‘to do no more than the promisor is bound to do’.[159]

Nathan may deny that duty. Firstly, he may say the ‘estimated fee’ and ‘A draft agreement will be prepared’ gave only a forecast; yet ‘estimated’ qualifies the fee, the date followed ‘We understand the urgency in this matter’, and both parties called the A$5,000 ‘extra’. Secondly, he may say the A$5,000 was agreed in the same 28 June call as acceptance, forming part of the original bargain; yet ‘Please proceed’ accepted the letter before Nathan raised delay. Thirdly, illness did not release him: desertion in Stilk was ‘an emergency of the voyage as much as their death’,[160] and staff illness was likewise a risk his undertaking bore. Nor did he claim he was not bound, so no compromise arises.[161] Delivery on 10 July gave, if anything, less than ‘before 10 July 2021’.

Nathan’s best route is practical benefit, adopted in New South Wales by Santow J, sitting alone, in Musumeci.[162] Nathan’s forecast of a 28 July draft gave James reason to doubt timely performance, and James’s ‘otherwise we may lose the deal to another competitor’ identifies the benefit: a draft 18 days earlier, protecting an A$10 million transaction, was capable of being ‘worth more’ than any likely remedy, even at A$5,000.[163] Element (iii) speaks of a promise by A, the performer, which Nathan never gave; but the proviso turns on ‘A’s performance’, and delivery, the bargain’s intended result, gave more than a promise.[164]

The contest is Santow J’s element (v): whether New Auto’s promise was induced by ‘unfair pressure’ from Nathan, ‘having regard to the circumstances’.[165] James’s best point is that in Williams v Roffey the payer, persuaded by its own surveyor that the price was ‘too low’, chose to pay a bonus.[166] Here Nathan, who had promised the date knowing of the urgency, demanded the extra, like Glidewell LJ’s obiter subcontractor who ‘declines to continue with it unless’ paid more.[167] Even unforeseen hardship does not ‘justify a demand for re-negotiation backed by unfair pressure’.[168]

The better view is Nathan’s, though finely balanced. Decisively, he did not decline to continue: he gave a cause, ‘Many of our lawyers are unwell’, and replied ‘we can try but we will need to charge an extra A$5,000’, while James framed the condition himself without objecting to the price. Genuine illness bears on the ‘proportionality of any pressure’,[169] and A$5,000 is only 17.9% of the A$28,000 Stage 2 fee.

Nathan is therefore likely entitled to A$35,000, leaving A$5,000 owing; if a court found unfair pressure, New Auto would owe nothing beyond the A$30,000 paid. Further information is needed on whether the illness was genuine; if the delay was contrived, element (v) likely defeats Nathan.

2022 T3: JammyJam: @#@, Ninja and Sventy7

First draft 84/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 84/100; main losses were the opponent’s best formality rule left unstated, doctrinal branches not followed into later Parts, and attribution in footnotes.

-   Classify every message in a chain (offer, acceptance, counter-offer, inquiry) before any formality doctrine: v1 went straight to Masters although ‘Yes’ plus a new term is a counter-offer that the next message accepted, which is what puts the stipulation inside the bargain.
-   When you rely on a rule’s fallback (construction where words are not express), first state the presumption the opponent invokes in the source’s own words and pin (here Masters 363, ‘of similar import’ words prima facie create an overriding condition), then answer it. Asserting the fallback alone answers a weaker argument than the one the examiner planted.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2021_T3 branches): follow each branch of a multi-class doctrine into every later Part. v1 conceded class 2 in a clause (no waiver, no mutual duty to bring the document into existence) and never noticed that on class 3 a later ‘agreement’ forms the contract, so the existing-duty problem in the next Part disappears. Write one sentence per branch saying what it does to each later issue.
-   Markers can reintroduce old errors: the examiner proposed proving essentiality from negotiation history, which Whitlock 461 excludes (2022_T1). Rule: test every marker-proposed application against the passage’s own evidential limits before accepting it; negotiation facts go to formation, not to essentiality.
-   Tie each factual inference to the fact that proves it and check the other side’s words before characterising an act: knowledge came from ‘then remembers’, not ‘subscribes’; ‘all day’ and the auditor’s ‘unprompted’ were wrong (JammyJam had told Ninja to ‘just log in’). Adjectives about conduct (‘unprompted’, ‘uncommunicated’, ‘all day’) need a quoted fact.
-   RECURRED (2020_T3): a dissenting judge’s words were credited to ‘four judges’. When several judges share a principle in different words, quote one, name him and his status in the body, and mark dissents in the footnote.
-   Verifier (the marker-crossing, dissent-label and quoting issues are fixed in the tool, 9 Oct). Nested double marks trip the lint, so end a quotation before an inner quoted word (‘play for at least 20 minutes’ per war).
-   RECURRED (every run): the revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,813 words. Rule: before rewriting, list each accepted addition with its word cost beside a named cut; the cuts that paid here were the threshold sentence, the weakest third factor of a walk, facts quoted twice, and a second authority for one point.

Final answer

Word count: 1,496

I. @#@’S CLAIM AGAINST JAMMYJAM

A. Parties

Whether @#@ is a party turns on ‘the written instrument itself’.[170] Kai’s ‘We agree to pay you’ made the bargain one with both developers, so JammyJam’s promise to play was made to them jointly, as ‘our real names’ confirms; Coulls is distinguishable, as that contract ‘purports expressly to be one made between’ husband and company.[171] However, the discussion was ‘mostly between Kai and JammyJam’ and payment comes ‘from me’; yet a joint promise needs only, in the dissenting Windeyer J’s words, ‘a consideration given on behalf of them all’, a principle four judges accepted, though not as ratio.[172] @#@ therefore likely has standing, but must join Kai, who wants ‘nothing to do with the game’, as a defendant after tendering costs.[173]

B. Formation

Kai’s message, stating every term and asking only ‘All good?’, was an offer; JammyJam’s ‘Yes’ added that they ‘need final agreement to be sent through for electronic signatures under our real names’, a counter-offer which Kai’s ‘Strange but OK’ accepted.[174] Masters asks whether parties were then bound at once, bound with performance ‘conditional upon the execution of a formal document’, or not bound until execution.[175]

JammyJam’s strongest argument is the third class: ‘need final agreement’ is arguably an expression ‘of similar import’ to subject to contract, which prima facie creates an overriding condition.[176] With the ‘Key points of contention’ left as formulae, ‘the possibility of new terms’ remained.[177]

However, the reply is not expressly subject to contract, so construction decides ‘whether the parties intended that the terms agreed on should be put into form’.[178] Unlike Masters, where solicitors could add ‘whatever else’ seemed appropriate,[179] the stipulation adds no terms, only signatures, and Kai’s ‘Strange’ shows he saw a formality. As in Empirnall, signing went to ‘the manner of acknowledging’ terms, not their substance.[180] Post-contractual conduct is admissible on formation,[181] and decisively JammyJam acted as bound: they told Ninja of a ‘launch gig’ with ‘good money’, promoted the game, logged in with no final document, and said ‘their job is done’. Intention is likely, as a ‘professional gamer’ agreed a fee after ‘much negotiation’, though ‘All good?’ reads casually.[182]

On balance, the better view is the first class, a contract on Kai’s ‘OK’, though ‘need’ and ‘final’ keep the third arguable. On the second, JammyJam’s play fell due only once both sides brought the document into existence,[183] unless JammyJam, by playing, waived a stipulation arguably ‘inserted solely for the benefit of one of the parties’.[184] On the third, launch-day conduct may still form a contract, including Part D’s 20-minute term, if ‘capable of proving all the essential elements of an express contract’,[185] though the period problem remains.

C. Certainty and breach

On the fee, JammyJam will say ‘market expectations’ for launch fees, like share packages in ‘a new and speculative field’, are unprovable.[186] Yet under a firm promise to pay for services, a conclusion of illusory consideration ‘will only be drawn where no standard exists by which the promise can be valued’.[187] Like Barwick CJ’s bridge at cost, a measure fixed ‘at the time of launch’ is certain though disputed in application.[188] The fee is therefore likely certain if a market is proved.

JammyJam owed ‘at least three’ wars ‘every 24 hours for the period of the launch’, held only to that minimum.[189] Firstly, no end date was agreed, and a standard must be one ‘which is proved’,[190] whereas a week is only what the developers ‘claim is the industry standard’. Secondly, Kai’s ‘Anything less than a week is pointless’ is post-contractual, so inadmissible on meaning.[191] @#@ replies that the launch was a real event with a set start, so the term is not ‘so obscure and so incapable of any definite or precise meaning’ as to fail.[192] On balance, the period likely fails unless a one-week standard is proved and, defining JammyJam’s performance, cannot be severed, so the contract fails, as JammyJam may assert though they stopped.[193]

JammyJam played at least eleven wars in the first 24 hours, which performs any one-day launch, but on a one-week launch is at least fifteen wars short, three for each 24 hours after hour 48. Further information is needed on hours 24 to 36, where up to three more may be owed.

D. The promise to play 20 minutes per war

The first question is what the developers gave for JammyJam’s promise to ‘play for at least 20 minutes’ per war; no new promise appears, and continuing to pay, doing ‘no more than the promisor is bound to do’, is no consideration.[194] @#@’s best route is a ‘bona fide compromise of a disputed claim’.[195] For it, the developers, as the parties giving the existing promise, must have asserted that JammyJam was in breach, honestly and, on the stricter test Mason J applied, not vexatiously or frivolously, though not necessarily soundly.[196] JammyJam’s reply that they ‘never promised to play for a minimum period of time’ suggests the developers claimed a breach, settled by the ‘further discussion’, though their ‘disappointment’ may be mere grievance. Practical benefit does not fit, as Williams v Roffey concerns a payer promising more.[197] Further information is needed on whether a breach was asserted: if so, the promise likely binds; if not, it is gratuitous, unless on the third class the promise to pay was fresh. Even if binding, the promise, read commercially, bars quitting early rather than requiring long wars, since a war ends when a team reaches 1,000 points or loses them all.[198] The eight Ninja wars, played ‘very successfully’, thus likely breach nothing, unlike, arguably, the later ‘short and ineffective playing’.

@#@’s claim therefore likely fails unless a one-week standard is proved, and then covers at least fifteen missed wars; quantum is outside this advice.

II. NINJA’S CLAIM AGAINST JAMMYJAM

Whether Ninja’s reply rejected the $20 offer is a matter of construction, and JammyJam may say it was mere ‘posturing’, leaving the offer open to acceptance by logging in.[199] Yet ‘way too little money for me to be bothered’ named her own price, $50, a counter-offer whose effect was ‘to kill the original offer’.[200]

Ninja’s best argument is that an offeree who, able to reject services, ‘takes the benefit of them under circumstances which indicate that they were to be paid for in accordance with the offer’ may be held to accept.[201] JammyJam read her reply and could have refused her, yet teamed up for eight wars as viewers rose, taking her play ‘with knowledge of its terms’;[202] JammyJam’s private plan to ‘negotiate a little more’ is irrelevant to ‘a reasonable bystander’.[203]

The strongest counter is that silence is not acceptance,[204] and teaming up is equivocal, not conduct that ‘necessarily’ implies acceptance;[205] Ninja logged in and sent no message, and JammyJam teamed with random players too. Teaming up might revive JammyJam’s offer to ‘team up with you in-game’, on Heydon JA’s minority reasoning.[206] Yet JammyJam singled out the one player whose price they knew, and, as in Brambles, the benefit could not be ‘severed from the obligations proposed’.[207] That Ninja is an ‘old gamer friend’ does not displace intention in a paid ‘launch gig’.[208]

Ninja therefore likely recovers $400, eight wars at $50, though $160 if the $20 offer survived or was revived, and nothing if teaming up was not acceptance.

III. SVENTY7’S CLAIM AGAINST JAMMYJAM

A. Offer

Sventy7 will argue that the video was an offer to the world, binding to anyone who ‘performs the condition’,[209] as ‘$300 up for grabs if you’re the first person to jam me’ names a sum and a defined act. JammyJam replies that a generally accessible online proposal, which a video arguably is, ‘is to be considered as an invitation to make offers’ unless it clearly shows an intention to be bound,[210] and that ‘I dare you’ is banter, with no Carlill deposit.[211] On balance, the dare invites the act, and a reward for the first performer clearly shows that intention, so it is likely an offer. Further information is needed on whether JammyJam, promoting the game, spoke as the developers’ agent, making them party to any contract.[212]

B. Acceptance

The decisive question is whether Sventy7 acted ‘on the faith of’ the offer.[213] Performance with knowledge of the offer ‘establishes prima facie an acceptance’,[214] and Sventy7, who ‘then remembers the YouTube post’, knew of it and did jam JammyJam. However, the inference ‘may be excluded by evidence’, including his own statements or conduct.[215] Firstly, he was throwing ‘haphazardly in every direction’. Secondly, he answered congratulations with ‘?’. Thirdly, he remembered the post only once another player mentioned the $300, so his ‘Oh yeah’ came after the jam. Like Isaacs ACJ’s swimmer, he performed ‘without any thought of the offer’.[216] Clarke is analogous on its decisive ground, as the claimant’s own statements rebutted the presumption;[217] that Clarke alone acted ‘to clear himself’ matters little, since motive is only evidence and the offer was not in Sventy7’s mind.[218]

Sventy7’s claim to $300 therefore likely fails, though knowledge and exact performance keep it arguable.

2023 T3: Djarren, Thé, Greg and Igii: lost pets, fee increase, reward

First draft 80/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 80/100; main losses were three passages applied beyond what they say (a joinder rule read as a bar, a notice illustration read as deciding who performed, a hedged dictum stated as settled), the advisee’s own formation case left unargued, and facts added by inference.

-   A supplement entry can launder a misreading: register_supp S1 recorded Bowen LJ’s lost dog sentence for ‘finding is the essence’, but the passage answers whether notice of acceptance is needed and its own offer paid for bringing the dog to a place. Rule: before adding or using a passage, write down the question the court was answering in that paragraph and compare any hypothetical’s facts with ours; use it only for that question.
-   Words like ‘must have been brought by both’ or ‘would fail if brought by one alone’ are joinder rules, not bars. Rule: read the same and adjacent pages for what happens when the co-party will not join (joined as defendant, judgment for both) and conclude on that remedy, never ‘no claim’.
-   Hedges are part of the proposition. Quoting ‘not justify a demand … backed by unfair pressure’ without the next sentence (‘But … proportionality’), ‘without extortion’ without ‘though by no means conclusively’, and Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps’ as ‘excepted’ each overstated the law for the opponent. Rule: for every quotation read the next sentence; if it opens ‘But’, ‘However’ or ‘Perhaps’, or the source hedges, quote or state the hedge.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2022_T3 inferences): ‘on Djarren’s instructions’, ‘the writing never came’ (it came on day one) and Roffey ‘offered the extra money’ (its surveyor persuaded it) were all inferences. Rule: list every verb of who did, said, instructed or proposed what, in the problem and in each distinguished case, and match each to a quoted line before drafting.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2020_T3): on a threshold that goes against the advisee, write the advisee’s case first with its authority (here Empirnall 535, photo as acceptance by conduct) and answer it with the opponent’s best planted fact (the requested writing added new terms); then follow both branches to the money.
-   One planted phrase can test two doctrines (‘two fees for no extra work’: evidence rebutting reliance, and consideration from someone already paid by a third party). Rule: map each planted phrase to every doctrine it could serve, and read ambiguous references (‘Claim it if you can’: the job or the fee) in each meaning before building on one.
-   Docx: pandoc rendered ‘$$ !!Reward!! $$’ as display maths and read the apostrophe in “(k)’s” as an opening mark, flipping the next quotation; the markdown verifier could not see either. Rule: no paired dollar signs in the body and no possessive after a closing bracket; after make_docx.py, scan word/document.xml for oMath and for reversed marks, and rerun the verifier on the .docx.
-   RECURRED (every run): the first revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,815 words. The cuts that paid were a second pin for the same test, a second authority for the same answer (Isaacs ACJ on motive, Woolworths on adequacy), facts already stated in the next Part, and quoting a counter-offer’s terms twice; paraphrasing a lettered formula (A and B) instead of quoting it saved words and bracket substitutions.

Final answer

Word count: 1,494

PART 1: DJARREN

I. DJARREN’S CLAIM AGAINST THÉ

A. Formation and the first day

Djarren’s counter-offer killed Thé’s ‘$100’ offer,[219] and her hesitant reply was an inquiry that left his offer open.[220] Djarren’s best case is that Thé, knowing his terms, accepted by conduct when she sent her photo, since a reasonable bystander would read it ‘as signalling to the offeror that his offer has been accepted’.[221] The first day would then be payable, and her later ‘OK’ would adopt the written terms as a variation supported by the new promise in clause (k).

Thé’s main defence is that she asked ‘Do you have anything in writing?’, and the writing added clauses (k) and (l); while a contract ‘involving the possibility of new terms’ remains to be adopted, the parties are still negotiating.[222] Nor does a bare photo ‘necessarily’ lead to the inference of acceptance.[223] On balance, the contract more likely formed at her ‘OK’ to the email carrying that writing. The first day then rests on the Pao On exception:[224] Thé asked for the search (‘I really need Loth back’), his stated fee showed both expected payment, and that fee would have been enforceable if promised in advance. Intention is plain between professionals.[225]

B. Consideration for the increase

Thé first argues that a promise ‘to do no more than the promisor is bound to do’ is no consideration.[226] Djarren’s ‘I don’t think I can complete it for the current fee’, she will say, shows he had sold his search until Loth was found, like the crew who ‘had sold all their services till the voyage should be completed’.[227]

Decisively, however, clause (j) pays ‘per day’, and his only visible promise is the daily update in clause (k), so ‘complete it’ describes the job, not a duty. He was thus ‘at liberty to quit’, a position Lord Ellenborough CJ treated as different,[228] so his fourth day was likely fresh consideration.

If Djarren was bound, practical benefit applies: Thé had reason to doubt completion, promised more, and gained Loth within the five days, which damages could never secure. Santow J counts her cost, and the fee ‘may end up costing her more than she will earn’; yet her ‘online reviews and ratings’ made finishing worth more to her than any likely remedy.[229] The contest is unfair pressure.[230] Unlike the promisor in Williams v Roffey, whose own surveyor persuaded it to pay a bonus,[231] Thé faced a demand, which Glidewell LJ thought might be duress where a subcontractor ‘declines to continue’.[232] Djarren’s ‘really challenging work’, for a cat that ‘would certainly be hard to miss’, cannot ‘justify a demand for re-negotiation backed by unfair pressure’.[233] Yet hardship bears on the ‘proportionality of any pressure’, and his was slight: no express threat, $50 a day more, and Thé agreed after ‘much thought’.[234] A concession so given ‘supports an inference, though by no means conclusively’ of real consideration.[235]

On balance, the increase likely binds. Further information is needed on whether the omitted clauses bound him to finish; if so, it turns on unfair pressure and is finely balanced.

C. Investigation expenses

Thé’s strongest counter, echoing ‘Your terms seem a bit vague’, is that ‘any investigation expenses claimed’ leaves a vital matter to Djarren, so there is ‘no concluded bargain’, as Gibbs J suggested obiter, noting Cussen J drew no distinction where the promisee decides.[236] Yet a cost concept is certain however wide the disagreement over what it covers,[237] and Gibbs J added, tentatively, ‘Perhaps it may be different’ where only subsidiary matters are left to one party.[238] ‘Claimed’ lets Djarren choose which expenses to claim, not what counts as one, and Karga, the clause (l) arbitrator, can settle the boundary, though arbitration cannot save meaningless words.[239] The carrier ‘he bought for this very purpose’ is likely recoverable and the flashlight that found Loth arguably so, though he ‘lost his previous one’; the raincoat and lunch are personal, likely outside the term.

Djarren therefore likely recovers $250 (three days at $50, one at $100), or $200 if the increase fails, less $50 if the first day is unpaid, plus the carrier and possibly the flashlight.

II. DJARREN’S CLAIM AGAINST IGII

A. Acceptance and consideration

Igii’s poster is an offer binding Igii to anyone who, ‘before it is retracted, performs the condition’.[240] Igii’s main defence is Djarren’s own thought, ‘two fees for no extra work’: he was searching for Loth and found Moff beside it, so the reward induced nothing. Yet anyone ‘knowing of the offer who performs its conditions establishes prima facie an acceptance’, and because Igii dispensed with notice, that uncommunicated thought is admissible to show what induced him.[241] The pocketed poster, the carriers ‘he bought for this very purpose’ and the prescribed text confirm the inference.

Igii’s stronger point is that the poster pays for ‘the return’, and performing some conditions gives no right to the reward ‘until he has completely performed them all’.[242] Yet the poster does not require the finder to return Moff personally, so Greg’s return likely completed Djarren’s performance.

Igii may add that Djarren, already paid by Thé to search, gave ‘no extra work’. Yet his duty to Thé covered Loth, not Moff. Even a duty owed to a third party can support a promise, as in Pao On, which Glidewell LJ described as a promise to perform an obligation ‘owed to B, in return for a promise of payment by C’.[243]

B. Intention

Igii next relies on ‘this was always just a social, community thing’, and Djarren bears the onus.[244] Yet the test is ‘not a search for the uncommunicated subjective motives’.[245] Igii spoke only after performance, while the poster, headed ‘!!Reward!!’ between dollar signs, invited strangers ‘to claim reward’. Intention is therefore likely, though the sum is unnamed.

C. Certainty

Igii’s strongest defence is that ‘Big reward’ names no sum, so the promise is ‘simply too vague and uncertain’.[246] Read ‘as the public would understand it’,[247] the dollar signs answer ‘the reward isn’t money’. Kirby P would fill the amount from ‘a readily ascertainable external standard which is proved’,[248] but none is proved here. Further information is needed on customary lost-pet rewards; without a provable standard, the claim likely fails for uncertainty or, on McHugh JA’s alternative view, yields nominal damages.[249]

Djarren therefore likely has a reward contract but may recover little.

PART 2: GREG

III. GREG’S CLAIM AGAINST THÉ

Greg’s best case is that he became a party: Djarren’s email copied him with ‘I’ll need your help with this one’, he replied to all with a thumbs-up, and Thé sent her photo to both men. Clause (j) then promises to pay ‘the investigator(s)’, unlike Coulls, where there was ‘no express promise by the company to pay royalties to the wife’.[250] Alternatively, Djarren contracted as his agent, having enlisted him before sending the terms.

Yet party status is ‘a question to be resolved upon a consideration of the written instrument itself’.[251] The terms are Djarren’s standard form, their ‘investigator(s)’ names no one, and they came by an email not said to be copied to Greg, whose thumbs-up answered Djarren, not Thé. Agency fails too: Lord Reid’s test requires the contract to show Djarren contracting as Greg’s agent,[252] yet Djarren dealt in his own name from the first call.

‘Claim it if you can’ does not help. If ‘it’ means the job, Greg gains nothing against Thé; if it means the fee, it resembles the testator’s ‘authorise’ in Coulls, a mandate rather than a promise to Greg,[253] and words that permit rather than transfer preclude an equitable assignment.[254]

Even as a joint promisee, on Taylor and Owen JJ’s conditional view, Greg could recover though Djarren gave the consideration, but ‘an action to recover must have been brought by both promisees’.[255] Barwick CJ and Windeyer J, dissenting, would let Greg join an unwilling Djarren as defendant, and Barwick CJ would give judgment for both.[256]

Greg therefore likely has no claim of his own, except jointly with Djarren.

IV. GREG’S CLAIM AGAINST IGII

Greg’s best case is that the poster rewards ‘the return’ and treats the text only as the way ‘to claim reward’. He alone returned Moff, knowing of the reward, since he asked ‘for payment of the reward’, which prima facie establishes acceptance.[257] Yet he neither found Moff nor made the prescribed claim, and he delivered with ‘Igii’s details’ after Djarren handed Moff over, likely completing Djarren’s acceptance rather than acting ‘upon its faith’ for himself.[258] Igii’s defences also apply, so Greg’s claim likely fails.

V. GREG’S CLAIM AGAINST DJARREN

Read objectively, Greg’s thumbs-up likely accepted Djarren’s request for help, as an emoji did in South West Terminal, where past dealings, absent here, also counted.[259] Services under a commercial agreement are ordinarily ‘not intended to be performed gratuitously’,[260] but if ‘Claim it if you can’ meant the fee, Greg’s pay was whatever he could collect from Thé. Further information is needed on whether they share fees; if not, his claim likely fails.

2024 T1: Carol Danvers, Nick, Monica and Kamala: holograms

First draft 80.5/100; final re-marked cold at 85.5/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 80.5/100; main losses were the advisee’s own Part 2 case cut to a clause, a dissent’s remedy passage misstated again, and a textbook gloss and a timing rule presented as law.

-   RECURRED despite the 2019_T3 lesson: Windeyer J’s damages view in Coulls (501 to 503) was again narrowed to the creditor case and treated as reaching the third party, and ‘cannot compel’ was stated without his hedge. Stronger rule: before writing any sentence on a promisee’s remedies, open W4 C4A Casebook pp 334 to 336 and copy into plan.md, verbatim, his four holdings with their labels: (1) he rejects the nominal-damages view (‘I do not see why’, 501; ‘(I do not think it is)’, 503); (2) three substantial-loss examples (creditor; someone the promisee feels a duty to reward or recompense; an activity the promisee wishes to promote); (3) the damages are the promisee’s own (‘why should A hold for C the proceeds’, 502); (4) ‘not persuaded’ that C could force A to sue, ‘always on the assumptions that there was no trust and that the transaction was as between A and C wholly gratuitous’ (502), with specific performance only ‘as at present advised’ (503). Every sentence on the point must be checked against that block, and the word ‘dissenting’ must appear.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2020_T3, 2023_T3): the advisee’s case in Part 2 got 46 words against Carol’s 200. Rule: when a Part’s advisee is a third party, list every route by which she could be a party or give consideration herself (joint promisee; offer accepted by her own act on an implied request, Australian Woollen Mills 458 and Clarke 244; a duty owed to a third party, Pao On as the textbook and Glidewell LJ report it; the dissent’s reading of the instrument), write them as her paragraph first, then answer each on the ground the promise was bargained for.
-   A textbook’s framing sentence beside a quoted judicial illustration is not the judge’s words (‘a party who is not a joint promisee’ before the Trident gate example). Rule: when quoting an illustration known only through the textbook, describe it by its own facts (A, B, C, the act), name the case and judges in the body, cite ‘quoted in’ the textbook, and put no textbook sentence in the judges’ mouths.
-   A test’s elements do not carry an unstated timing rule (‘the benefit is judged when Carol promised’). Rule: a proposition about when or from whose view a test is applied needs words in the passage that say so; otherwise reason from the element’s own words (Santow J’s ‘obtains in practice’, ‘capable of being viewed by B’).
-   A message classification must follow the majority’s analysis, not a both-ways formula that only the minority’s approach supports (Butler: a reply adding a stipulation is a counter-offer on Lawton and Bridge LJJ’s analysis). Rule: classify each reply once, on the ratio, and cite the judge who applied it.
-   Inferred facts about who did the work: the problem never said Kamala did it. Rule: when a route depends on a performance the narrator only implies, write ‘if, as planned, …’.
-   RECURRED (every run): the revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,783 words. What paid this time: removing every second authority for one proposition, the agency clause that could not be reasoned in the space, quotations replaced by paraphrase where the citation carries the point, and facts quoted twice.
-   Verifier: a short-form textbook reference (‘Paterson and Robertson (n 32)’) in a ‘quoted in’ citation gives a CHECK CASE/JUDGE although the full form passes; keep the AGLC short form and record the CHECK as expected.

Final answer

Word count: 1,497

PART 1: CAROL DANVERS

I. CAROL’S CLAIM AGAINST NICK

A. Formation at the meeting

Nick’s ‘$100,000’ rejected Carol’s opening fee, and her ‘$200,000’ subject to ‘satisfactory materials’ was a counter-offer.[261] Nick’s ‘Okay but I don’t do anything unless it’s in writing’ added a stipulation, so on the majority’s analysis it too was a counter-offer, which Carol’s ‘Great’ accepted.[262] Under Masters v Cameron, a contract binds if the writing only restates settled terms (the first class) or conditions performance (the second), but not if the parties intend no ‘concluded bargain at all’ until it is signed (the third).[263] Intention to create legal relations, ordinarily present in business, turns on the same stipulation.[264]

For Carol, firstly, as the Court said in Masters, ‘All the essentials of a contract are there’: the holograms, price, deadline and her condition were settled, and Nick said ‘Okay’.[265] Secondly, Nick used no formula such as ‘subject to contract’, so ‘it becomes a question of construction’,[266] and a stipulation for a formal agreement ‘does not, by itself, show that they continue merely in negotiation’.[267] Thirdly, ‘I don’t do anything’ speaks of Nick’s performance, fitting the second class, where, as Rich and Starke JJ held in Niesmann, payment due on signing made signing ‘a condition of the obligation to pay’.[268] Fourthly, Carol promptly engaged Monica, and post-contractual conduct is admissible on formation.[269]

The strongest counter is that writing ‘for my lawyers to look at’ is of similar import to ‘subject to contract’, words which ‘prima facie create an overriding condition’.[270] Masters itself turned on solicitors who could add ‘whatever else the solicitors may fairly consider appropriate’.[271] Carol’s ‘standard contract’ may likewise add terms, and Nick’s silence and resort to Dar-Benn point against a contract. Godecke v Kirwan, where a vendor’s solicitors could add terms yet a contract bound, is distinguishable: Walsh J (Mason J agreeing) confined them to consistent terms reasonable ‘in an objective sense’, whereas nothing confined Nick’s lawyers.[272] Carol’s conduct cannot displace ‘the intention disclosed by the language the parties have employed’.[273]

On balance, the better view is the third class: no contract was made, and Nick, who signed nothing, could ‘withdraw at any time until the formal document is signed’.[274] The second class remains arguable; on that view, Nick was bound to join in executing the writing and pay $200,000, so his ‘Good bye!’ was a refusal to perform.[275]

B. The materials condition

If a contract was formed, Nick may call ‘satisfactory’ uncertain or illusory, as a promisor with ‘a discretion or option as to whether he will carry out’ a promise makes no contract.[276] Yet in Meehan v Jones all four judges upheld a condition of finance satisfactory to the purchaser.[277] Gibbs CJ found ‘nothing uncertain’ in terms satisfying the protected party, here Carol, and held that a discretion over fulfilling a condition, not over performance, is not illusory.[278] For Mason J (Wilson J agreeing), the purchaser’s judgment ‘is not an unfettered discretion’ but must be honest, or honest and reasonable, a choice he left undecided.[279] Murphy J added that the protected party may waive it.[280] Since the holograms were built, Carol found satisfactory materials or waived the condition.

C. The emailed contract

On the third class, Carol’s emailed ‘standard contract’ was at most an offer, and silent acceptance is ‘generally insufficient’.[281] Empirnall, where a developer that never signed was bound, turned on ‘taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms’, and Nick took nothing.[282] An email to an address found on LinkedIn is probably not received until Nick ‘has become aware’ that it was sent there.[283]

Further information is needed on whether Nick contracted for EPEE, since the parties must be identified; if so, Carol’s claim may lie against EPEE.[284] Carol therefore likely has no contractual claim and bears the $100,000 paid to Monica, or $150,000 if Monica enforces the extra $50,000; on the second class, she sues on a $200,000 contract.

PART 2: KAMALA KHAN

II. KAMALA’S CLAIM AGAINST CAROL

A. Party status

Only a party may sue on a contract, as even the dissenting judges in Coulls accepted.[285] Carol’s promise of the extra $50,000 answered Monica’s proposal and was payable ‘once I deliver the holograms’.

For Kamala, firstly, a promise made in her presence about her work and pay may have been made to her and Monica jointly, resting on consideration ‘given on behalf of them all’, as Windeyer J (dissenting) held and Taylor and Owen JJ conditionally accepted.[286] Secondly, by agreeing that Monica would ‘bring in Kamala to get it done’, Carol arguably requested Kamala’s work by implication.[287] If, as planned, Kamala did the work knowing of the promise, that ‘establishes prima facie an acceptance’, and her work would be consideration even if she owed it to Monica, a third party.[288] Thirdly, Windeyer J read the promisee’s ‘I authorise’ in Coulls as ‘equivalent to a requirement’, so ‘You can pay’ could make payment to Kamala a term.[289]

Decisively, however, Carol and Monica met Kamala’s ‘we’re a team!’ with ‘We’re not a team’ before Carol agreed, a reply that objectively excluded Kamala from the bargain.[290] Carol’s promise was offered for Monica’s delivery, not as the price of Kamala’s work, which was Monica’s means of performing, and a request alone does not establish a contract.[291] Kamala is then like C in Mason CJ and Wilson J’s illustration in Trident: where A promises B and C to pay C if B erects a gate, C, though a party, is ‘a stranger to the consideration’.[292] Windeyer J’s reading of ‘authorise’ was a dissent; the majority treated it as a mandate.[293] Carol’s ‘I don’t even know who you are’ is immaterial. Kamala therefore very likely cannot herself sue Carol.

B. Consideration for the extra $50,000

Between Carol and Monica, intention to create legal relations is likely despite the family tie: presumptions are of doubtful utility, Monica is ‘an engineer who specialises in holography’, and Carol paid her from business funds.[294] If their original deal was not contractual, Monica owed no existing duty, but the same family facts would then undermine the $50,000 promise.

On every route through Monica, Carol’s defence is that promising to perform an existing contractual duty to the promisee is no consideration.[295] Monica may answer that the $100,000 bought only the act of ‘developing the two holograms’, so that, unlike the crew in Stilk, she was ‘at liberty to quit’.[296] Yet her ‘I can’t complete the work in time for the current fee’ likely treats timely completion as her undertaking.

The stronger answer is practical benefit, as Musumeci v Winadell recast Williams v Roffey.[297] Monica’s words gave Carol reason to doubt completion, and by promising more Carol obtained the holograms on time and obviated the risk that Nick would sue her, as Roffey sought to avoid a penalty for delay.[298] Monica’s performance was ‘capable of being viewed’ by Carol as worth more than any likely remedy against her.[299] If Nick was never bound, the feared suit was illusory, but Carol still obtained in practice the timely holograms any deal with Nick required.

The strongest counter is element (v), Santow J’s fifth condition, which excludes a promise induced by ‘unfair pressure’.[300] Monica resembles Glidewell LJ’s subcontractor who ‘declines to continue’ unless paid more and may thereby take unfair advantage.[301] Unlike Roffey, whose own surveyor persuaded it to pay, Monica initiated the increase a week before delivery, and Carol agreed only after ‘some consternation’.[302] Yet Monica, whose task proved ‘even more complicated to create than she expected’, stated an inability and offered a solution. Unforeseen difficulty does not ‘justify a demand for re-negotiation backed by unfair pressure’, but may influence fairness through the proportionality of any pressure.[303] On balance, practical benefit likely supplies consideration, though element (v) is finely balanced.

C. Enforcement through Monica

On Deane J’s view alone in Trident, a trust intention ‘should be inferred if it clearly appears’ that the promisee intended the third party to be entitled to insist on performance, and if trust is the appropriate mechanism.[304] ‘You can pay’ reads, like Arthur Coulls’s ‘authorise’, as Monica’s revocable direction, not Kamala’s right to insist, so a trust is unlikely.[305]

Otherwise, Monica may sue. Windeyer J, dissenting, would, ‘as at present advised’, order a promisor to perform a promise to pay a third person, here Kamala.[306] He also rejected the view that the promisee’s damages are only nominal, giving examples such as a third party she owes or feels bound to recompense, but those damages, which could be ‘less, or more’ than $50,000, would be Monica’s own.[307] Assuming no trust and a wholly gratuitous arrangement, he was ‘not persuaded’ that the third party could force the promisee to sue.[308] A trust or Monica’s suit could thus yield Kamala $50,000.

III. KAMALA’S CLAIM AGAINST MONICA

Further information is needed on whether Monica promised to pay Kamala for the work; if so, Kamala can likely recover the promised sum.[309] If Kamala, who ‘has always dreamed of working with’ Carol, helped without any promise, she has no claim.

2026 T1: Advanced Technology, Tim, Helen and Smarty

First draft 82/100; final re-marked cold at 84/100.

What the first draft got wrong

Draft v1 marked 82/100; main losses were an invented fact used to reconcile the Parts, a case cited for its test against the advisee when its holding favoured the advisee, a speculative route in place of the planted one, and recurring AGLC slips.

-   A reconciling sentence must rest on quoted facts. v1 made an internal ‘both directors must agree’ rule bite in Part (b) by saying Thomas ‘was absent’, which the problem never says. Rule: when a rule decides one Part one way and another Part the other, decide both on one doctrinal footing (here the objective test, Ermogenous [25], plus privity’s burden side) and point to the quoted fact that differs between the Parts; never supply the differing fact.
-   When you cite a case for a strict test, state whether the court found it met and on what facts. v1 gave Tim Ipp AJA’s ‘necessarily’ test from Brambles and omitted that the majority found it met by an offeree that protested and then took indivisible benefits (197), the Company’s closest analogy. Rule: for every test quoted, write one line on the result and on which side of our facts that result lies.
-   On an existing-duty point, look first in the parties’ own words for completion and a separately priced category (‘After a full testing round’, ‘maintenance/repair work … standard hourly rate’) before any cause the problem does not state; v1 built fresh consideration on an unplanted ‘data beyond scope’ cause. Then compare who proposed the extra payment: in Roffey and Musumeci the payer offered it, so a payee’s demand weakens practical benefit (Santow J 744, ‘extended by B, without extortion’).
-   State statutory conditions in full and say what they do not prove: s 13A receipt needs a designated address or awareness, and fixes only the time of receipt, not knowledge of the terms.
-   Do not truncate a quotation before the words that confine it (‘of a contract of carriage or bailment’), and put the footnote straight after the quoted words when the rest of the sentence is your own inference (v1 footnoted ‘goes to consideration, not assent’ to McHugh JA).
-   A promisee who paid an outlay gets her own route first (request; Pao On’s ‘was to be remunerated’; Roscorla’s ‘implied by law’) before the condition that defeats it; a planted ‘on your behalf’ gets a one-line agency flag.
-   RECURRED (2023_T3 ‘Perhaps’; 2020_T3 judge named for a whole-court judgment, Roscorla; 2022_T3 and 2024_T1 unmarked dissent, Beaton). Rule: before the verifier, run a three-question footnote pass on every citation: does the passage open or contain ‘Perhaps’, ‘But’ or ‘though’ (quote the hedge); is it a judgment of the whole Court or Board (no judge); is the judge dissenting (write ‘dissenting’ in the footnote as well as the body).
-   RECURRED (every run): the revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,823. What paid: cutting a second illustration of the same point (Glidewell LJ’s subcontractor), a roll call (McPherson J and Abbott v Lance), an unplanted further-information line, and a sentence that only restated a footnoted characterisation; then splitting four sentences over 45 words.

Final answer

Word count: 1,497

I. PART (A): THE COMPANY’S CLAIM AGAINST TIM

The parties come first:[310] the claimant is the Company, not Thomas or Tiffany, who emailed the offer ‘using the Company’s email account’.

A. The development contract

Tim’s request for a ‘cost estimate’ invited the email’s offer: ‘pleased to offer a fixed fee of $25,000’ is firm, unlike the fatal ‘may be prepared to sell’ in Gibson.[311] Tim’s reply added that the system be ‘ready for use’ before 15 September 2025, so on the classical rules Lawton LJ applied in Butler it was likely a counter-offer.[312] Since the offer invited ‘any further instructions’, it may instead have accepted with an invited instruction; either way the deadline is a term. Thomas’s ‘Let me double check with Tiffany’ withheld assent, but Tiffany’s email seeking the data within two days, to meet the deadline, accepted.

Tim may invoke the Company’s requirement of ‘agreement from both of them’, but the inquiry is objective, ‘not a search for the uncommunicated subjective motives or intentions of the parties’.[313] Objectively both founders assented: the offer came from both, Thomas left only Tiffany’s assent outstanding, she gave it, and both performed. The same inquiry decides Part (b) the other way. Tim’s reference to ‘the initial agreement’ is admissible on formation,[314] and he refuses only ‘the extra amount’, so a $25,000 contract including the deadline is very likely.

Incorporation of the unread standard terms is doubtful. Stephen J’s ticket-case reasoning treats failing to reject after an opportunity to read as acceptance,[315] but the email cited the terms only for the displaced hourly rate, as the Butler reference went only ‘as to the price’.[316] If they charge maintenance hourly, which is further information, and are incorporated, the $3,500 is due under them.

B. Agreement to pay for the repair

Tim’s strongest argument is that he never agreed to pay: he ‘did not read the email properly’, and his reply merely repeated his demand to ‘fix the issues ASAP’. Conduct must be ‘of such a character as necessarily to lead to the inference’ of acceptance,[317] and Empirnall turned on actual ‘knowledge of its terms’,[318] which Tim arguably lacked.

However, the email was received once retrievable at an address Tim designated, or, if not designated, once he was aware of it, as his reply shows;[319] that fixes timing, not knowledge. McHugh JA held that where an offeree able to reject takes the benefit of services in circumstances indicating ‘that they were to be paid for in accordance with the offer’, acceptance may be found.[320] Tim replied to an email saying such work ‘will be charged’, then took a day’s work. In Brambles, Ipp AJA, for the majority, found acceptance where an offeree that had protested took benefits which ‘could not be severed from the obligations proposed’;[321] Tim likewise took a repair offered only on paid terms. In McHugh JA’s analogy, an offeree who has or ought to have knowledge ‘of the terms of a contract of carriage or bailment, is generally bound unless he raises objection’,[322] and Tim objected only once invoiced. The Laurel Race Course owner, who ‘made no reply’, was bound;[323] Tim replied.

On balance, a reasonable bystander would likely read Tim’s reply and conduct as assent,[324] though this is finely balanced, as the reply also fits a repeated claim of right.

C. Consideration for the repair

Tim’s main defence is that ‘the repair work was part of your duties under the initial agreement’. Repairing is no consideration if it was ‘to do no more than the promisor is bound to do’.[325] Tim will say a system ‘ready for use’ for ‘a large group of new clients’ had to work during the carnival, as the Stilk crew ‘had sold all their services till the voyage should be completed’.[326]

The Company’s first answer is fresh consideration. Firstly, ‘After a full testing round, Tim was very happy’: evidence of what was done, not a gloss on meaning, which post-contractual conduct cannot supply.[327] Secondly, the fixed fee bought development, whereas Tiffany priced ‘maintenance/repair work’ separately, so on-site repair was work the Company was ‘at liberty’ to refuse.[328] Thirdly, ‘ready for use’ fixed a date, which was met, and the system ‘operated well initially’. Further information is needed on whether the slowdown came from a defect present on delivery; if so, the repair was owed.

If owed, the Company’s best exception is Mason J’s: performing an existing duty is consideration if given ‘by way of a bona fide compromise of a disputed claim’ after asserting that one is not bound.[329] Like the Wigan purchasers, the Company arguably asserted it need not repair without charge, and that claim, though perhaps wrong, was honest and not frivolous after successful testing.[330]

Practical benefit, from Roffey and adopted in Musumeci at first instance, is weaker. In Roffey the promisor’s own surveyor persuaded it to pay more,[331] and Santow J treated a concession ‘extended by B, without extortion’ as supporting, not conclusively, an inference of consideration;[332] here the payee demanded the extra mid-carnival. Consideration is thus likely, though it matters only if Tim assented under B.

The Company therefore very likely recovers $25,000 and likely $3,500 (seven hours at $500), $28,500 in all, or $25,000 if Tim did not assent, subject to any quality cross-claim outside these materials.

II. PART (B): HELEN’S CLAIM AGAINST TIFFANY

Tiffany said ‘Deal!’, so she is the promisor, to Helen or to ‘Live Together™’ if that is an entity.[333] Her ‘We need to pay you’ may make Thomas a joint promisor, but nothing shows he assented. On Part (a)’s objective inquiry the Company is not bound: Tiffany bargained about her own wedding, not for the Company, and a contract cannot impose obligations on a non-party.[334] Any promise of Smarty binds Tiffany alone.

A. Intention to create legal relations

Tiffany will call this a favour between friends: Helen said ‘I don’t want to charge you!’, and Tiffany later said ‘Thanks for your help’. Helen bears the onus,[335] and the objective inquiry weighs status, relationship and ‘other surrounding circumstances’.[336] Firstly, Helen acted ‘via her own business’, and Tiffany said ‘We need to pay you for this’. Secondly, Helen sought Smarty ‘to assist my business’, a commercial return. Thirdly, she did the requested work, and Mayo J in Todd preferred a reading not leaving such a party subject to ‘no more than the whim of the defendant’.[337] Tiffany’s thanks may serve ‘to explain, but not to contradict’ her assent.[338] Intention is likely, though finely balanced.

B. Bargain and Tiffany’s withdrawal

Helen’s tentative ‘it would be great if’ named Smarty instead of money, and ‘Deal!’ made it firm. Tiffany will say Helen would have helped anyway, so Smarty was a conditional gift, as where in Australian Woollen Mills A is ‘merely announcing’ a gift if B arrives in Sydney.[339] However, Tiffany asked Helen to ‘go ahead with the arrangements’ after offering to pay; a request ‘may often provide a useful test’,[340] and that offer shows the services were bought. Work finalised afterwards was consideration; earlier organising was past.[341]

Tiffany’s best reply is that Helen never did the requested act, booking a $9,000 hotel approved only ‘if our budget allows’. Yet that condition qualified the hotel, not the program, which Helen finalised before Tiffany withdrew, so her ‘I have done my work as agreed’ likely holds. Her withdrawal thus refused performance or came after a completed act. If ‘the arrangements’ ran to the wedding, revocation during performance is contested: Mobil, in alternative reasoning, rejected any universal bar,[342] unlike McHugh JA, dissenting in Beaton.[343] Yet Mobil may imply a promise not to revoke where the offeror knows performance began and the detriment is real, with damages for the lost opportunity.[344]

C. Certainty

Tiffany may say the months are a vital matter left to one party, which Gibbs J, obiter, doubted could bind. Yet he added, ‘Perhaps it may be different’ where all essential terms are agreed and only ‘subsidiary matters’ are left,[345] as the months likely are, with robot, period and year fixed. Nor is it illusory, for Tiffany lacks a promisor’s discretion ‘as to whether he will carry out’ the promise.[346]

D. The booking fee

Helen’s best route is an implied promise to reimburse an outlay Tiffany requested (‘Please go ahead with the arrangements’). An act done at request on an understanding that it ‘was to be remunerated’ can support a promise to pay,[347] and a past act supports a promise ‘such as would be implied by law’.[348] Decisively, however, Tiffany wanted the hotel only ‘if our budget allows’, so she never requested a $9,000 commitment. A discretion over a condition, not performance, is not illusory,[349] and is fettered by honesty, perhaps also reasonableness, which Mason J left undecided;[350] ‘Our business is not going very well’ likely meets either. Any agency question from her payment ‘on your behalf’ lies outside these materials.

Helen therefore likely holds Tiffany alone to three months of Smarty in 2026, but recovers none of the $1,000 and no part of the $9,000 hotel fee.

Full lessons log

Lessons log

Every agent reads this first. Each practice run adds the mistakes it made and the fix, so later runs do not repeat them. Entries are short and concrete. Newest runs at the bottom of each section.

Standing lessons (seeded before the first run)

Law and sources

-   The register (_register/*.md) is the only law the answer may state. If a proposition has no register entry, either find it in the sources and add it to the paper’s register_supp.md with a verbatim quote and pin, or cut it.
-   Count the bench. Say who held what: majority, concurrence, dissent, obiter. Traps already met: Lord Denning MR’s Butler patterns were his alone; Heydon JA’s ‘much to be said’ in Brambles is obiter (Ipp JA, with whom Mason P agreed, is the majority route); Birkett LJ in Boots adopts Lord Goddard CJ; Lord Diplock in Gibson quotes Lord Denning MR to reject him; Coulls joint promisee principle is supported by four judges but is not ratio (Taylor and Owen JJ conditional, obiter at 486); Beaton splits three ways (Kirby P no consideration; Mahoney JA and McHugh JA a promise for an act; result: Kirby P and Mahoney JA dismissed, McHugh JA dissented); Meehan v Jones has no majority on honest versus reasonable; Mobil refused any universal revocation rule and its revocation reasoning is arguably obiter; Ermogenous doubts the utility of presumptions in that context.
-   Never quote the slides or the casebook editors’ notes as law. Cases known only through other sources (Trident, Placer, middle of Pao On, Henthorn, Tallerman, Bressan, Goldsbrough Mort p 56) are cited to their report, pinned only where the materials give a pin, and never given words the materials do not attribute to the judge.
-   Scope: Weeks 1 to 4 only. Topics beyond (promissory estoppel, terms and incorporation in depth, frustration, termination, damages quantum, duress as a vitiating factor, the ACL, agency beyond the privity chapter) get one line flagged as outside scope or as further information. Do not argue them.
-   The Electronic Transactions Act 2000 (NSW) is in the 1B register; use it for email timing questions.

Verifier behaviour (after the fixes of 8 Oct 2026)

-   Run: python3 -I /home/claude/LAWS1150/_tools/verify.py check draft.md -c /home/claude/LAWS1150/_tools/corpus.json --facts question.txt --crops crops -o verify.json. Quotations from the problem pass as PASS (facts).
-   Expected, explained CHECKs (confirm by hand, do not ‘fix’ by changing pins): Pao On has no printed AC pin in the extract; Meehan v Jones Mason J passages pinned 589 (no [589] marker printed; Kirby P in Pace cites 589); Milne v A-G pinned 473 from the casebook lead-in; Henthorn, Bressan and Tallerman as quoted in the casebook commentary at [3.210]; Brambles Heydon JA quoting Lord Wilberforce at 176-7; (fixed 9 Oct: Ipp JA’s words after the misprinted ‘[172]’ in Brambles, from ‘the increase in fees’ onward, are pinned 197, and the verifier maps the misprint); Pao On p 131 economic duress passage. Each register file has the detail.
-   Two quotations separated only by a footnote marker can be merged by the parser: put words between them. A quotation that crosses a printed report-page marker should be split at the marker or pinned as a range. An apostrophe after a letter or digit is not read as an opening mark.
-   Use your own scratch subfolder; never write to a shared r.json.

Citation details settled

-   Brambles: cite Ipp as ‘Ipp AJA’ (Mason P at 155 calls him ‘Ipp AJA’, as does the textbook; the casebook’s ‘IPP JA’ heading is editorial). Footnotes in the 1B register now read (Ipp AJA); body text may say ‘Ipp AJA’.
-   make_docx.py runs pandoc, which converts straight quotation marks and apostrophes to curly ones in the .docx; straight marks in the markdown are fine. Dollar signs are no longer read as maths (fixed 9 Oct). Pandoc can still flip a quotation mark after a possessive like “(k)’s”; always run the verifier on the .docx.
-   The verifier now checks two-word quotations as well, and a quotation found in the problem passes as facts even when the same words appear in a source.

Writing

-   See STYLE.md. No dashes, no double quotes, no contractions, no invented abbreviations, no bullet points, no block quotes, footnotes citation only.

Run lessons

Verifier changes, 9 Oct

-   Footnotes are now matched citation by citation, and an ‘Ibid’ citation takes its case from the citation before it (and drops the earlier pin when it has its own). Short titles in brackets are never read as quotations. These were the causes of several ‘explained’ CHECKs in earlier runs; a CHECK now usually means a real pin or attribution problem. Also fixed: ‘(X J, dissenting)’ labels; ‘quoting’ and ‘quoted in’ citations (each case and its own judge are checked separately); statute footnotes (PASS (statute), confirm the section by hand); quotations that cross a printed page marker or a word split by one (pin the range).

2019_T3

Draft v1 marked 79/100; main losses were one-sided argument on the two most valuable contested points, and three source misreadings.

-   Typography is fact. question.txt drops italics; here they marked pencil on a printed form, which decides the battle of forms and the third party’s status. Read the page images and treat italics, handwriting, strike-through and attachments as planted facts. Then quote only what the image shows: v1 said Bea pencilled the whole heading when only one word was pencilled. Rule: never describe who wrote or added a word without checking the image for exactly which words.
-   Strongest counter, not the easiest one. v1 rebutted a weak counter (a narrow, price-limited dictum) and omitted the opponent’s best (the planted remark plus a broader alternative test). Rule: for each contested issue list every argument for the losing side, pick the one a good opponent would lead with, state it at full strength, then answer it; if a word budget forces a cut, cut the weak counter.
-   No contested issue settled in one flat sentence. Rule: any point worth real money or a whole claim gets ‘likely … though …’ and, where it changes the advice, the figure each way.
-   Meet the other side’s best facts on formation, and keep Parts consistent. v1 used the third party’s signature line to make him a party in Part II while calling it irrelevant to formation in Part I. Rule: when the same facts serve two issues, write the reconciling sentence (eg the offer to one offeree was accepted, the offer to the other was not).
-   Argue even the easy elements both ways in a sentence. Intention on social facts needs the onus, the counter, and the decisive answer (later conduct, Todd v Nicol).
-   Quantify every ‘is X entitled’ question: give the per-unit figure and the totals on each scenario, and say which clause limits the base.
-   Read remedy passages of dissents to the end. v1 turned Windeyer J’s doubt about nominal damages into a rule that damages are nominal unless the promisee owed a debt; he gave several substantial-loss examples and rejected the nominal view. Rule: before stating what a judge ‘would’ award, read the whole passage and the next pages for the judge’s own conclusion and the ‘as at present advised’ or dissent label.
-   Describe a distinguished case’s facts from the judgment, not memory: Meehan’s condition went to the obligation to complete, not to whether the contract bound at all. A test quoted from a case (Trident, Deane J) must keep its form: ‘should be inferred if … and if …’ is sufficient, not necessary, and has two limbs.
-   Pin each footnote to the passage that supports the proposition stated, not only the quoted words (a ‘left open’ proposition needs the page where it is left open).
-   Quote-stitching and length: one quotation from a source per sentence, split at the footnote; no sentence over about 45 words. Absolute constructions (‘X being obiter’) and trailing ‘besides’ read as broken.
-   Do not quote three function words (‘at least where’); paraphrase. Do not put a judge’s words about the case before him into his mouth about your parties (‘on his view a promisor in X’s position …’).
-   Verifier: the false CHECK PIN from a statute year in the .docx is fixed in the tool (8 Oct). The first full rewrite ran to 1,633 words: write it, count with the verifier, then cut low-yield roll calls of judges and repeated facts first.

2020_T3

Draft v1 marked 82/100; main losses were a one-sided treatment of the client’s own claim, dicta applied to the wrong party, and AGLC form.

-   RECURRED, sharpened: one opening sentence for the advisee followed by five factors for the other side is still one-sided.
