Rule: on a claim the advisee brings, give its case a full paragraph built from every planted fact (costing, promotion, a minister’s ‘committing’, the closest case on its side), then answer each point, even when you expect the claim to fail.
-   Where the register maps a point as contested (eg revoking a unilateral offer once performance has begun), work through each layer: the authority each way with its status and who rejected it, then the factor test applied to the facts, then the remedy. Settling it on the decisive fact alone loses most of the marks.
-   Before applying a dictum, check whose position it describes (promisor or promisee, offeror or offeree, payer or payee) and whether your party is in that position. v1 applied ‘a discretion within specified parameters’ (a promisor’s discretion) to a payee’s choice of its own fee.
-   When distinguishing a case or a court’s illustration, rely on the ground the court made decisive; reread the passage. The Woollen Mills Sydney example turns on request, not on benefit to A.
-   When one doctrine appears in two claims (eg the range rule), apply it the same way in both and say why it helps one claimant and not the other (‘up to’ has a ceiling but no floor; ‘$2,000 to $4,000’ has a floor).
-   RECURRED: never let a phrase like ‘like X in Case’ carry a single judge’s view, least of all a dissent’s. Write the judge, his status and his words. No adjective doing legal work (‘uncommunicated’, ‘expressly’, ‘all members’) may go beyond the problem’s own words.
-   RECURRED: a threshold sentence still needs a pinpoint that states the proposition. If the cited paragraph only implies the point, cut the sentence or restate it as the paragraph says it.
-   AGLC: name no judges for a judgment of the whole court or the whole Board (Woollen Mills HC, Mobil, Roscorla, Pao On). Use ‘quoting Case (year) report pin (Judge)’ and ‘citing’; never ‘adopting’ or ‘discussing’, and never a citation inside the judge’s brackets. Put en dashes in footnote pin ranges. Define a short title for every case later named in short form, in the body or by (n x). (The verifier quirk with two (‘Short’) titles in one footnote is fixed in the tool, 8 Oct.)
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2019_T3 ran to 1,633): the first full revision, with every marker addition, ran to 2,036 words. Rule: before revising, set a word budget for each claim (about 36% for the claim worth the most marks) and pay for each addition with a named cut; cut repeated authorities for one point and unplanted further-information lines first.

2021_T3

Draft v1 marked 78.5/100; main losses were a case distinguished on facts it did not have, a rule cited to a case that does not state it, and a multi-party Part analysed without its parties.

-   Check a case’s own facts before distinguishing it. v1 said Mary, unlike the Empirnall offeree, took no benefit she was not already owed; the casebook facts say Empirnall had admitted an oral contract, so the case was Faulkner’s best authority. Rule: before writing ‘unlike X in Case’, read the editors’ facts bracket and the passage the court decided on; if the case’s facts match the other side, present it as the opponent’s best case and distinguish on the ground the court made decisive (here knowledge of the terms, 536).
-   Some basic rules are stated only in the textbook or slides, never in an extracted judgment: revocation must be actually communicated (textbook [3.110], fn to Byrne v Van Tienhoven); a bare promise to hold an offer open is not binding (textbook, Goldsbrough Mort); the postal rule’s probable non-application to email (textbook, Olivaylle); privity’s burden side (textbook [11.60]); the Pao On third-party holding (casebook note, Glidewell LJ, textbook). Rule: before citing a case for a rule, find the rule’s words in that judgment; if only the textbook states it, cite the case the textbook footnotes (report only, no pin, no quoted words) or reason from what the extracted cases do say. Never borrow a case that decides a neighbouring point (v1 used Felthouse, an acceptance case, for revocation).
-   When a Part has three or more organisations or people, first name the parties to each contract and promise (Ermogenous [33]), then run privity both ways and the third-party-duty exception before any existing-duty consideration defence; v1’s ‘which it already owed’ ignored that the duty might be owed to a third party.
-   Where a Part’s conclusion rests on one contested threshold (here a binding oral contract before the documents), give the other branch and its result in two sentences; otherwise the conclusion is unreasoned if the threshold fails.
-   Apply a qualification by its own test, not by the words that explain its rationale. v1 used Mason J’s ‘threatening unscrupulously’ as a bar; the Wigan test is an honest claim, not vexatious or frivolous. Likewise ask the first question of a doctrine before its exceptions (did the event change the existing duty: Stilk ‘at liberty’).
-   RECURRED, sharpened: the advisee’s best argument can lie in its own words (Mary’s ‘If you finish … I will pay’ reads as a unilateral offer). Read the advisee’s own communications for the reading that defeats formation.
-   Bench labels in the register can be wrong: four judges in a joint judgment with a fifth concurring is a majority, not a plurality. Check the bench in the casebook before labelling.
-   RECURRED: the revision with every marker addition ran to 1,882 words. Rule: draft the revision against a 1,450 budget and cut whole low-yield sentences (second authorities, unplanted further-information lines, duplicate quotations of the same fact) before polishing. Verifier: a (‘Short title’) after a pin page where the case name does not appear gives a false CHECK, and a report citation the materials cannot pin (Pao On) gives a lint line; both are expected and explained, not ‘fixed’ with an invented pin.

2022_T1

Draft v1 marked 80.5/100; main losses were a planted doctrine cut as ‘note only’, a test applied with the very evidence it excludes, and misquoted facts.

-   A doctrine whose definition matches a planted phrase must be argued even if the materials hold it only in a casebook note (the fourth Masters class and Sunny’s ‘needs to be further negotiated’). Rule: map every planted phrase to its doctrine before budgeting, and cut weak analysis, never the doctrine the examiner planted.
-   Apply a test by its own evidential limits. v1 proved essentiality under Whitlock from James’s later outburst, though Whitlock (461) excludes extrinsic evidence of importance. Rule: before applying a test, read what the passage says may not be used to satisfy it, and apply it only to what it admits (there, the contract’s terms).
-   Read a party’s words in every legal character they could bear and keep the readings consistent. v1 read ‘we do need to ensure there will be sufficient supply’ only as a promise; as a condition for the buyer it is certain (Meehan’s crude oil condition). Rule: for each disputed clause, state its effect as a promise, as a condition and as no term, and say which reading each Part relies on.
-   Quote the speaker, the whole utterance and the right speaker. v1 gave the narrator’s ‘merely a handful of minor edits’ to Sunny, halved James’s 18 July sentence and cut Nathan’s ‘but we will need to charge an extra A$5,000’. Rule: before quoting, check who says it in the problem and read the full sentence; if the omitted half bears on the issue, quote it or do not quote at all.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2020_T3 decisive ground): a judge’s conclusion about a clause rests on its words (Mason J’s ‘each party’ on ‘null and void’). Rule: before transposing a judge’s result, set the clause he construed beside ours and say whether the operative words match.
-   When a fact names a non-party entity (‘will be the buyer’), run privity with the majority’s holding, not a dissent’s general statement, and reconcile it with the formation finding (who is party on each branch).
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2021_T3 first question): on an existing-duty point, exhaust the promisee’s routes around the duty from the problem’s own words (‘estimated’, ‘will be prepared’, a variation agreed in the same call as acceptance) before any exception; and when you characterise a deal as unilateral, reconcile each element of the test that speaks of a promise.
-   RECURRED: the revision with every accepted finding ran to 1,838 words; per-section estimates ran about 10% under the verifier’s count. Rule: draft each section at 90% of its budget and run the verifier after each section, not at the end.

2022_T3

Draft v1 marked 84/100; main losses were the opponent’s best formality rule left unstated, doctrinal branches not followed into later Parts, and attribution in footnotes.

-   Classify every message in a chain (offer, acceptance, counter-offer, inquiry) before any formality doctrine: v1 went straight to Masters although ‘Yes’ plus a new term is a counter-offer that the next message accepted, which is what puts the stipulation inside the bargain.
-   When you rely on a rule’s fallback (construction where words are not express), first state the presumption the opponent invokes in the source’s own words and pin (here Masters 363, ‘of similar import’ words prima facie create an overriding condition), then answer it. Asserting the fallback alone answers a weaker argument than the one the examiner planted.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2021_T3 branches): follow each branch of a multi-class doctrine into every later Part. v1 conceded class 2 in a clause (no waiver, no mutual duty to bring the document into existence) and never noticed that on class 3 a later ‘agreement’ forms the contract, so the existing-duty problem in the next Part disappears. Write one sentence per branch saying what it does to each later issue.
-   Markers can reintroduce old errors: the examiner proposed proving essentiality from negotiation history, which Whitlock 461 excludes (2022_T1). Rule: test every marker-proposed application against the passage’s own evidential limits before accepting it; negotiation facts go to formation, not to essentiality.
-   Tie each factual inference to the fact that proves it and check the other side’s words before characterising an act: knowledge came from ‘then remembers’, not ‘subscribes’; ‘all day’ and the auditor’s ‘unprompted’ were wrong (JammyJam had told Ninja to ‘just log in’). Adjectives about conduct (‘unprompted’, ‘uncommunicated’, ‘all day’) need a quoted fact.
-   RECURRED (2020_T3): a dissenting judge’s words were credited to ‘four judges’. When several judges share a principle in different words, quote one, name him and his status in the body, and mark dissents in the footnote.
-   Verifier (the marker-crossing, dissent-label and quoting issues are fixed in the tool, 9 Oct). Nested double marks trip the lint, so end a quotation before an inner quoted word (‘play for at least 20 minutes’ per war).
-   RECURRED (every run): the revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,813 words. Rule: before rewriting, list each accepted addition with its word cost beside a named cut; the cuts that paid here were the threshold sentence, the weakest third factor of a walk, facts quoted twice, and a second authority for one point.

2023_T3

Draft v1 marked 80/100; main losses were three passages applied beyond what they say (a joinder rule read as a bar, a notice illustration read as deciding who performed, a hedged dictum stated as settled), the advisee’s own formation case left unargued, and facts added by inference.

-   A supplement entry can launder a misreading: register_supp S1 recorded Bowen LJ’s lost dog sentence for ‘finding is the essence’, but the passage answers whether notice of acceptance is needed and its own offer paid for bringing the dog to a place. Rule: before adding or using a passage, write down the question the court was answering in that paragraph and compare any hypothetical’s facts with ours; use it only for that question.
-   Words like ‘must have been brought by both’ or ‘would fail if brought by one alone’ are joinder rules, not bars. Rule: read the same and adjacent pages for what happens when the co-party will not join (joined as defendant, judgment for both) and conclude on that remedy, never ‘no claim’.
-   Hedges are part of the proposition. Quoting ‘not justify a demand … backed by unfair pressure’ without the next sentence (‘But … proportionality’), ‘without extortion’ without ‘though by no means conclusively’, and Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps’ as ‘excepted’ each overstated the law for the opponent. Rule: for every quotation read the next sentence; if it opens ‘But’, ‘However’ or ‘Perhaps’, or the source hedges, quote or state the hedge.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2022_T3 inferences): ‘on Djarren’s instructions’, ‘the writing never came’ (it came on day one) and Roffey ‘offered the extra money’ (its surveyor persuaded it) were all inferences. Rule: list every verb of who did, said, instructed or proposed what, in the problem and in each distinguished case, and match each to a quoted line before drafting.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2020_T3): on a threshold that goes against the advisee, write the advisee’s case first with its authority (here Empirnall 535, photo as acceptance by conduct) and answer it with the opponent’s best planted fact (the requested writing added new terms); then follow both branches to the money.
-   One planted phrase can test two doctrines (‘two fees for no extra work’: evidence rebutting reliance, and consideration from someone already paid by a third party). Rule: map each planted phrase to every doctrine it could serve, and read ambiguous references (‘Claim it if you can’: the job or the fee) in each meaning before building on one.
-   Docx: pandoc rendered ‘$$ !!Reward!! $$’ as display maths and read the apostrophe in “(k)’s” as an opening mark, flipping the next quotation; the markdown verifier could not see either. Rule: no paired dollar signs in the body and no possessive after a closing bracket; after make_docx.py, scan word/document.xml for oMath and for reversed marks, and rerun the verifier on the .docx.
-   RECURRED (every run): the first revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,815 words. The cuts that paid were a second pin for the same test, a second authority for the same answer (Isaacs ACJ on motive, Woolworths on adequacy), facts already stated in the next Part, and quoting a counter-offer’s terms twice; paraphrasing a lettered formula (A and B) instead of quoting it saved words and bracket substitutions.

2024_T1

Draft v1 marked 80.5/100; main losses were the advisee’s own Part 2 case cut to a clause, a dissent’s remedy passage misstated again, and a textbook gloss and a timing rule presented as law.

-   RECURRED despite the 2019_T3 lesson: Windeyer J’s damages view in Coulls (501 to 503) was again narrowed to the creditor case and treated as reaching the third party, and ‘cannot compel’ was stated without his hedge. Stronger rule: before writing any sentence on a promisee’s remedies, open W4 C4A Casebook pp 334 to 336 and copy into plan.md, verbatim, his four holdings with their labels: (1) he rejects the nominal-damages view (‘I do not see why’, 501; ‘(I do not think it is)’, 503); (2) three substantial-loss examples (creditor; someone the promisee feels a duty to reward or recompense; an activity the promisee wishes to promote); (3) the damages are the promisee’s own (‘why should A hold for C the proceeds’, 502); (4) ‘not persuaded’ that C could force A to sue, ‘always on the assumptions that there was no trust and that the transaction was as between A and C wholly gratuitous’ (502), with specific performance only ‘as at present advised’ (503). Every sentence on the point must be checked against that block, and the word ‘dissenting’ must appear.
-   RECURRED, sharpened (2020_T3, 2023_T3): the advisee’s case in Part 2 got 46 words against Carol’s 200. Rule: when a Part’s advisee is a third party, list every route by which she could be a party or give consideration herself (joint promisee; offer accepted by her own act on an implied request, Australian Woollen Mills 458 and Clarke 244; a duty owed to a third party, Pao On as the textbook and Glidewell LJ report it; the dissent’s reading of the instrument), write them as her paragraph first, then answer each on the ground the promise was bargained for.
-   A textbook’s framing sentence beside a quoted judicial illustration is not the judge’s words (‘a party who is not a joint promisee’ before the Trident gate example). Rule: when quoting an illustration known only through the textbook, describe it by its own facts (A, B, C, the act), name the case and judges in the body, cite ‘quoted in’ the textbook, and put no textbook sentence in the judges’ mouths.
-   A test’s elements do not carry an unstated timing rule (‘the benefit is judged when Carol promised’). Rule: a proposition about when or from whose view a test is applied needs words in the passage that say so; otherwise reason from the element’s own words (Santow J’s ‘obtains in practice’, ‘capable of being viewed by B’).
-   A message classification must follow the majority’s analysis, not a both-ways formula that only the minority’s approach supports (Butler: a reply adding a stipulation is a counter-offer on Lawton and Bridge LJJ’s analysis). Rule: classify each reply once, on the ratio, and cite the judge who applied it.
-   Inferred facts about who did the work: the problem never said Kamala did it. Rule: when a route depends on a performance the narrator only implies, write ‘if, as planned, …’.
-   RECURRED (every run): the revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,783 words. What paid this time: removing every second authority for one proposition, the agency clause that could not be reasoned in the space, quotations replaced by paraphrase where the citation carries the point, and facts quoted twice.
-   Verifier: a short-form textbook reference (‘Paterson and Robertson (n 32)’) in a ‘quoted in’ citation gives a CHECK CASE/JUDGE although the full form passes; keep the AGLC short form and record the CHECK as expected.

2026_T1

Draft v1 marked 82/100; main losses were an invented fact used to reconcile the Parts, a case cited for its test against the advisee when its holding favoured the advisee, a speculative route in place of the planted one, and recurring AGLC slips.

-   A reconciling sentence must rest on quoted facts. v1 made an internal ‘both directors must agree’ rule bite in Part (b) by saying Thomas ‘was absent’, which the problem never says. Rule: when a rule decides one Part one way and another Part the other, decide both on one doctrinal footing (here the objective test, Ermogenous [25], plus privity’s burden side) and point to the quoted fact that differs between the Parts; never supply the differing fact.
-   When you cite a case for a strict test, state whether the court found it met and on what facts. v1 gave Tim Ipp AJA’s ‘necessarily’ test from Brambles and omitted that the majority found it met by an offeree that protested and then took indivisible benefits (197), the Company’s closest analogy. Rule: for every test quoted, write one line on the result and on which side of our facts that result lies.
-   On an existing-duty point, look first in the parties’ own words for completion and a separately priced category (‘After a full testing round’, ‘maintenance/repair work … standard hourly rate’) before any cause the problem does not state; v1 built fresh consideration on an unplanted ‘data beyond scope’ cause. Then compare who proposed the extra payment: in Roffey and Musumeci the payer offered it, so a payee’s demand weakens practical benefit (Santow J 744, ‘extended by B, without extortion’).
-   State statutory conditions in full and say what they do not prove: s 13A receipt needs a designated address or awareness, and fixes only the time of receipt, not knowledge of the terms.
-   Do not truncate a quotation before the words that confine it (‘of a contract of carriage or bailment’), and put the footnote straight after the quoted words when the rest of the sentence is your own inference (v1 footnoted ‘goes to consideration, not assent’ to McHugh JA).
-   A promisee who paid an outlay gets her own route first (request; Pao On’s ‘was to be remunerated’; Roscorla’s ‘implied by law’) before the condition that defeats it; a planted ‘on your behalf’ gets a one-line agency flag.
-   RECURRED (2023_T3 ‘Perhaps’; 2020_T3 judge named for a whole-court judgment, Roscorla; 2022_T3 and 2024_T1 unmarked dissent, Beaton). Rule: before the verifier, run a three-question footnote pass on every citation: does the passage open or contain ‘Perhaps’, ‘But’ or ‘though’ (quote the hedge); is it a judgment of the whole Court or Board (no judge); is the judge dissenting (write ‘dissenting’ in the footnote as well as the body).
-   RECURRED (every run): the revision with all accepted findings ran to 1,823. What paid: cutting a second illustration of the same point (Glidewell LJ’s subcontractor), a roll call (McPherson J and Abbott v Lance), an unplanted further-information line, and a sentence that only restated a footnoted characterisation; then splitting four sentences over 45 words.

Cold re-mark of the 2024_T1 and 2026_T1 finals

Finals re-marked cold at 85.5 and 84 (first drafts 80.5 and 82). A fresh tracer still found 3 and 2 certain errors, all in how a passage was used, none in quotation or pin. Hence Stage 5 for the real paper.

-   Read the rest of the sentence you quote: Masters’ ‘All the essentials of a contract are there’ continues ‘but whether there is a contract depends entirely upon …’, and the Court then held no contract. A court’s description of the document it held not binding cannot be quoted for the party who lost.
-   State multi-limb tests whole: Lord Scarman’s Pao On conditions are three (request; understanding that the act ‘was to be remunerated’; payment that ‘must have been legally enforceable had it been promised in advance’). Past-consideration authorities need a later promise; where there is none, the route is an implied promise from the request.
-   Quote the full scope of what a reply referred to (Butler, Lawton LJ at 406: ‘the price and the identity of the machine’, not the small print).
-   Words like ‘held’, ‘mandate’, ‘revocable’, ‘the majority’ must be the source’s: ‘observed’, McTiernan J’s ‘mandate’, Windeyer J’s ‘revocable’.
-   Close each Part with one unambiguous concluding line; a closing sentence that reopens a route the Part rejected costs about 1.5 marks.
-   About 50 quotations in 1,500 words reads as a string of quotations; aim for about 35, paraphrasing where the exact words carry no weight.

## FILE: drive/txt/Rocky - LAWS1150 Mid-Term T3 2026 (INTERIM v2).txt
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Breach, damages and guarantee law lie outside Weeks 1 to 4, and nothing shows Grace promised reimbursement; the ‘legally binding’ Development Agreement pays only ‘if the Project made a profit’, which is unproven.

I. ROCKY v GRACE

A. Offer

Grace’s call ‘proposed that Rocky offer’, an invitation to treat, and bullets 2 and 3, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing. On construction, unlike Gibson’s ‘may be prepared to sell’, ‘I will lend’ and ‘Please confirm agreement’ sought assent.[1] Yet Gibson’s indicative paragraph could read as a firm offer only absent its disclaimer, which ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ may resemble.[2] Bullet 1 is therefore likely an offer in form.

B. Acceptance

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent:[3] Grace’s ‘Confirmed’, sent ‘15 minutes later’, added nothing, so it was no counter-offer and accepted the whole email.

C. Consideration

Consideration is a price for the promise:[4] Rocky’s promise to lend was given for Grace’s promise to repay at ‘5% interest’, arguably implied by ‘Confirmed’. Grace’s promises to AMPL were likely given for its promise of ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’.[5]

D. Intention to create legal relations

Intention is assessed objectively, without presumptions, Rocky bearing the onus; the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours it.[6] Masters, asking whether a document was ‘only a record of terms’,[7] assumed a contemplated formal contract. Where none is stipulated, the question is whether terms ‘should be put into form’ or await ‘a new agreement’ on terms ‘not expressed in detail’.[8] Although ‘Confirmed’ settled amount, date, term and rate, as in Niesmann, where signing conditioned only ‘the obligation to pay’,[9] ‘satisfactory conditions’ left further terms of the loan to Rocky. On balance, the better view is that the parties likely did not intend to be bound, unless those terms were settled ‘this morning’.

E. Certainty

Rocky’s promise is illusory if its performance rests on his ‘unfettered discretion’.[10] Meehan, on ‘satisfactory terms and conditions’, is distinguishable: there the discretion concerned only ‘the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends’.[11] Here the conditions, as construed above, are the loan’s own terms, which an implied duty to judge ‘satisfactory’ honestly cannot supply.[12] In Godecke, Gibbs J, obiter, doubted that terms left ‘to be settled by one of the parties’ bind, ‘Perhaps’ excepting ‘subsidiary matters’, which the loan’s own conditions arguably exceed.[13] The promise is therefore arguably illusory.

F. Privity

Even if the email bound, AMPL was Rocky’s agent only if purporting to act for him, not solely for itself:[14] though ‘Rocky asked’, AMPL lent ‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and took his guarantee, so Rocky lent nothing.

Only a party can enforce a contract, and only if he provided consideration;[15] whether one is a party turns on ‘the written instrument itself’, not signature.[16] Mrs Coulls signed, yet the contract ‘purports expressly’ to be between her husband and the company;[17] likewise AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’ the Loan Agreement. Nothing makes Grace’s promise one to Rocky, so his joint promisee argument fails.[18] Grace’s ‘I never signed anything’ is therefore right, though not for that reason, and the 5 March demand, arguably premised on the 12 months having run, fails.

AMPL, the contracting party, enforces its loan, agency fails and no trust or estoppel appears, so nothing circumvents the privity rule.[19]

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

A. Offer

Pierre’s ‘expected’ proposed nothing Rocky could accept, so it was likely an invitation to treat;[20] Rocky’s ‘if you also promise’ sought a return promise, so he offered a bilateral contract.[21]

B. Acceptance

Pierre ‘agreed’, manifesting assent to Rocky’s offer, so he accepted for whomever he represented.[22] AMPL would say nothing bound until execution. Yet, as Lord Greene MR said of exchanges of contracts, parties are bound when and how they contemplate:[23] nothing required a document or reserved a right to withdraw.[24] The oral bargain, the undertaking for the $10,000, therefore likely bound.

C. Consideration

The $10,000 promise, sought by ‘if you also promise’, priced Rocky’s undertaking,[25] which moved from him as promisee;[26] if Pierre promised, Rocky’s detriment likely suffices, though AMPL benefits.[27]

A promise to perform an existing legal duty is no consideration ‘at least when’ made by a party to a pre-existing contract to the promisee under it.[28] AMPL would say ‘also’ and the clause show a guarantee already given; as in Sundell, a promise to ensure performance already owed is no consideration.[29] Yet no earlier promise binds Rocky: his 27 February request did not itself establish a contract,[30] and the clause was arguably included after the exchange. If Pierre promised, Rocky’s promise to him to perform a duty owed to AMPL, a third party, can be consideration.[31] Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ also exceeds ‘repayment of the Loan’, so, on balance, Rocky likely gave consideration, though an earlier clause would favour AMPL.

D. Intention to create legal relations

No presumption governs cousins; Rocky bears the onus.[32] However, the undertaking resembles a letter of comfort, which in Banque Brussels conditioned the facility,[33] marking the letter as serious, whereas AMPL had already advanced. Yet the undertaking was priced at ‘$10,000’ and given ‘at AMPL’s office’. Intention is therefore likely present on both sides, the price outweighing cousinhood even if Pierre promised.

E. Certainty

Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, measured by the loan’s timetable, is not ‘so obscure’ that no intention can be attributed.[34] AMPL’s promise, depending on Grace’s repayment, not its choice, is not illusory.[35]

F. Privity

Rocky, the promisee and payee ‘to me directly’, gave consideration, so privity does not bar him.[36] The clause ‘included’ most naturally means the guarantee clause, the only one named; even a written $10,000 term would leave him the oral promise.

Who promised turns on the doctrine of agency: whether AMPL consented to Pierre acting for it, and whether he purported to act for it or solely for himself.[37] AMPL, ‘owned and controlled’ by Pierre, likely consented; his purporting to act for it is contested: Rocky asked ‘you’ to ‘also promise’. Yet Pierre spoke ‘at AMPL’s office’ about ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’, and AMPL called under the guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’, arguably his undertaking. On balance, AMPL likely promised, because Pierre spoke throughout about AMPL’s loan, though ‘you’ keeps Pierre arguable.

G. The 12 months

The ‘12 months’ are construed objectively: pre-contractual conduct is admissible only if the words are ambiguous, and post-contractual conduct cannot show meaning.[38] The words are arguably ambiguous: the instrument ‘recorded’ the sum ‘advanced’ on 27 February, the transaction’s ‘genesis’.[39] Although the rate, term and ‘appropriate’ interest appear first from 8 April, the period on balance likely ran from 27 February, though only slightly, the ‘12 months’ attaching to ‘the Loan’ then advanced, unless the agreement dates them otherwise.

H. Condition precedent

The bargain binding at once, ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ conditions AMPL’s obligation, not the contract, which becomes ‘completely binding’ on fulfilment;[40] on 9 March 2025 Grace ‘had not yet repaid’, so nothing was payable. Rocky’s payment on the call would not literally meet words naming Grace, nor commercially: the $10,000 falls due on what his undertaking secured, Grace’s repayment.[41] Rocky would invoke the duty to co-operate, ‘to do everything necessary’ for his benefit.[42] Yet nothing suggests AMPL’s call stops Grace repaying, so AMPL has omitted nothing necessary. His payment therefore likely does not meet the condition.

I. Privity: AMPL’s call

A contract cannot impose an enforceable burden on a non-party:[43] the guarantee clause binds Rocky only if he manifested assent,[44] signature being neither necessary[45] nor decisive.[46] His ‘I will do that’ likely binds him, but to AMPL only if Pierre accepted for it; otherwise AMPL has only the clause.

Rocky promised what Pierre ‘expected’, ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, whereas the clause concerns ‘repayment of the Loan’. He assented to the clause if, with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’, he took the benefit of AMPL’s offer ‘with knowledge of its terms’:[47] his entitlement to the unpaid $10,000 was itself a benefit,[48] and the clause was included, arguably at the meeting he ‘attended’. The guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’ proves he gave one, not that he knew the clause’s words; he likely assented unless he never saw them.

If AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise is its consideration. If Pierre promised, AMPL’s advance was past consideration,[49] sufficing under Pao On only if, besides Rocky’s request, the parties ‘understood that the act was to be remunerated’.[50] Nothing shows that understanding on 27 February, whereas in Pao On it existed ‘at the time of the main agreement’.[51] AMPL would rely instead on entering the Loan Agreement; yet Rocky priced his undertaking at ‘$10,000’,[52] so AMPL arguably gave no consideration.

If the 12 months ran from 27 February, the call was not premature; from 8 April, it was premature as to principal, which only postpones liability. Interest shown paid only to ‘8 February 2025’ makes a March default arguable. If AMPL promised, Rocky likely owes AMPL on Grace’s default and, if he pays, likely loses the $10,000; if Pierre promised, Rocky claims against Pierre and is likely liable to him.

I. ROCKY v GRACE

A. Offer

Grace’s call ‘proposed that Rocky offer’, an invitation to treat; the later bullets, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing. On construction, ‘I will lend’ and ‘Please confirm agreement’, unlike Gibson’s ‘may be prepared to sell’, sought assent.[1] Yet Gibson’s mortgage paragraph might read as a firm offer without its disclaimer,[2] and ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ may be one; intention and certainty decide this. On balance, bullet 1 is likely an offer in form.

B. Acceptance

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent:[3] Grace’s ‘Confirmed’, sent ‘15 minutes later’, added nothing, so it was no counter-offer. Grace therefore accepted the offer as made.

C. Consideration

Consideration is a price for the promise:[4] Rocky’s promise to lend was, in form, given for Grace’s promise to repay at ‘5% interest’, arguably implied by ‘Confirmed’. Grace’s promises to AMPL were likely given for its promise of ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’.[5]

D. Intention to create legal relations

Intention is assessed objectively, presumptions doubted, Rocky bearing the onus; the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours it.[6] Masters, asking whether a preliminary agreement was ‘only a record of terms’,[7] assumed a contemplated formal contract; it applies by analogy. Where none is stipulated, the question is whether terms ‘should be put into form’ or be subject to ‘a new agreement’ on terms ‘not expressed in detail’.[8] As in Niesmann, where signing conditioned only ‘the obligation to pay’,[9] ‘Confirmed’ settled amount, term and rate; yet ‘satisfactory conditions’ left further loan terms to Rocky. On balance, the better view is that the parties likely did not intend to be bound, unless those terms were settled ‘this morning’.

E. Certainty

Rocky’s promise is illusory if its performance rests on his ‘unfettered discretion’.[10] Meehan, on ‘satisfactory terms and conditions’, is distinguishable: there the discretion concerned only ‘the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends’.[11] Amount, term and rate are ‘specified parameters’,[12] and an implied obligation to act honestly, or honestly and reasonably, would confine Rocky;[13] yet the conditions (D) are terms he would set, which could withhold the loan itself. In Godecke, Gibbs J, obiter, doubted that terms left ‘to be settled by one of the parties’ bind, ‘Perhaps’ excepting ‘subsidiary matters’, which conditions deciding whether Rocky lends, not how, arguably exceed.[14] The promise is therefore arguably illusory.

F. Privity

Even if the email bound, AMPL was Rocky’s agent only if it contracted for him, not solely for itself:[15] though ‘Rocky asked’, AMPL lent ‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and took his guarantee, so Rocky lent nothing.

Only a party can enforce a contract, and only if he provided consideration;[16] whether one is a party turns on ‘the written instrument itself’, not signature.[17] Mrs Coulls signed, yet the contract ‘purports expressly’ to be between her husband and the company;[18] likewise AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’ the Loan Agreement. Nothing there makes Grace’s promise one to Rocky, so he is no joint promisee.[19] Grace’s answer is therefore right, though not because he ‘never signed anything’, and the 5 March demand, arguably premised on 27 February (II.G), fails.

AMPL enforcing its loan, agency failing and no trust or estoppel appearing, nothing circumvents the privity rule.[20]

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

A. Offer

What Pierre ‘expected’ proposed nothing Rocky could accept, so it was likely an invitation to treat;[21] Rocky’s reply, ‘if you also promise’, sought a return promise, so he offered a bilateral contract.[22]

B. Acceptance

Pierre ‘agreed’, manifesting assent to Rocky’s offer, so he accepted for whomever he represented.[23] AMPL would say nothing bound until execution; yet, as Lord Greene MR said of exchanges of contracts, parties are bound when and how they contemplate:[24] nothing required a document or reserved a right to withdraw.[25] Both promises therefore likely bind.

C. Consideration

The $10,000 promise, sought by ‘if you also promise’, priced Rocky’s undertaking,[26] which moved from him as promisee;[27] if Pierre promised, Rocky’s detriment likely suffices, though AMPL benefits.[28]

The existing legal duty rule applies ‘at least when’ a party to a pre-existing contract promises the promisee under it no more than it requires.[29] AMPL would say that ‘also’ and its clause show a guarantee already given; as in Sundell, a promise to ensure performance already owed is no consideration.[30] Yet no earlier promise binds Rocky: his 27 February request did not itself establish a contract,[31] and the clause was arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’. If Pierre promised, even a promise to him to perform a duty owed to a third party, AMPL, can be consideration.[32] Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ exceeds ‘repayment of the Loan’, so Rocky likely gave consideration, though an earlier clause would favour AMPL.

D. Intention to create legal relations

No presumption governs cousins; Rocky bears the onus.[33] Against intention, the undertaking resembles a letter of comfort, which in Banque Brussels conditioned the facility it was made ‘to induce’,[34] whereas AMPL had already advanced. Yet the undertaking was priced at ‘$10,000’ and given ‘at AMPL’s office’. Intention is therefore likely present on both sides, the price outweighing cousinhood even if Pierre promised.

Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, measured by the loan’s timetable, is not ‘so obscure’ that no intention can be attributed.[35] AMPL’s promise, depending on Grace’s repayment, not its choice, is not illusory.[36]

F. Privity

Rocky, the promisee and payee ‘to me directly’, gave consideration, so privity does not bar him.[37] The ‘included’ clause most naturally means the guarantee clause named before it; even a written $10,000 term would leave him the oral promise.

Who promised turns on the doctrine of agency: whether Pierre, with AMPL’s authority or ratification, contracted for it, not solely for himself.[38] AMPL, ‘owned and controlled’ by Pierre, likely authorised him; his contracting for it is contested: Rocky asked ‘you’ to ‘also promise’. Yet Pierre spoke ‘at AMPL’s office’ about ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’, and AMPL called under the guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’, arguably his undertaking. On balance, AMPL likely promised, though ‘you’ keeps Pierre’s promise arguable, which proof that he disclaimed acting for AMPL would establish.

G. Construction

The ‘12 months’ are construed objectively: pre-contractual conduct is admissible only if the words are ambiguous, and post-contractual conduct cannot show meaning.[39] The words are arguably ambiguous: the instrument ‘recorded’ the sum ‘advanced’ on 27 February, the transaction’s ‘genesis’.[40] Although the terms appear first on 8 April, the ‘12 months’ attach to ‘the Loan’, whose use Grace had from 27 February, so the period likely ran from then, though narrowly, unless the agreement dates it otherwise.

H. Condition precedent

The bargain binding at once, ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ conditions AMPL’s obligation, not formation;[41] on 9 March Grace ‘had not yet repaid’, so nothing was payable. Read literally or commercially, words naming Grace do not cover Rocky’s payment:[42] the $10,000 falls due on what his undertaking secured, Grace’s repayment. Nor does the duty to co-operate, ‘to do everything necessary’ for Rocky’s benefit, assist:[43] nothing suggests AMPL’s call prevents Grace repaying. Rocky’s payment therefore likely does not meet the condition.

I. Privity: AMPL’s call

Only a contract’s parties are bound by its terms:[44] the guarantee clause binds Rocky only if he manifested assent,[45] signature being neither necessary[46] nor decisive.[47] His ‘I will do that’ likely binds him, but to AMPL only if Pierre accepted for it; otherwise AMPL has only the clause.

Rocky promised what Pierre ‘expected’, ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, whereas the clause concerns ‘repayment of the Loan’. He likely assented to the clause if, with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’, he took the benefit of AMPL’s offer ‘with knowledge of its terms’.[48] If AMPL promised, its $10,000 promise was arguably that benefit.[49] The guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’ proves he gave one, not that he knew the clause’s words; having ‘attended’ the meeting, he likely assented unless he never saw them, but not if Pierre promised, AMPL conferring no benefit.

If AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise is its consideration. If Pierre promised, AMPL’s advance was past consideration,[50] sufficing under Pao On only if, besides Rocky’s request, the parties ‘understood that the act was to be remunerated’.[51] Nothing shows that understanding on 27 February, whereas in Pao On it existed ‘at the time of the main agreement’.[52] AMPL would rely on entering the Loan Agreement, the clause included; yet Rocky priced his undertaking at ‘$10,000’, not that entry,[53] so AMPL likely gave no consideration.

As the 12 months likely ran from 27 February, the call was not premature; if from 8 April, it was premature as to principal. Nothing shows interest paid after ‘8 February 2025’, so a March default is arguable. If AMPL promised, Rocky likely owes AMPL on his undertaking when Grace defaults and, paying, loses the $10,000; if Pierre promised, AMPL’s call, lacking consideration, likely fails, and Rocky claims against Pierre and is likely liable to him.

Nothing shows Grace promised to reimburse Rocky for paying AMPL; the ‘legally binding’ Development Agreement entitles Rocky to repayment ‘if the Project made a profit’, not yet shown.

I. ROCKY v GRACE

A. Offer

Grace’s call ‘proposed that Rocky offer’, an invitation to treat; the email’s later bullets, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing. Gibson’s mortgage paragraph might read as a firm offer without its disclaimer,[1] and ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ may be such a disclaimer; intention and certainty decide this. Yet, on construction, ‘I will lend’ and ‘Please confirm agreement’, unlike Gibson’s ‘may be prepared to sell’, sought assent,[2] so bullet 1 is likely an offer in form.

B. Acceptance

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent:[3] Grace’s ‘Confirmed’, sent ‘15 minutes later’, added nothing, so it was no counter-offer. Grace therefore accepted the offer as made.

C. Consideration

Consideration is a price for the promise:[4] Rocky’s promise to lend was, in form, given for Grace’s promise to repay at ‘5% interest’, arguably implied by ‘Confirmed’. Grace’s promises to AMPL were likely given for its promise of ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’.[5]

D. Intention to create legal relations

Intention is assessed objectively and Rocky bears the onus, presumptions being doubted; the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours intention.[6] Masters, asking whether a preliminary agreement was ‘only a record of terms’,[7] assumed a formal contract, absent here, so it applies by analogy. Where none is stipulated, the question is whether terms ‘should be put into form’ or be subject to ‘a new agreement’ on terms ‘not expressed in detail’.[8] As in Niesmann, where signing conditioned only ‘the obligation to pay’,[9] ‘Confirmed’ settled amount, term and rate; yet ‘satisfactory conditions’, those satisfactory to Rocky as lender, arguably remained to be agreed. On balance, the better view is that the parties likely did not intend to be bound, unless those conditions were settled ‘this morning’.

E. Certainty

Rocky’s promise is illusory if its performance rests on his ‘unfettered discretion’.[10] Meehan, on ‘satisfactory terms and conditions’, is distinguishable: there the discretion concerned only ‘the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends’.[11] Amount, term and rate are ‘specified parameters’,[12] and an implied obligation to act honestly, or honestly and reasonably, would confine Rocky;[13] yet the conditions (D) are terms he would set, which honesty cannot supply. In Godecke, Gibbs J, obiter, doubted that terms left ‘to be settled by one of the parties’ bind, ‘Perhaps’ excepting ‘subsidiary matters’; conditions deciding whether Rocky lends, not how, arguably exceed these.[14] The promise is therefore arguably illusory.

F. Privity

Even if the email bound, AMPL was Rocky’s agent only if it contracted for him, not solely for itself:[15] though ‘Rocky asked’, AMPL lent ‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and took his guarantee, so Rocky lent nothing.

Only a party can enforce a contract, and only if he provided consideration;[16] whether one is a party turns on ‘the written instrument itself’, not signature.[17] Mrs Coulls signed, yet the contract ‘purports expressly’ to be between her husband and the company;[18] likewise AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’ the Loan Agreement. Nothing there makes Grace’s promise one to Rocky, so he is no joint promisee.[19] Grace’s answer is therefore right, though not because he ‘never signed anything’, and the 5 March demand, arguably premised on 27 February (II.G), fails.

AMPL enforces its loan and agency fails; no trust or estoppel appearing, nothing circumvents the privity rule.[20]

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

A. Offer

What Pierre ‘expected’ proposed nothing to accept, so it was likely an invitation to treat;[21] Rocky’s ‘if you also promise’ sought a return promise, offering a bilateral contract.[22]

B. Acceptance

Pierre ‘agreed’, manifesting assent to Rocky’s offer, so he accepted for whomever he represented.[23] AMPL would say nothing bound until execution; yet, as Lord Greene MR said of exchanges of contracts, parties are bound when and how they contemplate:[24] nothing required a document or reserved a right to withdraw.[25] Both promises therefore likely bind.

C. Consideration

The $10,000, sought by ‘if you also promise’, priced Rocky’s undertaking,[26] which moved from him as promisee;[27] if Pierre promised, Rocky’s detriment likely suffices, though AMPL benefits.[28]

The existing legal duty rule applies ‘at least when’ a party to a pre-existing contract promises the promisee under it no more than it requires.[29] AMPL would say that ‘also’ and its clause show a guarantee already given; as in Sundell, a promise to ensure performance already owed is no consideration.[30] Yet no earlier promise binds Rocky: his 27 February request did not itself establish a contract,[31] and the clause was arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’. If Pierre promised, a promise to him to perform a contractual duty owed to a third party, AMPL, can be consideration.[32] Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ exceeds ‘repayment of the Loan’, so Rocky likely gave consideration, though an earlier clause would favour AMPL.

D. Intention to create legal relations

No presumption governs cousins; Rocky bears the onus.[33] Against intention, the undertaking resembles a letter of comfort, which in Banque Brussels conditioned the facility it was made ‘to induce’,[34] whereas AMPL had already advanced. Yet the undertaking was priced at ‘$10,000’ and given ‘at AMPL’s office’. Intention is likely present on both sides, the price outweighing cousinhood even if Pierre promised.

E. Certainty

Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, measured by the Loan’s timetable, is not ‘so obscure’ that no intention can be attributed.[35] AMPL’s promise, depending on Grace’s repayment, is not illusory.[36]

F. Privity

Rocky, the promisee and payee ‘to me directly’, gave consideration, so privity does not bar him.[37] The ‘included’ clause most naturally means the guarantee clause named first; even a written $10,000 term would leave him the oral promise.

Who promised turns on agency: whether Pierre contracted for AMPL, not solely for himself, with its authority or, arguably, ratification.[38] AMPL, ‘owned and controlled’ by Pierre, likely authorised him; his contracting for it is contested: Rocky asked ‘you’ to ‘also promise’. Yet Pierre spoke ‘at AMPL’s office’ about ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’, and AMPL called under the guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’, arguably his undertaking. On balance, AMPL likely promised, though ‘you’ keeps Pierre’s promise arguable, decisively so if he disclaimed acting for AMPL.

G. Construction

The ‘12 months’ are construed objectively: pre-contractual conduct is admissible only if the words are ambiguous, and post-contractual conduct cannot show meaning.[39] The words are arguably ambiguous: the instrument ‘recorded’ the sum ‘advanced’ on 27 February, the transaction’s ‘genesis’.[40] The terms and ‘appropriate monthly repayments’ date from 8 April; yet those payments are post-contractual conduct, and the ‘12 months’ attach to ‘the Loan’, which Grace had from 27 February. The period likely ran from then, though narrowly, unless the agreement dates it otherwise.

H. Condition precedent

The bargain binding immediately, ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ conditions AMPL’s obligation, not formation, the contract becoming ‘completely binding’ on fulfilment;[41] on 9 March Grace ‘had not yet repaid’, so nothing was payable. Read literally or commercially, words naming Grace do not cover Rocky’s payment:[42] the $10,000 falls due on what his undertaking secured, Grace’s repayment. Nor does the duty to co-operate, ‘to do everything necessary’ for Rocky’s benefit, assist:[43] nothing suggests AMPL’s call prevents Grace repaying. Rocky’s payment therefore likely does not meet the condition.

I. Privity: AMPL’s call

Only a contract’s parties are bound by its terms:[44] the guarantee clause binds Rocky only if he manifested assent,[45] signature being neither necessary[46] nor decisive.[47] His ‘I will do that’ likely binds him, but to AMPL only if Pierre accepted for it; otherwise AMPL has only the clause.

Rocky promised what Pierre ‘expected’, ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, whereas the clause concerns ‘repayment of the Loan’. He assented to the clause if, with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’, he took the benefit of AMPL’s offer ‘with knowledge of its terms’.[48] If AMPL promised, its $10,000 promise was arguably that benefit.[49] The guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’ proves he gave one, not that he knew the clause’s words; having ‘attended’ the meeting, he likely assented unless he never saw them.

If AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise is its consideration. If Pierre promised, AMPL’s advance was past consideration,[50] sufficing under Pao On only if, besides Rocky’s request, the parties ‘understood that the act was to be remunerated’.[51] Nothing shows that understanding on 27 February, whereas in Pao On it existed ‘at the time of the main agreement’.[52] AMPL would rely on entering the Loan Agreement; yet Rocky priced his undertaking at ‘$10,000’,[53] so AMPL likely gave no consideration.

As the 12 months likely ran from 27 February, the call was not premature; if they ran from 8 April, it was premature as to principal. Nothing shows interest paid after ‘8 February 2025’, so a March default is arguable, engaging only Rocky’s undertaking. If AMPL promised, Rocky likely owes AMPL on his undertaking when Grace defaults and, if he pays, likely loses the $10,000; if Pierre promised, AMPL’s call, lacking consideration, likely fails, and Rocky claims against, and is likely liable to, Pierre.

I. ROCKY v GRACE

A. Offer

On 5 February Grace’s proposal ‘that Rocky offer’ a loan was an invitation to treat.[1] The 12 February email’s ‘Confirming discussions’ suggests a record; however, its first bullet, ‘I will lend’, fixes amount, date, term and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ invites assent. Unlike Gibson’s ‘may be prepared to sell’,[2] these words show readiness to be bound; ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ goes to intention and certainty. Rocky’s first bullet is therefore likely an offer in form.

B. Acceptance

Grace may say his ‘Confirmed’, echoing ‘Confirming discussions’, confirmed only the record and was not ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’.[3] Yet the reply answered ‘Please confirm agreement’, a request to agree, not to vouch for accuracy, so it objectively signals agreement; adding no term, it was no counter-offer.[4] Grace accordingly likely accepted the first bullet with its qualifier.

C. Consideration

By accepting, Grace impliedly promised repayment at ‘5% interest’, the price of Rocky’s promise,[5] unless that promise was illusory.

D. Intention to create legal relations

Intention, assessed objectively, weighs ‘the status of the parties’:[6] as ‘project developers’, Rocky and Grace dealt commercially, favouring intention. Against it, the qualifier raises the preliminary agreement question; no formal contract being stipulated, it is whether the terms were to be ‘put into form’ or ‘subject to a new agreement’.[7] Amount, date, term and rate being fixed, the qualifier may condition only performance, not agreement, as signing conditioned payment in Niesmann.[8] Yet each party there was impliedly bound to sign,[9] whereas ‘satisfactory’ names no external event and qualifies Rocky’s own promise, so the conditions are likely further loan terms he would set. On balance, the parties likely did not intend to be bound, unless the conditions were settled ‘this morning’.

E. Certainty

Rocky’s promise is illusory if it ‘depends upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor’.[10] Meehan is the counter: there ‘satisfactory’ finance had to be honestly judged; yet Gibbs CJ saved only a discretion over ‘the fulfilment of a condition’, not over performance,[11] and honesty cannot supply further loan terms fixing his performance. Nor does Gibbs J’s obiter ‘Perhaps’ for ‘subsidiary matters’ left to one party assist:[12] these conditions, qualifying ‘I will lend’, decide whether Rocky lends. His promise is therefore arguably illusory, so the email likely binds neither party, sparing Rocky any claim for not lending ‘by 15 February’.

F. Privity

Even if the email bound, Rocky lent under it only if AMPL advanced as his agent, not solely for itself.[13] His 27 February request suggests agency; yet AMPL advanced ‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and later took a guarantee of ‘repayment’, pointless had it lent as his agent. Rocky therefore likely lent nothing.

Rocky’s 5 March demand raises privity: only the parties to a contract can sue on it, and a plaintiff must show consideration provided by himself.[14] Party status turns on ‘the written instrument itself’,[15] which AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’, Grace’s promises there being the price of AMPL’s promise of ‘12 months’ alone. The guarantee clause makes Rocky at most a promisor, not a joint promisee:[16] Grace promised him nothing, not even reimbursement for paying AMPL. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ therefore defeats the demand, though not for his reason, signature being neither necessary[17] nor decisive: Mrs Coulls signed yet was no party.[18]

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

A. Offer

Pierre’s expectation, promising nothing,[19] was likely no offer; Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ sought a return promise, offering a bilateral contract.[20]

B. Acceptance

Pierre ‘agreed’, manifesting assent;[21] as nothing suggests that Rocky’s bargain awaited the Loan Agreement, which was ‘signed by Grace and AMPL’, or that anyone reserved ‘a right to withdraw’ until signing,[22] both promises likely bound at the meeting as one bargain.

C. Consideration

Rocky’s ‘if you also promise’ made his undertaking the price of the $10,000 promise.[23] AMPL may invoke the existing legal duty rule, reading ‘also’ as adding to an earlier guarantee, as in Sundell, where promising to ensure delivery already owed was no consideration.[24] Yet the rule presupposes an existing duty, as under ‘a pre-existing contract’ with the promisee.[25] Nothing shows Rocky owed one: his 27 February request created no contract,[26] and ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included’ suggests the clause followed the bargain. Even if a guarantee bound him first, ensuring ‘all payments’ were prompt exceeds guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’. Rocky therefore likely gave consideration.

D. Intention to create legal relations

Ermogenous doubts the utility of presumptions, so cousinhood raises none; Rocky, asserting the contract, bears the onus.[27] Against intention, his undertaking resembles a letter of comfort and induced no lending, AMPL having already advanced, unlike the letter in Banque Brussels, sought as a condition of the facility.[28] However, business statements ‘appropriately promissory in character’ should be enforced absent a ‘clear indication’ otherwise.[29] Rocky’s ‘I will do that’ was such a statement, priced at ‘$10,000’, so intention, binding him too, is likely present even if Pierre promised, the price outweighing cousinhood.

E. Certainty

Ensuring prompt ‘payments’ is not ‘so obscure’ as to fail,[30] nor is AMPL’s promise, turning on Grace’s repayment, illusory.[31]

F. Privity

Who promised turns on agency: whether Pierre, with AMPL’s authority, contracted for AMPL, not solely for himself.[32] Rocky’s ‘you’ points to Pierre; however, Pierre’s control of AMPL likely gave him authority, and he spoke ‘at AMPL’s office’. AMPL therefore likely promised, unless Pierre said he spoke for himself; either way Rocky, the promisee, gave consideration, so privity is no bar.[33]

G. Condition precedent

Rocky’s ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ conditions payment, not formation: obligations attach ‘immediately’ though a condition is unfulfilled.[34] As Grace ‘had not yet repaid’ on 9 March 2025, nothing is payable. Read commercially, Rocky would say, the term rewards repayment by whoever pays;[35] yet his words name Grace. Nor does AMPL’s duty to co-operate, ‘to do everything necessary’ for his benefit, assist him:[36] nothing suggests its call stops Grace repaying. Decisively, the $10,000 was the price of his ensuring that Grace paid, so if Rocky pays in Grace’s place, he likely loses it.

H. Construction

Whether the call was premature turns on when the Loan’s ‘12 months’ began. Construed objectively, the term admits surrounding circumstances only if ambiguous, and never post-contractual conduct;[37] fixing, as described, no start in an instrument that ‘recorded’ a loan already advanced, it is arguably ambiguous, admitting the advance as ‘the genesis of the transaction’.[38] For 27 February, the period attaches to ‘the Loan’, advanced that day. For 8 April, the Loan Agreement, monthly interest included, was ‘entered into’ that day; yet interest from when its rate was fixed fits equally a repayment period from the advance. The period therefore arguably ran from 27 February, so the call was not premature; if it ran from 8 April, it was, though interest is shown paid only to ‘8 February 2025’.

I. AMPL’s call

AMPL called on ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’, yet only a contract’s parties are bound by its terms:[39] the clause binds Rocky, a non-party, only by assent. AMPL would say he accepted it by conduct: an offeree with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’ who takes an offer’s benefit ‘with knowledge of its terms’ may be held to have accepted it.[40] Rocky, present at the meeting, took the $10,000 promise without objection. Rocky would answer that the $10,000 priced only his oral offer, not the clause’s promise to answer for ‘repayment of the Loan’. However, the clause arguably recorded his side of that bargain, and a party taking a proposal’s benefit may have to ‘make plain’ that he refuses its disadvantages.[41] A reasonable bystander would likely see his silence as assent if, as his presence suggests, he knew the clause’s words; otherwise his undertaking likely binds him to AMPL, if it promised, exposing him for Grace’s default, including any missed March payment, though not to the call as such.

If AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise supplies consideration for the guarantee; if Pierre did, AMPL’s advance was past consideration,[42] counting only if requested and the parties ‘understood that the act was to be remunerated’.[43] Rocky ‘asked’, meeting the first condition, but in Pao On the understanding existed ‘at the time of the main agreement’,[44] whereas Pierre’s expectation first appears on 8 April. AMPL’s fallback is its entry into the Loan Agreement, binding it for 12 months. Yet Rocky’s undertaking was ‘really offered as consideration’ for the $10,000, not for that entry.[45] If Pierre promised, the call therefore arguably fails.

Rocky likely has no claim against Grace, and his $10,000, not yet payable, is likely lost if he pays AMPL. If AMPL promised, as is likely, he is likely liable on its call if he knew the clause’s words and the 12 months ran from 27 February, which he should contest; otherwise he is exposed on his undertaking for Grace’s default. If Pierre promised, the call arguably fails, but his undertaking runs to Pierre, whom he must sue for the $10,000.

Word count: 1,495

I. ROCKY v GRACE

A. Agreement and certainty

The issue is whether the 12 February exchange formed a contract. While new terms remain to be adopted, the parties are still negotiating.[1] A promise leaving performance to the promisor’s discretion is illusory,[2] but not where the discretion relates only to the fulfilment of a condition, which must be assessed honestly, or honestly and reasonably.[3] However, Gibbs J doubted that an agreement leaving further terms, at least on a vital matter, to one party is a concluded contract.[4]

Here, the email settled the amount, date, term and rate, and Grace’s unqualified ‘Confirmed’ would ordinarily accept it. However, Rocky would lend only ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’, which the email does not specify. Grace will argue that these were subsidiary or, as with the finance in Meehan, for Rocky to assess honestly. Yet they identify no subject matter, so they are arguably further loan terms for Rocky alone to settle, not a condition whose fulfilment he would assess.

On balance, a court would likely find that no contract was formed, because whether Rocky lent depended on terms that he alone would settle. Further information is needed on what the conditions were, as Meehan-type conditions would likely bind. That finding protects Rocky, as nothing shows he lent by 15 February, but gives him no claim.

B. Privity

The issue is whether Rocky can enforce the Loan Agreement, as his 5 March demand assumed. Prima facie, only a party can enforce a contract, and a signature alone does not make one: in Coulls, the wife signed, yet was not a party, as the company made no promise to pay her.[5]

Here, Grace promised repayment to AMPL alone, and neither Rocky’s request for the loan nor the guarantee, which makes him at most AMPL’s promisor, makes him Grace’s promisee. Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ therefore reaches the right result. Nor does agency assist, as nothing suggests AMPL purported to lend as Rocky’s agent.[6]

Rocky therefore likely cannot enforce the Loan Agreement and, as the Development Agreement discloses no breach, would likely fail in any claim against Grace.

II. ROCKY v AMPL OR PIERRE

A. Agreement

The issue is whether the 8 April exchange formed a contract, and with whom. AMPL, a company, is bound if Pierre acted as its agent and purported to act for it,[7] and its consent may be implied where it placed him so that a reasonable person would understand him to have its authority.[8]

Here, Rocky offered his promise for a promise to pay him $10,000 ‘directly’, and ‘Pierre agreed’. Pierre ‘owned and controlled’ AMPL, the meeting was at AMPL’s office, AMPL had performed his 27 February agreement the same day, and his expectation concerned payments to AMPL. Against this, Rocky addressed Pierre as ‘you’.

AMPL is therefore likely the promisor, because Pierre spoke as its controller about its loan; Rocky should sue Pierre in the alternative.

B. Intention to create legal relations

The issue is whether the parties intended to create legal relations, which Rocky must prove and which is judged objectively; presumptions, such as those about ‘family arrangements’, are of doubtful utility.[9] Appropriately promissory statements made in the course of business should be enforced absent a clear indication otherwise.[10]

AMPL will rely on Pierre being ‘Rocky’s cousin’, but that is only one circumstance, and the $10,000 was payment for a specific undertaking about a $1,150,000 loan, with nothing indicating otherwise.

A court would therefore likely find intention, because the commercial setting outweighs the family relationship, though less clearly against Pierre personally.

C. Consideration

The issue is whether Rocky’s promise to ensure prompt payment was consideration. Prima facie, a promise to perform an existing duty is not consideration, at least where a party to a pre-existing contract promises the promisee under it no more than it requires.[11] In Sundell, the supplier was already bound to ‘do what was necessary to ensure’ delivery.[12]

AMPL will argue that Rocky, as guarantor, already owed it that duty. Firstly, he promised before the Agreement was signed, so no contract yet bound him. Secondly, if Pierre promised personally, Rocky promised Pierre, and a promise to perform a duty owed to a third party can be consideration.[13] Thirdly, ensuring that Grace made all payments promptly, including monthly interest, differs from guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’. Were the promises identical, practical benefit would not assist, as nothing suggests AMPL had reason to doubt Rocky’s performance.[14]

Rocky’s promise was therefore likely consideration because, unlike the Sundell promise, it was not identical with an existing obligation, even if the guarantee bound him first.

D. Privity

If ‘the clause’ is the $10,000 term, the issue is whether Rocky, like Mrs Coulls, is a stranger to the Agreement. The clause in Coulls merely authorised payment to her,[15] whereas Rocky gave his own promise for AMPL’s promise to pay him ‘directly’. Coulls is therefore distinguishable, and privity is likely no bar.

E. Condition of payment

The issue is when the $10,000 is payable. As with the signing in Niesmann, a stipulation may make an event a condition of the obligation to pay rather than of agreement.[16]

Here, the promise to pay ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ makes repayment such a condition, which may never be fulfilled if Rocky pays under the guarantee, given Grace’s ‘might not pay at all’.

On balance, Rocky would likely hold an enforceable promise of $10,000, payable only if Grace repays.

III. AMPL v ROCKY

A. Agreement

The issue is whether Rocky is bound by the guarantee. Prima facie, a contract ‘signed by Grace and AMPL’ cannot impose obligations on Rocky.[17] Silence is generally insufficient acceptance, but an offeree who takes the benefit of an offer, knowing its terms and with a reasonable opportunity to reject it, may be held to have accepted it.[18]

Rocky’s recorded words promised to ensure payment, not to guarantee it. However, he requested the loan, attended the settling of an Agreement naming him as guarantor, and raised no recorded objection. The guarantee is also described as ‘provided by Rocky’. If ‘the clause’ is the guarantee, it was arguably included as part of his $10,000 bargain; if it is the $10,000 term, Rocky’s benefit was written into that Agreement.

On balance, a court would likely find that Rocky accepted the guarantee by conduct, because he took a benefit tied to the Agreement without recorded objection. Further information is needed on whether he knew of, signed or expressly agreed to the guarantee.

B. Consideration

The issue is whether the guarantee, given after AMPL’s 27 February advance, is supported by consideration. Prima facie, a past act supports no promise beyond what the law implies,[19] unless it was done at the promisor’s request, the parties understood that it was to be remunerated, and the remuneration would have been enforceable if promised in advance.[20] However, consideration need not move to the promisor,[21] and may be a creditor’s forbearance.[22]

Here, ‘Rocky asked’ for the advance, but nothing shows an understanding on 27 February that he would guarantee it. Yet, in the Loan Agreement, AMPL promised Grace 12 months’ credit at 4%, unless the advance was already made on that term. If ‘the clause’ is the guarantee, AMPL also arguably promised Rocky $10,000 for it. Rocky’s two defences therefore conflict: if 8 April created the term, as his timing argument requires, AMPL gave fresh consideration that day.

On balance, the guarantee is likely supported by consideration, because AMPL’s 8 April promises, not the past advance, were given in exchange for it.

C. Certainty and construction

The issue is whether AMPL’s 9 March call was premature, which depends on when ‘the expiry of 12 months’ fell. A term is uncertain only if the court cannot decide which of its possible meanings the parties intended.[23] If a term is ambiguous, mutually known facts showing the genesis of the transaction are admissible to construe it,[24] but post-contractual conduct is not.[25]

Rocky will argue that the Agreement created the term, as nothing shows a term was agreed on 27 February, when ‘Pierre agreed to provide the money to Grace’. AMPL will reply that the loan ‘was recorded as $1,150,000’, so the Agreement recorded money already lent, and that the advance, known to all three, shows the term ran from 27 February. Later conduct, including the interest payments and Rocky’s own 5 March demand, cannot construe the term.

On balance, a court would likely find the term certain, running from 8 April 2024, because the Agreement created the term, and the advance shows only when the money was lent. Likewise, ‘recorded’ describes the amount, not the start of the term. Further information is needed on whether the Agreement tied the term or interest to the advance. If it did, the call was timely, and Rocky likely also breached his promise to ensure prompt payment.

AMPL would therefore likely hold an enforceable guarantee but could not call on it before 8 April 2025, so Rocky should resist the 9 March call.
