Word count: 1,488

I. ROCKY v GRACE

A. Agreement

Whether Rocky’s email was an offer accepted by Grace’s ‘Confirmed’ turns on its true construction, as present promise or future possibility;[1] since the problem records no advance by Rocky, a contract could only oblige him to lend ‘by 15 February’. Rocky’s best point is that ‘Confirming discussions’, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’ mark the email as minutes. Yet ‘I will lend’, unlike Gibson’s ‘may be prepared to sell’,[2] fixed the amount, date, term and rate, and its ‘1 year’ matched Rocky’s 5 February refusal of the ‘long-term loan’ Grace had invited him to offer; ‘Confirmed’ answered ‘Please confirm agreement’.

On balance, Rocky’s promise was likely an offer, because its terms were fixed, though its qualifier decides whether he was bound.

B. Intention to create legal relations

Whether a promise ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ was intended to bind is judged objectively;[3] under Masters, words like ‘subject to contract’ prima facie create an overriding condition, though no formula is decisive[4] and Tasman calls its categories ‘intellectual aids’.[5] Grace’s best point is that co-developers ‘since 2017’ exchanged promissory words and contemplated no formal contract. Masters, however, asks what intention the language discloses, and words leaving conditions to be settled, like the solicitors’ approval there, prima facie disclose none.[6]

Therefore, the better view is that no contract likely formed, because the conditions were left open.

C. Certainty

Even if intention were found, Grace would rely on Meehan, which upheld a sale conditional on finance satisfactory to the purchaser, though Mason J left open whether the purchaser must be honest or also reasonable.[7] However, Meehan is distinguishable: its sale terms were concluded and the satisfaction had an identified object, finance to complete.[8] Rocky’s conditions have no stated object and arguably govern his own lending, a discretion over performance which Gibbs CJ left within the illusory-promise rule; they leave the court ‘at large’, where Mason J said uncertainty would have force.[9] Even on Grace’s reading, Rocky’s duty to lend awaited his honest satisfaction, which nothing shows.[10]

Therefore, the better view is that the promise was likely illusory or uncertain, because its conditions had no stated object.

D. Privity

Rocky’s demand for ‘the principal amount’ succeeds only if the contract between ‘AMPL and Grace’ contains a promise to him.[11] Rocky’s case is that he procured the advance and that signature is neither sufficient nor necessary,[12] so Grace’s ‘I never signed anything with you’ applies the wrong test. Yet Grace is right in result: Rocky’s guarantee does not make him the promisee of Grace’s repayment promise, which runs to AMPL.

Rocky therefore has no claim against Grace.

II. ROCKY v AMPL

A. Agreement

Rocky’s ‘I will do that if you also promise’ answered Pierre’s request; whether ‘Pierre agreed’ concluded a promise for a promise, and with whom, is judged objectively.[13] The clause then included may be the guarantee, the only clause named and so likelier, or a term recording this exchange. The strongest counter is AMPL’s: ‘Pierre agreed’, and on the guarantee reading AMPL’s instrument omits the $10,000. However, the bargain was oral, so that silence matters little; Pierre ‘owned and controlled’ AMPL and, at its office, sought an undertaking protecting its loan, and AMPL had performed his 27 February agreement.

A contract was therefore likely concluded, with AMPL as promisor, alternatively Pierre, because the undertaking Pierre sought served AMPL.

B. Intention to create legal relations

Intention is tested objectively, and a family presumption does no more than identify who bears the onus.[14] Pierre, if he promised personally, might call the $10,000 a favour to a ‘cousin’; yet Rocky bargained for it at a loan signing in AMPL’s office.

Intention is therefore likely, because the bargain was commercial.

C. Certainty

Both promises are certain if each bears a definite meaning:[15] the Loan Agreement fixes what Rocky must ensure, like the promise to ‘ensure’ a debtor could repay that Banque Brussels held enforceable at first instance,[16] and the $10,000 term fixes amount, payee and time.

Both promises are accordingly certain.

D. Consideration

Even if the guarantee binds Rocky, his ‘ensure’ promise faces the existing duty rule: a promise to perform an existing duty is no consideration, at least when made by a contracting party to its promisee to do no more than the contract requires.[17] On the guarantee reading, the rule does not arise: the guarantee was itself Rocky’s undertaking for the $10,000. On the exchange reading, AMPL’s strongest counter is that Rocky, already guaranteeing ‘repayment of the Loan’, added nothing, like the seller’s ‘ensure’ promise in Sundell.[18]

Firstly, however, Pierre agreed before AMPL accepted the guarantee, arguably by signing, so no guarantee duty yet bound Rocky. Secondly, Rocky’s promise covers monthly interest and prompt payment, whereas the guarantee arguably secures only the principal; Sundell is distinguishable: there the new promise was identical with the old. Thirdly, if Pierre promised personally, any guarantee duty was owed to a third party, AMPL; a promise to perform it can be consideration, as Glidewell LJ, in the English Court of Appeal, read the Privy Council’s Pao On.[19] Nor does practical benefit assist: Rocky contracted to supply no work, goods or services.[20]

On balance, a court would likely find Rocky’s promise good consideration, because the undertakings differ and arguably no guarantee duty yet bound him.

E. Privity

Rocky’s right to the $10,000 turns on whether a promise was made to him, not his signature.[21] On the exchange reading, AMPL may liken Rocky, a payee named in another’s contract, to Mrs Coulls; yet Coulls is distinguishable: it turned on there being no promise to her,[22] whereas Pierre accepted Rocky’s terms for payment ‘to me directly’.

Rocky is therefore likely the promisee, because Pierre accepted Rocky’s own offer.

F. Terms of payment

The $10,000 is payable ‘once Grace repays the Loan’, a condition to be fulfilled first;[23] on 9 March 2025 ‘Grace had not yet repaid’, and payment by Rocky would not be Grace’s repayment.

AMPL, alternatively Pierre, accordingly likely owes Rocky $10,000, but only once Grace repays.

III. AMPL v ROCKY

A. Agreement

Whether Rocky is bound turns on his promise, not his signature:[24] he ‘personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, and AMPL called on ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’.

Rocky therefore promised AMPL as guarantor.

B. Consideration

Rocky’s 8 April guarantee came after AMPL’s 27 February advance, and past consideration supports only a promise the law would imply.[25] The Privy Council in Pao On excepted a requested act understood to be remunerated by a benefit enforceable if promised in advance; AMPL advanced the money after ‘Rocky asked’, and a guarantee would have been enforceable if promised then.[26] However, a request alone makes no contract,[27] and nothing shows a guarantee was understood as the advance’s price.

AMPL’s stronger case is fresh consideration: on 8 April it bound itself to Grace for 12 months at 4%, a detriment.[28] Rocky may answer that the instrument merely recorded a 27 February loan; yet no terms for the advance are stated, so the instrument likely created the period. AMPL’s commitment was also the price of Rocky’s promise: the guarantee and credit were settled in one instrument, at a meeting he attended, arguably at his implied request.[29] On the guarantee reading, AMPL’s $10,000 promise was also the guarantee’s price, if AMPL, not Pierre, promised, since consideration must move from the promisee.[30]

On balance, a court would likely find the guarantee binding, because AMPL’s 8 April commitment was its price, though the 27 February terms are unknown.

C. Construction of the repayment term

The Loan was ‘repayable at the expiry of 12 months’, with no stated start, so whether it fell due on 27 February or 8 April 2025 is ambiguous. Pre-contractual conduct showing the genesis is admissible, but later conduct and subjective beliefs are not;[31] Rocky’s emails, the interest payments and Grace’s ‘I have until 8 April 2025’ therefore cannot fix the meaning.

The strongest counter is AMPL’s: the instrument ‘recorded’ money advanced on 27 February, so the period runs from then; yet ‘recorded’ may fix only which money is lent, not when the period began. Decisively, the period is likely a term the 8 April instrument created, and absent words tying it to the advance, it runs from the instrument.

Therefore, the better view is that the Loan likely fell due on 8 April 2025, though the admissible advance date keeps it finely balanced.

Further information is needed on whether the guarantee is payable on demand: if so, Rocky must pay now, but if not, he is liable only on Grace’s default, so on the 8 April view the call was premature. On the 27 February view, Rocky must pay $1,150,000 if the guarantee is supported, and has broken his ‘ensure’ promise regardless. On the 8 April view, that promise is broken only if Grace missed the March 2025 interest or fails to repay by then.

Rocky therefore likely need not pay AMPL now, because the call was premature.

1. The answer (v4)
Nothing shows Grace promised to reimburse Rocky for paying AMPL; the ‘legally binding’ Development Agreement entitles Rocky to
repayment ‘if the Project made a profit’, not yet shown.


I. ROCKY v GRACE

A. Offer

Grace’s call ‘proposed that Rocky offer’, an invitation to treat; the later bullets, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing. On
construction, ‘I will lend’ and ‘Please confirm agreement’, unlike Gibson’s ‘may be prepared to sell’, sought assent.1 Yet Gibson’s
mortgage paragraph might read as a firm offer without its disclaimer,2 and ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ may be one; intention
and certainty decide this. On balance, bullet 1 is likely an offer in form.

B. Acceptance

Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent:3 Grace’s ‘Confirmed’, sent ‘15 minutes later’, added nothing, so it was no
counter-offer. Grace therefore accepted the offer as made.

C. Consideration

Consideration is a price for the promise:4 Rocky’s promise to lend was, in form, given for Grace’s promise to repay at ‘5% interest’,
arguably implied by ‘Confirmed’. Grace’s promises to AMPL were likely given for its promise of ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’.5

D. Intention to create legal relations

Intention is assessed objectively, presumptions doubted, Rocky bearing the onus; the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours
it.6 Masters, asking whether a preliminary agreement was ‘only a record of terms’,7 assumed a contemplated formal contract; it
applies by analogy. Where none is stipulated, the question is whether terms ‘should be put into form’ or be subject to ‘a new
agreement’ on terms ‘not expressed in detail’.8 As in Niesmann, where signing conditioned only ‘the obligation to pay’,9 ‘Confirmed’
settled amount, term and rate; yet ‘satisfactory conditions’ left further loan terms to Rocky. On balance, the better view is that the
parties likely did not intend to be bound, unless those terms were settled ‘this morning’.

E. Certainty

Rocky’s promise is illusory if its performance rests on his ‘unfettered discretion’.10 Meehan, on ‘satisfactory terms and conditions’, is
distinguishable: there the discretion concerned only ‘the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends’.11 Amount, term
and rate are ‘specified parameters’,12 and an implied obligation to act honestly, or honestly and reasonably, would confine Rocky;13
yet the conditions (D) are terms he would set, which could withhold the loan itself. In Godecke, Gibbs J, obiter, doubted that terms
left ‘to be settled by one of the parties’ bind, ‘Perhaps’ excepting ‘subsidiary matters’, which conditions deciding whether Rocky
lends, not how, arguably exceed.14 The promise is therefore arguably illusory.

F. Privity

Even if the email bound, AMPL was Rocky’s agent only if it contracted for him, not solely for itself:15 though ‘Rocky asked’, AMPL
lent ‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and took his guarantee, so Rocky lent nothing.

Only a party can enforce a contract, and only if he provided consideration;16 whether one is a party turns on ‘the written instrument
itself’, not signature.17 Mrs Coulls signed, yet the contract ‘purports expressly’ to be between her husband and the company;18
likewise AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’ the Loan Agreement. Nothing there makes Grace’s promise one to Rocky, so he is no joint
promisee.19 Grace’s answer is therefore right, though not because he ‘never signed anything’, and the 5 March demand, arguably
premised on 27 February (II.G), fails.

AMPL enforcing its loan, agency failing and no trust or estoppel appearing, nothing circumvents the privity rule.20

II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

A. Offer

What Pierre ‘expected’ proposed nothing Rocky could accept, so it was likely an invitation to treat;21 Rocky’s reply, ‘if you also
promise’, sought a return promise, so he offered a bilateral contract.22

B. Acceptance

Pierre ‘agreed’, manifesting assent to Rocky’s offer, so he accepted for whomever he represented.23 AMPL would say nothing bound
until execution; yet, as Lord Greene MR said of exchanges of contracts, parties are bound when and how they contemplate:24
nothing required a document or reserved a right to withdraw.25 Both promises therefore likely bind.

C. Consideration

The $10,000 promise, sought by ‘if you also promise’, priced Rocky’s undertaking,26 which moved from him as promisee;27 if Pierre
promised, Rocky’s detriment likely suffices, though AMPL benefits.28

The existing legal duty rule applies ‘at least when’ a party to a pre-existing contract promises the promisee under it no more than it
requires.29 AMPL would say that ‘also’ and its clause show a guarantee already given; as in Sundell, a promise to ensure
performance already owed is no consideration.30 Yet no earlier promise binds Rocky: his 27 February request did not itself establish
a contract,31 and the clause was arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’. If Pierre promised, even a promise to him to perform a duty
owed to a third party, AMPL, can be consideration.32 Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ exceeds ‘repayment of the Loan’, so Rocky
likely gave consideration, though an earlier clause would favour AMPL.

D. Intention to create legal relations

No presumption governs cousins; Rocky bears the onus.33 Against intention, the undertaking resembles a letter of comfort, which in
Banque Brussels conditioned the facility it was made ‘to induce’,34 whereas AMPL had already advanced. Yet the undertaking was
priced at ‘$10,000’ and given ‘at AMPL’s office’. Intention is therefore likely present on both sides, the price outweighing cousinhood
even if Pierre promised.

E. Certainty

Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, measured by the loan’s timetable, is not ‘so obscure’ that no intention can be attributed.35
AMPL’s promise, depending on Grace’s repayment, not its choice, is not illusory.36

F. Privity

Rocky, the promisee and payee ‘to me directly’, gave consideration, so privity does not bar him.37 The ‘included’ clause most
naturally means the guarantee clause named before it; even a written $10,000 term would leave him the oral promise.

Who promised turns on the doctrine of agency: whether Pierre, with AMPL’s authority or ratification, contracted for it, not solely for
himself.38 AMPL, ‘owned and controlled’ by Pierre, likely authorised him; his contracting for it is contested: Rocky asked ‘you’ to
‘also promise’. Yet Pierre spoke ‘at AMPL’s office’ about ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’, and AMPL called under the
guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’, arguably his undertaking. On balance, AMPL likely promised, though ‘you’ keeps Pierre’s promise
arguable, which proof that he disclaimed acting for AMPL would establish.

G. Construction

The ‘12 months’ are construed objectively: pre-contractual conduct is admissible only if the words are ambiguous, and post-
contractual conduct cannot show meaning.39 The words are arguably ambiguous: the instrument ‘recorded’ the sum ‘advanced’ on
27 February, the transaction’s ‘genesis’.40 Although the terms appear first on 8 April, the ‘12 months’ attach to ‘the Loan’, whose
use Grace had from 27 February, so the period likely ran from then, though narrowly, unless the agreement dates it otherwise.

H. Condition precedent

The bargain binding at once, ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ conditions AMPL’s obligation, not formation;41 on 9 March Grace ‘had not
yet repaid’, so nothing was payable. Read literally or commercially, words naming Grace do not cover Rocky’s payment:42 the
$10,000 falls due on what his undertaking secured, Grace’s repayment. Nor does the duty to co-operate, ‘to do everything necessary’
for Rocky’s benefit, assist:43 nothing suggests AMPL’s call prevents Grace repaying. Rocky’s payment therefore likely does not meet
the condition.

I. Privity: AMPL’s call

Only a contract’s parties are bound by its terms:44 the guarantee clause binds Rocky only if he manifested assent,45 signature being
neither necessary46 nor decisive.47 His ‘I will do that’ likely binds him, but to AMPL only if Pierre accepted for it; otherwise AMPL
has only the clause.

Rocky promised what Pierre ‘expected’, ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, whereas the clause concerns ‘repayment of the Loan’.
He likely assented to the clause if, with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’, he took the benefit of AMPL’s offer ‘with knowledge of
its terms’.48 If AMPL promised, its $10,000 promise was arguably that benefit.49 The guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’ proves he gave
one, not that he knew the clause’s words; having ‘attended’ the meeting, he likely assented unless he never saw them, but not if
Pierre promised, AMPL conferring no benefit.

If AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise is its consideration. If Pierre promised, AMPL’s advance was past consideration,50
sufficing under Pao On only if, besides Rocky’s request, the parties ‘understood that the act was to be remunerated’.51 Nothing
shows that understanding on 27 February, whereas in Pao On it existed ‘at the time of the main agreement’.52 AMPL would rely on
entering the Loan Agreement, the clause included; yet Rocky priced his undertaking at ‘$10,000’, not that entry,53 so AMPL likely
gave no consideration.

As the 12 months likely ran from 27 February, the call was not premature; if from 8 April, it was premature as to principal. Nothing
shows interest paid after ‘8 February 2025’, so a March default is arguable. If AMPL promised, Rocky likely owes AMPL on his
undertaking when Grace defaults and, paying, loses the $10,000; if Pierre promised, AMPL’s call, lacking consideration, likely fails,
and Rocky claims against Pierre and is likely liable to him.

P. Preliminary (claims C3 and C4)

v4 text: ‘Nothing shows Grace promised to reimburse Rocky for paying AMPL; the ’legally binding’ Development Agreement entitles
Rocky to repayment ‘if the Project made a profit’, not yet shown.’ No footnote (no proposition of law).

(a) Issue. Two minor claims disposed of in substantive terms (R-B decide-once; R-Z(1)): C3, any promise by Grace to reimburse or
indemnify Rocky if he pays AMPL under ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’; C4, the Development Agreement, stipulated
binding, as a source of a present claim.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘Grace and Rocky entered into a legally binding agreement that determined the scope of their development
relationship and included a valid and binding clause that if the Project made a profit, Rocky, as the investor for the Project, would be
repaid his investment and a portion of the profit in priority to Grace (the ’Development Agreement’).’ - Narrator: ‘In January 2024,
the Hail Mary Project was near completion, and Rocky and Grace realised that the profit from the Project would be minimal and, due
to the terms of their Development Agreement, Grace was unlikely to make a profit.’ - Narrator: ‘He was quite angry at Rocky, who he
blamed for the delays to the Project, and demanded Rocky’s assistance.’ - Narrator: ‘AMPL called for payment of the Loan under the
personal guarantee provided by Rocky.’ - No sentence of the problem records any promise by Grace to Rocky to reimburse him;
Grace’s only promissory word to Rocky is ‘Confirmed’ (12 February 2024), dealt with at I.C.

(c) Arguments. - Rocky (C3): Grace ‘demanded Rocky’s assistance’, so the guarantee was given at his request, and a service ‘moved
by a suit or request of the party that gives the assumpsit … will bind’ (Lampleigh v Braithwait, as quoted in the PO extract; no AC
page pin) and ‘the fact of a past service raises an implication that at the time it was rendered it was to be paid for’ (Bowen LJ in Re
Casey’s Patents, as quoted in the PO extract). Raised by OPPOSING r3 row P1. - Grace (C3): both passages need a later promise to
pay; none appears. OPPOSING r3 rated the point MINOR and answered by ‘Nothing shows’. - Rocky (C4): the clause is stipulated
‘valid and binding’ and gives him priority repayment; the parties foresaw a ‘minimal’ profit, which is still a profit (OPPOSING r3 P2;
SHEET P Credit, U22). - Grace (C4): a forecast in January 2024 is not a profit made; no breach appears. - No authority is cited: the
paragraph states no proposition of law (WORK/v4/REGISTER rows 1 and 2).

(d) Decisive reason. C3: no promise by Grace to Rocky appears on the facts, and an implied promise needs a later promise or a
contemporaneous understanding that the facts do not show. C4: the entitlement is conditional on a profit that the facts show only as
forecast.

(e) Conclusion and strength. No present claim on either. C3 strong; C4 strong (ISSUES_SETTLED header table, C3 and C4; S-24
withdrew assignment as a stated route for C3).

(f) Further information. - Whether a profit is realised on completion (‘minimal’ is still a profit): if so, the Development Agreement
claim arises; cuts for Rocky (credit, U22; not funded). - Any later promise by Grace to reimburse: would found a promise, cuts for
Rocky, but its consideration would then be tested (past consideration, II.I3’s law).

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. v2 opened ‘Breach, damages and guarantee law lie outside Weeks 1 to 4, and nothing
shows Grace promised reimbursement’. Round-2 MARK_1 and MARK_2 both graded P VG: C3 was ‘gestured at as ’reimbursement’
without saying for what’ (UPGRADES_r1 U31; SHEET P Drops). Settled in v3: ‘to reimburse Rocky for paying AMPL’. 2. R-Z(1) then
removed the ‘outside Weeks 1 to 4’ clause as meta language (v3, −12 words). 3. Round-2 MARK_1 R1 flag: ‘the Development
Agreement pays’ (an agreement does not pay). v3: ‘entitles Rocky to repayment’. 4. TRACER r3 P7: ‘only’ was an unmarked
inference, the narrator saying the agreement ‘included’ the clause and being silent on its other terms. v4 removed ‘only’ and ‘which
is’ (−3). 5. M2 r3 margin note: ‘reimburse Rocky for paying AMPL’ when Rocky has not paid. Not deducted. v4 rejected a change:
the claim is reimbursement if he pays, and SHEET P Core (1)‘s own accepted form is ’Grace promised Rocky no reimbursement for
paying AMPL’. 6. OPPOSING r3 P2 (‘though a ’minimal’ profit was foreseen’, +6) and r2 row 1: credit (SHEET P Credit; U22);
drafted and cut for funding in v3; not funded in v4. 7. R-X(7): ‘Frustration,’ deleted in v2. 8. VOICE r1 M22 (note-form tails): P
rewritten in v2.
(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 2.0, tier L. - M1 Exc, on v3’s ‘Nothing shows Grace promised to reimburse Rocky for paying
AMPL; the ’legally binding’ Development Agreement entitles Rocky to repayment only ‘if the Project made a profit’, which is not yet
shown.’: Core (1) C3 named and disposed of; Core (2) the Development Agreement as stipulated, ‘not yet shown’; a fact claim, not a
conclusion first. - M2 Exc on the same sentence, checked at question.txt lines 11 to 15. - v4 change: ‘only’ and ‘which is’ removed;
the condition and ‘not yet shown’ kept, which is what Core (2) requires.

(i) Residual risks. - ‘not yet shown’ now trails as a reduced clause after a quotation; a strict R1 reader could call it note-form (R1
lapse type: a clause whose verb must be supplied). Cost to restore ‘which is not yet shown’: +2. - ‘for paying AMPL’ while Rocky has
not paid (M2’s margin): no deduction recorded; ‘if he pays AMPL’ would cost +1. - The ‘minimal’ forecast (OPPOSING P2): credit,
+6.



PART I. ROCKY v GRACE

I.A Offer

v4 text: ‘Grace’s call ’proposed that Rocky offer’, an invitation to treat; the later bullets, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise
nothing. On construction, ‘I will lend’ and ‘Please confirm agreement’, unlike Gibson’s ‘may be prepared to sell’, sought assent.[fn 1]
Yet Gibson’s mortgage paragraph might read as a firm offer without its disclaimer,[fn 2] and ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ may
be one; intention and certainty decide this. On balance, bullet 1 is likely an offer in form.’

(a) Issue. Whether bullet 1 of Rocky’s 12 February email is an offer capable of acceptance by ‘Confirmed’; whether anything else
(Grace’s 5 February call; bullets 2 and 3) could be.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘On 5 February 2024, Grace called Rocky and proposed that Rocky offer Grace a’$1 million dollar working
capital loan for 2 years at 5% interest’.’ The inner words are Grace’s. - Narrator: ‘Rocky told Grace he was not interested in offering
Grace a long-term loan but proposed that they meet in person to discuss.’ - Rocky’s email: ‘Confirming discussions from our meeting
this morning’. - Rocky’s email: ‘I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory
conditions.’ - Rocky’s email: ‘Potential project over in Eastwood subject to success of Hail Mary Project.’ - Rocky’s email: ‘Threatened
litigation from subcontractor from Bowral Project’ and ‘wait and see at present.’ The problem prints a dash between the two, which
is why the answer quotes only ‘wait and see’ (D9). - Rocky’s email: ‘Please confirm agreement.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294, 298 (Lord Diplock; House of Lords; ratio; Lord Keith
agreeing): the words ‘may be prepared to sell’ ‘are fatal to this; so is the invitation, not, be it noted, to accept the offer, but’ ‘to make
formal application to buy’ (CB1A 42; quoted in fragments so as not to nest the casebook’s inner quotation marks). Correspondence is
read by ‘the conventional approach’ of seeing whether ‘upon their true construction’ the documents contain an offer and an
acceptance (297, CB1A 41; credit). - For an offer (Grace’s interest if she sued; Rocky’s if he did): ‘I will lend’ fixes amount, date, term
and rate, and ‘Please confirm agreement’ invites the assent that concludes a bargain, unlike ‘may be prepared to sell’. - Against an
offer (Rocky’s interest, who lent nothing and wants no binding promise to lend; OPPOSING r3 row I.A): ‘subject to satisfactory
conditions’ does what ‘may be prepared to sell’ did. Lord Diplock at 298: the Council’s second paragraph, ‘with its use of the
indicative mood …, might have been understood by council tenants to whom it was addressed as indicating a firm offer of a
mortgage’ only ‘If the final sentence had been omitted’; the final sentence was ‘This letter should not be regarded as firm offer of a
mortgage’ (CB1A 42). - Direction: a disclaimed indicative promise could NOT be read as a firm offer; the answer must keep that
direction or commit a D2 fault (CRIT_fidelity_3 M1; CRIT_round3 M1).

(d) Decisive reason. - ‘I will lend’ and ‘Please confirm agreement’ sought assent, which ‘may be prepared to sell’ did not. - The
qualifier may be the disclaimer’s analogue, but its effect goes to whether the parties meant to be bound and whether the promise is
illusory, so it is carried to D and E rather than decided here (decide-once, R-B; SHEET §1 rule (i)). - That beats the counter because
classification at A decides only the form of the communication; the qualifier’s legal effect is then decided once, at I.D. - Grace’s call
‘proposed that Rocky offer’, so it invited an offer and made none (an invitation to treat, R-X(4)). - Bullets 2 and 3 promise nothing on
their own words (‘Potential’; ‘wait and see’).

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘On balance, bullet 1 is likely an offer in form.’ Moderate (SHEET I.A Strength), the ‘in form’ leaving
bindingness to D and E (SHEET Part 9 item 43; trap T20 avoided at I.C). ISSUES_SETTLED S-51 (I.1 A1, ‘bullet 1 an offer in form’,
stands; D2a).

(f) Further information. What was said at the meeting ‘this morning’ (SHEET I.A Credit): conditions specified there would make
the offer clearer; cuts toward an offer, and so toward a binding email if D is also met. Not written at I.A; I.D carries the same item
with its direction.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Bullets on no deciding word: round-1 A1, A2, B1, B2 and C1 graded I.A VG (‘bullets 2 and
3 promise nothing’). UPGRADES_r1 U15 made the deciding words core (+5). v2 added ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’. 2. ‘Lord
Diplock’s indicative paragraph’ misattributed the Council’s letter to the judge (U27). v2: ‘Gibson’s indicative paragraph’. M2 r3
margin: ‘which paragraph?’ (not deducted). VOICE r3 M2: ‘opaque’, with a verbless tail. v4: ‘Gibson’s mortgage paragraph’ (an
accepted form, SHEET I.A Core (4)), direction re-checked at CB1A 42. 3. Carry to D and E: round-2 MARK_1 and MARK_2 both
graded I.A VG, the qualifier not carried in terms. v3: ‘which ’subject to satisfactory conditions’ may resemble, a matter for intention
and certainty’ (+7). VOICE r3 M2: verbless tail. v4: ‘and ’subject to satisfactory conditions’ may be one; intention and certainty
decide this’ (−1). 4. Garden path: VOICE r3 M1 (‘proposed’ read as the main verb, then a second main verb ‘promise’). v4: the
semicolon form (−2). 5. Course name: VOICE r1 M4 (invitation to treat unnamed). v2 named it. 6. VOICE r3 S1 (‘the first bullet’ for
‘bullet 1’, +1): residual, ‘bullet 1’ being unambiguous. 7. OPPOSING r3 I.A: MINOR, answered as written.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 3.0, tier C. - M1 Exc on v3’s four sentences, from ‘Grace’s call ’proposed that Rocky offer’, an
invitation to treat, and bullets 2 and 3, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise nothing.’ to ‘On balance, bullet 1 is likely an offer in
form.’: Core (1) to (5), the direction checked at CB1A 42, 298. - M2 Exc on the same, direction checked (‘might have been
understood … as indicating a firm offer’ only ‘If the final sentence had been omitted’). - v4 change: sentences 1 and 3 rewritten
(VOICE M1, M2). Core (4)‘s similarity, direction and carry survive: ’might read as a firm offer without its disclaimer’ states Lord
Diplock’s direction correctly, and ‘intention and certainty decide this’ is the carry.

(i) Residual risks. - ‘may be one’: the pronoun’s intended antecedent is ‘disclaimer’ (the nearest noun); a reader who takes it as ‘a
firm offer’ would read the sentence as saying the qualifier may be a firm offer, the opposite of the point. Map-writer’s observation,
untested by any agent on v4; R1 lapse risk (an unclear antecedent: R-V(1)). Cost: ‘may be such a disclaimer’, +2. - ‘bullet 1’ (VOICE
S1), +1.


I.B Acceptance

v4 text: ‘Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent:[fn 3] Grace’s ’Confirmed’, sent ‘15 minutes later’, added nothing,
so it was no counter-offer. Grace therefore accepted the offer as made.’

(a) Issue. Whether ‘Confirmed’ accepted the email as sent, qualifier included, or did anything else.

(b) Facts. - Rocky’s email: ‘Please confirm agreement.’ - Narrator: ‘Grace responded to the email 15 minutes later saying,’ - Grace:
‘Mr Rocky, Confirmed. Best, Grace.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Empirnall Holdings Pty Ltd v Machon Paull Partners Pty Ltd (1988) 14 NSWLR 523, 534 (McHugh JA;
Samuels JA agreeing; Kirby P to substantially the same effect; NSW Court of Appeal; ratio): ‘The objective theory of contract requires
an external manifestation of assent to an offer.’ (CB1B 71). Counter-offer: a reply with additions ‘was in law a rejection of the offer
and constituted a counter-offer’ (Butler 404, Lord Denning MR; credit). - Rocky (against a binding email; OPPOSING r3 I.B):
‘Confirming discussions from our meeting’ and ‘Confirmed’ acknowledged a record of discussions, not assent to be bound. - Answer
to that: Rocky’s own ‘Please confirm agreement’ asked for assent, and ‘Confirmed’ answered it; whether the parties meant to be
bound by what was assented to is the Masters 360 question decided at D (SHEET I.B Credit).

(d) Decisive reason. ‘Confirmed’, in the mode the email asked for, within fifteen minutes, adding nothing, is an external
manifestation of assent and no counter-offer.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘Grace therefore accepted the offer as made’, that is, the whole email, qualifier included. Strong on
correspondence; bindingness turns on D and E (SHEET I.B Strength). S-51 (I.1 B1 to B4 stand); S-30 (‘Best, Grace’ is a sign-off;
whether it is a signature does not matter).

(f) Further information. None that changes the advice. Credit only: receipt under Electronic Transactions Act 2000 (NSW) s
13A(1)(a).

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. VOICE r1 M6: counter-offer unnamed and a grammar fault. v2: ‘so it was no counter-offer
and accepted the whole email’ (+3). 2. VOICE r2 F6: split into two sentences, needed for the under-12 share (without it 6 of 66,
9.09%, below the 9.1% floor). v3, +2. 3. M1 r3: ‘as made’ read as the whole email, qualifier included, the sheet’s accepted
alternative form.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 2.0, tier L. - M1 Exc: criterion (CB1B 71, 534), deciding facts, counter-offer excluded and named,
result ‘as made’. - M2 Exc: ‘Acceptance requires an external manifestation of assent: Grace’s ’Confirmed’, sent ‘15 minutes later’,
added nothing, so it was no counter-offer. Grace therefore accepted the offer as made.’ - v4: unchanged.

(i) Residual risks. None recorded. ‘as made’ carries ‘qualifier included’ only by implication, which SHEET I.B Core requires to have

I.C Consideration

v4 text: ‘Consideration is a price for the promise:[fn 4] Rocky’s promise to lend was, in form, given for Grace’s promise to repay at
’5% interest’, arguably implied by ‘Confirmed’. Grace’s promises to AMPL were likely given for its promise of ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per
annum’.[fn 5]’

(a) Issue. Whether a price was given for Rocky’s 12 February promise; whether Grace’s promises in the Loan Agreement had a
price from AMPL.

(b) Facts. - Rocky’s email: ‘at a rate of 5% interest’. - Grace: ‘Confirmed.’ - Narrator: ‘The loan was recorded as $1,150,000 (’Loan’)
with an interest rate of 4% per annum. Interest was to be paid by Grace monthly, and the Loan was repayable at the expiry of 12
months.’ - Narrator: ‘the $1,150,000 was advanced by AMPL on the same day’ (27 February 2024).

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Beaton v McDivitt (1987) 13 NSWLR 162, 168 (Kirby P; NSW Court of Appeal): ‘consideration must be
satisfied in the form of a price in return for the promisor’s promise or a quid pro quo. The price can be in the form of an act,
forbearance or promise.’ (CB2A 104). Status: Kirby P was in the majority on the result (the casebook prints ‘Appeal dismissed.’ at
CB2A 111 after Mahoney JA; McHugh JA alone would have given Beaton the block, CB2A 109); alone on the consideration question;
no weight issue (R-F). - 12 February: the inference that ‘Confirmed’ implied a promise to repay at ‘5% interest’ is marked ‘arguably’
(CRIT_harsh_2 F14; R-M). - Loan Agreement (Grace’s best answer to Rocky’s demand, run only if it were useful to her; OPPOSING r3
I.C): AMPL’s advance on 27 February was past, so nothing was given for Grace’s 8 April promises (Roscorla 237). - Answer: AMPL’s
fresh 8 April promise of the term (‘12 months’) at ‘4% per annum’ is the price (Beaton 168). - Strategy (trap T12): Rocky should not
run that point, needing Grace bound for the $10,000 ‘once Grace repays the Loan’.

(d) Decisive reason. A promise for a promise is a price; the Loan Agreement’s recorded term and rate are AMPL’s price for Grace’s
promises. ‘in form’ because whether Rocky’s promise is illusory, and so the consideration good, is decided at E (Pace 150: ‘A
contract made for a consideration which is illusory is unenforceable’).

(e) Conclusion and strength. 12 February: strong that a bargain was struck in form. Loan Agreement: moderate to strong (S-21;
Heydon JA’s ‘contractual entitlement’ route at Brambles 182 is his alone, O-9c, and is not used). S-51 (I.1 C1 to C4 stand).

(f) Further information. None that changes the advice.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. T20 (I.C unqualified beside I.E ‘arguably illusory’): round-2 MARK_1 and MARK_2 both
graded R10 VG for it. UPGRADES_r1 U10. v3 added ‘in form’ (+2). 2. ‘not the past advance’ with Roscorla 237: credit since SHEET
v5 (Part 9 item 25), past consideration being decided at II.I3. 3. VOICE r3 S2 (‘its promise to lend for’, +2): residual. SHEET I.C Core
(2) prints ‘its promise of ’12 months’’ as the counted form (CRIT_round4 m3; CRIT_round5 M7). 4. Kirby P’s status: AGLC r3 noted
on fn 4 that ‘Kirby P was in the minority on the result ([173]: no enforceable contract)’. That note is wrong at source: the appeal was
Beaton’s and was dismissed, and Kirby P found no enforceable contract, so he was in the majority; McHugh JA was the minority
(CB2A 109, 111). The register (row 7), the tracer (r3 row 8) and SHEET I.C (‘majority on the result; alone on the consideration
question’) are right. The note asked for no change, and none was made.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 2.0, tier L. - M1 Exc: ‘Consideration is a price for the promise: Rocky’s promise to lend was, in
form, given for Grace’s promise to repay at ’5% interest’, arguably implied by ‘Confirmed’. Grace’s promises to AMPL were likely
given for its promise of ‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’.’ Criterion CB2A 104, 168; ‘in form’; AMPL’s price, ‘likely’. - M2 Exc on the
same; checked CB2A 104. - v4: unchanged.

(i) Residual risks. VOICE S2 (+2), stylistic only.


I.D Intention to create legal relations

v4 text: ‘Intention is assessed objectively, presumptions doubted, Rocky bearing the onus; the parties’ status as ‘project developers’
favours it.[fn 6] Masters, asking whether a preliminary agreement was ‘only a record of terms’,[fn 7] assumed a contemplated formal
contract; it applies by analogy. Where none is stipulated, the question is whether terms ‘should be put into form’ or be subject to ‘a
new agreement’ on terms ‘not expressed in detail’.[fn 8] As in Niesmann, where signing conditioned only ‘the obligation to pay’,[fn 9]
‘Confirmed’ settled amount, term and rate; yet ‘satisfactory conditions’ left further loan terms to Rocky. On balance, the better view
is that the parties likely did not intend to be bound, unless those terms were settled ‘this morning’.’

(a) Issue. Whether the parties objectively intended to be bound at once by the email exchange, or exchanged ‘only a record of terms
… as a basis for the negotiation of a contract’. The meaning of ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ is decided here, once (decide-once
rule (i)).

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘Mr Grace and Mr Rocky are both project developers who pursued various projects together since 2017 to
stellar success.’ - Rocky’s email: ‘Confirming discussions from our meeting this morning’. - Rocky’s email: ‘I will lend $1 million to
you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory conditions.’ - Rocky’s email: ‘Please confirm agreement.’
- Grace: ‘Confirmed.’ - No formal document is mentioned anywhere in the exchange.

(c) Arguments. - Rule, objective test and onus: Ermogenous v Greek Orthodox Community of SA Inc (2002) 209 CLR 95, [25] to [26]
(Gaudron, McHugh, Hayne and Callinan JJ; High Court majority; ratio). [25]: ‘an objective assessment of the state of affairs between
the parties’; the inquiry ‘may take account of the subject-matter of the agreement, the status of the parties to it, their relationship to
one another, and other surrounding circumstances’. [26]: ‘we doubt the utility of using the language of presumptions in this context.
At best, the use of that language does no more than invite attention to identifying the party who bears the onus of proof.’ (CB3A
137). - Rule, the question: Masters v Cameron (1954) 91 CLR 353, 360 (the Court: Dixon CJ, McTiernan and Kitto JJ; ratio): whether
the document ‘constitutes a binding contract … or only a record of terms upon which the signatories were agreed as a basis for the
negotiation of a contract’ (CB3A 154). The classes are framed for parties who ‘also agree that the matter of their negotiation shall be
dealt with by a formal contract’ (CB3A 155, 360), so on an email that mentions none they apply by analogy (S-4; CONTRA 3 adopted).
- Rule, the decisive authority for a qualifier not referring to a formal contract: 363, adopting Jessel MR in Winn v Bull (1877) 7 Ch D
29, 32: ‘When it is not expressly stated to be subject to a formal contract it becomes a question of construction, whether the parties
intended that the terms agreed on should be put into form, or whether they should be subject to a new agreement the terms of which
are not expressed in detail’ (CB3A 156; the official text reads ‘should merely be put into form’, the casebook drops ‘merely’, so the
answer quotes around it: R-K). - Rocky’s best case, for a binding email (the onus being his as the party alleging the contract):
Niesmann v Collingridge (1921) 29 CLR 177 as the Court reports Rich and Starke JJ at Masters 361: signing ‘did not make the
signing of a contract a condition of agreement, but made it a condition of the obligation to pay’ (CB3A 155). ‘Confirmed’ settled
amount, term and rate, so ‘satisfactory conditions’ arguably conditions only the obligation to lend. Also ‘Please confirm agreement’;
no formal document; a three-day deadline to ‘15 February’ (OPPOSING r3 I.D; credit). - Grace’s best case, against a binding email:
‘satisfactory conditions’ reserved further terms of the loan to Rocky, a ‘new agreement’ on terms ‘not expressed in detail’, not
Niesmann’s mere condition of performance. Lord O’Hagan, adopted at 361: ‘if any prospective contract, involving the possibility of
new terms … remains to be adopted, matters must be taken to be still in a train of negotiation’ (credit). - Status of the parties:
‘project developers’ who ‘pursued various projects together since 2017 to stellar success’ favours intention (U4, core from v11). -
Not used (official-only, credit, cap reached): Masters 362 adopting Jessel MR in Crossley v Maycock (‘if the agreement is made
subject to certain conditions then specified or to be specified by the party making it … until those conditions are accepted, there is
no final agreement such as the Court will enforce’), which would raise S-4 to moderate to strong (O-10); Walsh J’s indicators at
Godecke 640 (official-only).

(d) Decisive reason. - ‘satisfactory conditions’ left further loan terms to Rocky, which is Winn v Bull’s second alternative, ‘a new
agreement’ on terms ‘not expressed in detail’. - That beats Niesmann because Niesmann’s further stipulation was a condition of the
obligation to pay on terms already complete, whereas here the terms of the loan itself remained to be settled by one party. - Amount,
term and rate are named as settled (not ‘the essentials’), so the paragraph does not concede the premise of Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps’
exception, which I.E resists (trap T19; U26).
(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘On balance, the better view is that the parties likely did not intend to be bound, unless those terms
were settled ’this morning’.’ S-4: moderate on the course materials, the open-point tier. Result for Rocky (no claim on the email)
strong regardless, because Rocky lent nothing (I.F1).

(f) Further information. Whether the conditions were settled at the meeting ‘this morning’ (and accepted by Grace): if so, the
email likely bound. That cuts toward Grace’s counterclaim for a failure to lend ‘by 15 February’ (X4, weak, nominal for Grace, S-4, S-
5) and gives Rocky nothing, he having lent nothing.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. D2 (Masters or Meehan for the qualifier): [R] had class 3 via Winn v Bull at moderate to
strong; CONTRA 3 and GAPS A4, B12, C3 argued that Masters assumes a formal document. S-4 settled it: by analogy only, objective
intention governs, moderate; [R]‘s ’adopted for exactly this case’ withdrawn. 2. Niesmann as support or as Rocky’s case: TRACER r1
PE-2 and OPPOSING r1 6. v2 put it as Rocky’s best case and met it (+10). 3. Analogy disclosure: round-2 MARK_1 graded I.D VG (v2
‘assumed a contemplated formal contract’ never said it was absent here or that Masters applies only by analogy). v3: ‘, absent here,
so applies by analogy’ (+7). 4. VOICE r3 M3: ‘absent here, so applies by analogy’ elides its subject. The auditor’s rewrite kept the
absence (‘it applies here only by analogy’, 0). The reviser took ‘; it applies by analogy’ (−2), relying on the next sentence’s ‘Where
none is stipulated’ to carry the absence (v4 CHANGES §3.4). See (i). 5. TRACER r3 P3: ‘without presumptions’ states as settled what
[26] put as doubt. v4: ‘presumptions doubted’ (the Court’s own verb), 0 words. II.D’s ‘No presumption governs cousins’ was kept
(II.D (g)). 6. ‘the essentials’ against Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps’ (T19): round-1 C2 graded R10 VG. U26. v2: ‘amount, date, term and rate’; v3
cut ‘date’ for funding (M1 r2’s list). 7. M1 r3 U2: name the Masters category (‘akin to the third class’, +4) as core, because reading
guide 3A asks ‘What are the different categories of preliminary agreement?’. Not adopted: SHEET I.D Core (2) and Part 9 item 36
make the class name credit where the reasoning runs through Winn v Bull 363, as it does. Residual. 8. M2 r3 margin: the crux (‘left
further terms of the loan to Rocky’) is asserted rather than argued; M2 found it sufficient through Winn v Bull. 9. Round-2 MARK_2
margin (‘the better view … likely’ a double hedge): rejected, his own form (VOICE 1.9, ‘the better view is that SPC likely owes no
DoC’). 10. OPPOSING r3 M3 (I.D limb): Lord Blackburn and Lord O’Hagan at 361, the Godecke majority (Walsh J, 642 to 643), ‘by 15
February’ as immediacy, and ‘left further terms’ as assertion. Addressed at I.E (the whether-not-how reason); Walsh J not put
(residual, I.E (i)). 11. Funding cuts OPPOSING r3 proposed here (F3: drop ‘only a record of terms’; F5: drop ‘the better view is that’):
rejected, each removing a core item (I.D Core (2); Core (5)’s open-point tier).

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 6.0, tier K. - M1 Exc on v3’s five sentences: Core (1) (‘Intention is assessed objectively, without
presumptions, Rocky bearing the onus; the parties’ status as ‘project developers’ favours it.’); Core (2) and (6) (‘Masters, asking
whether a preliminary agreement was ’only a record of terms’, assumed a contemplated formal contract, absent here, so applies by
analogy.’); Core (4) (the Winn v Bull sentence, casebook form without ‘merely’); Core (3) (the Niesmann sentence); Core (5) (the
verdict with its direction). - M2 Exc on the same five sentences, each core checked at CB3A 137, 154 to 156. - v4 change: sentence 1
(‘presumptions doubted’), sentence 2 (‘; it applies by analogy’, ‘absent here’ removed), sentence 4 (‘further loan terms’).

(i) Residual risks. - ‘absent here’ removed: SHEET I.D Core (2) reads ‘Masters and its classes assume a contemplated formal
contract, absent here, so they apply by analogy’. v4 states the assumption and the analogy but not, in terms, the absence that makes
it an analogy; the next sentence’s ‘Where none is stipulated’ is Jessel MR’s condition stated generally, not a finding about this email.
Round-2 MARK_1 graded exactly this gap VG on v2. Map-writer’s observation, untested on v4. At risk: I.D VG, 1.5, plus R2’s cap if
the marker treats Masters as applied without the distinction (0.75). Cost: ‘assumed a contemplated formal contract, here absent, so
it applies by analogy’, +3. - M1 U2 (the category named): 0 under SHEET_v12; I.D VG (1.5) if the sheet adopts U2. Cost +4. - R5: I.D
(115) plus I.E (109) is 224 against R5’s guide of about 215; both round-3 markers accepted 218.


I.E Certainty

v4 text: ‘Rocky’s promise is illusory if its performance rests on his ’unfettered discretion’.[fn 10] Meehan, on ‘satisfactory terms and
conditions’, is distinguishable: there the discretion concerned only ‘the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends’.[fn
11] Amount, term and rate are ‘specified parameters’,[fn 12] and an implied obligation to act honestly, or honestly and reasonably,
would confine Rocky;[fn 13] yet the conditions (D) are terms he would set, which could withhold the loan itself. In Godecke, Gibbs J,
obiter, doubted that terms left ‘to be settled by one of the parties’ bind, ‘Perhaps’ excepting ‘subsidiary matters’, which conditions
deciding whether Rocky lends, not how, arguably exceed.[fn 14] The promise is therefore arguably illusory.’

(a) Issue. Whether a promise to lend ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ is illusory because it leaves the promisor a discretion
whether to perform, or leaves terms to be settled by one party, on the reading of ‘conditions’ decided at D (further terms of the loan).

(b) Facts. - Rocky’s email: ‘I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory
conditions.’ - Rocky is both the promisor and the judge of what is ‘satisfactory’. - The email says ‘satisfactory’, not ‘reasonable’, and
names no object of the conditions.

(c) Arguments. - Rule, illusoriness: Biotechnology Australia Pty Ltd v Pace (1988) 15 NSWLR 130, 151 (McHugh JA; Kirby P
agreeing in the result; Hope JA dissenting; NSW Court of Appeal): ‘A consideration is illusory if its payment or fulfilment depends
upon an unfettered discretion vested in the promisor.’ (CB3B 166). - Grace’s best authority (if a binding promise were in issue) and
the answer’s distinction: Meehan v Jones (1982) 149 CLR 571, 580 to 581 (Gibbs CJ; High Court; unanimous in the result; Aickin J
died before judgment): a clause speaking of ‘satisfactory terms and conditions’ bound because the principle ‘does not apply where
the discretion or option of the contracting party relates, not to the performance of the contractual obligations themselves, but only to
the fulfilment of a condition upon which the contract depends’ (CB3B 183); 582: ‘There is a concluded agreement as to the terms of
the contract which, if the condition is satisfied, leaves no discretion in either party as to whether he shall carry them out’ (CB3B
184). - The fetters put for the binding view (U1; R-X(5); OPPOSING r3 M3): - McHugh JA at Pace 151: ‘the consideration will not be
illusory if the discretion must be exercised within specified parameters’; ‘even when no objective criterion of measurement is
available, it may still be possible to infer a promise to act honestly and/or reasonably’ (CB3B 166). - Gibbs CJ at Meehan 581: ‘No
doubt it may be implied that the purchaser will act honestly’ (CB3B 183). - Mason J at 588: ‘an implied obligation that he will act
honestly, or honestly and reasonably’; at 589 to 590: ‘The limitation that the purchaser must act honestly, or honestly and
reasonably, takes the case out of the principle’ (CB3B 185). Wilson J inclined to honesty alone (597 to 598); no majority on
‘reasonably’. - Not put (credit; residual): - Gibbs CJ at 579, on the objective reading he did not prefer: with evidence of ‘the prevailing
rates and conditions on which loans are made’ a court ‘should not find it unduly difficult’ to decide what finance is satisfactory (CB3B
183). - The Godecke majority, Walsh J (Mason J agreeing) at 642 to 643: what could be required ‘must be reasonable in an objective
sense’; the purchaser ‘is agreeing presently to accept as part of the bargain such additional provisions’ (CB3B 188 to 189). - Walsh J
at 641 to 642 adopting Bray CJ, ‘there is no reason in principle for holding that there cannot be any binding contract if some matter
is left to be determined by one of the contracting parties’ (official-only; O-11; it lowered S-5 to weak to moderate). - The obiter on
point: Godecke v Kirwan (1973) 129 CLR 629, 646 to 647 (Gibbs J; obiter; ‘unnecessary to express any concluded opinion’): ‘it does
not necessarily follow from what I have said that an agreement which left further terms to be settled by one of the parties, rather
than by his solicitors, would be treated as a concluded contract’; ‘Perhaps it may be different where agreement has been reached on
all essential terms but the determination of subsidiary matters has been left to one of the parties’; his contrast at 647 is ‘a vital
matter (such as price or rental)’ (CB3B 190).

(d) Decisive reason. - The parameters and an honest, or honest and reasonable, judgment confine a discretion exercised within
agreed terms: Kitto J’s Thorby principle as McHugh JA quotes it at 151, ‘a latitude of choice as to the manner in which agreed
stipulations shall be carried into effect’. - On D’s reading, the ‘conditions’ are terms Rocky himself would set, and they could
withhold the loan itself. That is a discretion over whether he performs, not how. - Meehan’s discretion concerned only a condition
(finance from a third party) on which a concluded bargain depended. - The same reason answers Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps’: conditions
deciding whether Rocky lends are not ‘subsidiary matters’ but closer to his ‘vital matter (such as price or rental)’. - Why it beats the
counter: the fetters presuppose a concluded agreement as to the terms (Gibbs CJ 582); Mason J’s own limit at 587 is that the point
‘would have force if the contract left the court at large … yielding no indication as to what the parties meant’; here the terms
themselves are left open.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘The promise is therefore arguably illusory.’ S-5 as revised at O-11: weak to moderate on certainty
alone, decided at D (R-X(5) fixes ‘arguably’). Either result for Rocky stands on I.F1.

(f) Further information. What ‘conditions’ meant (carried from D by ‘(D)’). If external conditions on which Rocky’s promise
depends (security from a third party; the success of the Hail Mary Project), the email is Meehan-shaped and not illusory, which cuts
toward a binding promise and so toward Grace’s nominal counterclaim. If further loan terms for Rocky’s satisfaction, illusory.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. McHugh JA at Pace 154 to 155 (‘throws no light’): [R] used it against binding force; GAPS
B5 and CONTRA 3 showed that read with the sentence before it the passage points toward the Thorby side of the line. S-5 withdrew
the use; SHEET I.E Drops grade it Poor. 2. Gibbs CJ at 579 (GAPS C2): an objective reading of loan conditions against a market. S-5
recorded it as strengthening validity; credit; not put. 3. Walsh J adopting Bray CJ (O-11, official-only): moved S-5 down to weak to
moderate. Credit (R-L(5)); not put. 4. The honesty fetter, in four rounds: - v1 did not put it; UPGRADES_r1 U1 and R-X(5) made it
core. - v2: ‘which an implied duty to judge ’satisfactory’ honestly cannot supply’ (fn Meehan 581, Gibbs CJ). - OPPOSING r2 row 7
(MATERIAL): McHugh JA’s ‘specified parameters’ unmet. v3: ‘The conditions, as construed at D, are the loan’s own terms beyond its
’specified parameters’, terms Rocky would set and judge, so an implied duty of honesty confines nothing.’ (+8). - OPPOSING r3 M3
(MATERIAL): v3 used Pace 151 against the party it helps, answered the honesty fetter by assertion, left the ‘reasonably’ limb (Mason
J; Pace 151), Gibbs CJ 579 and the Godecke majority unanswered, and gave no reason for ‘arguably exceed’. VOICE r3 T1: ‘implied
duty of honesty’ is a proxy found in no course source; S4: ‘as construed at D’ is a parenthetical cross-reference. v4 rebuilt the
sentence: parameters conceded in McHugh JA’s words; ‘an implied obligation to act honestly, or honestly and reasonably’ in Mason
J’s words (CB3B 185) with fn 13 moved from Gibbs CJ 581 to Mason J 588 to 590; met by ‘terms he would set, which could withhold
the loan itself’; carry written ‘(D)’, the counted form SHEET I.E Core (2) prints (+10 in the unit). - PART adopted: Walsh J and Gibbs
CJ 579 not put (residual). 5. Both round-3 markers had graded v3’s sentence Excellent, the sentence OPPOSING r3 then rated
MATERIAL. The panel role, not the marks, drove the rebuild. 6. ‘or honestly and reasonably’ now in the text: SHEET I.E Core (2A)
makes honesty alone core and the ‘reasonably’ limb credit, ‘never stated as settled by a majority’ (credit-wrong line, VG). v4 states it
as the fetter Rocky would rely on (‘would confine’), footnoted to Mason J alone, not as the Court’s law (register row 17). 7. fn 14
judge: AGLC r3 held ‘(Gibbs J)’ unnecessary where the text names him (identity apparent). M1 and M2 each graded R8 VG for its
absence, Godecke’s majority being Walsh J. v4 added ‘(Gibbs J)’; the markers prevail. 8. ‘In Godecke,’ before ‘Gibbs J’ (+2): SHEET
Part 9 item 39 records the clarity risk (a reader taking ‘Gibbs J’ for the Meehan judge). Funded in v3; kept. 9. M2 r3 margin on v3’s
sentence: ‘terse to the point of being cryptic’. Superseded by the rebuild. 10. The ‘Perhaps’ answered with a reason: CRIT_round5
M4 made it core (‘which the loan’s own conditions arguably exceed’). v4 states the reason in Gibbs J’s own terms (‘deciding whether
Rocky lends, not how’), from OPPOSING r3 M3’s suggestion, +3.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 3.0, tier C. - M1 Exc on v3’s five sentences: criterion (CB3B 166, 151); Meehan similarity named
then distinguished on Gibbs CJ’s limit (CB3B 183, 581); the carry from D; Core (2A), the honesty fetter put and met, on ‘The
conditions, as construed at D, are the loan’s own terms beyond its ’specified parameters’, terms Rocky would set and judge, so an
implied duty of honesty confines nothing.’; Core (3), both hedges and the reason; Core (4), ‘arguably’. The fn 14 judge was graded
once, at R8. - M2 Exc on the same, checked at CB3B 166, 183 to 184, 190. - v4 change: sentences 3 and 4 rewritten (OPPOSING M3;
VOICE T1, S4); fn 13 now Mason J 588 to 590; fn 14 ‘(Gibbs J)’. The rebuilt sentence has not been graded.

(i) Residual risks (v4 CHANGES §4.1, §4.2). - Walsh J (Mason J agreeing) at 642 to 643 and Gibbs CJ at 579 not put. Both SHEET
I.E credit; the whether-not-how reason answers them in substance. A marker who knows the majority may want it named. At risk
only if Core (2A) is read as unmet: I.E VG 0.75, plus R2’s cap 0.75. Cost: about +12 to +15 for a clause such as ‘and, unlike
Godecke’s majority, ’satisfactory’ imports no objective standard’, with its own marker to Godecke 642 to 643 (Walsh J). - The
reasonableness limb is met by statement, not argument. If ‘reasonably’ were implied, the conditions Rocky could set would be
reasonable ones, and a court could fix them, which weakens ‘which could withhold the loan itself’. The answer’s implicit replies are
that the email says ‘satisfactory’, not ‘reasonable’, and that D decides the outcome. Cost of an express reply: about +8. - Two
parenthetical cross-references in Part I (‘(D)’ here; ‘(II.G)’ at I.F2) against R1’s ‘at most about one per Part’. The sheet’s own counted
model spent three in Part I (‘(D, E)’, ‘(D)’, ‘(II.G)’). Low risk.
I.F1 Privity: Rocky lent nothing (agency)

v4 text: ‘Even if the email bound, AMPL was Rocky’s agent only if it contracted for him, not solely for itself:[fn 15] though ’Rocky
asked’, AMPL lent ‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’, and took his guarantee, so Rocky lent nothing.’

(a) Issue. Even if the 12 February email bound, whether Rocky lent anything under it, that is, whether the 27 February advance was
Rocky’s loan made through AMPL as his agent. Rocky and Grace are the email’s only parties, so privity of the email is not the
question.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘On 27 February 2024, Rocky asked A-Maize Pty Ltd, (’AMPL’) a company owned and controlled by Rocky’s
cousin, Pierre, to advance $1,150,000 to Grace. Pierre agreed to provide the money to Grace and the $1,150,000 was advanced by
AMPL on the same day.’ - Rocky’s email: ‘I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest’. - Narrator:
‘The Loan Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘The loan was
recorded as $1,150,000 (’Loan’) with an interest rate of 4% per annum.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Port Jackson Stevedoring Pty Ltd v Salmond & Spraggon (Aust) Pty Ltd (1978) 139 CLR 231, 269 (Mason
and Jacobs JJ; majority on the result), quoting Lord Reid in Scruttons Ltd v Midland Silicones Ltd [1962] AC 446, 474: ‘(secondly) the
bill of lading makes it clear that the carrier, in addition to contracting for these provisions on his own behalf, is also contracting as
agent for the stevedore …, (thirdly) the carrier has authority from the stevedore to do that, or perhaps later ratification by the
stevedore would suffice’ (OFF Port Jackson, line 262, the paragraph closing ‘(at p269)’; read for this map). - Course statement of the
same elements (CB4 336, [11.70], editors): the principal ‘expressly or impliedly consented to the agent acting on the principal’s
behalf’ and the agent ‘was purporting to act on behalf of the principal and not solely on the agent’s own behalf’. - Rocky’s argument
(agency, so he lent through AMPL): ‘Rocky asked’; ‘Pierre agreed to provide the money’; Lord Reid’s ‘or perhaps later ratification’
(OPPOSING r3 I.F(1)). - Grace’s best: AMPL lent its own money on its own terms. ‘$1,150,000’, not ‘$1 million’; 27 February, not ‘by
15 February’; ‘4%’, not ‘5%’; and AMPL took Rocky’s guarantee, which no lender takes from its own principal.

(d) Decisive reason. - A lender that takes its supposed principal’s guarantee in its own document contracts for itself. - The sum
differs from the sum promised. - ‘Rocky asked’ goes at most to consent; it says nothing of whom AMPL purported to act for. - The
guarantee is the fact that goes to purporting; the sum alone would show only non-performance (U5).

conclusion is Poor with D6.

cutting for Rocky); why ‘$1,150,000’.
