I.F2 Privity: Rocky and the Loan Agreement

v4 text: ‘Only a party can enforce a contract, and only if he provided consideration;[fn 16] whether one is a party turns on ’the
written instrument itself’, not signature.[fn 17] Mrs Coulls signed, yet the contract ‘purports expressly’ to be between her husband
and the company;[fn 18] likewise AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’ the Loan Agreement. Nothing there makes Grace’s promise one to
Rocky, so he is no joint promisee.[fn 19] Grace’s answer is therefore right, though not because he ‘never signed anything’, and the 5
March demand, arguably premised on 27 February (II.G), fails.’

(a) Issue. Whether Rocky is a party to Grace’s promise to repay in the Loan Agreement and gave consideration for it; whether his
best argument (a joint promisee with AMPL) succeeds; whether Grace’s reason (‘I never signed anything with you’) is the law; what
follows for his 5 March demand.
(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘At the meeting, AMPL and Grace entered into a written loan agreement (the ’Loan Agreement’).’ - Narrator:
‘the clause was included in the Loan Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL.’ - Narrator: ‘On 5 March 2025, Rocky
instructed his solicitor to send a letter of demand to Grace requiring repayment of the principal amount under the Loan Agreement
with AMPL.’ - Grace, by telephone to Rocky on 7 March 2025: ‘I never signed anything with you, so you can’t enforce anything.
Leave me alone!’ (the answer quotes only ‘never signed anything’, avoiding the contraction under D9). - Narrator: ‘AMPL argued
that the Loan was advanced on 27 February, and thus the 12 months had begun then.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule, both limbs: Coulls v Bagot’s Executor & Trustee Co Ltd (1967) 119 CLR 460, 494 to 495 (Windeyer J
dissenting on construction; High Court). 494: ‘only those who are parties to a contract can sue upon it. For us that statement is
incontrovertible’. 495: ‘For us the rule prevails that a plaintiff who sues on a promise must show a consideration for it provided by
him’ (CB4 333; OFF Coulls paragraph 18 ‘(at p495)’). - Rule, who is a party: 487 (Taylor and Owen JJ; majority; ratio): ‘the mere fact
that her signature appears does not make her a party; this is a question to be resolved upon a consideration of the written
instrument itself’ (CB4 331). 486: ‘the contract purports expressly to be one made between Arthur Leopold Coulls and O’Neil
Construction Pty Ltd’ (CB4 330). - Rocky’s best argument: he is a joint promisee with AMPL, who may recover though he gave no
consideration (486, conditional: ‘If, however, the correct conclusion is that the widow was a party to the contract it is, to our minds,
clear that she is entitled to receive the royalties payable after her husband’s death notwithstanding that she, personally, gave no
consideration for the company’s promise’). - Rocky’s further point (OPPOSING r3 I.F(2)): if he assented to the guarantee clause
(II.I2), he is a party to a multi-party instrument. - Grace’s best: AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’ the instrument; 487: ‘there was no
express promise by the company to pay royalties to the wife nor is it possible to imply such a promise’; nothing makes her promise
one to Rocky; limb (b) also fails, AMPL having lent (S-19). - Grace’s planted reason: non-signature (wrong in law: signature neither
necessary, Empirnall 536, nor decisive, Coulls 487).

(d) Decisive reason. - Party status turns on the instrument. - The instrument is one AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’. - Nothing in it
makes Grace’s promise one to Rocky, so the joint-promisee argument fails at its premise, a promise made to both. - The Coulls
comparison is the distinction: Mrs Coulls signed and was still no party, because the instrument purported to be between others. -
Assent to the guarantee clause (II.I2) would make Rocky party to that promise only, not promisee of Grace’s (T2; ‘as to that clause
only’ is credit).

(e) Conclusion and strength. Grace’s answer is right in result, wrong in reason; the 5 March demand fails. Strong (header table
C1; S-8; S-19, limb (a) decisive, limb (b) also failing; S-25). The cross-reference to II.G marks the demand’s premise ‘arguably’ (R-M;
CRIT_fidelity_4 Finding 1).

(f) Further information. The Loan Agreement’s heading, parties clause and signature blocks (S-8; they decided Coulls at 482 to
483 and 486). They would change the result only if they named Rocky as a promisee of Grace’s promise, cutting for Rocky; nothing
suggests it. Not written (credit).

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Footnote for the rule: v5 of the sheet stacked Barwick CJ 478 with Windeyer J. R-S(1):
Coulls 494 to 495 alone (478 states only the privity limb and in the same passage says ‘That C provided no part of the consideration
seems to me irrelevant’). Slide 2 states only the party limb (R-U(1)). 2. Privity and consideration fused: VOICE r1 M23. v2 split the
two requirements (+5). 3. Joint promisee: VOICE r2 M11 (unclear ‘Grace’s promise’). v3: ‘Nothing there makes Grace’s promise one
to Rocky, so he is no joint promisee.’ 4. Applying limb (b) in terms: round-2 MARK_2 upgrade 2. Not adopted in v3: a bare ‘Rocky
gave Grace nothing for it’ would meet OPPOSING r2 row 9 (if bound by the clause, Rocky arguably gave consideration on behalf of
the parties to the instrument, Windeyer J at 493 to 494) and so cannot be done in a clause. The party limb decides. Residual credit. 5.
The planted line, in three forms: - v2: ‘right, though not for that reason’. - v3: ‘Grace’s ’I never signed anything’ is therefore right,
though not for that reason’. VOICE r3 M4: the antecedent contradicts itself (‘I never signed anything’ is itself a reason). - v4:
‘Grace’s answer is therefore right, though not because he ’never signed anything’‘. 6. The cross-reference, in three forms: - v2: in
words. - v3: ’arguably premised on the 12 months having run’, which M2 r3 accepted as R1’s preferred verbal form. - M1 r3
comment 3: the counted form ‘27 February (G)’ is clearer, the heading ‘G. Construction’ not saying what is construed. - v4: ‘arguably
premised on 27 February (II.G)’, with ‘II.G’, not ‘G’, because R3 grades a bare letter crossing Parts VG (−2). 7. OPPOSING r3 I.F(2)
(‘even a joint promisee must sue with AMPL’, Coulls 486, ‘an action to recover must have been brought by both promisees and …
would fail if brought by one alone’, +9): credit; unfunded. 8. VOICE r3 O1 (‘In Coulls, Mrs Coulls signed’, +2): unfunded. 9.
Signature reasoning symmetrical (R-R(4); trap T10, with II.I1).

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 7.5, tier C. - M1 Exc on v3’s four sentences: Core (1) and (2) (‘Only a party can enforce a
contract, and only if he provided consideration; whether one is a party turns on ’the written instrument itself’, not signature.’); Core
(3) (the Coulls comparison, no D4 assertion that the Loan Agreement ‘purports expressly’); Core (4) (no joint promisee); Core (5) (the
planted line, right in result and wrong in reason, the demand failing on an ‘arguably’ premise). M1 noted, without deduction, the
thinness of the verbal cross-reference. - M2 Exc on the same, checked at CB4 330 to 331, 333. - v4 change: the last sentence (VOICE
M4; M1 comment 3).

(i) Residual risks. - ‘(II.G)’ is a second parenthetical cross-reference in Part I (with I.E’s ‘(D)’); see I.E (i). - ‘Grace’s answer’ has no
earlier mention in the unit; it is identified by the quoted ‘never signed anything’ in the same clause. Low. - Limb (b) stated in the rule
but not applied (credit).


I.F3 Privity: circumventing the rule

v4 text: ‘AMPL enforcing its loan, agency failing and no trust or estoppel appearing, nothing circumvents the privity rule.[fn 20]’

(a) Issue. Whether any route around privity (the contracting party’s enforcement, agency, trust, estoppel) lets Rocky recover the
principal from Grace.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘On that same date, AMPL contacted Grace directly’. - Narrator: ‘AMPL required the $1,150,000 as soon as
possible and so on 9 March 2025 … AMPL called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky.’ - No
representation by Grace to Rocky, and no holding of Grace’s promise by AMPL for Rocky, appears.

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Trident General Insurance Co Ltd v McNiece Bros Pty Ltd (1988) 165 CLR 107 (Brennan J dissenting on the
result; cited by report, judge named, no pin, R-Y(1)): ‘It was not suggested that agency, trust or estoppel availed McNiece’ (TRI 115);
‘McNiece endeavours to turn aside from the familiar path of privity, trust, agency and estoppel. But there is no other path’ (TRI 201).
Both verified in the reading for this map. - Rocky’s arguments (OPPOSING r3 I.F(3)): - Estoppel: Grace paid interest throughout
while Rocky ‘would check in consistently’, without protest until 7 March. - Trust: courts ‘no longer feel the reluctance to infer the
existence of a trust’ (Brennan J, Trident [24]). - The Trident majority relaxed the rule. - The other side: - No representation by Grace
preceded or induced anything Rocky did. - Nothing shows AMPL intending to hold Grace’s promise for Rocky. - The contracting
party, AMPL, is enforcing for itself. - The majority’s relaxation was confined to third parties named in liability insurance (Mason CJ
and Wilson J).

(d) Decisive reason. Each route fails on a fact: AMPL is enforcing its own loan; agency failed at I.F1; no trust or estoppel appears.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘nothing circumvents the privity rule.’ Strong (C1; S-24 withdrew assignment as a stated route).

(f) Further information. None that changes the advice.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Source of the routes: - v1 and v2 cited ‘Class 4A Slides, slide 3’. R-Z(2) bars slides. - v3
checked Mason CJ and Wilson J first: v3 CHANGES §1 found they discuss trust and estoppel but mention agency only in reporting a
Law Reform Commission conclusion. - So v3 chose Brennan J, who names all three, with ‘dissenting’ in the footnote (R-F). - TRACER
r3 P2 (status-attribution): the majority recognised a further route for insurance third parties, so ‘nothing circumvents’ leans on the
judge who denied any. Its zero-cost alternative was Mason CJ and Wilson J (paras 23, 32 to 33: ‘a trust, an agency relationship or an
enforceable agreement’, and estoppel). - Kept in v4: Brennan J’s list matches the sentence most exactly, the dissent is disclosed, and
the tracer itself called keeping it defensible. The result is unaffected (no insurance). 2. Verdict first: VOICE r3 M5 (‘AMPL enforces
its loan; …’ opens with its conclusion). The auditor’s rewrite dropped the contracting-party route, which SHEET I.F3 Core requires
(Drops VG ‘one route missing’). v4: an absolute clause before the verdict keeping all three (his VOICE 2.7 item 42 form), −1. 3.
Wrong collocation: ‘AMPL enforces its own money’ (U29). v2: ‘AMPL, the contracting party, enforces its loan’. 4. The statutory fifth
route ([11.10]; OPPOSING r2 row 11): rejected under R-Z(4); never named.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 1.0, tier L. - M1 Exc on v3’s ‘AMPL enforces its loan; agency having failed and no trust or
estoppel appearing, nothing circumvents the privity rule.’: all routes on facts; course term; fn 20 verified in the reading. - M2 Exc on
the same (three routes in one line, each on a fact). - v4 change: the absolute-clause order.

(i) Residual risks. Trident without a pin (R-Y(1)): a real marker may note a report citation without pinpoint at R8 (SHEET Part 9
item 7). Brennan J’s dissent on the result (TRACER P2): a weight comment is possible. Both cost 0 body words.



PART II. ROCKY v AMPL (ALTERNATIVELY PIERRE)

Settled frame (ISSUES_SETTLED header C6 to C8; SHEET Part 6 opening). An oral bargain for the $10,000 was formed at the 8
April meeting: moderate to strong against AMPL or Pierre; moderate as to AMPL. Consideration was given (moderate to strong);
intention and certainty are present; nothing was payable on 9 March 2025 (strong). Rocky’s own payment probably does not meet
the condition (moderate to strong against him, R-O). The clause alone cannot bind Rocky (strong). Rocky is probably bound by his
oral undertaking to whoever accepted it (moderate as to AMPL). Timing is open. ‘Answer with specificity to individual Ps’: AMPL and
Pierre are run separately wherever promisor, promisee or onus differs.

II.A Offer

v4 text: ‘What Pierre ’expected’ proposed nothing Rocky could accept, so it was likely an invitation to treat;[fn 21] Rocky’s reply, ‘if
you also promise’, sought a return promise, so he offered a bilateral contract.[fn 22]’

(a) Issue. Who offered what at the 8 April meeting: whether Pierre’s expectation was an offer, and what kind of offer Rocky’s words
made.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘Pierre expressed during the meeting that he expected Rocky to ensure that Grace made all payments under
the Loan Agreement promptly.’ The words are the narrator’s report; Pierre is never quoted. - Rocky: ‘I will do that if you also
promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the Loan.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule for the offer: Gibson 298 (Lord Diplock): a letter is an offer only if ‘a contractual offer capable of being
converted into a legally enforceable open contract … by Mr Gibson’s written acceptance of it’ (CB1A 42). - Rule for the bilateral
contract: Brambles Holdings Ltd v Bathurst City Council (2001) 53 NSWLR 153, 177 (Heydon JA), quoting McHugh JA in Integrated
Computer Services Pty Ltd v Digital Equipment Corp (Aust) Pty Ltd (1988) 5 BPR 11,110, 11,117 to 118: ‘In classical theory, the
typical contract is a bilateral one and consists of an exchange of promises by means of an offer and its acceptance’ (CB1B 78). -
AMPL’s or Pierre’s alternative (OPPOSING r3 II.A): ‘expected’ was itself the offer, and Rocky’s ‘if you also promise’ a counter-offer
(Butler 404, Lord Denning MR: a reply with additions ‘was in law a rejection of the offer and constituted a counter-offer’; credit; S-
31). - Answer: the same bargain results either way, since Pierre ‘agreed’ last.

(d) Decisive reason. An expectation contains no promise by Pierre that Rocky could accept so as to bind Pierre. Rocky’s ‘if you also
promise’ sought a promise in return, not an act, which is the bilateral form.

(e) Conclusion and strength. Pierre’s words ‘likely an invitation to treat’: S-31, moderate to strong. Rocky ‘offered a bilateral
contract’: strong; a unilateral contract found against ‘if you also promise’ is Poor (SHEET II.A Strength).

(f) Further information. None.
(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Course name: VOICE r1 M5 (invitation to treat unnamed at II.A). v2 named it. SHEET II.A
Core accepts ‘likely an invitation to treat, not an offer’ as equally Excellent; R7 needs the name once. 2. Speaker. TRACER r3 P6
(possible error): v3’s ‘Pierre’s ’expected’’ attributed the narrator’s word to Pierre. TRACER r2 P5 had raised the same point at low
risk; v3 drafted and cut it for funding. VOICE r3 M6: quoted words used as nouns (‘Pierre’s ’expected’‘; ’Rocky’s ’if you also
promise’‘). v4: ’What Pierre ’expected’ … Rocky’s reply, ‘if you also promise’, …’ (+2).

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 2.5, tier L. - M1 Exc on v3’s ‘Pierre’s ’expected’ proposed nothing Rocky could accept, so it was
likely an invitation to treat; Rocky’s ‘if you also promise’ sought a return promise, so he offered a bilateral contract.’: criterion and
deciding word for each; two markers. - M2 Exc on the same, checked at CB1A 42 (298) and CB1B 78 (177). - v4 change: the speaker
attribution and the noun phrases.

(i) Residual risks. None recorded.


II.B Acceptance

v4 text: ‘Pierre ’agreed’, manifesting assent to Rocky’s offer, so he accepted for whomever he represented.[fn 23] AMPL would say
nothing bound until execution; yet, as Lord Greene MR said of exchanges of contracts, parties are bound when and how they
contemplate:[fn 24] nothing required a document or reserved a right to withdraw.[fn 25] Both promises therefore likely bind.’

(a) Issue. Whether Pierre’s assent concluded the bargain at the meeting, or whether nothing bound until the Loan Agreement was
executed.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘On 8 April 2024, Rocky, Grace, and Pierre attended a meeting at AMPL’s office.’ - Narrator: ‘Pierre agreed
and the clause was included in the Loan Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL.’ - Nothing says Rocky was to sign
anything.

(c) Arguments. - Rule for acceptance: Empirnall 534 (McHugh JA), ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’ (CB1B 71). -
AMPL’s argument (or Rocky’s, against his own undertaking), from OPPOSING r3 II.B: nothing bound until execution. Heydon JA lists
among the cases where offer and acceptance ‘does not work well’ ‘contracts between numerous parties, or even two parties,
negotiated at meetings but not assented to until each party executes counterparts’ (Brambles 176; CB1B 77). The clause was
included ‘before it was signed’, which shows a signed instrument was the contemplated mode. - Rocky’s answer, from the same page:
Lord Greene MR, of exchanges of contracts, ‘Parties become bound by contract when, and in the manner in which, they intend and
contemplate becoming bound. It is a question of the facts of each case’ (Brambles 176, Heydon JA, quoting Eccles v Bryant [1948] Ch
93, 104; CB1B 77). No document was required of Rocky and no right to withdraw was reserved (Masters 361: parties who ‘wish to
reserve to themselves a right to withdraw’; CB3A 155). - Status: Heydon JA’s meetings example is an example, not a rule that
meetings bind only on execution (S-17); Lord Greene MR’s words are never attributed to the meetings example (D2). The answer
says ‘of exchanges of contracts’.

(d) Decisive reason. Parties are bound when and how they contemplate. Only AMPL and Grace were to sign the Loan Agreement;
nothing in the exchange between Rocky and Pierre made their bargain subject to a document or reserved a right to withdraw.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘Both promises therefore likely bind.’ The two promises stand or fall together (trap T8). S-15:
formation with someone moderate to strong. S-17: binding without the document, moderate.

(f) Further information. None written. Credit: whether Rocky was ever asked to sign.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Eccles v Bryant report: AGLC r1 major 1 found ‘[1948] 1 Ch 93’ copied from CB1B 77. R-
X(2): ‘[1948] Ch 93’ (CB3A 156; official Masters), the first-named parties only. TRACER r2 P4(a) (‘Eccles v Bryant and Pollock’)
rejected under AGLC r 2.1.1. 2. ‘whoever … for’: VOICE r1 M2 and round-1 C1 and C2 (R1 lapse). v2: ‘for whomever he represented’.
3. ‘reserved a document’: round-1 C2 (note-form; the verb cannot govern ‘a document’). v2: ‘nothing required a document or
reserved a right to withdraw’. 4. M2 r3 R1 lapse 1: ‘Both promises therefore likely bound.’ reads as a missing verb. v4: ‘bind’ (0
words). 5. VOICE r3 S5: intransitive ‘bound’ in ‘nothing bound until execution’ (and I.F1’s ‘Even if the email bound’): kept; ‘bind’ is
used intransitively of contracts in the sheet’s own counted forms, and neither marker flagged those two (+1 each to change). 6.
AGLC r3 optional item 3: ‘(Lord Greene MR)’ in fn 24 is redundant where the text names him (identity apparent). Kept for
consistency with fn 14, where both markers required the judge. 7. VOICE r2 M5 (one-clause counter-frame) and F1: v3 merged the
frame into the ‘yet’ sentence and shortened the verdict (−6).

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 3.0, tier C. - M1 Exc on v3’s three sentences: Core (1) criterion and ‘agreed’, subject to who
accepted; Core (2) AMPL’s argument put and met with the analogy disclosed, Masters 361 on its own marker; Core (3) ‘likely’ and

II.C1 Consideration: the price of Rocky’s promise

v4 text: ‘The $10,000 promise, sought by ’if you also promise’, priced Rocky’s undertaking,[fn 26] which moved from him as
promisee;[fn 27] if Pierre promised, Rocky’s detriment likely suffices, though AMPL benefits.[fn 28]’

(a) Issue. Whether the $10,000 promise and Rocky’s undertaking stood in the relation of price and promise, and whether
consideration moved from Rocky, on each alternative of who promised.

(b) Facts. - Rocky: ‘I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘Pierre
agreed’.

(c) Arguments. - Rule, the bargain: Australian Woollen Mills Pty Ltd v Commonwealth (1954) 92 CLR 424, 456 to 457 (the Court;
ratio; said of unilateral contracts, adopted as the bargain requirement by Kirby P in Beaton 168): ‘it should be made to appear that
the statement or announcement which is relied on as a promise was really offered as consideration for the doing of the act, and that
the act was really done in consideration of a potential promise inherent in the statement or announcement’; ‘the relation of a quid
pro quo’ (CB2A 101). - Rule, moving from the promisee: Beaton 181 (McHugh JA), quoting Patteson J in Thomas v Thomas (1842) 2
QB 851, 859; 114 ER 330, 333 to 334: consideration ‘must be moving from the plaintiff’ (CB2A 107). McHugh JA was in the minority
on the result in Beaton; he states Patteson J’s rule, so no status word (R-F). - Rule, detriment: Musumeci v Winadell Pty Ltd (1994) 34
NSWLR 723, 745 (Santow J; NSW first instance): ‘It is of course long settled that detriment to the promisee suffices as consideration’
(CB2B 122). First-instance status not disclosed: the proposition is stated as long settled (R-F). - Pierre’s argument (OPPOSING r3
II.C(1)): a cousin’s promise of ‘$10,000 to me directly once Grace repays’ was a conditional gift; Australian Woollen Mills 457: there
‘may be no relation whatever’ between statement and act. - Answer: ‘if you also promise’ makes the $10,000 the price of the
undertaking.

(d) Decisive reason. Rocky’s own words ask for the $10,000 as the price of ‘I will do that’. The undertaking moved from Rocky. If
Pierre promised, the detriment to Rocky (undertaking to procure another’s payments) suffices though the benefit runs to AMPL.

(e) Conclusion and strength. Consideration moved from Rocky: strong if AMPL promised; moderate to strong if Pierre did (SHEET
II.C1 Strength; header C6, consideration moderate to strong).

(f) Further information. None.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Direction of ‘priced’: OPPOSING r1 5 (MATERIAL) found ‘priced’ used both ways. v2 fixed
one direction throughout: II.C1 ‘The $10,000 promise … priced Rocky’s undertaking’; II.H ‘the $10,000 falls due on what his
undertaking secured’; II.I3 ‘Rocky priced his undertaking at’$10,000’‘. 2. ’given’ and ‘though AMPL benefits’: VOICE r1 S6. v2
‘sought by ’if you also promise’‘; ’though AMPL benefits’ kept. 3. VOICE r3 S6: ‘though AMPL benefits’ reads as a concession that
weakens Rocky’s detriment; ‘though AMPL, not Pierre, benefits’ (+2) unfunded. 4. Tension with II.I2, where AMPL’s $10,000
promise is ‘arguably’ the benefit Rocky took of AMPL’s written offer. II.C1 makes the $10,000 the price of Rocky’s own oral
undertaking. OPPOSING r3 M2 named this; v4 marks II.I2’s use ‘arguably’ (II.I2 (g)).

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 1.5, tier L. - M1 Exc: the grammar right (the undertaking moves from Rocky); promisee named;
‘likely’; three markers (456 to 457; Beaton 181; Musumeci 745). - M2 Exc: the same, checked at CB2A 101, 107; CB2B 122. - v4:
unchanged.

(i) Residual risks. VOICE S6 (+2).


II.C2 Consideration: the existing legal duty rule

v4 text: ‘The existing legal duty rule applies ’at least when’ a party to a pre-existing contract promises the promisee under it no more
than it requires.[fn 29] AMPL would say that ‘also’ and its clause show a guarantee already given; as in Sundell, a promise to ensure
performance already owed is no consideration.[fn 30] Yet no earlier promise binds Rocky: his 27 February request did not itself
establish a contract,[fn 31] and the clause was arguably included after Pierre ‘agreed’. If Pierre promised, even a promise to him to
perform a duty owed to a third party, AMPL, can be consideration.[fn 32] Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ exceeds ‘repayment of
the Loan’, so Rocky likely gave consideration, though an earlier clause would favour AMPL.’

(a) Issue. Whether ‘I will do that’ was only a promise to do what Rocky was already bound to do, and to whom any prior duty was
owed.

(b) Facts. - Rocky: ‘I will do that if you also promise’. - Narrator: ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included in the Loan Agreement
before it was signed by Grace and AMPL.’ - Narrator: ‘The Loan Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed
repayment of the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘Pierre expressed during the meeting that he expected Rocky to ensure that Grace made all
payments under the Loan Agreement promptly.’ - Narrator, 27 February 2024: ‘Rocky asked … AMPL … to advance $1,150,000 to
Grace.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Wigan v Edwards (1973) 47 ALJR 586, 594 (Mason J; Walsh and Gibbs JJ agreeing on this point; majority
reasoning): ‘The general rule is that a promise to perform an existing duty is no consideration, at least when the promise is made by
a party to a pre-existing contract, when it is made to the promisee under that contract, and it is to do no more than the promisor is
bound to do under the contract.’ (CB2B 131). - AMPL’s best: ‘also’ and the clause, described before the exchange, show a guarantee
already given. TA Sundell & Sons Pty Ltd v Emm Yannoulatos (Overseas) Pty Ltd (1955) 56 SR (NSW) 323, 327 (the court, as the
editors quote it at [4.190]; no judge named): the promisor ‘would do what was necessary to ensure that the goods were delivered.
But we are satisfied that the [defendant] was bound to do so under the original contract.’ (CB2B 114). The answer paraphrases and
cites by report (SHEET Part 9 item 18). - Rocky’s four answers, numbered as SHEET II.C2 Core (3) numbers them: - (i) No earlier
binding promise by Rocky appears. - (ii) His 27 February request did not itself establish a contract: Australian Woollen Mills Pty Ltd
v Commonwealth (1955) 93 CLR 546, 550 (Privy Council): ‘The presence of a request does not, however, in itself establish a
contract.’ (CB2A 103). - (iii) On ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included’, the clause arguably followed the agreement (R-M). - (iv)
Ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ (interest included; procuring performance) exceeds a guarantee of ‘repayment of the Loan’ (the
defined principal), so it is ‘more than’ the limb allows. - Rocky on the Pierre alternative: the rule’s second premise fails (the promise
was made to Pierre, any duty owed to AMPL). Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614, 632 (the Board): ‘Their Lordships do not doubt
that a promise to perform, or the performance of, a pre-existing contractual obligation to a third party can be valid consideration’
(OFF Pao On, line 169; course-stated at CB2B 125, [4.300], heading ‘Duty owed to a third party’; the brief-verified pin).

(d) Decisive reason. No pre-existing contract bound Rocky to the promisee when he promised, so the rule’s first premise fails. The
promise also exceeds what a guarantee of the principal would require. On the Pierre alternative the third-party exception applies in
any event.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘so Rocky likely gave consideration, though an earlier clause would favour AMPL.’ S-11: moderate to
strong (re-founded on ‘no earlier binding promise by Rocky is narrated; the clause was included after Pierre agreed’; GAPS’ ‘circular
second limb’ objection rejected).

(f) Further information. The order in which the clause and the $10,000 were agreed. A clause agreed first would favour AMPL (a
pre-existing guarantee to the same promisee, Sundell’s shape). Direction stated (U3).

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Sundell named without its holding: round-1 A1 and A2 graded II.C2 VG (U6). The holding
has been stated since v1 (‘a promise to ensure performance already owed is no consideration’). 2. The rule unnamed: round-2
MARK_1 R7 proxy instance (the existing legal duty rule stated in Mason J’s words but never called the rule); VOICE r1 M7 and r2 M2
(third limb missing). v3 named the rule with its third limb (‘no more than it requires’), −2. 3. ‘AMPL would say ’also’ …‘: garden path
(round-2 MARK_1 R1). v3 ’say that’. VOICE r3 S7: ‘the clause’ had no antecedent in Part II. v4 ‘its clause’. 4. M2 r3 R1 lapse 2: the
Pao On sentence argued on a premise the previous sentence denied (‘Yet no earlier promise binds Rocky’ and then ‘Rocky’s promise
to him to perform a duty owed to AMPL’), with no ‘even if’. v4: ‘even a promise to him to perform a duty owed to a third party,
AMPL, can be consideration’ (+1). VOICE r3 T2 and S11: the course’s own words for the exception are ‘a duty owed to a third party’
([4.300] heading), now matched. 5. Wigan 595 (a volunteered addition as an element of the bargain; S-35): credit, an analogy only,
never a rule of interdependence. 6. The contrary branch (practical benefit exception; bona fide compromise): not engaged, because
the answer does not accept AMPL’s sequence (SHEET II.C2 conditional core). 7. Funding cut proposed by M1 r3 (‘say that’ to ‘say’,
−1): rejected; v4 funded elsewhere, keeping ‘that’ against the garden path.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 5.5, tier K. - M1 Exc on v3’s five sentences: Core (1) (the rule named, hedge kept, premises); Core
(2) (AMPL’s best and Sundell by holding, cited by report); Core (3)(i) to (iv); Core (4) (Pao On 632); Core (5) (tier, reason, direction).
- M2 Exc on the same, checked at CB2B 131 to 132, CB2B 113 to 114, CB2A 103, OFF Pao On 632. The unsignposted alternative was
graded at R1. - v4 change: ‘its clause’; the Pao On sentence.

(i) Residual risks. - ‘exceeds’ unhedged: accepted on the preferred branch (SHEET Part 9 item 38(h)), the verdict’s ‘likely’ carrying
strength. - The practical benefit exception not named on the preferred branch: credit.


II.D Intention to create legal relations

v4 text: ‘No presumption governs cousins; Rocky bears the onus.[fn 33] Against intention, the undertaking resembles a letter of
comfort, which in Banque Brussels conditioned the facility it was made ’to induce’,[fn 34] whereas AMPL had already advanced. Yet
the undertaking was priced at ‘$10,000’ and given ‘at AMPL’s office’. Intention is therefore likely present on both sides, the price
outweighing cousinhood even if Pierre promised.’

(a) Issue. Whether a bargain between cousins, one of them acting through his company, was intended to be legally binding, on both
sides and on both alternatives of who promised.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘a company owned and controlled by Rocky’s cousin, Pierre’. - Narrator: ‘Rocky, Grace, and Pierre attended a
meeting at AMPL’s office.’ - Rocky: ‘if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘the
$1,150,000 was advanced by AMPL on the same day’ (27 February 2024, before the 8 April undertaking).

(c) Arguments. - Rule, onus: Ermogenous [26] (CB3A 137): presumptions doubted; ‘it was for the appellant to demonstrate that
there was such a contract’. - The editors at CB3A 146, [5.90]: ‘no presumption should be made about the enforceability of
agreements made in a social or domestic context’ (read for this map). - Against intention (OPPOSING r3 II.D): cousins; ‘expected’
and ‘ensure’ are words of assurance, the shape of a letter of comfort, ‘not a full-sized guaranty’ (Proscour, adopted by Rogers CJ at
Banque Brussels 521 as French law, credit only, S-23); given after the advance, so not ‘made to induce’. - Banque Brussels Lambert
SA v Australian National Industries Ltd (1989) 21 NSWLR 502, 521 to 523 (Rogers CJ; NSW first instance): ‘the facility was subject
to BBL obtaining a suitable letter of comfort’ (between 521 and 523); statements ‘made to induce another business person to enter
into a business transaction’ (523) (CB3A 144). - For intention: the price (‘$10,000’, ‘to me directly’) and the setting (‘at AMPL’s
office’, in the course of a company’s loan).

(d) Decisive reason. The difference from Banque Brussels (the comfort there conditioned the lending; here the advance came first)
is put against intention. It is outweighed by the price, which marks a bargain whoever promised, and by the commercial setting.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘Intention is therefore likely present on both sides, the price outweighing cousinhood even if Pierre
promised.’ S-33 rates it strong. SHEET II.D departs to moderate to strong with its reason stated (Part 9 item 6: Ermogenous [25] to
[26] make it an objective weighing; no High Court authority in the materials decides a family-and-company weighing). The ‘both
sides’ clause binds Rocky to his undertaking likewise (trap T3).

(f) Further information. None that changes the advice.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. TRACER r3 P3: ‘No presumption governs cousins’ overstates [26] (same point as I.D);
offered ‘Presumptions about cousins aside, Rocky bears the onus’. Rejected at II.D: SHEET II.D Core (1) requires ‘No presumption
either way ([26])’, the editors read Ermogenous so at [5.90], and the rewrite would cost a semicolon near the colon and semicolon
floors. 2. The direction of the comfort-letter point: VOICE r1 M27 and r2 M3 (‘a mark of seriousness’; ‘serious’). v2 and v3 settled on
‘conditioned the facility it was made ’to induce’‘, with ’whereas AMPL had already advanced’ as the difference (U28; S-33). 3. A
contrast connective with nothing to contrast: round-2 MARK_2 R1 (‘However’ after the onus sentence). v3: ‘Against intention’. 4. M1
r3 comment 4 (no deduction): a marker who knows Banque Brussels enforced the letter may want the significance stated, ‘a mark of
seriousness weaker here’ (+6), the grid line’s own words. Residual. 5. The Pierre alternative re-weighed, not merely named:
CRIT_round5 M2. The verdict’s ‘even if Pierre promised’ has carried it since v1.
(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 5.0, tier C. - M1 Exc on all four sentences: Core (1) the onus; Core (2) the course term, the
difference with its reason, direction carried by ‘Against intention’; the price as the answer; Core (3) Pierre re-weighed, ‘both sides’
the consistency clause. - M2 Exc on the same, checked at CB3A 137 [26] and CB3A 144. - v4: unchanged.

(i) Residual risks. ‘weaker here’ not written (M1 comment 4; the grid line says ‘with its direction (’weaker here’)‘): both markers
graded the ’Against intention … whereas’ form Excellent. At risk only on a stricter reading: II.D VG, 1.25. Cost +6.


II.E Certainty

v4 text: ‘Ensuring ’all payments … promptly’, measured by the loan’s timetable, is not ‘so obscure’ that no intention can be
attributed.[fn 35] AMPL’s promise, depending on Grace’s repayment, not its choice, is not illusory.[fn 36]’

(a) Issue. Whether the undertaking and the $10,000 promise are certain enough, and whether AMPL’s promise is illusory.

(b) Facts. - Narrator, reporting Pierre’s expectation: ‘ensure that Grace made all payments under the Loan Agreement promptly’. -
Rocky: ‘once Grace repays the Loan’. - Narrator: ‘Interest was to be paid by Grace monthly, and the Loan was repayable at the expiry
of 12 months.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule, uncertainty: Council of the Upper Hunter County District v Australian Chilling and Freezing Co Ltd (1968)
118 CLR 429, 437 (Barwick CJ), quoting Lord Wright in G Scammell & Nephew Ltd v Ouston [1941] AC 251, 268: a contract fails
only if ‘so obscure and so incapable of any definite or precise meaning that the court is unable to attribute to the parties any
particular contractual intention’ (CB3B 161). The 268 pin is printed in the course at CB3B 184, Mason J reciting the words at
Meehan 587. - Rule, a condition within another’s control: Meehan 581 to 582 (Gibbs CJ): ‘The fact that the condition is one whose
performance lies wholly or partly within the power of one of the parties to the contract does not mean that there is no binding
contract once the condition is fulfilled’ (CB3B 184). - AMPL’s argument (OPPOSING r3 II.E): payment hangs on ‘once Grace repays’,
which may never occur; ‘promptly’ is vague.

(d) Decisive reason. ‘all payments … promptly’ takes its content from the Loan Agreement’s own timetable. AMPL’s obligation
depends on Grace’s act, not on AMPL’s discretion.

(e) Conclusion and strength. Both certain; AMPL’s promise not illusory. Strong (header C6). A contrary conclusion is Poor (D6 if
‘ensure’ or ‘once Grace repays’ is held void).

(f) Further information. None.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Scammell 268: round-2 MARK_1 R8 said the pin is not printed at CB3B 161. v3 rejected
that at source: CB3B 184 prints ‘[1941] AC 251 at 268’ in Mason J’s recital at 587; TRACER r3, AGLC r3 and M2 r3 confirm. 2.
Verdict before reason: VOICE r1 M18. v2: ‘AMPL’s promise, depending on Grace’s repayment, not its choice, is not illusory’. 3.
VOICE r2 S6: ‘AMPL’s promise’ anticipates II.F2’s conclusion (+2). Unfunded.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 2.5, tier L. - M1 Exc on both sentences, each on its own marker. - M2 Exc, checked at CB3B 161
(437), CB3B 184 (581 to 582). - v4: unchanged.

(i) Residual risks. VOICE r2 S6 (+2).


II.F1 Privity: Rocky the promisee; ‘the clause’

v4 text: ‘Rocky, the promisee and payee ’to me directly’, gave consideration, so privity does not bar him.[fn 37] The ‘included’ clause
most naturally means the guarantee clause named before it; even a written $10,000 term would leave him the oral promise.’

(a) Issue. Whether privity bars Rocky’s claim to the $10,000; which clause ‘the clause’ means.

(b) Facts. - Rocky: ‘pay $10,000 to me directly’. - Narrator: ‘The Loan Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally
guaranteed repayment of the Loan.’ (the clause named first). - Narrator: ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included in the Loan
Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Coulls 494 to 495 (Windeyer J dissenting on construction), both limbs (as at I.F2). - AMPL’s argument
(OPPOSING r3 II.F(1)): on the other reading the $10,000 is a term of an instrument AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’, of which Rocky
is not a party (Coulls 486; [11.10] example 1). - Rocky’s answer: the oral promise was made to him for his own consideration and
survives a written record. - Reading A (the guarantee clause) is preferred: the definite article refers back to the only clause
previously named in that passage (S-10, moderate to strong).

(d) Decisive reason. Rocky is the promisee and named payee of an oral promise made for his own undertaking. On either reading of
‘the clause’ the oral promise carries the claim.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘privity does not bar him’. SHEET II.F1: either reading Excellent if both are run and the result is
shown unchanged (Part 9 item 17, a disclosed departure from S-10’s moderate to strong). Header C7: a written $10,000 term adds
nothing.

(f) Further information. Credit: the Loan Agreement’s words, which would show which clause was included.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. A reason for ‘most naturally’: CRIT_harsh_2 F7 and the SHEET core required one. Round-2
MARK_1 upgrade 3 (‘the only one named’) was refined in v3 to ‘named before it’, because the problem also names the Development
Agreement’s clause. 2. ‘just named’: v10’s sheet form was an answer-external deictic (U29). 3. ‘The clause ’included’‘: round-2
MARK_2 R1 (a quotation that makes the clause the subject that included). v3: ’The ’included’ clause’. 4. VOICE r3 S8 offered ‘The
clause later ’included’’ (−2). Rejected in v4: it drops ‘named before it’, the reason SHEET II.F1 Core requires. 5. OPPOSING r3
funding F1 (shorten to ‘’The clause’ most naturally means the guarantee clause’, −5): rejected for the same reason.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 1.0, tier L. - M1 Exc: criterion, both readings, the reason for ‘most naturally’, Coulls 494 to 495
alone. - M2 Exc: both limbs on the oral promise; both readings with the sheet’s accepted ‘named before it’; checked at CB4 333. - v4:
unchanged.

(i) Residual risks. None recorded. Credit: ‘he being party to neither document’ (+6).


II.F2 Privity: who promised, AMPL through Pierre or Pierre personally

v4 text: ‘Who promised turns on the doctrine of agency: whether Pierre, with AMPL’s authority or ratification, contracted for it, not
solely for himself.[fn 38] AMPL, ’owned and controlled’ by Pierre, likely authorised him; his contracting for it is contested: Rocky
asked ‘you’ to ‘also promise’. Yet Pierre spoke ‘at AMPL’s office’ about ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’, and AMPL called
under the guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’, arguably his undertaking. On balance, AMPL likely promised, though ‘you’ keeps Pierre’s
promise arguable, which proof that he disclaimed acting for AMPL would establish.’

(a) Issue. Whether the $10,000 promisor, and so the promisee of Rocky’s undertaking, is AMPL (Pierre acting as its agent) or Pierre
personally. The answer carries the result conditionally into II.C1, II.C2, II.D, II.I1, II.I2, II.I3 and II.I4 (trap T11).

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘a company owned and controlled by Rocky’s cousin, Pierre’. - Rocky: ‘I will do that if you also promise to pay
$10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘Rocky, Grace, and Pierre attended a meeting at AMPL’s office.’ -
Narrator: Pierre ‘expected Rocky to ensure that Grace made all payments under the Loan Agreement promptly.’ - Narrator: ‘AMPL
called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky.’ - Narrator, 27 February (credit): ‘Pierre agreed to
provide the money to Grace and the $1,150,000 was advanced by AMPL on the same day.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Port Jackson 269 (Mason and Jacobs JJ, quoting Lord Reid in Midland Silicones 474): the agent must be
contracting for the principal ‘in addition to contracting … on his own behalf’, with ‘authority from the stevedore to do that, or
perhaps later ratification by the stevedore would suffice’ (OFF, line 262). Course statement at CB4 336, [11.70]: consent, and
purporting ‘not solely on the agent’s own behalf’. - For AMPL as promisor (the better view, S-7): - consent is readily inferred from
‘owned and controlled’; - Pierre spoke ‘at AMPL’s office’ about ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’ (payments to AMPL under
AMPL’s loan); - AMPL later called under the guarantee ‘provided by Rocky’, arguably his undertaking (R-M); - credit: the problem’s
own 27 February usage, ‘Pierre agreed’ preceding an advance ‘by AMPL’. - For Pierre personally (Rocky’s alternative and AMPL’s
possible denial; S-18): - Rocky asked ‘you’ to ‘also promise’; - ‘$10,000 to me directly’ reads as a side payment outside AMPL’s loan; -
the cousinhood; - on Reading A, the $10,000 is nowhere in AMPL’s document (S-10). - OPPOSING r3 II.F(2) added for AMPL: Lord
Reid’s ‘perhaps later ratification’, AMPL’s call adopting the bargain.

(d) Decisive reason. Pierre dealt, at AMPL’s premises, about AMPL’s loan and payments to AMPL. AMPL then asserted Rocky’s
side of the same bargain. Those facts go to whom Pierre purported to act for; ‘you’ is consistent with addressing the company’s
controller.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘On balance, AMPL likely promised, though ’you’ keeps Pierre’s promise arguable’. S-7: AMPL,
moderate; Pierre in the alternative. Ratification does not tip it (S-7 (i); O-7: no court in the set states a rule of ratification in terms).

(f) Further information. Proof that Pierre disclaimed acting for AMPL would establish Pierre’s own promise. That cuts toward the
Pierre branch: Rocky claims the $10,000 from Pierre; AMPL has only the clause; AMPL’s call likely fails for want of consideration
(II.I3, II.I4). Credit: AMPL’s later adoption of the $10,000 promise, cutting toward AMPL.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Promisor strength. [R] (ISSUES.md D4) had AMPL at moderate to strong on ratification,
Ipp AJA’s ‘Those benefits could not be severed’ and Windeyer J’s ‘the company (by its agent O’Neil)’. CONTRA 4 and GAPS A7, C6
challenged it. S-7 settled: moderate. Ratification cannot supply ‘purporting’; Ipp AJA’s is an acceptance rule (analogy); Windeyer J is
illustration; CONTRA’s ‘benefit-only agency’ point rejected. 2. Further information with direction: round-2 MARK_1 and MARK_2
both graded II.F2 VG (none given; U3, core (5) from v11). - v3: ‘, decisively so if he spoke only for himself’ (+1 net). - VOICE r3 M7:
circular (‘Pierre’s promise is decisively arguable if Pierre promised’) and ungrammatical; the auditor preferred cutting the tail (−8).
OPPOSING r3 F2 proposed the same cut, or a ratification clause. - Reviser: cutting would drop SHEET II.F2 Core (5), so v4 used the
further-information form, naming the information (whether Pierre disclaimed acting for AMPL) and its direction (+2). 3. Ratification.
TRACER r3 P1: Lord Reid’s third condition admits ‘or perhaps later ratification’, which v3’s ‘with AMPL’s authority’ omitted. v4:
‘with AMPL’s authority or ratification’ (+2). - OPPOSING r3’s further step, AMPL’s call as ‘later ratification’ deciding who promised,
rejected: O-7; SHEET II.F2 Drops grade ratification as the decisive reason Good. 4. ‘consented’ and ‘purporting’: VOICE r1 M32 and
TRACER r1 PE-5 (‘consent stated as fact’). v2: ‘likely consented’. v3 restated in Port Jackson’s terms: ‘likely authorised him; his
contracting for it is contested’. 5. ‘throughout’ overstated, and a restated reason: OPPOSING r2 row 19 and VOICE r2 F4. v3
removed ‘because Pierre spoke throughout about AMPL’s loan’. 6. Citation: [11.70] (casebook) to Port Jackson 269 under R-Z(3) in
v3. SHEET prefers 240 (Barwick CJ). As at I.F1 (g) 2 and 4.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 4.0, tier K. - M1 Exc on v3’s four sentences: Core (1) both questions as ‘whether’ clauses, a case
cited; Core (2) consent on ‘owned and controlled’; Core (3) Pierre’s best fact put and met; Cores (4) and (5) the alternative pleaded,
the further information with direction (‘decisively so if he spoke only for himself’). M1 noted the R-M inference was marked. - M2
Exc: ‘cores (1) to (5) in full; R-M inference marked’, checked at OFF Port Jackson 269. - v4 change: ‘or ratification’; the tail.
Untested.

(i) Residual risks. - ‘which proof that he disclaimed acting for AMPL would establish’ fronts the relative pronoun’s object; a reader
may parse ‘which proof’ as a determiner phrase and stumble. Map-writer’s observation; R1 lapse risk. Cost: ‘and proof that he
disclaimed acting for AMPL would establish it’, +2. - ‘or ratification’ states Lord Reid’s alternative without his ‘perhaps’, while fn 38
cites the hedged passage at 269. ‘perhaps’ cannot be added (R1 bars it outside quotations as a distanced hedge). Barwick CJ at 240

II.G Construction (the 12 months)

v4 text: ‘The ’12 months’ are construed objectively: pre-contractual conduct is admissible only if the words are ambiguous, and post-
contractual conduct cannot show meaning.[fn 39] The words are arguably ambiguous: the instrument ‘recorded’ the sum ‘advanced’
on 27 February, the transaction’s ‘genesis’.[fn 40] Although the terms appear first on 8 April, the ‘12 months’ attach to ‘the Loan’,
whose use Grace had from 27 February, so the period likely ran from then, though narrowly, unless the agreement dates it
otherwise.’

(a) Issue. Whether ‘repayable at the expiry of 12 months’ ran from the advance on 27 February 2024 or the agreement on 8 April
2024. Decided once here and carried to I.F2 and II.I4 (R-Q; decide-once rule (ii)). It is a question of construction, not uncertainty.

(b) Facts. - Narrator, 27 February 2024: ‘the $1,150,000 was advanced by AMPL on the same day.’ - Narrator, 8 April 2024: ‘The
loan was recorded as $1,150,000 (’Loan’) with an interest rate of 4% per annum. Interest was to be paid by Grace monthly, and the
Loan was repayable at the expiry of 12 months.’ - Narrator: ‘Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025, Grace made appropriate
monthly repayments of the interest on the Loan to AMPL.’ - Grace to AMPL, 7 March 2025: ‘I have until 8 April 2025 to repay and
you won’t see a cent before then’. - Narrator: ‘AMPL argued that the Loan was advanced on 27 February, and thus the 12 months
had begun then.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule, method: - Brambles 163 to 164 and 167 to 168 (Heydon JA; unanimous by adoption, Ipp AJA at 184 and
Mason P at 155, S-2 and O-9): pre-contractual conduct ‘only admissible on questions of construction if the contract is ambiguous and
if the pre-contractual conduct casts light on the genesis of the contract, its objective aim, or the meaning of any descriptive term’
(163); post-contractual conduct ‘not admissible on the question of what a contract means as distinct from the question of whether it
was formed’ (164); ‘the actual opinions of the parties are irrelevant’ (168) (CB1B 73, 76). - 191 (Ipp AJA; Mason P agreeing on the
contractual claim): ‘Where ambiguities exist, mutually known facts establishing the commercial purpose of the contract, the genesis
of the transaction, the background and the context in which the parties are operating will be admissible’ (CB1B 82). Conditional on
ambiguity, and silent on which date a genesis favours (S-3). - For 27 February (AMPL’s argument; the premise of Rocky’s own 5
March demand): the term is said of ‘the Loan’, the defined sum ‘recorded’ as advanced on 27 February; Grace had the use of the
money from then; that advance is the mutually known genesis. - For 8 April (Grace’s argument; Rocky’s best defence to AMPL’s call;
OPPOSING r3 II.G): - the ‘12 months’ and ‘4% per annum’ were first agreed on 8 April, when AMPL and Grace ‘entered into’ the
instrument; - a 12-month term priced at 4% runs from the bargain; - before 8 April Grace held the money on no agreed terms; -
‘appropriate’ monthly payments from 8 April fit that timetable (R-M: proves compliance in that period and no more); - Heydon JA at
167, ‘cannot be resorted to unless the … contract is ambiguous: it is not’. - Excluded on meaning: Grace’s ‘I have until 8 April 2025’,
AMPL’s ‘the 12 months had begun then’, and Rocky’s 2025 emails and demand (post-contractual conduct and subjective beliefs).

(d) Decisive reason. The ‘12 months’ attach to ‘the Loan’, and the Loan was the sum advanced, and in Grace’s use, from 27
February. S-1 calls this the stronger textual point: a reasonable reader of a 12-month term for an advance already in the borrower’s
hands may read it as the life of that advance. It beats the 8 April reading only narrowly, for three reasons S-1 gives: - the terms first
appear on 8 April; - ‘recorded’ governs the new 4% rate as much as the sum, so it does not show the terms pre-existed (CONTRA
1(3), adopted); - the ‘appropriate’ payments from 8 April are consistent with an 8 April anchor. Hence ‘though narrowly’.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘the period likely ran from then, though narrowly, unless the agreement dates it otherwise.’ S-1:
open; best-reasoned a slight lean to 27 February (weak), 8 April a real alternative; both branches carried (II.I4). ‘though narrowly’ is
the weak-strength marker; ‘likely’ alone would be the moderate tier.

(f) Further information. The Loan Agreement’s words: a term dating the period from 8 April reverses the lean, and the call was
then premature as to principal (II.I4). Credit: who drafted; whether interest ran from 27 February (pointing to 27 February); the
parties’ shared beliefs before 8 April (admissible under 191).

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. D1. [R] held 27 February moderate, ‘a course authority tips it’ (Ipp AJA 191; ‘recorded’;
post-contractual conduct excluded; contra proferentem declined). GAPS C1 and A5 and CONTRA 1 challenged it (‘an admissibility
rule, not a commencement rule’; ‘appropriate’ a proven fact; Carlill, Kitto J, Walsh J omitted). S-1 settled: open, slight lean, weak;
‘tips it’ withdrawn. 2. Masters class 1 ‘restatement’ analogy for 27 February: withdrawn (S-50), contradicting IV.3’s finding that the
27 February terms were incomplete. 3. Kitto J’s ‘commencing date’ in Whitlock (456): an analogy too weak to tip it (S-26). 4. Carlill
263 contra proferentem. OPPOSING r2 row 20(iv) proposed it; rejected: the drafter is not stated, and SHEET II.G grades Lindley LJ’s
‘It is for the defendants to shew what it does mean’ as a burden rule Poor (S-27). 5. The lean’s own reason. Round-1 C1 and C2 both
graded II.G VG: the verdict’s only preceding sentence was the 8 April counter (U24). - v2 added a reason. - OPPOSING r2 row 20
(MATERIAL) and TRACER r2 P3: v2 weighed ‘appropriate’ interest after excluding post-contractual conduct. - v3: ‘whose use Grace
had from 27 February’, ‘appropriate’ removed, one hedge. 6. ‘the rate and term’ to ‘the terms’ (v4, −2; SHEET II.G Core (4)‘s
