II.H Condition precedent (‘once Grace repays the Loan’)

v4 text: ‘The bargain binding at once, ’once Grace repays the Loan’ conditions AMPL’s obligation, not formation;[fn 41] on 9 March
Grace ‘had not yet repaid’, so nothing was payable. Read literally or commercially, words naming Grace do not cover Rocky’s
payment:[fn 42] the $10,000 falls due on what his undertaking secured, Grace’s repayment. Nor does the duty to co-operate, ‘to do
everything necessary’ for Rocky’s benefit, assist:[fn 43] nothing suggests AMPL’s call prevents Grace repaying. Rocky’s payment
therefore likely does not meet the condition.’

(a) Issue. Two questions in one unit (decide-once rule (viii)): whether ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ conditions AMPL’s obligation
rather than formation, so that nothing was payable on 9 March 2025; and whether the condition can be met if Rocky, not Grace, pays
AMPL (so that Rocky could pay $1,150,000 and lose the $10,000: trap T13).

(b) Facts. - Rocky: ‘I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace repays the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘on 9
March 2025, when Grace had not yet repaid the Loan, AMPL called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided
by Rocky.’

(c) Arguments. - Rule, classification: Meehan 582 (Gibbs CJ): ‘It is clear that the condition in Special Condition 1(b) is not a
condition precedent to contract. Certain obligations under the contract attached immediately the contract was signed although the
condition had not been fulfilled.’ (CB3B 184). - Rule, construction: Upper Hunter 437 (Barwick CJ): ‘no narrow or pedantic approach
is warranted, particularly in the case of commercial arrangements’ (CB3B 161). - Rule, the duty to co-operate: Beaton 185 (McHugh
JA, citing Mason J in Secured Income Real Estate (Aust) Ltd v St Martins Investments Pty Ltd (1979) 144 CLR 596, 607): ‘The
McDivitts have a contractual duty to do everything necessary on their part to enable the plaintiff to have the benefit of the contract’
(CB2A 109). The principle is Mason J’s in the High Court; McHugh JA’s minority on the result does not change its weight, so no
status word (R-F; never ‘a minority view’). - Rocky’s arguments (OPPOSING r3 II.H; R-O; S-16): - commercially the $10,000 rewards
the Loan’s repayment, which AMPL receives whoever pays; - once Rocky pays under AMPL’s call, the Loan is discharged and Grace
can never repay it, so AMPL’s call, if met, makes the condition impossible, contrary to the duty to co-operate; - prevention by analogy
with Mobil 500 (credit only, with its status: reasoning on an assumed unilateral offer). - AMPL’s answers: - the words are Rocky’s
own and name Grace; - the $10,000 priced Grace’s repayment, the outcome Rocky undertook to procure, not his own payment after
her default; - nothing suggests AMPL’s call stops Grace repaying (a fact, not guarantee law: R-O); - contra proferentem, if anywhere,
runs against Rocky, who used the words (S-32).

(d) Decisive reason. - The bargain bound at once (II.B), so the term conditions AMPL’s obligation; on 9 March Grace ‘had not yet
repaid’. - On construction, literal or commercial, the $10,000 falls due on what Rocky’s undertaking secured, Grace’s repayment.
That meets the commercial reading on its own terms: the commercial purpose was to reward procuring Grace’s performance, not to
reward its failure. - The duty to co-operate is met on its own terms: AMPL omitted nothing necessary to give Rocky the benefit of the
contract, since nothing suggests the call stops Grace repaying. - The pricing point also answers the stronger form (that payment
under the call ends any possibility that Grace repays), because the benefit of this contract is a reward conditioned on Grace’s own
repayment (SHEET II.H Core (4); Part 9 item 4; CRIT_round8 m6).

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘Rocky’s payment therefore likely does not meet the condition.’ S-16: a condition of AMPL’s
obligation, moderate to strong; not payable on 9 March 2025, strong; Rocky’s own payment not meeting it, moderate to strong
against Rocky (R-O; a contrary conclusion capped at VG). T13 is drawn at II.I4 (‘paying, loses the $10,000’).

(f) Further information. Credit: on the 8 April reading of the 12 months, Grace may still repay by 8 April 2025, and the $10,000
then falls due (cuts for Rocky). Whether Grace repays within a reasonable time (S-16: weak to moderate that AMPL is free of the
$10,000 if she does not). Round-3 M2 noted, as a credit gap and without deduction at R6, that whether Grace repays by 8 April 2025
is not addressed.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Strength. S-16 rejected CONTRA 10’s ‘moderate’ in part (moderate to strong against
Rocky). R-O fixed it, and fixed that the narrated non-prevention is a fact, never graded Fair as guarantee law. 2. The commercial
reading. CRIT_round7 M1 and R-T(1): it must be put and met on Upper Hunter 437, not hidden behind Ermogenous [25]. 3.
Classification without its reason: CRIT_round5 M3. ‘The bargain binding at once’ since v6 of the sheet. 4. ‘which becomes
’completely binding’’ misled: OPPOSING r2 row 21. v3 removed it (−7). 5. ‘nor commercially’: VOICE r2 M10. v3: ‘Read literally or
commercially, Rocky’s payment would not meet words naming Grace:’. 6. VOICE r3 M8: dangling modifier (‘Read literally or
commercially’ attached to ‘Rocky’s payment’). v4: ‘Read literally or commercially, words naming Grace do not cover Rocky’s
payment:’ (0). 7. ‘His payment’ with a wrong antecedent: VOICE r2 M1. v3: ‘Rocky’s payment therefore likely does not meet the
condition.’ 8. The stronger co-operation form (payment discharging the Loan). OPPOSING r2 row 22 and r3 II.H: MINOR, ‘+19
unfunded’. SHEET II.H Core (4) records that the pricing point answers it. Residual. 9. McHugh JA’s status. AGLC r1 item 6 wanted
‘dissenting’. Rejected: R-F; the principle is Mason J’s; SHEET II.H Core (3) forbids a status word. 10. The heading. VOICE r1 M10:
‘condition precedent’ unnamed. v2: ‘H. Condition precedent’ (R-X(6), three words for three; Gibbs CJ’s term at 582).

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 4.5, tier C. - M1 Exc on v3’s four sentences: Core (1) the classification with its reason (CB3B 184,
582); Core (2) the commercial reading put and met by the pricing point (Upper Hunter 437); Cores (3) and (4) the duty to co-operate
named, put and met (‘Nor does … assist:’, his signpost); Core (5). - M2 Exc on the same, checked at CB3B 184, CB3B 161, CB2A 109.
- v4 change: sentence 2’s subject (VOICE M8).

(i) Residual risks. - ‘do not cover’ is now unhedged where v3 had ‘would not meet’. The sentence states the construction with its
reason after the colon, and the unit verdict (‘likely’) comes after the counters, so it is not a verdict before analysis on SHEET II.H
Core (2)’s terms. Low. - The stronger co-operation form stated in terms: +19 (credit). - Grace repaying by 8 April 2025: credit, about
+10.


II.I1 Privity: AMPL’s call, the burden aspect

v4 text: ‘Only a contract’s parties are bound by its terms:[fn 44] the guarantee clause binds Rocky only if he manifested assent,[fn
45] signature being neither necessary[fn 46] nor decisive.[fn 47] His ’I will do that’ likely binds him, but to AMPL only if Pierre
accepted for it; otherwise AMPL has only the clause.’

(a) Issue. Whether the clause, in a contract between AMPL and Grace, can by itself bind Rocky; if not, whether he is bound by his
own undertaking, and to whom.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘The Loan Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan.’ This is
the narrator’s description of the clause’s effect, not its words, so the answer never says the clause ‘states’ or ‘records’ a guarantee
(D4). - Narrator: ‘before it was signed by Grace and AMPL’. - Rocky: ‘I will do that’.

(c) Arguments. - Rule, burden aspect: Trident (Deane J; majority on the result; by report, no pin, R-Y(1), (2)): ‘the general rule that
only the parties to a contract are bound by, and entitled to enforce, its terms’ (TRI 203; Deane J’s opening sentence, confirmed
against the official text by TRACER r3). - Rule, assent: Empirnall 534 (McHugh JA): ‘an external manifestation of assent to an offer’. -
Signature not necessary: Empirnall 536: Empirnall was bound though ‘Eric does not sign contracts’ (CB1B 72). - Signature not
decisive: Coulls 487 (Taylor and Owen JJ): ‘the mere fact that her signature appears does not make her a party’ (CB4 331). - AMPL’s
argument: the clause binds Rocky as the narrator’s ‘personal guarantee provided by Rocky’. - Rocky’s argument: he never signed;
and AMPL is no party to his undertaking if Pierre accepted for himself.

(d) Decisive reason. - A contract between AMPL and Grace cannot burden a non-party, so the clause binds Rocky only by his assent
(II.I2). - Signature cuts neither way (T10, matching I.F2). - His oral undertaking binds him to whoever accepted it, which is AMPL
only if Pierre acted for AMPL (II.F2).

(e) Conclusion and strength. The clause alone cannot bind Rocky: strong (S-8; D6 lists ‘the clause in the Loan Agreement binds
Rocky by itself’ and ‘Rocky is not bound to anyone because he never signed’ as confidently wrong conclusions). Bound to someone:
moderate to strong. Bound to AMPL: moderate, capped by S-7 (S-9).

(f) Further information. None beyond II.F2’s.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. Source of the burden aspect. - v1 and v2 cited ‘Class 4A Slides, slide 2’ under R-J and R-N
(no extracted judgment then stated the burden aspect). - R-Y made Trident a course reading; R-Z(2) barred slides. - v3: Deane J. 2.
TRACER r3 side finding: in the course-reading file, lines 206 to 290 under the ‘DEANE J’ heading are in fact Toohey J’s judgment
(official text, TOOHEY J at line 768), and Dawson J is absent. fn 44 rests on line 203, Deane J’s own opening sentence (official line
458), so it is unaffected; any later quotation from lines 206 to 290 must be attributed to Toohey J. 3. ‘to it’, ‘own’ (v2): cut for words,
meaning unchanged. 4. T2 reconciliation (‘as to that clause only’, +4): credit (SHEET II.I1 Credit). 5. VOICE r3 O3 (‘His promise, ’I
will do that’, likely binds him’, +1): unfunded.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 4.0, tier C. - M1 Exc on both sentences: burden aspect (Trident, Deane J, verified); T10; one
marker per proposition (534; 536; 487); ‘likely’; the AMPL/Pierre dependency. - M2 Exc on the same, checked at Trident, CB1B 71 to
72, CB4 331. - v4: unchanged.

(i) Residual risks. Trident without a pin (R8, real-marker risk only).


II.I2 Privity: AMPL’s call, content and assent

v4 text: ‘Rocky promised what Pierre ’expected’, ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’, whereas the clause concerns ‘repayment of the
Loan’. He likely assented to the clause if, with ‘a reasonable opportunity to reject’, he took the benefit of AMPL’s offer ‘with
knowledge of its terms’.[fn 48] If AMPL promised, its $10,000 promise was arguably that benefit.[fn 49] The guarantee ‘provided by
Rocky’ proves he gave one, not that he knew the clause’s words; having ‘attended’ the meeting, he likely assented unless he never
saw them, but not if Pierre promised, AMPL conferring no benefit.’

(a) Issue. What Rocky promised (his oral undertaking, against the clause as described) and whether he assented to the written
content.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘Pierre expressed during the meeting that he expected Rocky to ensure that Grace made all payments under
the Loan Agreement promptly.’ - Narrator: ‘The Loan Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment
of the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘Rocky, Grace, and Pierre attended a meeting at AMPL’s office. At the meeting, AMPL and Grace entered
into a written loan agreement’. - Narrator: ‘the clause was included in the Loan Agreement before it was signed by Grace and
AMPL.’ - Narrator: ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’. - Nothing says Rocky read or was shown the clause’s words, or
objected.

(c) Arguments. - Rule: Empirnall 535 to 536 (McHugh JA; Samuels JA agreeing; Kirby P to substantially the same effect; ratio): -
535: ‘where an offeree with a reasonable opportunity to reject the offer of goods or services takes the benefit of them under
circumstances which indicate that they were to be paid for in accordance with the offer, it is open to the tribunal of fact to hold that
the offer was accepted according to its terms’; ‘This formulation states acceptance in terms of a rule of law. However, the question is
one of fact’; - 536: ‘taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms’ (CB1B 72). - The ticket-case words ‘has or ought to
have knowledge’ are McHugh JA’s analogy confined to carriage and bailment, never his rule (CRIT_fidelity_3 M2; CRIT_round3 M3).
- AMPL’s argument: Rocky attended the meeting at which the clause was included; he took the benefit of AMPL’s $10,000 promise;
the narrator says a guarantee was ‘provided by Rocky’. Brambles 179 (Heydon JA, his route; Ipp AJA, Mason P agreeing, reached
acceptance differently): ‘Applying the test stated by McHugh JA in Empirnall … The commercial benefit was a contractual right’
(CB1B 80). - Rocky’s argument (OPPOSING r3 M2): - silence is generally insufficient: an offeror ‘cannot erect a contract between
himself and the offeree by the device of stating that unless he hears from the offeree he will consider the offeree bound’ (Empirnall
534); - knowledge of the clause’s words is not shown; - he was the offeror of ‘that’ and Pierre the acceptor (II.A, II.B), so he accepted
nothing; - the $10,000 priced his own words (‘ensure … all payments … promptly’), not the clause’s (‘personally guaranteed
repayment of the Loan’), and is unpaid; - he did not sign.

(d) Decisive reason. - On the AMPL branch, AMPL’s $10,000 promise is arguably the benefit of AMPL’s offer, and attendance is the
fact going to knowledge. He likely assented unless he never saw the clause’s words. - On the Pierre branch, the benefit the criterion
requires must be the offeror’s (‘taking the benefit of an offer’), and AMPL conferred none, so there is no assent to AMPL’s written
content. - ‘provided by Rocky’ proves a guarantee was given, not that he knew the clause’s words (R-M).

(e) Conclusion and strength. AMPL branch: ‘likely assented … unless he never saw them’. S-9: assent to the written ‘personally
guaranteed’ content moderate on Reading A, conditional on knowledge. Pierre branch: ‘not’, S-18 (the Pierre position weak to
moderate overall, AMPL being the better view).

(f) Further information. Whether Rocky saw the clause’s words: if he never saw them, no assent to the written content (cuts for
Rocky: his exposure is then on his oral content, ‘all payments … promptly’). Credit: the clause’s actual words; whether he objected.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. The longest-running dispute in the answer. 1. Round 1. OPPOSING r1 1 (MATERIAL): ‘taken
nothing’; silence. v2: ‘took the benefit of AMPL’s offer ’with knowledge of its terms’: his entitlement to the unpaid $10,000 was itself
a benefit’ (fn Brambles 182, Heydon JA). U13 (core from v11): ‘of AMPL’s offer’ named so that ‘its terms’ keeps its antecedent. 2.
Round 2. - Round-2 MARK_1 R8, TRACER r2 P1 and OPPOSING r2 rank 1 (MATERIAL): 182 is Heydon JA on consideration, not
assent; ‘unpaid’ implies a sum due against II.H; wrong offer; the Pierre branch. - R-Y(4): replace 182 with Heydon JA where he
applies Empirnall. - v3: ‘He assented to the clause if, … ’with knowledge of its terms’. If AMPL promised, the clause arguably
recorded the bargain whose $10,000 he accepted at the meeting he ‘attended’, without the objection it was for him to make.’ (fn 49
Brambles 179; fn 50 Brambles 181, ‘it was for the defendant to make plain’). 3. Round 3. - M2 R10 VG: II.I2’s unconditional ‘he likely
assented unless he never saw them’ against II.I3’s ‘it entered it for Grace’s promises, not Rocky’s’. - M2 upgrade 2: the verdict on
the same condition as its benefit. - OPPOSING r3 M2 (MATERIAL): ‘the bargain whose $10,000 he accepted’ misdescribes II.A and
II.B (Rocky offered, Pierre accepted), and the verdict presumes knowledge from ‘attended’. - TRACER r3 P4: Empirnall 535 says the
question is one of fact, so ‘He assented … if’ states a rule; P5: Heydon JA’s route at 179 and 181 is not the majority’s. - VOICE r3 S9:
‘whose $10,000 he accepted’ reads as money received. 4. v4’s resolution (v4 CHANGES §1): - ‘He likely assented … if’ (P4, +1); - ‘If
AMPL promised, its $10,000 promise was arguably that benefit.’ (benefit named without making Rocky the acceptor; ‘arguably’
because the $10,000 priced Rocky’s own words); - fn 50 and ‘without the objection it was for him to make’ cut (−17; credit, M2’s
funding note); - ‘having ’attended’ the meeting’ as the stated knowledge fact; - ‘but not if Pierre promised, AMPL conferring no
benefit’ (the Pierre branch on Empirnall’s own element, +12). 5. SHEET Part 9 item 33 (CRIT_round5 m14): Empirnall concerns
goods or services taken on terms; applying it to a conditional promise that was the price of Rocky’s own offer may strike a lecturer
as strained. A drafter who says so loses nothing; v4 does not say so.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 3.5, tier C. - M1 Exc on v3’s four sentences: Core (1) contents with the right speakers; Core (2)
criterion with the offer named (U13), the benefit named, ‘attended’ with the inference marked; Core (3) tier and direction (‘unless he
never saw them’). - M2 Exc on the same, checked at CB1B 72 and CB1B 79 to 81. M2 graded the tension with II.I3 once, at R10. - v4
change: sentences 2 to 4 rewritten. Untested.

(i) Residual risks. - ‘but not if Pierre promised’ is unhedged. S-18 rates the Pierre position weak to moderate, and SHEET II.I2
Credit describes the Pierre benefit point as one that ‘weakens’ assent, not one that negates it. A marker may read ‘not’ as
overstatement (§2: VG at II.I2, 0.875, with R6 capped at VG, 0.5). v4 CHANGES §4.3 records it. Cost: ‘but likely not if Pierre
promised’, +1. - The $10,000 as the benefit of AMPL’s written offer sits against II.C1’s ‘priced Rocky’s undertaking’ (OPPOSING
M2’s point); ‘arguably’ carries it. R10 risk (0.25) if a marker reads two footings. Cost of an express reconciliation: about +8. - The
last sentence carries three qualifications in 27 words; R1 clarity risk, no figure.


II.I3 Consideration from AMPL for Rocky’s undertaking

v4 text: ‘If AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise is its consideration. If Pierre promised, AMPL’s advance was past
consideration,[fn 50] sufficing under Pao On only if, besides Rocky’s request, the parties ’understood that the act was to be
remunerated’.[fn 51] Nothing shows that understanding on 27 February, whereas in Pao On it existed ‘at the time of the main
agreement’.[fn 52] AMPL would rely on entering the Loan Agreement, the clause included; yet Rocky priced his undertaking at
‘$10,000’, not that entry,[fn 53] so AMPL likely gave no consideration.’

(a) Issue. Whether AMPL, calling on Rocky’s undertaking, gave consideration for it, on each alternative of who promised the
$10,000.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘On 27 February 2024, Rocky asked A-Maize Pty Ltd … to advance $1,150,000 to Grace. … the $1,150,000 was
advanced by AMPL on the same day.’ - Rocky, 8 April: ‘I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once Grace
repays the Loan.’ - Narrator: ‘the clause was included in the Loan Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL.’ - Pierre’s
expectation is first reported on 8 April.

(c) Arguments. - Rule, past consideration: Roscorla v Thomas (1842) 3 QB 234, 237; 114 ER 496 (Lord Denman CJ delivering the
judgment of the Court): ‘a consideration past and executed will support no other promise than such as would be implied by law’
(CB2A 113). - Rule, the exception: Pao On [1980] AC 614, 629 to 630 (the Board; Lord Scarman delivering; the extract carries no AC
page markers; pins verified per the brief): ‘The act must have been done at the promisors’ request: the parties must have understood
that the act was to be remunerated either by a payment or the conferment of some other benefit: and payment, or the conferment of
a benefit, must have been legally enforceable had it been promised in advance.’ Applied: ‘The parties understood at the time of the
main agreement that the restriction on selling must be compensated for by the benefit of a guarantee’ (PO extract). - Rule, the
bargain: Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457 (as at II.C1). - AMPL’s case on the Pierre branch (S-12; S-13; OPPOSING r3 M1): - the
advance was made at Rocky’s request (‘Rocky asked’); - a past service ‘raises an implication that at the time it was rendered it was to
be paid for’ (Bowen LJ via the PO extract); - its entry into the Loan Agreement, with the clause ‘included … before it was signed’, was
‘really done in consideration of’ Rocky’s undertaking, a request being ‘expressed or implied’ (Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 458),
detriment sufficing though the benefit goes to Grace; - Pao On 632, a promise to a third party. - Rocky’s case: - nothing shows on 27
February an understanding that AMPL’s advance would be remunerated by a benefit from Rocky; Pierre’s expectation is first voiced
on 8 April; - AMPL’s return was Grace’s interest (credit); - Rocky’s own words price his undertaking at ‘$10,000’, not at AMPL’s
entry, so AMPL’s entry was not what he asked for (Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457: ‘really offered as consideration for the doing
of the act’).

(d) Decisive reason. - AMPL branch: AMPL’s own $10,000 promise is fresh consideration. - Pierre branch, the past advance: it fails
Pao On’s second condition on timing (the comparison named: same shape, different timing). - Pierre branch, the fallback: met by the
bargain requirement; the promise Rocky offered named a different price, so AMPL’s entry was not really done in consideration of the
undertaking as offered.

(e) Conclusion and strength. ‘so AMPL likely gave no consideration’ (Pierre branch). S-12: the past advance unproven under Pao
On’s second condition, moderate to strong against AMPL. S-13: AMPL’s fallback moderate. Either conclusion Excellent if the bargain
requirement is applied (SHEET II.I3 Strength).

(f) Further information. Credit: evidence of an understanding on 27 February (would reverse the Pao On limb, cutting for AMPL);
a recital of consideration in the guarantee clause (O-3: on Pao On’s own reasoning the second precondition ‘is simply one of the
construction of the words of the contract in the circumstances of its making’).

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. The fallback, put but not met (SHEET Part 9 item 41, ‘the residual a lecturer is likeliest to
press’). U2 made the meeting core in v11. v2: ‘AMPL would rely instead on entering the Loan Agreement; yet Rocky priced his
undertaking at’$10,000’, so AMPL arguably gave no consideration.’ 2. Round 2. - Round-2 MARK_1 and MARK_2 both graded II.I3
VG: ‘arguably’, after the fallback was met, takes no lean (§2). - R-Y(4): ‘likely’. - OPPOSING r2 rank 2 (MATERIAL): the price alone
does not answer AMPL on the content gap or the Pierre branch. - v3: ‘AMPL would rely on entering the Loan Agreement; yet, having
already advanced, it entered it for Grace’s promises, not Rocky’s, so it likely gave no consideration.’ 3. Round 3. - M1 comment 5 and
U1: v3 never confronts AMPL’s best fact, that the clause sits in the very document AMPL entered. - M2 R10 and upgrade 1: II.I3
against II.I2 (proposed trap T21). - OPPOSING r3 M1 (MATERIAL): ‘having already advanced’ answers the advance, not the entry,
and one entry can be the price of two promises. - VOICE r3 S10: the pronoun pile-up ‘it entered it … so it’. - v4: ‘AMPL would rely on
entering the Loan Agreement, the clause included; yet Rocky priced his undertaking at’$10,000’, not that entry, so AMPL likely gave
no consideration.’ This is M2’s exact recommended form in substance, AMPL’s best fact put (+1). 4. Pao On’s first condition (U32,
core from v11): ‘besides Rocky’s request’. 5. Past consideration named (VOICE r1 M9; R-X(4)). 6. Roscorla’s ER pin. - AGLC r3 (its
one FIX): the QB report carries a pin and the ER parallel does not, unlike fn 27. Either read the ER page on the ER reprint, or cite
without pins as the casebook heading prints it. - v4 did neither. No course file or saved official text gives the 114 ER page for 3 QB
237; the reviser may not save a new official text; SHEET II.I3 Citation prescribes exactly ‘Roscorla v Thomas (1842) 3 QB 234, 237;
114 ER 496’ (QB pin before the parallel, ‘the ER pin is not in the course materials’). - fn 27 carries ER pins because McHugh JA’s
Beaton 181 prints them (CB2A 107). - Recorded as a disclosed residual (AGLC 1). 7. OPPOSING r3 II.I(3a) (‘, its price being Grace’s
interest’, +5): credit; unfunded.

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 4.0, tier C. - M1 Exc on v3’s four sentences: Core (1) conditional, past consideration named; Core
(2) the first condition on ‘Rocky’s request’, the second on timing with the comparison; Core (3) the fallback put and met with
Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457, ‘already advanced’ being one of S-13’s own ‘against’ reasons. Comment 5 recorded the
unconfronted clause-in-document fact, without deduction. - M2 Exc, checked at the PO extract (629 to 630), CB2A 113, CB2A 101;
the reconciliation with II.I2 graded once at R10. - v4 change: the last sentence. Untested.

(i) Residual risks. - The fuller meeting (the entry not ‘really done in consideration of’ the undertaking, stated in terms): credit. - ‘its
price being Grace’s interest’ (+5): credit. - Roscorla ER pin: an AGLC auditor would again flag it (R8 minor; 0.625 only in
combination with a second minor). Cost 0 body words; needs a verified ER page or the unpinned heading form.


II.I4 Timing and consequences

v4 text: ‘As the 12 months likely ran from 27 February, the call was not premature; if from 8 April, it was premature as to principal.
Nothing shows interest paid after ’8 February 2025’, so a March default is arguable. If AMPL promised, Rocky likely owes AMPL on
his undertaking when Grace defaults and, paying, loses the $10,000; if Pierre promised, AMPL’s call, lacking consideration, likely
fails, and Rocky claims against Pierre and is likely liable to him.’

(a) Issue. Whether AMPL’s 9 March 2025 call was premature, on both readings of the 12 months; the client’s position on each
alternative of who promised.

(b) Facts. - Narrator: ‘the Loan was repayable at the expiry of 12 months.’ - Narrator: ‘Between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025,
Grace made appropriate monthly repayments of the interest on the Loan to AMPL.’ - Narrator: ‘on 9 March 2025, when Grace had
not yet repaid the Loan, AMPL called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky.’ - Grace to AMPL: ‘I
have until 8 April 2025 to repay and you won’t see a cent before then’. - Narrator: ‘AMPL required the $1,150,000 as soon as
possible’ (motive only; it cannot accelerate the term).

(c) Arguments. - Timing: carried from II.G by ‘As the 12 months likely ran from 27 February’, the lean applied. - AMPL on the 8
April reading (OPPOSING r3 II.I(4)): nothing shows interest paid after 8 February 2025, so Rocky’s undertaking to ensure ‘all
payments … promptly’ was engaged by March whatever the principal’s date. The answer says exactly this (‘a March default is
arguable’). - Consequences, AMPL branch: Rocky’s undertaking binds him to AMPL (II.I1), he likely assented to the clause if he saw
it (II.I2), AMPL’s promise is its consideration (II.I3). So he likely owes AMPL when Grace defaults and, paying, loses the $10,000
(II.H; T13). - Consequences, Pierre branch: AMPL has only the clause (II.I1), Rocky took no benefit from AMPL (II.I2), AMPL likely
gave no consideration (II.I3). So AMPL’s call likely fails, and Rocky’s $10,000 claim and his exposure lie against Pierre (T11; S-18).

(d) Decisive reason. Each consequence carries its reason in the sentence: ‘on his undertaking’ (II.I1) and ‘lacking consideration’
(II.I3). That satisfies §1’s tier rule, under which ‘likely’ needs its reason in the sentence or the one before (R-V(1); CRIT_round10
m2).

(e) Conclusion and strength. Timing open (S-1), carried from II.G. AMPL branch: Rocky likely liable (S-9, moderate). Pierre
branch: AMPL’s call likely fails; Rocky likely liable to Pierre (S-18, weak to moderate; S-13 moderate keeps AMPL’s fallback
arguable, which the ‘likely’ respects).

(f) Further information. - Whether the March 2025 instalment was paid: struck from R6’s list, because the ‘arguable’ clause states
the uncertainty and its effect (U3). - Whether Grace repays by 8 April 2025 (credit; M2 noted it unaddressed, without deduction): if
she does, the $10,000 falls due on the 8 April reading, cutting for Rocky.

(g) Disagreements and how settled. 1. ‘only postpones liability’ (v2): TRACER r2 P2 and AGLC r2 10 objected that it states
guarantee law; R-Y(4) removed it. v3 applied G’s lean instead (round-2 MARK_2 upgrade 1). 2. Round 3: M1 and M2 both graded
II.I4 VG. - M1: ‘if Pierre promised, AMPL’s call likely fails’ has no reason in its sentence or the one before. - M2: both alternatives’
‘likely’ verdicts carry no reason and no cross-reference. - M1’s fix: ‘lacking consideration’. M2’s fix: ‘bound by his undertaking’ and
‘unsupported by consideration’, +7. - v4: ‘on his undertaking when Grace defaults’ and ‘lacking consideration’ (+3), funded by the
cuts in v4 CHANGES §2, not by M1’s proposed cuts. 3. VOICE r3 M9: ‘Interest shown paid only to ’8 February 2025’’ is a note-form
reduced relative, and ‘only to’ asserts more than R-M allows. v4: ‘Nothing shows interest paid after ’8 February 2025’, so a March
default is arguable.’ (+1; his ‘nothing suggests’ form). 4. ‘paying,’: VOICE r1 M35 flagged ‘paying,’ and the zeugma ‘exposure lie
against’. v2: ‘if he pays’; ‘Rocky claims against Pierre and is likely liable to him’. v4 returns to ‘paying,’ within its funding (v4
CHANGES §1 table, II.I4 S3). See (i). 5. Hedge density: VOICE r2 S24. v3 removed ‘likely’ before ‘loses’. ‘likely’ at the head of the
predicate governs both verbs; both round-3 markers accepted the unhedged ‘loses’ under R10 (T13). 6. OPPOSING r2 row 28 (a
March interest default engages the undertaking, not the clause; +6): credit; unfunded. 7. v4 CHANGES §4.5: ‘lacking consideration’
names II.I3’s reason; the want of assent (II.I2) is not repeated (+2).

(h) Weight and round-3 grades. 5.0, tier C. - M1 VG, 3.75: Cores (1) to (3) met; Core (4) failed the tier rule on ‘if Pierre promised,
AMPL’s call likely fails, and Rocky claims against Pierre and is likely liable to him’ (no reason in the sentence or the one before, and
no cross-reference to II.I3 in terms). - M2 VG, 3.75: the same failure on both alternatives. - v4 change: both consequences now carry
their reasons. Untested.

(i) Residual risks. - ‘paying,’ reintroduced: round-1 VOICE M35 treated it as a lapse. Map-writer’s observation; R1 lapse risk. Cost:
‘if he pays,’ +2. - The want of assent not repeated in the Pierre consequence: +2. - Whether Grace repays by 8 April 2025: credit,
about +10.

5. Proposed rubric upgrades (only where a real lecturer would demand what the sheet lacks)

U1. II.I3: the fallback must confront the clause in AMPL’s own document. On the alternative that Pierre promised, AMPL’s
strongest fact for consideration is that the guarantee clause was part of the very Loan Agreement AMPL entered: ‘The Loan
Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ and ‘the clause was included in the Loan
Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL’ (question.txt). The bargain test asks whether AMPL’s promise was ‘really done
in consideration of a potential promise’ (Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457, CB2A 101). A lecturer would ask of the answer’s
meeting (‘having already advanced, it entered it for Grace’s promises, not Rocky’s’) why a guarantee written into the document
AMPL signed was not part of what AMPL bargained for; nor does the sheet’s pricing point answer it, since AMPL may read ‘also’ as
‘in addition to entering the Loan Agreement’ (II.I3 Core (3), the sheet’s own words). Proposal: II.I3 Core (3)‘s meeting must name the
clause-in-document fact and answer it (for example, that the clause recorded a bargain struck orally with Pierre for a $10,000 price,
so AMPL’s entry was not given for it), or accept the fallback; a meeting that relies on ’already advanced’ or on the price alone is VG.
Cost about +8; funding is the reviser’s under R-X(3). Material under R-S(5)(b).

U2. I.D: name the category the analogy points to. Reading guide 3A asks ‘What are the different categories of preliminary
agreement? Which are binding on the parties?’, and Masters states the classes at CB3A 155 (360 to 361). An answer that applies
Masters ‘by analogy’ (as this one does) but never says which class the email resembles leaves the reading guide’s own question
unanswered; a lecturer would write ‘Which category?’. Proposal: where the answer relies on Masters by analogy, core (2) requires
the class named in a clause (‘akin to the third class’, +4), the sheet’s current credit item (‘as the third class contemplates’, Part 9
item 36) moving to core. Material under R-S(5)(b), low cost.

U3. Further headings must name their subject. The Instructions mark ‘whether the layout and structure are logical and easy to
follow’ (Instructions p 1). A bare ‘G. Construction’ in a Part with three further headings does not tell the reader what is construed,
and Part I’s cross-reference to the 12 months then has no heading to land on. Proposal: R3 and §5 accept a G, H or I heading only if it
names its subject in course or problem words (‘G. Construction of the 12 months’; ‘G. The 12 months’); a bare doctrinal word is one
heading variant (VG at R3). Cost +2 to +3. Minor to material; the reviser may treat it as MINOR under R-S(5).

1. Margin notes (read cold, as the lecturer)

Preliminary paragraph. - ‘reimburse Rocky for paying AMPL’: Rocky has not paid; ‘if he pays AMPL’ is what you mean. Clear
enough to a lawyer; not deducted. - The Development Agreement is disposed of on its stipulated words, ‘legally binding’ and ‘if the
Project made a profit’, with ‘not yet shown’. Good: a non-issue named and left.

I.A Offer. - ‘an invitation to treat’: the call is classified by the course’s name on its own words. Good. - ‘Gibson’s indicative
paragraph’: which paragraph? It is the Council’s letter’s second paragraph, as Lord Diplock read it. A reader who knows Gibson
follows; a weaker reader would not. Not a misattribution to Lord Diplock, so not deducted. - Direction of Gibson 298 is right: a firm
offer ‘only absent its disclaimer’.

I.B Acceptance. Clean L line: criterion, facts, ‘so it was no counter-offer’.

I.C Consideration. ‘in form’ and ‘arguably implied by ’Confirmed’’ carry the two inferences. AMPL’s price named. Good.

I.D Intention to create legal relations. - Onus, no presumption and the status factor applied to ‘project developers’: good. -
Masters applied ‘by analogy’, the reason stated: good. - ‘As in Niesmann … ’Confirmed’ settled amount, term and rate’: Rocky’s best
case with its authority, and the three settled terms named (so I.E’s ‘Perhaps’ answer is not undercut). - ‘yet ’satisfactory conditions’
left further terms of the loan to Rocky’: this is the crux, and it is asserted rather than argued; it carries Winn v Bull’s ‘a new
agreement’ limb by application, which is enough here. - Further information with its direction (‘unless those terms were settled ’this
morning’’): good.

I.E Certainty. - Meehan distinguished on Gibbs CJ’s own limit, the shared ‘satisfactory’ formula named first: good. - ‘so an implied
duty of honesty confines nothing’: terse to the point of being cryptic; the reason (‘terms Rocky would set and judge’) is there, so it
meets the honesty fetter. - fn 14: no judge in the bracket. Gibbs J is named in the text, but every other footnote carries the judge;
AGLC wants ‘(Gibbs J)’.

I.F1. Criterion in Lord Reid’s form, ‘Rocky asked’ conceded and met by the guarantee taken, figures used. Model L line.

I.F2. - Both limbs, 487 for ‘the written instrument itself’, Coulls compared on its facts, joint promisee named and met: good. - ‘right,
though not for that reason’: the planted line answered as it should be. - ‘arguably premised on the 12 months having run’: this is the
cross-reference to G written in words, the form R1 prefers to ‘(II.G)’. Accepted.

I.F3. Three routes in one line, each on a fact. Good.

II.A to II.B. Classification on ‘expected’ with the criterion; bilateral contract on ‘if you also promise’; Eccles analogy disclosed in the
text; Masters 361 on its own marker. - ‘Both promises therefore likely bound.’: read cold, this parses as ‘are likely bound’ with the
verb missing. Write ‘Both promises therefore likely bind’ or ‘were therefore likely binding’. (R1 lapse 1.)
II.C1. Each proposition has its own marker; ‘Rocky’s detriment’ names the promisee. Good.

II.C2. - Rule named, hedge kept, Sundell put at full strength by holding, Rocky’s four answers with the request tied to ‘27 February’
and ‘arguably’ on the order. - ‘Yet no earlier promise binds Rocky … If Pierre promised, Rocky’s promise to him to perform a duty
owed to AMPL … can be consideration.’: you have just said no duty bound him; the Pao On sentence only works as an alternative
(‘even if a guarantee were already owed to AMPL’). As written the two sentences read against each other. (R1 lapse 2.)

II.D. Letter of comfort, the Banque Brussels difference with its reason (‘whereas AMPL had already advanced’), the price as the
answer, Pierre re-weighed, ‘on both sides’ for Rocky bound likewise. Good. ‘to me directly’ is not used here (it is at F); the price
carries the point.

II.E, II.F1. Clean.

II.F2. Both agency questions in one ‘whether’ clause; consent on ‘owned and controlled’; ‘you’ put; three facts met; ‘arguably his
undertaking’; further information with its direction. K standard met.

II.G. Method, ambiguity decided with ‘arguably’, genesis, both readings, lean with its own reason (‘attach to ’the Loan’, whose use
Grace had from 27 February’), ‘though narrowly’, ‘unless the agreement dates it otherwise’. Good.

II.H. Classification with its reason, condition precedent named in the heading, literal and commercial readings with the pricing
answer, ‘Nor does the duty to co-operate … assist:’ met on its own terms. Good.

II.I1, II.I2. Burden aspect from Deane J; ‘neither necessary nor decisive’ on two markers; Empirnall’s criterion with the offer

II.I3. - Conditional on F; past consideration named; Pao On first condition conceded on ‘Rocky’s request’, second contested on

6. Rubric upgrades a real lecturer would demand (proposed; none changes this mark)

    1. II.I3 core (3) and Appendix A: AMPL’s entry meets a clause in its own instrument. The fallback’s strongest form is not
       ‘AMPL entered the Loan Agreement’ in the abstract but that AMPL executed an instrument that contained Rocky’s guarantee
       clause, ‘included in the Loan Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL’ (question.txt lines 50 to 55), so its promises
       to Grace (‘12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’) are arguably the price of the package, the clause included. The bargain test is
       whether the act ‘was really done in consideration of a potential promise’ (CB2A 101, Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457), and
       detriment to the promisee suffices though the benefit goes to Grace (CB2B 122, Musumeci 745; Pao On 632 for a promise to a
       third party). Proposed: core (3) requires the ‘gave none’ verdict to meet the clause’s place in the instrument (or to concede the
       fallback), and a new trap T21 (an unconditional II.I2 assent finding against a II.I3 ‘not for Rocky’s promise’ finding) is added to
       Appendix A, graded once at R10. Cost about +6 words.
    2. II.I2 core (3): the verdict on the same condition as its benefit. Where the benefit named is AMPL’s $10,000 (‘If AMPL
       promised, …’), the verdict must carry that condition or the Pierre alternative must be addressed; otherwise the verdict reaches
       further than its reasoning. Source: CB1B 72, Empirnall 536 (‘taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms’: the
       benefit must be the offeror’s own). The sheet makes the Pierre weakening credit (S-18); a lecturer reading an unconditional
       verdict after a conditional premise would write ‘Answer with specificity to individual Ps’. Cost about +3 words.
    3. R8: name the only AGLC r 1.3 signals. State that the second-hand forms are ‘, quoting’ and ‘, citing’ only, and that any other
       word (‘discussing’, ‘considering’, ‘applying’) is one minor non-compliance. The sheet’s I.D credit names ‘, citing’ for Niesmann
       but does not say other signals are faults. No body cost.
    4. R1 lapse types: (d) an unsignposted alternative and (e) an intransitive ‘bound’ verdict. (d) a sentence that argues on a
premise the previous sentence denied, without ‘even if’ or ‘were’, is a clarity lapse (his own frame is ‘Even if a duty arose, …’,
VOICE.md 2.1 item 8); (e) ‘X likely bound’ without an object or auxiliary reads as a missing verb and is note-form ellipsis under
the existing type. No body cost.

SHEET_v10_appendix_NOT_FOR_DRAFTERS.md; their counts total 1,494 with the headings, a v10 record that from v11 no longer proves the
v11 cores fit: R-X(3), §1, Part 8; their voice statistics sit inside VOICE.md’s Part ranges; the appendix also carries the identity table,
core item by core item against the sentence that carries it, so that a critic can check R-L(2) line by line, the five counted contrary-
branch paragraphs (II.C2, I.D, I.E, II.G and II.F2) with the whole-body substitution test, and the per-unit first-demotion list).
Everything the core does not list is credit: it earns nothing extra and loses marks only if stated wrongly. The Drops at each unit
trigger only on core items. Official-only passages (Masters 362 on Crossley v Maycock; Godecke 641 to 642, Walsh J adopting Bray
CJ) are credit, never core, because the marker reads against the course materials (R-L(5)). The mandatory quoted facts are reduced
to those that decide a unit’s core (Appendix B); every other fact is credit.

Locator form. [CB4 331 | 487 | Taylor and Owen JJ | majority, ratio] = casebook file, printed casebook page, report pin, speaker,
status. Unit codes in this version: Part I units are I.A to I.F3; Part II units are II.A to II.F2, II.G (the 12 months), II.H (the condition
‘once Grace repays the Loan’) and II.I1 to II.I4 (AMPL’s call); v3’s G, II.G1, II.G2 and II.H1 to II.H5 are those units under their old
codes. CB1A Offer; CB1B Acceptance; CB2A Consideration 1; PO the Pao On extract; CB2B Consideration 2; CB3A Intention; CB3B
Certainty; CB4 Privity; S1A to S4A the slide decks (slide numbers are the PDF page where the deck prints none, as in 4A; a slide
locator in this sheet tells the marker where the course states a point and is never a citation the answer may use: R-Z(2)); OFF = the
official judgment text under 96 Official judgments/text/ (R-H). ‘RG skip’ marks a reading-guide skip range, recorded for the register
and never required or deducted in the answer (R-F).


1. Core and credit (R-B as made precise by R-L)

Every graded unit lists its Core as numbered requirements and its Credit as everything else. Excellent = every core item present
and correct, and no credit item wrongly stated. A core item missing or wrong drops the unit as the Drops say; a credit item is graded
only if stated wrongly (then by the Drops’ ‘credit wrong’ line, never above Very Good for a wrong rule and never above Fair for a
wrong status or speaker that matters). Until v10 the core was exactly what the unit’s appendix paragraph carried, so the floor in the
grid was the measured cost of the core; from v11 that is no longer so (next paragraph).

The cores are the requirement; the floors are a feasibility proof, not a quota (R-X(3)). The 1,495-word ceiling is binding, and
every unit’s Core, as this version states it, is what Excellent requires. The floors printed in the grid and in each unit heading are the
v10 counted paragraphs: a record that the v10 cores fitted in his voice, never a word quota a drafter must hit or may not exceed at a
unit. The v11 cores cost more than the v10 floors (Part 8 states each unit’s v11 core cost at the v10 counted forms; about 1,571
words in all), so no appendix now proves feasibility: the answer itself is the proof, and the answer reviser re-allocates words by
marks at risk per word, funding first every certain error, every UPGRADES_r1 ADOPT AS CORE item and every core this sheet adds,
by (a) zero-cost rewrites; (b) cutting duplication, cross-references, restatements and credit text; (c) compressing units whose result
is not in doubt (Rocky lent nothing on 12 February, I.F1; the preliminary paragraph, P; I.F3; II.E; II.F1), never dropping any unit’s
core. A core item still unfunded is recorded in the map as a residual risk and graded by the unit’s Drops (or Part 8’s first-demotion
list); it is never dropped silently, and this sheet never relaxes a descriptor to make the words fit. A marker grades each unit on its
Core whatever its length: a unit longer than its v10 floor is not over-length, and one shorter is not short, unless R5’s prioritisation or
R1’s conciseness is engaged. References in the descriptors and Part 9 to ‘the slack’, ‘not funded at slack 1’, ‘the counted form’ or
‘credit, written where words allow’ record the v10 word budget and the v10 counted model; from v11 the counted forms are
examples of wording that meets the core, never the only accepted wording, and the answer reviser may fund any credit item under
R-X(3) once the cores are funded.

Four accepted depths (R-B), three of them the tiers in the grid and the fourth a cross-reference (the floor figures in this paragraph
are the v10 records; Part 8 gives the v11 core costs). K (core full IRAC; three units; floors 95 to 126, being II.F2 95, I.D 122 and
II.C2 126: CRIT_round8 m1): the issue in course terms; the governing rule as the source states it with authority, pin and speaker; the
deciding facts quoted; the opposing side’s best point put and met; the decisive reason; a conclusion in the tier for the strength with
its consequence; further information where it changes the advice. C (compact; eleven units; floors 56 to 89, II.I1 56 the lowest and
II.H 89 the highest: CRIT_round8 m1): the issue; the rule’s operative words with authority; the deciding fact; the opposing point in a
clause; the decisive reason; the conclusion with strength. L (one-line disposition; nine units; floors 20 to 48, I.F3 20 the lowest and
I.C 48 the highest, as counted; I.C, II.C1 and II.E are two-sentence L units, at 48, 26 and 35: CRIT_round6 m8): one or two sentences
in which the quoted deciding fact and the operative words of the rule precede the result, joined by ‘so’, ‘therefore’ or a colon, with
the authority footnoted; it is NOT a conclusive statement and is NOT caught by D5. A bare verdict, or a verdict followed by its
reasons in a later sentence, remains conclusion-first (D5). A colon-joined claim-then-proof sentence is his form (VOICE.md 1.3: ‘Colon
= claim, then its proof’) ONLY where the claim before the colon is a classification or a fact claim that the words after the colon prove
(‘The words are arguably ambiguous: the instrument ’recorded’ the sum ‘advanced’ on 27 February …‘;’Meehan is distinguishable:
…‘; ’Purporting is contested: …’); a unit’s verdict stated before its proof (‘Rocky lent nothing: AMPL was his agent only if …’) is
conclusion-first at any level (brief R6; VOICE.md section 4 item 10, ‘Verdict first, proof after a colon’, a feature not to copy) and is
never licensed, whatever follows the colon (R-R(2); CRIT_round4 M8, adopted; v4’s wider carve-out is withdrawn and I.F1’s counted
sentence is rewritten in the L order). The fourth depth: a cross-reference to a doctrine decided in another unit or Part, graded on
the clause that applies the earlier finding to the unit’s own question (§4), as at II.I4 (‘turns on the 12 months (G)’) and I.F2 (‘(II.G)’).

‘The operative words of the rule’ means the criterion the governing authority itself applies (its test, not its label): ‘an external
manifestation of assent’ (Empirnall 534), not ‘an acceptance’; ‘purporting to act on behalf of the principal and not solely on the
agent’s own behalf’ ([11.70]; in a case’s words, the agent ‘contracted for the [principal’s] protection as well as for his own’, Lord
Reid’s requisite (2) as Barwick CJ states it at Port Jackson 240, the case form R-Z(3) prefers), not ‘an agent’; ‘so obscure and so
incapable of any definite or precise meaning’ (Upper Hunter 437), not ‘certain enough’; ‘the fulfilment of a condition upon which the
contract depends’ (Meehan 581; the words sit before the [582] marker), not ‘a condition’. A line that names a category (‘an
unqualified acceptance’; ‘objectively intended to bind’; ‘capable of meaning’; ‘the promisee’) without the criterion is conclusive,
however short, and is graded Good (CRIT_harsh_2 F2, adopted); ‘communicated assent’ or ‘manifested assent’ states the Empirnall
534 criterion in substance and passes (CRIT_round3 m8, adopted).

‘Conclusive’ (the marker’s own usage). A statement is conclusive if it (a) asserts a result without reasons, or (b) quotes facts and
asserts that they meet a test without applying the criterion the governing authority itself uses, or without naming the fact that
satisfies each element of that criterion. Calibration: his LAWS1061 marker graded ‘Jia is partially paralysed, in ’ongoing pain’, and
‘can no longer work in the tech industry’: lasting impairment and lost livelihood apt to produce MDD, an RPI, in a person of NF’
Good, with ‘Further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive’, because Tame and Lederer were not applied. A sentence of
that shape is Good here, however fluent. A sentence of three or more semicolon-joined clauses each of which is a conclusion without
its reason is conclusive (the unit capped at Good) and an R1 lapse.

Verdict tiers (core item at every K and C unit; the L result follows from its line). Unhedged, ‘therefore’ after the subject,
where strong or uncontested; ‘likely’ before the verb where moderate to strong; ‘On balance, the better view is that … likely …,
[reason], though …’ where moderate, weak or open. ‘Likely’ on a strong point is understatement (VG); ‘clearly’ or an unhedged
verdict on a moderate or open point is overstatement (VG). ‘Likely’ alone on a moderate, weak or open point is a tier fault (VG) only
where the sentence also omits the decisive reason; with the reason in the sentence or the one before it, it is accepted (CRIT_harsh_2
F13, adopted; the C and L forms carry strength by the single word ‘likely’). Two limits on ‘the one before it’ (v11): that sentence
counts only if it states a reason FOR THE LEAN, so a preceding sentence that states only the opposing point, or only that a category
of evidence is admissible, supplies no reason, and a lean whose only preceding sentence is the counter has no reason (VG;
UPGRADES_r1 U24, the deciding passage being Brambles 191, which makes ‘the genesis of the transaction’ admissible and says
nothing of which date it favours); and a reason given in another unit counts where the sentence cross-refers to that unit in terms (a
parenthetical or ‘as at …’), the fourth depth applied to a reason (R-V(1); CRIT_round10 m2: II.I4’s ‘likely exposure’ on the Pierre
alternative takes its reason from II.I3 by cross-reference).

Required authorities. The authorities in brackets on each grid line, without ‘eg’, are required for Excellent: one missing is VG;
none is Good. Authorities after ‘eg’ are alternatives, one of which suffices. Credit authorities are named in the descriptors and are
never required.

No meta language; no slide citations; a case for every proposition (R-Z; v12). The answer is advice to Rocky. Its body and
footnotes never mention weeks, classes, lectures, slides, the course, the readings, the syllabus, the rubric or the assignment, and
never frame anything as ‘outside the scope’ (or ‘outside Weeks 1 to 4’, or ‘not covered by this advice’ in course terms); the
restrictions that came from the task still govern what the answer covers, and the answer simply does not say so (R-Z(1), (4)). No
slide is ever cited (R-Z(2); R-A(3) and R-P’s slide limb are withdrawn): wherever this sheet’s Rules at source, Credit or R7’s term list
names a slide (S1A to S4A), that is the marker’s locator only, and the answer states the point in its own words with a case or omits it.
Every proposition is cited to a case, Trident included (R-Y(1)); the casebook is a last resort, used only where no case in the readings
states the proposition (R-Z(3)). Grading (R-Z(5)): a meta reference or a slide citation is an R1 and an R8 fault, each row capped at
Very Good for one instance and at Good for two or more; it is graded at those rows and not again at the unit (one error, one
deduction: Part 7). Every earlier line of this sheet to the contrary is superseded, whether or not v12 edits it.

Decide-once rules. (i) The meaning of ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ is decided once, at I.D (the reading of ‘conditions’ and
whether the parties intended to be bound), with I.E compact on its one decisive authority applied to that reading. (ii) The 12 months
is decided once, at II.G, and carried by cross-reference at II.H and II.I4. (iii) The $10,000 bargain and AMPL’s call are one bargain
whose elements are run once under II.A to II.F; I (AMPL’s call) is confined to the burden aspect, the content of what Rocky promised
and his assent to the written words, AMPL’s consideration, timing and consequences; intention and certainty of the undertaking are
carried by the clause at II.D (‘Rocky being bound likewise’; the onus flip to AMPL is credit). (iv) The objective test of intention is
stated once (I.D) and cross-referred. (v) Each aspect of the general rule in relation to privity is stated once where it bites: the benefit
aspect and the two limbs at I.F2; the burden aspect at II.I1. (vi) The consistency traps a position engages are stated once where they
bite (Appendix A). (vii) The minor claims (the Development Agreement; the Eastwood and Bowral items; any reimbursement by
Grace; the $10,000 as a clause of the Loan Agreement) are satisfied in a clause each. (viii) The condition ‘once Grace repays the
Loan’ is one unit (II.H): whether it is a condition of AMPL’s obligation and nothing is yet payable, and whether Rocky’s own payment
meets it.

2. Tilt rule and strength caps (R-E; symmetric)

Each unit states the settled strength of the better conclusion. Strong (authority decides): a contrary conclusion is Poor and, where
listed in D6, carries that deduction. Moderate to strong: a contrary conclusion is capped at Very Good. Moderate, weak or open:
either conclusion can be Excellent if best-reasoned, and the unit says what best-reasoned requires on each side; required items and
downstream consequences are stated conditionally on whichever conclusion the answer reaches. Overstating strength (an open or
moderate point called clear or stated without a lean) and understating it (‘finely balanced’ where authority decides) carry the same
cap, Very Good; where the misstatement changes the advice to the client (eg ‘the call was clearly premature, so do nothing’; ‘the call
was clearly valid, so pay now’), Good. The rule runs both ways: a tilt toward Rocky beyond the sources (eg ‘Rocky can enforce the
Loan Agreement’; ‘the $10,000 is payable now’; ‘the call was premature’ as clear; ‘Rocky can pay AMPL and still recover the
$10,000’ as clear) and a tilt against him beyond the sources (eg ‘Rocky is bound as guarantor of the principal’ as clear while II.I2 is
open; ‘the call was not premature, so pay now’) are graded alike. Correct advice that is bad news for Rocky is rewarded exactly as
good news is. At any moderate or open unit (I.A, I.D, I.E, II.B, II.F1, II.F2, II.G, II.I2, the fallback limb of II.I3 and the timing limb
of II.I4), a paragraph with no lean and no method is Good; with the method applied and no lean, Very Good; this rule is general and
not confined to II.G (CRIT_round3 m15, adopted). Three disclosed departures from ISSUES_SETTLED’s ratings, each with its reason
stated at the unit as R-R(9) requires (CRIT_round10 m6: v10 printed ‘Two’ and omitted the I.D departure): at I.D an answer that
deploys Crossley 362 and concludes ‘bound’ can reach Excellent, although S-4 rates the point moderate to strong where Crossley is
deployed, because the Court’s own hedges at 362 (‘no special form of words is essential’; ‘Nor is any formula … so intractable’) and
the absence of any contemplated formal contract are reasons the passage itself admits (I.D Strength; Part 9 item 5); at II.F1 either
reading of ‘the clause’ is Excellent if both are run and the result is shown unchanged, although S-10 rates the guarantee reading
‘moderate to strong’, because the ambiguity is textual and the legal result is the same on both readings (Part 9, item 17;
CRIT_round3 m14, adopted); at II.D the AMPL alternative is ‘moderate to strong’, not S-33’s ‘strong’, because Ermogenous [25] and
[26] make the point an objective weighing with the onus on Rocky and no High Court authority in the materials decides a family-and-
company weighing on these facts (II.D Strength; Part 9, item 6; CRIT_round4 m12).

3. Narrator statements (R-D as clarified by R-M; one rule, applied identically everywhere)

A narrator’s description in the problem is a fact to be taken as proven under the Instructions (‘You may assume the facts provided in
the scenario to be proven’), in its exact words and no further; what it implies beyond its words is argued as ‘arguably’, and the
inference is drawn for each side. The three phrases, in R-M’s words, applied the same way whichever party they help: - ‘the clause
was included in the Loan Agreement before it was signed by Grace and AMPL’ proves inclusion before signing and no more; its order
relative to ‘Pierre agreed’ and which clause it was are ‘arguably’ each way (II.C2, II.F1). - ‘the personal guarantee provided by
Rocky’ proves that a personal guarantee was provided by Rocky and that AMPL called under it, and no more; what ‘provided’
consisted of (an oral undertaking, assent to the written words, or both) is ‘arguably’ each way (II.I1, II.I2). - ‘appropriate monthly
repayments of the interest’ between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025 proves that interest was paid monthly, as the Loan
Agreement required, in that period, and no more; what that implies about the commencement of the 12 months is ‘arguably’ each
way (II.G). Likewise: ‘AMPL and Grace entered into a written loan agreement’ proves who entered into it and no more (the heading
and parties clause are not narrated: I.F2); ‘a letter of demand to Grace requiring repayment of the principal amount under the Loan
Agreement with AMPL’ is the narrator’s description of what the demand required, not Rocky’s quoted words nor the letter’s, so ‘the
Loan Agreement with AMPL’ is usable as the proven content of the demand and never as Rocky’s admission (CRIT_fidelity_3 M7,
adopted; I.F2; T5); ‘AMPL called for payment of the Loan under the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ proves the call and that a
guarantee was provided, so that AMPL called ‘on the undertaking’ (the oral promise) is the R-M inference and is written ‘arguably’ at
II.F2 exactly as at II.I1 and II.I2 (CRIT_round3 M8, adopted); ‘The Loan Agreement also included a clause that Rocky personally
guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ is the narrator’s description of the clause’s effect, not the clause’s words, so the answer says ‘the
clause is described as’ or quotes the narrator’s ‘that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, never ‘the clause states’
or ‘records’ (II.I1, II.I2; D4). The words ‘ensure that Grace made all payments under the Loan Agreement promptly’ are the
narrator’s report of what Pierre ‘expected’; Rocky’s words are ‘I will do that if you also promise to pay $10,000 to me directly once
Grace repays the Loan.’ Attributing ‘ensure … promptly’ to Rocky as his words is a D4 speaker fault. An answer that uses any
narrator phrase as evidence, says which use it makes, and marks the inference ‘arguably’, is eligible for Excellent whichever party
the inference helps. The words ‘narrator’, ‘narrated’, ‘narrative’ and ‘the facts narrate’ are this sheet’s analytic labels and
never words of the answer (R-R(1); CRIT_round4 M2): they join R7’s banned list, appear in no core requirement’s prescribed
wording and nowhere in the counted model; the drafter writes ‘nothing suggests’, ‘appears’, ‘is shown’, ‘the facts arguably place’,
‘the clause described first’, ‘as described’, as his Part A does (‘nothing suggests SPC knew or ought to have known’).


4. Evidence rule

A grade of Excellent is valid only if the marker (a) quotes the sentence or sentences of the answer that earn it, (b) names which core
items those sentences meet, and (c) confirms each rule the sentence states against the source page cited in this sheet (not against
this sheet’s paraphrase). A grade without that evidence is void. A sentence earns its full requirement in one unit only; where a later
unit cross-refers, that unit is graded on the clause that applies the earlier finding to its own question. For every grade below
Excellent the marker records the missing core item and a comment in the marker’s style.


5. Placement

Substance is marked, and so is the one placement a ruling fixes. Rocky v Grace may run one A to F walk covering the 12 February
email and the Loan Agreement (the counted structure) or two walks; AMPL’s call is a further heading inside Rocky v AMPL (‘I.
AMPL’s call’), never a Part III: the decide-once rule (§1 (iii)) runs the bargain’s elements once under II.A to II.F, so a Part III would
carry A to F headings with nothing under them or repeat Part II’s analysis, and v5’s Part III option is withdrawn (CRIT_round5 m2,
adopted; R-S(6)). The 12 months sits in Part II (Rocky v AMPL) as ‘G. The 12 months’, where it decides whether AMPL’s call was
premature, with a one-clause cross-reference from Part I where Rocky’s 5 March demand on Grace assumed the earlier date (R-Q;
CRIT_round3 M9, adopted: two headings lettered G and a bare ‘turns on G’ are removed); headings are lettered continuously within
each Part, so Part II runs A to F, G (the 12 months), H (the condition) and I (AMPL’s call). A 12 months placed under Part I is graded
on its substance but costs at R3 (VG), because its relevance to Rocky’s claim against Grace is then unstated and the cross-reference
crosses Parts. What is marked: headings exactly ‘A. Offer’, ‘B. Acceptance’, ‘C. Consideration’, ‘D. Intention to create legal relations’,
‘E. Certainty’, ‘F. Privity’ under each Part, in that order; further headings in course words or in the problem’s own words (‘G. The 12
months’; ‘H. The condition’ (the v10 counted form; ‘condition’ is Gibbs CJ’s word at 581 to 582) or ‘H. The condition ’once Grace
repays the Loan’‘; ’I. AMPL’s call’ or ‘I. AMPL’s call of 9 March 2025’); from v11 headings G, H and I may take a course-vocabulary
form where it costs no more words than the counted form (R-X(6)): ‘H. Condition precedent’ (three words for three; Gibbs CJ at
Meehan 582, CB3B 184: ‘not a condition precedent to contract’, and ‘a condition precedent to completion’), which also names that
doctrine once for R7; a longer course form (‘G. Construction of the 12 months’, +2; ‘I. Privity: AMPL’s call’, +1) is accepted and not
deducted, but its words must be found inside the answer’s own allocation under §1; the brief’s required A to F headings are
unchanged; the sheet’s own labels (‘the payment condition’, ‘prevention’, ‘the Pierre branch’) are never headings or text (R7;
CRIT_fidelity_3 m13, adopted); a heading that adopts the narrator’s ‘personal guarantee’ presupposes the content decided at II.I2
and is a VG at R3.

Part 3. Descriptor: PRELIMINARY

P. Preliminary: claim C3 and the Development Agreement (2.0; L; floor 34)

       Issue. What the advice covers: ‘advise Rocky on the success of any contractual claims he could make’, considering ‘only … the
       course materials from weeks 1 to 4’. The restriction governs what the answer covers; the answer never says so, never names
       weeks or the course, and never frames anything as outside the scope (R-Z(1), (4)).
       Core (v12; R-Z(1) and (5)). P’s core no longer requires excluded matters to be named: v11’s core (1), a clause naming
       breach, damages and guarantee law as ‘outside Weeks 1 to 4’, is withdrawn, and any such clause is from v12 a meta reference
       graded at R1 and R8 under R-Z(5), not here. Breach (including Rocky’s own ‘promptly’ exposure), damages, guarantee law and
       frustration are simply not argued, and an answer that says nothing of them loses nothing. (1) Claim C3 identified and disposed
       of in substantive terms: any reimbursement or indemnity by Grace if Rocky pays AMPL under ‘the personal guarantee provided
       by Rocky’, the claim NAMED so that a cold reader can follow it (reimbursement for paying AMPL: UPGRADES_r1 U31, three of
       six cold readers in Stage-5 round 1 having been unable to identify C3 from ‘no reimbursement’ alone), and disposed of because
       no promise by Grace to Rocky to that effect appears. An accepted form is ‘Grace promised Rocky no reimbursement for paying
       AMPL’ (eight words); the v11 absolute clause ‘Grace having promised Rocky no reimbursement for paying AMPL’ is equally
       accepted where it trails a substantive main clause (CRIT_round6 m11’s order), never one that names matters as excluded; the
       critic’s ‘Grace promised Rocky nothing’ is equally acceptable, though ‘no reimbursement’ does not read against I.C’s inference
       that ‘Confirmed’ arguably implied a promise to repay (CRIT_round5 M5; R-S(2); Part 9 item 29). (2) The Development
       Agreement as stipulated (‘legally binding’), Rocky’s entitlement arising only ‘if the Project made a profit’, which is not yet
       shown (the counted form; never ‘not yet narrated’: R-R(1)), so no present claim. Placement: both items may sit in a preliminary
       paragraph that states only what the advice covers in substantive terms, or, where the answer omits a preliminary paragraph
       (R-Z(1) permits it), wherever the answer first disposes of them (eg C3 in a clause at II.I4, the Development Agreement in a line
       at the head of Part I); they are graded here wherever they appear. A sentence restating the question’s own scope (‘assessed in
       New South Wales on the Weeks 1 to 4 materials’) is from v12 a meta reference graded under R-Z(5) at R1 and R8 (v3’s core
       (1), withdrawn by CRIT_round3 M15, stays withdrawn).
       Credit. ‘a valid and binding clause’ quoted; ‘minimal’ is still a profit, so the condition may be met on completion (further
       information, written with its direction, eg ‘unless the ’minimal’ profit, once realised, triggers it’: R6; UPGRADES_r1 U22
       records this as credit, first among credit if words remain; a drafter who writes ‘not narrated’ without ‘yet’ risks a marker
       reading the planted ‘minimal’ as missed: CRIT_round3 m17); NSW matters because the Electronic Transactions Act 2000

Part 4. Descriptors: PART I. ROCKY v GRACE (27%)
Settled results this Part reaches (ISSUES_SETTLED header table): the 12 February email gives Rocky no claim (strong on the result;
the formation route moderate, intention deciding); the Loan Agreement claim fails on privity (strong). One A to F walk for both is the
counted structure.

I.A Offer: the 5 February call and bullets 2 and 3; bullet 1 offer or invitation to treat (3.0; C; floor 73) [Gibson
298, distinguished and the similarity named with its direction]

     Issue. Whether ‘I will lend $1 million to you by 15 February for 1 year at a rate of 5% interest subject to satisfactory
     conditions’ is an offer capable of acceptance by ‘Confirmed’; and whether anything else in the call or the email could be.
     Rules at source. ‘you must manifest an intention to be bound by acceptance’ and ‘Cannot be an offer if there is not an
     intention to create legal relations’ [S1A slide 11 | slide only: the elements ‘overlap’]; ‘Invitation to treat | An invitation for
     others to make an offer or enter into a negotiation.’ [S1A slide 27 | slide only]; correspondence is read by ‘the conventional
     approach of looking at the handful of documents relied upon as constituting the contract sued upon and seeing whether upon
     their true construction there is to be found in them a contractual offer … and an acceptance of that offer’ [CB1A 41 | 297 | Lord
     Diplock, Gibson v Manchester City Council | ratio; Lord Keith agreeing, Lord Fraser agreeing with Lord Diplock and Lord
     Russell]; ‘The words “may be prepared to sell” are fatal to this; so is the invitation, not, be it noted, to accept the offer, but “to
     make formal application to buy”’ [CB1A 42 | 298 | Lord Diplock | ratio]; the second paragraph: ‘If the final sentence had been
     omitted the wording of the second paragraph, unlike that of the first, with its use of the indicative mood in such expressions as
     “the interest rate will change”, might have been understood by council tenants to whom it was addressed as indicating a firm
     offer of a mortgage’ [CB1A 42 | 298 | Lord Diplock | ratio: the paragraph that is Grace’s analogy]. The direction matters and is
     a D2 fault if reversed (CRIT_fidelity_3 M1; CRIT_round3 M1, adopted): the indicative paragraph might have read as a firm offer
     only WITHOUT its final sentence (‘This letter should not be regarded as firm offer of a mortgage’); with the disclaimer it could
     not. An answer that says a disclaimed indicative promise might be read as a firm offer states the opposite of the page; ‘The
     terms of the first sentence (“we have more work to do”, “where we’re at [499] the moment”, “maybe”) are not those of a
     present offer.’ [CB1A 57 | 498 to 499 | the Court, Mobil Oil Australia Ltd v Wellcome International Pty Ltd] (credit).
     Facts (deciding). ‘proposed that Rocky offer’; ‘I will lend’; ‘Please confirm agreement’; ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’
     (deciding here as well as at D, because the similarity cannot be named without it; Appendix B now agrees). Supporting (credit):
     ‘Potential project over in Eastwood subject to success of Hail Mary Project’; ‘wait and see at present’; ‘long-term’; ‘Confirming
     discussions from our meeting this morning’.
     Core. (1) Grace’s 5 February call classified in a clause on its deciding words, by the course’s name for it (‘proposed that Rocky
     offer’: an invitation to treat, the course’s ‘invitation for others to make an offer or enter into a negotiation’, S1A printed slide
     27; RG1A (2): ‘How is an offer distinguished from an invitation to treat?’; the v11 form, ‘Grace’s call ’proposed that Rocky
     offer’, an invitation to treat’, replaces v10’s ‘a request’, −3: UPGRADES_r1 U7; R-X(4)), and bullets 2 and 3 disposed of in a
     clause ON THEIR DECIDING WORDS as not promissory (the v11 form: ‘bullets 2 and 3, ’Potential’ and ‘wait and see’, promise
     nothing’, +5, ‘wait and see’ quoted on one side of the problem’s dash as D9 requires: UPGRADES_r1 U15, the deciding
     passages being the problem’s ‘Potential project over in Eastwood subject to success of Hail Mary Project.’ and ‘wait and see at
     present.’ against S1A slide 11, ‘you must manifest an intention to be bound by acceptance’; v10’s core asked only that the
     bullets be ‘disposed of in a clause as not promissory’ while the Drops graded ‘the bullets not classified on a deciding word’ VG,
     a contradiction now removed; Part 9 item 44). (2) The issue framed as construction of the exchange. (3) Gibson distinguished
     on its operative words (‘may be prepared to sell’ and an invitation ‘to make formal application’, against ‘I will lend’ with
     amount, date, term and rate and ‘Please confirm agreement’, which invites the assent that concludes a bargain). (4) The
     similarity named with its direction: the Council’s letter’s second paragraph, written in the indicative mood, which Lord Diplock
     construed (the v11 form is ‘the letter’s indicative paragraph’, or ‘the mortgage paragraph’, for v10’s ‘Lord Diplock’s indicative
     paragraph’, which misattributed the letter to the judge: UPGRADES_r1 U27, the deciding passage being CB1A 42, Gibson 298,
     ‘the wording of the second paragraph, unlike that of the first, with its use of the indicative mood … might have been
     understood by council tenants to whom it was addressed as indicating a firm offer of a mortgage’; zero words), an indicative
     promise, might have been understood (his words, or an accurate paraphrase such as ‘could read’) as ‘a firm offer’ only absent
     its disclaimer; ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ may be the disclaimer’s analogue, which is why the qualifier is carried to D
     and E rather than decided here (S1A slide 11: the elements overlap), and the cross-reference ‘(D, E)’ is written. The bare
     parenthetical is the accepted minimum for the carry (CRIT_round4 m2: a marker may read it as a cross-reference rather than a
    reason); the fuller ‘a question for intention and certainty (D, E)’ (+8 words) is credit, written where words allow. (5) A
    classification (an offer in form, or an invitation to treat) in the moderate tier, with the reason in the same or the preceding
    sentence; the counted form is ‘it is likely an offer’, and ‘it is likely an offer in form’ (+2), which says what A decides and leaves
    bindingness to D and E, is credit, written where words allow (CRIT_round5 m9, not funded).
    Credit. The Eastwood condition failing on the narrator’s projection (S1A slide 21, ‘A failure of a condition’, slide only); Rocky
    would be the Eastwood promisor in any case; Rocky’s reply states no terms, so it invites negotiation, not a counter-offer; ‘long-
    term’ explains ‘1 year’; ‘Confirming discussions’ as framing a record; the Restatement definition via [3.10] (editors’ text,
    attributed to the Restatement if used); Willes J’s alternative construction in Felthouse at 876 (a memorandum of a prior
    bargain; ‘the former is the more likely’ [CB1B 70 | 876]); the bullets as ‘discussions’ items that would not be terms of any
    bargain (the former I.E2 severance point is credit: severance presupposes terms, and Whitlock 461 (Knox CJ’s principle as
    adopted by Taylor, Menzies and Owen JJ) must never be stated as the joint judgment’s own words: D2). Further information:
    what was said at the meeting ‘this morning’.
    Strength and tilt. Moderate. Either classification earns Excellent if the qualifier is carried to D and E and the result for Rocky
    is the same; an answer calling it an invitation to treat must meet ‘I will lend’ and ‘Please confirm agreement’; an answer calling
    it an offer must name the second-paragraph similarity.
    Consistency. The qualifier is dealt with once (I.D) and carried; the answer must not hold the email an offer accepted by
    ‘Confirmed’ and then advise Rocky to sue on it without D, E and F (I.F1).
    Citation. Gibson v Manchester City Council [1979] 1 WLR 294, 298 (Lord Diplock) (297 for the conventional approach if
    stated). No slide is cited (R-Z(2); v11’s ‘Slide statements cited by deck and slide number’ is withdrawn): the slide-only points in
    this unit’s Rules (S1A slides 11 and 27) are stated, if at all, in the answer’s own words and footnoted to Gibson where Gibson
    carries them, the invitation-to-treat classification resting on Gibson 298 (‘to make formal application to buy’).
    Drops. VG: Gibson not distinguished on its words, or the second-paragraph similarity not named, or the qualifier not carried to
    D and E, or the 5 February call or the bullets not classified on a deciding word (for the bullets, ‘Potential’ and ‘wait and see’ or
    equivalent words quoted: U15), or the letter’s paragraph described as Lord Diplock’s own (a misattribution of the document,
    graded once here and not also under D2, the words being the letter’s and quoted correctly: U27). The call classified as ‘a
    request’ without the course’s name is graded at R7 (an applied doctrine unnamed), not here. Good: ‘the email is an offer’ with

    promissory. Poor: the direction of Lord Diplock’s second paragraph reversed (a disclaimed promise said to read as a firm offer:
    D2); the qualifier ignored and a binding loan contract declared at A; ‘Confirmed’ treated as the offer; a contract found on 5
    February or a claim on either bullet. Omitted: no offer analysis of the email. Credit wrong (VG): Rocky’s 5 February reply called
