    Poor (D2): Knox CJ’s severance words as the joint judgment’s own, a wrong speaker, which D2 grades Poor with its −3 and §1
    caps at Fair in any event, so v9’s listing of it on the VG line is withdrawn and the fault is graded once, by D2 (CRIT_round9 m4;
    R-U(6)).
    Marker comments. ‘Further analysis is required as your statement is conclusive.’ ‘Distinguish Gibson on its words, ’may be
    prepared to sell’ against ‘I will lend’, and meet the paragraph that resembles the email.’ ‘The second paragraph is the Council’s
    letter, not Lord Diplock’s.’ ‘Name the category: an invitation to treat.’ ‘The qualifier belongs to intention and certainty; carry it
    forward rather than deciding it twice.’

I.B Acceptance: ‘Confirmed’ takes the email as sent (2.0; L; floor 21) [Empirnall 534; eg Butler 404]

    Rules at source. ‘The objective theory of contract requires an external manifestation of assent to an offer.’ [CB1B 71 | 534 |
    McHugh JA (Samuels JA agreeing; Kirby P to substantially the same effect), Empirnall Holdings Pty Ltd v Machon Paull
    Partners Pty Ltd | ratio]; ‘To form a contract, the acceptance must be made in response to the offer.’ [CB1B 66 | [3.100] |
    editors]; a reply with ‘such additions … that it was in law a rejection of the offer and constituted a counter-offer’ [CB1B 94 |
    404 | Lord Denning MR, Butler Machine Tool Co Ltd v Ex-Cell-O Corp (England) Ltd | the traditional analysis shared by Lawton
    and Bridge LJJ; ‘the counter-offer kills the original offer’ is Megaw J’s, quoted]; ‘the offeror may always prescribe the method of
    acceptance’ [CB1B 68 | 233 | Isaacs ACJ, The Crown v Clarke | Higgins and Starke JJ concurring in the result] (credit); receipt
    ‘when the electronic communication becomes capable of being retrieved by the addressee at an electronic address designated
    by the addressee’ [CB1B 90 | Electronic Transactions Act 2000 (NSW) s 13A(1)(a)] (credit).
    Facts (deciding). ‘Confirmed’; ‘15 minutes later’; ‘Please confirm agreement.’
    Core. One sentence: the operative criterion (an external manifestation of assent) and the deciding facts (‘Confirmed’, ‘15
    minutes later’, in the mode the email asked for, adding nothing, so no counter-offer, the doctrine named in the course’s term:
    RG1B (2), ‘What is the legal effect of a counter-offer?’; S1B PDF page 42; the v11 form adds ‘so no counter-offer’, +3:
    UPGRADES_r1 U7; R-X(4)) preceding the result that the reply took the email as sent, qualifier included, so that whatever
    ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ does it does to the whole bargain (D, E). A form that says what ‘Confirmed’ did rather than
    what a word did (‘Grace’s ’Confirmed’ added no term, so it was assent to the whole email, not a counter-offer’) is equally
    Excellent; ‘qualifier included’ must have an antecedent the reader can see in the unit or the cross-reference (R1).
    Credit. Lapse and revocation (nothing suggests either on a fifteen-minute reply; not required: CRIT_harsh_2 F10); receipt
    under s 13A(1)(a) when retrievable at Rocky’s address, ‘arguably’ designated by his using it (one clause is neither required nor
    over-citation; a citation of s 13A for a point it decides nothing on invites ‘the reference should not include’); if anything formed,
    it formed on 12 February 2024; whether ‘Confirmed’ assented to a bargain or confirmed a record of ‘discussions’ is the Masters
    360 question decided at D; Grace’s private need and anger irrelevant (objective test). Lord Westbury’s ‘a term of the assent’
    (Masters 362) concerns an assent given ‘subject to a provision as to a contract’ and is not the rule for an unqualified
    ‘Confirmed’.
    Strength. Strong on correspondence; bindingness turns on D and E.
    Drops. VG: the criterion stated without the deciding facts, or counter-offer not excluded. Good: ‘Grace accepted’ bare. Fair:
    ‘Confirmed’ treated as accepting an unqualified loan. Poor: the postal acceptance rule applied to the email (law wrong: S1B
    slide 35; Brinkibon 41 to 42); ‘Confirmed’ treated as a counter-offer; Lord Westbury’s words applied to Grace’s unqualified
    assent as the rule. Omitted.
    Marker comment. ‘Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition for which it is relied: the postal rule has no
    relevance to an email reply.’

I.C Consideration: a promise for a promise; the Loan Agreement’s fresh terms (2.0; L; floor 48; AMPL’s price
named) [eg Beaton 168, Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457; Roscorla 237 credit here, required at II.I3]

    Rules at source. ‘consideration must be satisfied in the form of a price in return for the promisor’s promise or a quid pro quo.
    The price can be in the form of an act, forbearance or promise.’ [CB2A 104 | 168 | Kirby P, Beaton v McDivitt | majority on the
    result; alone on the consideration question]; ‘there must subsist, so to speak, [457] the relation of a quid pro quo’ [CB2A 101 |
    456 to 457 | the Court, Australian Woollen Mills Pty Ltd v Commonwealth | ratio; said ‘In cases of this class’]; ‘a consideration
    past and executed will support no other promise than such as would be implied by law’ [CB2A 113 | 237 | Lord Denman CJ
    delivering the judgment of the Court, Roscorla v Thomas | ratio]; a new contractual entitlement as consideration: ‘The effect of
    accepting the 19 September 1991 offer was to give a contractual entitlement. That is a benefit capable of amounting to
    consideration’ [CB1B 81 | 182 | Heydon JA, Brambles Holdings Ltd v Bathurst City Council | his reasoning alone: Ipp AJA
    (Mason P agreeing) found consideration in practical benefits (OFF Brambles [116], where Ipp AJA holds the 20 February 1990
    letter ‘a contractual offer … accepted by conduct’, against the premise Heydon JA calls ‘crucial’ at 182, that the 1990 letters
    ‘did not create a contract’; [175] to [176] for the benefits as consideration, ‘The benefits which I have outlined were adequate
    consideration for the October 1991 contract’: CRIT_fidelity_9 Finding 5, v9’s ‘[116], [176]’ corrected)] (credit).
    Facts (deciding). ‘at a rate of 5% interest’; ‘4% per annum’. Supporting (credit): ‘Confirmed’; ‘repayable at the expiry of 12
    months’; ‘the $1,150,000 was advanced by AMPL on the same day’.
    Core. (1) One sentence: the operative criterion (a price given in return for the promise) and the deciding fact: Rocky’s promise
    to lend was given for Grace’s promise to repay, ‘arguably’ implied by assenting to a loan ‘at a rate of 5% interest’ (the inference
    marked: CRIT_harsh_2 F14), the result stated as a bargain IN FORM (‘in form’, +2: UPGRADES_r1 U10), because whether
    Rocky’s promise is illusory, and so whether the consideration is good, is decided at E: ‘A contract made for a consideration
    which is illusory is unenforceable’ and ‘A consideration is illusory if its payment or fulfilment depends upon an unfettered
    discretion vested in the promisor’ (CB3B 166, Pace 150 to 151, McHugh JA), so an I.C that finds consideration without
    qualification and an I.E that finds Rocky’s promise illusory stand on two footings (brief Part 8 item 9; trap T20, Appendix A). (2)
    One sentence on the Loan Agreement with AMPL’s price identified and the inference marked: Grace’s promises to AMPL were
    likely given for AMPL’s promise of the term (‘12 months’) at ‘4% per annum’ (the counted form is ‘were likely given for its
    promise of ’12 months’ at ‘4% per annum’‘, footnoted to the price criterion: CRIT_round4 m3 and CRIT_round5 M7, adopted
    under R-S(2), because ’given for its ’12 months’’ elided the noun the price criterion needs and read as note form; ‘likely’ added
    in v7 because the problem states only that the Loan ‘was repayable at the expiry of 12 months’ and ‘recorded’ the rate, so that
    AMPL’s promise of the term is an implication from the recorded term (§3) and the legal point is moderate to strong (S-21), the
    tier ‘likely’ marks at II.A, II.C1 and II.I1: CRIT_fidelity_6 Finding 1, adopted, +1; ‘for its arguable promise of’ is equally
    acceptable; a drafter who writes ‘for AMPL’s promise of ’12 months’’ is graded the same). The words ‘not the past advance’,
    with Roscorla 237 footnoted, are CREDIT since v5 (moved from core under R-L(3) to fund the round-4 corrections, disclosed in
    Part 8 and Part 9 item 25): the one-line disposal of the Loan Agreement’s consideration survives with its authority, and the
    past-consideration point about the 27 February advance is decided at II.I3, where it bites and where Roscorla 237 remains
    required. The words ‘a bargain rather than a conditional gift’ are credit (moved in v4; the criterion ‘a price for the promise’
    already states the distinction).
    Credit. ‘not the past advance’ in terms, with Roscorla 237 (never stated wrongly: a past advance supports ‘no other promise
    than such as would be implied by law’, the Court’s contiguous words at CB2A 113; v6’s ‘no promise ’other than such as’’ split
    them: CRIT_fidelity_6 Finding 4, corrected); ‘a bargain rather than a conditional gift’ in terms; ‘with interest’ as the content of
    Grace’s promise; whether the 12 February promise is illusory is decided at E; Rocky’s motive irrelevant (‘Motive is not the
    same thing with consideration.’ [CB2A 107 | 181 | Patteson J in Thomas v Thomas, quoted by McHugh JA]); past consideration
    and the existing legal duty rule not engaged on 12 February (both promises executory and simultaneous); no bona fide
    compromise narrated; executory against executed contract (RG1A-Q4); Heydon JA’s ‘crucial’ qualifier with his status; Pao On’s
    first condition for Grace’s promises doubtful because the advance was at Rocky’s request, not Grace’s; the consideration for
    Grace’s promise moved from AMPL, not Rocky (I.F2); Rocky should not run the past-advance point, needing Grace bound for
    the $10,000 ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ (trap T12, credit).
    Strength. 12 February: strong that a bargain was struck in form; the Loan Agreement’s consideration moderate to strong (S-
    21), a contrary conclusion capped at Very Good.
    Drops. VG: the price not identified, or the inference of Grace’s promise asserted as fact without ‘arguably’ (D4 applies if
    quoted facts are altered); Rocky advised to run the argument that the Loan Agreement fails for want of consideration (the legal
    point is moderate to strong, S-21, so R-E caps the contrary conclusion at VG here; the strategic inconsistency, T12, is graded
    once at R10: CRIT_round4 m13; R-R(10)). An unqualified finding of consideration beside an I.E finding that Rocky’s promise is
    illusory (T20) is graded once, at R10, not here (UPGRADES_r1 U10). Good: ‘consideration is present’ bare. Fair: consideration
    found in Grace’s anger or the Development Agreement. Poor: consideration said to be lacking because Grace’s reply contained
    no express promise; Heydon JA’s route stated as the Court’s. Omitted.
    Citation. Beaton v McDivitt (1987) 13 NSWLR 162, 168 (Kirby P) is the counted citation for ‘a price for the promise’ in an
    exchange of promises (Kirby P’s words, ‘a price in return for the promisor’s promise’; CRIT_fidelity_4 Finding 5 identifies 168
    as the price-for-a-promise form); Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457 (the Court, ‘the relation of a quid pro quo’, said ‘In cases
    of this class’, unilateral contracts) is the accepted alternative; neither is deducted (CRIT_round4 m4, rejected as a swap: Kirby
    P’s statement of the orthodox bargain requirement is not a minority view of the law, though he was alone on the consideration
    question’s result, and 168 fits the proposition more precisely).
    Marker comment. ‘Identify the price on both sides: what did Grace give for Rocky’s promise, and what did AMPL give for
    Grace’s?’

I.D Intention to create legal relations: objective test and onus; ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’ decided once;
Rocky’s best case named with its authority (6.0; K; floor 122) [Ermogenous [25] to [26]; Masters 360, 361
(Niesmann) and 363]
Issue. Whether the parties objectively intended to be bound immediately by the email exchange, or exchanged only ‘a record
of terms … as a basis for the negotiation of a contract’.
Rules at source.
     The inquiry ‘requires an objective assessment of the state of affairs between the parties … (as distinct from the
     identification of any uncommunicated subjective reservation or intention that either may harbour)’ and ‘may take account
     of the subject-matter of the agreement, the status of the parties to it, their relationship to one another, and other
     surrounding circumstances’ [CB3A 137 | [25] | Gaudron, McHugh, Hayne and Callinan JJ, Ermogenous v Greek Orthodox
     Community of SA Inc | majority, ratio]; ‘we doubt the utility of using the language of presumptions in this context. At best,
     the use of that language does no more than invite attention to identifying the party who bears the onus of proof.’ [CB3A
     137 | [26] | same].
     The question Masters asked: ‘whether … this document on its true construction constitutes a binding contract … or only a
     record of terms upon which the signatories were agreed as a basis for the negotiation of a contract’; ‘All the essentials of
     a contract are there; but whether there is a contract depends entirely upon the meaning and effect of the final sentence’
     [CB3A 154 to 155 | 360 | the Court (Dixon CJ, McTiernan and Kitto JJ), Masters v Cameron | ratio].
     The three classes, framed for parties who ‘also agree that the matter of their negotiation shall be dealt with by a formal
     contract’ [CB3A 155 | 360]; class 2 requires parties who ‘intend no departure from or addition to that which their agreed
     terms express or imply’ [360]; Niesmann (Rich and Starke JJ, as the Court reports them): signing ‘did not make the
     signing of a contract a condition of agreement, but made it a condition of the obligation to pay’ [CB3A 155 | 361]; class 3
     where parties ‘have dealt only with major matters and contemplate that others will or may be regulated by provisions to
     be introduced into the formal document’ or ‘wish to reserve to themselves a right to withdraw’ [CB3A 155 | 361]; Lord
     O’Hagan, adopted: ‘if any prospective contract, involving the possibility of new terms … remains to be adopted, matters
     must be taken to be still in a train of negotiation’ [CB3A 155 | 361].
     ‘no special form of words is essential’ and ‘Nor is any formula, such as “subject to contract”, so intractable as always and
     necessarily to produce that result.’ [CB3A 156 | 362 | the Court]; Lord Westbury in Chinnock, adopted for the natural
     sense of ‘subject to contract’ [CB3A 156 | 362] (said of an assent given subject to a formal contract; not a rule for an
     unqualified ‘Confirmed’: I.B).
     Jessel MR in Winn v Bull, adopted, for a qualifier not referring to a formal contract: ‘When it is not expressly stated to be
     subject to a formal contract it becomes a question of construction, whether the parties intended that the terms agreed on
     should be put into form, or whether they should be subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not expressed in
     detail’ [CB3A 156 | 363 | the Court adopting Jessel MR; the official text reads ‘should merely be put into form’, the
     casebook dropping ‘merely’ (R-K): quote the casebook’s form or paraphrase]. This is the course passage nearest the
     planted qualifier and is the mandatory decisive authority.
     Official-only, CREDIT, never core (R-L(5)): the sentence the casebook elides at 362: ‘Again, Sir George Jessel M.R. said in
     Crossley v. Maycock (1874) LR 18 Eq 180: “if the agreement is made subject to certain conditions then specified or to be
     specified by the party making it, or by his solicitor, then, until those conditions are accepted, there is no final agreement
     such as the Court will enforce”’ [OFF Masters | paragraph 12, ‘(at p362)’ | the Court | the Court’s own second illustration
     of ‘the natural sense of such words’ | official-only (O-10)]. The Court adopted Jessel MR’s words as showing ‘the natural
     sense of such words’; Crossley’s own facts are not in the materials (gap: Z9), so the answer must not characterise them
     (CRIT_fidelity_2 M1, adopted); the limit to be disclosed if used is that the paragraph is framed on ‘subject to contract’ and
     ‘expressions of similar import’ and keeps the hedges ‘no special form of words is essential’ and ‘Nor is any formula … so
     intractable’.
     Fourth class: parties ‘content to be bound immediately and exclusively by the terms which they had agreed upon whilst
     expecting to make a further contract in substitution’ [CB3A 157 | [5.190] | McLelland J in Baulkham Hills quoting Sinclair,
     Scott & Co v Naughton | editors’ note; S3A slide 24]; the categories ‘are intellectual aids, but whether parties have come
     to a binding agreement is a matter of their objectively ascertained intention’ [CB3A 157 | [26] | Giles JA (McColl JA and
     Young CJ agreeing), Tasman Capital Pty Ltd v Sinclair | editors’ note quoting] (credit).
     Later conduct (credit): ‘post-contractual conduct is admissible on the question of whether a contract was formed … not
     admissible on the question of what a contract means’ [CB1B 73 | 164 | Heydon JA, Brambles | unanimous by adoption: Ipp
     AJA at 184, Mason P at 155 | RG skip (register only)]; Rocky’s ‘cure by later conduct’ argument (‘too uncertain or too
     illusory to enforce at a particular time … may by reason of the parties’ subsequent conduct become sufficiently specific’)
     and its limit (‘must be capable of proving all the essential elements of an express contract’) [CB1B 78 to 79 | 177 to 178 |
     McHugh JA in Integrated Computer Services, quoted by Heydon JA].
Facts (deciding). ‘subject to satisfactory conditions’; ‘Please confirm agreement’; ‘Confirmed’; ‘project developers’ (from v11,
the status factor under Ermogenous [25]: UPGRADES_r1 U4). Supporting (credit): ‘Confirming discussions’; ‘by 15 February’;
no formal document mentioned; ‘since 2017’ and the parties’ relationship; ‘$1 million’; ‘5% interest’; ‘this morning’; ‘I never
signed anything with you’ (post-formation; the planted line is answered at I.F2).
Core. (1) The objective test stated once with the onus on Rocky as the party alleging the contract, no presumption running
([25], [26]); the question framed as whether the parties meant to be bound at once; and the Ermogenous [25] factors WEIGHED
ON THESE PARTIES in a clause, at least their status: ‘the inquiry about this last aspect may take account of the subject-matter
of the agreement, the status of the parties to it, their relationship to one another, and other surrounding circumstances’ (CB3A
137, [25], Gaudron, McHugh, Hayne and Callinan JJ), against the problem’s first sentence, ‘Mr Grace and Mr Rocky are both
project developers who pursued various projects together since 2017 to stellar success’ (the v11 form, after the onus clause: ‘,
their status as ’project developers’ favouring intention’, +7, ‘intention’ as the short form under R7’s note: UPGRADES_r1 U4,
adopted as core because a marker applying [25] expects its factors applied to the parties before the email’s words are
construed; ‘since 2017’ and the relationship are credit; v10 recorded this as a residual risk at Part 9 item 36, now funded into
core). (2) The Masters question at 360 (‘only a record of terms’) framed for this email, with the analogy disclosed: Masters and
its classes assume a contemplated formal contract, absent here, so they apply by analogy (the counted form from v8 is
‘Masters, asking whether a document was ’only a record of terms’, assumed a formal contract, absent here, so applies by
analogy’, the words ‘a contract or’ before the quotation removed (−3) to fund CRIT_round7 M1 under R-R(7)‘s first tier;
’assumed a contemplated formal contract’ (+1), which removes the misreading ‘assumed that there was a formal contract’ and
uses the Court’s own ‘the contemplated formal document’ (CB3A 155, 360), is equally acceptable and is not funded, the slack of
1 being kept (CRIT_round8 m9; Part 9 item 36); the question at 360 is whether the document was a binding contract ‘or only a
record of terms’, so the quoted alternative frames it, and the I.D ‘bound’ branch counted in the appendix has carried this form
since v7 and was graded Excellent on it by two critics; the fuller ‘was a contract or ’only a record of terms’’ (+3) is equally
acceptable: Part 8; Part 9 item 38). The Masters categories need not be named (‘the third class’; ‘class 3’): the reasoning runs
through Winn v Bull at 363, which is the decisive authority for a qualifier that mentions no formal contract, and the reading
guide’s ‘different categories of preliminary agreement’ are credit here, ‘as the third class contemplates’ (+2) being written
where words allow (CRIT_round7 m1; Part 9 item 36). (3) Both best cases from the email’s words, each in a clause, either as
their own sentence or as the clauses of the verdict sentence, Rocky’s named WITH ITS AUTHORITY (CRIT_round4 M6, adopted
in part; R-R(7)): Rocky’s case is Niesmann as the Court reports it at 361, where ‘all the essential terms of a contract had been
agreed upon’ and the one further stipulation was ‘a condition of the obligation to pay’, not ‘of agreement’, so that ‘Confirmed’
settled the essentials and ‘satisfactory conditions’ arguably conditions only the obligation to lend (the v11 form: ‘despite
’Confirmed’ settling amount, term and rate, as in Niesmann’, footnoted Masters 361, the three settled terms named in place of
v10’s ‘settling the essentials’, +2: UPGRADES_r1 U26, because ‘the essentials’ concedes the premise of Gibbs J’s ‘Perhaps it
may be different where agreement has been reached on all essential terms but the determination of subsidiary matters has
been left to one of the parties’ (CB3B 190, Godecke 647), which I.E core (3) then resists, the two units otherwise standing on
two footings (trap T19, Appendix A); the analogy must attach to ‘Confirmed’ settling those terms and never read as authority
for the verdict, Niesmann having found a binding agreement (CB3A 155, 361: ‘all the essential terms of a contract had been
agreed upon’); credit: ‘Please confirm agreement’, the absence of any formal document in terms, and the fuller statement of
the analogy, ‘a loan conditioned only in performance’); Grace’s (‘satisfactory conditions’ reserved the loan’s terms to Rocky).
The fuller form of Rocky’s case (+13 words, the analogy stated in terms with ‘arguably’) could not be funded in any revision
from v5 to v9; Part 9 item 23 records the residual risk and names Niesmann 361 as the authority a drafter uses if words allow.
(4) The decisive authority applied in Jessel MR’s own condition, ‘When it is not expressly stated to be subject to a formal
contract’ (so ‘where no formal contract is stipulated’ or ‘where none is stipulated’, never ‘absent a formal contract’, which
could be read as ‘no formal contract was executed’: CRIT_fidelity_3 m14 and CRIT_round3 m19, adopted): the question is
whether the terms ‘should be put into form’ or be ‘subject to a new agreement the terms of which are not expressed in detail’
(Winn v Bull as adopted at 363), applied to unspecified conditions of the loan itself. (5) A verdict in the open-point tier (‘On
balance, the better view is that … likely …, [reason], though …’) with the further information that decides it (what ‘conditions’
were discussed ‘this morning’ and whether Rocky specified them and Grace accepted them) in the trailing clause, STATED
WITH THE DIRECTION IN WHICH IT WOULD MOVE THE ADVICE, in the ‘unless X’ or ‘if X, Y’ form (the v11 form on the ‘not
bound’ verdict: ‘unless the conditions were settled ’this morning’‘, −2 against v10’s ’though the conditions discussed ’this

the deciding passage being the Instructions p 1, ‘you may indicate what further information you require and how it would

its effect (VG, below; R6). (6) Where the answer relies on Masters’ classes or names one, it calls them by the course’s name,
the categories of preliminary agreement (RG3A: ‘What are the different categories of preliminary agreement? Which are
binding on the parties?’; S3A PDF page 22, ‘What are preliminary agreements?’; CB3A 154 heading ‘PRELIMINARY

I.E Certainty: illusory promise on the reading carried from D; Gibbs J’s dictum with its hedges and the ‘Perhaps’
exception answered with its reason (3.0; C; floor 76) [Meehan 580 to 582; Godecke 646 to 647 (Gibbs J); Pace
