II.E Certainty: ‘all payments … promptly’ measurable; ‘once Grace repays’ not illusory (2.5; L; floor 35) [Upper
Hunter 437 (Barwick CJ, quoting Lord Wright); Meehan 581 to 582]

    Rules at source. ‘So long as the language employed by the parties … is not “so obscure and so incapable of any definite or
    precise meaning that the court is unable to attribute to the parties any particular contractual intention”, the contract cannot be
    held to be void or uncertain or meaningless.’ [CB3B 161 | 437 | Barwick CJ, ‘to use Lord Wright’s words in G Scammell &
    Nephew Ltd v Ouston’, Upper Hunter | the inner quotation never nested; the quoted words are Lord Wright’s, so the footnote
    reads ‘(Barwick CJ, quoting Lord Wright in G Scammell & Nephew Ltd v Ouston)’ and R8’s second-hand list includes him;
    Mason J RECITES the same words at 587 as the respondents’ first proposition (‘The respondents’ case rests on three
    propositions: (1) a contract which is expressed in language “so obscure …” is void for uncertainty’), which he does not dispute,
    so 587 is a recited submission and not a second adoption; Upper Hunter 437 is the adoption and the citation (CRIT_fidelity_4
    Finding 4, adopted; CRIT_fidelity_3 m8)]; contrast Mobil: ‘find a way’ ‘is simply too vague and uncertain to be capable of giving
    rise to contractual obligation’ [CB1A 58 | 499 | the Court] (credit); ‘The fact that the condition is one whose performance [582]
    lies wholly or partly within the power of one of the parties to the contract does not mean that there is no binding contract once
    the condition is fulfilled.’ [CB3B 184 | 581 to 582 | Gibbs CJ, Meehan].
    Facts (deciding). ‘all payments … promptly’; ‘once Grace repays the Loan’. Supporting: ‘$10,000’; ‘to me directly’.
    Core. One or two sentences: the criterion (a term fails only if ‘so obscure’ that no contractual intention can be attributed to it)
    applied to ‘all payments … promptly’, which takes its content from the Loan Agreement’s own timetable (monthly interest;
    principal at the expiry of 12 months); and AMPL’s promise not illusory, its condition depending on a third party’s act, Grace’s
    repayment (credit: ‘once Grace repays the Loan’ quoted here; AMPL has no discretion once it is met). The counted form is two
    sentences, each carrying its own footnote (Upper Hunter 437 on the first; Meehan 581 to 582 on the second), the second a ten-
    word element sub-verdict with its reason in an absolute clause (‘AMPL’s promise is not illusory, its condition depending on
    Grace’), which is his form under R1; v5’s single sentence carried one marker for two sources (CRIT_fidelity_5 Finding 5).
    Credit. Mobil compared (similar: ‘find a way’ and ‘ensure’ both leave the means to the promisor; different: Mobil’s result was
    itself undefined, whereas Rocky’s result is defined by the timetable); the contrast with I.E (the same doctrine, opposite result,
    the discretion there lying with the promisor); any dispute about the 12 months is construction, not certainty (II.G); the sum,
    payee and trigger stated.
    Strength. Strong; a contrary conclusion is Poor.
    Drops. VG: the criterion absent (a bare ‘capable of meaning’); AMPL’s promise not addressed for illusoriness (the second
    sentence, the first-demotion item in Part 8, mirrored here: CRIT_round6 m8). Good: bare. Fair: the condition called uncertain.
    Poor: ‘ensure’ held void for vagueness; AMPL’s promise held illusory because Grace might never repay. Omitted.

II.F1 Privity: Rocky the promisee; ‘the clause’ both ways with the reason (1.0; L; floor 38) [Coulls 494 to 495
(Windeyer J dissenting) alone; never a slide (R-Z(2)) or [11.10] (R-Z(3); R-U(1)); Coulls 487 is not the citation]

    Rules at source. The two limbs (I.F2): Windeyer J at 494 (‘only those who are parties to a contract can sue upon it’) and 495
    (‘a plaintiff who sues on a promise must show a consideration for it provided by him’), dissenting on construction, alone: S4A
    slide 2 states only the party limb, and [11.10] is an editors’ note for a rule a course case states, so neither is the citation (R-
    Z(2), (3); R-U(1); CRIT_fidelity_9 Finding 1, v9’s ‘or S4A slide 2, or [11.10]’ withdrawn); Coulls 487 decides that signature does
    not make one a party and that there was no express or implied promise to the wife, and does not state the two-limb rule, so it is
    not the citation for ‘promisee for consideration, not barred’ (CRIT_fidelity_3 m6 and CRIT_round3 m6, adopted); example 1: ‘If
    A and B enter into a contract under which A promises B (for consideration) to pay $1,000 to C, and A fails to honour this
    promise, C has no right to sue A to recover the money.’ [CB4 327 | [11.10] | editors]; Coulls 487; Trident [14] (Mason CJ and
    Wilson J: ‘a stranger to the consideration cannot maintain an action at law upon it’; by report, no pin; [15] asks whether the two
    rules are one) (credit; CRIT_complete_bias_2 A-7 adopted).
    Facts (deciding). ‘to me directly’; ‘the clause’. Supporting: ‘Pierre agreed and the clause was included in the Loan Agreement
    before it was signed by Grace and AMPL.’
    Core. One sentence: Rocky is the promisee and named payee (‘to me directly’) of an oral promise made to him for his own
    consideration, so he is a party who gave consideration and privity does not bar the oral claim; and, in a clause, both readings of
    ‘the clause’ (CRIT_harsh_2 F7, adopted): it most naturally means the guarantee clause named before it (the reason stated in a
    few words: the definite article refers back to the only clause previously named; v10’s ‘just named’ pointed at a place in the
    answer rather than in the problem, an answer-external deictic a cold reader could not resolve, and is from v11 an R1 lapse; the
    v11 form is ‘the guarantee clause named before it’, +1: UPGRADES_r1 U29; ‘the guarantee clause the problem names first’ is
    equally Excellent; v3’s floor gave no reason, which the harsh critic graded VG: CRIT_round3 table 1.1), and even a written
    $10,000 term leaves him the oral promise made to him (accepted bare in the counted form; its reason, that Rocky is party to
    neither document and the materials state no rule displacing an oral promise by a later written record (gap G8), is credit, ‘he
    being party to neither document’ (+6) where words allow: CRIT_round4 m8, disclosed; credit also: example 1 named, Rocky
    being then a non-party to the Loan Agreement; the order of clause and $10,000 weighed in terms).
    Credit. The gap disclosed if relied on (no rule in the materials on an oral promise and a later written record); Grace is not a
    party to the $10,000 bargain; the order of the clause and the $10,000 weighed in terms, marked ‘arguably’ (R-M). From v11
    (UPGRADES_r1 U17, credit only; its proposed weight change REJECTED, the weights being R-C calibrated): the written-term
    reading’s reason, ‘he being party to neither document’ (+6), stays credit, example 1 at [11.10] (‘C has no right to sue A to
    recover the money’, CB4 327) supporting it.
    Strength and tilt. Either reading of ‘the clause’ is Excellent if both are run, the preferred reading carries its reason (the
    definite article for the guarantee reading; the order of clause and $10,000, marked ‘arguably’, for the written-term reading),
    and the result is shown unchanged; weighing the other reading’s reason in terms is credit (CRIT_round10 M1)
    (CRIT_complete_bias_2 B-5, adopted: the ambiguity is textual, not legal); one reading only is Good.
    Drops. VG: the criterion (party plus consideration) absent; ‘most naturally’ with no reason; Coulls 487 cited for the two-limb
    rule (a citation fault); [11.10] cited for the rule where Coulls 494 to 495 states it (a citation fault: R-Z(3); R-U(1)); a slide cited
    for either limb or for the rule is graded at R1 and R8 under R-Z(5), not here (v11’s slide-2 citation-fault line is withdrawn).
    Good: bare; one reading only. Fair: the written-term reading adopted and the claim said to fail on privity with the oral contract
    ignored. Poor: Rocky treated as a third-party beneficiary of the Loan Agreement for the $10,000. Omitted.
    Marker comment. ‘Identify the planted ambiguity in ’the clause’ and run both readings.’

II.F2 Privity: who promised, AMPL through Pierre or Pierre personally (4.0; K; floor 95) [the doctrine of agency,
one source per marker (R-R(3)): a case first under R-Z(3), Port Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ) for the criterion stated
in Lord Reid’s form; the casebook [11.70] only as a last resort, per R-A(4) as amended by R-X(1); either suffices
for the criterion; Ermogenous [24] credit]

    Issue. Whether the $10,000 promise (and so Rocky’s counterparty, and the promisee of his undertaking) is AMPL or Pierre.
    Rules at source. The doctrine of agency: S4A slide 16 (as at I.F1; a locator only, never cited: R-Z(2)); the course’s statement of
    what must be shown: the principal ‘expressly or impliedly consented to the agent acting on the principal’s behalf so as to effect
    the principal’s relations with third parties’ and, ‘with respect to the particular transaction under consideration, the agent was
    purporting to act on behalf of the principal and not solely on the agent’s own behalf. Ratification refers to the principal’s
    adoption or confirmation of a contract made without prior authorisation.’ [CB4 336 | [11.70] | editors’ note; cited from v12 as at
    I.F1: a case first, Port Jackson 240 (Barwick CJ) for the elements stated in Lord Reid’s form (‘contracted for the stevedore’s
    protection as well as for his own’; authority ‘antecedently or by ratification’), Trident (Brennan J or Deane J) by report only for
    the bare route, The New York Star only for authority; the casebook [11.70] a last resort (R-Z(3)), at most twice in the answer,
    never stacked with a case for the same proposition (R-R(3)); no slide (R-Z(2))]; ‘To be a legally enforceable duty there must, of
    course, be identifiable parties to the arrangement’ [CB3A 137 | [24] | Ermogenous] (credit); Windeyer J’s ‘the company (by its
    agent O’Neil) promised’ [CB4 332 | 492 | dissenting on construction] (illustration only). No court in the set states a rule of
    ratification in terms (O-7): ratification is not used to supply the purporting element.
    Facts (deciding). ‘owned and controlled’; ‘you’; ‘at AMPL’s office’; ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’; ‘the personal
    guarantee provided by Rocky’ (AMPL’s later call, quoted in the narrator’s words, the inference that it was a call on the
    undertaking marked ‘arguably’: R-M; CRIT_round3 M8, adopted). Supporting (credit): ‘Pierre agreed to provide the money to
    Grace and the $1,150,000 was advanced by AMPL’ (the narrator’s own 27 February usage, Pierre agreeing and AMPL
    advancing: moved from core to credit to fit the count); the $10,000 a payment outside the loan; ‘a cousin’ at ‘you’; on the
    guarantee reading of ‘the clause’ the $10,000 is nowhere in AMPL’s document.
    Core. (1) The issue framed on the doctrine of agency, and the two factual questions the course’s statement requires put in the
    answer’s own words as ‘whether’ clauses, never as a direct question with a question mark (his Part A has none; the counted
    form: ‘turns on agency: whether AMPL consented to Pierre acting on its behalf, and whether Pierre purported to act for AMPL
    or solely for himself’: CRIT_round4 m9, adopted), with one footnote for the criterion (Port Jackson 240 where the clause states
    it in Lord Reid’s form, as ‘whether Pierre contracted for AMPL as well as, or instead of, himself, with its authority’; [11.70] as
    the last resort where it states the editors’ form: R-Z(3)). (2) Consent answered on ‘owned and controlled’ (the counted form:
    ‘AMPL being ’owned and controlled’ by Pierre supplies consent’; credit: the problem’s own 27 February usage, ‘Pierre agreed’
    preceding an advance ‘by AMPL’). ‘Purporting is contested’ is accepted as the counted opening of (3) (CRIT_round4 m9, second
    limb: ‘Whether Pierre so purported is contested’ (+2) is equally acceptable); the counted form now joins (2) and the opening of
    (3) in one sentence (‘AMPL being ’owned and controlled’ by Pierre supplies consent; purporting is contested: ‘if you also
    promise’ was put to ‘you’‘), because the removal of the credit fact left a ten-word sentence beside a nine-word one, which R1
    forbids (no two under-12 sentences adjacent). (3) Purporting contested with the other side’s best fact met: for an AMPL
    conclusion, ’if you also promise’ put to ‘you’ (the deciding fact for Pierre; that the $10,000 was a payment outside the loan is a
    supporting fact, credit, as this unit’s Facts list has always rated it, and v5’s counted sentence carried it as ‘for a payment
    outside the loan’ against R-L(2); it was removed in v6, a disclosed move under R-S(4) named in Part 8, and a drafter who adds
    it is graded the same), met with ‘at AMPL’s office’, ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’ and AMPL’s later call under ‘the
    personal guarantee provided by Rocky’, ‘arguably’ his undertaking (never ‘AMPL called on the undertaking’ as fact: R-M); for a
    Pierre conclusion, those facts met with ‘you’, the cousinhood and, on the guarantee reading, the absence of the $10,000 from
    AMPL’s document. The three facts may be weighed inside one or two sentences, his stacked-facts form (VOICE.md 2.3,
     examples 14 and 15), or as ‘Firstly … Secondly, however … Thirdly …’ sentences; neither is required (R1 as restated;
     CRIT_round3 m9, adopted in part). (4) A conclusion in the open-point tier (‘On balance … likely …, because …, though …’)
     whose ‘because’ is Pierre’s dealing throughout about AMPL’s loan (v3’s ‘AMPL asserted its other side’ deleted as cryptic and as
     restating the R-M inference: CRIT_round3 M8); the other party pleaded in the alternative, which the trailing clause ‘though
     ’you’ keeps Pierre arguable’ does (the counted form from v8; v7’s ‘keeps Pierre arguable in the alternative’ carried three words
     the clause did not need, removed under R-R(7) to fund CRIT_round7 M1: Part 8; the words ‘in the alternative’ are not required
     and a drafter who writes them loses nothing) (credit: the consequence stated here that whoever promised the $10,000 is the
     person to whom Rocky’s undertaking ran, which II.I1 draws in any event). (5) The further information that decides it, with its
     direction, in the trailing clause (from v11 CORE, a K unit carrying none being the contradiction five of six Stage-5 round-1
     markers graded at R6: UPGRADES_r1 U3): what Pierre said about whom he spoke for, and which way it cuts; the v11 form
     adds ‘, decisively so if he spoke for himself’ after ‘though ’you’ keeps Pierre arguable’ (+7); a form naming AMPL’s later
     adoption of the $10,000 promise, with its direction, is equally Excellent.
     Credit. Ratification named and set aside (it concerns a contract ‘made without prior authorisation’, and prior authorisation is
     not the difficulty); in Port Jackson the carrier’s antecedent authority to contract for the stevedore was found as a fact on the
     evidence of their course of dealing (OFF Port Jackson, Barwick CJ [2] ‘(at p236)’: the stevedore ‘had for years acted as
     stevedore in the discharge of the carrier’s ships’ and ‘was aware of the use by the carrier of a form of bill of lading’ including
     the Himalaya clause; [21] ‘(at p241)’: the appellate Court ‘having reviewed the evidence’ found the carrier ‘was acting with the
     appellant’s authority’, ‘i.e. with its antecedent authority’, which Barwick CJ held ‘a correct conclusion of fact’; the trial judge
     had found ratification, [19]), and in The New York Star the Board records that the trial judge found agency ‘only by ratification’
     while the Court of Appeal ‘found that the necessary agency was directly established by the evidence, so that reliance on
     ratification was not necessary’ (OFF New York Star [7] ‘(at p303)’ for Sheppard J’s finding that ‘the necessary agency was
     established only by ratification’, and [8] ‘(at p303)’ for the Court of Appeal’s; v8 labelled both [8]: CRIT_fidelity_8 Finding 2);
     the stevedore’s knowledge of the offer and its reliance on it go to acceptance and consideration (OFF Port Jackson, Mason and
     Jacobs JJ [12] ‘(at p274)’: ‘the evident probability of the appellant acting in reliance on the shipper’s promise or offer when he
     discharges the goods so long as he has knowledge of the existence of that promise or offer’), and, in the authority finding
     Mason and Jacobs JJ adopted from Glass JA (OFF Port Jackson [5] ‘(at p271)’: the stevedore ‘proved that it was familiar with the
     terms of the bill of lading in general and with the clauses purporting to exempt independent contractors in particular’, and
     claims had been ‘rejected in reliance upon the exemption clauses’, from which there was ‘a clear implication’ that the carrier
     acted ‘as agent with the authority of its principal the stevedore’; ‘On this point we need do no more than state our agreement
     with what Glass J.A. has said’), the stevedore’s familiarity with the clauses and its reliance on them in rejecting earlier claims
     were part of the course of dealing from which authority was implied (CRIT_fidelity_9 Finding 3; R-U(6): v9’s ‘not to authority’
     was too wide and is withdrawn); so the cases support inferring Pierre’s authority from AMPL’s ownership and control, as a
     course of dealing supported it there, but neither addresses ‘purporting’ (v7’s gloss, ‘infer authority from the principal’s
     knowledge of and reliance on the clauses’, was imprecise rather than wrong, naming the familiarity and reliance without the
     course of dealing they formed part of, and is replaced by the statement above: CRIT_fidelity_7 Finding 2 and CRIT_fidelity_9
     Finding 3, adopted as corrections under R-T(3) and R-U(6); every span above checked verbatim against the saved official texts,
     which are credit, never cited for a course-stated proposition, and never quoted in the answer); Ermogenous [24]; intention re-
     weighed if Pierre promised (II.D); a second further-information item beyond core (5) (AMPL’s later adoption of the $10,000
     promise, or what Pierre said, whichever core (5) does not use), with its direction.
     Strength and tilt. AMPL likely the promisor (moderate, S-7); Pierre in the alternative. Either conclusion can be Excellent if
     both questions are answered from the stated facts, the other side’s best fact is met, the alternative is pleaded, and the
     consequences for II.C2, II.D, II.I1, II.I3 and II.I4 are drawn conditionally on the conclusion (T11).
     Citation. For the two elements, from v12 a case first (R-Z(3)): Port Jackson Stevedoring Pty Ltd v Salmond & Spraggon (Aust)
     Pty Ltd (1978) 139 CLR 231, 240 (Barwick CJ), where the sentence states the criterion in Lord Reid’s form (requisites (2) and
     (3), OFF Port Jackson [18] ‘(at p240)’); it does not count toward R-H’s cap of three, the proposition being course-stated at
     [11.70]; Trident General Insurance Co Ltd v McNiece Bros Pty Ltd (1988) 165 CLR 107 (Brennan J), or (Deane J), by report, no
     pin (R-Y(1)), only for the bare agency route. The casebook as the last resort, in the R-A(4) form as amended by R-X(1), Contract:
     Cases and Materials [11.70] ALONE (at most twice in the answer, counting I.F1; the v11 counted fn 35 read ‘Robertson and
     Paterson (n 13) [11.70]’; v10’s ‘Paterson and Robertson’ order is withdrawn), accepted without deduction where the sentence
     states the editors’ own ‘purporting … not solely’ form, which no case states in those words. No slide is ever cited (R-Z(2)): v11’s
     acceptance of ‘Class 4A Slides, slide 16’ for the bare route is withdrawn, and a slide citation is graded at R1 and R8 under R-
     Z(5). A footnote stacking a case and [11.70] for the same proposition is over-citation under R8 (CRIT_fidelity_4 Finding 2;
     CRIT_round4 M10; R-R(3)). An answer that states the two elements as law with no source is Good on the citation item; one that
     footnotes the editors by name outside R-A(4) is a D1 fault.
     Drops. VG: one question not answered from the facts; the alternative not pleaded; the other side’s best fact not met; the
     further information absent or given without its direction (core (5): U3); ‘AMPL called on the undertaking’ stated as fact (D4
     also). Good: ‘Pierre acted for AMPL’ bare; the elements stated as law with no source; no method and no lean (§2). Good also:
     ratification said to settle that AMPL promised (ratification is a course concept at [11.70], so using it as the decisive reason on a
     unit where either conclusion can be Excellent is a wrong decisive reason, not law wrong: CRIT_round4 m13; R-R(10); v4’s Poor
     exceeded R-E). Fair: agency assumed without the questions; corporate law beyond the course applied. Poor: ‘AMPL’ and
     ‘Pierre’ treated as interchangeable throughout. Omitted.
     Marker comments. ‘Answer with specificity to individual Ps as required: AMPL and Pierre.’ ‘Ask both questions the doctrine
     of agency requires, from the facts.’

II.G The 12 months (5.0; C; floor 76) [Brambles 163 to 164 and 191; for the objective reading eg Brambles 168
or Ermogenous [25]]

Why it is here (R-Q). ‘repayable at the expiry of 12 months’ states no start; it decides (i) whether AMPL’s 9 March 2025 call was
premature, (ii) whether Rocky’s undertaking was broken on 27 February 2025 (breach exposure, which the answer does not argue
and never frames as outside any scope: R-Z(1), (4)), (iii) when the $10,000 condition can be met. It does not decide Rocky’s claim
against Grace (privity defeats it on either reading), which is why it sits in Part II after F, with Part I carrying only the one-clause
cross-reference at I.F2 (the 5 March demand assumed the earlier date). The reader of II.I4’s ‘turns on the 12 months (G)’ is then in
the same Part (CRIT_round3 M9, adopted).

     Issue. Whether ‘the expiry of 12 months’ ran from the advance of 27 February 2024 or the agreement of 8 April 2024: a
     question of construction on which no reading or slide states when such a period begins (gap disclosed: Z9), and of construction,
     not uncertainty (Meehan 578: ‘It is only if the court is unable to put any definite meaning on the contract that it can be said to
     be uncertain’; the former I.E2 point, now carried here).
     Rules at source.
           Objective meaning: Ermogenous [25] (I.D; ‘in the same sense as it is used in other contractual contexts’) (eg).
           Ambiguity and genesis: ‘if the language of a contract is ambiguous, evidence of surrounding circumstances is admissible
           for the purposes of construing the contract … Where ambiguities exist, mutually known facts establishing the commercial
           purpose of the contract, the genesis of the transaction, the background and the context in which the parties are operating
           will be admissible … the shared beliefs of the parties as to their respective rights as they existed immediately before the
           contract was entered into are admissible’ [CB1B 82 | 191 | Ipp AJA (Mason P agreeing on the contractual claim),
           Brambles | majority; conditional on ambiguity throughout; RG skip (register only); ‘Ipp AJA’ per R-K, the casebook
           heading ‘IPP JA’ accepted and not deducted]; ‘pre-contractual conduct is only admissible on questions of construction if
           the contract is ambiguous and if the pre-contractual conduct casts light on the genesis of the contract, its objective aim,
           or the meaning of any descriptive term’ [CB1B 73 | 163 | Heydon JA | unanimous by adoption (O-9) | RG skip]; ‘whatever
           might flow from the factual matrix, it cannot be resorted to unless the 12 July 1990 contract is ambiguous’ [CB1B 76 | 167
           | Heydon JA].
           Exclusion: post-contractual conduct ‘not admissible on the question of what a contract means’ [CB1B 73 | 164 | Heydon
           JA, unanimous by adoption]; ‘the actual opinions of the parties are irrelevant’ absent rectification or estoppel by
           convention [CB1B 76 | 168 | Heydon JA]. Contra, older (credit): Mayo J admits subsequent conduct ‘where meaning is in
           doubt … to explain, but not to contradict, the language used’ [CB3A 147 | 74 | Mayo J, Todd v Nicol | first instance, SA,
           1957; the passage sits after the [74] marker and before any [75] marker: CRIT_fidelity_3 m11, adopted].
           Construction technique (credit): Lindley LJ declined to push ‘the doctrine of taking language most strongly against the
           person using it’ too far [CB1A 45 | 263 | Carlill | one of three concurring judgments]; ‘It is for the defendants to shew
           what it does mean’ is a step against a maker pleading vagueness, not a rule that the user of words bears a burden; Bowen
           LJ’s ‘two constructions … each of which is good sense’ [CB1A 46 | 267].
     Facts (deciding). ‘recorded’; ‘advanced by AMPL on the same day’; ‘the expiry of 12 months’; ‘appropriate’ (R-M: compliance
     in that period, no more). Supporting (credit): ‘4% per annum’; ‘Interest was to be paid by Grace monthly’; ‘I have until 8 April
     2025’; AMPL’s argument that ‘the 12 months had begun then’; Rocky’s 13 February 2025 email and 5 March demand; the
     drafter not stated.
     Core. (1) The issue framed as construction. (2) The method: objective meaning; surrounding circumstances admissible only if
     the words are ‘ambiguous’; later conduct excluded on meaning (Heydon JA 163 to 164 for the ambiguity gate and the exclusion
     of later conduct, and 168 (‘the actual opinions of the parties are irrelevant’) or Ermogenous [25] for the objective reading, the
     counted fn 36 reading ‘Brambles (n 19) 163–4, 168 (Heydon JA)’, because 163 to 164 do not state the objective limb
     (CRIT_fidelity_9 Finding 4; R-U(6)); Ipp AJA 191 in the footnote; the counted form from v8 is ‘later conduct excluded on
     meaning’, the grid line’s own words, replacing v7’s ‘later conduct never on meaning’, a clause whose predicate (‘admissible’)
     had to be supplied from the clause before it, the note-form ellipsis R1 names and said the model did not carry: CRIT_round7
     m5, adopted at no cost; ‘later conduct never admissible on meaning’ (+1) is equally acceptable). (3) Ambiguity decided, not
     assumed, with the reason and the inference marked: the instrument ‘recorded’ as the ‘Loan’ the sum ‘advanced’ on 27
     February, so it is ‘arguably’ ambiguous (the counted form is the classification-then-proof colon §1 and R-R(2) permit: ‘The
     words are arguably ambiguous: the instrument ’recorded’ the sum ‘advanced’ on 27 February, that advance its ‘genesis’‘;
     ’recorded an earlier advance without a commencement’ is a derived fact: CRIT_fidelity_3 m1, adopted; the stated terms give no
     commencement, and a drafter who says so says ‘as stated’ or ‘as described’, never ‘as narrated’: R-R(1)); if ambiguous, the
     admissible ‘genesis’ is the advance ‘on the same day’; if held unambiguous, the circumstances are excluded and the result
     follows from the words (either path applies the method: CRIT_complete_bias_2 B-6, adopted; ‘ambiguity assumed’ and
     ‘ambiguity denied without reasons’ are graded alike, VG). (4) Both readings, the opposing one in a clause: for 27 February the
     term attaches to ‘the Loan’, the defined sum advanced that day; for 8 April the terms (the rate, monthly interest, the 12
     months) first APPEAR then (the counted form is ‘though the terms appear first on 8 April’; v5’s ‘were fixed on 8 April’ stated a
     derived fact as fact, when the terms were first fixed being nowhere stated and ‘recorded’ being the problem’s word:
     CRIT_fidelity_5 Finding 2 and CRIT_round5 m3, adopted; ‘were arguably first fixed’ (+1) and ‘were recorded on 8 April’ (0) are
     equally acceptable) (credit: Grace’s ‘appropriate’ payments from 8 April fit that timetable, though equivocally; the fuller 8 April
     clause with ‘appropriate’ (+6) was not fundable and stays credit: CRIT_round4 m10, disclosed). (5) A verdict in the open-point
     tier with a lean, its reason, ‘though only slightly’ placed directly after the lean it qualifies (‘it likely ran from 27 February,
     though only slightly, the known starting point being …’: CRIT_round4 m10’s dangle fixed at no cost; the marker is the honest
     weak-strength marker and is not redundant with ‘likely’, which alone is the moderate tier: CRIT_round3 Part 3.4’s proposed
     saving rejected on the sheet’s own tier rule), and the further information that decides it (the Loan Agreement’s words; credit:
     its drafter; whether interest ran from 27 February) in the same sentence (credit: the readings cross-referred to II.H and II.I4,
     where they are applied). The v10 counted verdict was ‘On balance, it likely ran from 27 February, though only slightly, on that
     genesis; the agreement’s words would decide it’, its reason carried by reference to the sentence before (‘that advance its
     ’genesis’‘); v5’s verdict restated the genesis in a seven-word clause and was shortened under R-S(4) (Part 8). Two v11
     requirements on that verdict. (i) THE LEAN’S REASON says why the date is preferred, not only that the genesis is admissible:
     Ipp AJA’s passage makes ’the genesis of the transaction’ admissible where ‘ambiguities exist’ (CB1B 82, Brambles 191) and
     says nothing about which date it favours, so admissibility is no reason for either date, and a lean whose only preceding
     sentence is the counter has none (§1; UPGRADES_r1 U24); the reason is that the term attaches to ‘the Loan’, the sum
     ‘advanced’ on 27 February (eg ‘, the Loan having been ’advanced’ then’, about +6 where a draft lacks it; ‘that advance its

II.I AMPL’s call of 9 March 2025 (16.5; a further heading inside Part II; the Part III option was
withdrawn in v6, §5)

Why it is in the advice: it is the setter’s final fact and the reason advice is sought now; it is the other side of the bargain Rocky sues
on, so every argument on it is an argument on the $10,000; the 12 months (II.G) decides its timing. The elements of the bargain are
not re-run here; I is confined to the burden aspect, the content of what Rocky promised and his assent to the written words, AMPL’s
consideration, timing and consequences; intention and certainty of the undertaking are carried by the II.D clause. The four
paragraphs sit under the one heading ‘I. AMPL’s call’ (the Part III option is withdrawn: §5; CRIT_round5 m2); they may open
‘Whether …’ or with a classification; II.I2’s counted opening (‘Rocky promised what Pierre ’expected’, whereas …’) is a classification
of the two contents and is not a conclusion first (CRIT_round3 Part 3.5 noted the visible inconsistency; it is not a fault).

II.I1 The burden aspect; the clause alone; Rocky likely bound by his own undertaking, to AMPL only if Pierre
acted for it (4.0; C; floor 56) [Trident (Deane J) by report, judge named, no pin (R-Y(1), (2)), never a slide (R-
Z(2)); Empirnall 534 and 536; Coulls 487]

     Issue. Whether a clause in a contract between AMPL and Grace, described by the narrator as one ‘that Rocky personally
     guaranteed repayment of the Loan’, can by itself bind Rocky; and, if not, whether he is bound by his own undertaking, and to
     whom.
     Rules at source. ‘Nor can it impose an enforceable burden on a non-party.’ [S4A slide 2 | slide; a locator only, never cited: R-
    Z(2)]; ‘nor can it impose an enforceable burden on a non-party’ [CB4 327 | [11.10] | editors; ‘This chapter will focus on the
    benefit aspect of the rule’; a last resort only, never needed here: R-Z(3)]; the case statement of both aspects, the preferred
    source from v12 (R-Y(2)): ‘the general rule that only the parties to a contract are bound by, and entitled to enforce, its terms’
    [Trident, course reading (R-Y(1)) | Deane J, his opening sentence | verified in the corpus’s Deane J segment | by report, judge
    named, no pin, the reading carrying no CLR page markers], and Deane J’s further statement, ‘a contract between two or more
    parties does not, of itself, directly confer rights or impose liabilities upon persons who are not parties to it’ [same | Deane J |
    verified likewise]; either may be quoted or paraphrased; Trident being a course reading, the footnote never counts toward the
    R-H cap of three and there is no cap of one Trident footnote (R-J and R-N superseded: R-Y(1)); ‘The objective theory of contract
    requires an external manifestation of assent to an offer.’ [CB1B 71 | 534 | McHugh JA, Empirnall]; signature NOT NECESSARY:
    ‘Eric does not sign contracts’ and ‘Since Empirnall has taken the benefit of the work with knowledge of the terms on which it
    was offered, an objective bystander would conclude that Empirnall had accepted the offer’ [CB1B 72 | 536 | McHugh JA,
    Empirnall | a party bound without signing]; signature NOT DECISIVE: ‘the mere fact that her signature appears does not make
    her a party; this is a question to be resolved upon a consideration of the written instrument itself’ [CB4 331 | 487 | Taylor and
    Owen JJ, Coulls | signature not sufficient; whether it is necessary was not in issue, so 487 is never cited for ‘not necessary’:
    CRIT_fidelity_3 m7, adopted].
    Facts (deciding). ‘that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ (the narrator’s description); ‘I will do that’.
    Supporting: ‘signed by Grace and AMPL’; ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ (R-M).
    Core. (1) The burden aspect stated: a contract cannot impose an enforceable burden on a non-party, so ‘the clause as
    described’ (the narrator’s description is quoted or paraphrased at II.I2, whose unit it is: Appendix B; never ‘the clause states’
    or ‘records’: D4) binds Rocky only if he manifested assent to it (Empirnall 534), the question for II.I2; the reason is not that
    Rocky did not sign, signature being ‘neither necessary nor decisive’ (not necessary: Empirnall 536; not decisive: Coulls 487;
    T10), each footnoted to its own authority. (2) Rocky is LIKELY bound by his own ‘I will do that’, a promise in a bargain to which
    he was party (the hedge matching ‘bound to someone (moderate to strong)’: CRIT_round4 M4, adopted; the counted form is
    ‘His own ’I will do that’ likely binds him’); AMPL may enforce it only if Pierre accepted for AMPL (II.F2); if Pierre accepted for
    himself, AMPL is a non-party to the undertaking and can enforce only the clause, on II.I2’s assent and II.I3’s consideration, its
    entry into the Loan Agreement remaining arguable consideration on that alternative (S-13, moderate), so Rocky’s exposure to
    AMPL is then likely absent but arguable and is never stated as settled (CRIT_round9 M1; R-U(2): v9’s ‘has nothing to enforce’
    stated as settled a consequence II.I3 leaves arguable).
    Credit. The T2 reconciliation in four words, ‘as to that clause only’, after ‘binds him only if he assented’ (Rocky’s assent, if
    found, makes him party to the guarantee promise alone, not promisee of Grace’s promise to repay, so I.F2’s ‘not a party’ and
    II.I2’s ‘likely assented’ do not contradict: CRIT_round5 m12, credit, +4, written where words allow); Rocky differs in kind from
    Mrs Coulls (named as promisor, not payee); (v12: v11’s credit ‘the gap disclosed (no extracted judgment develops the burden
    aspect …)’ is withdrawn, Trident being a course reading that states it (R-Y(1)) and a statement about what the readings extract
    being meta language (R-Z(1))); joint promisees on the undertaking (if given to Pierre and AMPL jointly, ‘an action to recover
    must have been brought by both promisees’: Coulls 486; weak for Rocky); the Loan Agreement’s text not narrated (the answer
    never asserts it ‘purports expressly’ to be between AMPL and Grace: D4). From v11 (UPGRADES_r1 U11, credit only): ‘as to
    that clause only’ remains the first credit to write here; R10 accepts the T2 reconciliation without it only where I.F2’s joint-
    promisee clause states that no promise by Grace runs to Rocky, Taylor and Owen JJ framing two questions, ‘whether the
    testator’s wife was a party to the contract and whether, upon its true construction, the contract contains a promise by the
    company to pay to her’ (CB4 330, Coulls 486).
    Strength and tilt. The clause alone cannot bind Rocky (strong, S-8): ‘Rocky is bound because the clause is in the Loan
    Agreement’ is Poor with the D6 deduction; so is ‘Rocky is not bound to anyone because he never signed’. Bound to someone
    (moderate to strong); bound to AMPL (moderate, capped by the II.F2 conclusion and stated conditionally on it).
    Citation. Trident General Insurance Co Ltd v McNiece Bros Pty Ltd (1988) 165 CLR 107 (Deane J), by report with the judge
    named and no pin (R-Y(1), (2)): Trident is a Class 4A reading, so it is cited as any course case is, one source per marker, with
    no cap on the number of Trident footnotes; the reading carries no CLR page markers, so no pin can be verified, and the
    verifier’s lint ‘report citation with no pinpoint’ is an accepted, disclosed consequence, not a fault (R-Y(1); Part 9 item 7). v11’s
    alternative ‘Class 4A Slides, slide 2’ is withdrawn (R-Z(2)); a slide citation here is graded at R1 and R8 under R-Z(5). Residual
    risk, disclosed (CRIT_round7 m6, carried): the real marker reads the footnote, not this sheet, and may record a report citation
    with no pinpoint as a minor non-compliance at R8; the slide form that once removed that risk is barred, so the risk stands, and
    this sheet grades the no-pin form as no fault (Part 9 item 7); Empirnall 534 for assent; Empirnall 536 for ‘not necessary’; Coulls
    487 only for ‘not decisive’ and ‘the written instrument itself’. One footnote marker per proposition inside the sentence
    (CRIT_round3 m2, adopted): the counted form reads ‘neither necessary[fn Empirnall 536] nor decisive[fn Coulls 487]’, two
    markers; v5’s single marker listing both sources is withdrawn (CRIT_fidelity_5 Finding 5, adopted).
    Drops. VG: the AMPL/Pierre dependency not drawn; signature-not-the-test absent (T10); Coulls 487 cited for ‘not necessary’ (a
    citation fault); ‘binds him’ unhedged (the tier). Good: ‘the clause cannot bind a non-party’ bare; ‘Rocky is bound by his oral
    promise’ bare; ‘a fortiori because he did not sign’ as the reason for the right result (right result, wrong reason, conclusive: the
    same grade as I.F2’s ‘Grace is right because Rocky did not sign’, because the same signature reasoning with the same right
    result carries the same grade whichever party it helps: CRIT_round4 M11; R-R(4); v4’s Poor was asymmetric). Fair: the benefit
    aspect only; the oral route missed and liability rested on the clause; the clause said to ‘state’ or ‘record’ a guarantee as a stated
    fact (D4). Poor: either D6 conclusion. Omitted.
    Marker comments. ‘Privity has two aspects: the burden aspect decides whether the clause alone binds Rocky; signature is not
    the test either way.’ ‘Answer with specificity to individual Ps: to whom was Rocky’s undertaking given?’

II.I2 Content: what Pierre ‘expected’ against the clause as described; assent to the written words on Empirnall
535 to 536; the benefit named; ‘attended’ as the knowledge fact, the inference marked; ‘provided by Rocky’ (3.5;
C; floor 80) [Empirnall 535 to 536]

    Rules at source. ‘A more accurate statement is that where an offeree with a reasonable opportunity to reject the offer of
    goods or services takes the benefit of them under circumstances which indicate that they were to be paid for in accordance
    with the offer, it is open to the tribunal of fact to hold that the offer was accepted according to its terms. A useful analogy is to
be found in the “ticket cases” where an offeree, who has or ought to have knowledge of the terms of a contract of carriage or
bailment, is generally bound unless he raises objection’ [CB1B 72 | 535 | McHugh JA (Samuels JA agreeing; Kirby P to
substantially the same effect), Empirnall | ratio. McHugh JA’s OWN criterion has three elements: an offeree with a reasonable
opportunity to reject the offer of goods or services; who takes the benefit of them; under circumstances which indicate that
they were to be paid for in accordance with the offer; and his holding at 536 rests on actual knowledge (‘taking the benefit of
an offer with knowledge of its terms and knowledge of the offeror’s reliance’). The ‘has or ought to have knowledge of the
terms’ words are the ANALOGY (‘A useful analogy’), confined by its own words to ‘a contract of carriage or bailment’
(MacRobertson Miller is the course’s ticket case, CB1A 48); v3 spliced the analogy’s words into the rule as its second limb and
deducted for omitting an ‘ought to have’ limb the rule does not contain: CRIT_fidelity_3 M2 and CRIT_round3 M3, adopted];
‘Since Empirnall has taken the benefit of the work with knowledge of the terms on which it was offered, an objective bystander
would conclude that Empirnall had accepted the offer on those terms and conditions’ [CB1B 72 | 536]; ‘The ultimate issue is
whether a reasonable bystander would regard the conduct of the offeree, including his silence, as signalling to the offeror that
his offer has been accepted’ [535]; contra: ‘an offeror cannot erect a contract between himself and the offeree by the device of
stating that unless he hears from the offeree he will consider the offeree bound’ [CB1B 71 | 534 | McHugh JA]; Felthouse 876
(uncommunicated assent); ‘In all the circumstances it was for the defendant to make plain that its conduct amounted only to
taking advantage of the proposal but not to submitting to the disadvantages’ [CB1B 81 | 181 | Heydon JA, Brambles | his route]
(credit). Lord Denning MR’s ‘last shot’ (Butler 404 to 405) is his alone and concerns standard forms: a remote analogy at most.
Facts (deciding). ‘expected’ (and the narrator’s ‘ensure that Grace made all payments … promptly’); ‘that Rocky personally
guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ (the narrator’s description); ‘the personal guarantee provided by Rocky’ (R-M); ‘attended’
(Rocky, Grace and Pierre ‘attended a meeting at AMPL’s office’, at which the Loan Agreement was entered into and the clause
‘was included … before it was signed’: the attendance is the one fact in the problem that goes to McHugh JA’s knowledge
element, so it is DECIDING and is quoted in the counted paragraph, ‘included at the meeting he ’attended’‘: CRIT_round4 M5,
adopted; Appendix B). That the inclusion happened at the meeting rather than in a draft before it is itself an inference from ’At
the meeting … entered into’ and ‘included … before it was signed’; the counted form is now ‘included, arguably at the meeting
he ’attended’’ (CRIT_fidelity_6 Finding 2 and CRIT_round6 m6, adopted, +1 from the slack), so that the inference that helps
AMPL is marked exactly as the inference that helps Rocky at II.C2 (‘The facts arguably place the clause after the exchange’) is,
§3’s one rule applied identically whichever party it helps. v6 carried the unmarked form ‘included at the meeting he ’attended’’
and its changes file attributed that acceptance to words in R-S(6) that the ruling does not contain; the acceptance was a
reviser’s judgment call (CRIT_round5 m4, recorded rather than funded), disclosed as such in SHEET_v7_changes.md and now
moot. A drafter who writes the unmarked form is graded as the identity table graded v6: Excellent, the inference being carried
by the quoted word and by ‘likely’ in the verdict, though the marked form is the counted one. Supporting: ‘included … before it
was signed’; his presence at the inclusion is an inference from attendance, so ‘in his presence’ is written ‘arguably’ or as ‘at the
meeting he attended’ (CRIT_fidelity_3 m2, adopted); no objection shown; nothing narrated says Rocky read or was shown the
clause’s words; ten months of check-ins (admissible on formation of the oral bargain and on Rocky’s assent, inadmissible on the
meaning of ‘ensure’ or of the clause).
Core. (1) The two contents distinguished with the right speakers: what Rocky promised is what Pierre ‘expected’, reported by
the narrator as ensuring ‘all payments … promptly’ (interest included; procuring performance), whereas the clause is described
as one ‘that Rocky personally guaranteed repayment of the Loan’ (the defined principal; ‘on default’ is guarantee law and is not
said). (2) Assent to the written content decided on McHugh JA’s own criterion as the source states it: whether, with ‘a
reasonable opportunity to reject’, Rocky took the benefit of AMPL’s written offer ‘with knowledge of its terms’, THE OFFER
NAMED so that ‘its’ keeps its antecedent (McHugh JA at 536: ‘taking the benefit of an offer with knowledge of its terms’, CB1B
72; v10’s prescribed ‘took the benefit ’with knowledge of its terms’’ detached ‘its’ from ‘an offer’; the v11 form ‘took the benefit
of AMPL’s written offer ’with knowledge of its terms’‘, +4: UPGRADES_r1 U13; knowledge of the offeror’s reliance, which
describes Empirnall’s facts and appears in no statement of the rule, and the disclosure of the analogy (Part 9 item 33) remain
credit) (535 to 536; the ’under circumstances which indicate’ element may be stated in terms, credit); the BENEFIT NAMED,
because the criterion has a benefit element and a paragraph that names none is conclusive under §1(b): the $10,000 promise,
taken as the other side of the clause recording the bargain he had just proposed (CRIT_round3 M3, adopted: moved from credit
to core); the KNOWLEDGE ELEMENT APPLIED TO A FACT, because the holding at 536 rests on ‘taking the benefit of an offer
with knowledge of its terms’ and a paragraph that states the knowledge element and names no fact going to it before
concluding ‘assented’ is the conclusive shape his marker graded Good (§1(b); CRIT_round4 M5, adopted: moved from credit to
core): the fact is Rocky’s attendance at the meeting where the clause was included, carried by the quoted word (‘included,
arguably at the meeting he ’attended’‘, the counted form from v7), the inference from attendance to knowledge being marked
by ’arguably’, by the quotation and by ‘likely’ in the verdict, and a drafter who wants the knowledge inference itself explicit
writes ‘arguably knew’; the ticket-case analogy (‘has or ought to have knowledge’) is CREDIT, usable only with its confinement
to ‘a contract of carriage or bailment’ disclosed; for AMPL, the clause was included without objection shown (never ‘without
narrated objection’: R-R(1)), to record the bargain he had just proposed (credit), and the narrator’s ‘the personal guarantee
provided by Rocky’ proves that he provided one; for Rocky, that stipulation establishes neither the clause’s words nor that he
saw them (R-M) (credit: ‘provided’ arguably describes the oral undertaking; he was the offeror of ‘that’). (3) A conclusion in the
tier for the strength, with the further information named in the trailing clause (the clause’s words; whether Rocky saw them;
whether he objected) AND ITS DIRECTION (eg on a ‘likely assented’ verdict, ‘unless he never saw its words’; on a ‘likely did
not assent’ verdict, ‘unless he saw and accepted its words’; a same-count rewording of the counted trailing clause, which
named the information without its effect: UPGRADES_r1 U3; R6), which is also the answer to Rocky’s strongest counter, that
the $10,000 was the price of his own completed oral offer and not of the written clause (Kirby P at 170 by analogy: an
additional term arising after acceptance ‘cannot represent consideration’; credit in terms, met by the trailing clause because
whether he assented to the written content turns on the words he saw: CRIT_round4 M5).
Credit. Heydon JA’s ‘make plain’ (his route); the oral bargain complete before the clause was written (Kirby P at 170, by
analogy: an additional term arising after acceptance ‘cannot represent consideration’); Proscour only to frame the difference;
on either content Rocky is exposed if Grace defaults on a due date, the measure (a debt on call or damages) being remedies
law, which the answer does not argue and never frames as outside any scope (R-Z(1), (4)); whether the clause was in the draft
before the conversation; on the Pierre alternative the benefit taken was Pierre’s promise, not AMPL’s, which weakens assent to
AMPL’s written content (S-18, weak to moderate; CRIT_round9 M1, credit: the counted ‘the $10,000 promise being his benefit’
    names the promise whoever made it, and a drafter who states the weakening in a clause loses nothing).
    Strength and tilt. Assent to the written ‘personally guaranteed’ content moderate on the guarantee reading of ‘the clause’,
    weak to moderate on the other (S-9). Either conclusion can be Excellent if it applies McHugh JA’s criterion with the benefit
    named, meets the other side’s best fact (including ‘provided by Rocky’ on the R-M line), and names the further information; no
    method and no lean is Good (§2). An answer that treats ‘provided by Rocky’ as stipulated evidence of assent is eligible for
    Excellent provided it says what the stipulation does and does not establish (not the clause’s exact words).
    Drops. VG: further information missing, or given without its direction (U3); the offer whose benefit was taken not named, so
    that ‘its terms’ has no antecedent (U13); ‘provided by Rocky’ neither used nor tested; the ‘reasonable opportunity to reject’ or
    the knowledge element omitted so that AMPL’s best words are understated. Good: ‘Rocky is bound as guarantor’ bare; the
    benefit taken not named (§1(b)); the knowledge element stated and applied to no fact before ‘assented’ (§1(b); ‘attended’ or an
    equivalent fact absent). Credit wrong: the ticket-case ‘ought to have’ words stated as McHugh JA’s rule without the
    confinement (VG; a wrong rule). Fair: ‘ensure’ and ‘guarantee’ treated as the same with no reasons; ‘ensure … promptly’
    attributed to Rocky as his words (D4); the clause said to ‘state’ or ‘record’ a guarantee (D4). Poor: Proscour’s damages
    statement applied as the Australian rule; Rocky’s silence held acceptance on Felthouse’s facts; Butler’s ‘last shot’ used as more
    than a remote analogy. Omitted.
    Marker comment. ‘Empirnall asks whether an offeree with a reasonable opportunity to reject took the benefit with knowledge
    of the terms: what benefit did Rocky take, and what does the problem tell us he knew of the clause?’

II.I3 Consideration moving from AMPL, conditional on II.F2; Pao On’s second condition on timing; AMPL’s
fallback put (4.0; C; floor 73) [Pao On 629 to 630; Roscorla 237]

    Issue. Whether AMPL, as promisee calling on Rocky’s undertaking, gave consideration for it.
    Rules at source. ‘Must flow between the parties in both directions’ [S2A slide 2 | slide only]; past consideration: ‘a
    consideration past and executed will support no other promise than such as would be implied by law’ [CB2A 113 | 237 | Lord
    Denman CJ delivering the judgment of the Court, Roscorla]; Pao On: ‘An act done before the giving of a promise to make a
    payment or to confer some other benefit can sometimes be consideration for the promise. The act must have been done at the
    promisors’ request: the parties must have understood that the act was to be remunerated either by a payment or the
    conferment of some other benefit: and payment, or the conferment of a benefit, must have been legally enforceable had it been
    promised in advance.’ and its application, ‘The parties understood at the time of the main agreement that the restriction on
    selling must be compensated for by the benefit of a guarantee against a drop in price’ [PO | [1980] AC 614, 629–30 | the Board
    (Lord Scarman delivering) | ratio on the First Question]; the Board’s gloss, read in the official text; course-stated in substance
    only (Roscorla 237; Australian Woollen Mills (PC) 550, ‘The presence of a request does not, however, in itself establish a
    contract’), the words themselves sitting in the casebook’s omitted pp 126 to 130; never quoted, unpinnable (CRIT_fidelity_8
    Finding 4; ISSUES_SETTLED’s register line, ‘course-stated in substance’): the recital of a prior request ‘is not sufficient in
    itself’ and the second precondition ‘is simply one of the construction of the words of the contract in the circumstances of its
    making’ (O-3); a duty owed to a third party: Pao On 632 (II.C2); Glidewell LJ: ‘Pao On is a case of a tripartite relationship’
    [CB2B 119 | 15]; AWM ‘really offered as consideration … really done in consideration’ (456 to 457); Asquith LJ’s whole
    sentence [CB2A 102 | 460 | quoted by the Court | never cut to ‘an agreement to forbear … is a good consideration’ (D2)];
    detriment to the promisee suffices (Musumeci 745).
    Facts (deciding). ‘27 February’ as the date of the advance; ‘Rocky asked’ (from v11 the first condition, the request, met on
    that word: UPGRADES_r1 U32, reversing CRIT_round3 M5 option (a)‘s move to credit); ’I will do that if you also promise to pay
    $10,000’ (the pricing that meets AMPL’s fallback: U2). Supporting (credit): Pierre’s expectation narrated only on 8 April and
    AMPL’s return being Grace’s interest (the two reasons why nothing shows a 27 February understanding; credit for the same
    reason); nothing narrated on 27 February about a guarantee; AMPL entered the Loan Agreement with Grace at the same
    meeting.
    Core. (1) The point stated conditionally on II.F2: if AMPL promised the $10,000, that promise is fresh consideration moving
    from AMPL (strong on that view); if the $10,000 was Pierre’s, AMPL needs its own consideration and the 27 February advance
    is past (Roscorla 237 footnoted on the words ‘the past advance’, its own marker, with Pao On 629 to 630 on the exception
    carrying a second marker: one source for one proposition, R-R(3); the counted form is ‘AMPL’s own promise suffices; if Pierre
    promised, the past advance,[fn] under Pao On, suffices only where the parties ’understood that the act was to be
    remunerated’[fn]‘; from v11 the doctrine is NAMED once in the course’s term, past consideration (RG2A: ’What is the rule with
    respect to past consideration? Are there any exceptions to the general rule?’; S2A PDF page 20, ‘Past consideration’; S2A PDF
    page 23, ‘Exception to past consideration rule’; the v11 form ‘the past advance, past consideration,’ +2: UPGRADES_r1 U7; R-
    X(4)); v5’s ‘if AMPL, that promise suffices; if Pierre, the past advance’ elided the verb of each ‘if’ clause and read as note form,
    an R1 lapse under the type added in v6: CRIT_round5 M7, adopted under R-S(2)). (2) Pao On’s FIRST condition met on its fact,
    as the Board itself runs each condition on its fact (‘The act must have been done at the promisors’ request … All three features
    are present in this case. The promise given to Fu Chip under the main agreement not to sell the shares for a year was at Lau’s
    request’, Pao On extract, [1980] AC 614, 629 to 630): the advance was made at Rocky’s request, ‘Rocky asked’ (the v11 form
    ‘the past advance, made at Rocky’s request,’, +4: UPGRADES_r1 U32, folded into this item because the ‘similar shape’ below is
    a guarantee given after an act done at the guarantor’s request); the third condition is credit to state; and the SECOND
    condition as the contest: nothing narrated shows that the parties understood on 27 February that the advance was to be
    remunerated by a benefit from Rocky, whereas in Pao On the understanding existed ‘at the time of the main agreement’ (the
    comparison named: similar shape, different timing; credit: the two reasons, Pierre’s ‘expected’ narrated only on 8 April and
    AMPL’s return being Grace’s interest). (3) A conclusion in the tier for the strength on the alternative that Pierre promised
    (‘likely’), written ‘if Pierre promised’, never ‘on that branch’ (R7), WITH AMPL’S FALLBACK PUT in a clause (CRIT_round5 M6,
    adopted in the ‘put’ form under R-S(3)): AMPL’s entry into the Loan Agreement at the same meeting, tied by Pierre’s
    expectation to ‘payments under the Loan Agreement’, is the course’s second candidate for consideration moving from AMPL
    (ISSUES_SETTLED S-13, moderate), and a verdict that AMPL ‘gave none’ without naming it overstates the tier and leaves a C
    unit’s counter unput; the counted form is the absolute clause ‘its entry into the Loan Agreement remaining arguable
    consideration’ after ‘AMPL likely gave none’ (the noun ‘consideration’ added in v8, +1, so that the clause says what the entry is
    arguable as: CRIT_round7 m7, adopted; v7’s ‘remaining arguable’ is not deducted, the sentence being about consideration
    throughout); and, from v11, the fallback MET, not only put, or ACCEPTED with the bargain requirement applied
    (UPGRADES_r1 U2, adopted as core and as a grading fix, §2 already listing ‘the fallback limb of II.I3’ among the units where a
    paragraph with no lean and no method is Good while v10’s ‘remaining arguable consideration’ gave that limb neither): the
    bargain test asks whether AMPL’s entry was ‘really done in consideration of’ the undertaking (‘it should be made to appear
    that the statement or announcement which is relied on as a promise was really offered as consideration for the doing of the act,
    and that the act was really done in consideration of a potential promise inherent in the statement’, CB2A 101, Australian
    Woollen Mills 456 to 457, the Court), and Rocky’s own words name another price, ‘I will do that if you also promise to pay
    $10,000 to me directly’; the v11 form adds ‘, though Rocky priced his undertaking at’$10,000’’ after ‘remaining arguable
    consideration’ (+7), on its own marker to Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457. Accepting the fallback with the bargain
    requirement applied (AMPL may read ‘also’ as ‘in addition to entering the Loan Agreement’) is equally Excellent (S-13,
    moderate). Meeting it in the fuller form (the critic’s +12, the entry not ‘really done in consideration of’ the undertaking stated
    in terms) is credit.
    Credit. AMPL’s fallback met or accepted in a fuller form than core (3) requires: its entry into the Loan Agreement is arguably
    ‘really done in consideration of’ the undertaking (or, if AMPL was already bound to Grace from 27 February, a promise to
    perform a duty owed to a third party: Pao On 632), a detriment sufficing though the benefit went to Grace; against which the
    express words price the undertaking at $10,000 and AMPL had already advanced (S-13; either conclusion Excellent if the
    bargain requirement is applied and the pricing point met or accepted); Lampleigh’s ‘request’ and Bowen LJ’s ‘implication that
    at the time it was rendered it was to be paid for’ (the extract; cited as quoted by Lord Scarman without an AC page pin); the
    recital of consideration in the guarantee clause as further information (O-3); the AWM creditor-forbearance example labelled
    an analogy; the consistency points (T7: Rocky cannot say his undertaking was given only for past consideration while claiming
    the $10,000 was given for it; T17), each stated once; the further information that would reverse it (evidence of an
    understanding on 27 February).
    Strength and tilt. Two limbs, each with its own rating (corrected to ISSUES_SETTLED S-12 and S-13: CRIT_round5 M6; R-
    S(3)): the past advance as consideration, unproven under Pao On’s second condition (moderate to strong against AMPL; S-12),
    a contrary conclusion on that limb capped at Very Good; AMPL’s consideration on the Pierre alternative taken as a whole, once
    the fallback is live, MODERATE (S-13), so that a conclusion that AMPL gave consideration which rests on the fallback with the
    bargain requirement applied and the pricing point met or accepted is Excellent, and ‘AMPL gave none’ is Excellent only with
    the fallback put and met (from v11: U2). v5’s single ‘moderate to strong against AMPL’ line rated the whole question by its first
    limb and tilted the unit against AMPL beyond the settled ratings, which on the Pierre alternative was bad advice to Rocky (told
    that AMPL has nothing to enforce). An answer that uses Pierre’s ‘expected’ as evidence, marked ‘arguably’, that an
    understanding existed on 27 February (the narrator’s past tense permits the inference) is that capped contrary conclusion; an
    answer that places the understanding on 8 April misapplies the second condition’s timing (the condition’s own words do not
    state the time; the timing is read from the Board’s application, ‘at the time of the main agreement’) and is Fair on the brief’s
    ladder (a criterion misapplied, not law wrong), as the parallel item at II.G was moved in v7 (Part 9 item 37(d)); v7’s Poor
    (CRIT_complete_bias_2 B-7) is withdrawn to that extent, Poor being kept for the textbook (D1) and for Asquith LJ cut (D2), a
    Pao On pin or report error being VG with D11 from v10 (CRIT_round7 m14, adopted; Part 9 item 38; CRIT_round9 m5; R-U(6)).
    Not academic: live whenever the $10,000 is not AMPL’s promise.
    Citation. Pao On v Lau Yiu Long [1980] AC 614, 629–30 and 632 only, as the Board (no judge) or ‘(Lord Scarman for the
    Board)’, the course extract being headed ‘Judgement delivered by Lord Scarman’ and Glidewell LJ at 14 naming him as
    ‘delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee’ (R-P; CRIT_round3 M7, adopted: naming him is not deducted). Roscorla v
    Thomas (1842) 3 QB 234, 237; 114 ER 496 (the QB pin after the QB report, before the ER parallel, so that it does not read as
    an ER pinpoint: CRIT_fidelity_3 m5, adopted; the ER pin is not in the course materials); naming Lord Denman CJ, who
    ‘delivered the judgment of the Court’, is accepted (R-P). A Pao On pin other than 629–30 or 632, or a wrong report, is a D11
    deduction. Marker placement: the Pao On marker on the timing sentence sits directly after ‘at the time of the main agreement’,
    the words it supports, and the fallback clause that follows (‘its entry into the Loan Agreement remaining arguable
    consideration’) carries no marker, because Pao On does not support it and it states an arguable fact, not a rule (CRIT_round6
    m3, adopted at no cost; v6’s fn 48 closed the sentence and so appeared to cite Pao On for the fallback); a drafter who footnotes
    the fallback clause to Australian Woollen Mills 456 to 457 on its own marker, the bargain requirement it invokes, is graded the
    same.
    Drops. VG: the AMPL alternative not stated conditionally; the second condition applied without the ‘at the time’ comparison;
    the fallback (AMPL’s entry into the Loan Agreement) not put on the Pierre alternative, or put and neither met nor accepted
    (U2); the first condition stated without its fact (‘Rocky asked’: U32); ‘AMPL gave none’ stated as clear; Pao On cited as [1980]
    AC 615 (the slide misprint), with the D11 deduction, a citation slip graded once, as his marker graded a citation slip VG (‘the
    reference should not include ss 28 and 32(1)’), R8 then capped by R-C at the lowest citation grade (CRIT_round9 m5; R-U(6):
    v9’s Poor triple-counted it). Good: ‘Pao On applies’ or ‘past consideration fails’ bare. Fair: Pao On’s three conditions recited and
    declared met without the ‘understood … at the time’ requirement applied. Fair also: Pao On said satisfied by an understanding
    formed on 8 April (the timing of the second condition misapplied: CRIT_round7 m14). Poor: Pao On cited to the textbook (D1);
    Asquith LJ cut (D2). Omitted. Credit wrong: the fallback stated without the bargain requirement; Lampleigh given an AC pin
    (D11). The doctrine applied without its course name, past consideration, is graded at R7, not here.
    Marker comments. ‘Apply Pao On’s conditions to the facts; the second is the contest, and the timing is the difference.’
    ‘Ensure your citation precisely supports the proposition: 629–30 for past consideration, 632 for the third-party duty.’

II.I4 Timing on both readings of the 12 months; the arguable March instalment; consequences conditional on
II.F2 (5.0; C; floor 68)

    Facts (deciding). ‘repayment of the Loan’; ‘repayable at the expiry of 12 months’; ‘8 February 2025’. Supporting: ‘when Grace
    had not yet repaid the Loan’; ‘I have until 8 April 2025’; ‘you won’t see a cent before then’; ‘AMPL required the $1,150,000 as
    soon as possible’ (motive; cannot accelerate the term: Ermogenous [25]); AMPL called on 9 March 2025, ‘arguably’ the day
    after a monthly date if the instalments fell on the 8th (an inference: R-M).
    Core. (1) Whether the call was premature turns on the 12 months, cross-referred as ‘the 12 months (G)’ within the same Part
    (R-Q; never a bare ‘turns on G’), not on any rule of guarantee law (credit: the clause as described concerns ‘repayment of the
     Loan’, and the Loan was ‘repayable at the expiry of 12 months’, quoted again here). (2) Both readings applied: from 27
     February the call was not premature; from 8 April it was premature as to principal (v12: v11’s ‘which only postpones liability’ is
     a guarantee-law statement and is removed from the core and from credit under R-Y(4), the answer not arguing guarantee law)
     (credit: if Grace does not repay by 8 April 2025 the 12 months will then have run on either reading, and if Rocky then pays, the
     $10,000 condition fails: T13, II.H). (3) On the 8 April reading the bad news in a clause: the payment record ends at ‘8 February
     2025’, which makes an unpaid March 2025 instalment arguable (the hedged form is required: ‘appropriate monthly repayments
     of the interest’ between 8 April 2024 and 8 February 2025 ‘proves that interest was paid monthly, as the Loan Agreement

Part 7. Global rows (20%), scoring rule and automatic deductions
Global-row cap (R-C). A global row cannot be graded above the lowest grade, among the units, of the core item it summarises: R2
at most the lowest application grade (the authority applied by its own criterion; the comparison named at K and C units); R4 at most
Very Good if any unit is Omitted and at most Good if a claim is missed; R6 at most the lowest further-information or strength grade;
R8 at most the lowest citation grade; R10 at most the lowest consistency grade; R1, R3, R5, R7 and R9 are graded independently.
Reason: his real marker left the global rows ungraded in Part A, so the global block must compound unit failures, never offset them.

R1. Style, clarity of expression, conciseness, grammar & spelling, persuasiveness of argument: his voice (4.0)

Measured against his LAWS1061 Part A (the authority) and VOICE.md (the measurement), with python3 -I voice_stats_v2.py on the
body (headings, footnotes and the count line are stripped by the script). - Excellent requires all of: flowing multi-clause sentences
joined by semicolons (the next step) and colons (claim, then proof); whole-answer measures within the range of his Parts I to VI
(mean sentence length 17.8 to 24.7 words; sentences under 12 words 9.1% to 36.4%, all verdicts or one-line frames and never two in
a row inside a paragraph; semicolons 0.85 to 2.02 per 100 words; colons 0.81 to 2.57 per 100 words; sentences containing a
semicolon or colon 36.4% to 72.7%); the ranges apply to the whole body, not per unit, so K and C units are written in his 20 to 25-
word sentences and the one-sentence L forms are balanced by short verdicts (the appendix shows the balance: mean 24.0; 10.0%
under 12 words; 1.04; 0.90; 41.7%; the mean sits near the top of his range, so a drafter who lengthens sentences further falls out of
it: every fix that adds a clause to an existing sentence pushes the mean up, so additions go in as new sentences or by splitting a long
one, never as a further clause: CRIT_round4 m14); a short counter-frame (‘AMPL would say nothing bound until execution’) and an
element sub-verdict (‘AMPL being ’owned and controlled’ by Pierre supplies consent’; ‘His payment therefore likely does not meet
it’) count as his frames and verdicts under VOICE.md F9 (his Part A: ‘On the other hand, only SPC knew its finances and that GR
would rely’), so a drafter does not merge them to be safe and fall below the 9.1% floor (CRIT_round4 m14, adopted); the rule-then-
proof join written as a colon, because the L form (‘fact, rule, so result’) produces semicolons and ‘so’ but few colons; every semicolon
joins a step to the step it follows from (a sentence of three or more semicolon-joined clauses each a conclusion without its reason is
conclusive and an R1 lapse); his signposts (‘Firstly’, ‘Secondly, however,’, ‘Decisively,’, ‘Nor does … assist:’, ‘… is distinguishable:’,
‘… is analogous because …’, ‘The strongest counter is …’, ‘On balance,’, ‘the better view is that … likely …’) used where they fit and
never at a required rate: the requirement is ‘no signpost he never uses’, ‘Whether … turns on’ as an opener in at most about 1 in 6
sentences, ordinals where three or more factors are weighed as separate sentences (his stacked-facts sentence, VOICE.md 2.3
examples 14 and 15, weighs three or four quoted facts inside one sentence without ordinals and is equally his form), valence tags
only on factor sentences (CRIT_round3 m9, adopted in part: the appendix uses ‘Decisively’, ‘On balance’, ‘the better view’, ‘Yet’,
‘whereas’, ‘distinguishable’ and no ordinals, which is within his usage); no signposts he never uses (‘Moreover’, ‘Furthermore’,
‘Additionally’, ‘Here,’, ‘In this case,’, ‘Notably’; ‘Here,’ and ‘In this case,’ as sentence openers only, a mid-sentence locative ‘here’ not
being a lapse: I.F2 Credit; CRIT_round8 m3); no direct question with a question mark in the body (his Part A has none; a question is
put as a ‘whether’ clause: CRIT_round4 m9); none of this sheet’s analytic words (‘narrator’, ‘narrated’, ‘narrative’, ‘the facts narrate’:
R-R(1)); NO META LANGUAGE AND NO SLIDE CITATION (R-Z(1), (2), (5)): body and footnotes never mention weeks, classes,
lectures, slides, the course, the readings, the syllabus, the rubric or the assignment, and never frame anything as ‘outside the scope’
(or ‘outside Weeks 1 to 4’), the answer being advice to Rocky; one such instance, or one slide citation, caps this row at VG, and two
or more cap it at Good, whatever the rest of the row earns (the same instances are graded at R8; §1); parenthetical cross-references
(‘(D, E)’, ‘(D)’, ‘(II.G)’, ‘(G)’) are not in his register (his Part A carries none, writing ‘likewise’ and ‘again’), so at most about one per
Part is his form, the rest written as ‘a question for intention and certainty’ or ‘the 12 months’ where words allow; the counted model
spends four because the count forbids the longer forms, and they are counted words, not free (CRIT_round4 m19, adopted as the
rule); ‘both’ written with its nouns, and no pronoun whose antecedent is wrong or unclear, that is, whose nearest antecedent is a
different person or noun from the one meant (‘Rocky’s detriment’, never ‘his’ after an ‘If Pierre’ clause: CRIT_round4 M3, m17); a
pronoun whose antecedent is right and clear is never a lapse, wherever the antecedent sits (‘it is likely an offer’; ‘meet it’; ‘Rocky
likely gave none’ after a sentence about consideration), v10’s wider wording (‘written with its … antecedent in the same sentence’)
being withdrawn because the counted model itself breached it without any loss of clarity (R-V(1); CRIT_round10 m3); the scope of
the question never restated at length (a conciseness fault here, not at P: CRIT_round4 m17); verdict tiers matched to contest (Part
1); fact quotations short (median about 3 words), mid-sentence, inside his own grammar, the legal word outside the quote; no
sentence beginning with a quotation; quoted words in the body at most 20% of the body and no single quotation over 20 words (R-G;

Diplock’s ‘might have been understood’) is accepted where the quoted words would cost the count; no sentence whose only
reasoning is a quoted phrase followed by ‘so’ or ‘thus’ and a result; present tense for law, past for facts; third person; zero em

and documents (‘AMPL’, the ‘Loan Agreement’, ‘Loan’); no semicolon after a subordinate clause or before a fragment; no comma

and a UNSW marker reading such a clause as note form (CRIT_round5 M7, adopted; R-S(2)): each instance is a lapse under the VG
line below, two make VG, and the counted model carries none. THREE FURTHER LAPSE TYPES from v11 (UPGRADES_r1 U29; the
Instructions’ criterion ‘the quality of the writing and the clarity of expression’; four of six Stage-5 round-1 cold readers flagged
instances in forms this sheet had prescribed): (a) ZEUGMA, one verb governing two nouns it fits differently (‘claim and likely
exposure lie against him’: a claim lies against a person, an exposure does not); (b) WRONG COLLOCATION, a verb or noun that
cannot take the object it is given (‘AMPL enforces its own money’: money is not enforced, a loan or a contract is); (c) an ANSWER-
EXTERNAL DEICTIC, a pointer whose referent is outside the answer or cannot be found from the sentence (‘the guarantee clause
just named’, where nothing in the answer has just named it). Each is a lapse counted with the others under the VG line; v10’s claim
that the counted model carried none of these was untrue for the three forms quoted, each now corrected at its unit (I.F3, II.F1, II.I4).

against 3.2 and ‘though’ at 5.5 against 3.2 (8 in 1,442 words is 5.5 per 1,000, as the v10 appendix printed: CRIT_round10 m10),

form yields ‘so’ rather than a colon, so a drafter writes an L unit’s rule-then-application join as a colon where it reads naturally

parentheticals (’(F)‘,’(II.G)‘) count as words and are not free. - VG: one measure outside his range, or up to two lapses (eg a single
one-clause run; one stacked-assertion sentence); one meta reference or one slide citation (R-Z(5)). Good: a pattern of one-clause
runs, or two measures outside range; a quotation mosaic (quoted words over 20%); two or more meta references or slide citations, in

     stated as ‘Word count: 1,497’, and a stated count three words short of Word’s figure is a wrong count); N at most 1,500, so the
     body at most 1,497, and the sheet’s floors use 1,495 as the body ceiling; typed, double spaced, 12 pt Times New Roman, Arial
     or Calibri; page numbers; margins; MS Word; no coversheet, ‘unnecessary’ title page, headers or footers (page numbers
     excepted, the Instructions requiring them and forbidding only ‘unnecessary’ headers or footers: R-R(8); CRIT_round4 m16),
     bibliography, bullets or numbered points; no extended quotations. Any breach makes this row Poor (count wrong) or Omitted
     (over the limit or no count), with the Part 7 deductions.

     doctrinal footing, the six required ones (T4, T8, T10, T11, T13, T17) stated once in a clause where they bite and the rest

     into II.C2, II.D, II.I1, II.I3 and II.I4. VG: one tension unremarked. Good: two. Fair: a position in one Part undercuts another
     claim. Poor: the answer argues contradictory positions to win each claim.


Scoring rule

For each unit and each global row: points × multiplier (Excellent 1.00; Very Good 0.75; Good 0.60; Fair 0.45; Poor 0.20; Omitted 0).
Mark out of 100 = sum of all items − automatic deductions, never below 0, rounded down to a whole mark. 100 is awarded only if
every unit and every global row is Excellent (each with the quoted sentence that earns it and the source check) and no
automatic deduction applies.

Calibration (R-C). His real LAWS1061 Part A grades, re-read cell by cell from the .pdf pages (v5; the recount stands, was re-run for
v6 and v8, and was confirmed by the round-7 critic and, from the rendered pages, by the round-8 critic; the arithmetic is recomputed
for v10): Preliminary Exc; 1(a) 3 Exc, 2 VG, 1 Good; 1(b) 1 Exc, 5 VG; 1(c) 2 Exc, 1 Good; 1(d) 2 Exc, 1 VG; 2 (statutory authorities) 2
Exc, 3 VG, 1 Good: 11 Excellent, 11 Very Good, 3 Good, no Fair, no Poor (25 cells); the three global rows ungraded; Part A mark
82%. On these multipliers, with the printed Part weights (15/25/15/15/30, the preliminary row unweighted) and equal weight within
each Part, his dot grades give 0.850 × 15 + 0.792 × 25 + 0.867 × 15 + 0.917 × 15 + 0.808 × 30 = 83.5% of the dot points (v3
printed 83.7; the recount is 83.5); with the global block (20 of 100) capped at the grade of the units it summarises (Very Good on his
sheet), the whole-sheet mark is 0.835 × 80 + 20 × 0.75 = 81.8, and 81.4 if R2 is capped at Good (his two ‘conclusive’ units); both
within one mark of 82. The disclosure the result depends on (CRIT_round4 m15, adopted): the dot points alone give 83.5, which is
1.5 off, and the within-one-mark result holds only on the assumption that every ungraded global row is graded Very Good, the grade
of the units it summarises; if the five independent rows (R1, R3, R5, R7 and R9, 9.5 points) were Excellent, as his marker’s Part B
style comment might suggest, with R2 Good and the rest Very Good, the figure is 83.76 (v9 printed ‘83.7’, a truncation beside the
rounded 81.4: CRIT_round9 m6; R-U(6)). The assumption is a judgment call and is stated as the one on which the calibration rests.
The multipliers and the cap are unchanged from v2 and the grid change (23 units) does not touch the calibration, which is run on his
sheet’s own weights. The multipliers are a disclosed judgment call; the global-row cap is what makes them reproduce his result.


Automatic deductions (applied after the grades; each instance counts)

One error, one deduction (R-U(6); CRIT_round9 m3 to m5). Each error is graded once: where the same fault appears under
two Drops lines or two automatic deductions, only the heaviest applicable applies (eg ‘ensure … promptly’ attributed to Rocky is D4
and not also D2; Knox CJ’s severance words as the joint judgment’s own are D2 at I.A and not also a VG credit-wrong line; ‘[1980] AC
615’ is VG with D11 at II.I3 and not also Poor). The global-row cap (R-C) is not a deduction and still applies, because it is what makes
the global rows compound unit failures rather than offset them; D6’s ‘−2 each, in addition to the Poor grade’ is that deduction’s own
rule and is unchanged. One error carried into a later unit is deducted once, at the unit where it is made (R-V(1);
CRIT_round10 m9): a later unit that applies the earlier finding is graded on its own question and drops only for a new error of its
own (eg ‘AMPL clearly gave none’ at II.I3 is graded there, and ‘AMPL has nothing to enforce’ at II.I4, its consequence, is not
deducted again; but a later unit that turns the carried finding into new advice that the strength does not support, such as II.I4’s ‘so
do nothing’ or ‘so pay now’ on an overstated date from II.G, makes a new error in the advice and is graded at that unit, R-U(4)).
